17994-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Dated November 3, 1920, this is volume 159 of Punch, or the London Charivari, the famed British humor magazine. The issue opens with Charivaria, short jokes on the news of the week, from Ireland's parliament to the miners' strike.

Bits poke fun at a ragtime song, the Admiralty's silence on Jutland, and Lloyd George's bobbed hair, while a Euclid joke turns a rose bed into a geometry problem. Punch writes with the dry, upper-class wit of its age. The issue is a bright snapshot of Britain in 1920, best read as a period joke book, not as fair news.
18571-the-northmen-columbus-and-cabot-98:
Edited by Julius E. Olson and Edward Gaylord Bourne under general editor J. Franklin Jameson, this 1906 volume belongs to the Original Narratives of Early American History series. It prints first-hand accounts of the Northmen's voyages, edited by Olson of Wisconsin, and of the voyages of Columbus and John Cabot, edited by Bourne of Yale. Maps and a facsimile add to the text.

The series aims to give readers the words of eyewitnesses rather than later retellings, since many early narratives had grown scarce and costly. Here the span runs from 985 to 1503, covering the first European landfalls in the Americas. The volume is a core source book for early American history.
19878-the-passaic-flood-of-1903:
The Passaic Flood of 1903 is a federal water-supply paper by Marshall Ora Leighton. It was transmitted to the Geological Survey for publication in that series. The Passaic River drains a crowded corner of New Jersey. Its 1903 flood ranked among the worst then recorded there. Leighton's report measures the water and maps the damage. Government science treated floods as data problems first.

Leighton became a leading American hydrologist. His flood studies set methods for gauging and records. Mill towns along the Passaic suffered repeated inundations. A careful post-flood survey served engineers and insurers alike. The report preserves rainfall, flow, and loss figures. It is a primary source for New Jersey flood history.
20130-magazine-or-animadversions-on-the-:
Magazine, or Animadversions on the English Spelling, dates from 1703, a very early spelling tract. Animadversions means critical remarks, and spelling is the target here. English spelling was still unsettled in Queen Anne's time. Writers of tracts argued for simpler, more regular ways to spell words.

The modern edition lists scholars from Columbia, Chicago, Princeton, and other schools. Their names show how later editors framed this old text for study. Readers get a glimpse of English before spelling froze into place. It suits those who love the history of words and print.
2103-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle follows the Hohenzollerns into Brandenburg in Book Three, from 1412 to 1718, beginning with Burggraf Friedrich's cool reception as Statthalter on St. John's Day 1412. He came as a bearer of law to a land of robbery. Friedrich entered Brandenburg in 1412 as a stranger, sent by the emperor to restore order.

Towns harried to skin and bone welcomed order, while barons who lived by the saddle resisted it. Carlyle traces how the family turned a disordered march into a state, laying the ground for the Prussia Frederick would inherit. The towns, plundered by robber barons, welcomed a ruler who could keep roads safe.
23642-history-of-the-english-people-volu:
John Richard Green, honorary fellow of Jesus College, Oxford, wrote his History of the English People in eight volumes, and this fifth volume covers Puritan England from 1603 to 1644. First published in 1879 and reprinted in this Eversley edition of 1896, it opens with the England of Shakespeare before turning to the Puritan age proper.

Chapters follow England's break with Parliament under James I and the rule of royal favorites. They then cover Charles I's personal government and the rise of Puritan feeling that would soon break into civil war. Green writes narrative history with a storyteller's pace, making the clash of king, church, and Commons clear to readers without prior study.
24874-lucy-maud-montgomery-short-stories:
Lucy Maud Montgomery, born at Clifton, Prince Edward Island, in 1874, won world fame with Anne of Green Gables and wrote some five hundred stories and poems in her life. This volume gathers twenty-two of her short stories from 1902 to 1903, in order of first printing, from Davenport's Story to The Unhappiness of Miss Farquhar.

The tales range from Christmas baskets and runaway kites to a patent medicine testimonial and a sandshore wooing. Montgomery writes with warmth and humor about Island folk, stubborn uncles, and girls finding their way. Readers who love Anne will find the same eye for character and place in these shorter, lesser-known pieces.
25712-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Rossiter Johnson edits this third volume of The Great Events by Famous Historians, a readable account of world history in the master words of eminent historians, with Charles F. Horne and John Rudd as associate editors. A painting of Christ by Gabriel Max fronts the book.

The volume covers the Roman Empire period, from the Crucifixion in A.D. 30 through the rise of Christianity, Nero's burning of Rome, and the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70. Pompeii, the Jews' last struggle, Constantine, Nicaea, and the final division of the empire in A.D. 395 close a chronology to A.D. 409.
28880-recollections-of-a-tour-made-in-sc:
Dorothy Wordsworth wrote these recollections of a tour made in Scotland in 1803, edited by J. C. Shairp. The journal runs day by day for weeks, from Keswick through Grisdale and Mosedale to Carlisle, Gretna Green, and Dumfries. Early days bring Burns's grave, Ellisland, and the vale of Nith, then Thornhill, Drumlanrig, and the miners of Wanlockhead and Leadhills.

Later weeks follow the falls of the Clyde, Glasgow, Dumbarton, Loch Lomond, and the Trossachs, with Rob Roy's caves and the Highland girl of Inversneyde. Dorothy writes as a sharp-eyed walker, noting hosts, roads, and scenery. Readers get a classic of travel writing, and a companion to her brother William's poetry, in the voice of a woman who saw Scotland on foot.
29185-national-strategy-for-combating-te:
The United States government issued this national strategy in February 2003, in the wake of the September 11, 2001 attacks. It calls those attacks acts of war against the United States, its allies, and the idea of civilized society. No cause, it insists, justifies terrorism.

The strategy sets out four goals: defeat terrorists and their groups, deny them sponsorship, support, and sanctuary, diminish the conditions they exploit, and defend American citizens and interests at home and abroad. It also surveys the changing threat, from linked groups to weapons of mass destruction. Readers get the Bush administration's public doctrine for the war against terror, in its own formal terms.
30729-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume three of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works was printed in London in 1911. Its Roman date is MDCCCCXI, and it follows the limited pattern: two thousand sixty copies printed, two thousand for sale. An illustration shows Swanston Cottage, Stevenson's home from 1868 to 1876.

Contents gather Familiar Studies of Men and Books, opening with Victor Hugo's romances, some aspects of Robert Burns, and Walt Whitman. Henry David Thoreau, his character and opinions, and Yoshida-Torajiro follow. Stevenson judges writers with insight, affection, and critical edge, making the volume a classic of literary portraiture.
3079-original-short-stories-volume-03:
Thirteen tales ride out from Etretat in volume three, starting with Miss Harriet. Miss Harriet, Little Louise Roque, The Donkey, and Moiron lead the set. The Dispenser of Holy Water, The Parricide, Bertha, The Patron, The Door, A Sale, The Impolite Sex, A Wedding Gift, and The Relic complete it. The opening story rides from Etretat toward the ruins of Tancarville. Seven travelers on a drag, four women and three men, climb a winding coast road at a snail's pace, half asleep in fresh morning air.

Maupassant's irony sharpens in later tales, where a man sleeps a heavy, brutish sleep like one condemned to death, waiting for dawn to avoid suspicion. The volume shows his range from Norman comedy to dark moral tales.
30887-george-borrow-times-literary-suppl:
Held here is an appreciation of George Borrow from the Times Literary Supplement of July 10, 1903, written for the centenary year of his birth. It notes a singular coincidence: in one summer readers celebrated centenaries of Samuel Pepys, who died in early summer 1703, and Borrow, who was born in July 1803. Unlike each other in almost every respect, the two men share one material point, a reputation built chiefly on autobiography.

Among the world's autobiographers, the essay ranks the author of Lavengro with St. Augustine, Cellini, Pepys, Rousseau, and Franklin, and puts him, for truthfulness, very probably at the top. That veracity, it argues, came less from innate truthfulness than from a lack of invention and of a distorting literary style. In Borrow, wanderlust takes the place of Pepys's appetite for life. It is a sharp centenary judgment, still worth reading.
31593-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
John Mackay Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, volume three, was revised by Alexander Leighton, one of the original editors and contributors. It was published at London by Walter Scott in 1885. Its contents open with the Widow of Dunskaithe by Hugh Miller and the Whitsome Tragedy by Wilson himself. The Surgeon's Tales by Leighton follow, with the Diver and the Bell.

The volume continues with the Autobiography of Willie Smith by Alexander Campbell and the Professor's Tales by Professor Thomas Gillespie, including Phebe Fortune. These border tales mix history, tradition, and invention, and Leighton's revision keeps the collection's tales of the Scottish border country in readable order.
3341-the-wandering-jew-volume-03:
Eugene Sue's serial reaches Book Three in this volume, thick with conspiracy. A female Jesuit opens the chapters, with the plot and Adrienne's enemies. The skirmish, the revolt, and treachery follow, with the snare, a false friend, and the minister's cabinet. The visit, presentiments, and the letter lead to the confessional, my lord and spoil-sport, and appearances.

The convent, the influence of a confessor, and the examination close the movement. Adrienne de Cardoville, the serial's bright heiress, stands at the center of the snare, as Jesuit agents work through confessors and cabinets alike. Readers mid-serial will find Sue at his most theatrical: virtue besieged on every side, with rescue always one chapter late.
3553-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This third volume of Bourrienne's memoirs covers the Egyptian campaign in 1798 and 1799, from chapter fifteen to chapter twenty six. Bourrienne describes the divan set up in each Egyptian province, Desaix fighting in Upper Egypt, Ibrahim Bey beaten at Salehyeh, and the disaster at Aboukir. The army murmurs with dissatisfaction, and Bonaparte himself grows dejected.

The volume shows a campaign far from home, where victory in battle could not solve supply, disease, and politics. Bourrienne records his chief's plan for Egypt and his meditated descent on England, alongside daily worries of command. Readers get a close, troubled view of an expedition that made Napoleon's name while nearly breaking his army.
3570-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant's third volume settles into the life of the Tuileries, where Napoleon's household took on the full forms of a court. He describes audiences, levees, and the daily parade of ministers, generals, and foreign guests through the palace rooms. The valet's post gave him a view of both ceremony and the hurried work behind it.

The volume shows Napoleon learning to be an emperor in his own house: setting hours, choosing favorites, and guarding his privacy. Constant notes the clash between republican simplicity and imperial splendor. Readers interested in how a court is built, day by day, will find this volume a useful, intimate guide.
3583-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This third volume of Montaigne's Essays gathers chapters thirteen through twenty of Book One. They include the ceremony of interviews between princes, the punishment of men who obstinately defend a hopeless fort, the punishment of cowardice, the conduct of ambassadors, and the nature of fear. Later chapters ask whether we can judge a man's happiness before his death, and argue that to study philosophy is to learn how to die.

Montaigne writes by example, drawing on ancient history, his own travels, and the wars of religion around him. His method is to test a common saying against lived experience. The volume suits readers who enjoy short, searching essays that move from a small question to a view of human nature.
3764-coniston-volume-03:
Winston Churchill's third book of Coniston opens after William Wetherell's death, when Jethro Bass startles the village by moving into the tannery house beside the disused tannery. He will not leave young Cynthia alone on Thousand Acre Hill while his affairs carry him about the country, and the Reverend Mr Satterlee, gaunt and red faced, offers to teach her. Four years of happiness and peace follow in the little house, though Cynthia still weeps for her father on wakeful nights.

Cynthia serves Jethro with a devotion that fills his heart with strange joy and foreboding, while political letters, including a famous note of thanks to the president, show the boss's other life. The volume is the quiet center of the novel, with home, school, and loyalty in the foreground. Readers who like village chronicles will find it tender and steady.
3903-the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rou:
Jean Jacques Rousseau's third book follows him after leaving the service of Madame de Vercellis, back with a former hostess for five or six weeks. Health, youth, and laziness make his temperament importunate, and he weeps and sighs for a happiness he cannot name, sensible only of a deficiency. Thoughts of girls and women occupy him in a manner peculiar to himself, with shame confirming a natural timidity that no proposition in his favor can overcome.

The household around him buzzes with travellers, beggars, and visitors of every sort, and Rousseau grumbles and swears at the medley while his hostess laughs till tears run down her cheeks. His anger grows because he cannot refrain from laughter himself. Readers who like Rousseau's youth will find restlessness, desire, and comedy in a small compass.
3916-serge-panine-volume-03:
Georges Ohnet's third volume of Serge Panine moves the married couple to Nice, where their life resumes its Paris glitter. Visitors flock to the villa, and all that the colony counts of well known Parisians and foreigners of high repute present themselves. Fetes recommence, receptions run three times a week, and on other evenings Serge goes to the Cercle.

Two months of this absorbing life pass into early February, as spring begins to touch the coast. Then one evening three people, two gentlemen and a lady, step from a carriage at the villa gates and find themselves face to face with a new turn. Readers who like Ohnet's society drama will find a honeymoon of parties shadowed by arrivals from the past.
3921-the-red-lily-volume-03:
Anatole France's third volume of The Red Lily follows Therese to Florence, where love letters replace Paris talk. A letter from her lover closes tender and grave, with pious effusions that remind Therese of the prayer books of her childhood. He loves everything in her, he writes, the earth that carries her, the light that lets him see her, and the air she breathes.

He likes the bent tree of his yard because she has seen it. He has walked the avenue where he met her one winter night and culled boxwood she once looked at. In a city where she is absent, he sees only her. Readers who like France's lyric prose will find a volume of longing, art, and the slow work of a passion becoming fate.
3925-monsieur-madame-and-be-be-volume-03:
Gustave Droz's third volume of Monsieur, Madame and Bebe turns from courtship comedy to the pride of new parenthood. A young mother writes that room remains for mother and husband alike, and that her past life now seems trivial and colorless beside a life of deep love and delightful devotion. She feels she is beginning to live, proud as a soldier who has been in battle.

Wife and mother are her epaulettes, she says, and grandmother is the field marshal's baton. She weeps, she laughs, and she watches her good husband hold the child with pleasing awkwardness, at cost of great effort to lift so slight a burden. Readers who like Droz's domestic sketches will find a volume of tenderness without sentimentality.
5244-tales-from-the-arabic-volume-03:
John Payne's Tales from the Arabic, third and final volume, completes his translation of stories from the Breslau and Calcutta editions of the Thousand Nights. Its contents include Noureddin Ali of Damascus and the damsel Sitt El Milah, El Abbas and the king's daughter of Baghdad, the two kings and the vizier's daughters. The merchant of Cairo and the favourite of the Khalif appear among them.

The volume closes with the story of Sindbad the Sailor, giving his sixth and seventh voyages, and with tables of contents for the Calcutta and Boulac editions. Readers finishing Payne's collection here get both new tales and the famous voyages that crown the Arabian Nights tradition.
5277-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
In the third volume of La Fontaine's verse tales, readers meet The Muleteer, The Servant Girl Justified, and The Three Gossips' Wager. The Muleteer draws on Boccaccio, telling of Agiluf, a Lombard king who married Teudelingua, the beautiful widow of the last king, whose dominions became her new husband's share.

No beauty round could compare with the queen, and the tale that follows turns on love, loyalty, and court intrigue. The volume offers three stories in La Fontaine's light manner, where old Italian sources are retold with French wit and a moral that slips in almost unnoticed.
5358-the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-03:
Winston Churchill's Inside of the Cup continues in its third volume with four chapters: The Divine Discontent, The Messenger in the Church, The Lost Parishioner, and The Woman of the Song. It opens on the last Sunday in May, as breezes through open casements carry chancel flowers and summer gowns. Rector John Hodder surveys his decorous, fashionable congregation with a sense of extremity.

This volume holds only the middle portion of the novel, in which Hodder's doubts deepen and his parish divides. Readers following the story in order will find faith, wealth, and conscience in sharper conflict. Hodder moves toward the reconstruction of later volumes.
5367-richard-carvel-volume-03:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel continues in its third volume with chapters thirteen through eighteen: Mr Allen Shows His Hand, The Volte Coupe. Of Which the Rector Has the Worst, In Which Some Things Are Made Clear, South River, and The Black Moll complete the volume. It opens with news that Dorothy's beauty has taken London by storm, even as it conquered Annapolis.

Richard takes small consolation in hearing the Duke of Chartersea insulted, while better men dance attendance on Dorothy in Mayfair. He remains uneasy about the duke. This volume holds only this middle portion, in which London, love, and rivalry sharpen Richard's story.
5376-a-modern-chronicle-volume-03:
Winston Churchill's Modern Chronicle continues in its third volume with Book Two, opening with So Long as Ye Both Shall Live. It finds Honora late in November, sitting at the window of a sleeping car. Life seems as fantastic as the moss-hung Southern forest outside, and she feels the delight of a child on an unexpected outing.

At last her dull routine breaks, and wide possibilities open before her, though freedom has brought its own pangs of sorrow. This volume holds only this middle portion of Honora's story, following her marriage and its consequences through Stafford Park, the great unattached, and the new doctrine.
5385-the-celebrity-volume-03:
Winston Churchill's Celebrity continues in its third volume with chapter nine, in which the narrator lights a cigar and sits at the far end of the Asquith dock, alone with his thoughts. To say he was disappointed in Miss Thorn would set a mild value on his feelings; he felt anger, even aggression, at her defence of the Celebrity.

He had gone to Mohair hoping some good reason lay behind her tolerance. He came back without hope, since she not only tolerated the famous man but plainly liked him, praising and defending him. This volume holds only this middle portion, in which the Celebrity's charm divides Asquith's summer company.
5390-the-crisis-volume-03:
Winston Churchill's Crisis continues in its third volume with Book Two, opening with Raw Material. Summer, intolerable summer, lies upon the city, and the richest families have fled. Some brave the railroad journey to the Atlantic coast, while others retire to country places on the Bellefontaine road above the river.

This volume holds only this middle portion of the Civil War novel, in which Stephen learns something, meets Abraham Lincoln. He faces the question and the crisis itself, with Glencoe closing the book. Readers following the story in order will find St Louis at war's edge, and a young man's loyalties tested.
5411-the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volum:
Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont continues in its third volume with chapter six, on Grammont's arrival at the English court and its various personages. Curiosity about a man as famous for his crimes as for his rise had once before drawn the Chevalier to England, where reasons of state assume great privileges.

While the King of England sought protection in the Low Countries and Holland, other powers sent their envoys, and Grammont observed them all. This volume holds only this English-court portion of the memoirs, in which Restoration London and its king appear. Its courtiers pass before a witty French observer.
5441-uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-vo:
Georg Ebers carries his ancient Egyptian romance Uarda into the city of Thebes in this third volume. At noon, the narrow shaded streets stay cool while the broad dyke-road to the king's castle blazes in the heat. That road, usually deserted at midday, fills with foot passengers, chariots, riders, and litter-bearers, while workers pour water on the dust.

The crowded scene sets up the volume's court and city action, as characters move between temple, palace, and street. Ebers fills the background with the sights and labor of a great Egyptian capital. Readers get a vivid stretch of historical romance, rich in place and pageantry.
5452-an-egyptian-princess-volume-03:
Georg Ebers continues his historical romance An Egyptian Princess in this third volume with Prince Psamtik at the temple of the goddess Neith. Leaving his father's apartments, Psamtik asks for the high priest and is told to wait, since Neithotep is praying in the holiest sanctuary of the Queen of Heaven. Ebers pauses to explain how Egyptian temples were built to deepen a worshipper's devotion.

Temple politics, priestly power, and royal family tension drive the volume's action. The scene at Neith's shrine shows religion and rule working hand in hand in ancient Egypt. Readers get a richly detailed stretch of historical fiction, grounded in temple ritual and court intrigue.
5475-cleopatra-volume-03:
Messengers sent by Archibius to gather news return with nothing definite in the third volume of Georg Ebers's Cleopatra. A short time before, however, a royal runner delivered a tablet from Iras asking Archibius to visit her the next day. Disquieting but unverified tidings have arrived, and the regent strains to learn the truth while Archibius senses the government's distrust.

The volume works through rumor, messages, and guarded visits in Alexandria, as officials try to read a shifting political scene. Ebers builds suspense from uncertainty itself. Readers get a watchful, diplomatic stretch of the romance, where a tablet may matter more than an army.
5485-the-emperor-volume-03:
While anxiety broods over the steward's dwelling in the third volume of Georg Ebers's The Emperor, the hall of the Muses stays merry with feasting and laughter. Julia, the prefect's wife, has supplied the architect at Lochias with a meal fit for six hungry men. Pontius's slave unpacks dish after dish onto a humble table before fetching his master. The architect jokes that Titianus must take him for two crocodiles.

The volume contrasts a troubled household with a generous feast, showing how food, favor, and friendship work in Roman Alexandria. Ebers balances worry and comedy. Readers get a warm, busy stretch of the romance, where a great meal lightens a difficult day.
5496-homo-sum-volume-03:
Within minutes after Hermas flings himself from a window into the roadway, Phoebicius walks into his sleeping room in the third volume of Georg Ebers's Homo Sum. Sirona has barely had time to throw herself onto her couch, terribly frightened, her face turned to the wall. She wonders whether Phoebicius knows someone has been with her, who betrayed her, or whether he simply came home early by chance.

The volume turns on fear, suspicion, and a narrow escape in an early Christian household. Ebers keeps the tension close and domestic, even as larger questions of faith loom. Readers get a tense stretch of the desert romance, where a single return home changes everything.
5503-serapis-volume-03:
Agne's flight goes unnoticed for some time in the third volume of Georg Ebers's Serapis, since every member of the merchant's household is intent on a personal interest. After Karnis and Orpheus set out, Gorgo stays with her grandmother, and only later walks into the colonnade on the garden side of the house. From there she sees over the park and shore as far as the shipyard.

The volume follows a young woman's escape and the household that fails to notice it, in late Roman Alexandria. Ebers moves between garden, colonnade, and shore with an artist's eye. Readers get a quiet, suspenseful stretch of the romance, where a departure matters more than any arrival.
5510-arachne-volume-03:
Ledscha repeats a sentence to herself again and again in the third volume of Georg Ebers's Arachne: when the moon is over Pelican Island. While Hermon is detained by Daphne and her guests, Ledscha waits for that signal. After nightfall she enters a boat, hopeful and sure of her cause, declaring that he will come when the moon stands over the island. Her goal is quickly reached in the skiff.

The volume turns on a secret night meeting, jealousy, and divided loyalties among artists in ancient Alexandria. Ebers keeps the romance taut and moonlit. Readers get a suspenseful stretch of the story, where a single phrase becomes a promise and a test.
5519-the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-03:
After a night of great excitement, Paula throws herself on her bed with throbbing pulses in the third volume of Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile. Sleep will not come, so more than two hours after sunrise she goes to the window to close the shutters. As she does, she sees Hiram leap into a boat and push the light bark from the shore, daring neither to signal nor to call to him.

The volume follows Paula's sleepless watch and a boat's quiet departure, with loyalty and secrecy in tension. Ebers keeps the scene small and tense. Readers get a watchful stretch of the romance, where a glance from a window carries the whole plot.
5532-a-thorny-path-volume-03:
The sun has passed midday when Melissa and Andreas leave the house in the third volume of Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path. They walk in silence through deserted streets, the girl's eyes sadly fixed on the ground, warned by an inward voice that her lover's life is in danger. She does not sob, but more than once she wipes away a large tear, while Andreas is lost in his own thoughts.

To win a soul to the Saviour, Andreas reflects, is surely a good work, even amid danger. The volume pairs a girl's fear with a Christian's resolve in Roman Alexandria. Readers get a grave, tender stretch of the romance, where faith and love walk the same silent street.
5554-margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nurember:
Herdegen must return to Padua before Passion week in the third volume of Georg Ebers's Margery, a tale of old Nuremberg. Margery remembers with thankfulness the few months after worthy Veit Spiesz's burial and before her brother's departure, when not a day passed without their meeting. After she told Cousin Maud all that happened, with Herdegen's consent, the mystery that first weighed on them was gone for good.

The volume follows a sister and brother's close months, with confidences shared and secrets lifted. Ebers writes family affection in a young woman's voice. Readers get a warm, reflective stretch of the tale, where daily meetings matter more than great events.
5563-barbara-blomberg-volume-03:
During singing in the chapel on a fast day, Barbara waits vainly for a word of appreciation from the emperor in the third volume of Georg Ebers's Barbara Blomberg. The Queen of Hungary has gone to the chase, the monarch remains in his apartments, and Barbara does her best below before a few lords, ladies, priests, knights, and pages. Their small audience sorely irritates her easily wounded, sensitive nature.

The volume follows a singer's pride and disappointment at court, where praise withheld feels like rejection. Ebers writes Barbara's vanity with sympathy. Readers get a courtly stretch of the romance, where a chapel performance becomes a test of favor.
5574-a-word-only-a-word-volume-03:
For the first time in his life, Ulrich witnesses the death of a human being in the third volume of Georg Ebers's A Word, Only a Word. He often laughed at the fool or thought his words absurd and wicked, but the dead man inspires respect. The old jester's corpse exerts a deeper, more lasting influence on Ulrich than his father's supposed death.

The volume turns on a young man's first encounter with death, and how a jester's end reshapes him. Ebers writes the change from mockery to reverence. Readers get a somber, formative stretch of the romance, where a death teaches more than a life did.
5580-the-burgomaster-s-wife-volume-03:
On the afternoon of May sixteenth, Burgomaster Van der Werff's wife examines chests and boxes in the third volume of Georg Ebers's The Burgomaster's Wife. Her husband is at the town hall. Toward evening, several visitors will meet at his house for a confidential talk. They include the Prince's commissioner Herr Dietrich Van Bronkhorst, the two Seigneurs von Nordwyk, the city clerk Van Hout, and other heads of municipal affairs and friends of freedom.

The volume follows a household preparing for a secret council during the siege of Leyden. Ebers writes domestic order against political danger. Readers get a tense stretch of the siege romance, where a wife's housekeeping frames a city's resistance.
5586-in-the-blue-pike-volume-03:
Kuni's troubled soul gained much from a short pilgrimage to Altotting in the third volume of Georg Ebers's In the Blue Pike. She hopes for far more from a visit to Santiago di Compostella, famed throughout Christendom. Her old master Loni, met at Regensburg, permits her to join his band. Yet she sees he is far less prosperous than before, and that she cannot be useful to him in any way.

The volume follows a pilgrim girl toward Spain's great shrine, with an old master's decline shadowing her hope. Ebers writes pilgrimage as penance and longing. Readers get a devout, wandering stretch of the tale, where a shrine promises what a master cannot give.
5595-the-story-of-my-life-volume-03:
Georg Ebers recalls the night of revolution in the third volume of his autobiography, The Story of My Life, from childhood to manhood. When the family rose next morning, firing was over and all was said to be quiet, with the proclamation To my dear people of Berlin in hand. The horrors of the past night seemed the result of an unfortunate mistake, as the king explained that two shots by troops had begun the trouble.

The volume follows a Berlin boy through the March revolution of 1848, with royal proclamations, street fighting, and family fear. Ebers writes history as lived experience. Readers get a vivid stretch of autobiography, where a child's Berlin becomes a revolutionary city.
5647-sketches-by-seymour-volume-03:
Sketches by Seymour, part three, opens with The Jolly Anglers. On a grassy bank beside a meandering stream sit two gentlemen averaging forty years of age, on a sultry day. Weary of casting lines without effect, they stick their rods in the bank and turn to a well-filled basket of provisions and copious libations of bottled porter to dissipate disappointment.

One asks if this is not jolly, and whether Sam likes a day's fishing. Sam emphatically agrees, pipe in mouth, while his friend observes that some people do not know how to go fishing. Readers get Victorian comic verse about anglers, food, drink, and friendly boasting.
5666-the-arabian-nights-entertainments-v:
The Aldine Edition of The Arabian Nights Entertainments, illustrated by S. L. Wood from the text of Dr. Jonathan Scott, reaches its third volume, published by Pickering and Chatto in London in 1890. Contents include the story of Beder, Prince of Persia, and Jehaunara, Prince of Samandal. The history of Prince Zeyn Alasnam and the Sultan of the Genii follows, with the history of Codadad and his brothers.

The history of the Princess of Deryabar follows, with Abu Hassan or the Sleeper Awakened and Alla Ad Deen or the Wonderful Lamp. Adventures of Caliph Haroon Al Rusheed join them, with Baba Abdoollah and more. Readers get Aladdin and other great tales in handsome Victorian dress.
5690-the-innocents-abroad-volume-03:
This third part of Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad follows the pilgrims through northern Italy, from the Lago di Lecco and Bergamo onward. The opening chapter sends the party by steamer past mountain scenery, hamlets, and villas, then by open carriage with a wild driver along a smooth road between towering cliffs and the lake. Later chapters carry the same mix of sightseeing, local color, and comic complaint that marks the whole voyage.

Twain's gift here is to make a guided tour feel lived in: he notes the road, the driver, the pace, and the gap between guidebook praise and what the eye actually sees. Readers get Italy as American tourists of the 1860s met it, with churches, legends, and relics met by jokes as often as by awe. The part stands alone as travel writing, and it gains from the running jokes built up in earlier parts.
5784-a-tramp-abroad-volume-03:
Volume three of Mark Twain's A Tramp Abroad covers chapters fifteen through twenty-one, down the river through German country. Chapters treat German women's duties and bathing as the party went. Girls in the willows, steamers on the Neckar, and dinner aboard follow. Legends like the Cave of the Spectre, Lady Gertrude the heiress, and the Crusader fill later pages. The Lorelei, an unconquered monster, and an unknown knight follow.

Readers travel the Rhine and Neckar with Twain's running jokes about guides, legends, and fellow passengers. The volume balances real river scenery with invented and retold tales, letting Twain mock romantic guidebooks while enjoying their stories. It suits readers who enjoy travel humor, and it stands alone as a river journey even for those who skip earlier volumes.
5905-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Part three of Cervantes's Don Quixote, volume one, covers chapters six through eight, from scrutiny to second sally. Chapter six treats the diverting and important scrutiny the curate and the barber made in Don Quixote's library. Chapter seven covers his second sally. Chapter eight tells the good fortune he had in a terrible and unheard-of adventure. The library's fate and the road's dangers frame the part.

Readers watch friends try to cure Quixote by burning his romances, only to send him out again with Sancho at his side. The comedy sharpens as bookish madness meets real roads, inns, and giants that are not giants. This part suits readers following Quixote in order, since it moves the hero from home confinement back to adventure, with his squire newly in tow.
6048-works-of-john-bunyan-volume-03:
The third volume of John Bunyan's works, edited by George Offor, is allegorical, figurative, and symbolical, opening with The Pilgrim's Progress in the similitude of a dream. As Bunyan walks through the wilderness of this world, he lights on a den and sleeps. He dreams of a man in rags, his face from his own house, a book in hand and a burden on his back.

The man reads, weeps, trembles, and cries out, what shall I do, then carries his distress home to wife and children. It holds Bunyan's great allegory at its head, where burden, book, and road set the pilgrim walking.
6197-cumner-s-son-and-other-south-sea-fo:
The Planter's Wife opens Parker's third South Sea volume, with a ruined squatter's daughter married to Houghton the planter. She is not uncommon, he is not unusual, they are not happy, and they might never be. He almost knows they will not be, and she long ceased to think they could.

She told him at marriage she did not love him, and he waited in patience and devotion to win her love. Now both are sorry for each other, accept things as they are, and know danger in the situation, since she loves someone else and he knows it without speaking.
6245-the-right-of-way-volume-03:
Rosalie spends the day restless, and her unease holds into the evening as the tailor's wooden shutters close and only a flickering light shows through the cracks. At supper she answers her crippled father at random, while his mind turns on the lost iron cross and the threats of Filion Lacasse and his companions. The postmaster, the Cure, and Jo Portugais are among the few to whom the tailor talks much.

This third volume follows a sign from heaven, the tailor's return, and the Cure's inspiration, with two women at its centre, one who saw and one who did not tell. The Seigneur takes a hand in the game, a colonel tells his story, and a song, a bottle, and a ghost close the run. Parker keeps the village watching, whispering, and waiting for the cross to speak.
6448-mysteries-of-paris-volume-03:
Eugene Sue's Mysteries of Paris, volume three, opens Part Three, Night, in a notary's office. Paris, brain or heart of the land, claims nerves, muscles, and arteries centering in it, which few capitals can match for size, passions, horrors, loves, charms, and mysteries. To trace its emotions, impulses, secrets, wounds, cankers, and joys, these pages are devoted, picking up threads that lead deep into its labyrinths.

In 1819, a singular project grows from stories of left handed marriages and loving episodes, like the Prince of Capua and Miss Penelope Smith. Sarah Seyton, widow of the Earl of M'Gregor, puts it into operation, aided by her brother, the Honorable Tom Seyton, fully prepared to help his sister matrimonially entangle a victim. A mid scene shows Germain, advised by Rigolette, tossing ten sous to a speaker who hails him as a generous banker. Sue writes Paris as a maze of plots.
6772-the-thirty-years-war-volume-03:
Book three of Schiller's Thirty Years' War opens with the glorious battle of Leipzig, which changed Gustavus Adolphus in his own conduct and in friends' and foes' view of him. He had faced the greatest general of the age and matched his tactics and his Swedes' courage against the elite of the imperial army, Europe's most seasoned troops. From that day, confidence became the parent of great deeds.

Boldness, decision, and a loftier tone toward foes and allies mark his later campaigns, even in hard times. Schiller traces that rise with admiration and care. Book three is the high-water mark of Schiller's war history, where a Swedish king becomes a European hero.
6778-history-of-the-revolt-of-the-nether:
Book three of Schiller's Revolt of the Netherlands, on the conspiracy of the nobles in 1565, opens with a defense of Orange, Egmont, Horn, and their friends. Up to that point, Schiller says, peace had been their sincere wish, and they had served sovereign and common weal alike, as members of a free state and advisers of the king. Their only weapons had been remonstrances, modest complaints, and petitions.

No act yet showed a rebellious spirit or a suspect motive, Schiller argues, for they acted in bounden duty as men of honor. The book that follows tests that claim as plots thicken. Book three is a careful, sympathetic study of nobles on the edge of revolt.
6825-voyages-of-samuel-de-champlain-volu:
Volume three of Champlain's voyages, translated by Otis and edited by Slafter, completes the Prince Society's plan, covering 1611 to 1618 with ten maps and pictures. It holds journals issued in 1604, 1613, and 1619, covering fifteen years of Champlain's residence and exploration in New France. A later 1632 volume abridged those journals and carried the tale to 1631.

This closing volume thus gives Champlain's mature years as explorer and founder, in a scholarly dress. Slafter's memoir and notes aid the reader throughout. Its maps and notes aid a reader tracing Champlain's routes across New France. Volume three is the fitting close to a great early Canadian source.
7588-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part three of The Caxtons turns on one surprise in an otherwise tender homecoming. The narrator comes back to his father's house, welcomed warmly by the household, and led gently through the garden. His mother, tearful and cheerful at once, mentions that his father has company. The company is his brother, and that single fact stops him short.

The part's warmth comes from that reunion, not from any grand event. Servants and parents fuss over whether he has eaten, and the house gathers again under its own roof. Lytton lets humor soften the sentiment, so the scene feels lived in rather than staged. It is a family picture in miniature: arrival, affection, and a brother's unexpected presence changing the day.
7611-eugene-aram-volume-03:
In this middle part of Eugene Aram, trouble reaches the village of Grassdale. Peter Dealtry bursts from The Spotted Dog with news: two houses at Checkington have been forcibly robbed. Aram and Madeline are on their accustomed walk when the report reaches them.

The part pairs village alarm with the lovers' quiet happiness, then adds a reappearance that darkens both. Fraud and violence enter even Grassdale, as the chapter headings warn. Old faces from Aram's past close in, and the robberies give the village a reason to talk and fear.
7617-pelham-volume-03:
Pelham spends his last evening in Paris at a small party in this part. The Duchesse de B-- has invited him, and very few besides the royal family compose the gathering. He owes the honour to his intimacy with the duchesse's great friends.

Flattery, the narrator confesses, comes easily to one's mouth in the presence of royalty. The part is a study in court manners: a young Englishman among princes, watching faces and weighing words. Beneath the polish, the novel's darker business keeps moving. Every bow and compliment carries weight in such company.
7626-devereux-volume-03:
Book three of Devereux asks how much of life is design, and how much is a web we walk into ourselves. The Spinoza scene frames that question: the philosopher amuses himself by putting flies into a spider's web, and laughs at the imprisoned insects' struggles until tears course down his nose. The image returns whenever fortune turns against the hero. Philosophy and plot advance together here, each testing the other.

The part then drives the history forward at speed, and the chapter promises one important event in human life. Devereux's fortunes shift, and the web image gives those shifts a shape. Are his turns chosen, or caught? The book does not settle the question at once. It lets the hero move fast through events while the reader watches the web tighten.
7633-the-disowned-volume-03:
Mr. Copperas holds court at breakfast in this part of The Disowned, and the scene is comedy of money and manners. Mrs. Trinket's patter fills the room: talk of gloves, ribbons, and scents, over and over. The Copperas household gossips over wills, suitors, and Clarence's prospects, and shopping talk carries real stakes. What people buy, and what they hope to inherit, sit side by side at the table.

Copperas himself performs the scene, leg crossed over the other, a large piece of buttered cake in hand, asking his wife whether the old fool will leave the jackanapes all his fortune. She answers that she is out of patience with the young man's art. The posture is comic, the question serious: who gets the money, and on what terms? Breakfast, in this house, is also a court of opinion.
7642-ernest-maltravers-volume-03:
Book Three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Ernest Maltravers moves the young hero to Italy, where music and lake light set the mood. On Lake Como a boat song drifts toward a white villa, and the scene frames a story about art, feeling, and the search for a life worth living.

Maltravers listens to the young poet Cesarini read his own verse aloud on the water. The talk turns to taste, kindness, and the gap between fine words and daily conduct. Through Italian scenes and sharp talk, this part tests whether a gifted young man can grow past charm into steady character.
7652-kenelm-chillingly-volume-03:
Cecilia Travers stands at the heart of Book Three of Lytton's Kenelm Chillingly. She lost her mother young and ran a household while still a girl. Early care gave her poise and self-trust, yet left her sweetness intact, a rare and winning mix.

Kenelm meets her with wit and odd kindness, and their talk turns often to duty and feeling. The volume also takes him onto night streets where a poor girl begs for pity. Through country houses and town lanes, the book tests whether love can suit a hero who thinks in riddles and walks his own road.
7661-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-03:
Waife the gray cripple and little Sophy leave a friendly roof on a dull summer morning in Book Three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? She walks behind him in silence, past buttercups on dewy meads, too sad even to smile at the roadside flowers.

A shy lizard in the opening pages sets the tone: a small creature that hides yet finds joy in one sunlit hour. Through talk, gifts, and the puzzle of money given for no clear cause, the volume follows a grandfather and grandchild who depend on each other alone.
7674-harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-:
Book Three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Harold, titled The House of Godwin, opens with Duke William of Normandy curbing his vassals and wedding Matilda of Flanders. A papal blessing, won through Lanfranc, quiets the ban on the match, and England grows more Norman each day.

Then Harold's ships reach the Severn, and men of Somerset and Devon rise against him. In the Witan, clerks with the Great Seal hint at a new power that will one day grind men's hearts as Chancery. Saxon pride, Norman craft, and church power collide in these chapters.
7687-lucretia-volume-03:
Dalibard's plot ripens in the third volume of Lytton's Lucretia, titled The Discovery. He takes Lucretia by hired carriage to see her uncle's executor about her portion. On the short ride he turns solemn eyes on her with news he says may make her hate him forever.

The volume also crosses to France. There Chouan chiefs and old Jacobins weigh a plot against Bonaparte, the soldier who seized the fruits of revolution. Through drawing rooms and conspiracies, the novel shows how a teacher's cold art can steer a pupil toward ruin.
7694-a-strange-story-volume-03:
Margrave grows familiar in the third volume of Edward Bulwer Lytton's A Strange Story, calling at Dr. Fenwick's house before sunrise and meeting him again each evening. His extreme youth clashes with tales of travel over most of the known world, and he dodges a blunt question about his age.

A motherly warning at a ball adds unease: the stranger captivates yet revolts, and friends urge Fenwick to cool the friendship, above all after marriage. Through letters from Lady Haughton and Mrs. Ashleigh, the volume tightens a mystery around a man who seems too young for his past.
7704-my-novel-volume-03:
Pisistratus explains his title in Book Three of Lytton's My Novel, as his father praises the work so far yet balks at a sermon. Ladies rush to defend Parson Dale, and the young author, nettled, promises wider scenes beyond Hazeldean hall and parsonage, with new faces and longer views.

The volume also lingers in shops where haggling over weights and measures tries all patience, and quotes Aristophanes on peace. Through family debate, country detail, and jokes about authorship, it shows a novel growing in public, with its author learning his craft before his kin's eyes.
7717-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-03:
Sibyll muses alone at home in Book Three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons, after Marmaduke Nevile's sudden, broken farewell. His changed tone wounds her pride, yet a taunting rhyme from tymbesteres and a stranger's calm smile cut deeper, waking jealousy she cannot name.

Meanwhile a solitary sage meddles in worldly affairs at grave risk, speaking of steam power known to old sages and Roger Bacon, who dreamed of carts without horses and ships without sails. Allerton cuts him short, demanding letters for King Henry at once. Learning and peril meet in a scholar's cell.
7730-paul-clifford-volume-03:
Moonlight breaks over a lonely spot ten miles from Warlock in the third volume of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Paul Clifford. A masked horseman in a short cloak primes a large pistol, his dark gray horse standing still with ears alert, a scene fit for a painter of wild adventure.

The volume then moves to Bath, where Brandon, an early riser, wakes the luxurious Mauleverer, and a Punch and Judy show delights a crowd. Through highway scenes and town comedy, the novel follows Clifford's double life, where a gentleman's manners mask a robber's trade.
7739-the-parisians-volume-03:
Graham Vane arrives late at the Morleys' dinner in Book Three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Parisians, and his hostess pardons English lateness without asking. She presents him to the American minister, a sweet and powerful American poet, and other countrymen, then pairs him with Mademoiselle Cicogna at table.

Talk turns to America, where a fine singer might earn any sum, and Isaura colors at the praise. Later Raoul presses Alain's hand, urging him to meet his mother and settle family affairs with new-world candor. The volume blends dinner wit, art, and cousinly duty in Paris society.
7903-american-historical-and-literary-cu: Part three of Smith and Watson's American curiosities arrives as a text fragment. It holds an editor's note saying the volumes are illustrations and page images, plus the title page. Little prose could be scanned at all, which is why the note points readers to the HTML file for the real content.
8781-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This third part of Dante's Inferno, in Cary's translation, covers cantos five and six. From the first circle Dante descends to the second, a smaller space holding far more grief. Minos stands grinning, examining each soul's crimes and wrapping his tail around himself as many times as the degrees the soul must fall. The lustful, swept in an endless storm, dominate canto five.

Canto six turns to the gluttonous, lying in foul rain and hail under Cerberus, and to a prophecy of Florence's factions. Dante's encounters with Francesca and with Ciacco give the cantos their human weight: love and politics remembered from inside punishment. The part shows Dante's method at its most powerful, turning theology into meetings with people the reader already knows, or comes to know, in a few lines.
9765-alice-or-the-mysteries-book-03:
Book three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, opens on Lumley, Lord Vargrave, at a table covered with parliamentary papers. His face, once fresh, has faded and sharpened, with brows brooding over deep-set eyes. His mind's character now stamps his mouth in repose. Lytton paints a statesman whose ambition has etched his very features.

The book follows Vargrave's schemes and counsels, forked and quick, as Solon's verse promises harsh things mitigated. Lytton's prose favors moral portraiture. A reader gets the third book of a Victorian mystery romance, where a villain's face tells his story.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: The second volume of Robert Kerr's voyages continues early pilgrimages from England to the Holy Land between 1097 and 1107. It then treats the discovery of Madeira and the conquest of the Canary Islands. General voyages of discovery follow in the same systematic order. Kerr's history gathers the sources of navigation in one great collection.
a-modern-chronicle-volume-03:
Winston Churchill's A Modern Chronicle, volume three, opens Book Two with a wedding chapter: So Long As Ye Both Shall Live! Honora Leffingwell marries Howard Spence, the railroad magnate whose world she has entered. Stafford Park names his great house. The Great Unattached and The New Doctrine measure her married station.

Honora approaches New York by ferry in December, oppressed by its towers and its captains of industry. Quicksands, the Spences' Long Island seat, waits with its polo and its money-worship. The volume ends in Quicksands and with Gad and Meni, the biblical idols Churchill uses for wealth. Marriage has given Honora the world she glimpsed, and the chronicle begins to price it. Churchill's Book Two is the ascent: a wife installed among Titans, learning the doctrine of the great unattached — the rich who belong to nothing but themselves.
a-strange-story-volume-03: Edward Bulwer Lytton continues his strange story in this third volume, where the narrator's intercourse with Margrave grows habitual and familiar. Margrave comes to his house every morning before sunrise, and their evenings bring them together again at houses, hotels, and home. Nothing perplexes the narrator more than Margrave's extreme youthfulness set against travels that left little of the known world unexplored, and an age he evades with a jest.
a-thorny-path-volume-03:
Georg Ebers follows Melissa out of doors in Volume 3 of A Thorny Path, his novel of Alexandria under Roman rule. Ebers walks her through deserted midday streets beside Andreas, a freedman and Christian who serves her family. She keeps her eyes down, certain that the man she loves is in danger, and wipes away tears she will not explain.

Chapter VIII gives Andreas his own quiet hope as they walk. Baptism remade his life, and he longs to lead Melissa toward the same faith. He has known her since childhood, when her mother Olympias visited the estate where he served. Family memory, old loyalty, and new belief travel together here. The volume turns a simple walk home into a contest between pagan custom and Christian teaching for one girl's soul.
a-tramp-abroad-volume-03:
A Tramp Abroad, Part 3, by Mark Twain, floats down the Neckar on a raft and up into the legends of the Rhine. Twain's contents promise river bathing as the party went, then the ancient legend of the Lorelei, the siren rock where boatmen were said to perish. Another legend follows, of an unconquered monster and an unknown knight, told in Twain's driest deadpan.

Chapters XVIII to XXI bring breakfast in a garden, an old raven, and the castles of the Neckar valley, ending at walled Neckarsteinach and Dilsberg. Then Baden-Baden offers its comforts, described under headings about energetic girls and a comprehensive yawn. Throughout, Twain treats German scenery with real admiration and German legend with cheerful disrespect, rewriting each tale until its moral sits upside down. The raft journey gives the middle of his tramp its laziest, sunniest stretch.
a-word-only-a-word-volume-03:
Volume 3 of A Word, Only a Word, by Georg Ebers, gives young Ulrich his first sight of death. Ebers writes that the dead man is Pellicanus, an old jester Ulrich often laughed at or judged harsh and wicked. The corpse, stretched out stark and pale, stirs more respect and longer thought than the rumored death of his own father ever did in this volume.

Chapter XIV then turns to travel and art. Ulrich rides with an artist who speaks best in lines and colors, and grows lively only when talk turns to painting. At Toulouse the man buys three horses, hires French servants, and purchases chains and rings at a jeweller's. He packs the pieces in small boxes and labels them with neat Gothic writing. Names on the lids, none of them his children's, hint at young artists and plans the boy does not yet grasp.
alchimia-nova-das-ist-die-guldene-kunst-:
Alchimia Nova, printed at Frankfurt am Main in 1603, calls itself the golden art itself, or the mother of all arts. The book, associated with Giovanni Battista Birelli and the editor Peter Uffenbach, promises the art together with her secret secrets and her countless hidden children and fruits. It was printed by Nicolaus Hoffmann for the Palthenius publishing house, with its title page in red and black.

Woodcuts of alchemical apparatus illustrate the work, and an index closes it. Such German compilations gathered the scattered secrets of the art into one household volume for practitioners. Alchimia Nova preserves that Frankfurt trade in secrets at its height, when the golden art still mothered the crafts around it.
alice-or-the-mysteries-book-03: Edward Bulwer Lytton turns in the third book of Alice, or the Mysteries to Lumley, Lord Vargrave, seated among parliamentary papers with a face grown sharper and more brooding. The ambitious peer's scheming takes centre stage, and his character is weighed against the heroine's fortunes. Politics, pride, and plotting now press hard on the novel's romantic hopes.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol1-1803:
Amadis of Gaul is the great Spanish romance of chivalry that set the pattern for a whole age of fiction. Robert Southey, the English poet, translated it, and the first volume appeared in 1803. Its hero Amadis became the model knight for readers across Europe.

Amadis loves the lady Oriana and proves himself against giants, enchanters, and rival knights. Battles, shipwrecks, and magic fill this opening volume. The book bewitched Renaissance readers, and Cervantes honored it even while mocking its imitators. Southey's version brought the Spanish epic to English readers in full. Volume one launches the quest in high style.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol2-1803:
Robert Southey's translation of Amadis of Gaul ran to four volumes in 1803, and this is the second. The Spanish romance follows the peerless knight Amadis, the standard by which later heroes were judged. His deeds for his lady Oriana drive the whole vast tale.

Volume two carries Amadis through wars fought for Oriana's hand and fresh dangers in strange lands. Enchantments test his faith, and new knights enter the lists beside him. The pace is pure romance, with marvel piled on marvel. Readers of Cervantes will know this world well, since Don Quixote's library was full of such books. The epic here rides at full gallop.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol3-1803:
The third volume of Southey's Amadis of Gaul came out in 1803 with the rest of his translation. Amadis, the Spanish knight whose fame spread over Europe, faces his hardest trials of constancy here. His lady Oriana remains the center of all his deeds.

Sorcerers lay cunning traps, and magic isles rise out of the sea to test him. Amadis must hold his faith through long separation and false reports. The wonders come thick in this book, the richest in marvels of the four. Southey, himself a poet of romance, keeps the old Spanish fire alive in English. The volume brings the epic near its climax.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol4-1803:
Southey's Amadis of Gaul ends with this fourth volume, published in 1803. The Spanish romance had shaped European ideas of knighthood for three hundred years before Southey Englished it. Here the long tale of Amadis and Oriana reaches its close.

Final battles settle the wars that run through all four volumes. The last enchantments break, and old wrongs come right at last. The lovers win their hard reward after years of trial. With this volume ends the romance that taught Europe how to dream of knights. Its shadow falls across Don Quixote and across every chivalric tale written after it.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith offers a third instalment of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, again chiefly a gathering of illustrations rather than continuous prose. The editor warns that only a handful of sections scanned cleanly into text, so the HTML edition is the place to view the plates properly. What survives here is a window onto documents that shaped American memory.
an-egyptian-princess-volume-03:
Georg Ebers's An Egyptian Princess, volume three, in Eleanor Grove's translation, opens deep in the Sais court intrigue. Psamtik goes straight from his father's apartments to the temple, carrying his grievances to the priests. A night scene follows, bright with streaming light. Amasis receives his son with a burst of laughter that notices nothing.

The old Pharaoh's mirth is a statesman's mask: he knows his son plots and his kingdom totters. Psamtik's hatred of the Persian match, and of Bartja, ripens in these chapters toward open treason. Ebers keeps the historical frame tight — Amasis dying, Persia preparing, Egypt's priesthood intriguing. The middle volumes of his romance are court studies: a father's diplomacy against a son's wounded pride. Grove's English preserves the ceremonial pace. Readers of the whole set find here the hinge on which Egypt's fate begins to swing.
anselm-proslogium-monologium-cur-deus-ho:
Sidney Norton Deane published his translation of St Anselm's major works in 1903. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury in the 1100s, wrote the Proslogium and Monologium as prayers that reason through faith. Deane gathered those works with Cur Deus Homo in one English volume.

The Proslogium holds Anselm's famous argument that God, as the greatest conceivable being, must exist. Gaunilon, a monk, replied on behalf of the fool who denies God, and Anselm answered him. Cur Deus Homo explains why God became man, in the satisfaction theory of the atonement. These texts founded scholastic philosophy, the effort to prove the faith by reason, and they still anchor courses on medieval thought.
anthropography-or-bible-phrenology-of-th:
Anthropography or Bible Phrenology, published in 1903 by Rachel Bevington Webber, applies phrenology to the nations and tribes that sprang from Abraham. Where ordinary phrenology read an individual's head, Webber reads whole peoples: the descendants of Abraham are sorted and characterized by the science of skull and faculty. The Bible supplies her map of nations, and phrenology supplies her method.

Webber, who also wrote A New Race Phrenology, belonged to the fringe where the aging science met scriptural ethnology. Her book treats the peopling of the earth as a phrenological problem, with nations carrying inherited mental organs. It preserves a curious late chapter of head reading, in which Genesis and the calipers were made to agree.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-03:
Volume three of Burton's Arabian Nights, issued in 1885, carries Shahrazad's tales deeper into the cycle. By now the frame is familiar: night after night of story buys the teller her life. The tales turn through courts, markets, deserts, and islands of wonder in Burton's unabridged English.

Sea voyages and marvels grow more frequent as the volume proceeds. Burton refused to soften the Arabic text's frank passages, which kept his edition to private subscribers at first. His terminal essay and notes, spread through the set, made it a storehouse of lore. Later editors borrowed his learning even when they cut his text. The third volume sustains the pace set by the first two.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
The third supplemental volume of Burton's Nights, published from 1886, carries the overflow of the Arabic tradition further. Burton worked from manuscripts in several collections to catch tales the main cycle missed. Some are variants of known stories; others stand alone, rougher and stranger than the famous ones.

His method does not change: full text, kept verse, and notes that explain rite, dress, and law. The supplement as a whole shows how open the Nights remained, growing by copyists' hands for centuries. Burton wanted English readers to see that growth, not a polished extract. Volume three sits midway in the supplement's six books. It rewards readers who finished the main set and still want more.
arachne-volume-03:
Volume 3 of Arachne, by Georg Ebers, turns on a night meeting that one woman refuses to miss. Ebers follows Ledscha, who waits on a wooded island for the sculptor Hermon. Pirates once hid arms and loot there, and a walled passage under a grassy seat let fugitives vanish from anyone chasing them across the water.

Chapter X counts the hours with her as she repeats the agreed signal about the moon over Pelican Island. Hermon has been held back by Daphne and her guests from Pelusium, and the skiff ride feels longer for the delay. The gray water, the thick papyrus, and the hidden passage all promise secrecy. Love and vengeance share the same dark shore, and the reader waits with her to learn which one arrives.
arnaldi-de-villanova-philosophi-medici-e:
Arnaldi de Villanova Opera Chymica, printed at Frankfurt in 1603, gathers all the extant chemical works of Arnald of Villanova, the excellent philosopher, physician, and chymist who died in 1311. The collection opens with the Thesaurus Thesaurorum, the treasure of treasures, also called the Rosarius Philosophorum and the greatest secret of all secrets. Lumen Novum and Flos Florum stand with it.

The Speculum Alchimiae, the mirror of alchemy, closes the volume under its own title page, from the printing office of Matthias Becker. Woodcut initials and printed marginal notes furnish the text. The edition shows the seventeenth century still reading a medieval master as a living authority, his whole chemical corpus bound for working adepts.
arnim-svf-vol2-1903:
Chrysippus of Soli, the third head of the Stoic school, wrote hundreds of books, and none of them survive whole. Hans von Arnim devoted the second volume of his fragment collection, printed in 1903, to what remains of Chrysippus on logic and physics. The passages appear in Greek and Latin, as the sources kept them.

Here are the Stoic views on truth, signs, causes, fate, and the makeup of the cosmos, rebuilt from quotes in later authors. Chrysippus was the thinker who turned Stoicism into a tight system. This volume holds most of what can still be known of that system, and it stays a working tool for scholars of ancient thought.
arnim-svf-vol3-1903:
The third volume of Hans von Arnim's Stoic fragment collection, printed in 1903, turns from logic and physics to ethics. It gathers what survives of Chrysippus on how a person should live, and adds fragments from the Stoics who came after him. The texts stand in Greek and Latin, drawn from the authors who quoted them.

Readers find the roots of Stoic moral teaching here: virtue as the only true good, and the passions treated as errors in judgment. Duty is sorted by what fits nature and one's role in life. Because Chrysippus wrote the fullest defense of these views, his fragments form the core of Stoic ethics as later ages took it up.
arxiv-2509-00503:
Jialong Zuo leads eight authors in total, with Guangyan Zhang, Minghui Fang, Shengpeng Ji, Xiaoqi Jiao, Jingyu Li, Yiwen Guo, and Zhou Zhao, on compressing speech codes. Speech is often turned into discrete tokens, small units, at twenty-five or fifty per second, though speech carries only a few words per second.

Zuo and his co-authors use predictive entropy, a measure of how unsure a model is about the next token, to decide where to merge tokens into segments. A cross-attention step, which weighs links between parts, fuses each segment, and changing a threshold controls how much compression occurs. Tests on recognition, translation, and voice conversion match or beat dense token sequences.
arxiv-2509-00603:
Osama Abu Hamdan, with three co-authors, Hao Che, Engin Arslan, and Md Arifuzzaman, presents SmartFLow for cross-silo federated learning, where a few institutions train a shared model while keeping data private. Clients repeatedly swap model weights with a server, so slow networks stretch training time and congestion makes it worse.

SmartFLow uses Software-Defined Networking, central programmable control of network routes, to adjust paths as conditions change, cutting congestion and improving synchronization. Tests cut parameter synchronization time by up to forty-seven percent against shortest-path routing and forty-one percent against capacity-aware routing. Gains come with minimal extra compute, and the system scales to networks of up to fifty clients.
arxiv-2509-00703:
Osama Ahmad, with three co-authors, Lukas Wesemann, Fabian Waschkowski, and Zubair Khalid, proposes MAGN for spatiotemporal forecasting, predicting how values change across space and time. Complex volatility and spectral entanglement, signals mixing across frequencies, limit graph neural networks, and decomposition methods can be slow and need manual tuning.

MAGN turns iterative variational mode decomposition, a signal splitting method, into a trainable neural module with fixed depth, cutting decomposition time greatly on the LargeST benchmark. Mode-specific learnable bandwidth limits adapt to spatial differences and prevent spectral overlap. On LargeST, with thousands of sensors and hundreds of millions of observations, MAGN cuts prediction error sharply against its predecessor and beats leading baselines.
arxiv-2509-00803:
Saptarshi Saha and Rangeet Bhattacharyya propose a new use for prethermal states in NMR. Solid-state NMR probes a material's chemical and physical surroundings. A spin-locking pulse can drive spins into a long-lived prethermal state. That state has not been explored for measuring local environments before. The pair shows it can serve that purpose.

Such a state is described by two variables. They are its lifetime and its transverse magnetization. The lifetime grows as the surroundings' correlation time grows. The magnetization falls as the shift parameter strengthens. These two trends point in opposite directions. Together they let the method detect changes nearby. They also reveal chemical and dynamical shifts, such as Lamb shifts.
arxiv-2509-01203:
Black holes that spin, described by the Kerr geometry, differ from still ones described by Schwarzschild, yet the two may be linked by symmetry at the edge of spacetime. Nihar Ranjan Ghosh and Malay K. Nandy study that link through BMS supertranslations, shifts that act at null infinity, the far boundary where light escapes.

Ghosh and Nandy show the far structure of the Kerr spacetime can be produced from Schwarzschild by two supertranslations in a row. One class of shift, tied to center-of-mass moves, reflects plain translation. A second, built from an endless series of even Legendre terms, encodes Kerr's mass multipole structure. The result shows how these symmetries can connect distinct black hole geometries, with ties to soft theorems and gravitational memory.
arxiv-2509-01303:
Precise atomic measurements can reveal how a nucleus is built, but only if nuclear effects are understood well. Yilong Yang, Evgeny Epelbaum, Chen Ji, and Pengwei Zhao study hyperfine splitting in lithium isotopes, a fine energy shift in atoms. The shift is summarized by Zemach radii, and two kinds of radius, effective and elastic, have long disagreed for lithium six and seven.

The team shows nuclear polarizability, the way a nucleus stretches under electric fields, can resolve the gap. That effect is tiny in lithium seven but dominates in lithium six, explaining its large split between the two radii. They also prove a shared pattern across nuclei in a limiting case. In odd-odd nuclei the effect is boosted by a factor near three, a rule that helps read future precision data.
arxiv-2509-01803:
E D Paspaliaris, S Bianchi, E Corbelli, and A Concas link dust dimming to gas content across the disks of five nearby spiral galaxies. They measure dimming in two ways: from hydrogen line ratios and from fitting the full light pattern of each spot. Maps reach scales finer than half a kiloparsec, a unit for galactic distances. Gas maps for atomic and molecular forms complete the data set.

Both dust mass and line based dimming track molecular and total gas better than atomic gas alone. Dimming toward young stars from the fits matches the line based values well. That match lets the fit method stand in where line maps are missing. Dimming toward old stars fits a mixed stars and dust disk, while young star values fall between two layout extremes.
arxiv-2509-02203:
Dimos Aslanis, Alex Kehagias, Ioannis Kopsalis, and Ioannis Theodonis turn DECAL sensor noise into random numbers through time series analysis. A true random number generator harvests physical randomness rather than algorithmic pseudo-randomness. Their goals are to characterize the sensor noise without external stimuli and to test it as a randomness source. Statistical and time series tools examine the collected output.

An autoregressive integrated moving average model transforms raw noise into Gaussian white noise. That sequence then generates random bits for testing. The bits pass standard statistical suites, including the national standards battery. Bit generation rate, however, runs low for real time use under current settings. Further optimization could make the sensor a practical randomness source.
arxiv-2509-02703:
Peer Bilal Ahmad and Na Elah present a 2025 statistics paper proposing a new count model for health care data, with hospital length of stay as the target application. Count models describe data that arrive as whole numbers, such as days spent in hospital.

The authors establish the new distribution's key structural properties. A regression framework built on it lets researchers test how patient and treatment factors shift the counts. A three-inflated variant, which adds extra weight at three special values, handles datasets where certain stay lengths pile up unusually. Length of stay matters for hospital planning and cost control, so models that fit its skewed shape matter. The paper stays at the level of model construction, properties, and the regression setup.
arxiv-2509-03003:
Marko Ristić and 7 co-authors examined in 2025 whether some long gamma-ray bursts could come from colliding neutron stars. Gamma-ray bursts are the brightest explosions known, and long ones were long blamed on collapsing massive stars. Two recent long bursts, though, glowed afterward like kilonovae, the fading light of merged neutron stars forging heavy elements.

The team shows a collapsing star, called a collapsar, could match those same light curves. Their model uses one weak round of rapid neutron capture, the process that builds heavy atomic nuclei. It also omits the heaviest such elements, called lanthanides, and still fits the data. That weakens the claim that a red glow after a burst proves a merger origin.
arxiv-2509-03103:
Abdul Rahoof, Vivek Chaturvedi, and Muhammad Shafique set out in 2025 to run a full capsule network on a small programmable chip. Capsule networks group features into capsules that keep spatial relationships, aiming to understand image variation better than classic convolutional networks. Their routing step, which decides how capsules pass messages, is complex and slow in hardware.

Their two-step method first prunes the network with a look-ahead scoring scheme that judges parts by their future importance. It then simplifies nonlinear steps, reorders loops, and runs routing operations in parallel. On standard handwritten digit and fashion datasets, pruning removed nearly all of the network. Throughput on a low-cost chip rose from tens of frames per second to well over a thousand. That opens capsule models to cheap edge devices.
arxiv-2509-03203:
Christian Kanzow and Felix Weiß presented a 2025 penalty method for sparse optimization problems with general constraints. Sparsity here is enforced by an l0 term, which counts how many variables are switched on at all. Such problems are hard because that counting term jumps abruptly rather than changing smoothly.

A recent reformulation of the counting term lets the authors build a penalty approach, where breaking constraints adds cost instead of being flatly banned. Unlike their earlier work, the method needs no nonnegativity constraints, so variables need not be split into positive and negative parts. That keeps the problem smaller and preserves a one-to-one match between minima of the original and reformulated problems. They prove exactness for minima and stationary points, add practical subproblem techniques, and report extensive numerical tests.
arxiv-2509-03403:
Chenlu Ye and 7 co-authors tackled a flaw in reinforcement learning for reasoning models in 2025: rewarding only the final answer. When a model stumbles into a right answer through bad reasoning, outcome-only rewards still pay out fully. That outcome reward hacking biases training and teaches unfaithful reasoning.

Process reward models grade each reasoning step, but optimizing them directly, or mixing the two rewards naively, proved unstable as training shifts the data. Their method, PROF, instead uses agreement between process and outcome judges to select training samples. It keeps correct answers with strong process support and wrong answers with weak support, in balanced proportions. Experiments showed gains in both final accuracy and step quality over strong baselines. The method also leaned less on having a top-tier process judge.
arxiv-2509-03503:
Gwen Legate and two co-authors wrote a 2025 research paper on federated learning, where many edge devices train one model together without sharing raw data. Weak devices with little memory or bandwidth often fall below the level needed to join training. Excluding them hides their data and biases the final model.

Inspired by a memory-light method called MeZO, the authors build ZOWarmUp, a federated optimiser that estimates gradients without storing them fully. That zeroth-order trick had mostly served fine-tuning before, not training from scratch. Careful variance reduction, which tames noisy estimates, lets low-resource clients take part from a random starting point. Devices send only small random seeds instead of full updates, keeping upload costs tiny. Experiments across datasets and model shapes show the method holds up broadly.
arxiv-2509-03703:
Tristan Luca Saidi and three co-authors' 2025 research paper takes up EmbedOR, a visualisation method that keeps clusters intact when mapping high-dimensional data into a picture. Popular tools like t-SNE and UMAP squeeze tangled data into two dimensions for human viewing. They often tear connected regions apart spuriously and can miss clusters that are really there.

EmbedOR builds its distances from discrete graph curvature, a measure of how a network bends around each point.
