That curvature-enhanced distance emphasises the underlying cluster structure while the embedding proceeds stochastically, using controlled randomness. The authors prove the new distance extends known consistency guarantees for t-SNE to far more kinds of datasets. On synthetic and real data, EmbedOR fragments continuous high-density regions far less often than rivals. The same distance can also annotate existing visualisations, flagging where they broke geometry apart.
arxiv-2509-03803:
Mengyu Gao and one co-author's 2025 research paper is about teaching vision-language models to handle fine-grained recognition, where classes differ in subtle details. Prompt learning adapts a pretrained model like CLIP by tuning small text prompts instead of the whole network. Most prompt methods struggle exactly where classes look nearly alike, like bird species or car models.

Their method, CaPL, builds visual granules, small bundles of visual attributes, to guide the text prompt through causal inference. One module splits visual features into attributes shared across some classes and attributes unique to single classes, using a diffusion model of Brownian bridge type to do the splitting. A second module combines those attributes into granules under two causal inference strategies. The richer granules should yield a more discriminative learned prompt. Across fifteen datasets, CaPL significantly outperforms leading prompt learning methods, with the clearest gains on fine-grained benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-04003:
Wei-Tao Lu and one co-author's 2025 theoretical physics paper takes up electrical control of crossed Andreev reflection in antiferromagnet and superconductor junctions. Crossed Andreev reflection is an exotic process at a superconductor's edge: an electron enters and a hole leaves on the far side, entangling both sides. The junctions here are built from buckled honeycomb materials: germanene, silicene, and stanene.

With an electric field and an antiferromagnetic exchange field both present, spin-orbit coupling drives the honeycomb system into a spin-valley polarised half-metallic phase. That phase allows pure crossed Andreev reflection, uncontaminated by its two rivals, local Andreev reflection and elastic cotunnelling. The authors find the pure process persists over broad field ranges, uncontaminated. Adjusting the field flips the device between the two pure processes, a spin-valley switch effect. The device proposal suggests an electrical measurement of the crossed process.
arxiv-2509-04203:
Spencer Wadsworth and one co-author, Jarad Niemi, improve forecast blending with a Bayesian twist in a 2025 statistics paper. Weather and disease outlooks often pool several models into one ensemble forecast, weighting each model's voice. Weights are usually tuned by a proper scoring rule, meaning a score that rewards honest probability forecasts. Simple equal weights often beat fancy tuning, though, which hints that shrinking toward equality helps.

Their Gibbs posterior treats the stacking weights as uncertain quantities with a prior lean, possibly toward equal shares. Simulations and a real flu-forecasting contest from the US Centers for Disease Control test the idea. The stacked version often beat model averaging and equal weighting alike. Forecast teams also gain error bars on the weights themselves.
arxiv-2509-04403:
Jingen Qu and four co-authors build safety training data for multimodal AI by starting from pictures in a 2025 research paper. Models that read images and text together face growing safety risks in messy real situations. Older data-building methods start from known risks and miss much of that complexity, and no shared yardstick proved their worth. The new image-oriented method grows paired text and guidance replies outward from each image automatically, adapting as it goes.

Their generated set holds thirty-five thousand pairs of images and text, each with a guidance response. A standardized evaluation trick fine-tunes a safety judge model and tests it on other safety collections. Experiments confirmed the pipeline scales and works. The data set is posted publicly for other teams.
arxiv-2509-04603:
Justin Lin and one co-author, Julia Fukuyama, build an interactive toolbox for checking whether clusters in high-dimensional data are real in a 2025 research paper. Cluster analysis groups similar samples, but noise in many dimensions blurs patterns, and dimension reduction methods can invent false structure, especially when mishandled. Over-clustering, splitting one genuine group into several, often passes unnoticed. The authors develop checking techniques, from visual assessments to a formal hypothesis test, to expose fake clusters.

Everything ships in an R package called DRtool, designed for ease of use. Analysts can interrogate their clusterings interactively rather than trusting a single projection plot. Genomics and other high-dimensional fields gain a skeptical companion for exploratory analysis.
arxiv-2509-04903:
Long answers from language models are hard to train for because good long-form data are scarce and scoring is vague. Jianghao Chen, lead author with four co-authors, propose ACE-RL in a 2025 paper. Their framework turns subjective quality into fine-grained constraint checking for reinforcement learning.

Each instruction is first broken into adaptive constraint criteria across key dimensions of long-form writing. A reward mechanism then scores responses by how many constraints they satisfy. Reinforcement learning optimises the model on those signals. On a writing benchmark, the method beats supervised and reinforcement baselines and, in the authors' tests, surpasses a leading proprietary system.
arxiv-2509-05103:
Black hole phase transitions might be visible in the geometry of light orbits around the hole. Shi-Hao Zhang, lead author with four co-authors, build a differential geometric probe for such transitions in a 2025 paper. They locate the light ring using geodesic curvature in the optical metric and compute the associated Gaussian curvature.

During a first-order transition, the curvature-versus-temperature curve becomes multivalued, mirroring the swallowtail shape of the free energy. Numerical tests on a specific anti-de Sitter black hole family confirm the signature. Its jump between small and large black hole branches behaves like an order parameter, and a Lyapunov exponent extends the probe.
arxiv-2509-05403:
A bright hydrogen light line can misstate how fast distant galaxies form stars, and I. G. Kramarenko with five co-authors retune it in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The James Webb Space Telescope now records this H-alpha line in galaxies seen as they were long ago.

Standard scaling formulas assume typical metal content and steady star formation, both poor fits for early galaxies. Using the SPHINX simulations, the authors select galaxies like those the telescope observes and derive corrections that account for each galaxy's traits. Two new scalings cut forecast error compared with the old ones. Applied to recent data, they lower the estimated cosmic star-forming rate and steepen the main relation between galaxy mass and star birth.
arxiv-2509-05503:
Hiding how you see the board can itself be a winning move, Yue Guan, Dipankar Maity, and Panagiotis Tsiotras show in a 2025 game theory paper on competitive games. Each player acts on an internal representation of the environment, and a rival who infers that representation can exploit it.

In their defence scenario, one player watches the other's path, guesses its representation, and places barriers to block its goal. The other player disguises its type by randomising its route, bending the watcher's beliefs toward poor barrier choices. They solve the resulting Bayesian game for its perfect equilibrium with a bilinear program. Simulations confirm concealment emerges on its own from the incentives.
arxiv-2509-05603: A conjecture linking two filtrations in p-adic Hodge theory is formulated by Yukiyoshi Nakkajima in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is a proper scheme with a simple normal crossing log structure and a relative simple normal crossing divisor. Nakkajima states the logarithmic p-adic relative monodromy-weight conjecture for this zariskian, bifiltered complex, named for El Zein, Steenbrink, and Zucker, and proves the conjecture in certain cases.
arxiv-2509-05703:
Whale and dolphin calls drawn as spectrograms may be readable by vision-language models with the right support, Ragib Amin Nihal and three co-authors test in a 2025 paper. Marine mammal vocalisation analysis depends on these time-frequency pictures, but general vision models were never trained on them.

Their framework pairs a vision-language model's reading of a spectrogram with a language model check that builds domain knowledge. That loop adapts the system to acoustic data without hand annotation or retraining the models. The study asks a basic question first: can such models extract meaningful patterns from spectrograms visually at all? The design targets a low-cost route into underwater bioacoustics.
arxiv-2509-05803:
Black hole shadows under an alternative theory of gravity are examined in a 2025 paper by Xiao-Xiong Zeng and three co-authors. The theory is Horndeski gravity, a broad extension of Einstein's theory that adds a scalar field. Their test object is a spinning Kerr-like black hole carrying an extra hair parameter beyond mass and spin.

Using ray tracing with a fisheye camera model, the team renders shadows lit two ways: by a distant sky and by a thin glowing disk. As the hair parameter grows, shadows shift, their photon ring shrinks, and the outline bends toward a D shape, while spin strengthens frame dragging. Disk images differ for matter flowing with or against the spin. The authors then check the hair parameter against telescope images of two famous black holes, finding the theory still consistent with what was seen.
arxiv-2509-06003:
Coloring a graph so every vertex sees its neighbors' colors in perfect balance is the puzzle of a 2025 paper led by Maurice Genevieva Almeida with three co-authors. A neighborhood-balanced k-coloring uses exactly k colors, and each vertex must have equally many neighbors of each color. The notion generalizes an earlier two-color concept from the literature.

The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for such colorings and sort out which graph classes admit them. Deciding whether a given graph has one turns out to be NP-complete, so no fast general test is expected. They also prove no forbidden-subgraph characterization exists for the colorable class, closing a natural classification route.
arxiv-2509-06103:
Mining Mars's volcanic fields with a purpose-built rover is planned in a 2025 study by Divij Gupta and Arkajit Aich. Volcanic terrain offers resources but piles up hazards: steep unstable slopes, dust, and extreme conditions. The authors propose terrain-adaptive rovers with slope stabilization, terracing, and anchored drilling rigs for in-situ resource use.

Their mid-range rover design, about two tonnes, rides on a six-wheel rocker-bogie suspension with an anchoring drilling arm, dust-mitigating solar arrays, and advanced hazard sensing. Roads and rails are compared for transport infrastructure. Energy analysis favors combining solar with nuclear power for sustained work. The authors conclude that success in such terrain hinges on mechanical resilience, environmental adaptability, and autonomy working together.
arxiv-2509-06503:
Software that writes research code at expert level is described in a 2025 paper whose lead author is Eser Aygün, with forty-one co-authors. Scientific progress often stalls while researchers hand-build programs for their experiments. The system presented here, called ERA, aims to produce such software automatically, guided by a quality score it tries to maximize.

ERA pairs a large language model with tree search, a method that explores many branching paths and keeps the most promising ones. Given outside research ideas to draw on, it reached expert level on varied tasks. It found dozens of new methods for single-cell data analysis that topped a public leaderboard, and built epidemic forecasts that beat the CDC ensemble for COVID-19 hospitalizations. Strong results also came in geospatial work, zebrafish brain activity, numerical integrals, and time series forecasting.
arxiv-2509-06703:
Loading a shared machine learning model can quietly run hostile code, warn Gabriele Digregorio and four co-authors in a 2025 security paper. Model hubs and frameworks made sharing easy, and safety claims are common. The authors test whether those claims hold up in practice.

Their evaluation finds most frameworks and hubs handle risks only partly, often pushing responsibility onto users. Worse, checking products that advertise security settings turned up several previously unknown vulnerabilities allowing arbitrary code execution. The file format used for sharing, they argue, cannot by itself guarantee safety. A user survey adds a twist: safety marketing leads users to trust settings that the tests showed to be weak. The paper ends with suggestions for hardening the model-sharing ecosystem, aimed at both platform builders and practitioners.
arxiv-2509-07103:
Sergey Pozdnyakov and Philippe Schwaller introduce lookup multivariate Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in a 2025 paper. In most modern deep learning models, the big linear layers eat up most of the parameters and most of the computing cost.

Their design builds a large mapping out of many small ones. Each small function works in few dimensions, yet can hold dozens or hundreds of trainable parameters. Because each one is stored as a spline lookup table, working it out takes only a few multiplications. In tests, the networks cut the arithmetic needed at inference time by a large factor. At the same time they matched multilayer perceptrons at fitting general functions. In a second test they gave much higher throughput for the same accuracy. The authors also put the idea to work inside convolutional systems.
arxiv-2509-07203:
Mehdi Davoudi's 2025 paper, with 2 co-authors, studies long-term investment in rooftop solar panels through the lens of electricity markets. Homeowners and firms invest based on expected revenue over a panel's life. That revenue depends on short-term market prices and allocations, which in turn depend on how much total panel capacity gets installed.

The authors model investors as a non-atomic game, meaning many small players who each barely move the market. They compare three market designs: a plain real-time energy market, one that treats solar and grid power as distinct products, and a contract market that trades rights to future output. The product-based market reaches the social best outcome in their baseline case. The plain market underinvests, while the contract market can overinvest under some user conditions. The framework links daily market rules to long-term building choices.
arxiv-2509-07503:
Signals processed by two different sensor sets should stay stable even if some channels are lost. Ole Christensen, Hong Oh Kim, and Rae Young Kim study that stability in a 2025 research paper on frame theory. Frames are redundant signal representations used across mathematics and engineering. Two frames are woven when mixing their parts still gives a valid frame, guaranteeing no information loss.

The authors introduce information packets, a broader concept covering both frames and fusion frames. They show how to build woven packets from wavelet systems, a standard tool for analyzing signals at many scales. Certain wavelet systems split into any number of woven packets. Gabor systems, built from time and frequency shifts, behave differently: a separate frame is needed for each count. The results guide designs for robust signal processing with built-in backup.
arxiv-2509-07903:
Turbulence can be described by circulation, the swirling motion around a closed loop, but non-flat loops are hard to handle. L. Moriconi offers a new formulation of the vortex gas model in a 2025 research paper written alone. The statistical moments of circulation turn out to depend on special optimal surfaces spanning each loop. The model works in those curved spaces using operators that encode fractal density fluctuations.

Moriconi shows that minimal surfaces are the optimal choice within the inertial range of turbulence. Deviations should appear for loops sized near the smallest turbulent scale. As a case study, he evaluates the circulation distribution for a nonplanar loop by Monte Carlo simulation. The result agrees excellently with direct numerical simulations. The framework extends turbulence theory to the curved geometries that real flows often impose.
arxiv-2509-08003:
Flood prediction for climate-stressed cities is the target of a 2025 paper by Shahid Shafi Dar and 5 co-authors. Urban flooding threatens lives, infrastructure, and ecosystems, while older detection methods lean on single data sources and static rules that miss floods' dynamic, nonlinear behaviour. Attention and ensemble models also struggle with noisy, unstructured inputs.

The proposed network is explainable, meaning its decisions can be inspected, and it refines features by frequency awareness across channels and space. Hierarchical refinement and cross-modal integration aim to lift classification performance. City officials need warnings they can trust and defend, so a model that both predicts well and shows its reasoning fits the demands of sustainable urban planning.
arxiv-2509-08203:
Long language model answers become editable building blocks in a 2025 software paper by Ryan Lingo and 5 co-authors. Monolithic responses are hard to revise in parts, slowing collaborative work where a person wants to fix one claim and keep the rest. Their approach, componentization, decomposes model output into modular semantic units that stay linked to their context.

A decomposition method segments responses into coherent components, and a component-based architecture shows one implementation route. The reference prototype uses microservices with state-machine agents doing the splitting, independent of any single model vendor. Editable units could let teams review, reorder, and reuse machine text the way programmers refactor code, instead of regenerating whole answers and hoping the good parts survive.
arxiv-2509-08303:
M. Warizmi Wafiq and 16 co-authors release an open data set that maps oil palm farms in Indonesia, in a 2025 paper. Palm farms are a top cause of forest loss there. Good maps are needed for green rules and for checks by buyers. Experts drew the maps by hand from sharp satellite images taken from 2020 to 2024.

The labels cover whole regions, not samples. They span many farm zones and soil types. A tiered scheme splits palm by growth stage. It also splits palm from like crops that fool software. As a test bed, the set lets geo-AI models be scored on the same truth. Claims about forest loss then rest on maps that rivals can check, not on private data.
arxiv-2509-08503:
Marie-Pierre Béal and 2 co-authors give fast algorithms for a measure of how well a word compresses in a 2025 paper. The measure is the word attractor. An attractor is a small set of places in a word. Every distinct block of the word must touch one of those places, in a precise sense. The fewer places needed, the better the word compresses.

Two algorithms rest on suffix automata, compact machines that hold all blocks of a word. The first checks in linear time if a set of places is an attractor. The second builds one greedily. The smallest attractor is hard to find in general. Still, the greedy method gives tiny ones, and the true smallest for several classic word families. Storage systems live on compression, so sharp measures guide real design.
arxiv-2509-08603:
Anatoliy I. Lotkov and 4 co-authors study cat states in Rabi models with threefold symmetry in a 2025 paper. A Rabi model describes a qutrit, a three-level quantum system, interacting with light or vibration modes. The work covers one-mode and two-mode versions tied to circuit platforms.

A mathematical transformation lets the authors get the spectrum using perturbation theory in a magnetic field. In a strong coupling regime, the three lowest states become cat states that mix qutrit and boson parts. A new joint Wigner function, a picture of quantum state shape, identifies them clearly. Numerical checks confirm the tool across coupling strengths.
arxiv-2509-08903:
Alex Clay and 2 co-authors investigate useful information and filtering for language model driven knowledge base completion in a 2025 paper. The task is to complete triples, statements with a subject, relation, and object. In the 2025 LM-KBC challenge, common tools like retrieval were restricted.

Three facets are studied: generation, quality assurance, and parsing of model responses. Extra information improves generation quality in this constrained setting. Models can also filter poor triples effectively. The best parsing choice depends on the setting's need for flexibility versus consistency. The findings guide teams working under strict challenge rules.
arxiv-2509-09003:
Marlies Gerber and 1 co-author show non-classifiability of mixing zero-entropy diffeomorphisms up to isomorphism in a 2025 paper. Classifying dynamical systems up to isomorphism asks when two systems are essentially the same. For mixing, zero-entropy systems on a probability space, the task proves intractable.

The set of isomorphic pairs is shown not to be Borel, a measurability notion that marks classifiable problems. The result holds even for smooth diffeomorphisms of the five-dimensional torus. It also holds under a weaker equivalence called Kakutani equivalence. A cancellation argument for product systems drives the proof, with a counterexample showing cancellation fails in general.
arxiv-2509-09103:
Crop disease alerts help farmers most when the advice is specific, private, and cheap enough to run on a phone. Chanti Raju Mylay and 3 co-authors present AgriSentinel in a 2025 research paper. Existing alert systems, they argue, ignore data privacy, market pricing power, and usability. Farmers can end up exposed to breaches and exploitation by the tools meant to help them.

AgriSentinel classifies crop diseases with a lightweight model tuned for mobile devices. A differential privacy mechanism protects the farm images it learns from. An on-device language model, fine-tuned on a curated knowledge pool, gives concrete management advice rather than a bare alert. Experiments showed privacy held while classification accuracy stayed high. The system targets the farmer's real constraints: weak connectivity, sensitive data, and the need for an answer that says what to do next.
arxiv-2509-09503:
Di Wang and 1 co-author study CP asymmetries in two charmed baryon decays in a 2025 particle physics paper. Such asymmetries compare how matter and antimatter versions of a decay proceed, a clue to the cosmic imbalance between the two and to physics beyond the Standard Model. The decays end through a neutral kaon that later becomes two pions.

Wang and his co-author derive several time-based versions of the asymmetry, named by Greek letters, for the full decay chain. One neat result is that the kaon mixing contribution cancels in most of those versions. Using U-spin relations between the modes, they show the needed hadronic inputs can be drawn from measurable decay parameters, and one interference effect may reach a noticeably large size.
arxiv-2509-10003:
Tawfiq Ammari and 3 co-authors study how men facing infertility find support online in a 2025 analysis of a Reddit community. Traditional expectations of masculinity discourage men from voicing distress or asking for help, leaving many silent. The r/maleinfertility forum offers another route, and the authors mine more than eleven thousand posts and nearly eighty thousand comments from over eight thousand users to see how it works.

Topic modelling, network mapping, and time-lagged statistics reveal a hybrid place at once: an informal clinic, a shared emotional commons, and a moderated institution. Medical guidance dominates the talk, while a smaller stream of emotional support and a large share of moderation hold the space together. Members who also post in the mixed-gender forum act as guides, carrying knowledge between the two worlds.
arxiv-2509-10203:
Mohamed Majdoub and Ezzedine Mliki wrote this 2025 paper on equations for spreading that is slowed by random waiting times. Their focus is fractional diffusion. There, motion mixes plain local spreading with long-range jumps. They ask how solutions behave after a long time has passed.

The authors mix tools from probability, from asymptotic analysis, and from the theory of partial differential equations. With them, they pin down the long-run pattern of these time-changed solutions. Their results widen the classical theory of fractional dynamics. The work also tightens a link between two worlds. On one side stand random processes that change speed over time. On the other stand the fixed equations that mirror them. Later work on slow, uneven spreading gains a firmer base.
arxiv-2509-10303:
Factory scheduling from old records alone is the challenge Jesse van Remmerden, Zaharah Bukhsh, and Yingqian Zhang take on in this 2025 reinforcement learning paper. Online methods learn by trial and error in simulation, which costs many interactions. Their algorithm, CDQAC, instead learns good job-shop schedules from fixed datasets of mediocre solutions.

The method pairs a quantile-based critic, which estimates the full spread of returns for machine-operation pairs, with delayed policy updates for stability. On standard job-shop and flexible job-shop tests, it matches or beats the heuristics that produced its data and outperforms recent online and offline rivals. Strikingly, it needs only a small slice of the data, and broad coverage matters more than trajectory quality: random play with wide coverage beat strong genetic-algorithm data.
arxiv-2509-10503:
Haolin Yuan and four co-authors present FEDEXCHANGE, a federated object detection framework, in this 2025 computer vision study. Federated learning lets many clients train one shared detector without pooling their private images, but a model trained on sunny streets may stumble in the rain. Bridging that domain gap usually costs the edge devices extra computation, which they can ill afford.

FEDEXCHANGE moves the fix to the server. Rounds alternate between ordinary model aggregation and model exchange, where local models are clustered by distance and swapped so each client learns from other domains' models, never from raw data. Clients do no extra work. Tests show mean average precision up to 1.6 times better in hard domains like rainy scenes, while using only four-fifths of the baseline computation.
arxiv-2509-10603:
Thibault D. Décoppet and Matthew Yu classify topological orders enriched by symmetry in this 2025 paper. Topological order describes phases of matter. Their behavior depends on global structure, not local detail. The authors ask a focused question. How do such phases, in three spatial dimensions, combine with a finite symmetry group G?

Their tool is a two-categorical version of equivariantization, and its reverse. That machinery adds or removes symmetry inside category theory. They argue for an exact correspondence. Fermionic topological orders with G-symmetry match certain enriched crossed braided fusion 2-categories. The defining data also match a known construction. It is the Wang-Wen-Witten construction, adapted here to fermions, with an anomaly saturated. The same methods classify all braided fusion 2-categories. The field gains a complete map of this landscape.
arxiv-2509-10803:
Nafees Iqbal and Jed Brown bring Rust's type safety to MPI, the message passing standard of high-performance computing, in this 2025 software paper. MPI is powerful but low-level and type-blind, so mismatched messages surface as runtime errors or undefined behavior that are painful to debug at scale. Their framework builds on the RSMPI library and centers on a TypedCommunicator abstraction.

Using Rust's Equivalence trait, the framework ensures only compatible types can be sent and received, catching mismatches at compile time where possible and by validation otherwise. It handles single values and slices through an intuitive interface. The authors report that common MPI errors disappear, developers move faster, and performance holds, in keeping with Rust's zero-cost abstraction promise. Collective operations are the stated next frontier.
arxiv-2509-11303:
Dasol Choi, Jungwhan Kim, and Guijin Son introduce Ko-PIQA in this 2025 natural language processing paper. Datasets testing physical commonsense are mostly in English. They reflect English-speaking life. Other languages and cultures go untested.

The team started from millions of web-crawled Korean questions. Three language models filtered them. GPT-4o refined the survivors. Humans validated the final set. The result is a compact set of high-quality pairs. About a fifth of the questions hinge on Korean specifics. Kimchi and hanbok clothing appear. So do kimchi refrigerators. Translation alone cannot capture such items. Seven language models were tested. The best scored above eighty percent. The weakest scored near sixty. Culturally specific items tripped models up most.
arxiv-2509-11503:
Rishab Parthasarathy, Akshay Attaluri, and Gilford Ting built a video conferencing system in pure hardware. This 2025 engineering paper puts the whole stack on an FPGA chip. The board is a Nexys4 DDR. No computer software runs the call.

The design squeezes video with the M-JPEG codec. A custom UDP stack sends it on. An audio controller feeds the same stream. The rate reaches thirty frames per second to the receiving computer. A Python script there unpacks the packets. It plays video and audio back in real time. The team checked the design with simulation-driven tests in Cocotb. They also synthesized the SystemVerilog code in Vivado. Latency and throughput were measured on the real board.
arxiv-2509-11903:
Rainfall over Northeast India is tracked month by month from 1971 to 2023. Junmoni Saikia and two co-authors use that record in 2025 to test a hybrid way to forecast rain. Five weather subdivisions supply the data. The goal is sharper monthly forecasts for a wet, flood-prone region.

Their method first splits each rainfall series into layers. A wavelet transform does the split at several time scales. Four wavelet families are tried. A seasonal time-series model then handles the regular linear patterns. A Transformer network learns the leftover nonlinear parts. Last, the pieces are joined back into one forecast. On held-out data, the Haar-wavelet version won. It beat both single models and simpler hybrids. Its leftover errors also passed standard adequacy checks.
arxiv-2509-12003:
Fake voices made by AI are the target of a 2025 study by Pierre Serrano and 4 co-authors. Their detectors use frozen self-supervised encoders, models pre-trained on large amounts of speech and then left unchanged. Such systems work well on familiar data but often fail on new, out-of-domain recordings.

The team compared six encoders across four test collections, examining them layer by layer to see which layers helped most. Picking one strong layer matched more complex pooling methods while cutting the system's size by up to four fifths. Results varied widely with the test set and the encoder's pre-training. Combining scores from several encoders improved performance on unfamiliar attacks, pointing to a practical route for more robust detectors.
arxiv-2509-12103:
Compressible turbulence, where a fluid's density swings as it churns, gets a symmetry-first theoretical treatment from Olivier Coquand in a solo-authored 2025 article. Rather than simulate, Coquand asks what the energy spectrum across scales is even allowed to look like.

Starting from the symmetries and linear transformations of the microscopic action, the paper derives exact relations tying correlation functions to their generators. Those relations tightly restrict possible scaling laws at each scale. The headline result splits the action into two parts. One is an incompressible part identical to standard stochastic Navier-Stokes theory at any Mach number. The other is a longitudinal part matching the three-dimensional Burgers equation. That equation carries a far richer phase diagram than its one-dimensional cousin.
arxiv-2509-12203:
Drag-based image editing lets a user pull a point in a picture and expect the image to follow. Zixin Yin and 6 co-authors introduce LazyDrag in a 2025 paper for multi-modal diffusion transformers, a newer class of image generation models. Earlier methods matched points indirectly through attention, forcing weak inversion or costly test-time optimization.

LazyDrag instead builds an explicit correspondence map from the user's drag, giving attention a reliable reference. That reference allows full-strength inversion, a first for this task, and removes the need for test-time optimization. The method unites precise geometric control with text guidance in one edit. The authors show complex changes that were previously out of reach, such as opening a dog's mouth while keeping the image coherent.
arxiv-2509-12703:
Gyungmin Cho and Dohun Kim give a 2025 method to learn an unknown quantum state by testing one copy at a time with shallow circuits. Learning a full state can need huge numbers of tests, and tests that join many copies are hard to build on near-term machines.

Their plan uses no extra helper system and uses only short local circuits. For low-rank states the number of copies matches the best known limit up to a small extra factor. For full mixed states the count is fully best, with fast work to write the state out. The plan fits tools that labs can run today.
arxiv-2509-12803:
N. Bouteldja and 3 co-authors search for unusual electronic behavior in Heusler compounds in a 2025 paper. Heusler alloys are promising for spintronics, technology that uses electron spin as well as charge. The authors study two compounds with manganese and gallium paired with titanium or iridium.

Using density functional theory with a Hubbard correction, they examined two crystal structures for each alloy. One titanium compound switched from a metal to a spin gapless semiconductor, a state with special spin-dependent energy gaps, when the structure changed. The iridium compound showed gapless half-metallic behavior in one structure and half-metallic behavior in the other. Magnetic behavior was governed by hybridization between manganese and partner states. Both alloys were structurally stable with tunable traits.
arxiv-2509-13303:
Avior Almoalem, Sajilesh Kunhiparambath and ten co-authors find in 2025 a mixed singlet-triplet state in split monolayer sheets. Unconventional pairing that strays from plain s-wave stays a core puzzle. Layered dichalcogenides show odd signs despite a plain reputation.

A misfit stack pairs tin sulfide with tantalum disulfide sheets. Tin layers split the tantalum sheets into isolated layers. Tunneling shows a clear two-gap spectrum at low temperature. A model with broken inversion and finite-range pull reproduces the gaps as mixed pairing. Misfit stacks offer a lab for lone-layer exotic states.
arxiv-2509-13503:
Dahyeon Lee, Zoey Hu and nine co-authors reach in 2025 a record laser frequency stability in a silicon cavity with crystalline mirrors. Ultrastable lasers drive frequency metrology and quantum science. AlGaAs coatings promise low noise, yet excess noise curbed past cryogenic gains.

A new mirror pair in a short cryogenic silicon cavity at low temperature changes the picture. Stability beats dielectric expectations by fourfold at ten seconds. Coating loss drops by over tenfold. Two cavities combine for optical averaging gains. Multi-year drift records for four cavities are given. Paths to far higher stability and an all-optical timescale open.
arxiv-2509-13803:
Laura García-Sardiña and three co-authors set up a way to measure gender bias in job title matching in a 2025 paper. In languages with grammatical gender, job titles come in masculine and feminine forms, and automatic ranking systems that match candidates to titles might quietly favor one form over the other.

The team proposes comparison metrics that control for gender, centered on rank-biased overlap, a measure of how similar two ranked lists are. They built and released test sets in four grammatical gender languages, with titles in both forms annotated for gender and matching relevance. Running several ready-made multilingual models through the new benchmark showed every one of them carried some degree of gender bias, setting baselines for future work.
arxiv-2509-14003:
Liting Gao and seven co-authors edit audio with text in a 2025 paper. Changing one sound inside a recording, say swapping a dog's bark for a cat's meow, while leaving everything else untouched demands precise localization of the target and faithful rendering of the edit. Earlier methods leaned on full captions, masks, or expensive per-edit optimization and stumbled on complex scenes.

Their framework rebuilds the task on rectified flow matching, a fast diffusion-style generative method, in one end-to-end model that needs no auxiliary captions or masks at edit time. They also built a training and benchmark dataset of overlapping multi-event audio, the hard case where sounds pile on each other. Across metrics the system kept competitive editing quality with strong agreement to the text instruction.
arxiv-2509-14603:
Xingchen Wang and seven co-authors present PM-SFL in 2025, a privacy preserving split federated learning framework. Split learning divides a model between client and server to cut client computing. Shared activations and updates can still leak raw inputs through reconstruction attacks.

Probabilistic mask training adds structured randomness to the shared signals without injecting plain noise. That design aims to block reconstruction while sparing model accuracy, which noise defences often degrade. The framework also handles heterogeneous clients with unlike data and devices. Scalability is a stated design goal for large federations. Safer split learning could let phones and hospitals co train models without exposing the records behind activations.
arxiv-2509-14903:
Albert Peralta Amores and Marcin Swillo propose a way to make photon pairs far more efficiently in semiconductor waveguides, in a 2025 optics paper. The process is spontaneous parametric down-conversion, where one photon splits into two inside a nonlinear material. Two conditions must hold at once: phase matching along the guide and amplitude matching across it.

Their idea is to modulate one nonlinear coefficient unevenly across the waveguide cross-section. That shaping achieves amplitude matching across the width while keeping phase matching along the length. Analysis predicts about ten times the efficiency of the best unmodulated waveguide, and vastly larger gains over designs with phase matching alone. The authors also sketch a compact twin-photon source tunable across the telecom band for future quantum communication hardware.
arxiv-2509-15103:
Simin Li and fourteen co-authors ask which agents in a huge multi-agent learning system are the weak points whose failure hurts most, in a 2025 machine learning paper. When thousands of agents learn together, some failures are inevitable as systems scale. Finding the vulnerable subset in advance lets designers harden exactly the right places.

The authors frame vulnerable agent identification as a two-level adversarial control problem: an upper level picks the agents, a lower level learns their worst-case policies. The levels are coupled, and the upper problem alone is NP-hard. A Fenchel-Rockafellar transform decouples the levels so each can be learned independently at lower cost. The selection problem is then recast as a sequential decision process with dense rewards, so vulnerable agents can be picked one by one with feedback.
arxiv-2509-15203:
Sasan Rahmanian shows tiny light cavities hidden inside MEMS chips in a solo 2025 paper. MEMS are micro machines etched in silicon. The test device is a curved microbeam fixed at both ends. It faces a fixed side mirror across a thin gap and sits on a silicon-on-insulator wafer.

A laser beam fills the gap while the chip sits in vacuum. Beam and mirror form a small cavity that links light to the beam's shaking. The setup makes soliton frequency combs by phonon lasing, with no electric drive. Tests and models both show that the two plates of a plain capacitive gap can form such a cavity by chance. A side effect becomes a tool for chip-scale combs.
arxiv-2509-15403:
Yangyi Li and Mengdi Huai ask how sure we can be of a model's own words. Large language models now answer questions and can explain their answers in plain text. Those explanations help users, even for closed models. Yet no one had set a firm bound on how much trust an explanation deserves. Noise in the input, such as in medical queries, makes this harder.

The pair build a method that puts valid bounds on doubt for such explanations. It works after the model has run and needs no access to its insides. A second, tougher version keeps its bounds even when the input is noisy. Tests on question answering tasks show both methods work as claimed. The work adds a check on model talk.
arxiv-2509-15503:
Vishnu Nandakumaran and Gábor Székelyhidi settle a uniqueness question for least area surfaces. The Plateau problem asks which surface of least area fills a given closed edge. They study surfaces inside a unit ball whose edge on the ball is a slight shift of a known shape: the link of a least area cone built from a quadratic rule.

The pair show that such a surface is fixed by its edge alone. In plain terms, for edges near that cone link, the Plateau problem has just one answer. Uniqueness matters because it rules out rival surfaces that meet the same edge. The result holds for small shifts of the edge. The paper is a compact proof in geometry.
arxiv-2509-16003:
People often share private facts online without meaning to, and that slip can lead to theft or misuse of their data. Reza Shahriari and Eric D. Ragan survey past user studies on this kind of unwanted sharing. Their review covers 101 papers from six top meetings held between 2018 and 2023.

The survey sorts studies by method, both number-based and talk-based, and by topic area. Hot topics include data privacy, web browser safety, and privacy tools. By comparing study styles, the authors map where research effort has gone. Their map can guide new work on ways to cut the risks of daily online life.
arxiv-2509-16403:
A prior study by E. Aydiner proposed a new physical law meant to cover both particle and heat systems, along with fresh definitions of chaos and self-organization. Here the scheme is extended to a range of thermodynamic systems to test whether the law holds broadly. The dynamics of those systems also turn chaotic under varied conditions, the author reports.

The work links chaotic dynamics with the least action idea and proposes a Chaotic Action Principle for the first time. It also examines the physical and philosophical roots of the law and offers a new conceptual definition of complexity built on the principle.
arxiv-2509-16503:
An X-ray method that images soft tissue by refraction and scatter, not just absorption, suffers striped Moiré flaws when its grating sits slightly off. Hunter C. Meyer and nine co-authors write a recovery method that estimates the true grating steps using several harmonics of the fringe pattern, with a smoothing rule that keeps edges sharp. The stripes vanish from all three image types at once.

Tests on plastic bead samples and a mouse with two interferometer designs show the cleanup works in practice. Cleaner phase images could aid lung imaging and other clinical uses where this young modality promises detail that plain X-rays miss.
arxiv-2509-16603:
Maurício do V. M. da Costa and Eloi Moliner design a new sound generator in a 2025 paper. Their system builds audio with a diffusion process, which starts from noise and shapes it step by step. A transform that splits sound by octave guides the design. Each octave gets a time and pitch sharpness that fits it.

Their system is named MR-CQTdiff. It can be run forward and backward without loss. Tests used a standard score for audio quality across two datasets. The new design earned top scores against rival systems. Better scores mean clips that sound closer to real recordings. The work may help music and sound tools.
arxiv-2509-16803:
Qiang Li and co-authors sharpen brain maps from primate scans in a 2025 paper. A method called ICA splits mixed brain signals into separate parts. In monkey studies, the maps it gives are often too dense to read. The team use a sparse form of the method, which favors maps with clear, focused zones.

Applied to real primate scan data, the sparse method found several clean networks. Each network lit up well-defined areas. The clarity held across brain systems. Cleaner maps help researchers compare brain wiring across species. They also give a firmer base for studies of brain disorders that use animal models.
arxiv-2509-16903:
Nawar Turk, Daniele Comitogianni, and Leila Kosseim report a shared-task system for discourse labels in a 2025 paper. Discourse relations link clauses, such as cause or contrast. The task unifies many labels across dozens of corpora, many languages, and six frameworks. That mix makes the task hard for any single model.

Their system stacks adapters in a hierarchy to share strength across frameworks. It earned the highest overall accuracy in the task. It also trained far fewer weights than full fine-tuning. Bigger models helped only a little. Prompt-based models lagged well behind. Efficient adapters could widen access to multilingual discourse tools.
arxiv-2509-17003:
Jonathan Morag, working alone, tackles atomic line opacity in a 2025 astrophysics paper. When light passes through hot gas, atomic transitions block it at many frequencies. Modelers cannot resolve every line, so they average in rough ways. That averaging is a prime source of error in radiative transfer models.

Morag argues no fully consistent coarse-frequency solution exists yet for these systems. He describes new features in an updated public opacity table. The table works at high frequency resolution. Better opacity data sharpen models of stars and explosions, where light transport sets what telescopes see and how energy moves through the gas.
arxiv-2509-17103:
Yuhki Hosoya is the sole author of a 2025 arXiv paper on dynamic programming, the method that breaks a long chain of choices into step-by-step decisions. The paper proves the envelope theorem for a fixed, non-random version of that model. The theorem tells how the best outcome shifts when a condition of the problem shifts.

The proof uses the Clarke differential, a tool built for functions that are not smooth. Earlier proofs of the same result asked for more from the model. Hosoya's version does not need the functions to be smooth, the sets to be convex, or the values to be bounded. That weaker set of demands makes the theorem usable in more economic models.
arxiv-2509-17203:
Yifei Sun, writing alone, asks where a classic flow-splitting tool helps city traffic analysis and where it does not. His 2025 arXiv paper applies Hodge decomposition to traffic in Los Angeles. The tool splits a flow into a smooth gradient part, a swirling part, and a leftover part that loops around holes in the network.

On dense trip graphs that link every start to every end, the swirl and loop parts come out near zero. There the smooth part just mirrors raw inflow and outflow, so the tool adds little. On a real road network in downtown Los Angeles, with data every fifteen minutes, the picture changes. The smooth part departs from raw counts and flips between morning and evening, matching commute tides. Sun also proposes map embeddings that mix road layout, two-way volume, and net flow for grouping streets.
arxiv-2509-17503:
David Steiner and seven co-authors free a trapped nanoparticle and watch its wave packet spread. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves proposals to make non-classical states of levitated particles, where clean expansion of the packet is a core step. Letting the particle evolve freely after release is a simple expansion scheme, but stray forces can drag its center and spoil the state.

The team uses an optical trap, release, and recapture sequence with a charged particle. An electrostatic compensation scheme cancels gravity and stray electric fields, so the packet grows without a large mean drift, in all three dimensions. Free evolution lasts on the order of a hundred microseconds. New tools map and fix force cross-talk and tame the particle's charge state. With a low-decoherence setting, the approach prepares broadly spread states without long drops or a space-like platform.
arxiv-2509-17703:
Zhou Ziheng and nine co-authors use language model agents to ask why morality evolved. Their 2025 arXiv paper revisits a classic puzzle: selection should favor self-interest, yet humans built moral systems that push altruism. Older models must strip cognition down to bare rules, so they cannot show how thinking itself shapes moral change.

The team's agents carry varied moral dispositions inside a simulated hunter-gatherer society. They perceive, remember, reason, and decide in richer ways than rule-based agents, and the setup can vary traits no classic model can express, such as how visible a moral type is. Across twenty runs in four settings, cooperation and mutual help drove survival. Universal and reciprocal morality proved most stable, while selfishness was strongly disfavored. A cost of moral judgment emerged as a key mediator that can flip which moral type wins.
arxiv-2509-17803:
Nabila Amadou, Kazi Injamamul Haque, and Zerrin Yumak ask how real a fake human should look and move. Their 2025 study uses 3D virtual humans that show feelings on the face. Such figures are now used in health, school, work, and calls.

In a user test, the team varied how real the face looked and how real the motion looked. More real looks and motion led to higher marks for charm and for feeling present. Motion also changed how real the figure felt and how strong the feeling seemed. The results give design clues for next builds.
arxiv-2509-17903:
Roberto Stassi and 6 co-authors design a chain of linked qubits whose joint state lasts longer. Their 2025 theory paper deals with a core hurdle for quantum computers: qubits lose their state too fast. The chain uses super-strong links that swap between two types along its length.

The two lowest states of the chain act as one logical qubit. Its loss rates beat those of a lone qubit, and one loss rate can fall to zero as links grow or the chain lengthens. Gates on one or two such qubits also run with high truth scores. The design is a theory plan, not yet a built device.
arxiv-2509-18003:
Wave checks stay bounded on all scales for a perturbed fractional operator, in a 2025 paper by M Burak Erdogan, Michael Goldberg, and William Green. The trio study the same class of operator as in their companion work: a fractional Schroedinger operator with a real bump term. Here the ask is how wave operators act on scale spaces.

Under terms on the bump that rest on dim and power, the wave maps extend to bounded maps on every such space. From that fact, spread and mixed space-time bounds follow for the perturbed operator. The result mirrors what holds when the power is a whole number.
arxiv-2509-18303:
Ozgur Can Seckin and 3 co-authors hunt posts that spark hot debate yet stay civil. Their 2025 paper deals with a gap in social feeds: bridging posts that join opposed views are rare, while toxic rows are common. The team says curation could lift such posts if a clear trait marked them.

Two traits define their target: how controversial a post is, and how well it resists toxic replies. Models built to score both traits reach high accuracy. Resilient posts are not the same as low-toxicity ones. Political posts draw heat, yet some stay resilient, and they tend to use polite cues such as thanks and hedges.
arxiv-2509-18503:
A companion too heavy for a planet but perhaps too light for a star blurs a key boundary in astronomy. Md Redyan Ahmed and 16 co-authors present TOI-2155 b, a transiting companion found by a NASA survey satellite. Their 2025 paper confirms it with ground-based velocity measures and follow-up light data from several observatories. The companion circles its star in under four days.

Its size is about that of Jupiter, but its mass is about eighty times Jupiter's. That gives it a very high density. Its host is a hot, slightly evolved star, larger and heavier than the Sun. The companion's mass sits near the minimum needed to burn hydrogen. So it may be a massive brown dwarf or a very low-mass star. The authors offer it as a benchmark for models of that borderline zone.
arxiv-2509-18703:
Pesticides must kill pests without undue harm to bees and other wildlife. Jakub Adamczyk reports on graph machine learning for safer pesticide design in this 2025 paper. The work borrows the in-silico playbook of drug discovery, where computer screening guides lab work. Its focus is ecotoxicology, above all harm to honey bees.

A first contribution is ApisTox, described as the largest curated data set on pesticide toxicity to honey bees. The study then benchmarks many model types: fingerprints, graph kernels, graph networks, and pre-trained transformers. Methods that shine in drug research often failed to carry over to farm chemicals. That gap, the author argues, calls for domain-specific models and benchmarks. Next, the author plans a full benchmarking suite and models shaped for pesticide discovery. The paper reads as a research report with a forward plan.
arxiv-2509-18903:
Can a person fall into a black hole that sits inside an expanding universe, and live to tell it? Brien C. Nolan, writing alone, takes up the McVittie spacetime, a model that joins a black hole with a universe filled with a perfect fluid. The fluid itself drifts outward and escapes, but Nolan asks what happens to a free-falling test body.

He proves that such a body can reach the black hole horizon in a finite amount of its own time. With a positive cosmological constant, all the curvature measures he checks stay finite on the way in. With none, some second-order curvature terms blow up at the horizon. That split leaves open whether a real, extended body could survive the crossing.
arxiv-2509-19103:
E. Castillo-Ruiz and two co-authors generalize a classic formula that links a particle's electric charge to its weak isospin and hypercharge. That formula, tied to the names Gell-Mann and Nishijima, sits at the heart of the standard model. Their version is built for bookkeeping in model building, where particles can sit in large, exotic multiplets of gauge groups. The method uses indices on tensors rather than case-by-case tables.

Starting from how the Cartan generators, the diagonal members of the group algebra, act on tensor products, they use the fact that weights simply add. The result is a compact operator that hands out charges for tensors of mixed type in any dimension. They work through examples for the groups SU(2), SU(3), and SU(5). The tool should speed up charge assignment in new model proposals.
arxiv-2509-19303: Béla Bajnok, writing alone, presents the problems and solutions of the 63rd Annual International Mathematical Olympiad. The report collects that year's contest questions. It pairs each question with a worked solution. Nothing more is claimed in the source. Readers get the full problem set of that Olympiad in one place. Such reports serve students who train for math contests. They also serve teachers who set hard problem-solving work.
arxiv-2509-19403:
Brain-computer interfaces read EEG signals to let people control devices by thought, but every brain differs, so systems usually need slow calibration for each new user. Sheng-Bin Duan and seven co-authors propose an online adaptation algorithm that adjusts to unseen users as it runs. Alignment happens in two stages: first the raw EEG data are aligned in their own space, then normalization statistics are updated in the model's representation space. A self-supervised loss steers updates.

That loss uses the decoder's own soft guesses as stand-ins for the unknown truth, weighted by their entropy so confident guesses count more. Across five public datasets and seven decoders, the method plugged in cleanly. Updating from a single trial at a time, it raised accuracy by about five points on steady-state visual tasks and about four on motor imagery. Fast, calibration-light operation is the goal.
arxiv-2509-20303:
Cells crawl toward chemical signals by pushing out actin-filled protrusions, and Samuel Johnson and three co-authors model that motion in a 2025 arXiv paper. The protrusions also help the cell sense the gradient it follows. Experiments show protrusion patterns change with conditions, but the governing principles stayed unclear. The authors treat protrusion growth as an energy problem.

Their model assumes cells balance two things: sensing quality and the energetic cost of building each protrusion. Built on energy minimization, the model reproduces observed protrusion patterns across several biological systems and environments. That match suggests energetic efficiency may shape how motile cells look and move. The model also predicts responses to conditions no experiment has tried yet. Those predictions give future experiments clear targets for testing the idea.
arxiv-2509-20503:
Attention layers compare every element of a sequence with every other, so their cost grows quadratically. Evgenii Egorov and three co-authors propose a structured alternative called Myosotis in a 2025 arXiv paper. Existing escapes either drop most comparisons through sparsity or force the sequence through a recurrent state model. Each escape gives something up. The authors aim to keep the advantages of both.

Their algorithm rests on the efficient inversion of tree-structured matrices. That structure lets pairwise interactions be handled without materializing the full quadratic cost. The design targets the same sequence-to-sequence role that attention plays inside modern networks. The paper is brief and presents the algorithm as a foundation. Efficiency claims are framed at the level of the method's design, awaiting the fuller benchmarking the authors leave open.
arxiv-2509-20703:
Teaching a robot by showing it a human video sounds easy, but robot bodies differ from human hands. Xiaoxiang Dong, Matthew Johnson-Roberson, and Weiming Zhi tackle that gap in a 2025 paper on learning from demonstration. Their framework is called Joint Flow Trajectory Optimization, or JFTO.

Instead of copying hand motion directly, JFTO treats the video as a guide for the object being moved. It balances three goals at once. It picks a grasp pose the robot can actually reach. It shapes the object path to match the shown motion. It also keeps the motion collision-free within the robot's joint limits. The approach handles the fact that one demonstration can allow several valid robot motions.
arxiv-2509-20903:
Overlapping labels on a map, or clashing jobs on a schedule, can be fixed by moving things apart. Nicolas Honorato-Droguett and four co-authors study that dispersion problem as graph editing in a 2025 paper. Objects become nodes, overlaps become edges, and moving objects costs distance.

The team continues work on the geometric graph edit distance problem. They give an efficient algorithm that makes the intersection graph of unit circular arcs both edgeless and free of large cliques. The running time grows almost linearly with the number of arcs. The same algorithm solves related variants. Their results sharpen what is known about rendering geometric intersection graphs sparse by moving objects as little as possible.
arxiv-2509-21003:
Damaged speech may arrive at one sampling rate and need repair at another. Ui-Hyeop Shin and three co-authors build a restoration model for that mismatch in a 2025 paper accepted for ICML 2026. Their framework is called TF-Restormer.

They name the setting extended sampling-frequency-independent restoration, where input and output rates are decoupled. Older methods assume matched rates and waste effort on resampling. TF-Restormer encodes only the observed input band. Extension queries, handled by band-partitioned cross-attention, synthesize the missing high-frequency band. The asymmetric design spends computation where information is missing instead of reprocessing everything. Speech restoration covers noise, reverberation, and bandwidth loss, and the model aims to handle all of them natively at varied rates.
arxiv-2509-21103:
X-ray pulsars flare in episodes, and the brightest flares seem tied to how fast the neutron star spins. Shan-Shan Weng and eight co-authors test that link statistically in a 2025 astrophysics paper. These systems pair a magnetized neutron star with a donor star, usually a Be star.

Using long-term X-ray monitoring data, the authors correlate spin periods with outburst properties for type II outbursts. They report strong correlations for the first time: faster-rotating neutron stars show more violent eruptions. The same relationship shows up in pulsating ultraluminous X-ray sources in nearby galaxies. Most of these systems sit close to spin equilibrium, the authors show. The pattern links accretion physics across ordinary pulsars and the most extreme accretors known.
arxiv-2509-21203:
Sofia V. Sosa Fiscella leads a large team of pulsar researchers in a 2025 data paper. The work uses the NANOGrav fifteen year data set. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose pulses arrive with great regularity. Timing those pulses well needs exact maps of where each pulsar sits in the sky.

The team uses positions from very long baseline radio work as prior guides in the timing fit. They first align the radio frame and the timing frame. Then they blend both sources to get a best position for each pulsar. Wrong positions can soak up slow noise and hide faint signals, such as waves from space. Cleaner positions should sharpen the search for those signals.
arxiv-2509-21403:
Proposals to use language models as experimental designers face a direct test in a 2025 paper by Rushil Gupta and 2 co-authors. The tasks come from genetic perturbation and molecular property discovery. Both open and closed instruction tuned models were evaluated as design agents. Claims of in context experimental design motivated the study. Feedback sensitivity is the key property under test.

Replacing true outcomes with randomly permuted labels did not change agent performance. That shows the agents ignored experimental feedback. Classical methods, such as linear bandits and Gaussian process optimization, beat the language model agents across benchmarks. The authors propose a hybrid that pairs language model prior knowledge with nearest neighbour sampling. Their hybrid matched or beat rivals without much in context adaptation.
arxiv-2509-21803:
Francisco Arana-Herrera, Jayadev Athreya, and Giovanni Forni study a family of flows in dynamical systems in this 2025 mathematics paper. The flows live on circle bundles that sit over translation surfaces, flat surfaces built from polygons. They arise through a process called prequantization and extend a classic family known as Heisenberg nilflows to more general base surfaces.

These flows are basic examples of parabolic systems, which mix slowly and have a strong central direction. The authors prove the flows are relatively mixing: correlations fade away once the part that stays fixed along the fibers is set aside. They then draw out what this means for the dynamics of the flows. Further uses reach the theory of wave functions on the same spaces, and, through surface-of-section methods, skew products built over interval exchange maps.
arxiv-2509-22003:
Kshitij Sinha, writing alone, studies how fast a smoothing process takes over in equations with a repeating microscopic pattern. The 2025 paper treats parabolic equations, which describe diffusion-like change over time, with two large extra terms: a drift and a potential. Homogenization replaces the rapidly varying equation by an averaged one, and the quantitative question is how fast the two solutions merge as the pattern shrinks.

Sinha shows the solution splits into a product of three parts. One part depends only on time. Another is the ground state of an exponential eigenvalue problem posed on a single pattern cell. The third solves an averaged equation whose effective drift is zero. For that last part, the paper derives rates of convergence in the energy norm as the pattern scale goes to zero. The result clarifies how strong drift and potential terms shape the averaged behavior of such equations.
arxiv-2509-22403:
Fanjin Meng and 5 co-authors give movement models a sense of meaning, not just of place and time. Models of human mobility predict trips well but hit a ceiling from data scale and weak semantics. Language models reason well yet lack a feel for real travel patterns. Their framework, MoveFM-R, joins the two strengths.

Three parts do the joining. A location code carries meaning a language model can read. A staged training plan aligns the language model with mobility patterns step by step. A self-check step then shapes trips that fit a text request. Tests beat prior models and held up on new places with no retraining data.
arxiv-2509-22603:
Rakesh Thakur and 4 co-authors model how opinions shift during deliberation. Group discussion weighs many views before a decision, and language tools can now track those shifts. The team collected opinions from people of varied backgrounds into their own data set. They simulated deliberation with product presentations laced with striking facts, which often moved audience views in measurable ways.

Two models were compared against prior state-of-the-art systems. One modulates discourse by word frequency; the other uses a quantum deep learning framework. Both beat the existing models in their tests. The authors point to uses in policy-making, debate scoring, decision support, and opinion mining on social media.
arxiv-2509-22703:
Srikant Panda, Amit Agarwal, and Hitesh Laxmichand Patel benchmark disability bias across twenty-one language models. Their benchmark, AccessEval, spans six real-world domains and nine disability types. Each query comes in two forms: a neutral version and a disability-aware version. Outputs are scored for sentiment, social perception, and factual accuracy.

Responses to disability-aware queries skewed more negative in tone. They also showed more stereotyping and more factual errors than neutral replies. The gaps varied by domain and disability type. Hearing, speech, and mobility disabilities were hit hardest. The authors argue these patterns reflect ableism in model behavior with tangible harms for disabled users. The data set is public.
arxiv-2509-22803:
William W. Meynardie and 12 co-authors test whether a distant companion world formed like a star or like a planet. Ross 458c orbits its host binary at over a thousand astronomical units, among the widest low-mass companions known. If its makeup matches its host star, it likely condensed from the same cloud. Heavy-element enrichment would instead point to disk formation and later migration. The team took high-resolution near-infrared spectra with the James Webb Space Telescope.

They fit the spectra with three model grids and with atmospheric retrievals. The grids prefer a metal-enriched atmosphere, while retrievals give a host-like metal content within uncertainty. The split verdict also tests how far grid fitting and retrievals can be trusted for directly imaged companions.
arxiv-2509-23103:
Multiplications dominate the energy bill of neural networks on small edge devices. Emadeldeen Hamdan and Ahmet Enis Cetin cut them with Hadamard transforms plus in-memory computing. Their HTMA-Net swaps some middle convolutions for hybrid transform layers. Inside those layers, convolutions run as multiplication-avoiding operations in SRAM. Prior work hit only convolutions or only the memory side.

Tests used ResNet models on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. The design removed up to fifty-two percent of multiplications. Accuracy stayed comparable to baseline models. Parameter counts and compute load both fell. The pair see structured transforms plus in-memory math as a strong path for edge AI.
arxiv-2509-23503:
Corrosion models come in local and nonlocal families that rarely speak to each other. Christian J. Cyron and 5 co-authors extend the Kim-Kim-Suzuki phase-field corrosion model so that it bridges the two. Gradient terms give way to integral terms over a finite reach, which adds a built-in length scale like the one in peridynamics. A nonlocal free energy combines the usual bulk term with this interaction term.

From it the team derives nonlocal versions of the Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard equations. They prove the equations are well-posed and that the model settles to the classic local one as the reach shrinks to zero. Numerical tests confirm the predicted convergence and show what the nonlocal term changes.
arxiv-2509-23803:
Running federated learning across hospitals is as much an operations problem as a modeling one. Pramit Saha and 4 co-authors introduce FedAgentBench, a benchmark for LLM agents that would run that operation on their own. Client agents at hospitals and a server agent handle client choice, coordination, data preparation, label harmonization, and algorithm selection. The framework covers forty federated algorithms matched to task and data traits.

The test suite spans more than two hundred curated data sets across six imaging types, from MRI to histopathology. Twenty-four models were assessed. Strong cores like GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek V3 automated many stages, but tangled tasks with implicit goals still defeated even the best.
arxiv-2509-24003:
A semigroup representation on a Banach space splits into a part that cycles back and a part that fades. Micky Barthmann and 2 co-authors develop the Jacobs-de Leeuw-Glicksberg decomposition for a broad class of such representations. The reversible part turns out to match a unitary representation on a Hilbert space, itself a direct sum of finite-dimensional pieces. The almost weakly stable part is characterized through the unique invariant mean on weakly almost periodic functions.

For bi-amenable measured semigroups, Følner averages give further characterizations. An ultrafilter description yields the projection onto the reversible part, with combinatorial consequences. Examples probe the sharpness of the results, several of which extend known facts to nonseparable spaces.
arxiv-2510-00103:
Alberto Torralba and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 astronomy paper on a class of objects called Little Red Dots. These compact red sources may mark a key phase in the growth of giant black holes. The team studied one bright example with deep spectra from the James Webb Space Telescope. They wanted to learn what kind of gas surrounds such an object.

The spectra revealed a forest of faint iron lines coming from a warm, dense outer layer. That same layer scatters hydrogen light and gives the broad hydrogen lines their wide wings. The layer is mostly opaque to hydrogen light, which shapes the object's sharp Balmer break. A simple glowing-slab model matches much of the spectrum well. The picture that emerges is of a black hole wrapped in a warm cocoon of excited gas.
arxiv-2510-00203:
Robert Hayek, Joaquin Chung, and Rajkumar Kettimuthu wrote this 2025 review paper on software for quantum networks. Quantum networks promise secure communication, distributed sensing, and linked quantum computers. Moving from lab demos to dependable service takes software matched to quantum hardware's odd constraints. The authors survey what exists for designing such networks and for running them.

The review organizes tools into three planes: infrastructure, logical, and control or service. Design simulators such as SeQUeNCe, QuISP, and NetSquid get detailed coverage. Operating functions, from entanglement handling to resource management, are sorted into a proposed taxonomy. A stubborn gap separates protocol papers from working simulator or testbed code. The gap is worst for changing topologies and day-to-day network management. The authors close with open challenges and a roadmap toward large hybrid quantum networks.
arxiv-2510-00403:
Huan Yu, Qi Xia, and Jun Fang published this 2025 astrophysics paper simulating particle acceleration at relativistic shocks. Their plasma mixes electrons and positrons with a small share of protons, about five percent by number. Particle-in-cell simulations follow the shock that forms when this flow reflects off a wall. Such shocks power the glowing jets and bursts seen across the universe.

Downstream, positrons reached energies comparable to the protons themselves. Their spectrum grew a hard nonthermal tail, while electrons stayed stuck at lower energies. The authors blame waves driven by the protons, whose polarization favors positron acceleration. Density and magnetic field behind the shock fluctuated strongly in the runs. The lesson is that a pinch of protons reshapes who gets accelerated in pair plasmas. That composition effect should inform models of pulsar wind nebulae and gamma-ray bursts.
arxiv-2510-00703:
Bussolan and six co-authors release MultiPhysio-HRC in this 2025 arXiv paper, a multimodal dataset of physiology recorded during industrial human-robot collaboration. Robots that share factory work should sense stress and cognitive load so they can adapt, yet training such perception needs labelled data. Volunteers performed controlled cognitive tasks, virtual reality experiences, and industrial disassembly work, both manually and with robotic assistance. Sensors captured brain, heart, skin, breathing, and muscle signals.

The release includes voice recordings and facial action units, which widen the signal mix beyond body sensors. Validated psychological questionnaires supplied ground-truth labels for the participants' mental states. Baseline models for stress and cognitive load classification showed the signals carry information, though accuracy stayed hard to push high. The authors argue that gap invites better multimodal fusion methods. The dataset is public, aimed at affective computing and safer, human-aware factory robots.
arxiv-2510-01203:
Kadiyala and Mirzaeinia forecast minute-by-minute stock prices by blending market data with news sentiment scored by ten different language models. Short-term prices whip around on headlines, so raw price history alone misses the story. The team aligned a month of Apple news articles with one-minute trading data.

Each article received sentiment scores from every model, later merged with prices and technical indicators. Two modern architectures, Mamba and Reformer, trained on the enriched stream. Mamba predicted more accurately and ran faster across the sentiment sources. Pairing it with the strongest sentiment models sharpened short-term adaptability most. Ten sentiment judges disagree, and that disagreement itself carries signal. Hyperparameters were tuned systematically rather than guessed. A three-day evaluation window tested the freshest behavior. Lower error and higher speed rarely arrive together. Minute-level trading is the harshest classroom for forecasters of all kinds.
arxiv-2510-01303:
Sonthalia, Murray, and Montúfar explain why the gradients that train small neural networks are simpler than they look. Learning theory usually assumes tidy, isotropic data, which real datasets violate cheerfully. The team studies two-layer networks under a spiked, anisotropic data model instead.

The input-weight gradient turns out to be approximately low rank in both major scaling regimes. Two rank-one components dominate, one tracking the bulk data and one tracking the spike. Data properties, scaling, and activation choice set the balance between them. Common regularizers, from weight decay to Jacobian penalties, tune the components selectively. Mean-field and neural-tangent scalings both obey the same low-rank story. Input noise joins the list of knobs that modulate the balance. Synthetic and real data both confirmed the theoretical split. Feature learning gains a concrete mechanism from the decomposition. Two terms carry the gradient.
arxiv-2510-01403:
Nyland and co-authors image a tiny double-lobed radio source that a piggyback survey noticed flickering at low frequency. The instrument collects data during other astronomers' observations, turning spare capacity into a transient watch. One source varied by about a fifth over roughly a year, earning closer inspection.

Very-long-baseline imaging resolved two lobes spanning only tens of parsecs, a compact symmetric object. Its spectrum peaks in the hundreds of megahertz under either of two standard absorption models. Variable boosting by relativistic motion was ruled out as the flicker's cause. Interstellar scintillation and intrinsic changes remain the live explanations. Three hundred forty megahertz is the survey's home frequency. Photometric redshift places the source deep in the distant universe. Free-free and synchrotron self-absorption both fit the turnover. Milliarcsecond scales are where the double structure lives. Commensal observing turns idle antennas into discovery machines.
arxiv-2510-01503:
Evans and Norris couple the geometry of an irradiated surface to where the ions actually deposit their energy, inside continuum models of nanopattern formation. Ion bombardment sculpts astonishingly regular ripples on semiconductors, yet no unified model explains every detail. The collision cascade matters twice: it moves material quickly, and it creates defects enabling slow viscous flow.

Their asymptotic approximations track the deposition profile and the buried amorphous boundary together. Predictions for ripple wavelength, onset angle, and roughening prove surprisingly sensitive to coupling details. Both the early linear and later nonlinear growth regimes receive matched approximations. Surface amplitude and slope define the two regimes being bridged. The amorphous layer's thickness mediates the viscous response. Sputtering handles the fast transport the cascade initiates. Patterning onset angle is exquisitely sensitive to deposition shape. Details of coupling stop being details at all.
arxiv-2510-01803:
Stival and five co-authors study how Italians judge their environment's effect on health in this 2025 statistics paper. Their data come from PASSI, Italy's nationwide health surveillance system. Survey answers are merged with town-level data on income, pollution, and geography. The team models which personal and local factors push perceptions toward positive or neutral views.

Their tool is a penalized ordered regression model with partly parallel effects. It lets some factors act uniformly across response levels while others vary, and it regularizes unstable estimates.
