Yelyzaveta Satynska and Daniel T. Robb revisit how dynamic phase transitions are described in a standard mean-field model of a magnet driven by a repeating field. Earlier accounts used one order parameter and one companion field, but the authors argue both choices were too narrow for the model's actual behavior.

Careful numerical integration and wave-by-wave analysis show that the true companion field is the whole even part of the applied field, not a single number. Below the critical driving period, the order measure grows with the square-root scaling expected from earlier work across many wave modes. Exactly at the critical period, small even additions produce a distinct cube-root response, with even and odd modes following different but consistent rules that persist in extended versions of the model.
arxiv-2510-21903:
Xuhui Zhou and five co-authors pair a coding agent with a second agent. The co-authors are Valerie Chen, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Graham Neubig, Maarten Sap, and Xingyao Wang. The second agent has one job: understanding the user. Coding agents can plan, edit, run, and test large codebases. Yet they often misread what a person wants. Instructions can be vague or depend on past exchanges.

The partner agent practices a simple theory of mind. It infers goals, constraints, and preferences. It keeps a lasting memory of the user. It then feeds suggestions to the worker agent. On two benchmarks, the duo raised task success and user satisfaction. One benchmark used ambiguous tasks. The other used a simulated user with past interactions. That stateful test showed the largest gap over a leading single-agent system. Memory of the person, not just the code, got the credit.
arxiv-2510-22003:
Stefan Julian Kooy, Jean Paul Sebastian Piest, and Rob Henk Bemthuis review what generative AI is doing to enterprise architects, the specialists who keep a company's systems coherent, inside agile software organizations. Evidence was scattered across many small reports, so the team ran a systematic review following standard protocols.

From nearly seventeen hundred records they kept thirty-three studies spanning enterprise, solution, domain, business, and IT architecture roles. The clearest benefits were faster idea generation and trade-off exploration, quick drafting of artifacts such as code, models, and documents, and help with decisions and knowledge lookup. Risks included hidden bias, plausible but wrong output that caused rework, privacy and compliance worries, and people leaning on the tool too much. The review maps uses and risks and names the new skills architects now need.
arxiv-2510-22103:
Michael Carrion, Melissa M. Fuentes, Zaphenath Joseph, and Alexander Nappo revisit a classic question about families that all overlap. The Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem caps the size of a family of same-sized subsets that pairwise share an element. The team asks the analogous question for independent sets inside pendant graphs, networks made by hanging a clique of chosen size off every vertex of a base graph.

They give a fresh, purely combinatorial proof, using shifting and shadow arguments, that the pendant complete graph meets the bound whenever the base is at least twice the set size. Strictly so beyond that, then extend the result to pendants whose attached cliques vary in size. For pendant paths the story flips: careful constructions show the property fails in several ranges. The paper maps where the classical behavior survives decoration and where it breaks.
arxiv-2510-22403:
Camryn L Phillips leads seventeen co-authors in reporting spectra of quasar host galaxies seen with the James Webb Space Telescope. The twelve quasars sit at redshifts just above six, when the universe was young. The team models and subtracts each bright quasar so that only the fainter extended galaxy light remains in the spectra.

Ten of the twelve systems show extended line emission and five show extended starlight. One galaxy shows an outflow and another shows orderly rotation, while star formation rates in several hosts match normal galaxies of that era. Line ratios also suggest active nucleus style ionisation.
arxiv-2510-22503:
Searching for new materials means balancing many goals that often pull in opposite directions. Nikhil Abhyankar, Sanchit Kabra, Saaketh Desai, and Chandan K Reddy present LLEMA in 2025, a system that pairs large language models with evolutionary search for multi objective materials discovery.

At each round, the language model proposes crystal candidates under clear property limits. A fast stand in model estimates their traits, and a scorer keeps success and failure memories to guide later rounds. Across fourteen tasks spanning electronics, energy, coatings, optics, and aerospace, LLEMA finds plausible, stable candidates more often than rival approaches, with better trade off fronts.
arxiv-2510-22603:
Some tokens inside a language model attract far too much attention and trigger huge internal activations. Anand, Umberto Cappellazzo, Stavros Petridis, and Maja Pantic study those attention sinks in 2025, in models that recognize speech from audio, lip movement, or both together.

Sinks appear not only at the first token but also at weak meaning tokens in the middle of sequences. The huge activations start in specific internal layers and share the same feature slots across sink tokens. A simple decorrelation loss, which pushes token patterns apart, reduces the effect. It also lowers word error rates in the harder noise condition tested.
arxiv-2510-22803:
Doctors need clear reasons before they trust AI answers. Hai-Dang Nguyen, Minh-Anh Dang, Minh-Tan Le, and Minh-Tuan Le address that need in 2025. Their system is called MedXplain-VQA. It answers questions about medical images. Five explainable parts work together in the frame.

A tuned BLIP-2 model forms the backbone. Query reformulation sharpens each question. Better attention maps highlight key regions. A language model then gives structured reasoning steps. The team built a clinical scoring frame. It checks terminology, structure, and attention relevance. On five hundred pathology samples, scores rose a lot over baselines. Each case flagged three to five key regions.
arxiv-2510-22903:
Low dose radiation seems to help a joint disease called osteoarthritis. The reason for that help is not yet clear. Diana Shvydka and Victor Karpov wrote a 2025 paper with a proposed cause. Radiation may speed up how molecules move in cartilage. Faster movement could help cartilage heal itself.

The pair give numbers for how large that speed up could be. A linked effect is a build up of electric charge. That charge could favor one type of molecule over the next. In turn, dose plans could be tuned to that aim. The authors call for more tests in the lab and in clinics. They urge a curative aim, not just relief of pain. Sports medicine could gain from this work too.
arxiv-2510-23003:
ZhengKai Huang, YiKun Wang, ChenYu Hui, and XiaoCheng present a smart irrigation system built to save water on real farms. Uneven ground and wasteful watering hurt precision farming. Their system fuses several sensors with computer vision and robotic control to aim water where plants need it.

A light YOLO model on a small vision chip spots plant containers in real time with accuracy above ninety six percent across lighting. A simplified hand-eye method guides the robot arm that carries the camera. Together the parts promise steadier watering with less waste, tested as a working system rather than a concept alone.
arxiv-2510-23103:
B Molina leads a team of twenty six astronomers hunting for pairs of supermassive black holes hidden in blazars. Two long radio programs together give light curves of about forty six to fifty years for 83 bright, fast-flaring blazars. Such a long record is ideal for spotting slow periodic swings that a black hole pair would cause.

The team tested for periodicity with Lomb-Scargle, wavelet, and sine-fitting methods, and used simulations to judge false alarms. Confirmed candidates would be prime targets for gravitational wave follow-up. Even null results from this sample set useful limits on how common close pairs are.
arxiv-2510-23203:
Lukas Bierling, Davide Pasero, Fleur Dolmans, Helia Ghasemi, and Angelo Broere introduce DecoDINO for predicting where a human body touches objects in a scene, vertex by vertex. Accurate contact maps support human-object interaction models for robotics, augmented reality, and behavior simulation. The earlier DECO estimator gave only binary contact and struggled with soft surfaces, occlusion, children, and false foot contacts.

DecoDINO uses three branches with two large DINOv2 encoders, balanced loss weighting, and patch-level cross-attention. It adds semantic classification of contact, not just yes or no. Finer contact knowledge should make virtual humans and robots interact more believably.
arxiv-2510-23403:
Ş. Ekmen and H. Lee test, in a 2025 study, a newer way to capture a full sound field, called the Spherical Wavelet Framework. The framework blends Ambisonics, which encodes sound from all directions, with object-based audio, which treats each sound as a separate item. Its basis functions stay tightly local, so the field can be stored with few numbers.

Earlier checks used narrow tests with no perceptual measures, so the pair ran a wider comparison. They used hearing measures and listening tests with realistic sources. Several sphere layouts were tried, each with matching Ambisonics orders and channel counts. Listeners rated the framework much closer to the reference than Ambisonics, in both space and tone. The gain depends heavily on how the sphere is divided. The method also cannot place a wave from an exact in-between direction on its own, and the authors suggest fixes.
arxiv-2510-23503:
Fatemeh Zahra Safaeipour, Jacob Chakareski, and Morteza Hashemi tackle a squeeze faced by mobile devices such as augmented and virtual reality headsets. These gadgets must run neural network tasks fast, yet they carry little computing power and small batteries. Their study examines split inference, where part of a task runs on the device and the rest on a nearby edge server over a wireless link.

Their method, called Bayes-Split-Edge, uses Bayesian optimization to pick both the sending power and the split point of the network. A new scoring rule weighs task quality, few test runs, and penalties for breaking energy or delay limits. Tests on image models and real wireless channel data cut evaluation cost by up to 2.4 times compared with standard Bayesian optimization, while needing at most twenty trial runs.
arxiv-2510-23703:
Gino Isidori and three co-authors explore the neutrino side of flavor deconstruction, a framework that builds the pattern of fermion masses by breaking flavor symmetry in steps. With an inverse-seesaw mechanism added, the setup ties the steep hierarchy of charged-fermion masses to the anarchic, patternless mixing seen among light neutrinos. The question is what parameter space survives today's data and what experiments can see next.

Fitting oscillation data first, the authors map the allowed region and study heavy neutral leptons, hypothetical heavier neutrino partners. They also examine lepton-flavor-violating decays, rare processes that would signal new physics. Current searches already push the right-handed neutrino scale to a few trillion electronvolts, and planned muon-to-electron experiments will probe most of the remaining region. Among model variants, two gauge group choices allow the lowest deconstruction scale, making them the most exposed to near-term tests.
arxiv-2510-23803:
Christopher W. Churchill presents the second paper in a two-part series building mathematical models of the circumgalactic medium, the gas halo around a galaxy. The goal is to synthesize quasar absorption line profiles from tidy spatial-kinematic models of a galaxy and its gas structures. Paper one set up the geometry and three-dimensional velocity fields for the disk, halo, wind, and accretion parts.

Here Churchill adds the physics that fills those structures with gas. The formalism distributes multiphase gas, ionized by starlight or by collisions, through each component, then generates hydrogen and metal absorption profiles for any viewing angle and sight line. Worked examples through a reference galaxy model show the machinery in action. The models are built to be bent and extended, for fitting real systems, testing rival pictures of the gas cycle, or teaching. A graphical interface for the models is in early development.
arxiv-2510-24103:
Kang Zhang and five co-authors present MGAudio, a system that makes sound for open domain video. The task is to create audio that fits what is seen, with good timing and realistic quality. Older methods lean on outside guidance during generation, which can limit how well sight and sound line up.

MGAudio uses a flow based transformer model that learns to guide itself through a special training goal. Its audio visual encoder both conditions the generation and aligns features across sight and sound. On the VGGSound benchmark, the system reached a top score, cutting the main error measure to a low value and beating prior best results by a wide margin.
arxiv-2510-24203:
Lukas Bartl and two co-authors extend a fault tolerant version of multiparty session types with a new kind of global escape loop. Session types describe communication protocols in abstract form and can verify traits like progress, meaning no deadlock. Distributed algorithms often look like such protocols, but proving they terminate can be elaborate work.

Since distributed systems are built to cope with faults like crashes and unreliable links, the base system already models failure patterns. The new escape loops let a protocol leave a loop in a coordinated global way. The extension aims to bring session type verification closer to real distributed algorithms that must keep progressing despite failures.
arxiv-2510-24403:
Matteo Giordano comments on a claim about chiral symmetry in hot quantum chromodynamics, working alone. Aoki, Fukaya, and Taniguchi had argued for a strong result. They claimed the Dirac spectrum at zero and a key susceptibility must both vanish for small quark mass. That claim held in the symmetric phase, under some technical terms. Giordano argues that one key step in their proof is not justified.

He concludes the claims should be reassessed. In an added note, he answers objections from Aoki and Fukaya. He shows that the analyticity term they invoke against him does not hold up. He also shows their claim that his arguments break down is wrong. The note is part of a live debate on the axial anomaly at high heat.
arxiv-2510-24803:
Milad Yazdani, Mahdi Mostajabdaveh, Zirui Zhou, and Ying Xiong score the mid steps of a team of AI agents as they work. Search over such teams wastes compute when it can not tell which agent's note moved the task on. Their scorer, MASPRM, grades the full routed chain of notes in order.

It was trained on team search roll outs marked just by end wins, with no human marks on mid steps. The scorer then steers two search styles at run time. On math, fact, and logic sets, it beat a like sized end score tool by a clear gap. Rank of good chains rose too, most where step search used mid marks.
arxiv-2510-25003:
Gian Marco Orlando, Jinyi Ye, Valerio La Gatta, Mahdi Saeedi, Vincenzo Moscato, Emilio Ferrara, and Luca Luceri study how AI agents may team up in fake sway campaigns on social sites. Such campaigns, run to shift public views, were once hand led and hand made. Agent AI could make them more auto, more quick to adapt, and more hard to spot.

In a fake world, they set sway agents and plain user agents side by side, in modes from loose goal match to joint picks. As modes grew more set, sway webs grew dense and tight knit. Posts grew more alike, boosts fired more in sync, and shared posts grew. The work is a first map of that risk.
arxiv-2510-25103:
Minghai Lu, Zhe Zhou, Danning Xie, Songlin Jia, Benjamin Delaware, and Tianyi Zhang build Adapt, a frame that fixes failed math proofs by pick of the right fix plan for each flaw. Proof tools give strong checks of code truth, but proofs take much hand work. Chat models can draft proofs, yet first drafts are most oft wrong, and one fixed fix path fits all drafts poor.

Adapt lets a chat model read the proof tool's state and the wrong draft, then pick which fix plan to run. On two bench sets, it proved far more claims than the best past ways. The gain came from match of plan to flaw, not more brute tries.
arxiv-2510-25203:
Y Balaji leads a team with nine co-authors who made and tested Josephson links from hafnium, a low heat metal, for use as fine particle ears. Such links are known from quantum bits, but small gap stuffs could catch far more weak hits: lone waves at the terahertz scale and lone sound bits. Those hits are sought in dark matter and sky work.

Their links put a thin oxide skin between two hafnium films. Form and chem reads showed clean films and sharp oxide walls. Flow tests at room and cold heats showed clear Josephson acts, from which the gap and key marks were drawn. This is the first full such study.
arxiv-2510-25603: Matthew Bradshaw, Titus de Jong, and Wencai Liu wrote with Audrey Wang, Xueyin Wang, and Bingheng Yang. Their 2025 paper bounds quantum changes for quasi-periodic Schroedinger operators. The frequencies are Liouville in type. Their method mixes semi-algebraic discrepancy values for Kronecker sequences. Quantitative Green function values are adapted to that setting. The paper is short and specialized.
arxiv-2510-25903:
Vishnu Kumar, Nishta Arora, Bhargavi B. A., Akshay Naik, and Saurabh A. Chandorkar study paired vibrating beams that can amplify one shared motion while leaving another alone. The device is a double ended tuning fork resonator, two beams joined by a coupling beam, driven by electric forces. Parametric driving, where a property is varied in rhythm, can boost a vibration if timed well.

Kumar and the team find the out of phase mode, where beams move in opposite senses, shows strong nonlinear response and gain, while the in phase mode stays mostly linear. Driving through the coupling spring lets them select the mode and tune gain up or down by phase. The gain reached about thirteen decibels, which suits signal and logic uses.
arxiv-2510-26003:
Eirini Poimenidou and K. A. Draziotis present an attack that can recover a secret message from the NTRU-HPS cryptosystem when part of the message is already known. NTRU is a lattice based encryption scheme designed to resist quantum attacks. Their attack assumes a fraction of the message and nonce coefficients, each drawn from minus one, zero, and one, are known at random positions in advance.

Poimenidou and Draziotis turn decryption into a modular knapsack problem, a packing puzzle with a remainder condition, then encode it as a short vector search in a lattice. A lattice reduction tool recovered the message in practice when the known fraction was near forty five percent, within minutes on a desktop in their tests.
arxiv-2510-26103:
Maximilian Schreiber and Pascal Tippe measure how often AI generated code in public repositories carries known security flaws. They collected seven thousand seven hundred three files on GitHub that are explicitly attributed to four AI tools, with ChatGPT accounting for over ninety percent. Using CodeQL static analysis, a tool that scans code for weakness patterns, they found four thousand two hundred forty one weakness instances across seventy seven types.

About eighty eight percent of files had no mapped weakness, but clear patterns emerged. Python files showed higher weakness rates than JavaScript and TypeScript files across all tools, and tool rankings differed by language. The authors also note that a large share of collected files were documentation, an underexplored use of the tools.
arxiv-2510-26303:
Beomhan Baek, Minhak Song, and Chulhee Yun study the hidden bias of the Adam optimizer when it is fed one sample at a time. Adam is the default training optimizer in deep learning, and theory says that in the full batch regime it favors solutions aligned with a particular geometry. That geometry is the max margin classifier under the infinity norm. Whether that bias survives in the per sample, incremental regime was open.

Baek and the team show the bias can depart from the full batch behavior. On constructed data sets, incremental Adam provably converges to the Euclidean max margin classifier instead. For general data, they characterize the bias through a proxy algorithm whose margin uses a data adaptive Mahalanobis norm, set by a dual fixed point problem. Concrete cases reduce to each classic classifier.
arxiv-2510-26603:
Reda El Makroum, Sebastian Zwickl-Bernhard, and Lukas Kranzl put a large language model in charge of home energy use. Home energy systems can shift when appliances run to match cheap power, but adoption stalls because users must turn plain wishes into technical settings. Earlier work used such models only to write code or pull out parameters.

El Makroum and his two co-authors build a system where one orchestrator agent and three specialist agents schedule many appliances from plain-language requests, with no worked examples. It reads deadlines from Google Calendar and reasons in a loop. Tested with real Austrian day-ahead prices, the largest open model matched cost-optimal schedules in every scenario. Smaller models handled single appliances well but stumbled on full coordination, and prompt tuning alone did not fix analytical slips.
arxiv-2510-27103:
Jack Lonergan, Andrew Benson, and Xiaolong Du compare two ways of predicting small dark matter clumps around galaxies. Warm dark matter, made of lighter, faster particles than the cold standard, should suppress low-mass subhalos. The team contrasts a semi-analytic model called Galacticus with the COZMIC suite of direct N-body simulations across several particle masses.

Both approaches predict fewer low-mass subhalos as particle mass drops, plus lower peak speeds and larger peak radii than cold dark matter at fixed mass. The semi-analytic model gives tighter statistics from larger samples, while simulations show the same broad trends. Differences trace to halo finders, resolution, and modeling choices. The agreement supports using the faster model to explore warm dark matter effects widely.
arxiv-2510-27303:
Lifang Feng, Bin Pei, and Yong Xu build a new equation for systems with long memories in this 2025 paper. The systems are driven by noise, random pushes, of a kind whose past lingers for a long time. Classic tools assume each step forgets the last, so they fail here. The equation they build tracks how the odds of each state change over time.

Their equation adds a memory kernel, a weight that says how much each past moment still counts. To build it, they first extend a basic rule of random calculus to this noise type. A flexible shortcut then makes the equation solvable in practice. Worked examples check the method and show it stays accurate. The equation is not tied to one drift or spread form, so many systems fit it.
arxiv-2510-27403:
Junkang Liu, Fanhua Shang, and four other co-authors speed up learning spread across many devices in this 2025 paper. In federated learning, phones or sites train a shared model locally and swap updates, not raw data. Fewer swap rounds mean faster learning. Most local training still uses simple per-number optimizers that ignore matrix shape.

Their method puts the Muon optimizer on each device. Muon reshapes updates using matrix orthogonalization, a step that keeps update directions clean and balanced. With alike data, it cut rounds sharply versus standard local methods. With unlike data, though, each device's reshaping pulled the model apart. Their fix, FedMuon, shares momentum, the running push from past updates, so devices start each round aligned.
arxiv-2510-27603:
Ruiwen Dong and Doron Shafrir settle the Skolem Problem for a broad class of rings in 2025. The problem asks if a sequence built by a fixed repeat rule ever hits zero. A ring is a set where add, subtract, and multiply all work. Here the rings are finitely built and have positive characteristic, which means some fixed count of ones sums to zero.

The pair prove that a computer method can always decide the question for such rings. Their proof rests on two fresh results about unit equations and about powers of two linked numbers. A side result shows the zero spots of such a sequence form a finite union of structured sets. Decidable cases map the edge of what math can test by machine.
arxiv-2511-00003:
Eric Ngondiep offers an unconditionally stable numeric method for a nonlinear Sobolev model with distributed delay, where the delay is spread over a past span rather than fixed at one lag. Time derivatives are approximated by interpolation, while spatial derivatives use finite element approximation, keeping the scheme simple to build. Stability and error estimates are proved in a strong norm equal to the standard energy norm.

Theory shows unconditional stability and fourth-order accuracy in space. Numerical analysis readers get a method whose reliability does not depend on tight step limits. Distributed delay Sobolev models arise in flows with memory, where stability assures are mainly valuable.
arxiv-2511-00103:
Rotem Ezra, Hedi Zisling, and Nimrod Berman introduce FreeSliders, a training-free, modality-agnostic way to steer diffusion models along individual concepts. Concept sliders let users continuously vary one trait, like age or smile, without disturbing other content, but earlier sliders needed per-concept training and architecture-specific tuning. FreeSliders discovers semantic directions through textual contrasts without any training.

Images, audio, and video are all handled by the same approach. Generative media readers get fine-grained control that scales to new concepts and modalities cheaply. Training-free steering matters because the set of traits users want to adjust is open-ended.
arxiv-2511-00603:
Yubo Wang and seven co-authors present EPARA, a framework that squeezes more AI inference out of existing edge hardware. Edge clouds run language models and vision services close to users, but demand keeps rising faster than hardware budgets. EPARA sorts tasks by how sensitive they are to latency and how much GPU power they need, then matches tasks to resources at two levels: per request and per service.

Three parts do the work: an allocator that picks each task's parallel mode, a distributed handler that runs requests, and a state-aware scheduler that refreshes service placement over time. A prototype was tested on edge servers, embedded devices, and microcomputers, running language model and segmentation workloads. Goodput rose to more than double that of prior frameworks on production workloads.
arxiv-2511-00803:
Sohini Guin and a large team report transport measurements on thin films of a copper oxide high temperature superconductor. Such materials host many electronic phases, from the strange pseudogap to the superconducting state itself. The team probes these phases by breaking time reversal symmetry with a magnetic field. The record notes that the paper's central conclusions have since changed greatly.

Without a field, the current and voltage data point to two dimensional superconductivity of a topological kind. With a field applied, a weak antilocalization signal appears before superconductivity, as bound vortex pairs break apart through an intermediate localized phase. In highly disordered films, three dimensional weak localization dominates instead, and superconductivity is fully suppressed.
arxiv-2511-00903:
Ahmed Masry and colleagues present ColMate, a retrieval model for documents that mix text, layout, and images. Retrieval augmented generation needs such documents, yet most retrieval methods were copied from text only search, in how documents are encoded, trained, and scored.

ColMate changes all three parts. It pretrains with an OCR based objective, learns from a self supervised masked contrastive task, and scores matches with late interaction. That compares fine details between query and document rather than single summary vectors. On the ViDoRe V2 benchmark it improves over existing retrieval models by about three and a half percent, and it generalizes better to benchmarks outside its training domain.
arxiv-2511-01103:
Piet Groeneboom studies estimation from interval censored data, where each subject's event time is known only to fall inside an interval between observation times, a common pattern in medical follow up studies. With several observation times per subject, the limit distribution of the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator is still unknown in general.

Groeneboom proves consistency for a related isotonic least squares estimator and sketches its limit distribution. Simulations at sample sizes of one thousand and ten thousand show that the conjectured limit behavior is not yet clearly visible even there, a caution about relying on asymptotics. He also compares a simpler one step least squares estimator, which is easier to compute but uses less information and performs worse.
arxiv-2511-01203:
Pavel Rumiantsev, Soumyasundar Pal, Yingxue Zhang, and Mark Coates propose a fair way to evaluate test time compute methods. These techniques spend extra computation at answer time, often through chains of thought, to improve language model results. Model performance and API prices drift over time, which can silently invalidate comparisons published earlier.

Their protocol, FEval-TTC, standardizes evaluation across several models and a diverse set of mathematical and commonsense reasoning data sets. Few shot prompting and answer extraction are fixed across data sets, cutting researcher overhead, and a cost model estimates both token usage and dollar cost per query. The goal is comparisons that stay equitable as prices and models change. The protocol is released as open source software.
arxiv-2511-01303:
Tomer Shoham, Moshe Shenfeld, Noa Velner-Harris, and Katrina Ligett build confidence intervals that protect privacy while assuming almost nothing about the data's distribution. Differential privacy is the standard guarantee, but existing private resampling methods lean on strong demands, or on one set noise mechanism, and can fail at real sample sizes.

Their framework is black box. Take any private estimator meeting mild conditions. Apply it repeatedly to subsamples of the data. Post process the resulting distribution into an interval for any target quantity. They prove the induced distribution converges to the estimator's true sampling pattern, which makes the interval asymptotically valid and tight, and they give plain guidance on choosing the method's settings. Experiments beat rival methods.
arxiv-2511-01803:
Samuel Moore and dozens of DESI collaborators present galaxy luminosity functions from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument's second data release. A luminosity function counts how many galaxies shine at each brightness; measured in the g, r, z, and w1 bands for the Bright Galaxy Survey out to redshift 0.6, it is a basic census of the nearby universe.

With DESI's statistical power, the functions reach extremely faint magnitudes. North and South survey regions agree well around the function's knee. But the tiny uncertainties expose failures of simple analytic shapes. The bright end falls off more gently than an exponential. The faint end bends in complex ways, with a pronounced upturn for the faintest galaxies, stronger among red galaxies. The team shows the census is largely complete above a surface brightness threshold and traces a residual North-South offset at the bright end to red galaxies and possibly shallower northern photometry.
arxiv-2511-01903:
Krishna Kingkar Pathak builds a deliberately simple benchmark for one of quantum chemistry's basic effects. A proton tunnels through a hydrogen bond. That splits energy levels by a tiny amount, one that spectroscopy can measure. Fully multidimensional instanton and path-integral methods compute such splittings well, but a transparent one-dimensional model remains valuable for concepts and cross-checks.

Pathak's framework uses a Cornell-type double-well potential. It solves for the wavefunctions directly. It compares analytical WKB estimates with numerical finite-difference solutions, across barrier shapes. The two agree consistently. As a test case, the formic acid dimer's barrier is mapped onto a quartic double well matched to its reported height, and the model's splitting, about 0.037 inverse centimeters, matches the reduced-dimensional calculations of Qu and Bowman, while the comparison clarifies where one dimension must give way to many.
arxiv-2511-02103:
Boyu Pang and Kostas Margellos work on making forecast uncertainty honest for time series data. Conformal prediction wraps a forecaster with error regions that carry guarantees, but designing the score function behind those regions is tricky: poor choices give bloated regions or heavy computation. Their method, Optimal Selection Conformal Prediction, builds the score from adjustable offset terms.

The offsets are chosen by solving a mixed-integer linear program that minimises a stand-in for region size, then reformulated into a smaller problem that runs faster. The authors prove guarantees for both validity and efficiency. In numerical experiments their method produced smaller uncertainty sets than the leading alternative while needing much less computation.
arxiv-2511-02303:
Zhiwei Zhang and ten co-authors diagnose a failure mode in teams of language models: one agent does all the work while the other coasts. In the setup they study, a meta-thinking agent plans and monitors while a reasoning agent executes subtasks over several conversational turns. This lazy agent behaviour quietly collapses the team back into a single agent, wasting the design. The authors first explain theoretically why laziness arises so naturally in this arrangement.

They then introduce a stable way to measure each agent's causal influence, which helps counteract the imbalance. A second problem follows success: as collaboration deepens, the reasoning agent can get lost among earlier noisy replies. Their verifiable reward mechanism lets it discard bad outputs, consolidate the instructions, and restart cleanly. Experiments showed the framework easing the laziness and unlocking stronger performance on complex reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2511-02403:
Marius Wilm Menzel validates the first wafer-scale prototype of a new kind of particle detector for the ALICE experiment at CERN. The planned Inner Tracking System upgrade will stitch monolithic active pixel sensors across whole silicon wafers for the first time in high-energy physics, keeping the material per layer extremely thin. The prototype, called MOSS, went through serial production testing to check that enough working sensors can be manufactured.

Beam tests showed detection efficiency above ninety-nine percent, meeting the upgrade's requirement, while the fake-hit rate stayed below the allowed ceiling. Performance held up after irradiation doses expected in service. The sensor also collected charge excellently, with a clean linear relation between signal timing and deposited energy for soft X-rays in the tested range. The paper walks through the validation steps and the characterisation results behind those numbers.
arxiv-2511-02903:
Radouane Gannouji, Ayan Mukhopadhyay, and Nicolas Pinochet use a classic entanglement inequality to probe how typical quantum states are organized. Working in a two-dimensional holographic theory, they apply the Araki-Lieb inequality, whose flat plateau in entanglement carries structural clues. Their 2025 paper studies pure states at fixed energy and angular momentum in that setting.

On the field theory side, the plateau suggests the state space factors into ultraviolet, middle, and infrared parts, with part of the middle purifying the ultraviolet part. In the dual bulk picture, the ultraviolet sector becomes an outer corona reachable by short probes, whose size depends only on the conserved charges. Small corrections at finite size lift the plateau slightly. The team frames a generalized thermalization ansatz to explain those corrections.
arxiv-2511-03103:
Rafael Jose Moura Silva, Maria Gizele Nascimento, Fumio Machida, and Ermeson Andrade detect software aging, the slow decay of long-running programs, even as workloads shift. Aging systems lose performance and risk failure, but a detector trained on one workload can go blind under another. Their 2025 approach adds drift detectors, built for changing data streams, to a machine learning model so it can adapt.

They compared a fixed model with adaptive ones using two drift methods, DDM and ADWIN. Under sudden, gradual, and recurring workload changes, the fixed model dropped sharply on unseen profiles. The ADWIN version held an F1 score above 0.93 in every scenario. The result argues for detectors that expect change, in systems that run for months without restarts.
arxiv-2511-03303:
Ruth H Tichauer, Maksim Lednev, Gerrit Groenhof, and Johannes Feist merge two simulation styles to study light trapped with molecules at tiny scales. Quantum and molecular mechanics dynamics follow the molecules, while a compact field model captures the trapped light in lossy, uneven nano spaces. Shape-driven molecular traits are computed as the run unfolds rather than fixed in advance.

Tests with a paired nanoparticle and several light emitters show strong light-matter coupling survives once motion and disorder enter. At the same time, neat degeneracies promised by simple two-level models break apart. The runs also reveal how field patterns shift with position. The framework gives chemists a fuller way to predict how nano light devices will behave in real, messy conditions.
arxiv-2511-03603:
Victor Gracia, Pablo Krupa, Filiberto Fele, and Teodoro Alamo fit advanced predictive control onto small industrial embedded chips. Predictive control plans moves ahead using a model, but weak chips usually force stripped-down versions that drop useful features. Their build uses a tracking scheme with an artificial reference, solved by a fast splitting algorithm that exploits problem structure.

Practical touches needed on real hardware are included at small extra cost. Chance-based validation backs the performance claims rather than best-case runs alone. Factories run countless small controllers, so bringing full predictive control to cheap hardware widens where smarter control can replace fixed rules. Tests on embedded targets show the solver keeps pace with real-time demands.
arxiv-2511-03703:
Prashanth Amireddy and co-authors give the first construction of a probabilistically checkable proof with only one alphabet-shrinking step. Such proofs let a verifier check a huge claim by reading a few random spots, a pillar of hardness theory. All prior builds needed at least two composition steps, or many more, to shrink large alphabets down.

The missing piece is a basic proximity proof of near-exponential size that asks only a constant number of queries. At its core sits a new family of alternatives to the classic sum-check protocol, built with ideals and Macaulay bases. One-step composition simplifies the whole architecture and may tighten the price paid in soundness error.
arxiv-2511-04003:
Jiangtao Li, writing alone, introduces a curvature condition called two-positive bisectional curvature for compact Kahler manifolds and proves a characterization theorem for manifolds that satisfy it. The result is framed as a variant of the classical Frankel conjecture and its later forms, using the Yang-Mills flow as the route.

Frankel-type results sort manifolds by positivity of curvature, linking analytic conditions to concrete shape models. By working through the Yang-Mills flow, Li obtains the stated result for this new positivity notion. The note is short, and its abstract gives the condition and conclusion without listing the model spaces, so the contribution is best read as a sorting step inside Kahler geometry.
arxiv-2511-04103:
Moses Charikar, Chirag Pabbaraju, and Ambuj Tewari characterize when a learner can identify a target language in the limit. The learner may offer a list of k guesses at each step instead of one. Gold showed single-guess identification fails for most interesting language families, and Angluin later pinned down exactly when it succeeds.

Their exact characterization rests on a recursive version of Angluin's condition, generalized to lists. A cleaner equivalent form also emerges for collections that can be list-identified. Allowing several guesses enlarges what can be learned in the limit, and the result maps that enlargement precisely, linking a classic learning theory question to recent progress on language generation.
arxiv-2511-04503:
Jongchon Kim and his co-author extend a classic square function estimate to weighted settings. The Córdoba-Fefferman estimate concerns the parabola, a basic curve in Fourier analysis. Weights change the picture, since mass can pile up unevenly across scales.

Their weighted bound grows out of a wave envelope estimate for the parabola. Terms involve families of tubes at many scales plus parameters describing the weight's spread. As applications, they obtain weighted estimates for a class of Fourier multipliers. The same bounds cover solutions of the free Schrödinger equation, linking a geometric estimate to wave evolution.
arxiv-2511-04703:
Andrew M. Bean leads forty-two authors reviewing construct validity in language model benchmarks. A benchmark only helps if it truly measures the trait it names, like safety or robustness. Weak measures can mislead decisions made before a model ships.

Twenty-nine expert reviewers examined four hundred forty-five benchmarks from top venues. Patterns in the measured traits, tasks, and scoring rules undercut many published claims. The team closes with eight recommendations and detailed, actionable guidance for researchers. Their message is simple: measuring what matters takes as much care as building the models themselves.
arxiv-2511-05003:
Ruifen Ma, Yanjing Sun, and Xiaofei Qi sort out kinds of Gaussian channels tied to quantum steering, a resource that sits between entanglement and Bell nonlocality. Gaussian channels are core tools in quantum protocols and secure links.

The authors define channels that kill steering, break steering, or cannot be steered, plus the largest such classes. For each class they give exact tests for when a channel falls in it, and map how the classes relate. They also chart the free superchannels for the unsteerable cases, which are needed to score steering strength.
arxiv-2511-05203:
Linus Nwankwo and co-authors present SIL, a learning frame where a human and a robot agent teach each other. Most current frames are one-way: the agent just takes orders and acts, with no learning back from the person.

SIL sets up two-way co-adaptation in a shared latent task space, guided by language. Both sides adjust as they work through long tasks in turns. The frame aims to match how people adapt to each other in daily joint work. Tests probe whether this mutual tuning beats the old master and apprentice style.
arxiv-2511-05703:
N Frolov and co-authors measure how stiffly a thin flake of hexagonal boron nitride bonds to the surface beneath it. Such layered materials are stacked for new devices, and the coupling between layers sets how they behave. Sound waves running along the surface can reveal that hidden stiffness.

A focused laser pulse launched ultrasonic waves across a silica surface partly covered by the flake. An optical probe then tracked the surface motion point by point. The wave pattern changed over the flake, showing dispersion the bare surface lacks. Fitting a layered model to the data gave the two elastic constants that describe how the flake grips the substrate along and across the bond.
arxiv-2511-06003:
Atsushi Miki and Toshiyasu Matsushima pin down exactly when a private information retrieval scheme can be as efficient as theory allows. Private retrieval lets a user download one message from servers without revealing which one. Real servers may collude, go silent, or answer with noise, and schemes exist for each threat.

Upper bounds on download efficiency were known for the robust, Byzantine, and colluding variants. What was missing was a systematic way to build schemes that reach those bounds. The authors prove necessary and sufficient conditions on the queries a scheme sends. Meeting those conditions is exactly what capacity requires. The result gives designers a checklist for building optimal private retrieval under adversarial servers.
arxiv-2511-06303:
Noor Muhammad, Md. Nur Alam, and Zhang Shiqing model the spread of Ebola with help from control theory and a neural network. Ebola is a severe hemorrhagic fever passed through infected fluids and surfaces, including contact after death. Their fractional-order model uses Caputo derivatives to capture memory effects in how the disease moves through a population.

Eight compartments separate symptomatic, asymptomatic, and post-mortem transmission routes. The authors prove the model is well posed, derive its basic reproduction number, and rank which factors drive it most. Treatment joined with safe burial gave the strongest control in their analysis, and a disease-informed neural network reproduced epidemic behavior with very high accuracy.
arxiv-2511-06403:
Kumar Ghosh uses quantum annealing to test replica symmetry breaking, the theory describing how spin glasses organize their many low-energy states. Checking the theory beyond about one hundred spins had been computationally out of reach. Annealing hardware let Ghosh reach ground states of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model with up to four thousand spins.

Five separate measures lined up with the theory's predictions, from ground-state energies to the hierarchical shape of the overlap distribution. Diluting the network left the complexity unchanged until a sharp threshold, where the hierarchy collapsed in a narrow avalanche-like window. The study casts quantum computation as a working tool for probing complex disordered matter.
arxiv-2511-06503:
R. Malaspina and colleagues model how the strong force coupling changes with momentum while keeping it analytic. Analytic perturbation theory keeps the coupling finite at zero momentum, which blocks the blow-up at the origin that confinement seems to demand. Their workaround studies the inverse of the coupling instead, within an inverse coupling concept.

A two-parameter regularizing factor forces that inverse to vanish at zero momentum, restoring the divergent coupling wanted at low energy without spoiling high-energy behavior. Three candidate shapes for that factor were tried. After fitting the free parameters to trustworthy measured values, the model reproduces the running coupling at any other momentum, offering one consistent curve across both regimes.
arxiv-2511-07403:
Multimodal language models answer questions about pictures well but often stumble on space. Hunar Batra and co-authors present SpatialThinker, a model trained to reason about where objects sit and how they relate. Earlier systems needed extra three-dimensional inputs, special designs, or thin training signals.

SpatialThinker builds a mental scene graph while it reasons, listing task-relevant objects and their relations in one pass. Dense spatial rewards guide that process during online reinforcement learning. The team also built a seven thousand item question set for training and testing. Results suggest grounding each reasoning step in a scene layout sharpens spatial answers.
arxiv-2511-07503:
Asia Belfiore, Jonathan Passerat-Palmbach, and Dmitrii Usynin test whether synthetic genetic data stays private. Language models can generate fake mutation profiles for research, and differential privacy should stop them from leaking real donors. The team attacks their own models to check that promise.

Their hybrid membership inference attack mixes standard black-box probes with biology-aware genetic measures. It guesses whether a person record trained the generator more accurately than older attacks. Both small and large transformer models proved usable for small synthetic datasets. Results show privacy noise helps but must be tuned carefully, since genomic context gives attackers extra leverage.
arxiv-2511-07703:
J. Noel builds an expected goals model for ice hockey that credits skill, not just shot location. Standard models rate a scoring chance by where the shot came from. Shooters and goaltenders, though, differ sharply, and the same chance means different things in different hands.

A light gradient boosted model uses league tracking data with features for overall, locational, and situational skill for both shooter and goalie. Shot binning and similarity distances shape those features. Separate datasets by skill pairing feed baseline comparisons. Coaches and analysts gain chance ratings that respect who shoots and who guards the net.
arxiv-2511-07903:
Youneng Bao, Yulong Cheng, and Yiping Liu compress images with quantization that adapts to content. Learned image compression beats classic codecs in quality, but its neural networks need quantization for deployment. Static uniform bit widths ignore that layers and image regions differ wildly in sensitivity.

DynaQuant adjusts precision dynamically at two levels. Content-aware scaling and offsets track latent feature statistics, trained end to end with a distance-aware scheme. Rate and distortion balance improves over one-size settings. Efficient learned codecs could cut storage and bandwidth for photo services, provided compression models shrink without surrendering their quality edge.
arxiv-2511-08003:
Jialong Qin and colleagues present SharpV, a pruning method that makes video language models cheaper and more reliable. Such models process huge numbers of visual tokens, so computation and memory grow very fast with video length. Uniform compression wastes effort on frames and regions that carry little new information.

SharpV adjusts pruning rates by spatial and temporal information content, sometimes even beating unpruned models. A second stage removes degraded cache features by comparing them with original features in a self calibrating way. Tests on public benchmarks show strong gains, and the method works without exposed attention scores, keeping compatibility with Flash Attention.
arxiv-2511-08203:
Kyle Fogarty, Jack Foster, Boqiao Zhang, and Jing Yang show that image to three dimensional generative models carry a strong bias toward one standard viewing angle. These models turn a single picture into a three dimensional object, but their hidden preferences are poorly understood. Rotating the simple two dimensional input in controlled tests exposes how fragile viewpoint handling can be.

Performance of the leading Hunyuan3D model degraded noticeably under rotated inputs. A small convolutional network that detects and corrects input orientation restored results without touching the generative backbone. The authors ask whether sheer scale is enough for such models, or whether modular, symmetry aware designs are the better path.
arxiv-2511-08703:
Yaroslav Popryho and two co-authors build a tool that plants fake hardware Trojans inside industrial chip designs, so that detection software can be tested honestly. Real system-on-chip designs hold millions of connections, while public test benchmarks are small and hand-made, and sharing genuinely malicious designs would be risky.

The pipeline reads a gate-level design as a graph and hunts rare corners using testability metrics. It then applies function-preserving graph edits that create trigger and payload pairs with the statistical footprint of stealthy Trojans. User-visible behavior stays unchanged. On the generated benchmarks, leading graph-learning detectors fail to spot the planted patterns. The authors offer the framework as reproducible challenge material that closes the gap between classroom circuits and modern chips.
arxiv-2511-09003:
Zhouxing Tan and ten co-authors judge emotional support chatbots by the whole arc of a conversation, not by single replies. Snapshot evaluations miss the point of support, which is to leave a distressed user steadier over time, so the framework simulates long dialogues where feelings shift as events unfold.

The benchmark holds three hundred twenty-eight emotional contexts and over a thousand disturbance events, with model replies constrained by validated regulation strategies such as situation selection and cognitive reappraisal. User emotions are tracked as a first-order Markov process with causal adjustment to keep the estimates unbiased. Three trajectory metrics summarize performance: baseline emotional level, volatility along the path, and centroid position. Across many leading models the scores diverge sharply, exposing how uneven long-term support skill still is.
arxiv-2511-09203:
Robert Atkey and Roly Perera show that tracking where data came from can be built with the same machinery as automatic differentiation. Differentiation computes a program's derivative as a linear map, propagated forward or backward through the run. Swapping real numbers for dependency information turns that derivative into a record of provenance.

The choice of number system fixes the meaning of provenance. Over the two-element Boolean algebra, the resulting Jacobian records which input positions each output may depend on, recovering dependency analysis. Richer systems, such as distributive lattices, give measured interval provenance through the tropical semiring. The authors give meaning to a higher-order functional language in the approach and check every result in Agda.
arxiv-2511-09403:
Ian Low, Ming-Lei Xiao, and Yu-Hui Zheng build scattering amplitudes for Goldstone bosons that also carry gauge charge. Amplitudes are the quantities whose squares give particle interaction probabilities. Standard soft recursion builds them step by step, but it relies on Adler's zero condition, which gauge interactions break for charged scalars.

The authors introduce gauged soft recursion, which leans on the soft theorems of the gauge bosons themselves. Amplitudes are decomposed into gauge-invariant pieces where Adler's zero is partly restored. Internal gauge bosons enter through angular momentum constraints. The result constructs tree-level amplitudes with any number of Goldstone and gauge bosons. It covers both Abelian and non-Abelian theories, as explicit examples demonstrate.
arxiv-2511-09503:
Yilun Guan shows how to fold cosmic microwave background maps in phase to hunt for signals that oscillate over time. Passing gravitational waves would regularly deflect the background light, and axion-like particles could make its polarization rotate periodically. Standard time-divided maps cannot see frequencies above about a hundred-thousandth of a hertz, set by mapmaking cadence.

Phase folding aligns repeated cycles of a periodic signal, extending sensitivity up to the sampling rate near one hundred hertz. That widens the searchable band by more than seven orders of magnitude, Guan calculates. The approach supports two demonstrations: constraining a stochastic gravitational wave background through its lensing signature, and searching for oscillating polarization rotation. Microwave telescopes become broadband probes of the oscillating sky.
arxiv-2511-09703:
Stefan Kiefer and Andrew Ryzhikov compute the smallest rank achievable inside a matrix monoid. The monoid is generated by finitely many zero-one matrices. Those matrix monoids represent unambiguous finite automata, a generalization of deterministic automata with many of their good properties. Rank here measures how much an automaton can compress its state set under some input word.

Using linear algebra, they place the problem in the parallel complexity class NC. Their algorithms run in quartic time with modest space. A purely combinatorial algorithm matches that time bound. As a byproduct, a short straight-line program always describes a product attaining the minimum rank. For total deterministic automata, the answer equals the smallest image of the state set under any word.
arxiv-2511-09803:
Yufeng Wang, Lu wei, and Haibin Ling ask when a question-answering system should bother retrieving documents at all. Retrieval-augmented generation improves factual answers, but retrieving for every query wastes time and tokens and can even hurt quality. Their method, called TARG, makes the decision from a short draft answer the model writes without any context.

From the draft's opening token scores, TARG computes light uncertainty measures such as entropy, a margin between top choices, or variance across a few sampled prefixes. Retrieval fires only when uncertainty passes a threshold, and no extra training is needed. Across five question-answering benchmarks, the gate matched or beat always-retrieving systems while cutting retrieval by seventy to ninety percent and lowering total latency.
arxiv-2511-10203:
Stephane Da Silva Martins, Emanuel Aldea, and Sylvie Le Hégarat-Mascle present a trajectory prediction approach, also named VISTA, for crowded scenes with many interacting agents. Autonomous systems need forecasts that respect both each agent's long-term goal and the fine social negotiation between neighbors, which earlier methods often failed to combine. Their recursive goal-conditioned transformer fuses long-horizon intent with past motion through cross-attention.

A social-token attention mechanism models interactions flexibly, and pairwise attention maps expose who influences whom at prediction time. Judged not only on displacement error but on collision rates, the model reached state-of-the-art accuracy with far fewer collisions. On the dense MADRAS benchmark the collision rate fell from just over two percent to nearly zero. On SDD it recorded none.
arxiv-2511-10503:
Mateo Cárdenes Wuttig and Andrew J. Millis map out the magnetism of spin ladders, materials whose atoms form two-legged ladder structures that behave almost like one-dimensional chains. Many real materials fit this description, and the open question is what happens when ladders are weakly coupled sideways into a second dimension.

Using the Density Matrix Renormalization Group method together with a self-consistent mean-field approximation, they chart the full ground-state phase diagram. Depending on the couplings and magnetic field, the system can be spin-gapped, antiferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic, or fully polarized. They also show that measuring how magnetization responds to an applied field can place a real material on the diagram and pin down its Hamiltonian parameters, giving experimentalists a practical identification route.
arxiv-2511-10603:
Raymond T. Co, Keisuke Harigaya, Isaac R. Wang, and Huangyu Xiao propose a single mechanism that could explain both dark matter and the universe's excess of matter over antimatter. Their ingredients are the QCD axion, a hypothetical particle tied to a rotating field, and dark magnetic monopoles, which have never been observed.

In their picture, the monopoles gain mass from the axion field and hop between quantized charge levels as the field rotates, draining the axion's kinetic energy. That dissipation trims the axion abundance down to the observed dark matter density, while the rotating axion itself generates the baryon asymmetry through axiogenesis. The framework ties the two abundances together and predicts the axion's decay constant should fall below a stated bound.
arxiv-2511-10903:
Ramya Kumar, Dhruv Gulwani, and Sonit Singh compare a zoo of classifiers on a small, practical task. They sort exam questions and learning outcomes into the six cognitive levels of Bloom's taxonomy, from knowledge up to evaluation. Their dataset holds just 600 labeled sentences, a realistic size for an education team, and that smallness shapes every result.

Traditional models, recurrent networks, transformers, and large language models were all tested under different preprocessing and augmentation strategies. An augmented support vector machine won overall, reaching 94 percent accuracy with little overfitting, while the recurrent models and BERT overfit badly and RoBERTa began to as well. Zero-shot large language models from OpenAI and Google led their class at roughly 72 percent accuracy. The authors stress augmentation and simpler algorithms on small data.
arxiv-2511-11103:
Maryna Kachanovska and Adrian Savchuk derive approximate models for how waves scatter off many small particles of arbitrary shape over time. Exact boundary-value solutions are costly when particles shrink toward zero size, yet that limit is where simple models can take over. Their method starts from a boundary integral form, split in space with chosen basis functions.

Convergence comes as particle size vanishes, not from adding more basis functions, a swap that keeps the model lean. Because the matrix build needs double integrals over particles, they also derive a simpler model and a Born approximation for large counts. Error analysis for the high-order models is backed by numerical tests.
arxiv-2511-11403:
C. Hainaut, K. Ouahrouche, and their colleagues show a way to map photon counts across a surface in a single shot, with timing as fine as a picosecond. Photon counts show how light behaves when it is out of balance or changing fast. Mapping them in two dimensions at such speed is hard to do well.

Their setup uses a crystal that mixes light waves to read the counts. It can tell apart two basic kinds of light, coherent and thermal, across the surface. The counts found depart from the ideal shapes. The team traces that gap to vacuum noise and to how the amplifier reacts. A mode-based frame for the timing explains the gap and matches the data.
arxiv-2511-11703:
Jin Huang tests whether feeding a reinforcement learning agent semantic segmentation maps, rather than raw pixels, makes learning in three-dimensional games cheaper and steadier. Raw video input inflates the memory buffers that stabilize training and worsens partial observability, two chronic pains of game AI.

Experiments run in ViZDoom deathmatches with perfect segmentation for control. Using segmentation alone cut buffer memory by at least two thirds, and by far more with run-length compression, while a combined color-plus-segmentation input is also evaluated. Leaner inputs that preserve what matters could let smaller labs train capable game agents without server-class memory budgets.
arxiv-2511-12103:
Sayad Ibna Azad and Md. Atiqur Rahman introduce BdSL-SPOTER, a pose-based transformer system for recognizing Bengali Sign Language. Sign systems for low-resource languages often lack large datasets, so a model must learn well from limited examples. Their design adapts the SPOTER approach with preprocessing shaped for this language and culture.

A compact four-layer transformer reads body pose, with tuned position codes and a staged training plan that aids learning on small data. On the BdSLW60 benchmark the system reports a large gain over a Bi-LSTM baseline in top-one accuracy. It also uses fewer parameters and runs fast, which helps real access tools.
arxiv-2511-12403:
Mordecai Waegell and Kelvin J. McQueen argue that Everettian quantum mechanics, often praised as a local theory, in fact involves nonlocal action. In the Everett view the universe never collapses, and acting on one system cannot change the reduced state of a distant entangled partner. That fact is usually taken to prove locality.

The authors reply that such an action does change the global state shared with the remote partner, and that change should count as nonlocal. They reject a defense based on calling the change merely extrinsic, arguing that line cannot bear the weight placed on it. When the global state serves as an essential explanatory tool, they conclude, changing it at a distance is nonlocal action.
arxiv-2511-12803:
Yu-Han Huang and Venugopal V. Veeravalli study quickest change detection over a finite time window. The task is to raise an alarm soon after a system's statistics change, without crying wolf. Classical theory assumes an endless horizon; here the horizon ends, so the authors measure false alarms by the chance one fires before time runs out. Delay by a latency level that delay exceeds only with small probability. The goal is the smallest latency at chosen risk levels.

They derive a universal lower bound that no detector can beat, then build detectors that are order-optimal in the horizon length. Results first assume the before and after distributions are known, then extend to the case where only a sub-Gaussian shape and a mean shift are assumed. Simulations confirm the theory. The work fits monitoring in non-stationary environments.
arxiv-2511-12903:
Bo Hu and Jose C. Principe reinterpret two classic neural network tools through a Gaussian, Bayesian lens. In their view, training a model tightens a probabilistic bound, and the learned density is what makes the bound tight. Mixture density networks use a bound for the marginal distribution, while autoencoders use a conditional one. The paper focuses on networks with multiple outputs, where each output is the center of a Gaussian component, and asks what objective such networks should really optimize.

Their first result equates the autoencoder objective with maximizing the trace of a Gaussian operator. When one-to-one matching is not required, maximizing the operator's nuclear norm instead would raise its overall rank. Their second construction adds a norm term that increases sample diversity and blocks output collapse. The paper is theoretical, offering new objectives for density modeling.
arxiv-2511-13003:
Shota Ampuku, Yasuhiro Yamaguchi, and Masayasu Harada ask what the exotic particle Tcc(3875)+ is made of. Exotic hadrons might be loose molecules of two ordinary hadrons or compact multiquark objects. This doubly charmed state, seen by LHCb as a peak in the two-D-zero plus pion spectrum, is a prime test case. The authors build a model mixing molecular and compact components rather than forcing a choice, then fit the observed peak.

The best fit favors a predominantly compact tetraquark. Two further solutions fit nearly as well, and both make the state a molecule, differing in which pairing of charmed mesons binds and each predicting an additional molecular partner below threshold. The molecular states mix isospin zero and one. All three scenarios also match the near-threshold distributions in related channels, so the extra predicted states give experimenters concrete targets to separate them.
arxiv-2511-13303:
Sumana Hatui, Sanjay Mukherjee, and Kamal Lochan Patra study the deep commuting graph of a finite group. Vertices are group elements, and two are joined when their lifts in a Schur cover commute with each other. Earlier work showed the graph does not depend on which Schur cover is chosen.

The authors prove the graph is complete exactly when the group is cyclic, and they classify which finite simple, symmetric, and alternating groups give perfect graphs. They also study linked traits such as Euler paths, connectedness of reduced graphs, and dominant vertices. Separate sections treat abelian groups and familiar non-abelian families such as dihedral and Heisenberg groups.
arxiv-2511-13403:
Yuzhou Fang, Juha Kinnunen, and Chao Zhang prove regularity results for a class of degenerate fully nonlinear nonlocal equations with a Hamiltonian term. Regularity asks how smooth answers must be, given the shape of the equation. The answer here depends on how the degeneracy law interacts with the growth of the Hamiltonian part.

By pinning down that interaction, they prove a Lipschitz bound for viscosity solutions with the Ishii-Lions method. Perturbation arguments then give Hölder continuity of the gradient, meaning the slope itself varies in a controlled way. Under weak assumptions on that pattern, they also explore when answers gain a full first derivative.
arxiv-2511-13503:
Ioannis Diamantis offers a practical guide to topological data analysis for business and economic data, aimed at working analysts. Business data often bend and branch across scales in ways that straight-line tools miss. Topological methods instead track durable shapes such as clusters, loops, and voids as the scale changes.

Figure-led sections explain persistent homology and lay out a reproducible workflow, with advice on distance choices, complex building, and reading results. Case studies cover consumer behavior, stock markets, and currency dynamics, set against classical methods. A new Topological Stability Index turns persistence lifetimes into a simple gauge of structural change that managers can track.
arxiv-2511-14303:
Oscar Cosserat studies when long-run numeric schemes for Hamiltonian systems stay stable. The schemes he treats keep the Poisson form of the system and own a tweaked energy, a modified Hamiltonian. He argues that the mere fact that such a tweaked energy exists is the key to good long-run acts. His test cases come from Lotka-Volterra models, the classic prey and hunter laws of ecology.

For systems that can be solved in full, the link is made firm. To probe past that case, Cosserat builds a five-part Lotka-Volterra system that cannot be solved in full and studies it on the computer. The work ties scheme design to plain growth laws of populations.
arxiv-2511-14403:
Moyu Zhang, Yujun Jin, Yun Chen, and three co-authors make a click-rate model use its build skill at serve time, not just in training. Click models for ads and feeds more and more train in a build-it style, to learn how traits hang together. But at serve time they fall back to a plain yes-no score and waste that skill. The team's frame, SGCTR, makes training and serving match.

After masked build-style training, the model works on each live sample the same way. It reworks the sample's noisy traits step by step, then scores it. That clean-up blunts bad traits and lifts the hit rate. Wide tests show the matched design beats the lopsided build-style tools that came before it.
arxiv-2511-14503:
Xinzhuo Yu and five co-authors introduce a decoder for doing many dense image tasks at once. Dense tasks label every pixel, so tasks can help or hinder each other. Most past methods link tasks with convolution or attention blocks. The new model instead uses state space model parameters to carry task specific prior knowledge.

Dual parameter experts set and merge those priors for each task. A structured sequence model then mixes the priors globally. Multi direction Hilbert scanning builds feature sequences from many angles. Tests are meant to show sharper task interaction and broader context. The design targets precise multi task prediction in complex scenes.
arxiv-2511-14803:
Pranjal Gupta, Karan Bhukar, and four co-authors describe a deployed tool that uses large language models to read IT support logs at scale. Support teams drown in log volume, and manual reading cannot keep up with modern systems. Their tool processes the logs and drafts diagnoses and summaries for incoming tickets automatically.

A key trick lets the models run well on ordinary CPUs, so huge log volumes can be handled quickly without costly hardware. In production since March 2024, the tool has spread across dozens of products and thousands of tickets. The authors share the lessons from that rollout, including large reported savings in staff hours.
arxiv-2511-14903:
Ruixin Zhang, Jon Donnelly, and five co-authors present LIT, a framework that pushes language models to solve problems with inspectable external tools. Models that reason in private text can pick shaky solution paths that users cannot check, a real problem in high-stakes work. LIT instead forces the model to route work through tools whose steps can be seen and fixed.

The framework ranks solution paths by how reliable and easy to troubleshoot they are, even when a path needs several tool calls in a row. It builds on the tool-calling skills that current models already have. For fields like medicine, law, and engineering support, that shift from fluent answers to auditable steps is the point.
arxiv-2511-15503:
Peiming Yang, Sankeerth Durvasula, and five co-authors present DCC, a compiler for machine learning programs that run partly inside memory. Chips that compute in memory can speed up memory-heavy model parts, but host chips and memory chips want data laid out in opposite ways. Rearranging data is costly, and earlier compilers often ignored that cost while tuning the computing code.

DCC treats rearrangement and computing as one joint tuning problem, supported by a layered model that can target several kinds of memory hardware. It searches layout and loop choices together and uses a fast predictor to pick the best schedule. On separate model kernels, DCC reached speedups of several times over prior work.
arxiv-2511-15903:
Issei Kobayashi, Hiroyuki Kurokawa, Laura Schaefer, and Satoshi Okuzumi simulate how close-in sub-Neptune planets lose their original atmospheres and gain new ones. Such planets are common and are thought to start with primary atmospheres captured from their birth disk. Escape driven by stellar high-energy radiation, plus degassing from the rocky interior, can replace that envelope with a secondary atmosphere poor in gases that dissolve poorly in magma, such as helium.

Their one-dimensional evolution model couples escape with outgassing of hydrogen, helium, and water. Low-mass, close-in planets that lose the most atmosphere make the transition, showing helium depletion and water enrichment. A parameter survey finds a correlation between planet radius and helium escape rate, suggesting a testable observational signature.
arxiv-2511-16003:
David A. Neufeld, Kedron Silsbee, and ten co-authors map cosmic-ray excited hydrogen glow inside the dark cloud Barnard 68 with the James Webb Space Telescope. Barnard 68 is a starless Bok globule, and cosmic rays penetrating it excite molecular hydrogen, whose infrared lines reveal the otherwise invisible ray flux. Spatially resolved signatures of that excitation are reported for the first time.

Sixteen sight lines through the cloud separate cosmic-ray glow from ultraviolet-pumped emission. The cosmic-ray signal per hydrogen column varies significantly with position in a way dust extinction alone cannot explain, showing clear attenuation as shielding grows. Modeling the cloud as a Bonnor-Ebert sphere yields the unshielded ionization rate and its decline with depth, higher at a reference depth than absorption-based averages.
arxiv-2511-16703:
Seokcheon Lee runs controlled null tests on recent hints that dark energy might evolve with time. Combined analyses have shown mild departures from a cosmological constant. The question is whether a single probe, through its own degeneracies and calibration freedom, can fake such a signal.

Mock datasets resembling baryon acoustic oscillation, compressed microwave background, and supernova data were all made from one standard cosmology, then analyzed with probe-adapted parameterizations, convergence checks, and coverage tests. None of the three single probes falsely excluded the true model at the ninety-five percent level. The microwave background mocks did show stably displaced posterior medians alongside wide intervals, proving that a shifted posterior alone is not evidence for dynamical dark energy. Real claims, the paper argues, must survive mock-ensemble recovery tests like these.
arxiv-2511-16803:
Abdelmalek Boumali solves the scattering of spin-half particles in the spacetime of a spinning cosmic string that also carries torsion. He treats both a spacelike disclination and a dislocation, with and without a Coulomb potential. Cosmic strings are hypothetical line defects from the early universe, and their geometry imprints itself on quantum scattering.

Working in the tetrad formalism, Boumali treats balanced torsion, pure spinning, pure dislocation, and the general case. The geometry shifts the effective azimuthal quantum number, and strong rotation builds a radial cutoff that acts as a hard wall. Closed-form radial wave functions, phase shifts, and cross sections follow, showing Aharonov-Bohm-like effects and topology-renormalized Mott and Rutherford patterns. Even without the Coulomb term the scattering is purely geometric with a defect-controlled forward peak, and strained graphene may mimic the setup.
arxiv-2511-16903:
Marco Carmosino, Ngu Dang, and Tim Jackman tackle a problem in circuit complexity: how hard it is to find the smallest circuit that computes a given Boolean function. Earlier work showed a partial version of this problem is hard under a standard assumption, using the OR function. Extending that result to the full problem needs a different, slightly richer function.

The authors show that the extension task stays easy when the function is XOR, the next natural candidate. They build a general algorithm that works whenever a function's best circuits are small, few in number, and easy to list. XOR meets all three tests, so its extension problem runs in polynomial time under two ways of counting circuit size. The result maps where the hardness proof can and cannot be pushed.
arxiv-2511-17103:
Daiqing Wu and three co-authors work on visual emotion recognition: teaching computers to judge the feeling an image conveys. Pretrained visual models know a lot about what images show, but facts and feelings are only loosely linked, a gap the authors call the affective gap. Text, by contrast, expresses emotion directly and densely, so the team borrows knowledge from a pretrained text model instead.

Their method, Partitioned Adaptive Contrastive Learning, learns from noisy image and text pairs harvested from social media. It sorts the pairs into types and applies a different contrastive strategy to each, building positive and negative matches dynamically. Across experiments, closing the affective gap this way improved several pretrained visual models on emotion tasks. The code is publicly released for other researchers.
arxiv-2511-17203:
Yang-Hui He surveys how machine intelligence is starting to change pure mathematics. Drawing on early trials in geometry and theory from 2017 onward, he sorts the help into three kinds. It can check proofs with machine aid, form new conjectures from patterns in data, and handle the language tasks that surround research. Examples from across the maths sciences show learning tools spotting patterns that people had missed.

He then asks the deeper question of what such help means for discovery itself. If machines can suggest where a proof might lie, the mathematician's role shifts toward judging and guiding those hints. The survey reads as both a progress report and a prompt: the tools are already useful, and the field is still deciding how far to trust them.
arxiv-2511-17303:
Timmie M R Lagermann, Kristina Sophia Carter, Su Mei Gwen Ho, Luís Cruz, Kerstin Eder, and Maja H Kirkeby measure the energy cost of automated web testing. Teams test web pages with scripted actions such as clicks, typing, and scrolling, and four common frameworks can run those scripts. The team asks whether the choice of framework changes the power each action draws.

In a fixed setup with an outside power meter, each action was run thirty-five times per framework.
