Raster images fuse all content into one canvas, so edits often break consistency elsewhere. Design tools avoid that with layers, and this model aims to recover such layers automatically.

The system decomposes one RGB image into several semantically separate RGBA layers, each open to independent editing. Three parts make that work: an RGBA autoencoder, an architecture that handles a variable number of layers, and a multi stage training plan. Training data come from a pipeline that mines layered images from Photoshop documents. Tests show clear gains in decomposition quality over prior methods.
arxiv-2512-15703:
Erika Ye and Chao Yang study time integration of quantized tensor trains with a new low rank method in a 2025 paper. Quantized tensor trains compress high resolution, multi dimensional data in a low rank, multiscale form. They are promising for modeling hyperbolic systems such as Navier Stokes and Vlasov equations.

Standard dynamical low rank approximation projects the system using orthogonal projectors, which suits linear systems best, and it was mostly studied without the quantized form. The new version builds its low rank manifold from chosen interpolation points and polynomials. Tests show it handles nonlinear systems and steppers needing nonlinear element wise steps. Upwind schemes are one case, where the orthogonal version struggles.
arxiv-2512-15803:
Apurva Shet and Izzat Alsmadi analyze zero day vulnerabilities disclosed through the Zero Day Initiative in a 2025 paper, dated December 16. Zero day flaws are unknown to vendors when attackers exploit them, leaving systems defenseless until a patch arrives. Patterns in past disclosures could help teams prioritize their response.

The study covers 415 vulnerabilities reported from January to April 2024, with identifiers, severity scores, dates, and short descriptions. It tracks trends over time, compares severity across vendors, and asks which traits best signal high severity. Classical machine learning and deep learning models are compared for severity classification, using both structured metadata and free text descriptions.
arxiv-2512-16003:
Pere Ara, Alcides Buss, and Ado Dalla Costa introduce a new algebraic object in their 40-page 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is separated graphs, diagrams whose edges are split into labeled families. From such a graph they build an inverse semigroup, a structure capturing partial symmetries, and tie it to the tame Leavitt path algebra of the graph.

The authors describe the new semigroup as a product of a free group acting on a semilattice, pictured through branching trees. That picture yields a normal form, a standard way to write each element, and explicit bases for the algebra. They prove the semigroup embeds faithfully into the algebra. Applications include describing a key kernel, computing the socle, and locating isolated points in the spectrum, with examples to guide the reader.
arxiv-2512-16103:
Sandeep Neela presents a market surveillance tool in an arXiv preprint made public in 2025. Stock manipulation now often starts on social media, where coordinated campaigns pump a ticker before trades move. AIMM, the author's framework, links online chatter and coordination signals to market data to flag such schemes.

For each stock, AIMM produces a daily manipulation risk score from Reddit activity, bot indicators, and price and volume data, shown in an analyst dashboard. The author built a ground truth set of 33 labeled ticker-days across eight stocks, drawn from SEC enforcement cases and matched normal days. Because Reddit access is limited, the social features are calibrated simulations, while market data is real. AIMM flagged the GameStop episode 22 days before its January 2021 peak, though the small sample makes the results preliminary.
arxiv-2512-16403:
Matthew Edmonds and James Bateman model a nanoparticle launcher in a paper posted to arXiv in 2025. Laser-induced acoustic desorption knocks nanoparticles off a surface with a sound pulse, loading them into optical traps for levitated optomechanics under vacuum. Today's setups are tuned by trial and error with whatever lab lasers are at hand, making them bulky.

The authors solve the photoacoustic wave equation for how laser light becomes sound in a metal substrate. Clear scaling laws emerge: surface acceleration grows as the inverse square of pulse duration, and diffraction sets a minimum useful spot size. Material scores combining heat expansion and light absorption suggest alternatives to aluminum. The model matches experiments and shows compact lasers with sub-nanosecond pulses can rival big lab systems at far lower pulse energy, enabling portable designs.
arxiv-2512-16503:
Elias Guisado Villalgordo and three co-authors study derived equivalences in a mathematics paper shared on arXiv in 2025. Fourier-Mukai transforms are integral transforms between derived categories, the modern bookkeeping of algebraic geometry. They can prove two varieties share the same derived category, but testing that directly is hard.

The authors develop fiberwise criteria: a yoga of local algebra and fibers that checks an equivalence, or the weaker fully faithfulness property, piece by piece under base change. The results generalize a theorem of Orlov to singular varieties and strengthen earlier work by allowing arbitrary base fields. Arithmetic settings gain new insight too, including fibrations and their singularities over rings like the discrete valuation rings used in number theory. Local checks for global equivalences are valuable wherever these transforms appear.
arxiv-2512-16603:
Zipei Geng and coauthors build a new way to measure how wildfires cause poor air quality in the United States. Smoke effects are hard to pin down because weather and land features can hide the true link, and the harm may show up only at high pollution levels.

Their model swaps averages for quantiles, so effects can differ across the whole range of outcomes, and it handles hidden spatial factors. Tests confirm it cuts bias better than mean-based tools. On US data, fire strength shows a clear causal push on haze at high levels in western states such as California and Oregon, but little effect at low levels.
arxiv-2512-16803:
Wooil Yang and coauthors compare two first-principles ways to get Hubbard U and V values, the fix-up terms that make density-functional theory work for transition-metal and rare-earth compounds. No systematic check between the two routes existed.

One route uses linear-response theory, the other a Hartree-Fock-based pseudohybrid method, tested on oxides MnO, NiO, CoO, FeO, BaTiO3, ZnO, and ZrO2. For partly filled d shells both agree on U, but they split for near-empty or full shells. For oxygen states the first route gives large U near 10 electron volts, the second varies by system. Inter-site V splits most, under 1 versus near 3 electron volts.
arxiv-2512-17203:
Jiwoo Song, Daning Huang, and John Harlim tackle a hard forecasting problem: how to predict a complex system far into the future from data alone. Their answer, called DM-KRR, pairs kernel ridge regression with a kernel built from diffusion maps. A second piece is a dynamic-aware way of checking the model before use.

Because the kernel comes from the data, the method adapts on its own to the shape of the set where the system settles. It skips the step of rebuilding that shape by hand, a step that often hurts forecasts. Tests cover smooth shapes, chaotic systems, and large flows that change over space and time. In those tests DM-KRR beat leading random feature, neural network, and operator learning methods on both accuracy and data use.
arxiv-2512-17503:
Leonardo Bohac asks how much a quantum memory will reveal about the balance of bits stored inside it. The memory holds a yes-no table, and a reader may query it through a fixed quantum interface. The bias class of the table is its lean away from a half-and-half split, ignoring the mirror case where every bit flips.

Bohac proves a neat structure: for tables of exact weight, one query leaves the address register in a state with just two distinct directions. That structure yields exact formulas for the best possible measurement and its success rate. Mirror tables, it turns out, are perfectly indistinguishable in this setup, since they leave the same state up to a phase. The result sharpens what quantum read-only memory can and cannot tell.
arxiv-2512-17603:
Namhun Koo and three co-authors extend a family of near-perfect scrambling functions used inside ciphers. A good cipher function should change its output wildly for tiny input changes; APN functions are the gold standard for that resistance, and boomerang uniformity grades a second, subtler attack. The family here is a simple two-term power function over a finite field with odd characteristic.

Earlier work certified some members of the family under narrow conditions. The new condition is far broader: a single counting check on the field guarantees the function is locally-APN with boomerang uniformity at most 2. The team also maps the full difference patterns for three special members. Cipher designers gain a wider shelf of proven parts.
arxiv-2512-17803:
Gerard Marias Gonzalez and three coauthors examine a new Swiss policy that starts in 2026. Local Electricity Communities will let homes, solar owners, and storage operators in one town trade power over the public grid at reduced grid fees. Their case study looks at a rural community and asks who gains and who loses.

The study finds that such communities raise local use of solar power and bring modest savings. Bigger, more mixed groups match supply and demand best, and local solar works best at one to two times the load. Grid operators, though, lose 17 to 36 percent of distribution fee income, so rules will need to adapt.
arxiv-2512-18003:
Soumava Paul and four coauthors teach computers to cut a 3D object into named parts, like the legs, seat, and back of a chair. Past data sets name parts in clashing ways, which blocks steady training. Their method, ALIGN-Parts, treats naming as a matching task between shape pieces and word labels.

Shape clues, photo features from many views, and hints about how a part is used all feed the match, so new names can be added without new labels by hand. With human checks, the team merged three big data sets into one shared list of 1,794 parts. They also offer two new scores for judging named part work.
arxiv-2512-18303:
Giuseppe Desolda, Francesco Greco, Rosa Lanzilotti, and Cesare Tucci map the human side of cyber risk. Most breaches still start with a person: a clicked phish, a weak password, a wrong setting. Past studies treated each weak point as a lone, fixed trait. Their MORPHEUS frame instead treats 50 human factors as one moving, linked system.

Built on a thought, feeling, and action model plus a theory of how people assign blame, the frame charts 302 measured links among the factors. Twelve repeating pathways carry most of the action. A shelf of 99 tested survey tools lets teams measure their own weak points, and worked scenarios show how to turn the map into training and design fixes.
arxiv-2512-18603:
Joseph Samper Finberg examines a puzzle at the heart of relativistic quantum theory. Locally covariant quantum field theory respects Einstein causality: nothing signals faster than light. Yet entangled field states still show Bell-type correlations across spacelike separations. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, argues the tension is not about signalling at all. It is about covariance.

He proves a no-go theorem. No set of classical past variables can do three things at once. They cannot transform properly under spacetime embeddings, screen off the quantum correlations, and match the theory's statistics. Bell's local causality demands factorization given a common past. That demand clashes with the structure of the theory itself. The failure shows quantum correlations cannot be forced into a classical causal frame without cheating, by adding a preferred slicing of spacetime or hidden elements that break the symmetry.
arxiv-2512-18903: Valentin D. Ivanov outlines a plan to listen for alien lasers with European Southern Observatory telescopes. Most such searches so far have targeted radio waves. His white paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 for ESO's Expanding Horizons initiative, argues optical laser communication is a natural alternative for a ground-based observatory. Artificial monochromatic light would stand out as an unmistakable technosignature in the spectra that ESO's future high-multiplex facilities gather anyway. Ivanov also touts the outreach bonus: few programs capture public imagination like a search for other minds.
arxiv-2512-19203:
Prameshwar Thiyagarajan and Chad Williams argue that the usual score for intrusion detectors hides the attacks that matter most. Rare attacks drown in benign traffic, so plain accuracy can look high while every rare attack slips through. They test base and ensemble classifiers on the CSE-CIC-IDS2017 dataset, focusing on low-traffic attack kinds.

Two scores are compared head to head: accuracy, and the Matthews correlation coefficient, which weighs all four outcomes of a detector. Accuracy inflated results across the board. The correlation score exposed real gaps, and showed boosting ensembles catching more minority attacks. The authors urge imbalance-aware scoring as the standard for such research.
arxiv-2512-19303: Abdelhanid Hassairi and Gérard Letac extend a classic classification of probability families. Carl Morris united six familiar families by noting their variance is a polynomial of degree at most two in the mean. The authors take that program to several variables and to degree three, asking which natural exponential families on Euclidean space have simple cubic variance functions. Group actions and a multivariate Lagrange formula supply the tools. The work is the first part of the classification project.
arxiv-2512-19403:
Xiao-Bin Chen, Ruo-Yu Liu, and Xiang-Yu Wang test whether active galactic nuclei supply the universe's TeV neutrinos. IceCube has caught such neutrinos from the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068. The missing gamma rays there suggest the neutrinos are born in a compact, opaque zone near the black hole, likely the disk-corona.

Corona models tie neutrino output to X-ray output, since X-rays trace coronal activity. The team simulates future telescopes and asks whether the glow of diffuse neutrinos tracks the X-ray sky of these galaxies. They fold in how much of that X-ray flux current surveys resolve, and how much stays hidden in unresolved sources.
arxiv-2512-19703:
Siyuan Fu and nine co-authors present ASK, a tool for matching sounds to text. Most sound-text search trains two encoders on small batches of pairs. The authors say that habit creates a bottleneck. Rare sounds and unclear sounds never get checked against the wider world. Outside knowledge can help, but a fixed store of facts drifts out of sync with the growing model.

ASK attacks both flaws at once. Facts enter at several levels of detail to break the bottleneck. A live update step keeps the store in sync with the model. A weighting step filters out noisy matches by cross-checking sound against text. On many test sets and with several base models, ASK set new best scores. The authors report gains across the board.
arxiv-2512-19803:
Sumit Banik and Samuel Friot extend a toolkit for hard integrals in particle physics. Mellin-Barnes integrals are a standard route to multi-loop Feynman integrals. New methods based on conic hulls and triangulations work them out as series, step by step. But those methods took only integrands built from gamma functions. Real work, after an expansion step, grows polygamma functions too.

The authors show that polygamma terms can pass through the same hull machinery. The method finds the poles that feed each series. They then give two ways to finish the sums, one for straight contours and one for bent ones. All of it is coded in an updated Mathematica package, MBConicHulls. Tests on Feynman cases show the tool at work. The reach of the whole approach is now wider.
arxiv-2512-19903:
Kirk Vanacore and Rene Kizilcec benchmark how well today's language models can read a classroom. Their task is classifying instructional moves, the recognizable teaching actions inside authentic lesson transcripts, a simple-sounding job that matters for education technology built on top of these models. Six models were tested out of the box, under zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting, against expert-coded annotations.

Zero-shot performance was moderate. Comprehensive few-shot examples lifted state-of-the-art models substantially, the best configuration reaching a Cohen's kappa of 0.58 against expert coding, a moderate agreement level. Gains were uneven across move types, and better recall often arrived with more false positives. The authors conclude that foundation models show meaningful but limited capacity for interpreting educational discourse, with prompt design surfacing capability rather than creating reliability.
arxiv-2512-20103:
Mahfuzur Rahman and three co-authors measure a real satellite link end to end, in place of a simulated one. Non-terrestrial networks promise service for remote, maritime, and underserved places. Yet most studies judge them in theory or in simulation. Their SpaceNET testbed joins the Starlink low Earth orbit system to a Mininet emulation setup. The satellite segment stays genuinely live.

A two-way link tied a ground terminal in Blacksburg, Virginia to a ship terminal near Key West, Florida. The ship was a cruise vessel. The satellite acted purely as a transparent relay. Throughput and latency were measured for TCP and UDP traffic. Two user terminals were used, a smartphone and a small dish terminal. The results chart the limits and reliability of commercial LEO service. The platform can be extended to routing and mobility work.
arxiv-2512-20203:
Zhenlei Ye and co-authors present an automated repair approach for software vulnerabilities that uses large language models. Earlier tools focused only on what a patch should say. They often ignored where the patch belongs and never graded the candidate fixes produced during repeated attempts.

Their approach first predicts the locations that need patching, then scores each test-failing candidate patch. Scoring weighs whether a patch introduces new vulnerabilities and how much tainted code it covers. On a benchmark of forty real C and C++ vulnerabilities, the method produced more plausible and more correct patches than earlier systems. It repaired eight to thirteen more vulnerabilities than the strongest benchmarks tested.
arxiv-2512-20403:
Xuan-An Le, Minh-Nam Tran, and Son Nguyen shrink frontier language models into tiny ones without paying frontier prices. Direct distillation from a huge teacher to a sub-billion-parameter student fails twice over: the capacity gap is enormous, and teacher queries are expensive. Their approach, BRIDGE, inserts a mid-sized teaching assistant between them.

First the assistant learns from the teacher on a small, carefully chosen slice of data, picked for difficulty and diversity at zero query cost. Then the assistant freely generates rationales for the full dataset to train the student, after an instruction-tuning warm-up. Across medical, legal, and financial benchmarks, students gain substantially and close much of the gap to the teacher. BRIDGE uses a tenth of the teacher queries of direct distillation.
arxiv-2512-20603:
Shashank Mishra and Sayan Choudhury drive two halves of one spin system at different strengths and watch time itself split. Their platform is the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, a collective spin system with all-to-all interactions, under a periodic Floquet drive whose field differs between two regions.

Despite the shared interactions, distinct discrete time crystal orders settle into different parts of the system and coexist. Elsewhere in parameter space, a time crystal shares the system with a Floquet-synchronized or plain oscillatory phase, a chimera time crystal. When the two drive strengths are close, a tunable family of global time-crystal phases appears. The regimes survive in finite systems and the thermodynamic limit, making spatially structured driving a practical design tool.
arxiv-2512-20703:
Matthias Stierle, Karsten Kraume, and Martin Matzner argue that process mining has swallowed its own field. Data-driven analysis of business processes is older and broader than the fashionable term suggests, and the narrowing has pushed human and organisational questions off the radar. Their socio-technical proposal is process analytics, a perspective uniting the analysis with the organisation performing it.

The paper conceptualises process analytics and its dimensions by mixing inductive and deductive reasoning. A real-life case study from a large company implementing data-driven process analysis and automation tests the concept against practice. The contrast shows what a purely technical lens misses: stakeholders, responsibilities, and the analysis process itself shape what the data can say. Information systems researchers are the intended audience.
arxiv-2512-21003:
Xiangzuo Wu, Yuan Liu, and three co-authors recover what a scene is made of, from several photographs at once. Inverse rendering separates geometry, material, and lighting; single-view tools contradict each other across viewpoints, while optimization-based multi-view methods are too slow to scale. MVInverse instead predicts albedo, metallic and roughness maps, diffuse shading, and surface normals in one feed-forward pass. It swaps attention within and across views, so lighting interactions and material consistency are reasoned about together.

Synthetic training data alone carries poorly to real scenes, so a consistency-based finetuning stage learns from unlabeled real-world video. Benchmarks show state-of-the-art multi-view consistency and material and normal scores, with robustness in uncontrolled conditions. Seconds instead of per-scene optimization changes where inverse rendering can be used.
arxiv-2512-21403: Sen Zhang, Lei Yang, and their co-authors introduce a software framework for laying out quantum circuits across several linked quantum processors. The processors are connected by photonic links, meaning they exchange information with light. According to the authors, the framework is the first tool that compiles a single quantum circuit for such a distributed machine. It follows a divide-and-conquer design, splitting the circuit into parts, transpiling each part for its processor, and then assembling the pieces into layouts that can be both simulated and put into practice.
arxiv-2512-21503:
Sen Niu, D. N. Sheng, and Yang Peng give large-scale numerical evidence that doping a chiral topological phase produces a chiral superconductor. Their setting is the triangular Hofstadter-Hubbard model: electrons hop on a triangular lattice in a magnetic field while repelling each other on site. Earlier evidence came only from small, finite systems.

The authors advance a tensor-network method, fermionic projected entangled simplex states, that works directly in the thermodynamic limit. It captures superconducting long-range order and chiral topological order together, despite strong charge fluctuations. Undoped, the model shows a chiral spin liquid at intermediate interaction strength, separated from a Chern insulator by a Mott transition. Hole doping produces a uniform chiral superconductor whose pairing phase winds almost universally across a broad regime. The entanglement spectrum keeps the parent phases' chiral fingerprint, supporting the claim.
arxiv-2512-21803:
Ruochen Liu, Jingxin Liu, and their co-authors present CellMamba, a detector that finds individual cells in pathology images. Cell detection is hard for reasons: cells pack densely, classes differ subtly, and the background is cluttered. A useful detector must be accurate and light enough for high-resolution slides.

CellMamba is a one-stage detector built on a VSSD backbone. Its blocks pair a Mamba sequence model, or multi-head self-attention, with a coupling module that splits channels into two branches. One branch uses attention maps, the other a consensus map, and the three are fused adaptively to keep both local sensitivity and global consistency. A detection head merges features from several scales with learned weights, handling cells of different sizes. On the CoNSeP and CytoDArk0 datasets, CellMamba beat convolutional, transformer, and other Mamba baselines in accuracy while using a smaller model and lower inference latency.
arxiv-2512-22103:
Tomasz Denkiewicz and Hussain Gohar test a cosmology in which the universe's speeding expansion comes from entropy rather than a fixed cosmic constant. Their system starts from a general relation between mass and horizon size, which produces a matching general entropy. An entropic force on the cosmic horizon then drives the acceleration as an emergent effect.

Earlier work showed these models can mimic the standard model's expansion history. Here the authors add data on how structure grows, alongside supernova distances, baryon acoustic oscillations, and microwave background distance measures. A Bayesian comparison finds the entropic models preferred on the numbers over the standard scenario. The result supports entropy, not a basic constant, as the driver of late-time acceleration.
arxiv-2512-22303:
Noor Fatima, Hasan Faraz Khan, and Muzammil Behzad build a deepfake detector designed to survive deliberate attempts to fool it. Real deployments face counter-forensic tricks, recompression, warps, and re-graining meant to erase tampering traces. Their system pairs red-team training with randomized test-time defenses in a two-stream design: one stream reads semantic content, the other forensic residuals, and a small adapter fuses them.

A pyramid-style head also paints tamper heatmaps under weak supervision, guided toward face regions without pixel-level labels. Training applies the worst of several counter-forensic attacks per batch, while test-time jitters are aggregated into the final call. On standard and surveillance-style benchmarks, the detector kept near-perfect ranking across attacks, low calibration error, and graceful degradation under re-graining.
arxiv-2512-22403:
Chia-Yu Hsu and Shubhanshu Shekhar study how to test whether two data streams come from the same distribution when the tester chooses where to sample next. Data arrive from several heterogeneous sources; in each time slot the decision-maker picks one source and receives a paired sample. The aim is to decide as quickly as possible, with no assumptions about the distributions' shapes, a nonparametric setting where adaptive gains were earlier uncharacterized.

Their procedure mixes two instincts: favor sources that currently look most distinguishable, and keep exploring through a fading greedy rule. Observations feed a betting-wealth process that stays a nonnegative martingale if the distributions truly match, so the test rejects when wealth crosses a threshold. Type-I error is controlled, power reaches one, and expected sample size is bounded.
arxiv-2512-22503:
Xin Chen, Kang Luo, Yangyi Xiao, and Hesheng Wang present SCAFusion, a sensing model that helps lunar robots spot small rocks and meteor fragments. Reliable detection of such irregular obstacles is critical for roving and working on the Moon, yet earthbound multimodal methods lag off-world, with weak camera-LiDAR alignment and poor small-object sensitivity. Built on the BEVFusion system, SCAFusion adds four targeted components.

A smart adapter tunes the camera backbone cheaply, a contrastive alignment module tightens camera-LiDAR agreement, and an extra camera branch strengthens visual features. The centerpiece is coordinate attention designed around sections of the scene to lift small-target detection. On the nuScenes benchmark the model improved its baseline notably, and in simulated lunar environments built in Isaac Sim it reached about ninety-one percent mean average precision.
arxiv-2512-22703:
Angiolo Huamán shows that the optical response of atomically thin semiconductors can be captured by a strikingly small model. Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides lack inversion symmetry and are usually treated with heavy first-principles calculations using full Bloch wavefunctions. Around the band gap, though, their states are mostly d-orbital in character, and Huamán exploits that fact to reduce everything to three energy bands.

Within the minimal model, both the linear and quadratic optical susceptibilities are computed from the d-band structure alone. This simple approach reproduces first-principles results well up to about two electronvolts above the band gap. Huamán offers the model as a cheap starting point for adding many-body effects with only a few bands, where full calculations would be numerically expensive.
arxiv-2512-22903:
Chumeng Liang and co-authors tackle debugging of tabular logs, the structured records that track objects and events inside running systems. Inconsistencies in the real world show up as wrong log entries, but recent debugging tools lean heavily on large language models, which limits flexibility and scale. Their framework, GraphLogDebugger, instead rebuilds the system behind a log as a graph that evolves over time.

Objects and events become different kinds of nodes, linked by edges, so the log turns into a dynamic heterogeneous graph. On top of that representation, a comparatively simple dynamic graph neural network does the debugging. Experiments on real log datasets from computer systems and from academic publishing show the graph model debugs more accurately than language-model approaches. The result argues that recovering the right structure matters more than model size for this task.
arxiv-2512-23503:
Matthew Harper and Thomas Kerler write a 158-page monograph on quantum groups at roots of unity. These are the special parameter values where these algebraic structures develop a large center and rich ideal theory. They study skew-commutative subalgebras generated by primitive power elements inside Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum groups, classifying when those subalgebras are central and when merely commutative. Which case holds depends on the Lie type and the root's order modulo eight.

From ideals in those subalgebras they describe Hopf ideals of the whole quantum group, including a family indexed by Weyl group elements. The family arises both in building partial R-matrices and as vanishing ideals of Bruhat subgroups. Specializing to the longest element gives restricted quantum groups with no arbitrary choices. The treatment extends earlier results to even orders and non-simply laced types over minimal ground rings, with explicit PBW bases and new formulas.
arxiv-2512-23803:
Roman Buniy and Thomas Kephart construct Mermin devices for a family of entangled quantum states. A Mermin device packages the logic of Bell-type arguments: particles are measured in a few settings, and the pattern of outcomes either can or cannot be mimicked by preassigned instruction sets. The famous GHZ state famously defeats every instruction set. The authors ask the same question for W and Dicke states, other important entangled forms.

By bounding the expected values of Bell-Mermin operators, they generalize the three-qubit GHZ device to four qubits and build analogous devices for generalized Dicke states of three and four qubits. The GHZ and Dicke states of three qubits, and the four-qubit GHZ state, admit no instruction-set explanation. Among the four-qubit Dicke states, though, one allows such a description and the other does not, a split the authors establish exactly.
arxiv-2512-23903:
Charith Wickrema and nine co-authors report lessons from training vision models on a quadrillion pixels of satellite imagery. Foundation models for remote sensing lag those for ordinary photographs, because internet-scale data do not exist for high-resolution electro-optical satellite views. The scaling laws that guide text and natural-image training are poorly understood in this domain. The team used MITRE's Federal AI Sandbox to push far past prior scale.

They trained progressively larger vision transformer backbones on commercial satellite data, cataloguing successes and failure modes at peta-scale. Even at that size, performance behaved as if data, not model capacity, were the binding constraint. The practical conclusions target future programs: how to collect data, budget compute, and schedule optimization when building frontier-scale encoders for remote sensing, with an eye to bridging into further sensing modalities.
arxiv-2512-24003:
Hosein Rajabi, Zhejian Liu, Fereshteh Rajabi, and Martin Houde automate a measurement radio astronomers need for every fast radio burst. These millisecond cosmic flashes arrive smeared by their passage through ionized gas, and the dispersion measure quantifying that smearing encodes distance and plasma conditions. Estimating it by traditional dedispersion is computationally heavy and open to human bias.

As a proof of concept, the team trained three deep learning architectures, a plain convolutional network, a fine-tuned ResNet-50. A hybrid convolutional-recurrent model, on synthetic burst spectra modeled on the CHIME telescope's specifications. The hybrid model gave the most accurate and stable dispersion estimates at low computational cost across the tested range. Because the networks were trained on simulations, the authors note they can be fine-tuned on real CHIME observations and adapted to future facilities, aiming at real-time measurement in large burst surveys.
arxiv-2512-24103:
Bernd Bohnet and five colleagues test an idea about language models. Can a model improve its own plans by critiquing them? No outside checker would be involved. Earlier research had cast doubt on self-critique. Planning tasks give the idea a concrete test. Blocksworld is the main one. There, blocks must be stacked in the right order.

The base method starts from few-shot prompting. It then extends toward many-shot prompting. An iterative loop adds review and repair. The model corrects its own answers step by step. The gains were substantial. New best results were set for the model class studied. Logistics and Mini-grid sets improved as well. Strong baselines were beaten on both. The authors argue the method should transfer. Stronger models and richer search should benefit even more.
arxiv-2512-25003:
Lukas Anzeletti, Oleg Butkovsky, and Mate Gerencser give a broad approach for strong existence and uniqueness of random differential equations in Hilbert spaces with rough drift. Their formula combines a negative fixed map, a merely Holder steady drift, and noise shaped by a partial power of that map. Rough drift defeats standard Lipschitz arguments, mainly in infinite dimensions.

Under stated terms on roughness and noise, a unique strong answer is proved. Probability readers get tools for random partial differential equations with rough coefficients, common in fluid and surface models. A approach, rather than one-off tricks, lets later work reuse the same tools.
arxiv-2601-00303:
Yuxin Li leads six coauthors in building fake speech that sounds depressed while saying cheerful words. Speech can flag depression early in a cheap, gentle way. Popular datasets, though, tie sad content to sad labels. Models then learn a shortcut from word sentiment. Hidden depression breaks that shortcut in real life. People may sound flat while speaking bright lines.

Their three stage system first learns a depression voice mark. Adversarial training strips out speaker and content from it. A speech synthesizer then injects that mark at will. Severity slides smoothly along a prototype scale. The team builds an augmentation set from the mismatch. Depressed sound pairs with positive or neutral text. Three detector designs all gain in F1 score. Gains beat standard augmentation across the board. The tool also aids simulation where clinical data are scarce.
arxiv-2601-00403:
Lukas Liehr and Tomasz Szczepanski study phase retrieval, the task of recovering a signal when only sizes of measurements are known, not their phases. Their 2026 paper widens the problem: measurements may be observed only up to rotations drawn from a chosen set on the unit circle. That single setup covers both classic phase retrieval and sign retrieval, where only a sign can flip.

For countable rotation sets, the pair give a complete description of when recovery works, extending a known characterization. For cyclic sets, recovery matches the presence of certain recurrence relations. They apply this to exponential systems and obtain a sharp density rule. For uncountable sets, a topological split governs the answer, and sharp thresholds appear in finite dimensions.
arxiv-2601-00603:
Zihan Zhang and two co-authors tackle a hard question in a 2026 paper: how to judge cause and effect in network data. Two snags block the way. First, one unit's treatment can spill over to its linked peers. Second, some key drivers are never measured. The team build a frame that compares change over time between treated and untreated units. It also leans on stand-in measures that the treatment should not touch.

Graph neural networks, which learn from linked data, fill in the parts that are hard to model. The team show their setup can pick out both direct effects and spillover effects. Their estimates stay sound if one of two model parts is right. They prove the estimates settle into a known shape for large samples. Last, they apply the method to a policy case. They weigh how China's green credit policy shaped green innovation by firms.
arxiv-2601-00703:
Cory Fan and Wenchao Zhang revisit how camera images are reconstructed from sensor data. A camera sensor records only one color per pixel through a color filter array, and demosaicing rebuilds the full color image, a first step in every photo pipeline. Deep networks do this well, but the residual-style networks usually used avoid shrinking the image spatially, making them too expensive for phones.

The authors argue the opposite choice pays off: downsampling the image substantially inside an isotropic network can raise both efficiency and quality. They design simple fully convolutional networks to test that claim on demosaicing and on the joint task of demosaicing with denoising. If it holds, high-quality reconstruction becomes far more practical on mobile hardware.
arxiv-2601-00903: Joel Franklin, David Griffiths, and Darrell Schroeter examine a widespread misconception about magnetic field lines in static situations. Textbooks often leave the impression that these lines ordinarily form closed loops, yet the authors state that this is not generally true. The puzzle is why so many familiar examples do show closed loops, and what else is possible. Their article builds a taxonomy of magnetostatic field line shapes, cataloging the topologies the lines can take and identifying which configurations of electric currents generate each kind.
arxiv-2601-01003:
Amin Abyaneh and colleagues make diffusion-based robot policies more reliable by teaching their sampling process to contract. Diffusion policies learn from demonstrations and generate actions by reversing a noise process guided by a learned score function. In continuous control, small solver and score errors compound into failed actions, and the models are hungry for data.

Contractive diffusion policies reshape the sampling dynamics so nearby trajectories pull toward each other, a property called contraction. That pull damps the effect of numerical and modeling errors and reduces unwanted variance in the actions produced. The paper develops the theory in depth and gives a practical implementation, aiming to keep diffusion policies' flexibility in learning diverse behavior while making their execution dependable on real robots.
arxiv-2601-01103:
Abhinav Attri, Rajeev Ranjan Dwivedi, Samiran Das, and Vinod Kumar Kurmi present HAQAGen, a generative model that adds color to near-infrared images at any resolution. Near-infrared cameras see well in the dark, but their gray output is hard for people and some software to use. Turning it into natural color without blurring fine texture is the challenge.

The model balances several aims at once. A histogram-matching loss keeps the overall color mix realistic, while local hue and saturation guides steady the colors in each region. A Mamba backbone with texture-aware training guards fine detail, and an adaptive engine handles high-resolution inputs. Tests on four data sets, using many quality measures, show sharper textures and more natural colors than leading rivals. The method suits night imaging, surveillance, and other fields that rely on infrared views.
arxiv-2601-01203:
Seung-Yeon Ryoo studies the Winfree model, a classic setup for groups of oscillators, such as fireflies or heart cells, that pulse and influence each other. Sometimes the pulses die out entirely, a state called oscillator death, first seen in simulations decades ago. Ryoo asks how strong the coupling between oscillators must be to force the whole system to settle.

He proves that once the coupling passes twice the largest natural frequency in the group, the system converges for almost every starting state. The proof first ties the needed coupling to a measure of how synced the group is, then shows that measure cannot stay low forever for typical starts. A related argument shows death arrives in finite time except possibly on a tiny set of starts. He also checks that the results are sharp by counting the system's resting states. The work turns a numerical observation into a theorem.
arxiv-2601-01303:
Smith and 5 co-authors compare how three major firms label news stories for advertiser safety. Brands pay these firms to keep ads away from harmful content, and news pages are often flagged with care. When labels differ, ads can be blocked from sound reporting, costing publishers money they can ill afford.

The team gathered ratings for 4,352 articles on 51 news sites from DoubleVerify, Integral Ad Science, and Oracle. Labels often clashed across firms for the same story. The authors call for shared, open standards so choices are clearer and fairer. Their results show a quiet system with big effects on news funding.
arxiv-2601-01503:
The BESIII Collaboration, a large international team working at a Beijing electron-positron collider, measures how often a charmed baryon decays into twelve specific final states. These rates, called branching fractions, are basic data for particle physics, yet several were known only loosely. The team uses a double-tag method on collision data gathered at several energies near the pair-production threshold.

By counting events where both the baryon and its antimatter partner are reconstructed, they pin down absolute rates without relying on the total number produced. A joint fit across decay modes and energy points sharpens every number at once. Precision improves by a factor of two to three over earlier results, the best to date. The flagship decay into a proton, a kaon, and a pion lands at about six point six percent. The team also reports cross sections and form factors at record precision.
arxiv-2601-01603:
Tianshuo Yang studies matrix versions of Kloosterman sums, objects from number theory with uses in secure coding. Classic sums are well understood, but their matrix forms need new tools for computing values and for describing how those values spread out. Yang builds methods that use special polynomial functions to evaluate the sums efficiently.

Links to related L-functions, symmetric functions, and random matrix theory frame the statistical picture. Normalized values spread evenly in the same pattern seen for eigenvalues of random matrices from certain groups. Yang then uses that signature as a spectral test that can tell truly random sequences from ones hiding subtle algebraic bias, a check with clear value for cryptography.
arxiv-2601-01803:
Reinforcement learning agents can reach the same average score with wildly different behavior, and small training updates sometimes wreck a walking robot's gait. Dennis Jabs, Aditya Mohan, and Marius Lindauer trace part of the problem to the spread of returns an update produces, and propose correcting policy learning using the shape of the return distribution.

Rather than estimating that spread directly, which is expensive, their method reads skewness and kurtosis from a distributional critic and biases the advantage in the PPO algorithm, penalizing extreme tail behavior. In the Walker2D task the correction improved stability by up to seventy-five percent while keeping evaluation returns comparable. The idea offers a cheaper route to steadier, more transferable control policies.
arxiv-2601-01903:
Explaining a model's predictions feature by feature misses how features interact. The Faithful Shapley Interaction index is the one measure of interaction guaranteed to be faithful. But it is brutally expensive to compute. Ungsik Kim and Suwon Lee rebuild the computation with tensor-train methods borrowed from physics.

They prove the operator producing the index has a compact matrix product form. That yields a sweep algorithm. It uses far less time and memory than existing implementations. On six datasets the method ran up to two hundred eighty times faster than the baseline. It used about two hundred ninety times less memory. It scaled to twenty features, a million coalitions. Rivals failed there. Faithful interaction explanations become practical for larger models.
arxiv-2601-02003:
Horseshoe maps are the classic examples of chaotic dynamics. Abbas Fakhari, Maisam Hedyehloo, and Mohammad Soufi study a general version. Their method is a thermodynamic one. This paper is the first part of a two-part work.

The authors build a tailored Banach space with weighted norms. In it, the transfer operator has a spectral gap. That guarantees a unique physical measure. It also opens the door to limit theorems for the fluctuations. Under a virtually expanding condition, the measure is fully continuous. It is continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Its density has modest Sobolev regularity. The results give chaotic horseshoe dynamics a firm statistical footing.
arxiv-2601-02203:
Counting people through walls with WiFi signals preserves privacy where cameras cannot go. A model trained in one room usually fails in the next, though. Oliver Custance and three co-authors answer with two-stage learning. Self-supervised contrastive pretraining builds domain-invariant signal features first. Tiny adapter modules then adapt cheaply to a new space.

On their WiFlow dataset, the unsupervised approach reached a mean absolute error of under half a person. Only ten labeled examples were used. Supervised baselines fail at that task. A new Generalisation Index scores the approach near-perfectly. Adapter tuning matched full fine-tuning within one percent. It trained about ninety-seven percent fewer parameters. The system also set a state-of-the-art result on the public WiAR benchmark.
arxiv-2601-02303:
Nawatl is the most widely spoken Indigenous language of Mexico, with more than two million speakers and a written history reaching back to the fifteenth century. Juan-José Guzmán-Landa and five co authors work on a basic language technology task for it, telling its spoken varieties apart automatically. About thirty varieties are recognized, and spelling is not standardized, which makes the task harder.

Few computer resources exist for Nawatl at all, and even fewer for its separate varieties. The team applies machine learning and neural network methods to classify texts by variety. Reliable variety labels are a first step toward tools such as dictionaries, teaching aids, and translation that respect which form of the language a speaker actually uses.
arxiv-2601-02603:
Alec Kirkley, Helcio Felippe, and Federico Battiston ask how much of a hypergraph is really needed. A hypergraph records interactions among groups, not just pairs, which captures real systems more truly but costs more to read and compute than a plain network.

Their information theoretic framework measures how much extra structure a given hypergraph holds. It also identifies which orders of interaction, pairs, triples, and so on, are the critical ones, so redundancies can be removed while the essential higher order structure is preserved. The goal is a smaller, honest summary of a complex system.
arxiv-2601-02803:
Kasper Hagens and Cynthia Kop strengthen rewriting induction, a proof method for inductive theorems that began in equation based proofs and now serves program checking. Programs are turned into simply typed term rewriting systems with logical side conditions, where inductive theorems play the role of equality claims to prove. The soundness of the method rests on well founded induction, and the main hurdle is finding suitable well founded orderings on its own.

Naive approaches force every induction hypothesis to be oriented inside one well founded ordering, which imposes very strong termination demands and badly limits what can be proved. Bounded rewriting induction relaxes exactly that point. By bounding how the induction is applied, the termination requirements shrink to a minimum while the method stays sound. The change should widen the class of verification problems the tool can actually discharge.
arxiv-2601-03203:
Davi Valério and four co-authors make fairness audits of machine learning models honest about a hidden assumption: the causal graph they rely on. Counterfactual fairness judges bias through a causal model of how data were generated, but in practice that graph is rarely known for sure. Their procedure, CF-GU, folds the uncertainty about the graph into the audit itself.

The method bootstraps a causal discovery algorithm under domain knowledge constraints to produce a bag of plausible graphs. It measures the spread with normalized Shannon entropy, and reports confidence bounds on the fairness metrics. On synthetic data, different knowledge assumptions can support or refute an audit's conclusion. On the real COMPAS and Adult datasets, the method pinpoints well-known biases with high confidence, even from minimal domain knowledge.
arxiv-2601-03403:
Fitsum Gaim and Issayas Tesfamariam document how numbers are spoken in Tigrinya, a language with few computational resources. Their work formalizes the canonical rules for cardinal and ordinal numbers. It covers the conjunction system, the scale words for large values, and special cases for dates, times, and currency. From those rules they derive a formal algorithm for converting numerals into words. They also release an open-source implementation.

The authors test frontier large language models on the task. They find significant gaps in the models' ability to verbalize Tigrinya numbers correctly. That failure underlines why explicit rule documentation matters for low-resource languages. The resource is aimed at language modeling, speech synthesis, and accessibility tools. These serve Tigrinya-speaking communities.
arxiv-2601-03603:
Kaidong Feng and five co-authors run the first broad comparison of model families for forecasting mental health from smartphone data. Phones quietly record sleep, movement, and use patterns that often shift before stress, anxiety, or depression worsen. Most earlier work detects current problems; forecasting aims to warn early enough for just-in-time support to help.

Using the College Experience Sensing dataset, the largest long-running record of student mental health of its kind, they compared traditional learning, deep learning, and large language models. They varied time windows, feature detail, personalization, and class imbalance handling. Deep learning, especially a transformer model, performed best overall, while language models reasoned well about context. The study guides builders of early-warning tools toward designs that actually predict.
arxiv-2601-03703:
Lang Cao and seven co-authors improve group-based reinforcement learning for language models, the family that includes GRPO. In these methods, a group of sample answers is scored, but standard practice treats each answer as a flat sequence and gives every token the same advantage value. That wastes samples and rewards long, redundant chains of thought that add words without adding logic.

Their method, TreeAdv, makes the shared tree structure of grouped rollouts explicit. Sampling branches at high-uncertainty decisions while sharing calm stretches across rollouts. Advantages from full rollouts are then redistributed down to internal tree segments, so credit lands on the steps that diverged. The design targets both better exploration and fairer credit, two needs for training reasoning models efficiently.
arxiv-2601-04203:
Xueqing Wu and six co-authors introduce FronTalk, a benchmark for building website front ends through conversation with mixed feedback. In real front-end work, sketches, mockups, and marked screenshots carry design intent as much as words do. Multi-turn code tools, though, have barely been tested with such visual input.

FronTalk holds one hundred multi-turn dialogues drawn from real sites across news, finance, art, and more, each turn giving the same intent in text and in visual form. A web agent explores the built site to score both function and user experience. Across twenty models, two faults stand out: models forget and overwrite features built earlier, and visual feedback is hard to read, above all for open models. Their AceCoder baseline critiques each past instruction and cuts forgetting nearly to zero while lifting scores.
arxiv-2601-04503:
Anwesh Ray counts hidden symmetries in the arithmetic of cubic fields, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Every cubic field has a class group measuring how badly its numbers fail to factor uniquely, and the 2-torsion part of that group. The elements of order two — is a basic statistic whose average behaviour number theorists want. Ray adds a geometric condition: the field's shape, a point on a modular surface recording the shape of its ring of integers, must fall in a prescribed region.

Refining methods of Bhargava and Varma, he computes the averages exactly. Among fields with shape in such a region, the 2-torsion in the class group averages five-fourths for totally real fields and three-halves for complex ones. While the narrow class group's 2-torsion averages exactly two for totally real fields. Analogous results hold for cubic orders with prescribed local conditions at every prime.
arxiv-2601-04603:
Hoagy Cunningham and twenty-eight co-authors harden a production defence that keeps language models from being jailbroken, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Constitutional Classifiers screen conversations for attempts to extract forbidden help, but the first generation was expensive and examined replies in isolation, which attackers learned to exploit. The upgraded system reads each response in its full conversational context, closing that seam.

Three engineering ideas compound: a two-stage cascade lets cheap classifiers screen everything and escalates only suspicious exchanges. Small linear probes on the model's own activations are ensembled with external classifiers; and the exchange-level design cuts false refusals. The result, the authors report, is a forty-fold cut in computing cost at a refusal rate of a twentieth of a percent on production traffic. Over seventeen hundred hours of red-teaming found no universal jailbreak that extracted detailed answers to all eight target queries.
arxiv-2601-04703:
Yiqun Chen and seven co-authors split the searching agent in two so it stops tripping over its own notes, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agentic search systems let a language model interleave reasoning with tool calls for hard information seeking. a single monolithic agent produces bloated trajectories, gets only sparse end-of-task rewards that blur credit assignment, and trains unstably under search noise.

Their framework, M-ASK, divides the labour. Search Behavior Agents plan and execute the queries; Knowledge Management Agents aggregate, filter, and maintain a compact internal context the searchers then work from. Turn-level rewards supervise each decision and each knowledge update separately, stabilizing the coordination between the two roles. On multi-hop question answering benchmarks, M-ASK beats strong baselines on answer accuracy while training noticeably more steadily, which the authors attribute to each agent finally having one well-defined job.
arxiv-2601-04803:
Chenxi Deng, Emiel Lorist, and Mark Veraar prove a Fourier multiplier theorem for operator-valued functions in a 2026 mathematics paper. Fourier multipliers reshape a signal frequency by frequency, and the operator-valued kind acts on quantities living in Banach spaces, a broad class of measured spaces. Their result works across weighted Lebesgue, Besov, and Triebel-Lizorkin spaces.

The theorem assumes the multiplier's range is well controlled and that its bounded variation over dyadic intervals, doubling frequency bands, meets a summability condition. As the main tool, they prove a weighted variational Carleson inequality and an estimate of Littlewood-Paley-Rubio de Francia type. Such theorems underpin work on equations where solutions live in function spaces.
arxiv-2601-04903:
Plasma wakefield accelerators promise compact machines that surf charged bunches on waves in plasma. G. V. Sotnikov, K. V. Galaydych, and P. I. Markov address one practical obstacle in a 2026 paper: keeping drive and witness bunches high-quality and stable over long acceleration distances. Emittance, size, and energy spread all degrade if transport through the channel is poorly controlled.

Their proposal fills the transport channel with background plasma at lower density than the main accelerating plasma, forming a layered waveguide. The gentler environment should guide bunches more stably between stages. Better transport is a step toward wakefield machines serving high-energy physics and industry, where beam quality decides whether the compact promise is usable.
arxiv-2601-05403:
Zhiwei Liu and 24 co-authors built a 2026 benchmark that tests whether language models judge the same financial claim differently under different scenarios. Financial misinformation detection means deciding if a money-related claim is false. Such judgments can shift when a model is given a role, a region, or a persona.

Working with finance experts, the team created three kinds of scenarios and a dataset in English, Chinese, Greek, and Bengali. They then tested 22 mainstream models with that material. Pronounced biases appeared in both commercial and open-source systems. The benchmark gives researchers a shared way to measure a risk that matters for high-stakes financial advice.
arxiv-2601-05703:
Wiebe Vandendriessche and 4 co-authors present AIBoMGen, a 2026 proof-of-concept platform that automatically creates signed AI bills of materials during model training. An AI bill of materials extends the software version of that record, listing datasets, model details, and environment as a verifiable account of how a model was built.

The training platform acts as a neutral observer and root of trust, enforcing record creation for every job. Hashing, digital signatures, and attestation formats protect the records against tampering by dishonest model creators. Evaluation showed reliable detection of unauthorized changes to all artifacts, with negligible performance overhead. The authors position the system as groundwork for compliance with frameworks such as the European AI Act.
arxiv-2601-05803:
Congyao Zhang and 5 co-authors offer in 2026 a minimalist merger explanation for gas motions measured in the Coma galaxy cluster by the XRISM X-ray observatory. XRISM's precise velocity readings had sparked debate about what drives the cluster gas. Coma is a nearby, massive cluster long known to be disturbed.

Their scenario uses an off-axis minor merger caught early, when the infalling subhalo sits near its farthest point and its stripped tail has not yet mixed in. That single event reproduces a pronounced velocity gradient and a roughly uniform velocity spread in the core, and it also matches Coma's major X-ray shapes. A simple diagnostic based on velocity ratios is introduced for future cluster studies.
arxiv-2601-06103:
Leaked test items inflate model scores, but what happens after post-training? Muhammed Yusuf Kocyigit and 1 co-author run a controlled study on that question in a 2026 paper. Post-training, through supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, is now standard after the main training run.

Starting from clean checkpoints of two model families, they injected copies of math and coding test items into extended pre-training data. Contamination spikes faded with continued training. Both post-training methods resurfaced the leaked material, though differently: fine-tuning inflated only the leaked tasks, while the reinforcement method also inflated clean counterparts. Larger models memorized more under fine-tuning and generalized leakage more under reinforcement learning. The authors urge audits after post-training, not just before.
arxiv-2601-06303:
Moving a quantum state along a chain of qubits must be fast, before decoherence spoils it. Sofía Perón Santana and 3 co-authors compare two control design methods for that task in a 2026 paper. External control pulses, applied step by step, force the chain's evolution toward the target.

One approach uses a genetic algorithm, evolving candidate control sequences toward better performance. The other uses a reinforcement learning variant that learns a control policy. The genetic algorithm matched the learning method's short transmission times and surpassed its fidelity. Under noisy pulses, however, the learned policies proved more robust. The authors map the regimes where each method suits the job best, giving practitioners a practical guide.
arxiv-2601-06903:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Bingnan Xiao and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers Divergence-Based adaptive aggregation for byzantine robust federated learning. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Inherent client drifts caused by data heterogeneity. As well as vulnerability to Byzantine attacks within the system, hinder effective model training and convergence in federated learning (FL).

The work presents two new frameworks, named DiveRgence-based Adaptive aGgregation (DRAG) and Byzantine-Resilient DRAG (BR-DRAG). To mitigate client drifts and resist attacks while expediting training. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07403:
Burcu Gurbuz and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on dengue, a fever spread by mosquitoes. Dengue comes in more than one strain. A first bout with one strain can change how a second bout plays out. The authors build a math model with two strains at once. The model is deterministic, so its path is fixed by its rules, not by chance.

The model sorts people by stage: some are in a first bout, and some in a second. A short shield from the first bout can guard against the next strain for a time. But a past bout can also make a second bout worse, an effect called antibody-dependent enhancement, or ADE. Death is more apt in a second bout, and the model tracks that risk. It also tracks mosquitoes that bear both strains at once.
arxiv-2601-08003:
Weiyue Li and colleagues improve creative writing by language models with a peer review trick. Models often struggle with creative generation. Multi-agent frameworks that help reasoning can paradoxically hurt creativity by homogenizing content. Their system, LLM Review, implements blind peer review. Agents exchange targeted feedback but revise independently. Divergent creative paths survive the process. Their 2026 preprint describes the framework.

Blind review borrows the guardrails of academic publishing. Reviewers comment without knowing whose draft they read, and authors keep control of revisions. Independence prevents the group from collapsing onto one voice. Targeted feedback still fixes weak passages. The paper serves scholars in creative AI and multi-agent systems. It shows a social structure, not a bigger model, as the source of better writing.
arxiv-2601-08103:
Abby Bault, Andrei Cuceu, Julien Guy, and many collaborators measure baryon acoustic oscillations in a new tracer. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses data from the second release of the DESI survey. Baryon acoustic oscillations are a frozen sound-wave pattern that works as a cosmic ruler.

The team cross-correlates triply ionized carbon absorption with quasar and emission-line galaxy positions. The sample holds 2.5 million quasars plus a large galaxy set. Carbon forest absorption traces gas between galaxies along quasar sightlines. Measuring the pattern there extends cosmic distance checks to gas that most surveys ignore, which helps pin down how the universe expands.
arxiv-2601-08403:
Abhijnan Nath and four co-authors propose Owen-Shapley policy optimization for generative search models. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses reinforcement learning for personalized recommendation. Standard methods like GRPO use sparse, sequence-level rewards, which blur credit assignment.

When a long answer succeeds, no one knows which tokens drove the success. The gap worsens when models must infer latent user intent from vague language without ground truth labels. Such reasoning rarely appears in pretraining data. Owen-Shapley optimization borrows Shapley value ideas to spread credit more fairly across tokens. Fairer credit could train search assistants that learn from whole-answer rewards without guessing.
arxiv-2601-08503:
Aditya Kumar and co-authors present Temporal Fusion Nexus, an embedding model for clinical data after kidney transplant. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins irregular time series with unstructured clinical narratives. The model is multimodal and task-agnostic, so one embedding can serve many outcomes.

The team analyzes a retrospective cohort of 3,382 transplant patients. Three outcomes are studied: graft loss, graft rejection, and mortality. Irregular lab timing and free-text notes usually force separate pipelines. A fused embedding could give clinicians a single patient summary that many risk tools can reuse. Transplant care generates exactly the messy mixed data this model targets.
arxiv-2601-08603: Carlos Antonio Pinzon and co-authors estimate true data distributions collected under randomized response. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies a protocol for categorical data with local differential privacy guarantees. Randomized response lets people answer surveys while plausibly denying their true answer. Big technology companies have used it as a building block for collecting app and web user data. Recovering the true distribution from noisy responses is the statistical core. Better estimators mean firms can learn population trends without learning any person's answer.
arxiv-2601-08703: Kaivalya Rawal and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on whether short accounts of a model's logic can tell like models apart. A Rashomon set holds many models that score much the same. Accounts of each model's logic should help a user pick which one to deploy, by showing how their acts differ. But such accounts vary with the explainer tool used. So they need tests of their own. The authors test how well accounts split models in a set. The work counts for fields under strict rules.
arxiv-2601-08803:
Carina Hausladen, Christoph Engel, and Marcel Schubert study why gifts in a shared pot game shift so much. In the game, each player can give to a group pot that helps all. First round gifts can be read as a sign of how fair a player likes to be. But gifts jump up and down in later rounds in ways that view can not explain.

The team uses a large set of plays from close to three thousand players. They bring in a method that works back from acts to hid aims. Two new steps help them track aims that change over time. A reader in social science gets a fresh way to read group gifts. It splits firm traits from fast shifts in mood or plan.
arxiv-2601-09003:
Melody Molander gives a drawn rule set for a deep algebra tied to the E7 shape. The algebra codes how lines and zones can join in a plane web used in quantum work. A known plan, called the Kuperberg program, seeks drawn rules for such algebras. Rules let a user shrink any web to a count by set steps.

She gives the rules for the affine E7 case, in its plain, unshaded form. She then proves the shrink plan, called the jellyfish algorithm, works and hits all counts. That proof was the hard part of the case. A reader in algebra gets a closed case in a long program, with rules they can use.
arxiv-2601-09103:
Haijian Shao and four co-authors fix a flaw in heart wave sorting: some beats are rare. A heart wave, or ECG, is a trace of the heart's spark. Tools sort traces by the ill they show. Rare ills have few train traces, so tools learn them poor. A sick folk with a rare ill is then most prone to a wrong call.

The team grows rare traces in two ways. A wave shift tool bends known traces in sound ways. A fusion step then mixes traits across beat types. Both add rich, fair train cases for rare types. A reader in heart tech gets a data fix for a class gap that can cost lives if left.
arxiv-2601-09203:
Ao-Xiang Liu and Cong-Feng Qiao push tests of quantum links past the first order. A link here means two bits share a state that no lone bit can hold. Most tests check a mean, the first count of that state. High counts, such as spread and skew sums, hold more of the tale. They have been left near bare by past tests.

The team works on linked hyperon pairs, heavy bits that can be made in vast sets in charm decays. They set a new form of a classic test for those high counts. It uses sums of joint marks, not just means. A reader in core physics gets a way to hunt links where past tests were blind.
arxiv-2601-09403:
Yu-Ming Yang, Xiao-Jun Bi, Long Wang, and Peng-Fei Yin ask what ultralight dark matter does to small star systems. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies compact stellar systems living inside halos of this wavy dark matter. Waves in the dark matter field make the halo's gravity flicker over time.

That flickering heats the stars, pumping energy into the system step by step. Small systems are often used to set tight limits on ultralight dark matter for this reason. Yet systems far smaller than the dark matter's wavelength are still poorly explored. The authors ask when heating puffs a system apart and when it instead collapses.
arxiv-2601-09603:
Petros Vavaroutsos, Theodoros Palamas, and Pantelis Vikatos seek a leaner way to train music-understanding models. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses self-supervised learning with a random quantizer, aimed at linear complexity. Foundation models work well but carry hundreds of millions of parameters, which makes them costly to train and run.

Self-supervised learning lets a model learn from unlabeled audio, a big plus for music. A random quantizer turns sound features into simple codes the model can predict. Keeping the cost linear in input size keeps long tracks affordable. The work targets music tasks where labs cannot match the budgets of big tech.
arxiv-2601-09803:
Mariam Bouhmadi-López and Carlos G. Boiza model dark energy as a field that may already be ringing. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats a generalized axion-like quintessence field. The field rolls down its potential as the universe expands.

Depending on its mass and starting point, the field may still be sliding toward the minimum or already oscillating around it. Those two regimes need distinct treatments of cosmic perturbations. The split matters for matching the model to data. An oscillating dark energy would leave different fingerprints in the cosmic microwave background than a slowly rolling one.
arxiv-2601-10003:
Sanghyeok Choi, Woosang Jeon, Kyuseok Yang, and Taehyeong Kim build webs of facts from raw text. A fact web links things by typed ties. Such webs back search and smart tools. AI built webs face a hard trade off.

Cast the net wide and the web breaks into loose bits. Pull it tight too soon and facts are lost. The team made SocraticKG to ease that trade. It first turns a text into pairs of asks and replies. Those pairs lay out the sense of the text. Only then does it pull out the typed ties. The step keeps more facts while the web stays joined.
arxiv-2601-10203:
Zheng Zhao and co authors speed up the tune of quantum chips. Before a chip runs, its qubits must be set to the right tones. Tones that clash cause cross talk. The tune step is a known slow point for large chips.

The team recast a known tune tool in fresh math terms. The Snake tool, they show, is a form of block descent. That fact gives the tool a firm base. They then built a new tune plan that uses the chip graph. It tunes blocks with the graph in mind. The aim is a faster tune with fewer clashes.
arxiv-2601-10803:
Woorak Choi and co-authors present radio views of NGC 4522, a galaxy being stripped by ram pressure. As the galaxy plows through the Virgo cluster's hot gas, that gas pushes its own gas out. The team used the Very Large Array at two bands, three and ten gigahertz. The maps reach fine scales of a few hundred parsecs.

The study reads the galaxy's radio continuum, its spectral index, and its magnetic field under this battering. Ram pressure can compress fields on one side and stretch them on the other. Watching that struggle shows how cluster weather reshapes a galaxy's magnetism and star birth. The work speaks to how environment, not just inner life, drives galaxy evolution.
arxiv-2601-10903:
M. R. Norman examines superconductivity tied to the Slater mode in KTaO3 heterostructures. At the interface of KTaO3 with other oxides, a two-dimensional electron gas can superconduct. Its transition temperature is about ten times higher than in its cousin SrTiO3. The transition also depends strongly on which way the interface faces.

Norman tests whether the Slater mode, a particular lattice vibration, drives the pairing. Orientation dependence is a clue a good theory must match. If a single mode explains both the high temperature and the orientation effect, the mechanism comes into focus. The work bears on the hunt for the rules behind interface superconductivity, a puzzle with device stakes.
arxiv-2601-11003:
Shivaksh Rawat, Samyobrata Mukherjee, and Gennady Shvets generate lasting nanoscale magnetization in all-dielectric metasurfaces. A metasurface is a thin sheet patterned to steer light. When such a sheet changes in time, it forms a boundary in time for guided waves. Changing the sheet fast can shift a wave's frequency as it travels.

The authors use light-injected free carriers to write lasting magnetization at very small scales. A magnetic pattern that stays after the light leaves could store data or set a wave's path. The work joins optics with magnetism at scales where both are hard to control, and points to sheets that remember what light wrote on them.
arxiv-2601-11103:
Minju Park, Seunghyun Lee, Juhwan Ma, and Dongwook Yoon present AI Twin, a speaking practice system for ESL learners. AI conversation tools let learners practice English speaking. Most rely on explicit correction, which can break the flow and dent confidence. AI Twin takes a gentler path grounded in language acquisition research and motivational psychology.

The system rephrases a learner's utterance into more fluent English. It then delivers that better version in the learner's own voice, a self-clone of a better me. Hearing oneself speak well can motivate without shaming. The work, shown at CHI 2026, serves language learners who need practice that builds fluency and nerve together.
arxiv-2601-11203:
Riku Kuze, Kunihito Ioka, Kohta Murase, Shigeo Kimura, and Kohei Inayoshi study odd red galaxies. Their 2026 preprint looks at Little Red Dots at high redshift. These small, red systems were found by the James Webb Space Telescope. They sit far back in time, at redshift four to seven.

Their light shows broad emission lines from fast gas. Yet they lack the X-ray and radio signs one would expect. That odd mix hints at black holes that feed in dense gas. The gas wrap could hide the holes from most probes. The team asks if such hid holes could also emit neutrinos. If so, these dots would be a new source class for those ghost particles.
arxiv-2601-11303:
David Feldstein-Bofill and six coauthors tune how Cooper pairs tunnel in a qubit. Their 2026 preprint deals with a hybrid superconducting qubit. Superconducting circuits get their key trait from one relation. The Josephson energy-phase relation gives them strong nonlinearity.

That relation holds more than the basic cosine term. Higher harmonics can appear, as cosines of multiples of phase. Each harmonic marks pairs that tunnel together as a group. The count in the group sets the parity of the process. Parity here means whether that group count is odd or even. The team shows control of which parity rules the device. That control is a new knob for qubit design.
arxiv-2601-11403:
Michael Eides and Vladimir Yerokhin compute levels of bound states in QED. Their 2026 preprint uses the energy-momentum trace for the task. Some bound states depend on more than one mass at once. Muonic hydrogen is their worked example of such a system.

In muonic hydrogen, a muon orbits a proton like an electron. Its energy levels depend on both the electron and muon masses. The team writes the levels as matrix elements of one operator. That operator is the trace of the QED energy-momentum tensor. One-loop corrections to the levels follow from that form. The trick turns a hard multi-scale problem into clean algebra. It may serve other exotic atoms with mixed masses.
arxiv-2601-11503:
Viren Tyagi, Mike Pols, Geert Brocks, and Shuxia Tao track halide motion in perovskites. Their 2026 preprint studies mixed-halide crystals and heterojunctions. Perovskites are prized materials for solar cells and lights. Halide defects inside them guide how ions move around.

That motion sets the pace of halide mixing in the crystal. It also sets how fast phases separate into unlike zones. The team studies diffusion of two defect kinds. Halide vacancies are missing atoms that hop through the lattice. Interstitials are extra atoms squeezed between lattice sites. The test crystal mixes iodine and bromine in CsPb halide. Knowing both paths helps design stable perovskite devices.
arxiv-2601-11703:
Marco Chianese and six coauthors probe super-heavy dark matter with gamma rays. Their 2026 preprint refines lifetime constraints on such particles. Super-heavy dark matter spans a vast mass range here. Masses run from 10 to the 7 up to 10 to the 15 GeV.

Decaying particles of that kind would shed gamma rays. Ultra-high-energy gamma-ray data can catch that faint glow. No glow at a set level bounds how fast they decay. The team analyzes UHE gamma-ray data for those bounds. Refined constraints narrow where such dark matter can hide. The work tests a dark sector far above collider reach.
arxiv-2601-11803:
Lee D. Feinberg, Breann N. Sitarski, Michael W. McElwain, and a large NASA-linked team set out the plan for a future space scope. The Habitable Worlds Observatory is built to search for life on far worlds. The team call it the first scope designed for that task.
