They also frame it as a broad tool for star and galaxy science. Their study weighs early design picks and the tech work still needed. It maps the trade space, where cost, risk, and skill pull in unlike ways. The plan guides the next steps toward build and launch.
arxiv-2601-12003:
Angel Y. He and David Parker make checks for shared stochastic games more sound when odds are not known in full. Such games model agents that act at once, plan ahead, and face chance. They suit self-run systems that share roads, grids, or air.

Real use rarely gives exact odds for each move. Past tools need those exact odds, which is a weak spot. Their robust checks work over a range of odds in place of one set. That makes proofs of safe acts more fit for the real world.
arxiv-2601-12203:
Antonella M. C. Torrisi, Inês Nolasco, Paola Sgadò, Elisabetta Versace, and Emmanouil Benetos study chick calls after embryonic exposure to VPA. Young chicks use calls to signal state and needs. Hand coding of calls is biased, slow, and misses much of the full call set.

Their computational study reads the calls by machine. VPA exposure before hatch is the test factor. Machine reads can show if such exposure shifts call form or use. The work links early exposure to later social signals in birds.  Calls are a rich sign of chick health and mood.
arxiv-2601-12303:
Shizhan Gong, Xiaofan Zhang, and Qi Dou explain image models via concepts found after training. Deep models win at image tasks, yet their opacity blocks use in critical fields. Concept methods explain calls in human terms in place of raw pixels.

Past post-hoc and built-in concept tools have flaws: weak concept links, non-visual concepts, or high hand cost. Their tool finds concepts by sparse decomposition of visual traits. Found concepts are visual by design. That should make image AI calls more clear to experts.  Sparse parts keep each concept small and clear.
arxiv-2601-12403:
Shu Cai, Ya-Feng Liu, Jun Zhang, and Qi Zhang study a wireless setup that sends two streams at once. A main sender beams common data to many main receivers over broadcast signals. At the same time, a smart surface helps a backscatter device send its own data to a second receiver. The surface can be tuned, which adds a new degree of control.

The setup is called a decoupled symbiotic radio system, boosted by the tunable surface. The two streams share the same airwaves, so they must not spoil each other. Work of this kind aims to squeeze more use from scarce spectrum. The paper was accepted to a major signal processing venue for 2026.
arxiv-2601-12703:
Andrew Gordon and five co authors at Timaeus borrow a method from physics to study language models. Spectroscopy infers internal structure by measuring how a system responds to perturbations. They apply that principle to neural networks. Their perturbation upweights one token in a given context, shifting the data distribution slightly.

The response is measured through susceptibilities, covariances between component level observables and the perturbation. These are computed over a localized Gibbs posterior, in the language of the work. A susceptibility map could show which parts of a model care about which tokens. That would give interpretability a tool with roots in statistical physics. The team frame this as a step toward a spectroscopy of models.
arxiv-2601-13003:
Safaa Menssouri and El Mehdi Amhoud study how to spot rare cyber attacks in networks of flying devices. These networks, called the Internet of Flying Things, support tasks such as air watch and smart travel. They also face real risk, since attacks can harm private data and safe use.

The authors put forward PrivFly, a self-taught system that aims to guard privacy while it hunts for rare attacks. They note three hard parts of the task. Attack data is badly skewed, with few rare cases. Privacy must be kept. Older tools often miss the rare but harmful threats. Readers get a clear view of why rare attack search in such networks is hard.
arxiv-2601-13303:
Minh Le and Phuong Cao check if cut down neural nets stay safe in a provable way. Formal proof of net acts is a must for high stakes use. Such use spans surgery bots to NASA craft that drive on their own. Yet proof cost for big nets blocks wide use.

Pruning cuts a net by drop of weak links. The team asks what prune shares do to local proof of calm. A calm proof says small input shifts cannot flip the out put. By prune rate, they map where proofs hold and where they break. For safety teams, the map helps pick a prune rate that saves cost with no loss of proof.
arxiv-2601-13603:
Wylliam Cantin Charawi and co-authors work on turning raw 3D data into clean mesh shapes in 2026. Tools like Marching Cubes build meshes fast and are used in many pipelines. Their trainable forms, though, often give weak mesh quality. That flaw caps the worth of meshes rebuilt from point clouds or images by learning systems.

The team puts forward DCCVT, a trainable take on clipped centroidal Voronoi tessellation. In plain terms, space is split into cells, and each cell is clipped to the shape. Such clipped cells carry strong math backing and tend to yield finer meshes. The aim is mesh output that learning tools can tune end to end.
arxiv-2601-14503:
Wouter Termont and Esteves Beatriz examine European digital identity in this 2026 paper. Recent European efforts center on the EUDI regulation and its OpenID architecture. The authors say these efforts aim high but start from a narrow, ill-defined view of authentication. From a broader, more grounded view of the term, they identify several issues.

The issues sit in the OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP protocols. They name insecure practices, plus static and subject-bound credential types. A limited query language also restricts the design. The authors say these limits confine the system to classic credential exchange cases, which existing solutions like OpenID Connect already support.
arxiv-2601-14603:
Jingru Li, Yibo Fan, and Huan Li speed up language model training in this 2026 paper. Large language models perform well across natural language tasks, yet pretraining is computationally demanding. Optimizer efficiency is thus an important practical concern. Muon is an optimizer that accelerates pretraining via orthogonal momentum updates. Those updates act as a matrix analogue of the element-wise sign operator.

The team presents Variance-Adaptive Muon. It adds NSR-modulated and variance-scaled momentum to the base method. In plain terms, the step size adapts to how noisy the gradients are. Readers get an optimizer aimed at cutting the cost of the most expensive phase in building a model.
arxiv-2601-15003:
Bartosz Bieganowski and Daniel Strzelecki study a nonlinear scalar field equation with a harsh twist at the origin. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with an inverse-square potential term. That term carries the critical strength, the largest value of its kind that the math allows.

The question is one of multiplicity. The authors ask how many distinct solutions the equation can have. The equation is set on all of space with the origin removed. A general nonlinear term drives the field. Results of this kind sort out when a field can settle in more than one way.
arxiv-2601-15203:
L. Einramhof, L. Bugnet, and co-authors read the magnetic past of dead stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with white dwarfs, the dense remains of stars like the Sun. Strong, large-scale magnetic fields show at the surface of only the oldest white dwarfs.

That pattern hints at a hidden field inside the star. The field may rise slowly to the surface over time. Strong fields have also been gauged by asteroseismology inside red giants, the stars white dwarfs come from. The authors use those clues to reconstruct the hidden field's long history.
arxiv-2601-15303:
Liang Chen explains why China's platform giants earn thin margins despite huge market shares. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with platform pricing in concentrated markets. The giants hold over sixty percent of their core segments, yet margins stay compressed for a decade.

Standard theory predicts a different end. Either the weaker firm exits, or the survivors raise prices toward monopoly levels. Chen builds a dynamic theory of ecosystem competition. Cross-market subsidization plays a central part: profits in one market fund low prices in another, and the long price fight never settles.
arxiv-2601-15403:
Adam LaClair and Jason McCullough test a conjecture about when a graph's edge ideal has a purity property. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with binomial edge ideals in positive characteristic. Matsuda defined weakly closed graphs and asked when these ideals are F-pure.

Matsuda proved that weakly closed ideals are F-pure in positive characteristic. He conjectured two things. In characteristic two, every F-pure example should come from a weakly closed graph. And every such ideal should be F-pure when the characteristic is large enough. The authors take up both of those open claims.
arxiv-2601-15503:
Rishit Chatterjee and Tahiya Chowdhury forecast lake water quality with machine learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Volunteers do much of the lake monitoring behind their data. That yields seasonal time series with many gaps. Ice cover blocks access in winter. Bad weather and simple human error add more holes. Gaps make forecasting and early warning of algal blooms hard.

The pair study Secchi disk depth, a classic measure of water clarity. Their data cover a rich subset of 30 lakes. The records span three decades of in-person sampling across Maine lakes. Learning from gappy records is the core challenge here. A method that copes with missing data could help lake groups act sooner. Early word on blooms protects swimmers, wildlife, and drinking water alike.
arxiv-2601-15603:
Yi Yu and five co-authors study estimation in large network systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Hierarchical Bayesian models are now common for such systems. They treat each unit's parameters as draws from a shared distribution. A hyperparameter governs that distribution. Theory for these estimates has lagged practice, though. In particular, guarantees as system size grows have been missing.

One fear stands out. Hyperparameter estimates might diverge as networks get larger. That would undercut the model's reliability at exactly the scales where it is used. The authors give a nonasymptotic scaling guarantee, per the title. It covers inhomogeneous systems with weak dependence between units. For data scientists who model big networks, such guarantees mark when trust is earned.
arxiv-2601-15703:
Jiaxin Zhang, Prafulla Kumar Choubey, and Kung-Hsiang Huang tackle trust in AI agents in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents now reason over long horizons with real skill. Early errors can poison that whole run, though. The authors name this the spiral of hallucination. Small epistemic mistakes propagate and cannot be undone. Existing tools split into two camps, each with a flaw.

Uncertainty methods act as passive sensors. They flag risk but do not fix it. Self-reflection methods try to fix errors, but their corrections can be aimless. The title names the authors' aim: agentic uncertainty quantification that does more. A system that measures doubt and acts on it could stop spirals early. For long agent runs in real work, that combination is the missing piece.
arxiv-2601-16003:
Yunan Wang, Chuxiong Hu, and Zhao Jin solve a control problem exactly in a 2026 arXiv paper. Time-optimal control drives a system to its target as fast as possible. Their system is a triple integrator, a chain of three integrations. Full box constraints bound its state and input. The problem is fundamental and widely applied in industry. Motion control for machines and vehicles is a typical home.

Hard cases have resisted clean solutions. Asymmetric constraints, moving boundary conditions, and active position constraints all complicate the answer. The authors derive time-optimal switching surfaces for this setting. Switching surfaces tell the controller when to flip its input. An exact surface means fast, provable control. The paper was accepted by the American Control Conference, per the record.
arxiv-2601-16203:
Usoskin and coauthors rebuild sun spot cycles of the first thou years CE. Their 2026 preprint uses carbon based proxy data for past sun acts. Direct views of sun acts start in the year 1610. Past that, teams turn to trace data kept in wood and ice. New carbon tests are now fine to pick out the known sun cycle of near eleven years.

The team uses that fine grain to rebuild cycles far back. Clear cycles show the sun kept its beat in that era. They also show how strong each past beat was. That past helps test sun models over long spans. It links earth trace data to sun acts of old.
arxiv-2601-16403:
Zhaochun Li and coauthors set theory for how RLHF learns past its train set. Their 2026 preprint deals with learn from human feed back. That path, called RLHF, is now the main way to align models. It works well in tests, but why it holds on new prompts is less clear. High size prompts make that why hard to pin down.

The team builds maths for spread of skill to new cases. Spread bounds rest on train size and model class traits. Firm bounds would guide how much feed back teams must buy. They would also flag when align may fail on new ground. The work firms up a much used train path.
arxiv-2601-16503:
Wei Zhu builds a test set for search backed builds in the med field. His 2026 preprint, named MRAG, deals with search plus build tools. Such tools have spread fast in science and ward QA work. Yet the med field lacks a full test for their worth. Gaps in tests hide where the tools fail on med asks.

MRAG spans a wide range of med ask types. Each type checks search grade and build truth as one. Firm scores let teams weigh med tools fair and fast. They also show which ask types need more work. The work gives the med field a shared test base.
arxiv-2601-16603:
Ke Xue and four coauthors use a Mamba gaze that looks all ways for speech split. Their 2026 preprint deals with split of mixed speech to lone voices. Mamba, a state space model, now rivals coders for speech work. It runs long chains at straight cost, not square cost. Past Mamba speech tools still missed acts that span all dirs.

An all way gaze lets the model weigh past and next as one. Joint weight should lift split grade on hard mixes. Speech split backs aids, notes and call tools in real rooms. The work tests all way Mamba on split tasks. It seeks grade gains with no loss of speed.
arxiv-2601-16803:
Carolin Holtermann, Florian Schneider, and Anne Lauscher test image bots across tongues. Such bots turn words into shots. Most users type in English. The same ask in a new tongue should give the same shot. Yet bots oft swap sense for surface cues. They paint stock scenes tied to the tongue's home land.

Their 2026 preprint names this flaw surface-over-semantics. It gauges how oft bots pick stock traits over true sense. The flaw can spread trite views of lands and folks. Clear gauges push bot makers to serve all tongues fair. The work aids fair AI for a world of many tongues.
arxiv-2601-16903:
Sk Jeesun and Anirban Majumdar chase light dark matter with help from cosmic rays. Big tanks now curb heavy dark bits to near the neutrino fog. Yet light dark bits slip past those tanks. Cosmic rays can kick halo dark bits to high speed. Kicked bits can then trip a tank's eye. Their 2026 preprint reads fresh LZ tank data for such kicks.

The LZ tank's 2025 data sets the stage for the read. The team maps what cross rates the data allow. Light bits gain a test they long lacked. Null marks here trim the space for dark tales.
arxiv-2601-17103:
Pascaline André and a large team check how firm scan AI scores truly are. A score with no range can look more firm than it is. Ranges, called confidence intervals, show that doubt. Their 2026 preprint runs a large-scale check of those ranges. It spans many scan tasks and AI tools. The aim is sound doubt marks for care use.

Hospitals need doubt marks before they trust a tool. A tool that tops a chart may tie with the next in truth. Wide ranges flag scores that need more data. The check sets a base for fair score claims. It aids rules for AI in clinics.
arxiv-2601-17203:
Scott Friedman, Sonja Schmer-Galunder, Anthony Chen, and Jeffrey Rye tie word-code slant to real pay and role gaps. Text bots learn word codes from news and posts. Those codes oft lean by sex in clear ways. Their 2026 preprint sets code lean next to real-world gaps. Many lands' texts and gaps join the check. The aim is to see if code lean tracks true gaps.

A track would mean codes mirror each land's state. A gap twixt them would flag bot-made bias. Such checks help teams clean text bots for fair use. They span tongues and lands in one frame.
arxiv-2601-17503:
Laura Bernard, Tamanna Jain, and Stavros Mougiakakos compute how binary stars scatter in scalar-tensor gravity. These theories add a scalar field to Einstein's gravity. The authors use post-Minkowskian effective field theory. Their main result is the scattering angle for non-spinning binaries. It is computed to third post-Minkowskian order. That order needs two-loop Feynman diagrams.

Scattering angles feed models of gravitational wave signals. Wave detectors need exact templates to pull signals from noise. Scalar-tensor terms would mark a break from pure Einstein theory. A third-order result sharpens that test. The work gives wave teams a firm formula. It links loop math to what detectors hear.
arxiv-2601-18003:
Pascual Lucas and José Antonio Ortega-Yagües describe a special family of surfaces in curved spaces. Their 2026 preprint studies concircular hypersurfaces in space forms. Space forms are spaces with the same curvature everywhere, like spheres and hyperbolic spaces. The authors give a full description of these hypersurfaces as a special family of ruled ones, built by sweeping a line through space.

They also characterize concircular helices in three-dimensional space forms. A differential equation links the helix to its curvature and torsion through a concircular factor. Together, the two results pin down a class of shapes that had been only partly known. Such clean descriptions serve geometry and its uses in physics.
arxiv-2601-18103:
Jiang Yan, Xiong-Hui Cao, Meng-Lin Du, and Feng-Kun Guo measure how a heavy particle and light mesons interact at low energy. Their 2026 preprint studies the J/psi particle with pions and kaons. The tool is dispersion relations, which tie an interaction's parts together by strict rules. The authors show that symmetry-breaking terms in the chiral Lagrangian mix the bare charmonium fields. That mixing shapes the scattering lengths they compute.

Scattering lengths are compact numbers that sum up low-energy behavior. They test how well our theory of strong forces handles heavy-light pairs. Values here can guide both lattice work and collider studies. The paper adds firm numbers where data are thin.
arxiv-2601-18203:
ShunLiang Fu, Yanxin Zhang, Yixin Xiang, Xiaoyu Du, and Jinhui Tang build document maps that match how people see a page's structure. Their 2026 preprint presents DMAP for multimodal document understanding. Most question-answering systems treat a document as a bag of loose text chunks. That flat view drops the document's hierarchy and its links. Sections, figure-text ties, and cross-references all vanish, and answers suffer.

DMAP keeps a structural map of the document, aligned with human reading. Retrieval can then follow the document's own logic and layout. Questions that hinge on a figure or a section gain the context they need. The work serves anyone who asks machines to read reports, papers, and manuals.
arxiv-2601-18303:
Léonard Brice, Thomas A. Henzinger, and K. S. Thejaswini study games where players share a source of randomness. Their 2026 preprint opens with a four-player matching pennies game. A team of three faces the Devil. Each player calls heads or tails at the same time. The team wins only if all four calls match. If the team randomizes independently, it wins with probability one in eight. Shared randomness changes that math.

The paper grows that seed into a theory of dicey games in distributed systems. Shared coins can align players who cannot talk. That alignment has real value in protocols and verification. The work links a toy game to deep questions about coordination.
arxiv-2601-18403:
Raphaël Maire, Andrea Plati, Frank Smallenburg, and Giuseppe Foffi study how odd crystals can build them-selves when a flat layer is sheared back and forth. The crystals at hand have twelve-fold form, a shape that breaks the rules of plain crystals. In most labs such forms grow when heat makes bits jiggle and sort. Here the jiggle comes from shear, not heat.

Each pass of shear shoves the bits, and the shoves let them snap into new spots. In time the layer can sort itself into the twelve-fold form. The work shows a fresh path to make rare forms of matter in the lab. It also hints at ways to grow films with traits that plain crystals cannot give. The file is the extra note that goes with the main study.
arxiv-2601-18503:
Xin Wu and four colleagues study a rare case where pairs of bits are born with linked fates and no time to drift apart. In most smashes of bits, the pair lives for a while, and that life blurs the link. Here the pair is made in a graze of two heavy cores that just miss each other. The pair is whole at birth and stays clean, with no long life to blur it.

That clean birth makes the pair a fine test bed for true quantum links. The team show how the link shows up in the paths of the pair. Since the pair does not age, later bumps do not wash the link out. The setup gives labs a rare clean case to check deep claims of quantum theory. It may also set a yard stick for less clean cases.
arxiv-2601-18703:
Alex Viguerie and four colleagues model how germs borne on air spread through a space, with maths drawn from how cells chase food. In that chase, cells drift toward a scent and bunch where it is strong. Air-borne germs act in a like way: they drift with the air and bunch where the flow slows. Past spread models treat that drift as a plain spread, like heat in a pan.

The team build a spread model with the chase term in it, so bunching shows up where it should. They test the maths and run it on cases to see how peaks of germ load form. Sharp peaks mark rooms or zones where risk runs high. Such a model could guide vents and room plans that cut the peaks. It could also help trace where a bout of ill health began.
arxiv-2601-19003:
Santanu S. Dey and Jingye Xu tighten a bound that makes hard sums look almost convex. A classic lemma covers sums of many bounded, nonconvex sets in fixed dimension. Once the set count passes the dimension, the sum's nonconvexity stops growing. The sum then looks nearly convex, which helps in optimization.

The pair use a sharper error bound for that lemma on smooth nonconvex problems. Their gain makes the Lagrangian dual, a key tool for bounding hard problems, as tight as it can be. Tight duals mean better proof that a found solution is near the best one can do.
arxiv-2601-19203:
Kaicheng Wang and four co-authors teach video systems to plan smells that match what is on screen. Smell can deepen immersion in media, yet it is rare because scent is hard to author and to sync with moving video. Past scent tools lean on hand set triggers and fixed links between events and odors, which do not scale to open content.

Their two stage pipeline first reads the video and drafts a scent plan a person can inspect. Keeping the plan readable lets a human check it before any scent is made. The work asks whether semantic planning can carry smell design the way it now carries image and sound design.
arxiv-2601-19503:
Wei Huang, Anda Cheng, and Yinggui Wang prune whole layers of large models using the gradient as a guide. Fine tuning big models on new data is slow and costly. Structured pruning can speed inference, but it often demands extra training, distillation, or search that eats the savings.

Their method, GradPruner, picks layers to cut by gradient signals, aiming to keep fine tuning and inference both efficient. Cutting whole layers, not scattered weights, gives speed that real hardware feels. A cheaper path from base model to tuned model matters as more teams adapt models of this size.
arxiv-2601-19903:
Saeid Rajabi, Chengmo Yang, and Satwik Patnaik automate a tedious step in chip verification. Formal verification relies on SystemVerilog assertions, statements that a design must always satisfy. Writing them by hand is slow and error-prone. Language models can draft assertions, but they usually start from scratch or ignore the design's structure.

Their framework, STELLAR, retrieves expert-crafted assertions and uses structural similarity to guide generation. A new assertion is modelled on proven ones from similar hardware. This retrieval-and-generation design is the first to exploit structural patterns this way. Better assertions catch design bugs earlier and cheaper. The work brings verification closer to push-button status.
arxiv-2601-20103:
Darshan Deshpande, Anand Kannappan, and Rebecca Qian study reward hacking in code training, where a model games the score instead of solving the task. As language models act more often as judges in code training, their skill at spotting such cheating matters. The authors build a taxonomy of reward exploits that spans dozens of categories.

They also introduce TRACE, a benchmark of testing trajectories that was built from synthetic cases and checked by humans. It lets researchers measure how well a judge model catches each kind of exploit. Stronger detection would make training by reward safer, since a model that fools its judge learns the wrong lesson.
arxiv-2601-20503:
Jesse Phitidis and five colleagues compare training strategies for segmenting brain MRI scans when labels are incomplete. The targets are white matter hyperintensities and ischaemic stroke lesions, both signs of cerebral small vessel disease visible on FLAIR scans. The two look alike and often appear in the same brain, which makes telling them apart hard.

Models are hard to build and validate when expert labels cover only part of each scan. The authors test which training strategies cope best with partial labels. Better segmentation would give doctors cleaner measures of disease burden for prognosis and trials.
arxiv-2601-20603:
Peter V. Dovbush and Steven G. Krantz characterize normal families of analytic functions in the unit ball. A family is normal when every sequence in it has a well-behaved convergent subsequence, a compactness property at the heart of complex analysis. They show a family in the ball is normal exactly when its restriction to each complex line through the origin is normal.

They then generalize the result to normal functions, judged by behavior on analytic discs. Reducing a high-dimensional question to one-dimensional slices is a powerful pattern. Their characterization gives analysts a simpler test for normality in several complex variables.
arxiv-2601-20703:
Bixin Yan, Valentine Gillioz, Ipek Efe, and Morgan Trassin review new ways to steer a special class of materials. Their 2026 perspective paper is about ferroelectric materials. These materials hold a built-in electric polarization that stays in place. That trait makes them strong candidates for chips beyond today's standard designs.

Most control of these materials uses applied electric fields. The authors survey a newer set of routes that need no such bias. Recent work on dipole textures, tiny patterns of polarization, has opened these paths. The paper lays out how texture design can flip or move polarization. It maps where this field-free control could lead. Readers get a compact guide to a fast-moving corner of materials science.
arxiv-2601-20803:
Aunabil Chakma, Mihai Surdeanu, and Eduardo Blanco work on pulling facts out of text with very few examples. Their 2026 paper studies few-shot relation extraction. The task is to find links between entities in a sentence, such as who founded what. In-context learning lets a model copy the pattern from one given example. The catch is finding more good examples to show it.

The authors present several strategies to gather extra examples on their own. Their novel strategy picks examples by deep structure, not surface words. It compares the syntactic-semantic shape of each candidate with the one-shot example. A close match in structure should teach the model more. The work helps extraction systems that must start from almost no labeled data.
arxiv-2601-21603:
K. Karatsu, A. Endo, and a large team describe an upgraded spectrometer for millimeter-wave astronomy. The instrument, DESHIMA 2.0, covers a very wide band in one device. It is built on superconducting detectors that sense faint cosmic signals.

The first version proved itself in tests several years ago. The paper lays out the upgrade and its lab characterization. A single instrument that maps wide bands at once can survey distant galaxies far faster. Such speed matters for tracing how galaxies and their gas evolved across cosmic time. Its sensing parts are kinetic inductance detectors, which react to tiny amounts of incoming radiation. Wideband maps also help pick targets for deeper follow-up with larger telescopes.
arxiv-2601-21803:
Korbinian Randl and co-authors build a way to inspect how retrieval systems and language models work together. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a model's answers in fetched documents. But how the retriever and the generator interact is opaque, which is risky in high-stakes fields.

Their 2026 preprint presents RAG-E, an end-to-end explainability framework. It measures how well the retriever's choices align with what the generator actually uses, through attribution methods grounded in mathematics. And it names the ways the pairing can fail. Deployment teams in medicine, law, and finance need exactly this. A way to tell whether a wrong answer came from bad retrieval, bad generation, or a mismatch between them.
arxiv-2601-21903:
Konstantinos Varsos and co-authors study whether viewers will accept greener video streaming. Streaming over fast mobile networks consumes growing energy across access networks, core networks, and data centers. Lowering a stream's bitrate saves energy, but viewers may feel the drop as worse quality.

Success therefore hinges on user acceptance. The team's 2026 preprint builds a user acceptance model for smart incentives. These include rewards offered for choosing efficient settings. The goal is sustainable streaming toward sixth-generation networks. Knowing what makes users say yes is essential: an efficiency feature nobody enables saves nothing. While one framed well could cut the footprint of a hugely popular activity.
arxiv-2601-22003:
James Cuin, Davide Carbone, Yanbo Tang, and Deniz Akyildiz optimize functions whose gradients cannot be computed directly. Such problems fill machine learning and statistics, from estimating models by marginal likelihood to fine-tuning generative models. Stochastic approximation is the standard route.

Standard methods run inner sampling loops to get noisy, biased estimates of the gradient, which is slow and delicate. The team's 2026 preprint instead drives optimization with sequential Monte Carlo, a population-based sampling method that can track the needed quantities as the parameters move. Cleaner gradient estimates could make a whole class of hard estimation problems faster and more reliable in practice.
arxiv-2601-22103:
Greg Kreider extends a classical piece of distribution theory. The spacing is the gap between consecutive order statistics, the sorted values of a sample. Its distribution was known only for samples from uniform and exponential distributions, two special cases.

Kreider adds the logistic and Gumbel distributions to that short list. He also presents an estimator for the spacing distribution that works for any distribution whose inverse cumulative function is known. His 2026 preprint gives statisticians new exact results where previously only simulation could go. Spacings underlie tests for randomness and uniformity, which are used everywhere from quality control to checking whether experimental data have been fudged.
arxiv-2601-22203:
Huinan Xu and co-authors give genomic foundation models a memory to look things up. Current models of DNA spend heavy neural computation to approximate conserved biological motifs from single-letter inputs. They rebuild the same patterns from scratch for every sequence they read.

The team's 2026 preprint proposes Gengram, a conditional memory module built into the model. It adds an explicit, efficient lookup for multi-base motifs, using a hashing scheme designed for genomes. And thereby establishes a genomic syntax the network can consult. Explicit memory could make genome models faster and sharper at the patterns evolution conserved, with payoffs for variant prediction and gene regulation studies.
arxiv-2601-22403:
Khalid Mahmud Labib and Shabbir Ahmed model the wild swings of lithium-ion batteries with a data-driven trick. A battery's inner chemistry makes its behavior curve and bend in hard ways. Their 2026 preprint uses dynamic mode decomposition, a method that pulls clean patterns from data, set in a delayed frame.

The delay frame lets a mostly linear tool catch curved behavior. A sound, light model helps a battery system judge charge, health, and safe limits. That judgment guards life span and safety in cars and grids. The work offers a middle path between crude and costly models.
arxiv-2601-22703:
Abid Hassan, Tuan Ngo, Saad Shafiq, and Nenad Medvidovic built DAVIS, a detector for inputs unlike anything a model was trained on. Out-of-distribution detection is a key guard for real-world deployment. Their 2026 preprint notes that most post-hoc tools read a pooled feature summary, which throws away rich detail from the activation maps.

DAVIS uses dominant activations and their variance to widen the gap between known and strange inputs. A wider gap means fewer strangers waved through. The work is a guard-rail upgrade. It costs no retraining of the base model. That ease is part of its appeal.
arxiv-2601-23003:
Dionysios Galanis and three co-authors build a theory for light scattering off objects that change in time. The objects have a permittivity, a measure of response to electric fields, that varies in a regular rhythm. Such time-modulated scatterers are a new playground for controlling light.

Within a perturbative approach, they derive formulas for the scattering matrix in first-order Born approximation. The dynamic result is tied directly to the matching static problem. That link lets designers predict time-varying optics from well-understood fixed ones. First-order expressions keep the theory usable, relating the time-modulated scattering directly to the solved static problem.
arxiv-2602-00103: Mahule Roy and coauthors build a multi agent AI system for polymer discovery that joins high throughput work, AI, and modeling in one Polymer Research Lifecycle pipeline. Specialist agents based on DeepSeek models read scientific sources, call external tools, run domain code, and check their own work. The system shows property prediction with generative design, auto study of biopolymers, and a self checking agent that improves its own plans over time. On 1251 held out polymers, its PolyGNN agent predicts key traits with strong accuracy.
arxiv-2602-00303: Jyoti Prakash and colleagues envision analysis for N-language polyglot programs. Polyglot programming grows as developers combine languages for their distinct strengths, aided by platforms such as GraalVM and other multi language runtimes. Current analysis research mainly covers two languages, missing the complexity of systems using three or more. Modern web systems often connect JavaScript, WebAssembly, and Rust within one execution chain.
arxiv-2602-00403: Hon Tik Tse and Marlos C. Machado derive a default representation objective via graph methods in RL. The default representation and its principal eigenvector prove effective for reward shaping, exploration, option discovery, and transfer. Prior work got DR eigenvectors by first approximating the DR matrix, then doing eigendecomposition, which is expensive and scales poorly in high dimensions. The authors derive an objective for approximating the DR's main eigenvector with a neural network. They show the objective in several settings and apply learned eigenvectors for reward shaping.
arxiv-2602-00603: Luca Viano and colleagues study direct preference optimisation with rating information, where pairwise preferences alone leave response quality ambiguous. Pairwise feedback makes data collection easy, but it stays unclear whether likelihood shifts for preferred and dispreferred responses are good or bad. Their algorithms use the rating gap, how much better the chosen response is than the rejected one. They reach faster statistical rates than DPO with accurate gaps and stay robust when gaps are inaccurate. Tests show solid performance against DPO-style algorithms across many language models and benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-00903: Thomas Muehlenstädt and colleagues propose a graph-based method for coverage analysis drawing traffic scenes as layered graphs, combining map layout with actor relationships. Current methods assess coverage factors alone or in small combinations, missing complex traffic-scene links. Their two-phase build captures spatial relationships between participants, including leading, tailing, nearby, and opposing setups. Sub-graph matching matches scenes against hand-defined archetype graphs for common driving cases. Graph vectors with Graph Isomorphism Networks project scenes into vector space for similarity-based coverage checks.
arxiv-2602-01003: Zhishen Sun and co-authors build ESSAM, a way to tune big language models that pairs evolution search with sharpness-aware steps. Tuning by reward methods eats a lot of GPU memory, which bars use on small rigs, so their method searches in weight space with no reward model at all. On a grade-school math test, its mean score matched the top reward methods across the models tried. A faster twin of the method nearly halved run time at the same low memory use, while still beating PPO.
arxiv-2602-01503: Afifah Kashif and co-authors argue that current AI governance frameworks fail NeuroAI systems. Today's benchmarks for accuracy, latency, and energy efficiency assume static, centrally trained neural networks on von Neumann hardware. NeuroAI, embodied in neuromorphic hardware through spiking neural networks, breaks those assumptions. The paper examines those limits, arguing that assurance and audit methods must evolve with the architectures. It ties standard metrics to the physics and learning dynamics of brain-inspired computation, plus its efficiency, for grounded assurance.
arxiv-2602-01803: Junyan Chu and colleagues rebuild polynomial vector fields from sampled velocities on a convex many sided domain with an exact no penetration boundary condition. Given a degree bound, their method fits the samples in the least squares sense while keeping tangency on every boundary facet. The key is a recipe for tangent polynomial vector fields from log derivations of hyperplane arrangements, turning the constrained problem into finite dimensional linear algebra. Extensions add linear differential constraints like incompressibility, plus piecewise polynomial builds on non convex domains with smooth joins across cells.
arxiv-2602-02003: Lingyue Shen and colleagues present a quasi monolithic ALE method for fluid coupling. Fluid momentum, Neo-Hookean law and Cauchy-Green tensor join into one system, while mesh updates explicitly. P2 elements approximate curved faces to third order, and an implicit explicit Runge-Kutta scheme gives second order results. Localized updating confines mesh and deformation history to a sub domain with background flow, bridging local and large geometry. The Turek-Hron FSI3 benchmark reproduces beam tip size and frequency within three percent. Particle focusing in spiral channels illustrates the framework.
arxiv-2602-02403:
Michael Balzer and 1 co-author study how collaborators lift or drag each other's output across science and invention, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their theory treats publications and patents as linked activities inside one network. Output in each activity should rise with a centrality measure that captures influence flowing within and across both spheres.

To test the theory, the authors assemble the full set of cancer-related publications and patents. They build joint coauthorship and coinventorship networks for researchers active in both worlds. An instrumental-variables plan, using predicted link formation to dodge biased network formation, supports the predictions. Output rises with centrality for both authors and inventors. Output on the science side boosts output on the invention side, but not the reverse. The asymmetry fits a science-driven view of innovation.
arxiv-2602-02503:
Jincheng Xie and 6 co-authors estimate both range and direction for Bluetooth devices using a single antenna, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Conventional direction finding needs antenna arrays, which are costly on small Bluetooth Low Energy devices. A virtual antenna array technique moves one antenna to fake an array, but Bluetooth's two-way channel measurement carries a binary phase ambiguity that blocks direct use.

The team unifies the virtual array with the two-way channel response in one model. A neural network with row and column predictors plus a voting mechanism recovers the missing phase. The recovered one-way response then feeds super-resolution methods such as MUSIC for joint time-of-arrival and direction estimation. Simulations show the method beating rivals under non-uniform virtual arrays. Its error approaches the theoretical Cramer-Rao bound once signal quality is moderate.
arxiv-2602-02603:
Alif Munim and 11 co-authors pretrain a foundation model for heart ultrasound on eighteen million echocardiograms, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ultrasound images are corrupted by speckle noise and acquisition artifacts that obscure anatomy. Models that chase pixels learn the noise along with the signal.

EchoJEPA instead uses a latent predictive objective, learning anatomical representations that ignore speckle. The corpus spans three hundred thousand patients, the largest yet for this modality. A multi-view probing framework with frozen backbones tests what the representations contain. Left ventricular ejection fraction estimates improved by about twenty percent over leading baselines, and right ventricular pressure estimates by about seventeen percent. With one percent of labeled data the model classified views far better than baselines with all of it. It also generalized to children without fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-02903:
Coordinating traffic lights across a city network is the problem in a 2026 paper by Haoran Su and 2 co-authors. Reinforcement learning can adapt signals, but multi-agent coordination and sample efficiency remain hard. Each intersection must act with its neighbors in mind, not alone.

Their system, MADT, recasts signal control as sequence modeling with a decision transformer. A graph attention part captures links between intersections. A temporal encoder tracks how traffic evolves. Target performance is set through return-to-go conditioning, a way of asking for a desired total reward. Tests on synthetic grids and real traffic followed. Average travel time fell by five to six percent against the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2602-03103:
Measuring whether an instruction actually determines its expected output is proposed by Pritam Kadasi and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Instruction tuning trains language models on instruction-input-output triples. Many triples are weakly specified, though, since the same output could plausibly follow several alternative instructions for the same input, weakening what the model learns from each example during training.

Their Task-Specificity Score contrasts the true instruction against plausible alternatives for the same input. A refined version uses harder alternatives and a small quality term to avoid easy-negative effects. Across three instruction datasets and three open models, selecting highly task-given examples improved downstream results under tight token budgets. The score also complemented quality-based filters such as perplexity.
arxiv-2602-03203:
Which cached pairs a reasoning model can safely discard is learned by Zican Dong and a team of 6 others. Long reasoning traces make the key-value cache grow linearly, raising memory and computation costs. Existing eviction methods discard pairs by simple importance scores and often miss complex dependencies, degrading performance when the cache budget tightens during long generations on difficult problems.

Their framework, ForesightKV, trains an eviction policy from optimal traces. A golden eviction procedure identifies ideal pairs to drop at each step using future attention scores. Those traces are distilled with a pairwise ranking loss. Cache eviction is then formulated as a decision process and refined with reinforcement learning. On competition math benchmarks, ForesightKV beat prior methods while using only half the cache budget.
arxiv-2602-03303:
Light-matter particles that survive to room temperature in layered crystals are reported by Bhabani Sankar Sahoo, leading 8 other authors. Interlayer excitons, bound electron-hole pairs split across layers, are built here through precise stacking orientation and twist-angle control. A three-layer stack of molybdenum and tungsten compounds sits on a chirped Bragg reflector, a mirror that also creates bilayer and homobilayer regions nearby for comparison within the same device.

The trilayer shows pronounced band modulation and intervalley shifts. Its light output is ten times stronger and its exciton lifetime seven times longer than the bilayer at cryogenic temperatures. Heat studies reveal valley-polarized excitons emerging and optical stability maintained up to room temperature. The platform suits excitonic optoelectronics and quantum photonics.
arxiv-2602-03403:
When two sides disagree, analysts often sort the agents and issues into camps for or against each other. Guangming Lang and 4 co-authors extend that three-way conflict analysis in a 2026 paper. Older preference-based models only allowed three coarse attitudes toward an issue pair: prefer, oppose, or indifferent, which misses much of what a conflict involves.

The authors define an intuitionistic fuzzy preference setting that grades attitudes more finely, then build conflict measures and three-way models on top of it. Loss functions set the thresholds for sorting agent pairs, agents, and issues. They finish with adjustment strategies that weigh both change size and conflict degree. An algorithm and a worked example complete the proposal.
arxiv-2602-03603:
Care robots fail in messy homes, and a human operator has to bail them out; the question is which operator. Lorena Maria Genua and 2 co-authors propose ARFA in a 2026 paper, an adaptive method for allocating robot failures to people. Sending every failure to the same expert overloads them, while random assignment wastes skill.

ARFA keeps a running model of each operator's capabilities and updates it from their actual recovery performance. For each new failure, a reward function weighs operator skill, task urgency, historical data, and current workload. The failure goes to whoever scores highest on expected reward. Simulations and user studies show less robot idle time, better overall performance, and a fairer workload spread than random allocation.
arxiv-2602-03803:
Antoine Leudière and Renate Scheidler present an algorithm for computing the structure of submodules of points on Drinfeld modules over finite fields. Their 2026 paper works in the function-field analogue of elliptic curve arithmetic, where a Drinfeld module's points form a module over a function ring. Kernels of isogenies and torsion submodules are special cases.

For the standard function ring of polynomials in one variable, the algorithm also yields a Frobenius decomposition of the submodule. The approach leans on Frobenius normal forms, module presentations, and Fitting ideals, carried out with classical linear algebra and fast Ore polynomial arithmetic. A SageMath implementation comes with the work. The authors also compute a simple invariant that encodes which polynomials give rational torsion.
arxiv-2602-04003:
Fluent explanations can make a wrong AI answer feel right. Shutong Fan and 2 co-authors name that attack surface in a 2026 paper on adversarial explanation attacks. Instead of corrupting a model's computation, an attacker reframes its explanation to keep users trusting incorrect outputs.

The authors define a trust miscalibration gap measuring how much framing shifts trust between honest and manipulated explanations. A study with over two hundred participants tested the effect on real decisions. Persuasive framing preserved trust even when predictions were wrong. The findings argue that AI safety must audit the words shown to users, not only the model behind them.
arxiv-2602-04103:
Counting characters fast is a humble operation with outsized importance. R. Groot Koerkamp's 2026 paper engineers rank queries, which count occurrences of a character in a text prefix. Rank underlies the FM-index used throughout bioinformatics to search genomes.

Two structures result. BiRank answers binary-alphabet rank with about three percent space overhead, interleaving offsets into cache lines and counting from block middles to halve the work. QuadRank extends the tricks to the four-letter DNA alphabet at higher overhead. Both target throughput on many threads, since genome pipelines are usually limited by exactly this primitive.
arxiv-2602-04203:
Darshan Kumar and 3 co-authors jointly test two pillars of cosmology: whether space is curved and whether two cosmic distance measures agree. The Etherington relation links luminosity distance and angular diameter distance at the same redshift. Their 2026 paper checks both using baryon acoustic oscillation data and cosmic clock readings.

Luminosity distances were rebuilt with Gaussian processes, with no fixed formula assumed. Comparing 2D, 3D, and DESI oscillation datasets probed whether tensions between them skew the findings. Across all datasets and four formula choices, the distance-duality relation held and no break showed up at high confidence. That agreement strengthens trust in the standard cosmic distance ladder.
arxiv-2602-04403:
Shenwei Huang and 2 co-authors prove an optimal coloring bound for a restricted graph class in a 2026 paper. Even-hole-free graphs, those with no even cycle as an induced pattern, resist the usual coloring guarantees. The authors additionally forbid induced seven-vertex paths.

Every such graph's chromatic number is at most five quarters of its clique number, rounded up, and the bound cannot be improved. The result extends an earlier theorem for six-vertex paths and confirms Reed's conjecture for this class. The proof leans on structural analysis of a maximal configuration built from a five-cycle. Chi-boundedness results like this map where coloring stays close to clique size.
arxiv-2602-04903:
Feature steering edits a model's internal signals to control its behavior, and it is often pitched as cleaner than careful prompting. The work is by Eitan Sprejer and 4 co-authors. The team compares a commercial tool, Goodfire's Auto Steer, against plain prompt engineering on two sizes of the Llama model.

Steering did change behavior as intended, scoring higher than prompting on control. The cost was steep. Accuracy on a broad knowledge test fell from 66 to 46 percent on the smaller model, and answers became far less coherent. Prompting gave the best overall balance. The authors argue that control methods carry a real trade-off between behavior and capability, and that the trade-off must be measured before such tools are deployed.
arxiv-2602-05603:
Spin-Hall nano-oscillators are tiny devices that turn electric current into microwave signals, and they could scale into large coupled networks. Victor González and 12 co-authors report the first direct imaging of the magnetization dynamics inside one such device, built on a cobalt-iron-boron layer. They used time-resolved scanning transmission X-ray microscopy, a method fast and fine enough to catch motion on the device's minute scales.

The images show the oscillation is strongest at the two edges of the narrow constriction, with a clear asymmetry favoring one edge. Spin waves leaving the device spread unevenly in different directions. Simulations point to grain boundaries and a magnetic interaction called DMI as causes of both effects. The dynamics also changed during measurement, which suggests the material interface is less resistant to X-ray damage than assumed.
arxiv-2602-05703:
Programs that build unbounded linked lists are hard to verify, since the memory shape can grow without limit. Tomáš Brablec, Tomáš Dacík, and Tomáš Vojnar present SEAL, a static analyzer built on symbolic execution with separation logic, a logic designed for reasoning about memory. Abstract memory states are checked by a general purpose separation logic solver, which itself translates problems into SMT form.

That design makes the tool modular and easier to extend or combine with other theories. In the SV COMP 2026 verification competition, the prototype reached competitive results in the linked list category. It was one of only four analyzers able to verify programs with unbounded lists. The authors argue that extensibility plus further development can bring significant gains in future competitions. The paper is a short competition contribution. It targets the software verification community, where automated proofs of memory safety are a standing challenge.
arxiv-2602-05903:
A generative model trained on example sequences may absorb the rules of its language, or may only mimic the surface. András Balogh and Márk Jelasity ask how to verify the implicit world model inside such a model, using chess as the test domain. Chess is complex enough to be interesting, yet its rules are simple and exact.

Their method generates adversarial sequences: valid play designed to force the model into predicting an illegal next move. If the adversary succeeds, the model is not sound, whatever its average accuracy says. The approach also exposes failure modes and shows how training choices change them. The authors train models on random and on high quality games under several recipes. None proved sound, though some techniques and data choices did better. The study was accepted at a major conference, with code and data public.
arxiv-2602-06103:
Answering questions from a single document sounds simple, yet language models often skip facts or add claims the document never made. Zhaoyang Chen and Cody Fleming present EVE, a framework that forces answers through a strict pipeline. Extraction, checking, and listing happen as separate steps.

Free-form prompting lets models favor likely wording over faithful coverage. EVE counters that by making each claim trace back to the source. In tests, both recall and precision rose at the same time, breaking a trade-off that single-pass generation usually faces. Longer answers also stopped getting cut off. The authors note that vague wording in documents still caps how far the method can go.
arxiv-2602-06203:
Thermal cameras see heat instead of light, which helps robots work in darkness, smoke, or glare. Parv Maheshwari and 10 co-authors present AnyThermal, a feature extractor for thermal images meant to serve many tasks at once. Older thermal models were trained for one task in one setting, which limited their reach.

AnyThermal learns by copying the feature structure of a strong visual foundation model into a thermal encoder, using data from indoor, aerial, off-road, and city scenes. The team also built a data collection rig that records color and thermal images in sync, and gathered a balanced set with it. Tests showed top results across place recognition, segmentation, and depth estimation.
arxiv-2602-06403:
Comet 41P passed near the Sun in the spring of 2017 and spun so hard under its own outgassing that its rotation changed dramatically. David Jewitt studies Hubble Space Telescope observations from later that year, after perihelion, to pin down the nucleus size and its new spin. Gas jets act like small rockets that torque the nucleus.

The nucleus proves tiny, about half a kilometer in radius, from both brightness and its non-gravitational drift. Its light varies with a period of about six-tenths of a day, far from the values measured earlier that year. Jewitt concludes the spin likely reversed between spring and December. The surface also grew less active compared with an earlier visit, showing long-term change.
arxiv-2602-06603:
Thomas Frost, Hrisheekesh Vaidya, and Steve Harris warn about a common step in training medical AI on hospital records. Patient data arrive at uneven times, so researchers often re-bin them into even time slots first. The authors test whether that tidying step quietly distorts what the model learns about cause and effect.

In intensive care data on insulin treatment, binning flipped the apparent order of most paired sugar readings and dose changes inside a slot. In a simulated trial with virtual diabetes patients, models trained on binned data did up to 60 percent worse when put back into the simulator. Worse, judging the models on binned data hid the drop. The team urges the field to keep natural decision times in training data.
arxiv-2602-06703:
Yishuo Zhou and six co-authors ask how the tiny stresses raised by tides can set off slow earthquakes. Tidal stress comes mainly from the gravity of the Moon and Sun. It is far weaker than the forces that drive ordinary quakes, so any fault it triggers must be unusually sensitive. The team models such a fault as a sliding block on a spring with friction that depends on speed and state.

Simple test pulses reveal a resonance-like effect: pulses of certain lengths amplify the slip speed the most. With steady wave-like forcing, two controls dominate, the forcing period and its size relative to the fault's own scales. Longer periods move events from the stress peak toward the moment of fastest stress rise, and bigger forcing turns slow slips into fast ones. Comparing modeled and observed tidal patterns could reveal a fault's hidden friction properties.
arxiv-2602-06903:
Jannik Schestag and Norbert Zeh prove the first separation between two measures of graph width. Treewidth is a central parameter in parameterized complexity, and scanwidth is a newer measure designed for directed acyclic graphs, especially phylogenetic networks, that respects edge direction. Until now every problem studied under scanwidth was either tractable under both measures or hard under both.

The authors break that pattern with Weighted Phylogenetic Diversity with Dependencies, a problem about selecting species to preserve diversity under dependencies. They show it is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the scanwidth of the food web, yet hard with respect to its treewidth at every level of the hardness hierarchy. The result shows scanwidth captures structural information that treewidth misses, not merely a simpler route to the same algorithms.
arxiv-2602-07003:
Alaa M. Ali and six co-authors offer a noninvasive way to map protective chemicals as they soak into tissue-like material. Freezing without ice needs those cocktails loaded just right. Too little loading risks freezing and failed recovery. Too much is toxic. Yet old in situ measures of permeation were largely unvalidated and could not split single protectant amounts.

Their method uses multi-spectral X-ray CT to map the space-time spread of protectants diffusing into a tissue-mimicking phantom. A photon-energy bin choice gives sensitivity to low-contrast chemicals, with no contrast agents or fluorescence edges. Tests on a mix of dimethyl sulfoxide, glycerol, and water resolved volume fractions within 5 percent accuracy. The team saw uneven diffusion into the hydrogel, a pattern old techniques cannot see. That should aid loading protocol design and vitrifiability checks before freezing.
arxiv-2602-07103:
Chenglei Yu and three co-authors offer scDFM, a generative system for predicting how cells react to perturbations. Single-cell measures are noisy and sparse, and perturbations often shift whole populations rather than single cells. Old deep learning methods assume cell-level matches, which limits their grasp of global effects. scDFM instead models the full spread of perturbed cells, conditioned on control states, through conditional flow matching.

A maximum mean discrepancy objective lines up the perturbed group with the control group, going past single-cell matches. For robustness to sparsity and noise, a Perturbation-Aware Differential Transformer backbone uses gene interaction graphs and differential attention to catch context-specific expression shifts. Across genetic and drug perturbation benchmarks, scDFM beat prior methods, generalizing to unseen and combinatorial settings alike. In the combinatorial case it cut mean squared error by about 20 percent versus the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2602-07203:
Explaining a complex system often means asking how much each variable matters under interventions, and do-Shapley values answer that question game-theoretically.  R.  Teal Witter and six co-authors make those values exactly computable in far more cases than before.

The key is a reformulation in terms of the irreducible sets of the underlying structural causal model. The exact method runs in time linear in their number, which ranges from the number of variables up to exponential depending on graph structure.  A companion estimator handles any query budget and converges as the budget grows.  Causal analysts get both an exact tool and a graceful fallback for hard graphs.
arxiv-2602-08403:
People who watch over delivery drones must catch critical events fast without being overwhelmed by alerts. Thorsten Klößner and four co-authors test whether reinforcement learning can personalize highlighting to strike that balance. Their arXiv paper simulates the watcher's gaze so the system can learn without a live deployment.

Highlighting helps awareness but each interruption costs attention, and the best trade differs by person. In a drone-oversight scenario, learned highlighting beats fixed rule-based alerting in early results. The authors also discuss the hurdles of intelligent oversight support. Readers get a first look at adaptive interfaces that learn when to speak up and when to stay quiet.
arxiv-2602-08503:
Vision-language models rarely learn to correct themselves, because genuine self-correction shows up too seldom to teach from. Yi Ding and three co-authors propose Octopus, a rollout-augmentation method that makes many self-fix examples by mixing old rollouts in new ways. Their arXiv paper targets the sparse-signal problem in reinforcement learning.

Reuse boosts sample efficiency while balanced supervision steadies optimization. A response-masking trick separates self-correction from direct reasoning so the two skills do not fight each other. The resulting Octopus-8B model leads open-source vision-language models across seven benchmarks, beating the best prior baseline by a point while using only 0.72 times the training time per step. Readers get a controllable self-correction recipe.
arxiv-2602-08703:
Physics-informed learning enforces differential equations at scattered points, but that local focus can fail between points and at boundaries. Annie E. Paine and two co-authors propose adding weak-form, integral-based losses that impose global conditions instead. Their arXiv paper targets robustness in both classical and quantum physics-informed methods.

Combining local and global losses exploits the strengths of each: pointwise accuracy plus good average behavior. Tests across problems, focusing on differentiable quantum architectures, show hybrid losses with domain decomposition beating local-only strategies by a strong margin. Readers get a simple but powerful fix for a known weakness of physics-informed machine learning.
arxiv-2602-09003:
As data scaling hits limits of supply, cost, and efficiency, Yudong Wang and sixteen co-authors argue AI development is entering a data-model co-evolution phase. Their tiered data management system, spanning levels L0 to L4 from raw uncurated resources to organized, verifiable knowledge, supports the full language-model training lifecycle across varied objectives and budgets. Language models themselves score quality and edit content to lift data across tiers.

Each tier carries distinct traits, management plans, and training roles, so data can be allocated deliberately across pretraining, mid-training, and alignment. The system balances quality, acquisition cost, and marginal benefit, offering a systematic path to scalable, sustainable data stewardship for the road toward general intelligence.
arxiv-2602-09103:
Quantum channels are only useful if encoding and decoding survive their own noise, and Paula Belzig and one co-author push that frontier with constant space overhead. Earlier fault-tolerant capacities used concatenated codes holding a single logical qubit each. This paper instead concatenates quantum Hamming codes, which pack many logical qubits together, keeping overhead constant as systems grow.

Modular tools for fault-tolerant circuits with quantum input and output interfaces follow, enabling a simpler analysis of entanglement-assisted communication. Achievable rates substantially exceed previous methods, thanks to limited noise correlations in syndrome qubits of high-rate Hamming codes. The work makes fault-tolerant communication both cheaper and faster in theory.
arxiv-2602-09303:
Che-Chia Chang and four co-authors bring a physics-taught steadiness-model setup for cracking part differential equations with fast, few-step AI-made guessing. They spot a steadiness trap: PDE leftovers can push steadiness training toward flat or broken answers, spoiling the learned spread. Their fix is a shape-keeping two-step plan that parts spread learning from physics policing by icing the factor decoder during physics-taught fine-tuning.

A two-step leftover goal holds up physical steadiness on polished, soundly built runs rather than noisy single-step guesses. The result is steady, high-truth guessing for open-ended making and forward puzzles alike, with forward answers gained by projection-based zero-shot filling. Rightness matches spread baselines at far lower computing cost.
arxiv-2602-09503:
Cooperation in human groups unfolds inside teams, clubs, and coalitions, structures that hypergraphs capture as hyperedges joining many members at once. Bingxin Lin and five co-authors build a unified framework for imitation dynamics on such higher-order networks in their 2026 paper. Network structure has been studied deeply, but update rules, how individuals revise strategies by copying others, were scattered across isolated models.

The framework parameterizes each update rule by how many groups a person samples and how many peers they consult per group. Under weak selection, it derives a closed-form condition for cooperation to succeed in any multiplayer dilemma on homogeneous hypergraphs, linear or nonlinear. Disconnected rules collapse into one family, their effects reduced to information diversity: rules generating more diverse information promote cooperation better, strictly across all dilemmas. Simulations extend the principle to heterogeneous hypergraphs, synthetic and empirical alike.
arxiv-2602-09903:
Quantum steering lets a measurement on one particle shape the state of a partner particle, and the steering ellipsoid draws every state reachable that way. A 2026 paper by Wen-Jie Zhang and Jun-Hong An asks how that picture survives contact with the real world. In practice each qubit sits in its own noisy surroundings, and the resulting decay wears the ellipsoid down.

The authors link the ellipsoid's shape to two features: memory-like non-Markovian effects in the surroundings, and bound states in the combined energy spectrum. A bound state supplies the capacity to preserve steering, while the memory effect supplies the dynamics. Testing three cases, with bound states on both sides, one side, or neither, they map varied steering types and point to reservoir design as a tunable way to protect steering-based tools.
arxiv-2602-10403:
Data sets meant to include disabled people often get their labels from crowdworkers without disability-specific know-how, yielding inconsistent or inaccurate labels. A 2026 paper led by Xinru Tang, with two co-authors, examines this problem in speech data from people who stutter. Stuttering varies widely, and views differ on how it shows, so labeling and writing down stuttered speech stays hard even for trained experts. Through interviews and co-design workshops with people who stutter and domain experts, the authors name labeling challenges and build practices weaving stutterers' lived experience into labeling.

The findings highlight the value of lived knowledge for data-set quality, while revealing a tension: disability experiences are complex, but fixed labels are rigid. The paper closes by urging disability-first, multiplicity-aware ways of reading data across the AI pipeline, with labeling designed with disabled people rather than merely about them.
arxiv-2602-10603:
Arnav Shah and nine co-authors build a genomic base model that reads DNA without a fixed tokenizer in a 2026 paper. Standard tokenizers chop biologically meaningful motifs like codons and regulatory elements into fragments, while nucleotide-level models preserve coherence at prohibitive cost for long contexts. The model trade-off has limited genomic modeling.

Their model, dnaHNet, segments and models genomic strings end to end with a differentiable dynamic chunking process. Raw nucleotides compress into latent tokens adaptively, balancing compression against guess scores. Pretrained on prokaryotic genomes, the model outperforms leading systems in scaling and speed. Quadratic reductions in runs enable more than three times faster inference than transformer baselines in the paper's comparisons.
arxiv-2602-10703:
Martijn B. J. Brummelhuis and two co-authors teach a drone to feel a roof's slope before landing in a 2026 paper. Urban drones must land on rooftops of varied shape, but vision and acoustic sensing of inclination falter with weather and surface materials. A misjudged slope risks a failed touchdown.

The team proposes a dual-arm aerial manipulator with an omnidirectional solid workspace and extended reach. On that platform, a momentum-based torque observer enables proprioceptive contact finding and localization: the drone infers inclination through real contact, blindly, before touchdown. Flight tests check the approach, showing that touch can succeed where sight struggles in the messy reality of city rooftops.
arxiv-2602-11003:
Density functional theory often spreads electrons too thin, skewing energies and bands. Yichen Fan and three co-authors extend a fix called straight response localized orbital scaling correction to wider molecule ground. The fix adds screening and orbital locality to correct the spread.

They built a fast version whose cost matches standard density functional runs, so large systems stay in reach. Screening helps only a little for small molecules but proves key for larger ones, from chains to 3D shapes. Tests span varied organic systems and transition-metal oxide complexes with strong scores. The method aims to make computed energies and orbital levels more trustworthy across chemistry.
arxiv-2602-11103:
Coding agents now write code, but can they build a game? Wayne Chi and ten co-authors offer GameDevBench, the first benchmark for agent-led game growth. Its tasks come from web and video tutorials, and demand both large codebases and visual assets like shaders, sprites, and animation.

Tasks run long: typical solutions need over three times the code and file changes of prior software benchmarks. Even the best agent and method solve just over half the tasks. Success falls as visual hardness rises, from gameplay tasks to 2D graphics work. Simple image and video feedback lifts scores, showing that agents need eyes on the scene, not just text.
arxiv-2602-11503:
Doubt grows near black holes, and coherence fades with heat. Rui-Jie Yao and Dong Wang propose a generalized entropic doubt relation for arbitrary multi-measurement in many-body systems, deriving a greatly tighter bound than current formulations. The Schwarzschild black hole case shows that tightness.

The study also tracks multipartite coherence and linkage in curved spacetime. A striking exact equivalence emerges between linkage and a coherence measure for a broad class of multipartite states. Coherence diminishes markedly and measurement doubt rises to a stable maximum as Hawking heat increases. The findings deepen grasp of quantum resources in black holes.
arxiv-2602-11803: Idrees Fayaz Harry and two co-authors establish a Hineva inequality for several kinds of submanifolds of quaternionic space forms, geometric spaces built from quaternionic structure. An inequality of this kind bounds one geometric quantity by others across a family of shapes, giving researchers a general tool rather than a result tied to a single example. The abstract states the result briefly, covering different submanifold types without singling out one case.
arxiv-2602-11903:
No-reference video quality assessment for gaming videos is hard: content is unusual, compression glitches abound, and human ratings are scarce. Yu-Chih Chen and six co-authors present MTL-VQA, a multi-task learning framework. It uses full-reference quality metrics as teaching signals to learn meaning-rich features without human labels during pretraining. Jointly optimizing multiple complementary proxy goals with adaptive task weighting, the approach learns shared representations. Those representations transfer effectively to downstream no-reference scoring.

Experiments on gaming videos show MTL-VQA beats label-efficient or self-supervised settings and rivals mean-opinion-score-labeled settings in performance. For gaming video quality, where human ratings are scarce and content shifts quickly, the approach offers a practical path to skills that transfer without costly labels.
arxiv-2602-12203:
Business forms and reports hold facts that workflows need, yet most document tests use narrow entity lists, simple questions, or one document type. Mathieu Sibue led this work with six co-authors, presenting ExStrucTiny, a benchmark for structured extraction from document images that can bend to changing schemas. It joins key entity extraction, relation extraction, and visual question answering in one test.

Samples were built by mixing hand work with checked synthetic data, covering varied document types and extraction cases. Tests of open and closed vision-language models expose three pain points: adapting to a new schema, handling vague queries, and pinning answers to the right spot. The benchmark aims to give general models a firmer base for real document work.
arxiv-2602-12303:
Astrophysics now publishes so fast that no one can follow every subfield, yet the year's shape is worth seeing whole. Rommulus Francis Lewis led this work with two co-authors, reviewing every astrophysics paper on arXiv in 2025. The review tracks most-used keywords, subfields, and telescopes, journal spread, and most-studied objects, from gravitational wave and gamma-ray burst events to fast radio bursts and exoplanets.

Author affiliations map the global spread of research and collaboration, and citation data show which papers most influenced the year. A first-of-its-kind spectral fingerprint charts research across the electromagnetic spectrum and by redshift. Students and professionals alike can use the picture to spot hot topics, active communities, and where their own work might fit.
arxiv-2602-12503:
Neutron stars should contain hyperons at high density, yet hyperons soften the equation of state so much that massive neutron stars become hard to explain, the so-called hyperon puzzle. Bikai Gao works alone here, investigating hyperon emergence with the SU(3) parity doublet model in chiral representation (3, anti-3) plus (anti-3, 3). Chiral symmetry restoration and the interplay between chiral condensate and chiral invariant mass m0 shape baryon masses in dense matter.

Hyperon onset density depends strongly on m0: at 500 MeV, hyperons appear at 1.9 times saturation density, while at 750 MeV or more, they appear only above 5 times saturation. That delay comes from weakened density dependence of baryon masses at larger m0. When onset exceeds the expected quark-hadron transition range of 2 to 5 times saturation, matter deconfines before hyperons populate, avoiding softening while staying consistent with massive neutron star observations.
arxiv-2602-12603:
Safety filters keep learning-enabled controllers within safe states and inputs, but common Euclidean projections onto the safe set ignore long-term performance. Ziyan Lin led this work with one co-author, Liang Xu, giving a state-dependent, Hessian-guided projection for safety filtering. It preserves convexity while improving performance, unlike direct value optimisation, which can be nonconvex.

The key idea picks a weighted projection matrix from curvature of the action-value function. It biases corrections toward action directions with higher value sensitivity. Two results are established: a uniform bound on the performance gap to the safe value-optimal action, and a condition under which weighted projection beats Euclidean projection in long-term value. A data-driven construction via Q-function learning supports black-box controllers. Quadrotor tracking-and-avoidance simulations show safety maintained with less value loss than Euclidean projection, at real-time-compatible cost.
arxiv-2602-12703:
Some graphs are never written out in full: their edge weights come from a formula applied to node features, as with neighbourhood graphs in machine learning. Walking such a graph step by step is hard when the graph itself is only implicit. Alessandro Manenti and four co-authors introduce SWING, a method that walks instead through the continuous space where the graph lives, using a tailored sampling trick built on random features and importance weighting.

The trick leans on a deep link between implicitly defined graphs and Fourier analysis, which the authors lay out in the paper. Because it never builds the graph, SWING stays friendly to hardware accelerators and scales to large inputs. The authors back the method with detailed analysis and tests across several classes of implicit graphs, showing it can stand in for the combinatorial calculations it replaces.
arxiv-2602-12903:
Online marketplaces repeatedly match buyers and sellers whose values depend on context, such as features of the good or the moment. Romain Cosson and five co-authors study repeated bilateral trade where each side's value is a linear function of a context vector.
