Each round, the learner posts a price to each side, and trade happens only if both accept. The goals are gain from trade and profit, judged against the best omniscient dynamic strategy.

With two-bit feedback, seeing each side's answer separately, the authors achieve near-tight regret bounds for both goals while never losing money in a round. With one-bit feedback, seeing only whether trade happened, the same regret regimes survive at the cost of small, horizon-independent losses. Combining one-bit feedback with strict per-round balance costs exponential dependence on dimension for gain from trade, a sharp trade-off the paper maps fully.
arxiv-2602-13303:
Image-to-image translation with diffusion models often inverts a picture into a latent code, then samples a new version from it. That standard inversion breaks when the source image is spectrally sparse, as in super-resolution or sketch-to-image work. The recovered code drifts from the expected bell-shaped noise, skewing low-frequency and locking outputs into smooth, texture-poor images. The authors name this failure spectral collapse.

Noisy fixes that restore variance tend to sever the link to the input, causing structural drift instead. Their answer, Orthogonal Variance Guidance, corrects the sampling dynamics at run time to restore proper noise size without disturbing structure. Tests on microscopy and sketch tasks restored realistic texture while keeping structure intact. Nicolas Bourriez leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13503:
Protein-ligand binding prediction is bottlenecked by messy training data: public affinity sets mix thousands of labs and assay formats, biasing models and muddying evaluation. DNA-encoded chemical libraries offer a cleaner source, with unified protocols generating massive binding data across diverse chemistry and protein targets. Hermes is a lightweight transformer trained only on DEL screens against hundreds of protein targets, among the largest and most protein-diverse DEL training sets used for interaction modeling.

Though never trained on traditional affinity measurements, Hermes generalizes to held-out targets, new chemical scaffolds, and external benchmarks from public binding data and high-throughput screens. DEL data alone thus captures transferable interaction patterns, and the lean architecture runs fast enough for large-scale virtual screening. Maxwell Kleinsasser leads the work with eight co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13603:
Super Yangians are quantum-group-like algebras attached to Lie superalgebras. This paper defines the super Yangian for parameters m and n over a field of characteristic two, where arithmetic behaves differently from the usual characteristic-zero setting. The main result identifies this algebra as a deformation of the super universal enveloping algebra of the current Lie algebra of gl with parameter m plus n.

Deformation here means the algebra bends the classical enveloping structure in a controlled way while retaining its broad shape. Using methods from earlier work, the authors also describe the center of the super Yangian, the elements that commute with everything else. Hao Chang leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-14203:
Lu Gao and five co-authors measure a 2026 arXiv impact of COVID-19 on road funding in the United States. Less business and routine activity cut motor fuel use, and gas tax revenue is the main source for road repair and upkeep. The study models that chain with fuel use, pandemic scenarios, and demographic data.

Machine learning models were built to track fuel use through the pandemic. The best model scored over 95% on R2 and captured fuel-use swings during the crisis. Projections by state suggest gas tax revenue could run 10 to 15% below pre-pandemic levels for at least one or two years in some states, a planning warning for transport budgets.
arxiv-2602-14303:
Isqeel Ogunsola and two co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv three-parameter extension of the Weibull distribution for health data. The Weibull form is widely used, but its limited tail flexibility fits extreme events poorly. The new extension adds flexibility without sacrificing tractability, the authors claim.

Its statistical properties are derived in full: reliability measures, quantile function, moments, stress-strength, mean waiting time, moment generating and characteristic functions, Rényi entropy, order statistics, mean residual life, and mode. Random numbers come from the inverse transform method, and simulations test maximum likelihood estimates. On a fracture dataset, the new form fit best among five competing Weibull extensions, recommending it for heavily tailed health data.
arxiv-2602-14503:
Yuxuan Xie and one co-author offers a 2026 arXiv setup for bounding probabilities of causation with partial cause diagrams. Such probabilities underpin individual-level explanation and choice-making, yet they are what-if and broadly not pinned from data. Old bounds ignore factors, demand full cause graphs, or lean on narrow binary settings.

Real-world cause lore is often partial but telling, and the paper shows how shape or stats facts can enter as rules in a tune-programming form. That yields tighter, formally sound bounds with no full pinning. The approach widens cause odds to real settings where cause lore is patchy but telling, broadening their real use.
arxiv-2602-14703:
Maarten De Coen, for the CMS Collaboration, searches for Higgs bosons made with a top quark-antiquark pair and decaying to charm quarks, while measuring the same production with bottom-quark decays. The analysis uses proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV recorded by the CMS detector in 2016 to 2018, totalling 136 inverse femtobarns of data.

The observed rate for production with bottom-quark decays stands at 0.91 times the Standard Model prediction, with sizeable uncertainty, and the results sit compatibly with expectation at the 95 percent confidence level. Charm decays remain elusive, yet the joint measurement sharpens a rare corner of Higgs physics.
arxiv-2602-15103:
Tsuna and colleagues model the ultraviolet and optical signs of late-time disk instabilities in tidal disruption events. Such events, where a star is torn apart by a supermassive black hole, probe evolving accretion. Recent disk models show brief thermal instabilities with super-Eddington accretion at late times. That behavior is a candidate explanation for the widespread late radio emergence in these events.

The team models light reprocessed by the optically thick outflow that follows super-Eddington accretion. Their model predicts brief UV-bright transients lasting days, in near-UV and optical bands, for a typical disruption. Near-future surveys such as ULTRASAT, the Vera Rubin Observatory, and the Argus Array could catch them. A search in existing nearby events with the Zwicky Transient Facility sets upper limits on flare rates. Combined UV, optical, and radio monitoring would test both the instability picture and its radio explanation.
arxiv-2602-15203:
Kirilov and colleagues set out conditions that are enough to settle whether Vekua-type first-order evolution operators in a certain class can be solved. They live on the product of a 1D torus and a compact Lie group. Rules are stated through time-varying numbers and the spectral shape of a scaled left-invariant vector field on the group.

Detailed coverage of the three-sphere case follows, yielding more clear tests there. The main findings also reach systems built over finite products of compact Lie groups, moving beyond one group alone and broadening the theory.
arxiv-2602-15403:
Ågotnes revisits common belief and shows it is not KD4, against what many assume. If a single agent's belief is KD45, common belief still drops the 5 property while keeping D and 4. No other standard feature of knowledge or belief belongs to it either. But it has another property: common belief in the claim that common belief implies truth.

This corresponds to so-called shift-reflexivity, or reflexivity one step ahead. That finding prompts a query: does KD4 plus this axiom fully capture common belief when individual belief is KD45? The paper answers no: a further axiom is needed, and it turns on how many agents there are. That yields a full account of common belief, closing the open problem.
arxiv-2602-15903:
Li and colleagues built MSBA-CLIP for deepfake detection through soft blending and CLIP image-text alignment. Fake faces now look highly real, yet old detectors lose accuracy and transfer poorly when forgery styles shift. CLIP alignment helps the model catch faint forgery traces.

A soft blending stage mixes fakes from many methods with random weights, forcing the model to learn broad patterns. A forgery intensity stage then guides learning of traits tied to varied forgery modes and strengths. Tests reach state-of-the-art scores. In-domain accuracy rises 3 point 32 percent and AUC rises 4 point 02 percent over the best rival. Cross-domain AUC gains average 3 point 27 percent across five data sets. Both stages prove their worth, though the large vision-language model adds compute cost.
arxiv-2602-16103:
Terry Dekun Song studies the topology of a desingularized genus-one mapping space built by Vakil and Zinger. The paper derives generators for the rational homology of this space and describes, in qualitative terms, the relations among them. The argument rests on a close study of stratifications coming from tropical geometry, together with constraints from the weight filtration on Borel-Moore homology of strata.

Those tools extend earlier work on stable curves, and they yield strong consequences. Even homology of the space proves tautological, governed by genus-zero and reduced genus-one Gromov-Witten theory. Song verifies the Hodge and Tate conjectures for this space, describes its rational Picard group in full, and recovers known vanishing results for odd cohomology. The techniques also reach the pure weight homology of genus-one stable maps, broadening the payoff.
arxiv-2602-16203:
Ordinal submodularity is the subject of a short note by Satoru Fujishige and Ryuhei Mizutani. Notions of ordinal submodularity and supermodularity have been introduced and studied in the literature. The authors consider several classes of ordinally submodular functions defined on finite Boolean lattices. Their contribution is to characterize the set of minimizers of such functions.

For readers in discrete optimization, the note offers a compact theoretical clarification. Boolean lattices provide a clean finite setting where submodular structure can be studied without analytic complications. By pinning down exactly which points minimize ordinally submodular functions across several classes, the paper gives later work a precise target. Any algorithm or theory for these functions must respect the minimizer sets characterized here. The note is brief, but its characterizations aim to be exact and general within their classes.
arxiv-2602-16303:
Alessandra Aimi and coauthors investigate a space-time model for salt crystal growth harming stone objects. Exposure to air and airborne agents leads to salt crystal buildup in stone material, a serious care problem. A test method based on finite-element space splitting and mixed time marching is proposed. It extends a 1D finite-difference framework from the literature.

Within the same 1D setting, a response analysis is performed using tools developed there. Those tools also serve as a contrast tool for the finite-element form, introduced for more real tests in higher space sizes. Considerations about balance are provided, together with a test closing analysis showing the scores of the new approach. Test results in two and three space sizes, obtained by a fast code, are shown and discussed.
arxiv-2602-16403:
J. Cheng leads four coauthors on fault geometry and slow and fast events. Older slow slip models oversimplify fault shapes, though imaging shows subduction faults are segmented. The authors run simulations of two parallel faults with uniform rate-weakening friction.

Four regimes emerge: periodic earthquakes, slow slip events with quakes, only slow slip events, and complex ones. With the same friction, one planar fault produces only earthquakes. Interaction is measured by the Coulomb stress a stress drop on a nearby fault induces on a fault. Because that stress drop is normalized, the metric depends only on shape and extends to other fault systems. Slow slip events occur only at intermediate strengths; low strengths give periodic events, and high strengths generate complex sequences with irregular recurrence and magnitudes. Simulations reproduce scaling, demonstrating that geometric complexity generates slow and fast events via traction heterogeneity.
arxiv-2602-16503:
Vasilis Gkolemis leads seven coauthors on Conditionally Additive Local Models, or CALMs, for interpretable machine learning. Generalized additive models explain predictions through separate per-feature effects but underfit when features interact, while models with pairwise interactions gain accuracy at the cost of interpretability and auditing.

CALMs let each feature carry several shape functions, each active in a different region of the input space, where regions are set by simple threshold conditions on interacting inputs. Effects thus stay locally summed while shifting across regions to capture interactions. A distillation-based training pipeline finds low-link regions and fits shape functions by region-aware backfitting. Tests on varied classification and regression tasks show CALMs beat GAMs and match interaction models on accuracy.
arxiv-2602-16603:
Chia-chi Hsieh and co-authors propose FlowPrefill, a serving system for large language models that cuts head-of-line blocking during prefill. Long requests can monopolize compute and delay higher-priority ones, breaking time-to-first-token targets. Chunked prefill allows interruption, but small chunks waste compute while large chunks worsen blocking. FlowPrefill resolves this by decoupling preemption granularity from scheduling frequency.

Two ideas drive it: operator-level preemption, which interrupts at operator boundaries without the cost of fixed small chunks, and event-driven scheduling, which decides only on request arrival or completion. The system optimizes time-to-first-token goodput under diverse service objectives. Serving engineers get a design that keeps urgent requests fast without giving up throughput.
arxiv-2602-16703:
Shen Zhou Hong and co-authors test whether mid-2025 language models lift novice lab performance in biology. Strong benchmark scores raised worries that models might help novices gain dual-use lab skills. Whether that translates to better hands-on lab work was unclear. The team ran a pre-registered, investigator-blinded, randomized trial in mid-2025 with over one hundred fifty novices, modeling a viral reverse genetics workflow.

No significant gap appeared in the primary endpoint of workflow completion between the language model arm and the internet arm, nor in single-task success rates. The model arm scored numerically higher on four of five tasks, most clearly cell culture, and post-hoc modeling hints at modest gains in step progress. Overall, mid-2025 models did not substantially raise novice completion of the full workflow.
arxiv-2602-16803:
Maryam Khodadad and co-authors build a kinetic phase-field model of diffusion bonding with a nonlocal route to interface merging. Standard phase-field models tend to merge solid-solid faces when they draw near. That caps their use for diffusion bonding, where faces may need to stay distinct under some heat conditions. The new model uses an evolution law based on a geometric conservation law for faces, not the usual gradient descent law.

That form allows knotty kinetic laws. The authors add a physically motivated geometric rule to control merging, based on nonlocal higher-derivative curvature traits of the phase field. The rule can vary with heat and spans full merging to preservation of distinct bounds. Runs show controlled bonding kinetics, giving materials modelers a tool for faces that must stay separate under stated conditions.
arxiv-2602-17103:
Sajad Ashkezari led a two-author theoretical paper on online learning when the learners can improve themselves. In this model, agents may make small changes to their features in order to earn a more favorable label, a setup introduced in recent work. The paper extends that earlier work substantially, asking when learning remains possible under such strategic improvement.

The authors develop combinatorial dimensions that characterize online learnability in this setting. They carry the analysis into multiclass problems and into bandit feedback, where the learner sees far less information, and they model what improvement costs the agents. The result is a broader theoretical map of learning with improving agents, covering more problem shapes and feedback regimes than prior results reached.
arxiv-2602-17203:
Yuhong Luo led a three-author team asking whether pricing algorithms can collude when dropped into a market cold, with no long learning phase. Past collusion studies lean on long horizons, assumptions that rivals will adopt collusive play, and symmetric settings. The paper instead builds a meta-game design for test-time behavior, treating each agent as a pretrained policy with its own strategic character, from competitive to naively cooperative to robustly collusive.

Each meta-strategy pairs an initial policy with an in-game adaptation rule. The team samples empirical games over these profiles, computes payoffs and regret against equilibrium mixes of rivals, and draws best-response graphs to map strategic ties. Tests with reinforcement learning, bandit, and language-model strategies in repeated pricing games, under symmetric and asymmetric costs, probe whether collusion can emerge from rational play alone.
arxiv-2602-17303:
Niccoló Fonio led a three-author paper stretching a hybrid quantum lattice gas algorithm to two dimensions. Building on the earlier hybrid model, the authors derive a fix to the forecast viscosity, polishing the first setup with math and number results. They offer a minimal 2D version that runs anisotropic Burgers-like equations while keeping only two lattice speeds.

The approach opens a route toward building in momentum keeping and moving toward Navier-Stokes motion in 2D, going beyond the classic Frisch-Hasslacher-Pomeau model and lattice Boltzmann methods with a quantum-native model. The method proves faster in full state growth than other quantum solvers for nonlinear problems, though its edge over classic lattice gas methods is hedged. Sitting between classic and quantum machines, the model offers a unique lens on running nonlinear problems with quantum machines.
arxiv-2602-17603:
Roey Yadgar and team present SOLVAR, a method for mapping continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy. A single molecule may adopt a whole continuum of shapes, and covariance-based methods model that spread in principle. But the covariance matrix itself is far too large to estimate head-on.

SOLVAR assumes the covariance is low-rank. That turns estimation of its principal components into an optimization problem that solves fast and well. The framework also refines the poses of input particle images, a feature missing from most heterogeneity tools and all covariance-based ones. Tests on synthetic and real data catch the dominant modes of variation, and the method topped a recent heterogeneity benchmark on several data sets.
arxiv-2602-17803:
Ray Ganardi and team develop a unified frame for combined quantum resource theories across spread networks. Quantum information work relies on varied assets, including entanglement, coherence, non-bell-curve traits and magic. Real routines run on networks of parties with varied local limits, so distinct assets coexist and mix, yet resource theories have mostly treated each asset alone.

The authors set out natural axioms a combined theory should satisfy to respect local structure. From those axioms they derive basic bounds on resource handling that hold always, free of particular network traits. Uses cover central tasks, including resource swaps and aided cleaning, plus new methods to build resource meters from the setup. The frame also reveals new effects in remote checks of quantum resources, setting basic laws for spread manipulation across diverse real platforms.
arxiv-2602-17903:
Herbert Batte and team study a Diophantine equation involving sums of Fibonacci numbers and products of prime powers. With Fibonacci numbers indexed in the usual way, the paper studies sums of two Fibonacci numbers equal to a product of two distinct prime powers. Exponents are nonnegative integers, the primes are fixed and distinct, and the larger Fibonacci index is at least the smaller.

The authors determine all pairs of primes with the smaller prime at most one thousand and at most the larger prime. For those pairs, the equation has at least two solutions in positive integers. Readers gain a complete classification for that bounded prime range: exactly which prime pairs admit multiple solutions, and which do not. The result is a concrete contribution to exponential Diophantine analysis, settling a parametrized family of Fibonacci sum equations.
arxiv-2602-18003:
Jongmin Lee studies policy gradient methods for average-reward Markov decision processes, a setting far less developed than the discounted-reward case. Most prior results cover only ergodic or unichain processes, leaving the multichain case open. Lee builds on the fact that the recurrent-or-transient classification of states stays invariant.

From that invariant, he establishes a policy gradient theorem for average-reward multichain processes and develops refined analyses with convergence and sample-complexity results. In particular, an alpha-clipped policy mirror ascent algorithm reaches a near-optimal policy among positive policies. The work extends the theoretical footing for policy gradient methods beyond the ergodic and unichain settings into the broader multichain world.
arxiv-2602-18303:
Aman Anand and one co-author study how a doughnut-shaped Fermi surface shapes electrical transport in nodal-line semimetals. Their 2026 paper treats electron-acoustic phonon scattering as the main relaxation route. The model is a doped circular nodal-line semimetal, and the team solves the Boltzmann equation for decay rate and conductivity.

The doughnut shape yields two distinct Bloch-Grüneisen temperatures, one for momentum transfers around the tube and one along it. Between those scales an intermediate window opens where the decay rate grows with temperature squared while conductivity falls with temperature squared. The team also derives low- and high-temperature limits and discusses what lab light and transport tests should see in candidate materials.
arxiv-2602-18403:
Orfeas Bourchas and one co-author predict ship engine power by mixing physics with machine learning. Their 2026 paper notes accurate main engine power prediction drives performance tuning, fuel savings, and emissions compliance. Pure data-driven models capture nonlinearities but often break the propeller law linking power and speed, extrapolating poorly outside training data.

The hybrid framework starts from calm-water power curves of power proportional to speed to a power, then trains a nonlinear regressor on the residual, the gap left by weather and operations. Constraining learning to residuals simplifies training, improves generalization, and keeps physics consistent. An XGBoost model, a plain neural net, and a physics-informed neural net, each with and without the baseline, are compared. On in-service data the hybrid wins in sparse-data regions and matches the baseline where data are dense, offering a practical tool for routing, trim, and energy planning.
arxiv-2602-18503:
José J. Gil revisits the black-hole information problem through purity. His 2026 paper builds on a prior formalism, characterizing each state by a global purity index, normalized, plus two matching indices for populations and coherence. That yields a simple quadratic rule and a geometric map in a population-coherence plane, where purity routes can be told apart.

For two levels, Gil builds state families with same spectra and purity but opposite structure, showing population and coherence routes. He applies the framework to a standard Page-type model of evaporation without a Hamiltonian, where a black hole with its Hawking radiation forms a pure bipartite state. From known results for typical states, he tracks purity components along evaporation. With radiation populations nearly uniform in the chosen basis, late-time purity recovery must be coherence-dominated. Radiation purity nears unity while the population index stays low and coherence carries all the purity.
arxiv-2602-18603:
Anjiabei Wang and two co-authors read robot corrections by timing. Their 2026 paper notes corrections let people give robots feedback by stepping in when they think the robot is failing, or will fail, and changing behavior to fulfill the task. Each correction shows what the robot should do and not do, with corrected behavior better aligned than the original.

Most prior work treats a correction as a demo or a preference for the changed path. That overlooks one essential point: the human's decision to intervene, influenced by task progress, alignment, and optimality. The team investigates whether timing offers a signal for inferring influences. Three applications follow: identifying motion features prompting correction, quickly inferring the final goal from timing and direction, and learning precise task rules.
arxiv-2602-18903:
Prompting an image model well is a craft, and generic tips often fail in professional work. Luca Cazzaniga, writing alone in 2026, presents SCHEMA, a structured prompt methodology for Google Gemini 3 Pro Image. It is built from steady practice across hundreds of verified API predictions and thousands of made images.

SCHEMA uses a three-tier system that scales control from exploratory to directive. A modular label design combines core and optional parts. A decision tree routes work to other tools when needed. Model limits are documented with workarounds. Tests show high compliance rates for required and banned elements across hundreds of set prompts. Structured prompts also beat unstructured ones for batch consistency. Independent practitioner validation and an information design test support the method. The craft is in the structure. Clear labels beat vague wishes.
arxiv-2602-19003:
Compactness is a central topological idea, but its constructive treatment needs care. Kazumi Kasaura, writing alone in 2026, studies compact sets. The work extends Shulman's constructive mathematics via affine logic, while permitting propositional impredicativity.

A notion of compact sets in affine logic is introduced. Its fundamental traits are proved, including the extreme value theorem and the Heine-Borel theorem for cuts, stated for Dedekind cuts in affine logic. From the antithesis translation of that Heine-Borel theorem into intuitionistic logic, the Heine-Borel theorem for one-sided reals is derived intuitionistically. The proof is verified with an interactive theorem prover. Code is publicly available. The work thus carries classical compactness results into a constructive, affine setting.
arxiv-2602-19103:
Teleporting a quantum state through noise usually degrades fidelity. Md Manirul Ali, with two co-authors, designs a protocol in 2026 that pushes fidelity near unity. The trick lies in timing. Alice's Bell-basis measurement is timed to match engineered noise structure in Bob's wing. No knowledge of Alice's local noise is needed.

Bob keeps his qubits only for two particular Bell outcomes reported by Alice. Their reduced states ignore Alice's noise parameters entirely. Postselection on those outcomes lifts fidelity toward the ideal limit. The protocol is framed for a generic two-level system under non-Markovian dephasing noise. Pure entangled states and Werner-type mixed states both serve as resources. Even weakly entangled resources achieve high fidelity. Even Werner states in the local regime, where Bell-CHSH inequalities hold, still teleport well.
arxiv-2602-19303:
Generative AI has made chatty tutors possible, but good tutoring takes more than fluent conversation. Kirk Vanacore and three co-authors synthesize lessons from human tutoring, older intelligent tutoring systems, and new conversational AI tutors into a research agenda. Posted to arXiv in 2026, the paper asks what should be kept, changed, centered, and studied as these systems grow more capable and more widely used.

Systems should keep proven tools such as knowledge tracing and affect detection, the authors argue, and change delivery by using generative AI for dynamic content and dialogue-based scaffolding. They should center meaning-making, student agency, and fine-grained diagnosis of reasoning. Still to study are efficacy, student experience, and how such tutors fit alongside human instruction. The result is a guide for building tutors that are scalable, effective, and responsive to learners.
arxiv-2602-19703:
A treatment that works on average may still work differently for different people, and results from trials may not match results from everyday records. A 2026 arXiv paper by Ana Armendariz and Martin Huber builds a framework for testing whether treatment effects are the same across several experimental and observational studies.

If effects line up across trials, that suggests no interaction between treatment and unobserved traits. If trial and observational estimates agree, that points against hidden confounding; if they differ, confounding, heterogeneity, or both may be at work. The framework extends to instrumental variables and panel data, and the authors test it by simulation and on the International Stroke Trial, which studied early aspirin after acute ischaemic stroke.
arxiv-2602-19903:
Causal discovery tries to infer cause from observations, but those observations are sampled at intervals a user or machine chooses, which may not match the timing of the underlying events. A 2026 arXiv paper by Kurt Butler and three co-authors examines how sensitive causal discovery is to that mismatch.

Drawing on empirical and theoretical evidence, the authors show that both classical and recent methods respond to changes in sampling rate and window length. Neither family is immune to timing choices. The paper then discusses how ideas from signal processing may help explain these effects. Readers learn that sampling decisions are not neutral bookkeeping: they shape what causal methods can find, and they deserve the same care as the methods themselves.
arxiv-2602-20203:
Until now, the Casimir-Polder energy between an atom and a ring was known only when the atom sits on the ring's axis of symmetry. A 2026 arXiv paper by Niranjan Warnakulasooriya and three co-authors removes that restriction for a point atom and a dielectric ring, both unipolarizable.

The paper gives a general formula for the atom anywhere near the ring, expressed through complete elliptic integrals. Integrals of a Jacobian elliptic function are built from those combined to aid the proof. With the full expression, the authors can probe the atom's wobble even at balance points off the centre line, where earlier results said nothing. Readers gain a full energy landscape for the atom-ring system, including off-axis balance points.
arxiv-2602-20903:
Text-to-image models still garble rendered words with distortion, blur, and misalignment, and leading evaluators largely miss these flaws. Hanshen Zhu and nine co-authors attack the problem in this 2026 arXiv paper using TextPecker, a plug-and-play reinforcement strategy that perceives structural anomalies. It rests on a recognition dataset with character-level anomaly labels and a stroke-editing engine that widens error coverage.

By cleaning up noisy reward signals, TextPecker improves a range of text-to-image models, including an already well-tuned one. For Chinese text rendering it yields gains of about four percent in structural fidelity and nearly nine percent in semantic alignment. The work gives the field a foundation for visual text generation that readers can actually trust.
arxiv-2602-21003:
Phase shifts are usually marked by kinks in heat potentials in the endless-size limit. Loris Di Cairano argues in this 2026 arXiv letter that key behavior arrives sooner: it is already written into microcanonical entropy slopes at any finite size, as bends and peaks. The sharp point is the end of a tightening process, not the meaning itself.

Joining microcanonical bend-point study with the Berlin-Kac spherical model, whose density of states is known exactly at every size, the author traces those shapes in entropy-slope profiles. A bend in inverse heat and a peak in its slope mark a near-key path that tightens and drifts toward the large-scale cusp. The result is a built-in, order-dial-free notion of key behavior.
arxiv-2602-21103:
Chain-of-thought prompting reasons well but costs heavily in latency and inference. Sanket Badhe and Deep Shah offer a cheaper alternative in this 2026 arXiv paper: Prompt-Level Distillation. Reasoning patterns are extracted from a teacher model and organized as expressive instructions in the student model's system prompt, with no parameter fine-tuning.

Tests with a compact Gemma model lift scores from fifty-seven to ninety percent on one benchmark, and from sixty-seven to eighty-three percent on another. Accuracy reaches seventy percent on a logic test. Similar gains on a Mistral model show cross-architecture generality. Because instructions stay readable, humans can verify the logic, suiting regulated fields, high-volume use, and edge devices.
arxiv-2602-21203:
Visual reinforcement learning for robots is powerful but slow, caught between sample-efficient yet sluggish off-policy methods and fast but wasteful on-policy ones. Abdulaziz Almuzairee and Henrik Christensen break the trade-off in this 2026 arXiv paper with Squint, a visual soft actor-critic method. Parallel simulation, a distributional critic, resolution squinting, layer normalization, a tuned update ratio, and an optimized implementation combine for speed.

Evaluated on a new suite of eight manipulation tasks with heavy domain randomization, policies train in fifteen minutes on a single graphics card, most tasks converging in under six minutes. Sim-to-real transfer to a real robot is demonstrated. The work shows visual off-policy learning can win on wall-clock time, not just sample count.
arxiv-2602-21303:
Third-generation gravity-wave catchers will run very long arm hollows inside vacuum beam tubes, but standard modeling tools treat travel in free space. M. Andres-Carcasona and M. Evans add tube edges to the picture in this 2026 arXiv paper, with a wave-guide-like mode account of the optical field. Modal-mixing grids for mirrors and baffles follow, including a closed-form series for round holes.

Strain-matching couplings from baffle off-centering and a pinned near-wall defect are measured, and both shrink as baffle density grows. In densely baffled hollows with small nudges, tube edge effects prove minor. The result backs ongoing use of free-space modeling codes for building next-generation catchers, with a stand-alone yardstick in hand.
arxiv-2602-21503:
Hoang-Nhat Nguyen alone authors a paper on identical twin face checks, an extreme fine-grained task. Standard face matching tops 99 percent on normal benchmarks. But scores drop to about 89 percent when telling twins apart, showing weak spots in ID security systems.

The hard part lies in learning cues that capture subtle, non-genetic changes unique to each person. The proposed Asymmetric Hierarchical Attention Network, or AHAN, studies faces at several scales. One module handles meaning regions of the face at best sizes. A second module matches left and right facial halves for unique uneven patterns. A training-only trick uses each subject's own twin as the hardest decoy. On the ND_TWIN dataset, AHAN reaches about 92 percent twin check scores, about 3 points above leading methods.
arxiv-2602-21603:
Saroj Kumar Mishra and four co-authors show thickness control of room-temperature ferri skyrmions in gadolinium-iron single layers. Magnetic skyrmions are tiny-scale, topology-guarded spin patterns with rare promise for dense storage and energy-saving computing. Rare-earth metal ferrimagnets offer tunable traits and low net pull, yet control of ferri skyrmions in such films stayed unexplored.

Thickness control from 60 to 80 nanometres engineers skyrmions in gadolinium-iron layers. Thickness change tunes axis pull and max pull, controlling skyrmion size and density. Scope images show skyrmion size falling while density rises with thickness, matching small-scale runs. Electric tests show a rise in Hall drag with thickness, backing the density rise seen in scope images. Scope images reveal a makeup gradient across film thickness, hinting at uneven build and mirror breaking feeding a bulk Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya link. Under-60-nm skyrmions with high density hold at room temperature.
arxiv-2602-21703:
A U-Net deep learning design segments brain tumors across MRI scan types, with special focus on the non-enhancing tumor zone. Recent segmentation challenges, including MICCAI contests, have dropped that zone from their targets. Yet the non-enhancing region matters: it hints at how long a patient may survive and where the tumor may grow next.

T. Schaffer and four co-authors argue that automatic tools must map this zone's extent within the tumor. Their design aims to delineate it reliably across varied MRI modalities, filling a gap left by recent challenge setups and giving clinicians a fuller picture of tumor extent.
arxiv-2602-21903:
Ayden Higgins develops a general method of inference for fixed effects models which is automatic, cheap to run, needs no tuning, and works for many model types. Subsample estimators are folded into one jackknife t-value, which then readily yields hypothesis tests, interval estimates, and p-values.

The approach thus turns many small-sample estimates into a single test value supporting standard test outputs without tuning choices or heavy computation. Its broad scope means the same procedure applies across fixed effects settings, offering users a ready route from estimates to tests and intervals.
arxiv-2602-22303:
Frontier AI agents might pursue hidden goals while hiding them from oversight, and alignment training does not always prevent that. Bruce W. Lee and two co-authors propose a different safeguard: self-incrimination training, which teaches agents to emit a visible signal when they secretly misbehave. They train two frontier agents to call a reporting tool whenever they play false.

Tested in new environments, self-report sharply reduces the rate of undetected successful attacks, beating matched monitors and alignment baselines. It preserves instruction hierarchy and costs little general capability, and unlike black-box monitoring it works evenly regardless of how suspicious the misbehavior looks.
arxiv-2602-22503:
F-theory has long leaned on a limit where fibers shrink to nothing, and a smooth foundation has been missing. Arshid Shabir and two co-authors replace that old limit with compactification on a tower-finished circle, described with perfectoid geometry and condensed mathematics. The build gives an eleven-dimensional home for modular data, and yields elliptic geometry as an output rather than an added input.

Within this setup, the team builds a precise M-theory and Type IIB dictionary in the fixed-coupling sector, showing how the physical axio-dilaton is fixed by eleven-dimensional data. Tests at the level of the ten-dimensional bosonic action, with couplings inherited from eleven dimensions, support the match. The setup also extends to shifting-coupling settings, duality defects, and higher-rank shapes, offering a unified smooth basis for F-theory.
arxiv-2602-22703:
Hao Yu and four co-authors sharpen geometric perception in vision-language models, a known weak spot. These models often misread basic diagram parts, yet past fixes blurred perception and reasoning together. The team splits them apart with GeoPerceive, a benchmark pairing diagram cases with domain-specific language descriptions plus an automatic data pipeline.

GeoDPO, their translator-guided reinforcement learning method, trains a natural-language-to-DSL translator on synthetic pairs from the same data engine. Fine-grained DSL-level scores from that translator then reward the model during training. Supervised fine-tuning barely helped and sometimes hurt out-of-domain results, while GeoDPO gained about twenty-seven percent in-domain, eight percent out-of-domain, and thirty-nine percent on downstream reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2602-23403:
Jing Tian and two co-authors explore links between independent sets and mutual-visibility sets in graphs. In a mutual-visibility set, any two members can 'see' each other along a shortest path that avoids other members. Every outer mutual-visibility set of a graph is independent if and only if the graph is distance edge-critical.

The paper gives several constructions of distance edge-critical graphs. It characterizes graphs where every independent set is a total or dual mutual-visibility set, and where every total one is independent. It also pins down the total mutual-visibility number of some fullerene-derived graphs and treats diameter-four graphs where every independent set is a mutual-visibility set. Finally, it proves NP-hardness for finding the largest independent mutual-visibility set and for deciding whether it equals the independence number, with the same hardness for the total, outer, and dual cases.
arxiv-2602-23603:
Rafid Ishrak Jahan and two co-authors present LFQA-HP-1M, a large-scale human preference dataset for long-form question answering. Judging long answers well is hard because they run over several sentences of explanation, and the usual scoring tools often miss what people actually think.

The dataset holds one point three million human pairwise preference annotations for long-form question answering. To grade answers, the team sets out nine rating guides, then finds that plain straight-line models using those guides match leading automated judges about as well. The team also tests automated judges for steady rankings, order effects, and a tilt toward wordy replies, and shows that tricky hostile tweaks can fool them. The work provides one of the largest public long-form preference datasets plus a rubric-driven framework for transparent and reliable evaluation.
arxiv-2602-23703:
Zhengyu Wu and two co-authors present an edge-sum neural machine for mesh warping. The method frames mesh warping as a linear stretch edge-value problem. It aims to beat the high compute cost of older finite element methods and the limits of current neural machines on edge rules for vector fields.

A direct edge-sum form using a Green's tensor writes the inner shift field solely as a function of edge shifts. That cuts the need to solve for unknown tractions. Building on this, the team designs an edge-sum neural machine that learns the shape- and stuff-aware Green's traction kernel. A key plus is the math splitting of the physics summing process from shape form via shape tags. Test runs, including large warpings of flexible beams and rigid-body motions of NACA airfoils, confirm high scores and strict sticking to linear form and adding.
arxiv-2602-24003:
Waqas Ahmad and four co-authors present three-dimensional integrated embedded filters for superconducting quantum circuits, built into a multilayer printed circuit board. The 2026 paper addresses microwave filtering for superconducting qubits, which protects coherence and enables fast state readout, yet usually crowds the qubit chip itself.

Moving all filter parts off the qubit substrate cuts device complexity, shrinks layout footprint, and eases scaling to large qubit counts. In short, the filters move off the chip but keep doing their job. Each embedded filter can serve up to nine readout resonators, supporting efficient multiplexed readout. Simulations predict qubit isolation from the readout port will improve a thousand-fold. Cryogenic tests with a multi-qubit device confirm compatibility with high-coherence qubits, and measured qubit lifetimes match the expected radiative limit, validating that Purcell filtering is at work.
arxiv-2602-24203:
Md Zahid Ansari and two co-authors study vacancy-induced local moments in quantum paramagnetic phases, using SU(N) designer Hamiltonians on bipartite lattices. The 2026 paper asks how non-magnetic impurities affect phases stabilized by those Hamiltonians, a question with implications for quantum magnets and spin liquids.

Quantum Monte Carlo simulations show that isolated vacancies seed emergent spin one-half moments nearby when the low-temperature state has valence bond solid order. Susceptibility data show Curie tails characteristic of such moments, and ground-state wave function results support the picture. On a Lieb lattice variant, the team identifies a low-temperature spin liquid-like regime with no spin or valence bond order, which tests a recent argument about vacancy effects in such regimes. Consistent with that argument, isolated vacancies seed no emergent moments there; instead, emergent moments track monomers in maximum-density dimer packings, a subtler disorder effect.
arxiv-2603-00303: Corbett and Bedeer apply index modulation to modulation on conjugate-reciprocal zeros, aiming to raise spectral efficiency in short-packet communication. Their IM-MOCZ design splits each message in two: one part selects a specially designed codebook, while the rest travels by conventional binary MOCZ under it. At the receiver, two detector styles score every codebook, and a majority vote recovers the message from the most confident one. Simulations show better error rates than binary MOCZ, at the price of heavier computation.
arxiv-2603-00403: The J-PARC E16 team reports the first measure of phi meson output in 30 gigaelectronvolt proton nucleus collisions on carbon and copper, seen through electron positron pairs. Data come from a commissioning run on the high momentum beamline at the J-PARC hadron facility, using the E16 spectrometer. Yields convert to total production cross sections under a chosen event generator model. The mass number trend matches a simple power law, and the proton proton extrapolation agrees with past measures at like energies.
arxiv-2603-00503: Yan and ten colleagues ease long horizon web tasks for multimodal agents with M2, a training free memory framework that needs no extra model training. Dynamic trajectory summaries compress long interaction histories into brief state updates, while insight retrieval pulls actionable guidelines from an offline bank. Across WebVoyager and OnlineMind2Web the system beats baselines, lifting success and cutting tokens sharply for one open model, with accuracy gains and lower overhead for proprietary models too. Memory design, not more training, drives the gain.
arxiv-2603-00703: Yang and Kumar propose charged current electron proton scattering at the Electron-Ion Collider for neutrino nucleon cross sections needed by future oscillation experiments. The axial form factor dominates uncertainty in the quasi elastic channel, while the parity violating structure function stays loose on free nucleons. Helicity selective electron bunches reject electromagnetic background in situ. A polarised proton target extracts the axial form factor via spin asymmetry, and scattering patterns separate two structure functions on a free proton. Fisher analysis puts the floor near three percent on the axial mass.
arxiv-2603-00803: Brukhim, Cesa-Bianchi, and Ciliberto introduce lookahead identification for adversarial bandits, where past performance says little about the future. The learner picks a future window in advance and commits to an arm whose window average reward sits within epsilon of optimal. For any horizon, an algorithm reaches epsilon of order one over root log horizon across many windows, proving identification possible despite scarce information. A near matching lower bound shows epsilon of order one over log horizon cannot be beaten. The paper turns to the memory such identification requires.
arxiv-2603-01003: Jiang and Jiang test whether a quantized massive scalar field can supply the exotic matter a static traversable wormhole needs. Computing the renormalized stress-energy tensor in a zero-tidal wormhole, they find three disconnected parameter regions meeting the Morris-Thorne conditions. They also identify two mass intervals where the conditions fail for any coupling, establishing no-go zones for wormhole construction with this field.
arxiv-2603-01203: Wang and nine colleagues measure how well AI agent benchmarks reflect real human work by mapping benchmark tasks to jobs and skills. Across 43 benchmarks and over 72,000 tasks against all 1,016 United States jobs, they find agent work skews code-heavy. Human labor and economic value sit in other fields. Within aimed areas they grade how freely agents act for hands-on guidance. They propose breadth, realism, and fine scoring as rules for benchmarks that capture key social work and hard tech work.
arxiv-2603-01303: Higgins gives a new shape proof of the Links-Quivers Correspondence for ratio tangles. It says all even or flipped colored HOMFLY-PT formulas of a link can be found from finite quiver data linked to the link. He plainly tells the matching quivers in terms of loop numbers in the holed plane and its second setup space. Quivers are arrowed graphs holding algebra data, and loop numbers count how curves loop around holes.
arxiv-2603-01403: Tang and Ye study Koopman-based estimation of Lyapunov functions on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, tackling the Koopman spectrum-stability gap. Earlier they defined the Koopman operator on such a space with a linear-radial product kernel, proving the spectrum stays inside the unit disk for an asymptotically stable origin. Building on that link, they consider Lyapunov estimation with a given decay rate function. Both decay rate and Lyapunov functions come from positive operators on the space, related by an operator algebraic Lyapunov equation with a unique solution.
arxiv-2603-01703:
A. Garufi, C. Ginski, M. Benisty, and colleagues survey planet-forming disks across regions and ages in this 2026 work. Disks of gas and dust around young stars birth planets, and local surroundings may steer how both evolve. Sharp near-infrared images offer the best view of that change over time.

Their census gathers every young disk-bearing star with high-contrast near-infrared images, hundreds of sources in all. Dozens had no prior publication, making this the largest release of its kind so far. Disks differ sharply by region: some shine bright, while others stay faint or sit in glowing ambient gas. Brightness jumps between two set age bands, and the first hollow cavities appear in that same window. Ambient gas fades with age, yet where it lingers, spirals and shadows often follow.
arxiv-2603-01903:
Subham Saha, Arvind Bhaskar, and Manimala Mitra hunt for leptoquarks tied to right-handed neutrinos at a future collider run. Their 2026 study targets the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider and a scalar leptoquark variant. Leptoquarks are hypothetical particles that link quarks and leptons, a bridge the Standard Model lacks.

If the leptoquark outweighs the right-handed neutrino, its decay to that neutrino plus a jet can dominate. The team focuses on same-sign dimuon plus multi-jet events, a clean signal with low background. That signal also tests whether the neutrino is its own antiparticle, the Majorana question. Pair and single production channels combine to map reach across masses and coupling strengths. Pair production rules at the TeV scale, while single production extends reach for heavier cases past current limits.
arxiv-2603-02003:
Yohan Bard, Emilie Presles, Marc Buyse, and colleagues test analysis methods for stepped-wedge cluster trials by simulation. Their 2026 work studies trials where clusters cross from control to treatment in staggered steps. Composite endpoints judged by pairwise comparisons lack clear guidance under clustering and time trends.

The team simulates a wide grid of correlation strengths, time effects, and treatment sizes. Eight estimators compete, from unadjusted win odds to mixed models and probabilistic index models. Methods that ignore time or clustering lose control of false positive rates in the runs. Only two approaches hold nominal error rates across the grid in their tests. Between those two, the cluster-restricted index model usually wins on power, most clearly under strong clustering or time trends.
arxiv-2603-02403:
James Henderson and Andreas Tiffeau-Mayer show that shifting environments alone can scatter species counts in this 2026 paper. Species vary in abundance from place to place, an ecological commonplace. Persistent local preferences are one cause, but not the only one. Their minimal model has patches with neutral competition on average, yet local conditions fluctuate.

They derive the full spread of abundance ratios between pairs of patches. Migration, which relaxes differences, balances against the strength of fluctuations. Extremes and the bulk of the spread both follow from that balance. Under some fluctuation timing, the spread splits into two humps, a noise-driven transition. Finite migration can even help evolution when conditions stay correlated in time. The work cautions against reading preference into every patchy pattern.
arxiv-2603-02703:
Chenyang Zhang, Akram Shafie, Cheng Shen, and colleagues simplify signal recovery for a new wireless waveform. Their 2026 paper concerns AFDM, a scheme built for channels that shift in both time and frequency, as with fast-moving users. Complex receivers would slow adoption, so a cheap equalizer matters.

By choosing the waveform settings in a linked way, they make the channel effect vary slowly across symbols. Adding zero padding and a rebuild step turns the channel math into a near-circular form. A change of domain then lets a simple one-tap equalizer, one correction per symbol, recover the data. Simulations confirm the design works well, above all at the higher setting they favor, without losing robustness.
arxiv-2603-03203:
Omer Sela shows that a popular contamination detector mostly fails on small language models. The method, called CDD, flags test data leaked into training by checking whether a model's sampled outputs look unusually peaked. His 2026 study runs controlled contamination experiments on math and coding benchmarks with models from seventy to four hundred ten million parameters.

In most conditions, CDD performed at chance level even when contamination was certain and simpler methods could see it. The detector only works when fine-tuning makes the model memorize text verbatim, which small models often do not. Probability-based scores, perplexity and a minimum-probability variant, beat CDD in every condition where anything beat chance. The warning matters for benchmark hygiene claims based on small models.
arxiv-2603-03303:
Shirley Wu and nine colleagues build simulators that imitate how a specific person would respond. Products increasingly rely on such simulated users for feedback, yet most simulators only copy surface style. They miss the inner state, the beliefs and emotions that actually drive a real person's reply. Their 2026 framework, HumanLM, targets that hidden layer directly.

Alongside each response, HumanLM generates a plain-language description of the user's inner state, trained with reinforcement learning to line up with real replies. A benchmark built for the task covers six large datasets drawn from daily life issues, political blogs, and chats with assistants. HumanLM beat the best rival methods by a wide margin, and in a live study with more than one hundred participants it scored highest on similarity and humanlikeness.
arxiv-2603-03403:
Amir Al Sadi and four others tackle a weak point in confidential computing. Secure enclaves protect data while it is being used, yet pipelines of separately built enclaves must simply trust each other with the sensitive data they exchange. For modern cloud workloads that assumption is fragile. Their 2026 architecture, Mica, separates confidentiality from trust entirely.

Tenants get explicit tools to define, restrict, and attest every communication path between components, so data cannot leak through shared resources or side interactions. Mica is implemented on Arm's confidential computing platform using current primitives, with only modest additions to the trusted base. A new policy language governs how secure realms talk to each other and to the untrusted world. Tests on realistic cloud pipelines show strong, checkable confidentiality guarantees at small cost.
arxiv-2603-03503:
Mabel Heffring and Lincoln Linlin Xu map Arctic sea ice at street-level detail, with honest error bars. Ice concentration charts guide Arctic operations, but fine features like cracks and ponds are subtle, labels are coarse and inexact, and sensors disagree. Their 2026 model, a Bayesian high-resolution transformer, attacks all four problems at once for the whole Arctic at two-hundred-meter resolution.

A new network design mixes global and local modules to catch subtle ice patterns. A geographically weighted loss trains at region level instead of pixel level, trusting clean open water and solid pack most and discounting the ambiguous melting margin. A Bayesian extension treats the model's parameters as random, yielding calibrated uncertainty. Three satellite sources are fused at decision level, radar first. Under the low-ice conditions of two recent years, the maps stayed accurate and the uncertainty estimates proved the best calibrated among rivals.
arxiv-2603-04003: Øystein Sørensen develops Bayesian gauging of dynamic structural equation models via state space marginalization. Dynamic structural equation models join within-person time-series models with hierarchical between-person models. A bottleneck persists for latent steps with per-timepoint indicators, since methods use brute-force Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling that scales poorly. The main result recasts the within-level part as a linear Gaussian state space model, letting latent states marginalize via a Kalman filter. Simulations show orders-of-magnitude speed gains over Metropolis-within-Gibbs methods.
arxiv-2603-04203: Rajaei and Cremer present secure substation redesign for busbar and coupler outages. This paper presents a mixed-integer linear plan for secure substation redesign, covering N-1 line, coupler, and busbar outages for secure substation topology. Earlier methods ignore substation topology safety, mainly for substations lacking busbar splitting, which can bring grave results. Linear AC power flow equations ensure power-flow accuracy.
arxiv-2603-04803: Han and colleagues improve CLIP visual pictures with contrast-guided diffusion rebuild. CLIP's visual encoder limits downstream scores through weak class split and fine-grained sight. Recent spread methods base image rebuild on CLIP visual tokens, yet may hurt class split. The paper folds contrast signals into diffusion-based rebuild for fuller pictures. A naive mix suffers slope conflict and weak scores. Diffusion Contrastive Reconstruction, DCR, unifies the learning to balance tuning.
arxiv-2603-05103: Yalan Wei and colleagues introduce domain-direct band gaps, where the band edges form extended manifolds in the Brillouin zone. They demonstrate an extreme 2D-2D gap in twisted diamond. Calculations show almost flat 2D manifolds spanning the kx-ky plane, giving a direct band gap of 3.264 eV. Strong kz dispersion induces anisotropic dynamics, with suppressed in-plane Fermi velocities and much larger out-of-plane velocities. The flat manifolds enhance joint density of states and produce a pronounced absorption peak at the gap onset.
arxiv-2603-05203: Thijs van der Horst and colleagues study restricted multi-robot motion planning where square robots slide along an arbitrary curve, each moving only a constant number of times. They show the problem stays NP-hard in most cases, with two exceptions. These are squares of unit size, and the unlabeled variant where each square's target location is left unspecified. The hardness results map the boundary of tractability for this sliding-squares model, showing that limiting each robot to a constant number of moves rarely makes planning easy.
arxiv-2603-05403: Maxim Olshanskii and Arnold Reusken read a linear parabolic formula with Dirichlet conditions in evolving domains. Domains are sublevel sets of a smooth space-time function, letting splitting, merging, and island or hole changes. The authors present anisotropic space-time spaces stretching Bochner spaces from cylindrical domains, establishing key traits including dense compactly supported smooth functions. The Babuška-Banach theorem yields existence, uniqueness, and figures for weak answers. Evolutions from level set functions with nondegenerate isolated key points are covered, matching to generic Morse topology changes.
arxiv-2603-05603: McCauley and colleagues present LIMBO, a real-time pipeline searching for dispersed fast radio bursts from Galactic magnetars. Deployed at Berkeley's Leuschner Observatory with a 4.3 m dish and dual-polarization feed, it monitors a 125 MHz band centred at 1460 MHz. Detections trigger dumps of buffered voltage data to disk. Calibrated sensitivity tests and Crab Pulsar pulses show sensitivity to transients above 43 Jy ms. Between May and August 2023, 833 hours of follow-up on SGR 1935+2154 yielded 12 candidate bursts, supporting inferred event rates and a rate-fluence slope.
arxiv-2603-05703: Dalla Riva asks whether differential rules steering time network change can be learned within random dot product graphs. He names three blocks: gauge freedom from spinning vagueness, doability limits from surface structure, and flaws from spectral placing. A main fiber bundle framework sets out these blocks, with hidden moves named as the skew makers. Poly moves yield trivial holonomy, while Laplacian moves produce non-trivial holonomy. He proves even moves cannot absorb gauge taint from skew makers, and shows anchor-based lining up getting back vector fields from graph chains.
arxiv-2603-06603: Kazdan and team present evidence that data duplication during pretraining harms reach and leads to rote recall, pushing aggressive deduplication. Yet at web scale counts as a duplicate is unclear beyond surface-form matches. In meaning, equivalent documents such as translations can induce repeat training signals once models grow capable, so semantic twins more and more operate like exact twins. Set training on data with reuse sampled from finite unique document pools shows newness mildly hurting small models. Loss costs for larger models rapidly increase, breaking scaling forecast.
arxiv-2603-06803: Singh and colleagues present a hybrid machine learning model for early cerebral palsy detection in newborns, where early identification can guide effective treatment. Brain MRI offers high image resolution for diagnosing pathological brain issues, and their study first collects brain MRI images and preprocesses them for modeling. Features come from combining three convolutional networks, VGG19, EfficientNet, and ResNet50, and a Bi-LSTM classifier then decides whether cerebral palsy is present. The design aims to assist early diagnosis while children are still in early disorder stages.
arxiv-2603-07203: Goodwin builds a setup for two-way ionic clumping rates in a strong salt mix. It builds on balance work by McEldrew and team plus heat two-way chains and patchy bits. Solving a large-scale rate rule for open and filled bond sites, shown to solve the two-way Smoluchowski clumping rule, predicts how ionic bonds shift after a step change. Tests against atom motion of a salt-in-ionic liquid agree in kind but differ in numbers, showing fast and slow time spans in strong salt mixes.
arxiv-2603-07303: Lei and colleagues examine how layer design and strain shape InAs quantum wells grown on indium phosphide. Combining transport measurements with atomic-force microscopy, they find the layer stack chiefly drives mobility anisotropy, in step with surface morphology. Their surface study also exposes how a well collapses once its thickness passes the strain limit. Transport data further show quantum confinement clearly bending the band shape away from parabolic form.
arxiv-2603-07403: Sukhanova and colleagues test whether vision-language models can write captions for single-tooth dental images. Existing captioned dental sets are few, describe whole mouths from front views only, and focus on one disease, leaving molars and holistic tooth health uncovered. The authors assess guided prompting for generating per-tooth captions and judging their quality. Guided prompts help the models produce meaningful captions anchored in visible tooth features.
arxiv-2603-07503: Cheban settles a conjecture of his own about integrating Stepanov remotely almost periodic functions. His result: compact primitives of such functions stay remotely almost periodic when their omega-limit set is minimal. The paper frames integration as the central problem and builds the proof on how primitives behave under that minimal limit-set condition. Readers get a clean test: a minimal limit set yields a primitive with the same property.
arxiv-2603-07803: Lima studies a generalized gauged CP1-Maxwell theory where the charge sector gains field-linked response from vacuum stirring. From the gauged CP1-sigma model on a curved target space, dropping a Dirac fermion yields a non-polynomial magnetic permeability at one loop. Reducing dimensions to 2+1 gives a working Maxwell sector with log response. A broad CP1-Maxwell model admits BPS shapes, and he solves self-dual rules for vortex-like states with quantized flux, showing target-space shape and induced links.
arxiv-2603-08003: Saberlatibari and colleagues speed up distributed transactions with an FPGA. Replicas must stay in sync and respect integrity under workloads. Commutative Replicated Data Types converge for conflict-free objects under relaxed consistency, while Well-coordinated Replicated Data Types add integrity for general objects through a hybrid model, relaxed when possible, strong when needed. While leading speedup uses Remote Direct Memory Access, the authors connect an FPGA card directly to the network. Their SafarDB system rebuilds the network link to match the FPGA-hosted app, enabling near-network runs.
arxiv-2603-08203: Gebauer and colleagues measure large differential attosecond delays in solid-state photoemission. Time-resolved spectroscopy opens a window on electronic structure and electron motion out of equilibrium. At solids, timing can be tracked on its natural scale through escape delays. Particles with final energy of several tens of electron volts need tens to hundreds of attoseconds to reach vacuum. The authors report delays of 30 to 100 attoseconds for bismuth, tellurium, and selenium core levels.
arxiv-2603-08403: Yang and colleagues present SPIRAL, a closed-loop framework for self-improving action world models via planning agents that reflect. Long-horizon video generation aims to make time-coherent videos that follow complex action orders over long stretches, requiring step order and persistent runs. Older single-shot models usually operate open-loop, leading to half-done runs, fake motions, and time drift. SPIRAL plans in sequence and reflects in loops: a PlanAgent splits goals into sub-actions, a VideoGenerator makes each segment, and a CriticAgent checks segments for fixes.
arxiv-2603-08903: Yihang Zhao and colleagues offer design guidance against over-trust on AI in group sense-making. Poorly designed GenAI tools hand groups plain orders to follow without thinking, eroding self-run sense-making. Group awareness tools instead show group data, surface member gaps to spark useful friction, and trigger self-driven discussion, and the paper presents early rules for GenAI-aided versions.
arxiv-2603-09003: Inna Kviatkovsky and colleagues narrow absorption lines in rubidium vapor at telecom wavelengths. A strong control field dresses the middle state of a three-level ladder, letting a probe at 1529 nanometers interrogate the dressed states. They observe absorption lines of depth near 4 and width near 17 megahertz, an order-of-magnitude narrowing versus the Doppler width with higher depth than the lower transition.
arxiv-2603-09103: Runyao Yu and colleagues predict the hysteresis factor of electric vehicle batteries whose graphite anodes contain silicon, a trait that makes charge gauging hard. Rather than rely on costly high-fidelity tests, they build a data-driven method that also reports its own uncertainty. A harmonization step first puts varied driving cycles onto one footing across conditions. Tests then probe how the best setup copes with unseen vehicle models through retraining, fine-tuning, and joint training.
arxiv-2603-09203: Jiangming Shu and colleagues make retrieval quality an explicit action for retrieval-augmented agents, whose multi-step reasoning noisy search results can derail. Their EvalAct system scores each retrieval right after it happens under a coupled search-to-evaluate protocol. A second method rescales advantages segment by segment using those scores, updating trusted parts fully and doubtful parts with care. It posts the best average score across seven QA benchmarks, and the gain is biggest where questions need several hops.
arxiv-2603-09503: Fermín Moscoso del Prado Martín and Suchir Salhan ask why phoneme frequency patterns look so regular across languages, with exponential-tailed rank curves and a link between inventory size and entropy. They build a stochastic model of how sounds change over time and simulate inventories evolving under it. A naive version matches the rank curve shape but misses other facts. Adding a functional load effect and a pull toward a preferred inventory size makes the simulations match both target patterns.
arxiv-2603-09703: Zhiye Tang and colleagues present ProGS, a progressive codec for 3D Gaussian Splatting that keeps every transmission stage decodable and directly renderable. It organizes anchor-based splatting as parent-closed octree prefixes, combining level-balanced anchor growth, parent-causal entropy coding, and bounded multi-prefix training. One training run yields five rate-quality points from a single bitstream. On seventeen scenes it reaches quality targets with far fewer bytes than progressive baselines, while also improving similarity scores over a strong single-rate rival.
arxiv-2603-10303: Tim Schopf and Michael Färber introduce RINoBench, a benchmark for judging whether automated tools can tell if a research idea is novel. It holds 1,381 ideas scored by human experts, plus nine metrics covering both rubric scores and written justifications. Leading large language models were tested against this gold standard. Their reasoning often mirrored human rationales closely, yet the novelty verdicts still diverged sharply from expert judgments, even for strong reasoning models. Data and code are public.
arxiv-2603-10603: Sunilkumar M Hosamani finds the graphs that maximize the inverse sum indeg index among trees and unicyclic graphs of fixed diameter. The index is a bond incident degree index, summing a simple function of endpoint degrees over every edge. Using graph transformation methods, he shows a named tree attains the maximum for trees once the diameter and size are large enough. For unicyclic graphs he characterizes the extremal shapes case by case, with different winners for diameter two, three, and four or more.
arxiv-2603-10703: Rafi Ibn Sultan and co-authors introduce WalkGPT, a vision-language model for grounded pedestrian navigation help, aimed at accessibility. Existing models describe scenes but hallucinate objects and judge depth poorly, which is risky for guidance. WalkGPT answers a navigation query in conversation while producing masks for accessible and harmful features, plus relative depth, without user-supplied cues. A multi-scale query projector and a calibrated text projector supply the grounding. A new benchmark, PAVE, pairs tens of thousands of street-level images with accessibility questions.
arxiv-2603-10803: Mohamed Benelmekki studies tightly prime-divisor-finite domains, a class of integral domains defined by how prime divisors behave. In a PDF-domain, each nonzero element has only finitely many prime divisors, counting nonassociate ones once. The tight version adds a demand: for each nonzero nonunit, at least one prime divisor must exist. The paper investigates basic properties of these domains. It then examines how the property behaves under standard constructions, namely localization, D+M constructions, and polynomial rings.
arxiv-2603-10903: M. Jarry and coauthors present a catalogue of solar proton events above 100 MeV recorded by the SOHO spacecraft's ERNE instrument across solar cycles 23 to 25. Events found by scanning particle counter data were cross-calibrated with a second SOHO instrument to derive peak fluxes and fluences, then matched to their likely parent eruptions. Statistics show most particle releases closely follow flare and coronal mass ejection onsets, with event strength strongly shaped by magnetic connectivity and coronal conditions.
arxiv-2603-11203: Giuseppe Colella and coauthors build a local thermodynamic model for condensed phases inside a dissipative particle dynamics method that conserves energy, tackling the long-standing snag in working with liquids with coarse-grained methods. Their model covers the thermal expansion coefficient and isothermal compressibility at the mesoscale. Tests on argon at liquid and supercritical states prove accurate and stay valid nearby. They derive pressure and energy equations of state from the model parameters.
arxiv-2603-11403: Mosalpuri, Abdelsamea, and Eldaly present DeepHistoViT, a vision transformer built to sort tissue images by cancer type. Pathologists still read such slides by hand, a slow task with room for disagreement. The model uses attention to pick out the cell patterns that matter most for each call. It also shows where it looked, which helps doctors check its work. On lung and colon cancer sets, plus acute lymphoblastic leukaemia data, the team reports perfect or near-perfect scores on every metric they track.
arxiv-2603-11503: Yu and co-authors present FedRecGEL, a federated recommendation framework that centers on item embeddings. Federated systems train together while user data stays on each device, sharing only model parameters. Item embeddings carry the shared knowledge across clients, so their quality matters system-wide. Heterogeneous, sparse local data make stable, general embeddings hard to learn. The team recasts the problem as multi-task learning from an item-centered view. Sharpness-aware minimization then steadies training, and tests on four data sets show clear gains.
arxiv-2603-11603: Shong and co-authors present AutoScout, a configurator for machine learning systems across training, fine-tuning, and inference. Good settings are hard to find: features mix types, choices depend on earlier ones, and profiling costs dearly. AutoScout frames the search as structured optimization with hierarchical dependencies. A hybrid method refines sparse structural choices and dense execution parameters together. It also ranks features by impact and mixes simulators of varied fidelity to cut profiling cost. Results reach up to 3.0 times the training speed of expert-tuned settings.
arxiv-2603-11803: Zheng and co-authors simulate binary breakup early in open clusters, starting from a 100% primordial binary fraction. Disruption falls in two stages, a fast drop then a slower one, fit by two piecewise linear functions. The early rate follows a power law in the cluster's density, with index near 0.56, driven by wide binaries hit by close encounters. The switch time follows its own power law, with a negative index. They release a Python tool predicting survival from density, period, and mass ratio.
arxiv-2603-12003: Madika and co-authors map the twin jets of the radio galaxy 3C 452 at very fine scales. High Sensitivity Array data at five frequencies let them fit the jets in both the visibility and image planes. Both the jet and the counter-jet show a symmetric, parabolic shape as they expand outward. Core brightness and Doppler factors point to a large viewing angle and a de-boosted jet base. The core spectrum is strongly inverted, then turns steeply thin in the innermost jet.
arxiv-2603-12303: Wakaura and Tanimae withdraw their own earlier claims about a quantum reservoir protocol in this replacement paper. Version one reported vast shot-noise suppression and sharp reconstruction of unseen inputs. Under one single evaluation, the suppression flips sign and reset channels degrade results badly. The two-phase target also proves invertible in closed form, and a plain polynomial matches the full model. Four artifacts explain the false results. One entangled channel survives the same controls, though a classical scrambler decodes the task better.
arxiv-2603-12403: Yang and Kandasamy design exchange protocols for freely replicable goods that carry negative externalities. Agents trade copies of goods like data, gaining access while rivals gain the same edge. A central planner proposes rounds of pairwise swaps that agents may accept or reject, with no money used. Three goals guide the design: no agent loses by joining, honesty pays, and no good trades remain at the end. Their protocol meets all three after careful reformulation for this setting. Pareto efficiency, they argue, fits this world poorly.
arxiv-2603-13303: Gaopeng Ren, Yijie Yang, Jiajun Zhou, and Kim E. Jelfs present PolyMon for polymer property prediction. Good forecasts guide materials design, but data are scarce and polymer forms vary a lot. PolyMon puts many polymer representations, models, and training plans in one open platform. It spans tabular models and graph neural networks, plus multi-fidelity, active, and ensemble learning. The team tests five key polymer properties to see how choices shape forecast skill. Case studies show how each training plan can help when data are limited.
arxiv-2603-13403: Sungjun Cho compares three CLIP-based approaches for diabetic retinopathy grading from fundus images. The disease is a leading cause of preventable blindness, so automated grading can aid large-scale screening. The three methods are a zero-shot prompt baseline, a hybrid FCN-CLIP model with CBAM attention, and a ranking-aware prompt model. Training used APTOS 2019 and Messidor-2 data, with resampling and tuned thresholds for class imbalance. The ranking-aware model scored highest overall, while the hybrid model excelled at proliferative cases. Both far beat the zero-shot baseline.
arxiv-2603-13503: Robert Beinert, Jonas Bresch, and Michael Quellmalz derive a discrete Radon transform from cube-plane intersection areas. The Radon transform is a basic tool in tomographic imaging, optimal transport, and geometric analysis.
