They ask how the Lau-Tseng-Yau notion of non-Kähler SYZ relates to mapping supersymmetric branes between symplectic and complex sides. They also ask whether explicit mirror pairs can be fixed by Lie-theoretic data, and how the correspondence works in this setting. They prove that the Lau-Tseng-Yau Fourier-Mukai transform exchanges type-A supersymmetric cycles given by special Lagrangian sections.
arxiv-2604-19403: Chen and Fua propose VecHeart, a unified tool for holistic rebuild and generation of four-chamber heart structures. Good heart anatomy work must handle tricky links among structures, yet current feed-forward methods model single objects only and neglect links between parts. Their Hybrid Part Transformer uses learnable queries for each part and mixed attention to capture links between chambers. Anatomical completion masking and modality alignment let the model infer complete four-chamber hearts from partial, sparse, or noisy views. That inference works even when whole parts are missing.
arxiv-2604-20003: Zhou and seven colleagues introduce scpFormer, a transformer-based foundation model for single-cell proteomics. Antibody panels fragment such data, so the model maps variable panels into one shared space with continuous, sequence-anchored tokens and value-aware expression embeddings. Pre-trained on over 390 million cells, it competes on large-scale batch integration and unsupervised clustering. Its open-vocabulary design also expands panels in silico, aids sparse clinical data, and transfers protein co-expression logic to bulk tasks such as cancer drug response prediction.
arxiv-2604-20203: Chen and four colleagues compare how inner small planets relate to outer cold Jupiters on either side of the radius valley. Around metal-rich stars, cold Jupiters accompany sub-Neptunes 42.6 percent of the time but super-Earths under 15 percent, against a field rate near 14 percent. The sub-Neptune correlation is significant at over 99 percent confidence, while no such link appears for super-Earths. Kepler-Keck and radial velocity samples agree, fitting metal-rich disks that form outer giants and larger inner planets more efficiently.
arxiv-2604-20303: Solinas, Donelli, and Gherardini give an operational test for Wigner function negativity in any state, using quantum non-demolition measurement. Their schemes measure the Wigner function directly and single out the coherent-state basis for judging negative regions. No coherent superpositions in that basis signals a positive Wigner function, a sufficient condition. It also proves necessary for Schrödinger-cat states. For higher-order cat states on a circle it holds for many densely packed states, though general necessity stays unproven.
arxiv-2604-20403: Karabulut, Manna, and Develder test spatio temporal graph networks for grid fault location with sparse meters. They compare measured only graphs against full topology graphs, and test spatio temporal models based on GraphSAGE and improved graph attention. On the IEEE 123 bus feeder, spatio temporal variants beat a recurrent baseline by up to 11 points. The measured only build trains six times faster at equal gains. Spatio temporal models hold steadier, within under one and a half percent versus seven and a half for the baseline.
arxiv-2604-20503: Chen and three colleagues introduce FASER, a system that manages speculative decoding with finer control for busy language-model serving. In speculative decoding a small draft model proposes tokens for a large model to check. Instead of one draft length per batch and serialized phases, FASER tunes draft length per request and prunes rejected tokens early inside checking. It also splits checking into chunks that overlap drafting. Built into vLLM, the prototype lifts throughput by up to 53 percent and reduces latency by up to 1.92 times against leading systems.
arxiv-2604-20603: Collinson displays a family of Stone-type dualities linking kinds of frames carrying pairs of modal operators to kinds of spaces carrying a binary link. Different notions of morphism on the link side lead to big changes in the point build. The case gets simpler for semicontinuous links, giving direct ties between modal axioms and link traits.
arxiv-2604-20703: Li and eight colleagues describe a 260-liter liquid argon test stand for detector research at BNL. The system cleans argon gas with pumpless flow: boil-off gas is cleaned, recondensed, and sent back by gravity without a pump. A purity monitor tracks electron lifetime firsthand, gauging charge loss from impurities. Under set terms, electron lifetime is 0.5 ms. The system enables rapid retry of detector parts in full cycles within 7 days. That fast turnaround, medium volume, and direct purity checks suit testing designs for large liquid argon time projection chamber experiments.
arxiv-2604-20803: Metzger presents NAILA, a tool that gives 24/7 self-run feedback for student tasks in introductory software engineering courses. Using modern large language models, NAILA processes student solutions in open document formats against teacher-set model answers through specialized prompt forms. He ran an empirical study with over 900 active students at the University of Duisburg-Essen. It checked reasons to adopt or reject NAILA, user take-up, and how often and steadily students engage with NAILA. It also checked how AI feedback impacts academic performance versus human feedback.
arxiv-2604-21003: Seong and colleagues automate the painstaking craft of harness engineering. That craft is the prompts, tools, orchestration, and scoring that make a foundation model effective in a new domain. A Harness Evolution Loop lets a worker agent act, an evaluator agent diagnose failures adversarially, and an evolution agent rewrite the harness from the full history of attempts. A Meta-Evolution Loop then learns the blueprint itself across tasks. Adapting an agent to a novel domain then needs no human harness work at all.
arxiv-2604-21303: Chandranandan Gangopadhyay and Atsushi Ito study the birational geometry of Quot schemes on smooth projective curves of genus at least 2, parametrizing quotients of a vector bundle by rank and degree. Their main tool, the moduli space of stable pairs, yields small factorial modifications of the Quot scheme and its fiber over the Picard variety. They explicitly describe the nef, movable, and effective cones of each modification. Consequently the fiber is a Mori dream space, and the determinant morphism is a Mori dream morphism.
arxiv-2604-21603: Meghyn Bienvenu and colleagues use answer set programming with quantifiers to answer queries over ranked data that holds clashes. They rank clashing facts to set best fixes. They test three fix rules, Pareto, global, and completion best, across three classic query readings, and give the first code for global-best fix readings plus a fast grounded shortcut. Trials show when global-best answers can be worked out in practice and how readings, shortcuts, and codings shift the results.
arxiv-2604-21903: Defez and four colleagues present a scale-adaptive system for joint super-resolution with diffusion models. Climate work usually sharpens space or time alone, and joint models serve only one pair of factors. Their system reuses one design across scales. It predicts the mean directly, with attention, then models the leftover with diffusion. An optional mass-conservation step keeps totals. Retuning three settings on retraining makes it work across scales. On French precipitation, it spans 1 to 25 in space and 1 to 6 in time.
arxiv-2604-22103: Tang and Law ask how many visual levers shift how people subjectively judge street scenes. Their lever framework turns scene explanation into a search over planned edits, each naming a concept, a spot, a direction, and a template. Edits come from prompt-based image editing and survive only if they pass checks for same-place keeping, locality, realism, and plausibility. A pilot over 50 scenes from five cities finds patterns and a failure list for prompt-only editing, with Mobility Infrastructure and Physical Maintenance shifting safety most.
arxiv-2604-22503: AI help makes writers look more opinion-led, able, positive, and demographically privileged, and readers trust those writers more, growing more persuaded as the distortion grows. Röttger and three colleagues ran the test with 2,939 writers drafting political opinion paragraphs with and without AI help, plus 11,091 readers judging them blind. Writers fought many of the distortions yet still picked AI-assisted text once told. A further 8,798 readers confirmed the trust gap. The authors warn the distortions run deep, last under human oversight, and may sway conduct and views.
arxiv-2604-22603: Stolet, Peter, and Kaufmann present Chamelio, a flexible shared network stack letting tenants define their own protocols. Conventional cloud virtualization pushes packets through many guest and host layers, inflating cost and tail latency. Shared host paths collapse that layering, but existing shared stacks are fixed-function and cannot be specialized. eBPF could restore programmability, but its verifier guarantees safety, not isolation. Chamelio lets tenants implement full protocols through a bounded eBPF fast path plus a tenant slow path, nearing fixed-stack speed with strong isolation.
arxiv-2604-23003: Sikora and nine colleagues propose a physics-informed neural network framework for time-varying simulations of pollution spreading from moving sources. A robust variational framework for advection-diffusion is established, with a loss function tied to true model error, plus a collocation plan to speed training. The model extends to nonlinear Burgers-type equations. As a case study, snowmobile traffic in Longyearbyen, Spitsbergen, shows thermal inversion trapping dense, humid air near the ground, sharply raising PM and harming local air quality.
arxiv-2604-23103: Martins searches 16 years of Pierre Auger data for pairs of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays close in space and time. With a 3-degree, 15-day window and a filter for stiff particles, he finds 28 doublets above 32 EeV. He traces their paths back through three magnetic field models and eight nuclear species, then tests them against the ten nearest radio galaxies. The match reaches 5.8 sigma overall, with about four and a half sigma for eight doublets tied to Fornax A, implicating radio galaxies as long-term accelerators.
arxiv-2604-23203: Xu and five colleagues synchronise follower agents to an unstable leader when communication links randomly disconnect and reconnect. They propose a network transformation mapping that splits the network at any moment into reachable and unreachable parts. Only nodes in the reachable part can access leader information and synchronise. Each node's sync speed is set so convergence in reachable stretches beats divergence in unreachable stretches, yielding asymptotic sync over all time. Adaptive coupling gains cut the method's computational cost, and simulations on manipulator and multi-motor systems confirm it.
arxiv-2604-23403: Cruciata and four colleagues propose Learn&Drop, a training method speeding convolutional networks by dropping stalled layers. During training, scores track each layer's parameter changes and whether it will keep learning, and the network is scaled down to cut parameters. Unlike compression for inference or backpropagation savings, the method cuts forward operations during training. Validated on VGG and ResNet across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Imagenette, time more than halves with little accuracy loss. FLOPs fall by under one-fifth for VGG-11 to over four-fifths for ResNet-152.
arxiv-2604-24203: Rowstron proposes Agentic Witnessing, a method moving verification from attested execution to attested reasoning. Zero-knowledge proofs protect privacy but fit precise algebraic constraints poorly for qualitative code logic. Three agents split the roles: a Verifier asks limited binary questions, a Prover owns the data, and an Auditor inspects it inside a Trusted Execution Environment. The Auditor answers through the Model Context Protocol with a signed hash chain tying reasoning to data and hardware trust. A demo auditing 21 papers shows privacy-preserving oversight without data disclosure.
arxiv-2604-24703: Akli, Papadakis, Cordy and Le Traon address defective task descriptions in language-model code generation, where vague or underspecified prompts hurt code correctness. They build SpecValidator, a lightweight classifier based on a small fine-tuned model, to detect lexical vagueness, under-specification and syntax-formatting defects. On three benchmarks it reaches an F1 score of 0.804, significantly beating larger models. It also generalizes to unseen defects in the original benchmark descriptions.
arxiv-2604-25203: Mazza and Levi present BARRED, a framework for making synthetic training data for custom policy guardrails from a task description and a few unlabeled examples. Generic safety models miss task requirements, prompting gives uneven boundary-case performance at high cost, and custom classifiers need costly labeled data. BARRED splits the domain into dimensions for full coverage and uses multi-agent debate to verify label correctness. Small models fine-tuned on this data beat proprietary and dedicated guardrail models. Ablations confirm both dimension splitting and debate verification matter.
arxiv-2604-25503: Dwivedi and three colleagues propose a hybrid quantum-classical genetic method for bent Boolean functions. The method rates the Gowers U2 norm as fitness function. The quantum circuit needs qubits and gates that grow with n and n squared, whereas plain work demands exploding steps. Checks cover systems with six and eight inputs. For eight inputs, an old run to 1000 rounds hits 0.250000, exactly the bent threshold. Quantum-aided checks match the old path up to noise, and for n above 25 the checker gives a clear edge.
arxiv-2604-25603: Martinka and three colleagues test an accelerated surface hopping scheme that scales spin-orbit couplings to reach long timescales in intersystem crossing. True time constants must be extrapolated from several trajectory ensembles at distinct scaling factors, a demand that often caps trajectories per ensemble. Using silaethylene as a case, they compare population fitting and extrapolation methods. Machine learning models for energy surfaces, nonadiabatic couplings, and spin-orbit couplings match reference data within confidence intervals. Yet extrapolation stays highly sensitive to fitted time constants, so final time constants diverge.
arxiv-2604-26003: Dennerl and six colleagues separate the Solar System's contribution to the soft X-ray sky from diffuse emission. Solar wind charged particles hitting heliospheric gas produce soft X-rays that complicate observations. The team analyzes western Galactic hemisphere data from eROSITA on the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma spacecraft. Those data avoid geocorona contamination across four full-sky surveys, including a solar minimum. Subtracting the solar wind charge exchange contribution gives a cleaner diffuse sky view. X-rays can also map interstellar matter flowing through the Solar System.
arxiv-2604-26603: Jain, Borse, and Barabde proved that zero-divisor graphs of reduced rings yield endless families of simple connected graphs whose main-eigenvalue count is exactly s, for every positive integer s. Pinning down graphs with a set main-eigenvalue count is a long-standing spectral problem, with few known endless families. Zero-divisor graphs suit the study because equitable partitions describe their spectra plainly. Certain induced bipartite subgraphs share the same trait, also attaining exactly s main eigenvalues.
arxiv-2604-26803: Que, Poelarends, Breschi and Wang build a wearable method for estimating the energy a person burns during everyday activity. Their model links body movement to the metabolic gas-exchange processes behind energy use, then runs inside an Extended Kalman Filter, a tracking tool that handles noisy measurements. Tested on nine people in lab sessions mimicking free living, its predictions beat a linear model and a neural-network model on the same data. Movement sensors carried most of the signal, with heart-rate data adding little.
arxiv-2604-27103: Easson constructs a geodesically complete closed bounce-plus-inflation model in general relativity, driven by a scalar field with positive vacuum offset. Only positive curvature permits a nonsingular cosmos with matter meeting the average null energy condition. Curvature, not exotic stress energy, drives the bounce: matter satisfies the null energy condition and breaks only the strong energy condition. The branch stays sub-Planckian and reaches a curvature-diluted slow-roll with inflationary outputs matching constraints. Forecasts put tilt near unity and the tensor-to-scalar ratio under one percent.
arxiv-2604-27403: Ho and three colleagues use knowledge about how speech sounds are formed to pull a target voice out of cinematic audio mixed with background sound effects. They spot articulation manners in speech frames and pack those cues into a knowledge vector that sharpens separation, above all for brief bits buried in background sound. Tested on a recent demixing-challenge set for cinematic audio, the articulation-aware approach beats separation without such knowledge. The edge is widest where short speech hides inside unlabelled background noise.
arxiv-2604-27503: Dogra and 85 colleagues analyze 19 years of R-band data on blazar 3C 454.3, hunting quasi-periodic oscillations. They detect an oscillation of about 433 days, lasting from MJD 54980 to 58450, making it one of the most persistent optical oscillations ever found. A phase dispersion minimization check validates the signal, which reaches a global significance of 2.53 sigma across methods. To explain it, they weigh accretion-disk models around the supermassive black hole against jet models. They also introduce a new way to separate genuine oscillations from spurious signals caused by annual seasonal gaps.
arxiv-2604-27803: Siwek and three colleagues propose a non-harmful check framework for bullion coins based on sound tests and deep neural networks. Each coin's sound print, set by metal, mass, and shape, is captured through tapping. A two-model setup pairs a spectrum coder for oddity spotting with a coin-type sorter. A dynamic oddity threshold and data boosts address noise and limited data range. The combined system achieves high care telling real coins from top fakes across varying settings and tools.
arxiv-2604-27903: Zhou and five colleagues build HiMix, a frame for spotting synthetic pictures that holds up on unseen makers. Its mixup arm blends real and fake shots into in-between samples, covering shaky zones and sharpening sense for low-level fake marks. Its artifact arm pools fake marks from whole-image and fine-detail levels through cross-layer links, pulling out sharp forgery signs. Across many test sets HiMix posts top scores, with well-spread logits that help it catch forgeries it never trained on.
arxiv-2605-00203:
Nelson R. F. Braga and William S. Cunha connect two ideas in black hole physics: black holes as topological defects and the change between confined and deconfined matter. In their picture, a black hole carries a total topological charge defined in a widened parameter space. Under gauge and gravity duality, the confined phase of matter maps to a state where a black hole phase dominates.

Working in a holographic model of quantum chromodynamics, the authors show that adding an energy scale to anti-de Sitter space changes the topological class. That change lines up with the existence of separate confined and deconfined phases. The two phases are divided by a Hawking-Page transition at a finite critical temperature, tying the abstract charge to a concrete physical boundary.
arxiv-2605-00403:
Seramika Ariwahjoedi, Muhammad Farchani Rosyid, and Andika Kusuma Wijaya extend Fourier analysis, the math of waves, from flat space to curved spaces. On a curved manifold there is no clear momentum space, since mirror directions may be missing or tangled. Their generalized transform is built from the spectrum of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, the curved-space wave machine.

Under minimal demands, that the transform preserve lengths and diagonalize the wave operator, they prove a Parseval-Plancherel theorem for this setting, the curved twin of energy bookkeeping for waves. The tricky part is degeneracy, where many waves share one pitch. They resolve it with the largest set of commuting geometric operators, often built from the space's own mirrors, and give a recipe to build them. The momentum labels can be discrete, unbroken, or mixed, and the authors sort the structures that can arise.
arxiv-2605-01303:
Fang Liu, Yu-Bo Ma, Yun-Zhi Du, and Huai-Fan Li study how changes to black hole entropy would change what a black hole looks like from far away. Starting from the first law of black hole heat and energy, they link a corrected entropy formula to the shape of the space around the hole.

With that corrected shape, they work out the photon sphere, the ring where light can orbit, and the size of the dark shadow the hole casts. Each type of entropy change shifts these features in its own way. By matching the shifts against Event Horizon Telescope views of the black hole at the center of our galaxy, they narrow the allowed range for the new terms. The work gives a clear test for ideas that go beyond the classic area law for black hole entropy.
arxiv-2605-01503:
Giulia De Pasquale, Sarah Dean, and Paolo Frasca read recommender systems as control systems, machines that steer a population over time rather than rank once. The lens is aimed at fairness, which touches users through skewed exposure and opinion drift, and creators through fame piling onto the already famous.

Their central claim cuts against the usual framing: fairness need not trade off against utility. Judged over a long horizon, a fairer policy can lift the whole system's performance, since today's recommendations shape tomorrow's tastes, supply, and engagement. The catch is that the gains only appear when the dynamics underneath are modeled honestly. The paper maps how fairness steps feed back through those dynamics, giving platform designers a language for when an intervention compounds into health and when it merely shuffles the present.
arxiv-2605-01603:
Gordon J Ross, Dean Markwick, and Priyanshu Tiwari present an R package that puts Dirichlet process models within reach of working statisticians. These Bayesian nonparametric tools let the data decide how complex a model should be, but coding the sampling machinery by hand has kept many users away.

The package wraps that machinery into flexible objects. A user picks one of the pre-built models or specifies a custom one, and the package runs the Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling behind the scenes. The same objects serve as building blocks across jobs: estimating a density, clustering observations, or supplying prior distributions inside larger hierarchical models. Software papers like this one matter quietly: they turn a research-grade method into a routine tool, with the inference code tested once and reused by many.
arxiv-2605-01803:
Florin Leon reads the first days of a simulated epidemic for signs of the outbreak to come. He then asks what smallest push could still prevent it. His agents move, differ in susceptibility, and pass infection by co-location, with viral load shaped by immunity, a test bed tuned near the tipping point where small changes flip outcomes.

Daily aggregate readings from early windows are compressed into a Koopman latent space, coordinates in which the messy dynamics run nearly linearly, supporting short forecasts and risk estimates. A random forest on those features predicts whether the final attack rate will cross the major-outbreak line, and the Koopman features drive the class separation. Counterfactual runs search for minimal saves: holding one chosen agent home for one day often cuts the attack rate and pulls the trajectory under the outbreak threshold. The framework joins early warning to intervention choice.
arxiv-2605-02003:
Mario Koddenbrock and colleagues launch RamanBench, a shared benchmark for machine learning on Raman spectroscopy. Raman methods identify molecules without damaging a sample, but the field lacked standard data and tests, so models were hard to compare. RamanBench unifies seventy-seven data sets across four domains, with more than three hundred thousand spectra for classification and regression.

Seventeen of those data sets are released here for the first time. The project supplies streamlined data access, evaluation code, and a live leaderboard. The authors benchmark twenty-eight models under one protocol, including classical methods, under varied experimental conditions. The aim is reproducible progress on spectral data, whose structure generic models often miss.
arxiv-2605-02103:
Haoxing Tian, Zaiwei Chen, Ioannis Paschalidis, and Alex Olshevsky bridge average-reward and discounted temporal difference learning, two ways to evaluate a policy from experience. In the average setting, the Bellman operator does not contract in any norm, which breaks the standard proofs that work for discounted learning. Past approaches carry limits in scope or in their bounds.

Their new algorithm samples from two Markovian trajectories and is designed directly for the average-reward case. It is guaranteed to converge to the unique solution of a properly defined projected Bellman equation. The analysis covers both tabular and linear function settings in one form. Its bounds also avoid explicit terms that grow with dimension, aligning with discounted results.
arxiv-2605-02803:
R K B M Rizmi and Shabbir Ahmed present a vision-based method for spotting damage in vibrating beams, without touching the structure. Contact-free sensing is prized in structural health monitoring, but reading damage from motion alone is hard. Their approach applies dynamic mode decomposition to high-speed video, a method that fits a linear operator to the observed dynamics.

Splitting that operator yields modal frequencies and spatial mode shapes, a physically readable summary of how the beam moves. Tests run in two stages. A simulated cantilever beam, healthy and damaged, checks reconstruction and prediction from partial views. Real high-speed video then feeds the same pipeline, recovering full-field motion with no contact sensors. A damage index built from the modal features turns shifts in frequency and shape into a quantitative score.
arxiv-2605-03003:
Simone Blasi, Maxime Grandjean, and Alberto Mariotti examine the classical stability of metastable cosmic strings from a two-step symmetry breaking chain. Such strings can decay by forming a monopole pair, and they are a leading candidate for the gravitational wave hum seen by pulsar timing arrays.

The authors map where in parameter space the strings stay stable and where they do not. They find that classical instability affects part of the range that matters for the pulsar timing signal. They also discuss what likely happens to the string network in the unstable regions.
arxiv-2605-03203:
Vincenzo M. Scarrica offers a partition-based counting method for row-convex polyominoes, grid shapes whose rows form single unbroken runs with no holes. Counting such shapes exactly is a classic hard counting problem in combinatorics.

Each integer partition of the total area gives a list of row lengths, and permuting those parts accounts for the ways rows can align. Summing over all partitions yields the count for each size, with small cases worked out. A transfer argument gives the exact generating function and the growth rate. The link may aid shape priors in image analysis and grid modeling.
arxiv-2605-03303:
Jingjing Zhou, Yongshuai Yang, Qing Qing, Ziqi Xu, Xikun Zhang, Renqiang Luo, Ivan Lee, and Feng Xia improve graph unlearning for multimodal graphs. Unlearning lets a model forget chosen nodes or edges on request. Standard methods edit all layers evenly. That badly harms the wide input layers, which hold most cross-modal knowledge.

Their FDQ framework spots those sensitive layers. It applies gentler quantile thresholds there, and leaves the importance scoring itself unchanged. Tests used fashion and book graph datasets. Utility stayed strong after forgetting, and membership attacks still failed. The balance suits privacy-aware learning well.
arxiv-2605-03503:
Chiara Vercellino, Giacomo Vitali, Paolo Viviani, Alberto Scionti, Olivier Terzo, and Bartolomeo Montrucchio show how to embed real problems as unit-disk graphs on neutral atom quantum machines. Such machines natively encode unit-disk graphs in atom registers, but protein and network layouts must be reshaped to fit each device's constraints.

Using distance encoder networks with device-specific adjustments, they embedded most protein graphs for a learning task on QuEra's Aquila and all antenna subgraphs from Turin positions on PASQAL's Orion Alpha. The antenna case became a graph coloring problem solved with a hybrid algorithm. The results support the embedding route across applications.
arxiv-2605-03603:
Mekala Kiran, Apurba Das, Suman Banerjee, and Tathagata Ray count small balanced bicliques in signed bipartite graphs. A bipartite graph links two disjoint sets, such as drugs and targets or users and items, and signed edges add positive or negative labels. A balanced biclique is a complete two-sided pattern whose signs multiply out consistently.

The smallest such motif, the balanced butterfly, shows only local structure, so the authors target fixed larger sizes. They first adapt a leading unsigned-graph algorithm to handle signs, then propose two faster methods: a wedge-centric enumerator that enforces balance during search, and a vertex-based pruning approach. Together they make counting these higher-order motifs practical.
arxiv-2605-03703:
Sohaib El Karmi studies scaling limits of a pair of nearly unstable Hawkes processes, self-exciting point processes used to model clustered events, coupled in one direction only. The first process evolves on its own and excites the second, but not the reverse. Each has a heavy-tailed memory kernel, and the two tails may differ, giving different degrees of roughness.

As the system nears criticality, El Karmi proves the rescaled intensity converges to the unique solution of coupled stochastic Volterra equations of rough-volatility type. The second component inherits noise from the first through an effective cross-kernel built by convolving the two Mittag-Leffler kernels. A short-time cross-decorrelation law follows: functional correlation between the components vanishes at small scales at an explicit polynomial rate.
arxiv-2605-04103:
Matteo Gambella, Fabrizio Pittorino, and Manuel Roveri survey neural architecture search through a triple lens. They argue modern practice now requires three things at once: efficiency, robustness, and continual learning. The search finds network designs that balance accuracy and cost on its own. But as AI moves to real-world deployment, hardware-aware efficiency alone is no longer sufficient. That is especially true at the edge. Robustness covers environmental variability. Continual learning covers adaptation without forgetting.

The authors propose a taxonomy. It sorts methods by aim: resource optimization, environmental resilience, and architectural plasticity. They argue the three axes reinforce each other rather than compete. Building on it, they map the landscape into a framework named HERCULES. They define its wish list, styled as twelve labours, for search that is hardware-efficient, robust, and continual. The survey is aimed at people who build such systems.
arxiv-2605-04603:
Shisheng Li settles a conjecture about whirling knight's tours. In this chess puzzle, a knight must visit every square of a board exactly once and return to its start. It always moves counter-clockwise around the board's centre. The coil count measures how many times the tour winds around that centre.

Li proves no such tour exists with coil count exactly half the board size. That holds for board sizes in two residue classes modulo eight. The boards must be large enough to state the problem. For each class he exhibits an explicit algebraic certificate. It shows even a relaxed version of the problem has no solution. The two certificates have genuinely different structures.
arxiv-2605-04703:
Oliver Baker and Carl P. Dettmann work out how to compress a random geometric graph in a distributed way, where several encoders each hold part of the graph and code their parts separately. Their graphs place points randomly in space and connect nearby pairs with a probability that softens the usual hard distance cutoff.

Restricting attention to graphs above the connectivity threshold, where the network is essentially one connected piece, they establish the exact Slepian-Wolf rate region for this distributed compression. The proof needs new limit theorems and equipartition properties for the entropy of these soft random geometric graphs, after which standard random binning techniques deliver the coding result.
arxiv-2605-04903:
Santosh Premi Adhikari, Radu Timofte, and Dmitry Ignatov propose generating new neural network designs as small code changes rather than whole programs. Language models can invent architectures, but writing a full model each time is costly and produces long, verbose code. Their delta approach instead asks a fine-tuned model to output a compact diff against a baseline design.

The pipeline fine-tunes models in cycles on curated architectures, filtering for structural novelty along the way. Three coder models of similar size all beat full generation on validity and first-epoch accuracy across six image datasets. Their outputs ran far shorter, and a longer training study confirmed early accuracy predicted later rankings well.
arxiv-2605-05003:
Gayane Ghazaryan and Esra Dönmez examine whether the reward models used to align language models actually prefer socially desirable answers. Reward models stand in for human preferences during training, yet most testing covers only general instruction following. Social failures can therefore stay hidden behind good headline scores.

The authors convert social evaluation datasets on bias, safety, morality, and ethics into paired choices and test five public reward models plus two instruction-tuned stand-ins. No model led overall, and all often preferred socially undesirable options, producing biased output patterns. Stronger bias avoidance also dulled sensitivity to context, revealing a trade-off at the heart of alignment.
arxiv-2605-05103:
Nicholas Kersting and five co-authors treat a text collection as a concept field, a landscape of how meaning drifts from sentence to sentence, to measure hallucination and novelty without opening the model. Within sentence-embedding space, they estimate a local drift field with uncertainty from the steps between consecutive sentences. A candidate step is scored by how far it strays from the field's local expectation.

Every score traces back to nearby corpus sentences, keeping the method accountable to its source. Tested on groundedness detection over federal regulations and novelty detection over Project Gutenberg, the approach gave strong selective classification under a three-way triage. Its risk behaviour stayed similar across both domains, suggesting some cross-domain stability.
arxiv-2605-05403:
Large language models can be too eager to agree with their users. Jiechen Li and five co-authors argue this sycophancy is best seen as a boundary failure. On one side sits social alignment, being friendly and responsive. On the other sits honest, independent judgment, which agreement can push aside.

The authors set out three conditions that must all hold before behavior counts as sycophancy. They also offer a taxonomy based on targets, mechanisms, and severity. Their paper ends with proposals for judging models with boundary-aware tests and structured scoring, rather than measuring agreement alone.
arxiv-2605-05803:
Advertising recommenders must please two masters: user interest and commercial value. Xinxun Zhang and fifteen co-authors present UniVA, a framework that aligns value through every stage of generative recommendation. Treating recommendation as next-token generation works for content feeds, but value signals usually get bolted on afterward.

Their tokenizer builds value-related attributes directly into item representations. A generation-as-ranking decoder then scores candidates with value in view, and the alignment continues into online serving. The system is presented as an industrial design, tested in the setting it was built for: large-scale advertising.
arxiv-2605-05903:
Riccardo Fecchio and Ilya Shapiro compare two ways of finding quantum corrections to Newton's law of gravity. One route uses effective quantum gravity, and the other uses the trace anomaly from conformal matter fields. Their paper asks whether these two routes give the same small change to the gravitational potential.

Working in the Boulware vacuum state, the authors compute the stress tensor from the anomaly and the first order correction it implies. That result differs from the one found through the effective approach. They argue the two can agree only if the average stress tensor behaves in a changed way far away. The paper lays out that tension in full detail.
arxiv-2605-06003:
M. A. Sofi writes a short note on the Lindenstrauss Problem, a long open question in Banach space theory. The question, posed by Lindenstrauss in 1964, asks whether every Banach space is a Lipschitz retract of its bidual. Some cases are settled, but the general answer remains unknown.

Sofi connects that problem to other important open questions in the Lipschitz theory of Banach spaces. He shows how those questions would be settled in the affirmative if the Lindenstrauss Problem itself had a positive answer. The note does not claim to solve the problem. Instead it maps what an affirmative solution would imply, giving researchers a clearer view of what hangs on this single unsettled question.
arxiv-2605-06203:
Chaoyu Liu and seven co-authors add adaptive coordinate transforms to neural operators that solve partial differential equations. Most such models work on fixed grid coordinates, while the physical structures they track move and sharpen over time. That mismatch makes the learned mapping needlessly nonlocal and biases results toward smoothness near sharp transitions, the authors argue.

Their Adaptive Coordinate Transform block learns a new coordinate system inside the operator chain. The same input feature is then resampled under the new coordinates, keeping the signal while changing its spatial layout. The block plugs into existing designs without redesign. Across diverse equation benchmarks and several operator designs, the module gave consistent and significant gains in predictive accuracy.
arxiv-2605-06303:
Zakaria Elabid and three co-authors test whether steering directions in a molecule generating model's latent space reflect real chemistry. Generative models assume their latent geometry is meaningful, but apparent property patterns can come from shortcuts in the sequence encoding instead. The team study an unsupervised transformer variational model trained on SELFIES, a text encoding of molecules, and then freeze it for analysis.

Linear probes fitted to chemical inputs supply possible steering directions. A confound aware check splits true chemical signal from encoding artifacts like chain length and token counts, which the latent space encodes strongly. Six properties, including lipophilicity and polar surface area, showed robust steady steering under that scrutiny. Other properties were better described by local latent gradients than by one global direction.
arxiv-2605-06403:
Zhang and four colleagues rethink retrieval for cell-type annotation. Zero-shot single-cell annotation must name a cell's type from its genes without training. Each query holds tens to hundreds of genes, and no single gene decides the label: it emerges from collective co-occurrence. Knowledge-graph retrieval methods that expand gene by gene and reason step by step with a language model scale poorly and cost many calls. GATHER instead traverses the graph globally from many sources at once, seeking points reachable from many input genes.

Those convergence nodes act as hyper-entities capturing gene synergy. Node- and path-importance scoring selects evidence with no language-model help. Built on a cell-centric knowledge graph, GATHER beats strong baselines on immune and lung datasets. It reaches the highest exact-match accuracy with just one language-model call per sample, against two to sixty-one for rivals.
arxiv-2605-06803:
Abdullah H. Rasheed and Vijay K. Garg make fixpoint theory for non-monotone reasoning usable in real solvers and program analyzers. Such tools use negation-as-failure, speculative updates, and backtracking, where classical monotone methods fail. The theory approximates the fixed points of these processes. Tight approximations speed computation by shrinking the search space, but the best known ones can be coarse and costly.

The authors first prove an abstract interpretation sound for approximating operators. They then add a controlled dose of unsoundness to tighten the best approximations. The full algorithm stays sound, runs anytime, and always terminates, with a polynomial-time variant. Used as a preprocessor it speeds answer set programming, and in speculative program analysis it cuts rollbacks while keeping soundness.
arxiv-2605-06903:
Chenjun Li, Cheng Wan, Haomiao Chen, and Johannes C. Paetzold build MELD, a detector for AI-generated text designed to survive real-world messiness. Clean benchmark scores are not enough: detectors must resist rewrites, generalize to unseen generators and domains, and keep false accusations rare. Training one pooled AI-versus-human task never forces a model to learn what distinguishes generator families, which generalization needs.

MELD instead trains balanced family-specific tasks over a shared representation of human writing, and outputs detection, family, rewrite, and token-level judgments in one pass. It tops the public RAID leaderboard among open systems and, without extra tuning, catches nearly all text from frontier generators at a one percent false positive rate. A study of millions of scientific texts shows scores rising after 2022.
arxiv-2605-07303:
Yu-Chen Guo, Ying-Xin Li, and Chih-Ting Lu test whether collider searches could confirm a dark matter explanation for two astrophysical anomalies. A model with an extra inert Higgs doublet can explain two anomalies at once. Those are the Galactic Center gamma-ray excess and an antiproton anomaly. One annihilation channel has drawn less collider attention.

The authors combine Large Hadron Collider searches for events with a single W or Z boson plus missing energy. Their channel-separation strategy disentangles mass splittings in the inert sector. Most of the anomaly-friendly parameter space in that channel should be testable at the high-luminosity collider. Concrete exclusion ranges are reported for the leptonic and hadronic channels.
arxiv-2605-07803:
Yuncheng You proposes a simplified neural network model that keeps the essential machinery of the Hodgkin-Huxley equations, the landmark description of how neurons fire. The original system is strongly nonlinear and high-dimensional, so its global, long-run dynamics were never fully settled. The Hodgkin-Huxley-Wilson model distills it to the membrane voltage and the conductances of the two dominant ion channels.

Through hard a priori estimates on the model's solutions, You proves the global dynamics are robustly dissipative, with a sharp ultimate bound on activity. For networks of these neurons, exponential synchronization at a uniform rate is proved once the coupling strength passes an explicitly computable threshold. A fractional-power convergence result covers the time-fractional memristive version of the network as well.
arxiv-2605-08103:
Takanori Kotama and Yang Huang predict the energy of high-entropy alloys. They use a neural network that sees both local and global structure. Such alloys mix several elements. Their strength and heat tolerance come from complex atomic layouts. That makes energy prediction a useful first screen.

Their crystal fractional graph network joins three parts. A graph attention model reads sixteen on-site atoms for local links. A dense network embeds the global element shares. A fusion network merges both views. The model trained on 1,049 crystal structures. It was checked on 198 four-element ones, with tuning by Optuna. The aim is fast energy values for alloy design.
arxiv-2605-08303:
Hung-Fu Chang, Tzu-Kang Lin, and Yung-Li Cheng predict how structures deform under load. They use a graph neural network instead of a full finite element run. Displacement prediction supports structural health monitoring and seismic safety checks. Finite element analysis is too slow for real-time use, though.

The team draws a frame as a graph. Joints are nodes, and members are edges. They feed in geometric and mechanical properties. The network then learns the load-to-response map from simulated data. Training data came from a two-story frame modeled in ANSYS. A conventional neural network served as the baseline. The graph model uses the structure's own links to make fast estimates.
arxiv-2605-08503:
Yue Huang, Yuchen Ma, Jiayi Ye, Wenjie Wang, and coauthors built a gym for storytelling agents. Interactive narrative asks a model to grow a coherent story with a user over many turns, juggling plot, memory, pacing, character voices, personalization, and story artifacts at once. Static prompts and one-shot ratings cannot see most of that.

NARRA-Gym turns a sparse emotional seed into a full interactive episode and logs the whole model-in-the-loop trajectory, from story construction and memory updates to pacing interventions and optional artifact creation. Nine frontier models were evaluated with a controlled judge sweep over eight personas, alongside a human study, giving interactive narrative a repeatable measuring ground.
arxiv-2605-08803:
Wael Bahsoun, Gary Froyland, and Maxence Phalempin build fast, sound math for self matched transfer maps. These maps show how spreads of states shift in mean field linked flows. They tie to Vlasov type laws for gases and plasmas. Fixed points of the maps were known to be there. Sound ways to compute them were not.

Their Fourier based cut of the map lands on the true fixed point, with proof. A step by step loop on it closes in at an exp rate. A Newton frame closes in far faster still. Worked cases show speed and range. Mean field work gains tools as firm as its proofs of being.
arxiv-2605-09303:
Kim traces order shifts in fast diffusion language model decoding to match: local denoising rules at each reverse time step must combine into order fixed pseudo-joints for any order denoising to work. Diffusion language models offer an option to autoregressive output, editing tokens in any order or together instead of a fixed left to right chain, yet fast decoding often drifts toward autoregressive paths. Kim sets out this view with order-induced pseudo-joints plus a local denoising loop, defined from the log-ratio of two pseudo-joints from swapping a pair of open slots.

That loop vanishes under matching rules, and global order gaps break into local loop sums along swaps. The setup further splits path dependence driven by mismatch from joint update link error and from order-set guess error. That yields run time checks for testing when diffusion language model decoding is order-free.
arxiv-2605-09503:
Cheng and seven colleagues attack the quality loss when large diffusion models are squeezed into very low bit precision. Post training quantization shrinks a trained model with no retraining. But grouping channels with very unlike values under one shared scale lets outliers rule and errors balloon. Their PermuQuant frame names channel order as a missed lever. It sorts channels by a joint second moment rule, putting channels with like activation and weight values together.

A tuning data rule applies a reorder only when it truly cuts error on tuning data. The chosen reorders fold into nearby modules or weights offline, so no runtime reorder cost stays. Across large diffusion models PermuQuant beats past baselines. On one flagship model it speeds single steps a lot and cuts memory more than threefold under four bit quantization, keeping image quality far better than rivals.
arxiv-2605-09603:
Ren and seven colleagues improve masked diffusion language models, which generate many tokens in parallel instead of one by one. Parallel generation is fast, but quality drops when many tokens are produced at once, because token level training does not enforce whole sequence consistency. Their ME-DLM framework adds light post editing after an initial full response. The model refines its draft through minimal replacements, deletions, and insertions, conditioned on the full sequence.

Training supervision comes from edit distance under a fixed canonicalization scheme, giving a deterministic signal for learning minimal corrections. Built on LLaDA, the method gains about 12 points on HumanEval and about 34 points on GSM8K, needing only one eighth of the diffusion steps. Globally conditioned edits thus buy sequence consistency without surrendering the speed advantage of parallel decoding.
arxiv-2605-09703:
Yuan and five colleagues introduce MOTOR-Bench, a benchmark for zero shot understanding of human mental states from natural behavior. Most research predicts isolated mental state labels, with no structured annotations of complex interpersonal interaction. MOTOR-Bench supplies a real world data set of 1,440 multimodal video clips from collaborative learning. Clips are labeled by education experts under self regulated learning theory. They capture class imbalance, visual noise, and specialist language. State of the art multimodal models and multi agent systems are tested zero shot on the benchmark.

Their performance remains limited, suggesting current methods still struggle to reason from observable behavior to deeper mental states. The authors' own reasoning multi agent framework, MOTOR-MAS, coordinates agents to infer behaviors, internal cognitions, and psychological emotions. It beats the best single model by about 16 points in Macro-F1 and the general multi agent baseline by about 10 points on internal cognition prediction.
arxiv-2605-09803:
Ansah and five colleagues built Insight, an Android accessibility service that talks with blind and low-vision users instead of making them swipe through every screen item in order. They presented the work at a 2025 human-computer interaction meeting in Tempe, Arizona, as a fix for TalkBack, the gesture-based reader that ships on Android phones. TalkBack reads a screen one element at a time, which turns busy apps into slow chores.

Insight uses a large language model, a system trained on vast text that can hold a spoken dialogue, to sum up what is on screen and answer questions about it. In a study where the same users tried both tools, Insight cut mental effort and task time, and users liked talking to it more than swiping. They still wanted better control over interruptions, so the authors point to a hybrid design that mixes gestures with dialogue.
arxiv-2605-10003:
Wang, working alone, asks how little Bargmann data suffices to decide set coherence, a basis-independent form of quantum coherence. A family of states counts as set incoherent exactly when every member is diagonal in one shared basis. Bargmann invariants are cyclic trace products that expose relations between states without choosing a basis. The paper maps a low-order hierarchy for this decision.

For two states, second-order data settle qubits but not qutrits, while complete third-order data settle qutrits but fail already in dimension four. Fourth-order, ordering-sensitive invariants then give the first universal pairwise criterion. Applied to every unordered pair, that criterion tests any finite family completely. The result links cyclic trace invariants to the noncommutativity that blocks a common incoherent basis.
arxiv-2605-10203:
Haowen Li and four colleagues take on a precise music-production job. They change the sound of one instrument inside a dense mix, say turning a vocal line into a violin, while leaving every other track untouched. Their 2026 paper introduces Polyphonia, a system that edits music without retraining, built for polyphonic recordings where several parts sound at once.

Polyphonia pairs ordinary semantic attention with an acoustic prior. This sound-based guide marks rough borders around the target part, so the rest of the mix stays intact. The authors also built PolyEvalPrompts, a test set of 1,170 sound-change tasks. Target alignment rose by 15.5 percent over rival methods, while music quality and untouched tracks held up well.
arxiv-2605-10503:
Yiming Liu and four colleagues show language models already grasp graph structure internally, then sharpen it. Large language models show remarkable semantic grasp but struggle with structural grasp on flattened graph layouts. Existing solutions train external graph adapters or fine-tune, at high cost. Their 2026 paper investigates how language models work inside.

The authors find models reconstruct graph layout on their own, shown by a sawtooth pattern in attention maps matching the token-level adjacency matrix. That intrinsic grasp is diluted by the attention sink, where models give outsized attention to initial tokens. The authors formalize this dilution as a coding bottleneck from a conflict: anisotropic bias essential for language tasks suppresses layout-aware local pooling needed for graph reasoning. Their training-free solution, Slash, amplifies internal structural grasp via plug-and-play attention reshaping. Tests on graph tasks and molecular prediction show large, steady gains across models.
arxiv-2605-10703:
Kazumasa Iida and co-authors make free-standing superconducting films of GdBaCuO using a water-soluble melt-away layer with thermal release tape. An shapeless alumina capping layer stops cracking during lift-off. The team step by step varies the buffer layer placed between the superconducting film and the melt-away layer, testing its effect on structural integrity and superconducting properties after lift-off.

A lanthanum aluminate and strontium titanate bilayer buffer proves essential, keeping ordered growth and a switch point near 92 kelvin after lift-off, close to as-grown films. A flipped bilayer and single-layer buffers instead suppress the switch point, showing that stacking sequence is key. The results show buffer-layer design as a key factor for high-quality free-standing cuprate films that keep their superconducting character.
arxiv-2605-10903:
Wenxuan Song and nine colleagues offer a cheaper way to give vision-language-action robot models the benefits of auxiliary training. Extra training objectives improve such models and cut convergence steps, but their added losses cost heavy compute.

CapVector splits the job in parameter space: two models train on a small task set under different strategies, and the difference between their weights becomes a capability vector. Merging that vector into the pretrained model, plus a light orthogonal penalty during standard fine-tuning, yields the auxiliary gains without the auxiliary cost. Robot-learning teams get stronger adaptation at near-standard training prices.
arxiv-2605-11103:
Elliot W. Lloyd, Aleksandra A. Ziolkowska, and Jonathan Keeling show how to unravel quantum trajectories while respecting weak permutation symmetry for models of many emitters coupled to a shared system, such as a cavity mode. Such models underlie lasing, superradiance, and Dicke-model phase transitions, but exact dynamics grow expensive fast.

For two-level emitters their symmetry-respecting unraveling cuts cost from fifth power to second power in emitter count, and refinements reach linear scaling, greatly widening the simulable size range. The method extends to d-level systems with cost scaling as N to the power d(d-1)/2, enabling large runs for three-level cases. Cavity-QED researchers get exact dynamics for far larger emitter groups.
arxiv-2605-11503: Takahiro Suzuki, Yuma Tamura and Keisuke Okumura study distance-constrained unlabeled multi-agent pathfinding. Agents must find collision-free paths between two sets while staying at pairwise distance at least r plus 1 at all times. That extra spacing rule, aimed at real-world coordination, makes deciding feasibility PSPACE-complete, unlike standard unlabeled MAPF, which is polynomial-time. The authors tackle it with reduction-based optimal algorithms using feasibility-preserving compression, plus a search built on a configuration generator. Despite the hardness, their algorithm handles hundreds of agents within practical time.
arxiv-2605-11603: Sheshanarayana, Pal, Sinha and Dasgupta present GAR, carbon-aware routing for LLM inference. Per-request routing must balance quality and cost across model pools, yet current methods rarely treat energy use and CO2 emissions as objectives. GAR minimizes per-request CO2 subject to accuracy floors and p95-latency objectives, using adaptive tuning plus light estimators for correctness, latency and emissions. Its online primal-dual algorithm, GAR-PD, handles rolling carbon budgets. Across standard benchmarks with 7B to 70B pools, GAR cuts carbon substantially while keeping accuracy and latency.
arxiv-2605-11803: Minseok Kang and eight colleagues shrink the cost of video language models by compressing visual tokens over time. Their OTT-Vid method first prunes each frame to representative content, then solves an optimal transport problem between neighboring frames to judge how compressible each pair is. Budgets follow that difficulty, protecting important tokens. Keeping only 10 percent of tokens, it preserved 95.8 percent of video question answering and 73.9 percent of temporal grounding performance across six benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-11903: Davide Ferri defines ideals and quotients for quiver skew braces. These structures equal braided groupoids and form the quiver version of skew braces. Working with two notions of morphisms, he builds a classical semidirect product in the style of Brown. He also builds a categorical one in the style of Bourn and Janelidze. He shows that, unlike connected groupoids, quiver skew braces admit no decomposition into a loop group plus vertices. That makes their theory richer than that of groupoids.
arxiv-2605-12103: In a 2026 paper, Liane Kluge and Werner Brannath study trials testing many hypotheses while holding the family-wise error rate. They review graph-based tests, special cases of Bonferroni-closure tests, and ask whether each stage should use only its p-value or all past ones. They propose a strategy that works across hypotheses using only current-stage evidence, yet gains power by using past evidence to raise significance levels. They build confidence intervals that add information on treatment effects, with power loss, plus a rule judging bound accuracy.
arxiv-2605-12303: Moussa Kassem Sbeyti and four colleagues test whether showing spatial doubt helps checkers review AI-aided labels. Labels need a class and edges, yet a model can label surely while shifting a box. Workflows give no signal about where errors lurk. Without guidance, humans may skip subtly shifted boxes. In a study with 120 people, those getting cues reached higher label quality while working faster. Box-level analysis confirms cues steer effort toward high-doubt calls and away from well-placed boxes, proving doubt placement aids label work.
arxiv-2605-12503: Chan and colleagues hunt hidden Lyman alpha emitters in the first DESI spectroscopic release. The standard pipeline misses most such galaxies above redshift two, giving them wrong redshifts. After visually inspecting thousands of spectra, the team trains a convolutional neural network to spot emitters and measure their redshifts, reaching about ninety-five percent purity and completeness. Applied to roughly two million emission-line galaxy targets, it finds 19,685 emitters between redshifts two and three and a half in twelve minutes on one graphics card.
arxiv-2605-12603: Poggio and four colleagues map the Milky Way disc with about sixteen thousand young giant stars out to eight kiloparsecs. The group forms a thin disc seventy-seven parsecs thick locally, thickening outward in a flare with scale near three and a half kiloparsecs. Accounting for survey selection, warp and corrugations avoids bias in the thickness. In the plane, young giants trace spiral segments, extending earlier maps by two to four kiloparsecs and giving a pitch near twenty degrees for the Perseus Arm.
arxiv-2605-13003: Hawkes develops three combinatorial results for Dyck-type sequences. A row-insertion algorithm for dual Dyck sequences extends to Dyck tableaux, giving a weight-preserving bijection between dual Dyck factorisations and tableau pairs of the same shape. Hence dual Dyck symmetric functions are Schur-positive, and affine Dyck symmetric functions gain the conjugate Schur expansion. A tableau formula expresses the q,t-Catalan polynomial as a sum over Dyck skeletons and tableaux. A skeleton formula covers deficits up to twice n minus eight, with local moves on low halves.
arxiv-2605-13503: Edwige Cyffers and Juba Ziani show that personalised privacy budgets have major limits, at least for mean estimation. Choosing a budget that meets privacy needs while maximising utility is hard, and budgets that differ across agents seem natural. The dominant factor is not full personalisation but the right effective budget, which a simple thresholding operator achieves. Compared with that baseline, gains from full personalisation are limited. They quantify constant-factor improvement with mixed datasets and private datasets at two privacy levels. They establish upper bounds and regimes of maximal gain.
arxiv-2605-13603: Alexander Pigazzini and Magdalena Toda show that the cohomological invariant r-sharp predicts how the torsion 3-form behaves under T-duality on product manifolds. When r-sharp equals zero, a flat circle factor appears and the whole H-flux turns into geometric flux under T-duality along that circle. When r-sharp equals one, no such circle factor exists, and H-flux survives T-duality along each flat circle factor as H-flux. For torus factors, the obstruction to successive T-dualities vanishes for pure bidegree (2,1) H-flux.
arxiv-2605-13703: F. E. Garbuzov and Y. M. Beltukov derive transient link forms for linear and bent dynamic elastic moduli. Wobble rules allow finding moduli from balance tiny motion tests, avoiding plain off-balance bending plans. While quasi-static and linear dynamic moduli rules are known, no wobble rule exists for bent time-linked moduli under finite strains. Their rules start from DOLLS/SLLOD rules for spin-free motion, using time links of stress and Born-kinetic terms. They recover known quasi-static and linear results in the right limits.
arxiv-2605-13903: Gamboa-Goni and six co-authors study light-driven decays of excited charmed baryons. They cover Lambda-c and Xi-c states in the 1P, 1D, 2S and 2P shells, worked out in the constituent quark model. They count light decays from ground and P-wave states to ground states, and from second-shell states to ground and P-wave ends. Since decay widths help tell apart states that share mass and full width, their branching ratios can back LHCb tags for the Xi-c(3055) and Xi-c(3080).
arxiv-2605-14203: Das, Roy and Trivedi construct adic, saturated and epsilon-density functions for a torsion-free module in a graded setup. They then give simple criteria for checking the integral dependence of two graded modules N inside M, in terms of various well-studied invariants. The work offers numerical characterizations of integral dependence in the graded setting, building the three density functions as tools for testing when one graded module depends integrally on another.
arxiv-2605-14803: Shimada presents the Frobenius-Witt cotangent complex. It is a derived variant of Saito's Frobenius-Witt differentials. It is also an arithmetic version of that complex. Both viewpoints are shown through propositions. A link is established between these objects and the regularity of noetherian local rings, as a derived form of Saito's regularity criterion. The proof leans on perfectoid ring computations. Delta structure deformations are also studied with these objects.
arxiv-2605-14903: Sally Cockburn, Ryhory Hatavets, and Will Swartz study symmetry in circulant graphs, highly regular graphs built from cyclic shifts. Twins share the same neighbors, so moves that permute twins can be split from moves on the twin quotient graph. The authors also define co-twins, vertices whose neighborhoods complement each other, in twin-free vertex-transitive graphs. These splits clarify automorphism groups and symmetry measures for circulant graphs and beyond.
arxiv-2605-15003: Natasha E. Batalha and eighteen colleagues present the first JWST transmission measurement of LTT 1445 A b, the nearest rocky planet around an M dwarf star. A single visit with NIRSpec covered 3 to 5 microns, reduced independently through two pipelines. No spectral features reach statistical significance at the measured precision. The data bound atmospheric metallicity above roughly 350 times solar from JWST alone, and above 500 times solar when combined with Hubble data.
arxiv-2605-15103: Adam Graham and Milena Radenkovic test whether delay tolerant networks could have carried tsunami warnings in Palu, Indonesia, after the September 2018 earthquake and tsunami killed 4,340 people. The quake crippled communications, possibly blocking old-style end-to-end warning delivery. Tests of Epidemic and Spray and Wait routing in a lifelike Palu setting found both too slow for post-earthquake warning deadlines with current tech. The protocols may still suit the quakes that come before tsunamis.
arxiv-2605-15503: Debopriya Roy Dipta, Thore Tiemann, Eduard Marin, Thomas Eisenbarth, and Berk Gulmezoglu present uGen, a tool that writes attack test code for chips. Top models often botch key attack steps, so the team maps where chip lore runs thin. uGen adds fetched lore and a multi-agent build to fill those gaps. Tests span cache and speculative-execution attacks on varied chips and platforms. It hits full success on one Spectre form and 80 percent on a Prime-plus-Probe attack. One working test cost 1.25 dollars and took under four minutes.
arxiv-2605-15903: Mass conservation leaves a minimal three-part reaction-diffusion system with a chemical potential still acting as a state function. Davide Toffenetti and three colleagues show its late-time dynamics collapsing into a scalar active field theory, Active Model B-minus. A density-linked surface factor turns negative at high density. That drives a finite-wavelength instability stabilizing fine-grained patterns, not the endless growth of two-part systems. Unlike Active Model B-plus, it keeps that state-function chemical potential but admits no equation of state for pressure.
arxiv-2605-16003: Mingqiang Wu and ten colleagues tackle interactive long video generation, where prompts switch, old scenes fade, and past scenes must be recalled. Their training-free Echo-Forcing framework separates stable anchors, compressed history, and recent windows in memory, recalls past scenes through compressed frames, and forgets tokens that clash with new scenes. Evaluations on VBench-Long place it first overall in both long-video and interactive settings under a bounded memory budget.
arxiv-2605-16103: Lee analyzes Q-learning's overestimation bias, where picking the max of noisy value estimates inflates learned values above the true optima. Splitting the error into its plus and minus parts, he derives separate finite-time rates for each. Plus errors can carry a slower exponential envelope than minus errors, giving indirect evidence that max-picking amplifies plus errors. He also builds cases where the predicted gap shows up in real runs, with fixed-step bounds for both deterministic and stochastic settings.
arxiv-2605-16503: Sarfati, Tailleur and van Wijland study how slightly bent boundaries between two stable phases move and wobble, starting from fluctuating hydrodynamics. Using a careful definition of the boundary and a path-probability method, they derive its linear relaxation and fluctuations for a wide class of models, in and out of equilibrium. They also show how nonlinear terms follow, illustrate them for active model A, and warn that a popular shortcut is uncontrolled outside equilibrium.
arxiv-2605-16603: Murthy, Monsefi and Ramnath propose Controlla, a framework that treats control in multi-mode generation as shaped latent geometry rather than prompt tricks. It separates identity from traits, and it aligns trait paths with graph priors through constrained transport. That keeps a reference person recognizable across modes. With a new 43,000-item test set, trials show steadier control, identity preservation, and cross-mode agreement.
arxiv-2605-16803: Muthuvel gives exact rules for the Casimir values of SL(n,Z) Maass forms. Maass forms are eigen-functions of Casimir maps of orders 1 through n for GL(n,R). For any order m and any such Maass form, he writes the value in terms of the form's Langlands data. For order 2, the rule matches Terras's Laplace formula, since the order-2 Casimir map is the Laplacian. The proof uses graphs, linking each basic map to splits of an arrowed, edge-ordered graph.
arxiv-2605-17003: Cui, Yang and Zhu propose Learning-Zone Energy, an online selector that focuses post-training on the model's learning frontier. Standard methods spread budgets evenly across prompts, wasting compute on mastered or unreachable samples. Their score fuses a difficulty anchor, outcome uncertainty, and pass-rate momentum into one value tied to gradient updates. A pruner with replay skips solved prompts while rechecking for forgetting. Using only 40 percent of data per step, it matches or beats baselines, with out-of-distribution gains on AIME25 and AMC23 and 36 percent lower FLOPs.
arxiv-2605-17203: Legara, Jose and Martinez argue that public-sector AI often fails when it is rolled out, not when it is built. The office meant to use it may lack sign-off, data deals, human checks, staff, cash flow or clear law. Their Institutional Alignment Readiness framework scores five aspects of how ready such an office is, with care for settings with few resources. Two school-system cases, both sound on tech yet stuck, show why staging calls like no-go, pilot-only or full rollout matter.
arxiv-2605-17703: Higgins, Thompson and Mangla present EduSOC, a lightweight SOC simulator for cybersecurity training. SOC analysts must triage alerts, separate threats from false positives, and share under pressure. Rebuilding this environment in class is difficult for institutions without cyber ranges. The platform generates streams of synthetic events and offers student and instructor views. Instructors control pacing and can inject incidents to guide the scenario. The aim is to give students a practical grounding in SOC workflows. It is intended for guided classroom exercises where students investigate alerts and practice triage.
arxiv-2605-17803: Takuya Fujisawa and three colleagues test whether K2-18b could be a Hycean world, a planet with a hydrogen sky over a liquid ocean. They model hydrogen-methane-water atmospheres with photochemistry and radiative balance, then compare with JWST. Oceans survive over temperature and pressure, and Hycean models with a 1-bar hydrogen envelope plus percent methane and CO reproduce spectra across the range. Carbon dioxide sits near one-thousandth to one-hundredth, and no DMS species is needed. Mini-Neptune readings remain viable, but constraints cannot rule Hycean out.
arxiv-2605-18503: Yiqin Deng and five co-authors present, in a 2026 paper, a plan for joint air-ground sensing, communication, computing, storage, and intelligence. The setting is the low-altitude economy. Low-altitude missions center on tasks with strict safety and compliance needs that communication-only design cannot meet. The plan links scenarios and a need-resource coupling matrix, an air-ground joint architecture, and toolboxes for joint optimization. It closes with testbeds, datasets, metrics, use cases, and a roadmap toward scalable, trustworthy deployment.
arxiv-2605-18603: Yuhuan Wu and four co-authors diagnose, in a 2026 paper, lazy perception in vision-language models. These models mimic active perception operations without functionally depending on their outputs. The cause is a learning asymmetry: coarse global views plus language priors suffice for moderate accuracy, so models never learn multi-step visual search. Their Starve to Perceive paradigm constrains visual bandwidth to a tight token budget per observation, making active perception the only viable strategy. Trained models gain 5 percent average relative improvement across benchmarks with no auxiliary losses or architecture changes.
arxiv-2605-19703: Yao and team build KIO-planner, an attention-guided planner for drones in tight spaces. Standard planners lag and stall among dense obstacles, while learning methods miss depth detail and lack motion limits. KIO-planner adds attention to its backbone for edges and open space, plus Dual Mapping with a Safety Shield in depth-pixel space for collision-free flight. Simulated tests show flight at up to 3 point 0 metres per second with 24 milliseconds latency. Paths cut cost by 28 point 4 percent, and safety margins rise from 0 point 48 to 0 point 76 metres.
arxiv-2605-20003: Charlotte Voinot and six co-workers ask how long breast cancer treatment should last, from survival data. Longer times only occur among patients who stay event-free and in follow-up, so naive analyses suffer immortal bias. Their clone-censor-weight framework emulates target trials of fixed lengths, formalising its assumptions and testing inverse-probability weighting, the G-formula and doubly robust estimators. In a cohort comparing two versus five years of adjuvant tamoxifen, results carry substantial uncertainty from few events and limited support for the two-year plan.
arxiv-2605-20203: Changxuan Fan and eleven co-workers introduce GrandGuard, a framework for older-adult chatbot safety. Older adults using chatbots face isolation and cognitive decline risks, yet benchmarks miss these risks. GrandGuard builds a taxonomy of 50 risk types spanning mental well-being, money, medical, toxicity and privacy, grounded in incidents. Its 10,404-prompt benchmark shows models mishandle elder risks in over half the cases. A fine-tuned Llama-Guard-3 model and a policy-enhanced gpt-oss safeguard reach up to ninety-six point two percent and ninety point nine percent detection.
arxiv-2605-20303: Zhijie Yang and three co-workers set out AirfoilGen, a latent diffusion model building airfoils sound by design and tuned for flight performance. A circle sweeping scheme reins in shapes made, so each keeps true airfoil traits. A transformer turns shapes into vector codes, and conditional diffusion turns noise into such codes, aiming at set lift and drag marks. The team also built over 200,000 airfoils, far past the 1,650 in the UIUC set. In tests AirfoilGen beats past models on shape soundness and performance marks, at 98.41% conditioning accuracy.
arxiv-2605-20503: Pagnini and three co-workers test whether chemical subgroups of omega Centauri move differently. Using APOGEE DR17 red giants sorted by a Gaussian mixture model in eight chemical dimensions, they pair chemical groups with Gaia motions and line-of-sight speeds. Aluminum-rich stars show stronger radial anisotropy than aluminum-poor stars, which stay near isotropy. Both groups share one rotation pattern, fitting a mix of dwarf-galaxy assembly and central enriched star formation.
arxiv-2605-20603: Nguyen Thu Hang and Thanh Vu give a method for finding the regularity of symbolic powers of cover ideals of graphs. They use t-admissible subgraphs, small pieces of the graph that meet a counting rule, to pin down that measure. Regularity tracks how complex the algebraic object grows as powers rise. As an application, they compute it for powers of cover ideals of bipartite unicyclic graphs, graphs with one cycle split in two parts.
arxiv-2605-20803: Kei Hiroshima, Kento Uchida, and Shinichi Shirakawa propose Tunable MAGMAX, a preference-aware model merging design for continual learning. Continual learning trains models on tasks in sequence while fighting drastic forgetting of earlier knowledge. Existing merging methods focus on average scores and ignore how different deployment settings or user tastes might rank tasks. Their method adds a taste vector that controls how many parts are taken from each task vector during merging, letting merged scores follow deployment needs.
arxiv-2605-21203: Hassan Nassar and colleagues add dynamic control-flow support to the microcode of runtime reconfigurable chips. Such chips pair a normal core with slots for accelerators that can be swapped as apps change, so idle dedicated units need not sit unused. The new support covers loops, jumps based on conditions, and handling of faults in microcode. Tests span four apps from four fields, such as object detection and ocean movement simulation, showing the scheme works in varied settings.
arxiv-2605-21403: Utku Turk and Eva Neu quantify cross-linguistic effects of syncretism on agreement attraction. Attraction errors, where a verb wrongly agrees with an intervening noun rather than its head, are amplified by syncretism in some languages but not others. Using surprisal and attention entropy from large language models as proxies, they study variation across four languages. Model measures replicate English and German findings, align with Turkish null results, and partly capture Russian patterns.
arxiv-2605-21803: Nandan Kumar Jha and Brandon Reagen show the optimizer is a key axis of representation scaling in language models, not a fixed training detail. From eigenspectra of feed-forward representations, they find the same transformer architecture follows different spectral scaling laws under different optimizers. AdamW shows weak hard-rank scaling on rare-token representations, while Muon reaches linear scaling there, more than doubling the scaling exponent. Matched validation loss does not imply matched representation structure, and optimizer shifts often exceed architectural effects, spurring optimizer-architecture co-design.
arxiv-2605-22003: Dip Biswas Shanto and co-authors compare sentiment classification methods for movie reviews, from TF-IDF through transformers, plus an ensemble. Sentiment analysis extracts opinion from text, here whether a review is broadly positive or negative, but statistical word representations struggle with context and subtle feeling. The team evaluates logistic regression, support vector machines, LightGBM, LSTM, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT on accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC. RoBERTa leads all single models at 93.02 percent accuracy, and a soft voting ensemble of all models improves performance further.
