arxiv-2605-22703: Yang and others diagnose a clipping bottleneck in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: hard clipping discards signals just past the clipping edge. Their Near boundary Stochastic Rescue method keeps slightly out of bound tokens, recovering lost signal with a minimal plug and play change. Ablations show the stochastic boundary rescue beats deterministic gradient decay. Tests across dense and mixture of experts models from 7 billion to 30 billion parameters confirm steadier training and consistent gains over strong baselines. The fix is minimal and plug and play.
arxiv-2605-22903: Lan and three colleagues test whether vision-language benchmarks truly test vision, after finding that deleting many image tokens barely dented scores on a hallucination benchmark. Across open-source models and several levels of degradation, occlusion, and question reformulation, predictions proved far less sensitive to fine visual evidence than accuracy implied. Even unchanged predictions hid weakened internal support for the right answer. Deeper layers showed visual tokens growing more similar, a possible explanation.
arxiv-2605-23103: Luo presents Lepton, a fine-tuned BERT classifier for Classical Chinese wenji tables of contents. It predicts whether a title is a private letter or a closely confusable preface, especially the parting preface. Lepton fine-tunes bert-base-chinese with 5438 hand-labeled wenji works from thirty-three late-Ming plus early-Qing literati. Deployed at the China Biographical Database, it has identified roughly fifty-five thousand letters spanning mid-Ming through early-Qing collected works. Those letters populate the Ming Letter Platform.
arxiv-2605-23203: Durand and three coauthors verify vision networks against 3D camera motion, a key gap for safety-critical domains. Current methods cover only statistical checks or norm and affine robustness, missing camera motion. They map camera pose to pixel values, then extend Lipschitz optimization to derive tight linear bounds on perturbed pixels, enabling the first formal verification of projective transforms. It applies to planar scenes. Tests show 89 percent speedup and 7 percent tighter bounds. A runway case study reveals weaknesses to projective perturbations.
arxiv-2605-23403: Wang and colleagues test whether quantum circuits can sharpen weather downscaling, rebuilding fine detail from coarse forecasts. They slip variational quantum circuit layers into the tightest bottleneck of a diffusion model, leaving its regression branch classical, and try two circuit designs on 10-meter wind parts. On 2020 validation data the hybrids hold up and beat the classical model on error scores in several setups, keeping wind spectra and distributions. But 2021 out-of-sample tests show the gains do not always carry over time, and real hardware limits deployment.
arxiv-2605-23603: Frydrych introduces the Preisach Attention Layer, a sequence model grounded in the classical Preisach hysteresis operator from physics. It swaps softmax attention for a binary relay operator with learned on and off thresholds, keeping a stack of local extrema as its state. A single-layer Preisach transformer with constant depth is Turing-complete under arbitrary precision, unlike standard hard-attention transformers needing logarithmic depth. The extremum stack forms a minimal sufficient statistic for rate-independent functions, and total inference costs n log n versus n squared for standard attention.
arxiv-2605-24103: Habermann and Vanzella probe the limits of the semiclassical Einstein equation, used when quantum back-action on space-time matters yet meant to hold only when quantum jitters stay small. They exploit odd quirks of gravity, building a tidy, workable setting where mixed weak-gravity states push the system into a strong-gravity regime. Choosing a branch-tied measure, quantum and semiclassical calls can be compared, maybe marking the latter's reach. The work is a proof of principle, not a full verdict on the shortcut.
arxiv-2605-24403: Iliash and six co-authors present Artiverse, a set of jointed 3D objects built for lifelike working models. It holds about 5,400 human-authored objects across 88 groups, drawn from some static 3D stores. Objects carry labels for working parts, inner structures, joints with multi-degree-of-freedom motion, plus scale, stuff, and mass. A semi-auto setup mixing few-shot cutting, shape logic, and human checks cuts manual labels time by over 30 percent. Tests on part motion, object making, and physics-based contact show its value for working insight.
arxiv-2605-24903: Suresh Kumar Amalapuram leads SEED, a malware detector built for drift under scarce labels. Detectors age as apps drift, and recent fixes need full labels. Under partial labels, hierarchical contrastive loss degrades on unseen malware where semantic structure is weak. SEED drops the semantic-structure assumption, pairing a tailored cross-entropy goal with continual training and active learning. Unlabeled samples join labeled partners in a singular value space; the most uncertain go to analysts. Windows and Android tests show large unseen-malware gains with only a fifth of labels.
arxiv-2605-25003: Margam Ramprasad, Shubhadeep Mandal, and Pallab Sinha Mahapatra study upstream swimming, called rheotaxis, in colloid-crowded channel flow. Swimmers are modeled as squirmers in a multi-particle collision simulation. Without colloids, swimmers drift from walls and oscillate across the channel as flow rises, keeping an upstream tilt near walls. Adding colloids sends pushers to the center and upstream, while pullers leave the center at low flow. At high flow the current carries all swimmers, upstream motion dominates centrally, and speeds fall for all three types.
arxiv-2605-25103: The CMS Collaboration hunts for hypothetical spin-zero particles that decay into pairs of tau leptons. It uses proton-proton collisions recorded in 2022 and 2023. A fast trigger stream plus a new method for rebuilding low-momentum tau decays opens a mass window from 20 to 60 gigaelectronvolts, a range earlier searches had not covered. No surplus over ordinary background emerges, so the team caps the production rate times the decay share between 40 and 400 picobarns.
arxiv-2605-25203: Gorgi Pavlov applies a Walsh-geometry rotation to extreme low-bit quantization of language model weights. Each layer's weight matrix gets a Walsh-Hadamard rotation plus rescaling by per-coordinate activation energy before rounding. On four decoder-only models from 135 million to 1.5 billion parameters, wikitext-2 perplexity falls 15 to 58 percent against plain auto-round at two-bit weights. Extensions cover families the base recipe failed on, and all weights export to OpenVINO for Intel hardware. The author stresses the gain is engineering, not a transferred theorem.
arxiv-2605-25603: Shen and colleagues ask whether a language model's stated reasoning matches the computation that produced its answer. Outside checks of wording or consistency miss that gap, so they trace compact sentence-level circuits from informative tokens. They build separate graphs for the internal process and the outward trace, then score the mismatch with fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance. Their CIE-Scorer tops prior detectors on four FaithCoT-Bench datasets while cutting the cost of building full circuits.
arxiv-2605-25903: Zhao and colleagues present the Universal Activation Verbalizer, showing donor codes with a shared decoder. It learns an adapter turning codes into soft tokens. It also allows adapter-only transfer: a frozen decoder side LoRA stays put while a new adapter is trained. Across classification, retrieval and summarization it matches self explanation, enabling cross-model verbalization. Ablations show decoder side tuning improves behavior, while the adapter supplies grounded information.
arxiv-2605-26103: Pan, Schönberger and Pollefeys merge old and new methods for structure-from-motion, recovering camera poses and 3D scene shape from photos. Old methods fail on flat texture, scant overlap and symmetries, where feedforward rebuilding shines. Feedforward methods, though, trail old ones on scale, accuracy or toughness in standard scenes. The authors map those limits in detail and build a pipeline using each side's strengths. Tests plus an open-source release show gains where either method alone falters.
arxiv-2605-26403: Xiaohua Wang and seven colleagues confront distribution shift in multi-turn dialogue training. Fixed offline logs and prompt simulators suffer when training histories diverge from live conversation, a gap shown to compound quadratically over turns. Two roots explain it: policy shift from static histories, and simulator shift from fake users unlike real people. Their Calibrated Interactive RL couples interactive training with simulator alignment matched to human patterns. Tests confirm interactive training beats the static baseline, and calibration further narrows the sim-to-real gap.
arxiv-2605-26503: Jianzhe Gao and eight colleagues make navigation agents weigh perceptual doubt instead of ignoring it. Their agent builds a Semantic Gaussian Map from panoramic views, encoding scene shape and meaning in 3D Gaussian units. Shape doubt comes from small jitters of position and scale. Meaning doubt comes from jitters of meaning traits. Looks doubt comes from Fisher Information on view sensitivity. Folded into one 3D Value Map, these doubts act as affordances and constraints for reliable choices. Tests across several navigation benchmarks show the approach works.
arxiv-2605-26603: Xiaoran Liu and four others review thin films of pyrochlore iridates, oxides where spin-orbit coupling, electron ties, and lattice frustration clash. Bulk crystals already host rich linked and topological states, but film growth adds fresh knobs: tight layers, strain, and boundary coupling. The review covers a magnetic Weyl phase in tilted films, strain-shaped multipole order, a spin-liquid-like state in near-flat films, and odd states at mixed-material boundaries. Open questions close the piece.
arxiv-2605-26703: Foster and Hart extend two forecasting standards, calibration and calibeating, from the quadratic scoring rule to every bounded proper scoring rule. They show calibration always implies proper calibration, but calibeating does not always imply proper calibeating. They then give methods that guarantee proper calibeating, prove complete calibeating is always proper, and tie proper calibration to universal no regret in decision making.
arxiv-2605-27303: Pouya Fakharizadeh, Mohamed-Amine Lahmeri, Gerhard Krieger, and Robert Schober optimize drone swarm radar imaging by shaping its point spread function. They jointly tune the drone formation and the power used to send data down, using particle swarm optimization. Simulations show far stronger sidelobe suppression than benchmark schemes, under realistic sensing and communication limits.
arxiv-2605-27603: Candelaria Migliaro, Juan Martin Randazzo, and Renata Della Picca model how atoms ionize in strong fields from two combined light sources. They split the electron spectrum into direct laser ionization and high-frequency ion formation, picking out above-threshold ionization and laser-assisted photoemission patterns even when they mix. A special case where an ionization peak meets a sideband is treated in detail.
arxiv-2605-27803: Goswami and colleagues offer a full-system simulator for RowHammer, a hardware flaw in which repeated access to one memory row can flip bits in neighboring rows. Built on gem5, HammerSim models those flips with probabilities and lets researchers test hardware and software defenses, including targeted refresh of threatened rows and selective error correction. Its flip predictions were checked against real DDR4 memory modules.
arxiv-2605-28003: Son and colleagues assemble a large set of research-level mathematics problems to train language models where no human solutions exist yet. ResearchMath-14K gathers over fourteen thousand problems across eleven domains through a multi-agent pipeline. Training on it improved graduate- and research-level scores, while rival datasets left models flat.
arxiv-2605-28103: Wei and colleagues run a fair, head-to-head test of time-series anomaly detectors across five datasets and ten method families. No single approach wins everywhere, they find, and one event-dense dataset behaves more like a deployment workload than a sparse-anomaly test. Their own channel-graph detector tops the overall ranking and leads under noise, dropout, and time-shift stress.
arxiv-2605-28403: Sanjay Chandrasekaran, Florian Dörfler, and Silvia Mastellone give a decentralized way to pin down a power grid's equivalent model from local converter data alone. Grid voltage inputs bias a direct impedance estimate, so their gray-box plan splits the passive impedance effect from the active voltage effect. Least squares yields the parameters and a Kalman filter yields the voltages, across frequency samples. A five-converter grid-forming test shows the plan works well.
arxiv-2605-28603: Haonan Wen, Hanyang Chen, and Songhe Feng tackle online forecasting for irregular multivariate time series, where sampling gaps and shifting missingness break continuity. Offline methods degrade online as data distributions shift, and irregular sampling blocks standard online-learning tricks. Their Under-Cali framework uses an uncertainty estimator as the core control signal, routing high-uncertainty samples to an unreliable expert and keeping low-uncertainty samples with a reliable expert. The source forecaster stays frozen while a lightweight calibration module adapts, giving steady benchmark gains at low computational cost.
arxiv-2605-28803: Xinyu Wang and eight colleagues present HoloQ-VLA, the first training-free quantization of vision-language-action models to W4A4. Low-bit quantization destabilizes the head, so prior work keeps it at full or mixed precision, while uniform quantization stays open. HoloQ-VLA targets outliers with a weight-adapted rotation, a Hadamard transform, and scaling for drift across denoising steps. On LIBERO it compresses Pi-0.5 and GR00T-N1.5 to W4A4 at 98 and 88 percent success, matching FP16 references of 97 and 87, while cutting memory by 74 percent.
arxiv-2605-28903: Namit Chandak, Fulvio Melia, and Junjie Wei compare two pictures of the cosmos: the standard model and the R_h=ct universe. They test both against nearby galaxy and cosmic clock data. The four energy rules of general relativity forbid negative energy, repulsive gravity, and faster-than-light energy flow. Yet the standard model breaks them during inflation and dark-energy dominance, while the rival model fits the data at about 92 percent against 8 percent and obeys all four rules.
arxiv-2605-29103: Kara Fagerstrom classifies cohomological support varieties for monomial ideals with six generators. Earlier work had covered up to five generators; this paper extends the work to six. The authors also build two families of rings. One yields unbounded codimension, and the other yields an unbounded count of components. Finally, they answer a question of Gintz about which ones occur when the ideal is the edge ideal of a cycle. The results map the full range of shapes these objects can take in this case.
arxiv-2605-29503: Hao-Lei Chen and five colleagues compute the Polyakov-loop potential for pure gluonic matter under constant acceleration. They work in two linked settings, Euclidean Rindler space-time and optical space-time. The two versions describe distinct observables tied to their own parts of the energy-momentum tensor, settling a discrepancy for fields on conical backgrounds. In the optical version, real acceleration strengthens deconfinement. Moving to imaginary acceleration yields a bound phase, with echoes and contrasts to imaginary rotation.
arxiv-2605-29703: Maria del C. Valdes-Hernandez and nine colleagues track how deep brain shapes shift with thinking skills during people's eighties. Using scans and test scores from a long-running Lothian birth group, they map change in structures below the cortex across that decade. The hippocampus and ventral DC warped unevenly on left and right, while the thalami and globus pallidi shrank more evenly on both sides. Broad thinking change lined up most with inward and outward shifts at surface points between visits.
arxiv-2605-29803: Zhongtian Ma and four colleagues add two controls to graph attention networks: gating and a learnable temperature. Standard layers weigh neighbours by data-driven scores but leave shaky dimensions unchecked and fix attention sharpness. Gating filters feature and message responses to mute unreliable dimensions, while temperature tunes attention sharpness. Tests on uniform and mixed-type benchmarks show the variants beat their base models, and noise trials confirm gains under feature corruption. Theory backs the picture: gating helps when only some coordinates prove trustworthy, temperature when noise blurs node differences.
arxiv-2605-29903: Yousra Gati and Vladimir Petrov Kostov map where the spectrum of Ramanujan's partial theta function cannot lie. They show no spectral value falls in a wide sector plus a small disk around zero, of radius just over a fifth. One spectral value sits in the same sector plus a slightly larger disk, at about three tenths. Inside the safe zone, zero moduli split apart by negative half-integer powers of the parameter size. The result fences off most of the sector and pins the lone value inside it.
arxiv-2605-30103: Santosh Premi Adhikari, Radu Timofte and Dmitry Ignatov build a convergence theory for iterative LLM-based neural architecture search. They model the search as a parametric cross-entropy method over programs and prove six results. Elite fine-tuning matches the cross-entropy update, expected quality never decreases, and elite-set probability converges geometrically. Further results favour delta-based generation, show a novelty filter blocks mode collapse, and give a closed-form proxy reliability formula. A 22-cycle, three-model, six-dataset experiment confirms two predictions and two in direction.
arxiv-2605-30403: Abdelmalek Boumali studies a flat Dirac oscillator in a Yang-Mills field. The field setup holds a magnetic field and space and scalar strengths. The field strength gives an operator on spin-isospin space, with a Zeeman part and a mixing part. Splitting it gives one aligned branch and two mixed branches. The aligned Zeeman scale grows with the square of the space strength, while the singlet-triplet gap grows with space times scalar strength. The form states sign rules, checks edge cases, and clears up the plots.
arxiv-2605-30503: Vittorio Giammarino, Anastasios Manganaris and Ahmed H. Qureshi show that Pi-GCRL fails when applied naively to contact handling. Pi-GCRL adds optimal-control biases to value learning. While Pi-GCRL works in driving and object-free goal-reaching, its trust in contact tasks is unclear. They show these core traits can cause current Pi-GCRL methods to fail on contact handling. Spurred by this analysis, they present contact-aware and layered forms applying Pi-GCRL ideas in spots across the handling problem.
arxiv-2605-30703: Wang and colleagues show mid-infrared single-photon imaging with a single-element silicon detector, a single-pixel camera. Single-pixel cameras cost less and last longer than multi-pixel sensors, an advantage for IR work in industry inspection and biomedical diagnosis. Their method imprints encoded time-varying pump patterns onto the IR object image through sum-frequency generation, shifting IR radiation into the visible range for upconversion detection. Compressed sensing and deep learning algorithms then reconstruct images under sub-Nyquist sampling and photon-starving light.
arxiv-2605-31003: Che and colleagues improve credit assignment for e-commerce search relevance. Relevance needs reasoning over query, product, and facet matching, done as chain-of-thought. Outcome-only rewards treat the chain as one unit, so faulty steps cannot be told from correct ones. Process-reward methods treat steps independently, ignoring error propagation along them. Their Graph-GRPO builds a graph of steps, propagates outcome rewards over it for step credit, and tunes propagation with a controller. Tests on a platform show better classification and engagement.
arxiv-2605-31103: Amram, Letizia, and Kuusela review model-free signal discovery with machine learning, bridging theory and practice. Searches for new phenomena are model-based, tuned to chosen ideas, limiting coverage. New AI-based model-free strategies, started in high-energy physics, favor broad search over tailored studies, raising search potential where theory guidance is scarce. They review the framework behind classes of them, discuss pitfalls, and strategies for checks and reading. They aim for the document to serve as a reference for users and scholars keen on model-free search.
arxiv-2605-31503: Uselis, Koishigarina, and Oh ask how embedding models bind concepts. This is the skill of telling which colour belongs to which shape in a multi-object scene. Vision-language models like CLIP spot single concepts, yet fail to show which concepts form which object. The team finds scene embeddings split additively into object parts, so single-modality probes can recover object facts. But the binding rule CLIP learns is high-complexity, which likely blocks a shared rule that generalizes to unseen mixes.
arxiv-2606-00003:
Sorokoletova, Giarrusso, Suriani, and Nardi ask whether a language model can regain its safety alignment after being corrupted, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Alignment training teaches models to refuse harmful outputs, but jailbreaking attacks can break that behavior in chat. Most research responds with stronger training or output filters. This paper instead studies the model's intrinsic ability to self-recover, treating safety as a trajectory that unfolds across turns of talk.

The authors propose a method for modeling those safety trajectories and detecting recovery trends within them. They apply it to adversarial multi-turn dialogues built around jailbreaking scenarios. Their early analysis also examines how the choice of content moderation model used for scoring changes the conclusions, since different scorers judge safety differently. A data visualizer accompanies the work. This reframes alignment from a fixed training property into a dynamic pattern that can be monitored and supported during deployment.
arxiv-2606-00103:
Fan and co-authors evaluate reasoning as an interactive process rather than a one-shot answer, in this 2026 arXiv benchmark paper. Real reasoning means seeking missing information, updating beliefs, and choosing when evidence suffices. Their framework gives models only the rules of a hidden environment; models must issue targeted queries, merge observations across turns, and choose when to submit an answer. The benchmark contains 470 executable games across five difficulty levels, and also tests robustness to context changes and metacognition, meaning awareness of one's own reasoning.

A set of models showed differences in success rate and interaction efficiency, making it a discriminator. Context changes caused moderate, steady declines in performance. Much larger drops appeared on counterfactual revision and necessity judgment, tasks asking models to reconsider conclusions or judge whether information was needed. The authors argue benchmarks conflate missing knowledge with faulty thinking, while interactive evaluation separates the two failure sources.

arxiv-2606-04503:
Zhu and colleagues tackle a chicken-and-egg problem in training reasoning models: the best training examples are worth paying to label, but nobody knows which ones before labeling, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards needs annotated data, and picking a small golden subset normally requires a labeled pool already. Their 'pick in the dark' setup instead selects unlabeled samples that most deserve annotation, guided by a well-calibrated estimate of the model's own uncertainty.

Their framework, PivotTrace, traces metacognitive pivots, moments inside a reasoning trace where attention patterns signal the model shifting strategy. Pivot density turns those moments into an uncertainty score, and a three-way triage routes data for annotation and training. Empirically, PivotTrace surpassed a fully supervised reasoning model using only 29.3 percent annotated samples, and converged 2.75 times faster.
arxiv-2606-04603:
Jeunen proposes a retrieval method for recommender systems that takes embedding uncertainty seriously, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard candidate generation indexes a single point-estimate embedding per item. It queries the index with the user's embedding. But embeddings are learned from sparse interactions, so they are noisy. The pipeline ends up biased toward popular head items with well-estimated embeddings. It starves the long tail of niche content.

It builds the index on that augmented set. At query time it samples a user embedding. It changes neither model architecture nor index infrastructure. Analytically, dinosaur reduces to standard retrieval as uncertainty vanishes. Higher variance provably expands where uncertain items can be retrieved. Experiments align with the theory. They show large coverage gains with only small losses in offline recall. That trade favors diverse catalogs.
arxiv-2606-04903:
Sterling presents an agent architecture whose correctness is proved rather than hoped for, in a 2026 arXiv computer science paper. LLM agents acting in nontrivial domains need linear auditability: every decision reconstructible. His architecture, Agentic Redux, uses the typed lambda calculus to prove that executions on appropriate domains are semantically guaranteed correct. Two production-grade domains demonstrate it, healthcare billing compliance and security vulnerability disclosure.

Sterling also introduces Ontology-First Agent Design, a methodology in which a human expert first ontologizes the problem domain, and only then assigns a language model to derive roles. The order is the point: the domain's structure is fixed by accountable humans in a formal ontology, and the model's creativity is confined to roles inside it. The approach targets regulated work where a plausible answer is not enough.
arxiv-2606-05003:
He Liu and colleagues introduce PhysDox in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark that tests whether language models can audit biomedical sensing protocols for physical feasibility. Models increasingly help design experiments, yet a fluent protocol may still be impossible to run in the real world. PhysDox holds a 683-sample expert-checked Gold set and a 5,000-sample Silver set spanning six sensing domains.

The task runs in two stages: first label each protocol as valid, minor, or fatal, then diagnose the exact constraint a fatal case breaks. Across six models and four inference strategies, the best first-stage score reached only 53.0 on the macro-F1 measure, and strong diagnosis with oracle help collapsed in end-to-end runs because errors cascaded. Models also showed scaffold bias, mistaking procedural completeness for physical validity, and missed implicit constraints about twice as often as explicit hardware violations.
arxiv-2606-05103:
Karan Gandhi and colleagues present RuBR in this 2026 arXiv paper, a learning approach for spotting genuine astronomical transients in data from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Roman, set to launch as early as September 2026, will image wide fields in infrared and could discover millions of transients and variable objects. The RAPID alert pipeline must separate real events from bogus detections from day one. No real Roman data exist yet, which makes building that filter hard.

The team trained three models on simulated transients. One used combined locally injected and OpenUniverse2024 events. One trained on local injections and tested on OpenUniverse2024. One mixed in a fraction of OpenUniverse2024 data in adaptation mode. The work lays out a strategy for adapting the combined model to real observations during the early mission, when no ground-truth labels will be available. Experiments show the approach is effective for real-bogus classification.
arxiv-2606-05203:
Nikita Larin and Daniel Seipt bring time-frequency analysis to nonlinear Compton scattering in this 2026 arXiv paper. When charged particles collide with an intense laser pulse, the emitted radiation shows harmonics, broadening from the phase-dependent ponderomotive redshift, and fine sub-harmonic structures. These spectral features accumulate over the whole interaction, so they are nonlocal in time and hard to assign to moments within the pulse.

Joint distributions from time-frequency analysis can track energy and time jointly, and the authors show how to construct one inside strong-field quantum electrodynamics. They build a non-negative distribution, which allows a clean probabilistic reading that many quasiprobability tools lack. After studying the distribution itself, they apply it to nonlinear Compton scattering in complex laser pulse setups with carrier-envelope phase effects and variable polarization. The joint view can disentangle when spectral features are emitted during the interaction.
arxiv-2606-05303:
Aritra Banerjee, Arpan Bhattacharyya, Rudranil Basu, and Sayan Das probe flat band systems with Krylov complexity in this 2026 arXiv paper. Written in terms of their localized states, flat bands turn out to be invariant under supertranslation symmetries, the hallmark of Carrollian physics, where light cones collapse and motion freezes. That symmetry makes flat bands a place to test how quantum states spread after a sudden change.

The authors study quenches driven by perturbations that break the Carroll symmetry, measuring the response with Krylov complexity, which counts how far a state wanders through its Krylov basis. Specializing to fermionic ladder Hamiltonians with all bands flat, they follow complexity across critical lines. Its growth resolves how resilient a Carrollian sector is against delocalizing perturbations, phase by phase. A continuum study, a Carroll scalar field theory with a gradient deformation, shows growth with ultraviolet sensitivity, an instance of UV and IR mixing.
arxiv-2606-05403:
Rohan Pradhan and Steve Goley expose a blind spot in how language models weigh sources, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models act as evidence synthesizers for decisions, but whether they judge the quality of what they read, or aggregate by surface presentation, was unclear. The authors show the capability exists: models detect fabricated statistics at rates from 0.76 up to 1.00 for methodology checks.

Models produced similar numeric estimates whether the underlying statistics were fabricated or valid. Source influence is governed by a methodology-register gate: a sensitivity to how analytical a text sounds, not to whether its numbers are valid. The dissociation replicated across five models from three families and three domains. Analyses converged on the same account, with register representations used while numeric-validity signals were suppressed to chance. Even an oracle checklist prompt produced blanket skepticism rather than discernment.
arxiv-2606-05803:
Sayan Paul and Pati find a new lever for blocking heat flow in a crystal in a 2026 arXiv paper. Slow heat conduction is prized in thermoelectrics. Known tricks exploit near-misses between sound-like and light-like vibration branches. The team studies near-misses among the light-like, optical branches, long dismissed as minor carriers. Their test crystal is unusual: optical phonons carry most of its heat.

In the pure crystal, optical branches carry about sixty-three percent of heat flow. Swapping half the indium for gallium changes branch symmetries so branches can couple. Gaps open at the crossings, and optical phonon speeds drop hard. The optical share of conduction fell to about forty-four percent. Total conductivity at room temperature dropped from zero point five seven to zero point four eight watts per meter-kelvin. Symmetry-aware substitution, the authors argue, is a design tool for materials.
arxiv-2606-06103:
Tariq Khan and colleagues insist medical image segmentation should start from dataset demands, not the architecture zoo in a 2026 arXiv paper in Medical Image Analysis. What a dataset requires depends on occupancy, shape, boundary fuzziness, annotation quality, and clinical risk. The MS-DKC framework writes those requirements into a knowledge card. Descriptors for acquisition, morphology, supervision, context, and deployment risk map onto failure modes and design priors.

Three datasets stress different regimes. Retinal vessels in DRIVE are sparse and branching; skin lesions in ISIC vary; ACDC hearts need multi-class outputs. Card-guided compact models scored Dice values near zero point eight one on vessels with tens of thousands of parameters. On skin lesions the card's risk-aligned selection reached a higher Dice. Plausible add-ons that worsened the risk profile were rejected on evidence, not fashion. Traceable design, the authors argue, beats leaderboard-chasing in clinical imaging.
arxiv-2606-06303:
Hongkun Dou and co-authors steer discrete diffusion models without retraining them in this 2026 arXiv paper. Discrete diffusion generates sequences, such as DNA or protein chains, by gradually cleaning up noise token by token. Users often want the output to score well on some reward, like binding strength. Gradient based guidance is the natural tool, but in discrete spaces those gradients are unstable and costly.

Their framework, GILC, reuses the pretrained denoising network as a stand in for the guidance signal. Instead of differentiating through the discrete process, it directly corrects the model's predicted clean logits, the scores behind each token choice. A Jacobian free design keeps the correction stable. The method even accepts rewards that have no gradient at all. Across DNA, protein sequence, and molecule generation tasks, GILC reached state of the art results with no added training, often beating fine tuned approaches outright.
arxiv-2606-06403:
Sanchita Sharma separates look alike spaces with a finer spectral probe in this 2026 arXiv paper on geometry. Lens spaces are three dimensional shapes made by gluing a ball's boundary with a twist, classic test cases in spectral geometry. The eta invariant summarizes asymmetries in a space's vibration spectrum, but assigns the same value to certain lens space pairs. Sharma keeps each mode's full character data instead of only that number.

For a family of lens space pairs indexed by odd numbers at least five, she finds a clean separation. The ordinary eta values agree, and even the first derivative of the refined invariant vanishes by symmetry. The second derivative does not: for the pair built from twenty five, it equals minus six thousand eighty after normalization. So the refined invariant detects a difference the standard one provably cannot. The computation runs through explicit Fourier residues.
arxiv-2606-06603:
Umar Sohail Qureshi and co-authors undo detector smearing without bins or second chances in this 2026 arXiv paper on particle physics. Unfolding converts measured detector level distributions back to true particle level ones. It is a two level problem: constraints live at the detector, the target at the particle level, joined by a random detector response. When the two barely overlap, training destabilizes. Older methods falter or need repeated iterations.

Their Reweighting Adversarial Network learns a particle level reweighting function. A Wasserstein critic steers it, judging only detector level output. The method needs neither overlapping support nor multiple training rounds. In Gaussian simulations and jet substructure studies, including cases with vanishing overlap, it recovered the true distributions. It beat state of the art approaches like OmniFold in accuracy, at lower cost.
arxiv-2606-06703:
Two trusted solar observatories disagree about how plasma circulates inside the Sun, and nobody fully knows why. Zhao and co-authors dig into that mismatch in this 2026 arXiv paper. They compare Dopplergrams, maps of surface motion, from the HMI instrument in space and the ground based GONG network, processed in the same way for both.

The team found a lasting patch of phase anomalies, timing offsets in the Sun's sound waves, in the northwest of the solar disk, and it grew stronger from 2010 through 2024. Travel times for sound crossing north to south also differed between the east and west sides of the disk in both data sets, where they should have agreed. The authors conclude that both instruments carry built in artifacts, and that these flaws shift over time, which makes correcting them genuinely hard.
arxiv-2606-06803:
Inside an electron storage ring, every bump and cavity leaves an echo that can shake the beams behind it. Yao and co-authors present a faster way to measure those echoes in this 2026 arXiv paper, aimed at the HALF storage ring in Hefei, China. The echoes, called long range wake potentials, carry the fingerprints of trapped modes, resonances stuck inside ring components that can drive beam instabilities.

Their method fits a model of several resonators to the wake signal using particle swarm optimization, a search technique where many candidate solutions swarm toward the best fit together. On a test cavity, the extracted values matched both a commercial solver and an older evolution based method, at much lower computing cost. The team then applied it to three real HALF components, showing the method handles the messy, many mode shapes of practical accelerator hardware.
arxiv-2606-06903:
Most human animation systems first extract a skeleton from the driving video, and skeletons make mistakes. Yuan Zeng and co-authors cut out that middleman in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their DirectAnimator learns straight from raw driving videos. A static reference photo supplies the person to animate.

Instead of a skeleton, the system builds a driving cue triplet. The triplet carries pose, face, and location cues together. A fusion block blends those cues during the denoising process. Training across different identities is unstable, so they add a Same2X strategy. It aligns features from cross identity pairs with those from same identity pairs. Experiments show top visual quality and identity preservation. The system stayed robust under occlusion and complex bending poses. It also used fewer computing resources than rivals. Skeleton errors like flipped fronts and missing limbs disappear by design.
arxiv-2606-07303:
Raynal and co-authors propose a theory of how learning systems outgrow their own representations in this 2026 arXiv paper. They call the framework the Bootstrap Theory of Representational Emergence. Its central signal is explanatory insufficiency, the point where a representation still fits observations but can no longer explain their organization. Rather than treating that failure as mere error, the theory treats it as the trigger for building a new representation.

The proposed cycle runs through five stages, from stabilized observation to anomaly detection, recognition of insufficiency, emergence, and provisional restabilization. Each new representation then generates fresh observations that may expose new limits. The authors apply the lens to representation learning in AI, latent spaces, foundation models, and world models, plus digital twins and adaptive biological systems. Their design suggestion is concrete: future AI systems should monitor when their internal representations reach explanatory limits and refine themselves accordingly.
arxiv-2606-07703:
Hongxing Wang and co-authors ask how much dense attention a long-context language model really needs, in this 2026 arXiv technical report. During prefill, the first pass over a long prompt, attention layers score the whole history, which is costly. Hybrid models mix in cheaper sparse layers, but the remaining full layers still dominate the bill.

The team builds an oracle, an idealised selector that first computes full attention, then keeps only the top-scoring tokens under a fixed budget. This reference separates what a sparse budget could ever achieve from mistakes made by practical selectors. On retrieval-heavy tests with Qwen models, oracle rows stayed within one point of dense scores, even across contexts from four thousand to one hundred thousand tokens. A small indexer trained to imitate the oracle preserved quality closely at sixteen and thirty-two thousand tokens, showing the budget itself is rarely the problem.
arxiv-2606-08003:
Dong-Hui Yu and Yong Cai ask whether eternal inflation breaks a quantum energy bound, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The smeared null energy condition limits how much negative energy can accumulate along a light ray, averaged over a region. Eternal inflation seems to threaten it: rare random upward fluctuations of the inflaton field locally raise the expansion rate, apparently piling up the wrong kind of energy.

Working with a single-field model and the Fokker-Planck equation, the authors show the ensemble drift of the expansion rate is parametrically small. It is bounded by slow-roll parameters and semiclassical suppression. A single-trajectory analysis adds a timescale hierarchy. Gravitational backreaction destroys the assumed background long before any trajectory can approach the bound. Their conclusion: standard stochastic diffusion does not inherently violate the smeared null energy condition, within the semiclassical slow-roll regime.
arxiv-2606-08403:
Sinha and Chavan demonstrate a way to smuggle hidden instructions past text-based safety filters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Prompt-injection defenses assume the malicious signal is visible in some inspected text view. The authors study an indirect injection failure mode where that assumption breaks. A payload in plain English is caught by a detector. Yet the same payload slips through when it is carried as float parameters, arrays of decimal numbers, and rebuilt later as fragmented telemetry.

Across fourteen thousand attacked trials on three commercial model interfaces from different providers, the float-array carrier preserved a leakage attack success rate above ninety percent in the main experiments reported here. This held even under a strong dual-layer text-classifier defense. The pattern also replicated against a fine-tuned detector of a different design. The lesson is that defenses inspecting only text views have a structural blind spot.
arxiv-2606-08503:
Leisegang, Meyer, and Rudolph combine two logical frameworks for reasoning from multiple viewpoints, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standpoint logic expresses knowledge from several possibly contradicting viewpoints. Statements are sharpened or loosened by whose perspective is adopted. Defeasible reasoning captures beliefs that hold by default but can be withdrawn when exceptions appear. The authors integrate the two, so standpoints can hold defeasible beliefs.

The paper supplies a foundational representation result for the semantics of these logics. Several entailment relations are then lifted from the propositional case to the standpoint one, including preferential entailment and ranking-based closures. The result is a principled logic for knowledge bases where agents hold different default beliefs. The aim is a logic that fits how groups of agents really hold and revise their views over time.
arxiv-2606-08903:
Kuo, Gallego, and Jorm warn that synthetic patient records can look convincing on paper while failing clinical tests, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hospitals and researchers generate artificial electronic medical records to share data without exposing real patients. Judging usually rewards matching overall distributions and predictive accuracy. The authors instead built a framework grounded in epidemiology, checking whether the data describe patients faithfully, predict outcomes well, and keep the causal structure intact.

They tested four families of generators, based on GANs, variational autoencoders, diffusion, and masked modelling, on PRIME-CVD, a 50,000-person cohort with known true structure. Every model matched the overall shape of the data well. None preserved subgroup structure, effect estimates, and dependency structure at once. Some models with a strong surface match showed unreliable risk scores and warped links between variables, which would corrupt later analysis. Current practice can badly overestimate the data's quality.
arxiv-2606-09003:
Tang models a tension in modern crypto: trading concentrates on centralized exchanges while the blockchains traded promise decentralization, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In proof-of-stake systems, token holders lock up coins as validators securing the chain. Tang builds a continuous-time mean field model: many participants act as both validators and traders on a centralized market whose trades move prices. The question is how exchange activity feeds back into staking, token allocation, and decentralization.

Under assumptions, Tang proves the system is well-posed and derives a semi-explicit formula for equilibrium trading. The numerical results cut against the usual fear. Centralized trading may raise staking participation and spread validation, because market incentives reward staking. Transaction costs and token supply mechanisms shift the equilibrium staking ratio and its concentration. The study shows how market microstructure and centralized liquidity can influence independent decentralized protocols.
arxiv-2606-09203:
Harun Teper and colleagues make robot software run the same way every time, by routing a popular middleware through a deterministic coordination language, in this 2026 arXiv paper. ROS 2, the standard middleware for robots, structures computation as callbacks over a publish-subscribe network. Callback order is nondeterministic even on one machine; distributed setups add interleaving and latency, making safety analysis nearly impossible.

Their framework runs an unmodified ROS 2 app under Lingua Franca, a coordination language built on logical time, so the same input yields the same order. They characterize which ROS 2 features admit deterministic execution under logical time, then extract app structure and generate the program. Logical-time delays, federated runs, and fault handling then apply, without changing robot code. On a synthetic example and the Autoware reference system, the default setup varied callback order and latencies across runs. The converted system produced one fixed order and stable latencies.
arxiv-2606-09303:
Xinyan Gao and colleagues reframe image segmentation as a two-round job: first find candidate regions, then reason about which one the query really means, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reasoning segmentation asks a model to cut out what a complex description points to, and multimodal models struggle to pass reasoning into mask generators. Their framework, Rea2Seg, mines candidate masks from a segmentation model's attention maps. A second pass scores each candidate against the question.

The highest-scoring mask wins, turning segmentation into candidate discovery plus discriminative selection. Existing benchmarks lean on commonsense questions that barely test joint seeing and reasoning. So the authors built ReasonSeg-SGDR, probing perception, grounding, spatial and geometric reasoning, and multi-step inference with fine-grained masks. They also collected training data teaching models to score masks by reasoning. Results on their benchmark and ReasonSeg favor the unified generate-then-select design.
arxiv-2606-09603:
Kuanlin Chen and Cheng-En Ou build a local system that drafts special education plans from parent-teacher talks in Traditional Chinese in this 2026 arXiv paper. Each plan, called an IEP, takes teachers hours to write by hand. English tools exist, but Chinese data is scarce and privacy law is strict. Sending such files to cloud services is risky.

Their pipeline grows a training set from just twenty-five expert-scored seed transcripts. Style traits from the seeds guide a model to make more samples, and five hundred sixty-seven passed checks. That set fine-tuned a small open model that runs fully offline. A surprise came at the last step. Forcing a strict output schema slowed the system and hurt reliability. Without it, the model hit a perfect schema pass rate and beat big cloud models on the held-out test.
arxiv-2606-09803: Shared on the arXiv preprint server in 2026, this manuscript describes fresh findings. The subject named up front is Echo-Memory: A Controlled Study of Memory in Action World Models. The study operates inside artificial intelligence (the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data). The paper documents what the researchers found when they looked closely.
arxiv-2606-10003:
Wildeboer and colleagues generalize a family of exactly solvable quantum models into shapes once thought intractable, in a 2026 arXiv paper on condensed matter theory. Quantum dimer models place paired atoms on lattice bonds and can realize a topological phase, a state whose properties depend on global patterns rather than local details. Classic solvable versions live on trivalent lattices, where three bonds meet at each site, and connect to Ising gauge theories. The new work moves to tetravalent parent lattices.

The resulting models live on crossed-medial lattices with crossed plaquettes, so their transition graphs contain intersecting loops, a non-planar structure against the usual templates. On the checkerboard lattice, their simplest model maps exactly onto the toric code, linking it directly to Anderson's resonating valence bond picture. They also extend Kasteleyn methods to these non-planar graphs, keeping correlation functions efficiently computable.
arxiv-2606-10503:
Özdemir studies peaks in permutations in this 2026 arXiv paper in combinatorics, the mathematics of counting and arranging. A peak is a position where a permutation rises then falls, a hilltop in the sequence. The paper tracks two counts together: the peaks of a random permutation and the peaks of its inverse, which reverses the roles of positions and values. Using enriched P-partitions, a counting tool from algebraic combinatorics, Özdemir derives a generating function for their joint distribution, a two-variable peak polynomial.

The coefficients of that polynomial satisfy a second-order recurrence, and a martingale formulation of the recurrence yields a bivariate central limit theorem. For long permutations both counts behave like bell curves, and the two statistics become asymptotically independent: knowing one says nothing about the other in the limit. Özdemir also gives an exact closed form for their covariance, which shrinks like one over n.
arxiv-2606-10703:
Engmann, Adriano, and Giese audit a common inference in model interpretability in this 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Mixture-of-experts models route each token to specialist subnetworks, and pruning methods pick experts to delete using routing statistics: utilisation rates, activation norms, routing weights. The assumption: population-level summaries predict what an intervention would do. The authors test it, ablating experts token by token across three high-redundancy architectures and comparing measured causal importance against every observational metric.

The result is a null. Across 60 metric-layer combinations, effect sizes stay below 0.23 in Cohen's d, and no metric reliably predicts causal importance. A per-token control with identical sample size recovers a real signal at OLMoE's final layer, ruling out low statistical power. Pruning methods still work, the authors argue, because early layers are so redundant that any criterion succeeds. It is an explicit counterexample to reading observation as intervention.
arxiv-2606-11203:
Alpay and Kilictas reframe constrained text generation as a rare-event problem in a 2026 arXiv paper. Data-to-text systems must realize several required anchors, concepts or values from the input, inside one fluent output. Standard decoding favors fluent continuations and gives little probability to continuations satisfying every anchor jointly. Hard-constrained decoders can turn unstable.

LatticeBridge compiles each input instance into surface automata, formal checkers of the constraints, and decodes with twisted sequential Monte Carlo. Partial outputs are sampled, weighted, and resampled, with multilevel splitting and a proposal term drawn from the source's own phrases. Constraints compile per instance, with no hand-built lexical classes. On 2,610 attainable validation tasks spanning CommonGen, E2E NLG, and WikiBio, the particle decoder beat greedy, beam-filtered, and best-of-k baselines on exact anchor satisfaction and mean anchor coverage. The benchmark also reports source coverage, intrusion diagnostics, overlap, and runtime.
arxiv-2606-11303:
Kattel, Tang, and Andrei study exact dynamics across a phase transition in a 2026 paper. Their one-dimensional system can sit in a charge-density-wave phase, CDW, or a symmetry-protected topological phase, SPT. Starting from a CDW state, they study sudden quenches and slow ramps into the SPT regime, asking what happens to each order.

CDW order melts under both protocols, but topological order behaves differently. After a sudden quench, long-range SPT order does not emerge, because the post-quench state holds a finite density of excitations above the ground state. Slow ramps let the system follow the ground state away from the critical region, building SPT order with deviations set by Kibble-Zurek defect production. A unitary mapping to a quadratic fermionic Hamiltonian makes the dynamics solvable. They compute the Loschmidt echo, correlations, and string correlator; the Loschmidt rate function shows cusps signaling dynamical quantum phase transitions.
arxiv-2606-11603:
Gaohang Yu, Yihao Pan, Ailun Jian and Xiaohao Cai speed up a core data compression method in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tensor is a multi-way array of numbers, and tensor train decomposition rewrites a huge tensor as a chain of small three-way pieces. The bottleneck is repeated singular value decomposition, a standard but expensive matrix factorisation, on very large matrices.

Their algorithm, TT-subSKETCH, replaces those heavy steps with sketching, which multiplies the data by random test matrices to capture its essential shape in far fewer numbers. Sketching from both sides, plus subspace iteration to sharpen accuracy, produces the approximation in a single pass over the data. The authors prove error bounds and analyse robustness, meaning performance should not collapse on awkward inputs. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better accuracy and robustness than rival randomised methods, and much lower running time than deterministic ones.
arxiv-2606-11903: ArXiv received this research paper in 2026; it carries new results. The title assigns it the subject of Snapping Matters: Context-Aware Onset Refinement for Automatic Music Transcription. Expect science and technology throughout: careful study of how the natural and built world works. Its pages carry fresh research aimed at the field's practitioners.
arxiv-2606-12003:
Paula Ontalvilla, Gorka Azkune and Aitor Ormazabal extend a popular reasoning trick to open-ended tasks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-consistency samples several answers from a language model and picks the most consistent one. It traditionally needs exact matches, so it fails for code or summaries where no two outputs are identical. Their hypothesis is geometric: semantically compatible generations cluster in nearby regions of the model's inner space.

Their method, Embedding-Based Agreement, clusters sampled generations in embedding space and selects from the dominant cluster, with no training. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation and summarisation it beats random selection. Its scaling with more samples is more stable than selection by model evaluation. The signal survives across model families and embedding choices, even using the model's own hidden states. Generations near the centre of the sampled cloud tend to be reliable, while peripheral ones are less accurate.
arxiv-2606-12103:
Hendrik Reiter and five colleagues move factory data analysis to where the data is born in this 2026 arXiv paper. Process mining extracts workflows and checks conformance from event logs, guiding autonomous control in smart factories. Real-time decisions, though, cannot wait for a distant cloud, so the authors study process mining on edge devices near the machines.

They first propose a formalism describing both the datasets and the computing topology. Edge deployment brings specific implications: event data and algorithms are inherently distributed, and the topology itself must enter the formal framework. From this they derive quality attributes tailored to the setting, including processing time, resource use, load capacity and scalability. A case study implements real-time conformance checking at the edge, where each process step is verified against its model. The results demonstrate feasibility and concrete benefits: lower latency, less bandwidth, and privacy-aware handling.
arxiv-2606-12303:
Xian and co-authors give image fusion a small set of global dials alongside its usual detail map, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal fusion merges images from different sensors, like infrared and visible light, into one picture keeping both heat targets and fine texture. Standard methods share a two-dimensional feature grid, great for local structure but clumsy for whole-image traits like lighting and tone. The authors add a compact one-dimensional token list from a frozen pretrained tokenizer to carry those global appearance factors.

Their Selective Token Editing updates or replaces only a few critical tokens. This steers global coherence without touching the fusion backbone or adding training losses. The two-dimensional pathway still restores local detail as before. On four standard benchmarks the method achieves the best overall performance. Improvements show up across many metrics, in both global coherence and local fidelity.
arxiv-2606-12503:
Chiara Semenzin and co-authors teach a neural network dolphin, from dolphins, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-supervised learning trains models on raw audio without labels, but bioacoustic models spread across many species. The team instead recorded five dolphins for over five years in a semi-natural marine setting, gathering one hundred eighty thousand whistles. Adapting the Wav2Vec architecture, they trained Dolph2Vec, a large species-specific model of dolphin sound.

Dolphins communicate through signature whistles, personal calls that work like names. On two benchmark tasks, telling signature whistles apart and detecting whistles in recordings, Dolph2Vec beats general baselines. More interesting than the scores, its units prove interpretable. The learned embeddings and codebook entries line up with whistle categories, and with sub-whistle pieces. A model trained this way doubles as a scientific instrument. Researchers can probe the structure to test hypotheses about how dolphin communication is organized.
arxiv-2606-12603:
He and co-authors teach delivery robots sidewalk manners, moving them from mimicry to alignment, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sidewalk navigation is long-horizon and social: robots must thread past pedestrians for miles with one camera. Imitation learning copies human driving but compounds errors and ignores social norms. Their FlowPilot policy navigates from a single monocular camera. Anchored flow matching, an action representation, is pretrained on robot-fleet data.

Flow matching captures the multimodal ways humans navigate crowds. The base policy then gets a human-in-the-loop preference tune-up, learning from a set of human interventions. In simulation, the base reaches a forty-two percent success rate and sixty-six percent route completion. The preference-tuned version cuts the intervention rate by forty percent and a near-intervention measure by about half. Social compliance and counterfactual reasoning, knowing what would have happened otherwise, both improve.
arxiv-2606-12703:
Sharma presents SMSR, a defence with a security certificate against memory poisoning in persistent AI agents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented agents keep a memory store across sessions, and an attacker who talks to the agent can plant memories that later steer its behaviour. The author calls this multi-session memory poisoning. Existing defences assume a fixed knowledge base or use filters that fake text can bypass.

SMSR has 2 components. The first signs every memory with a cryptographic tag at write time, so unsigned injections are rejected. The second randomly ablates, dropping random subsets of memories at query time, then aggregates verdicts by majority vote, bounding what even authenticated attackers can achieve. Across 15 enterprise scenarios, signing cuts attack success from 93 to 100 percent down to zero for unsigned attacks. In a production-scale store, the second component cuts authenticated attack success to 8.0 percent, while clean-query utility stays at 85 percent.
arxiv-2606-12803:
Ali and Cui tackle a convergence failure that strikes power system simulations right after switching events such as faults or breaker events, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Transient simulation solves switched differential-algebraic equations, mixing differential equations for machine dynamics with algebraic equations for network constraints. After a discontinuity, Newton-Raphson iterations can stagnate or diverge even when a valid post-event solution exists.

The authors give a geometric explanation of the failure, showing why step-size reduction and globalised Newton methods, which shrink a merit function, can stall at points that are not true solutions. They then build a re-initialisation scheme based on homotopy continuation, which tracks a solution along a deformed problem from a starting point to the post-event system. In simulations, the scheme recovers convergence in cases where direct post-event solution fails, giving a robust restart for transient stability studies.
arxiv-2606-12903:
Kang and colleagues build a benchmark and an interpretable pipeline for handling contradictory Chinese and English evidence in retrieval-augmented generation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, answers questions using fetched texts, but in multilingual settings the Chinese and English sources may support opposed answers.

Their benchmark, X-RAMDocs-ZHEN, contains 300 cases across 6 conditions, including monolingual support, bilingual agreement, reversed conflict directions, and conflict with extra noise. Their pipeline, X-MADAM-RAG, splits evidence handling into per-document candidate extraction, visible-evidence repair, grouping, and conflict-aware aggregation. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct it reaches 0.9667 strict accuracy and 0.9767 conflict-aware success, beating an evidence-cleaning baseline. However, a zero-call rule-only extractor scores a perfect 1.0000, showing template regularity in the benchmark. On a stress test that removes the templates, the rule-only extractor falls to 0.0000 and X-MADAM-RAG drops to 0.3000, below both baselines.
arxiv-2606-13003:
Jwalapuram and colleagues challenge the assumption that multi-agent systems beat single-agent systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The authors focus on automatically generated multi-agent systems, tested against a single-agent baseline: chain-of-thought with self-consistency.

Across reasoning data sets and tasks with multi-step workflows such as BrowseComp-Plus, automatically generated multi-agent systems underperform the single-agent baseline despite costing up to 10 times more. To split these failures from task-structure limits, the authors present a synthetic dataset built for multi-agent strengths, with task breakdown, context separation, and parallel-work scope. On that dataset, expert-architected multi-agent systems beat automatically generated ones in performance and cost-efficiency. Deconstructing these architectures reveals bloat. Automated design paradigms produce complexity that does not translate into functional utility. That is a misalignment with multi-agent principles, which benchmarks mask by ignoring the utility of the compute.
arxiv-2606-13103:
Xie and colleagues present a magnetic torsional pendulum, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In 1 undergraduate lab setup it unifies forced resonance, parametric resonance, and degenerate parametric amplification. A permanent magnet hangs by thin wires and is driven by magnetic fields from Helmholtz coils. With separate control of a direct driving field and a bias field, the same system shows plain forced swings, parametric drive, and phase-sensitive amplification, effects usually taught apart.

A tiny cordless gyroscope inside the pendulum bob reads spin speed, giving live dynamic data. The authors derive 1 equation of motion for all 3 regimes. Studies of all 3 effects match theory well. The data reproduce their characteristic features and also show nonlinear effects.
arxiv-2606-13203:
Parma and colleagues embed ISO 10218 safety compliance directly into robot control for human-robot collaboration using control barrier functions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The standard's Speed and Separation Monitoring approach limits robot speed to keep a protective distance from humans. But standard filters assume constant human velocity, which prevents accurate prediction of minimum separation and causes needless halts.

The proposed barrier function uses human acceleration data to forward-predict the minimum human-robot separation distance during a worst-case robotic stopping trajectory. This predictive constraint is built into a sequential quadratic programming framework in 2 ways. Method I is a barrier-constrained PD safety filter. Method II is a task-scaling controller that enforces a spatial tube constraint. Method II modulated execution speed and confined spatial deviations, with a 63 percent reduction in mean trajectory error compared with Method I while avoiding wild evasive manoeuvres.
arxiv-2606-13303:
Troeshestova, Ustyuzhanin, and Kastryulin introduce DuET in this 2026 arXiv paper, a training-free method for editing images with diffusion models. Diffusion editors follow a text instruction while conditioning on the source image at every denoising step. That conditioning can hold the result back when the requested scene differs from the input. DuET relaxes the conditioning, passing through a text-to-image phase before returning to edit mode. The detour lets the image move toward the target while keeping the benefits of editing.

No model weights change and the sampling cost stays the same. Across models and benchmarks, DuET improves how well results follow the instruction, how faithful their meaning is, and how natural they look. Some cases trade a modest loss of source preservation for those gains. The authors note this trade-off is predictable, so users can anticipate when stronger edits will loosen ties to the image.
arxiv-2606-13503:
Vilella-Cantos and colleagues improve place recognition for robots in vineyards in this 2026 arXiv paper. Place recognition means realising that a robot has returned to a visited location, a core ability for long-term localisation. Unstructured environments such as farmland are hard: rows of vines look alike, and seasons change appearances. LiDAR sensors help because they capture 3D structure and ignore lighting. The authors combine two LiDAR sensors early in the pipeline, fusing a dense near-range unit with a longer-range spinning one, so each compensates for the other's blind spots.

Their system adds a re-ranking stage at inference time, which re-examines candidate matches and promotes true positives. That stage is important in repetitive environments where many places look identical. Evaluation uses a vineyard dataset with heterogeneous LiDAR recordings. The approach targets robots that must localise reliably over months of operation.
arxiv-2606-13603:
Scalena and colleagues probe whether the reasoning steps of large models actually cause their answers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chain-of-thought reasoning, writing out intermediate steps, is the dominant way to scale inference. Yet how much each step causes the final answer is poorly understood. The authors estimate each step's importance by exiting the reasoning early and checking the answer. Reasoning typically crosses a commitment boundary: a sharp transition from tentative guesses to a stable, high-confidence answer, often within a single step.

That transition usually happens well before the reasoning block ends. The steps after it are epiphenomenal, leaving the final answer's probability unchanged. Attention probes show the answer-forming stage can be decoded from intermediate steps with high accuracy, even on unseen tasks. The authors exploit that signal to exit reasoning early. The implication is stark: much generated reasoning is decoration after the fact.
arxiv-2606-13703:
Van Ditmarsch traces the history of a logic puzzle in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Muddy Children puzzle concerns children who can see mud on others' foreheads but not their own, and who reason, round by round, about what everyone knows. It has been foundational for epistemic logic, the study of knowledge and ignorance, and for the theory of common knowledge. Who invented it first is unclear. Van Ditmarsch follows its origin through publications over the past two centuries, showing how the puzzle surfaced repeatedly in different guises.

The puzzle inspired numerous variations, including versions with numbers and coloured hats. The paper also presents a novel hats puzzle involving self-reference. The note is dedicated to the memory of Joe Halpern, who popularised the puzzle through influential publications. Written in a non-formal style, the history doubles as a gentle introduction to why epistemic logicians care about a children's riddle.
arxiv-2606-13803:
Wiedemann, Jacquier, and Gonon tackle a stubborn problem: forcing a neural network to obey shape rules, such as always rising or always curving upward. Such rules matter in finance and engineering. Yet penalty methods only push back where a rule is already broken, so training drifts back into breaking it. Their 2026 arXiv paper adds a helper network. Its outputs are valid by construction, and they serve as targets for the main network.

On dense test grids, the method records zero measured violations on every run. Penalty and primal-dual rivals still leave some violations behind. The authors then fit volatility surfaces. These map option prices across strikes and maturities. They must rule out arbitrage, meaning risk-free profit from inconsistent prices. Their method is the only one of three satisfying the no-arbitrage rules in every test setting. It also posts the lowest fitting error.
arxiv-2606-13903:
Sarkar proves a negative result about a popular proof technique in quantum information. Mutually unbiased bases are sets of measurement directions that reveal nothing about each other. At most d plus one can exist in dimension d. Sum-of-Squares turns existence questions into semidefinite programs a computer can check. His 2026 arXiv paper asks whether degree four can prove that bound in vector coordinates.

It cannot. For every dimension and proposed count, Sarkar builds a degree-four pseudoexpectation from independent random orthonormal bases. This fake average obeys all degree-four constraints, even past d plus one. So degree four here cannot rule out impossible cases. The failure depends on formulation, though. In projector coordinates, degree four recovers the bound. The encodings are thereby separated, answering a Randomstrasse101 open problem.
arxiv-2606-14203:
Valentini and Chiani design codes making computer buses flip fewer bits, saving energy per transfer. Each flip costs dynamic power; in network-on-chip designs interconnects can dissipate over fifty percent of total dynamic power, and non-volatile memories wear out with writes. Their 2026 arXiv paper works in the write-efficient memory (WEM) framework, whose limit ties code rate to the entropy of the average flip fraction. The classic data bus inversion scheme is optimal there only for one redundant bit.

For larger redundancy, data maps to the lowest-weight codewords available, then is XORed with the previous message. They develop a simulation-free analysis of flip savings, and propose two new schemes, RI and SI. Well-designed sub-optimal techniques perform closely to the optimal but complex solution, far more simply. In data centers, small per-transfer savings compound into large energy reductions, and fewer flips extend memory endurance.
arxiv-2606-14303:
Danielsson and colleagues propose that one scalar field secretly sets two of the Standard Model's least-known couplings, staking the idea on collider signatures. In the One Scalar Theory, a single real singlet scalar dynamically generates both the Higgs self-coupling and the top Yukawa coupling. All production and decay are locked to one fundamental scale. Their 2026 arXiv paper works out the phenomenology.

A kinematic threshold at twice the top mass partitions the signals: below it, di-Higgs resonances; above, di-top resonances. Recasting current ATLAS data already sets lower bounds on the scale at the TeV level. The High-Luminosity LHC will probe it up to about four TeV. The rigidity is the point. The scalar bypasses the usual WW and ZZ decays. Its diphoton and digluon decays run only through top quarks, fixing their ratio with no free parameters: a veto against generic portal theories.
arxiv-2606-14403:
Ji, Nazzaro, and Ezzat introduce a 2026 arXiv model for tracking the North Atlantic right whale, a critically endangered species. Acoustic recorders on autonomous underwater vehicles listen for whale calls along the United States East Coast. The data are hard to model because most listening spots hold no whales, detection is imperfect, and habitat ties are complex.

Their DeepZIB model, short for deep zero-inflated Bernoulli, jointly estimates where whales are truly present and how likely calls are to be detected there. Simulations show the model recovers true parameters and hidden presence patterns well. On real recordings it fits better than rivals and produces high-resolution maps of presence that change over space and time. Managers can use those maps to balance shipping, fishing, and offshore energy against whale safety.
arxiv-2606-15303:
Maamache analyzes the inverted Dirac oscillator in a 2026 mathematical physics paper. The Dirac oscillator is a relativistic cousin of the harmonic oscillator, exactly solvable and used. A different momentum swap produces its inverted cousin. That version's Hamiltonian is not Hermitian, its potential is unbounded below, and its spectrum spreads out. Its solutions are not square-integrable, which breaks the norming rules. Maamache shows the operator is pseudo-PT-symmetric, a weaker pattern that can still organize its behavior.

The paper builds a non-unitary map linking the inverted system to the standard one. Through that link, spectra and solutions transfer over. Solutions come out in terms of radial functions, spherical harmonics, and spinor components. The slow-motion limit exposes a spring term plus spin-orbit coupling. The construction gives a handle on a non-Hermitian system. It may guide studies of balance and complex spectra in models.
arxiv-2606-15603:
Barua and Desai test in 2026 how much large-scale polarization data steer conclusions about dark energy. The low-multipole EE modes pin down the optical depth to reionization, and removing them might ease several cosmological tensions. The pair refit three dark energy parameterizations, called CPL, JBP, and BA, with and without that data.

They combine microwave background data from Planck and ACT with baryon acoustic oscillation and supernova data. Excluding the low-multipole EE modes pushes the reionization depth and the primordial amplitude higher, by roughly one and a half sigma in the standard model and JBP. For all three parameterizations the dark energy equation of state moves toward the quintessence regime, and in JBP it sits entirely there at one sigma. Hubble constant constraints stay robust throughout. Model comparison favours CPL and BA under most criteria, so the preference does not hinge on the disputed data.
arxiv-2606-15803:
Talalov studies a thin circular quantum vortex filament inside an infinite cylindrical pipe in 2026, where the surrounding fluid flows at a steady velocity. Using his earlier quantisation technique for closed vortex filaments, he computes the ring's energy spectrum as a function of total momentum. The spectrum turns out to depend strongly on the background flow speed.

That dependence produces exotic states: vortex rings whose effective mass is negative, or extremely large. Coupled vortex pairs can also appear with finite total mass, one partner positive, the other negative, at unrestricted magnitudes. Whether such pairs arise is decided by comparing a quantum analogue of the Reynolds number with its critical value for single-vortex flow. He proposes this as a mechanism for the onset of quantum turbulence, and a route to its critical Reynolds number. Negative-mass vortices, exotic on paper, may be the seeds of turbulent tangles in quantum fluids.
arxiv-2606-16303:
Agboola and co-authors build a neural controller in 2026 that keeps the optimality structure of classic control theory while running fast enough for real time. Model predictive control solves an optimization at every step, which is accurate but slow. Their adjoint-based neural regulator instead learns a co-state policy: the adjoint variables that, through Pontryagin's Minimum Principle, encode what an optimal controller should do. Safety is not left to the network.

At runtime, a convex projection enforces actuator limits and safety constraints written as control barrier functions. Tests use a unicycle robot moving through an unknown environment under real-time safety demands. The regulator matches model predictive control performance at more than one hundred times lower computational cost, per the report. Its performance also stays near-invariant on scenarios outside training, beating reinforcement learning baselines there.
arxiv-2606-16603:
Jin leads a 2026 team study of data-analytic agents, computer programs that use large language models to answer questions from data. Their outputs are rarely verifiable, because computation and judgment are mixed in one stream of text. A reader cannot easily check a number or trace how a claim was reached.

The proposed framework, VeriGraph, makes an agent build an explicit evidence graph while it works. Nodes in the graph link raw data, program variables, computed results and written claims. Three expansion steps handle computation, grounding in sources, and logical derivation. Training rewards correct answers, sound computation and coherent derivation together. On four benchmarks the eight-billion-parameter version scores highest overall among the systems tested. Its claims also reach a strong grounding rate under claim-level evidence checks, showing that auditable agent output is practical.
