arxiv-2606-16803:
Austin, Popović and Grima show that cell division can flip cell fate in a 2026 mathematical biology paper. Gene networks decide cell identity through multistable dynamics, where several stable states compete. The genetic toggle switch, two genes each repressing the other, is the classic toy model of such a choice.

Most analyses ignore the fact that cells divide, splitting their contents between daughters. The authors derive analytic separatrices, the boundary surfaces between fates, for a simplified Boolean toggle switch with and without division. Division can send two trajectories starting from identical states to opposite stable outcomes. They define a region of disagreement where predictions made without division are simply wrong. The result matters beyond the toy model: fate boundaries in real regulatory networks may be drawn incorrectly whenever division is treated as a detail. It also suggests division itself can act as a decision-making mechanism in development.
arxiv-2606-17003:
Zou and colleagues compute the hadronic tensor with quantum algorithms in a 2026 nuclear physics paper. The hadronic tensor packs everything a scattering experiment can learn about a hadron's interior, encoding the non-perturbative structure of quantum chromodynamics. Classical lattice methods struggle with the real-time correlations that define it.

The team works in simplified one-space-dimensional gauge theories with two kinds of gauge group, evaluating real-time current-current correlation functions directly. Quantum algorithms, run here on classical hardware as a proof of principle, produce the tensor, from which hadron form factors for both meson and baryon states are extracted. The extracted factors agree strongly with direct calculation and with exact diagonalization of the same systems. The validation matters: the method targets the real-time regime where classical lattice techniques falter. The work steps toward quantum computation of quantities experiments measure but theory struggles to reach.
arxiv-2606-17303:
Yu presents a 2026 arXiv paper on a famous open problem: whether the sum of the constants e and pi is irrational. Each constant alone is known to be transcendental, yet that does not rule out their sum being a simple fraction. Yu studies the question through finite irrationality certificates, asking what kinds of proof mechanisms could ever settle it and mapping where low-complexity attempts must fail for structural reasons.

One part gives exact equivalences between the sum being rational and tail patterns in factorial expansions of the number. Those criteria show what rationality would force, but also why tail behaviour alone is no finite obstruction. A second part audits Apéry-style constructions, from Padé approximation to lattice searches, using a set of no-go filters. Within the tested families, no non-circular mechanism survives, and the best signals prove to be continued-fraction shadows.
arxiv-2606-17703:
Zhou and Zhang present a KDD 2026 conference paper on strengthening a network by adding a few links chosen to shrink its total biharmonic distance. That distance is a connectivity measure summed over all node pairs. Biharmonic distance refines the classic resistance distance, capturing finer local and global structure for tasks like spotting critical edges. The authors ask which handful of new edges lowers that total most. It is a clean question with a hard core, since naive greedy search over candidate edges costs cubic time.

They first show the objective is monotone but lacks the supermodularity that would make greedy provably near-optimal. Algorithms follow anyway: greedy selection sped up by projection methods, fast Laplacian solvers, and convex hull tricks until the cost falls to nearly linear time with error guarantees. Experiments on real data sets confirm the speed-ups keep the quality. Link recommendation gains a principled, scalable tool.
arxiv-2606-17803:
Dorovatas and colleagues ask in a 2026 machine learning paper whether language models can keep learning from their own reasoning as they work. Models normally stay stateless, throwing away the reasoning traces they produce while solving problems. The authors test ways to turn that fleeting computation into lasting, reusable knowledge without outside supervision or future data.

They find that reusing raw traces through in-context learning fails to generalize, since single traces lack the abstraction needed for transfer. Lightweight per-instance training, rewarded by self-generated signals such as majority voting, does far better and can beat full offline training. Building on that, their method distills problem-solving experience into compact latent memories that capture reasoning structure, offering a path to models that improve continually from use.
arxiv-2606-18003:
Domini and colleagues tackle learning on fleets of moving devices whose data can never be gathered in one place, in a 2026 paper. Sensors on vehicles, drones, and phones see privacy-sensitive data, and nearby devices observe similar conditions while far ones see different worlds. Worse, movement shifts what each device sees over time, so yesterday's model quietly goes stale.

Their system, C²FL, lets devices self-organize into learning groups by spatial clustering, mirroring the geography they move through. Federated updates merge knowledge inside each cluster without raw data leaving the device. Experience replay fights the forgetting that hits when a node crosses into a new region, and a dwell-time-aware averaging step leans harder on the local consensus the longer a node stays. Experiments show standard clustered learning forgets badly under this drift, while their design retains it.
arxiv-2606-18103:
Kim-Baumann and Hiltmann rebuild retrieval-augmented generation around how historians actually work, in a 2026 paper. Standard RAG systems are tuned for factual question answering. Historical work runs on different values: care with sources, even coverage of a period, and arguments a reader can contest. Those values clash with defaults that grab whichever text chunks score highest on similarity.

Their framework, HistoRAG, turns method into design. Retrieval and generation are kept apart, so scholars can inspect sources before any synthesis happens. Time windowing forces even coverage across the study period. Model judgments of relevance are exposed, so others can challenge them. The test bed holds over one hundred thousand Der Spiegel articles from 1950 to 1979. Probing it shows why the fixes matter: asking with 1970s terms retrieved nothing at all from the 1950s, a time skew that windowing repairs.
arxiv-2606-18203:
Zhang and colleagues build a grading tree for personal health agents, in a 2026 paper. Language model health assistants that read a user's sensor data promise wider access to care. Judging their open-ended answers is a bottleneck, though. Physicians grade reliably yet slowly. Model judges are fast but inconsistent, and sometimes clinically off. The field needs evaluation that scales without drifting from expert standards.

RubricsTree answers with a hierarchy of over one hundred atomic, checkable yes-or-no rubrics, grown from four thousand real user queries through rounds of curation led by an experienced physician. A context-aware router activates only the rubrics relevant to each query and weights them, keeping throughput high. Meta-evaluation shows the system tracks expert judgment far better than a large-scale baseline, reliably penalizes degraded inputs in stress tests, and stays stable across judge models and sampling settings.
arxiv-2606-18303:
Miyagawa draws an exact bridge between fluid shock waves and the training of neural networks, in a 2026 theoretical paper. Modern networks carry heavy parameter symmetries: many weight settings compute the same function, so raw parameter statistics can mislead anyone monitoring training. Miyagawa quotients out those symmetries and coarse-grains the stochastic gradient descent dynamics with a local-entropy smoothing, working on the space of genuinely distinct models.

On that quotient space the effective dynamics obey a viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Under a gradient-field assumption, the gradient of the coarse-grained loss obeys a Burgers-type equation, the classic law whose solutions steepen into shocks, and shock formation is proved rigorously. The theory is checked against perceptrons, convolutional networks, Transformers, and mean-field networks. Miyagawa conjectures the payoff is practical: symmetry-corrected observables could monitor, forecast, and control abrupt phase changes during training.
arxiv-2606-18403:
Ghosh proposes a context-aware stress test for fast reconstruction pipelines, the simulation shortcuts used where full detector simulation is too expensive, in a 2026 paper spanning high-energy physics and medical imaging. Those pipelines assume reconstruction error depends only on local input values, ignoring the context of each event.

Ghosh tests that assumption on the dilepton decay of the Z boson in simulated High-Luminosity LHC data. Clustering events by kinematic quantities, such as the summed transverse momentum of the leptons and their angular separation, revealed regimes where the mass peak was biased. Resolution degraded there too, even though average performance looked fine. Recalibrating by regime restored peak stability and recovered the resolution. The paper argues the regime-mapping logic transfers to scans like MRI and CT, where signal quality and tissue density play the context role. That makes it a diagnostic for next-generation fast simulation tools.
arxiv-2606-18703:
Shao and the team at Yale School of Medicine teach biological language models to respect context without destroying the probability interface that makes the models useful. The work is a 2026 computational biology paper. Protein and genome language models output per-token probabilities, used for variant scoring and sequence design. But those probabilities come from broad unlabeled corpora. Existing contextual methods route around them through pooled embeddings or task-specific heads, warping the interface.

Their scheme LogiCA performs contrastive learning in output-logit space. It uses gated cross-modal adapters fitting each model's token head. So alignment is defined by context-sensitive token probabilities. It proved effective for mutation-local variant ranking. Across protein-ligand binding, T-cell receptor activity, and drug-conditioned resistance prediction, it beat prior state-of-the-art methods. On held-out-gene resistance prediction, it lifted discrimination from near-random to useful.
arxiv-2606-18803:
Lyu and the team bring language-model user profiling into the production dispatch system of the ride-hailing platform DiDi, in a 2026 data systems paper. Matching pipelines run on structured numerical features. Yet decisive signals are contextual, and naturally expressed as text profiles. Producing them at platform scale collides with context-window limits, long-tail users with almost no history, and the fact that fluent profiles may not help predictions.

ProfiLLM works entirely offline, in two modules. An agent with twenty-seven analytical tools mines platform-scale logs into reusable global knowledge and clustering rules. A second module then generates candidate profiles per cluster, scores them with a downstream utility proxy, and builds preference pairs for fine-tuning. Online serving is just a lookup of precomputed embeddings. In production, a fourteen-day A/B test showed gains in gross merchandise value and completion rate, with fewer early cancellations.
arxiv-2606-19103:
Khanna and colleagues tackle product identity preservation in instruction-based image editing in 2026. Editors can follow complex text instructions, yet they often distort the very product a brand needs kept intact. Logos, labels, and fine features drift or vanish, and no dedicated dataset has targeted product editing with text fidelity demands. The problem has been treated as a side effect of general editing skill rather than a goal in itself.

The team builds a ProductConsistency dataset with a large supervised fine-tuning set, a smaller reinforcement learning set, and a new benchmark for standardized tests. A cyclic consistency reward guides reinforcement learning. It compares captions of the original product description with captions from the edited image, rewarding edits that keep identity. Fine-tuning two leading editors on this data improves text reading accuracy and identity scores over baselines. The work gives commerce imaging a focused data and reward recipe.
arxiv-2606-19203:
Baik and colleagues propose DASH in 2026, a self-distillation framework for noise-robust speech recognition. Recognition degrades in real noisy settings, so robustness is essential for deployment. Noise-augmented fine-tuning is a common fix, but it can trade clean accuracy for robustness and overfit to specific corruptions. DASH instead learns clean-noisy consistency from paired views of the same speech, without needing labels for its extra stage.

The method distills hidden states from many encoder layers, from low-level acoustics to high-level meaning. It also aligns prototype assignments between clean and noisy views, which stabilizes training. On LibriSpeech, DASH improves recognition across diverse noise while preserving clean accuracy, with minimal extra training time.
arxiv-2606-19503:
William Jay and Matteo Saccardi build tools in 2026 for converting between smeared spectral functions. A smeared spectral function blurs a sharp energy spectrum with a chosen kernel, as used in quantum chromodynamics. One group may publish results with one blur while others need a different one to compare.

Jay and Saccardi state analytic conditions for exact kernel changes to exist and converge cleanly. No arbitrary regularisation is needed when those conditions hold. Explicit formulas cover cases of interest, including Cauchy-to-Gaussian changes and Gaussian-to-Cauchy width mixtures. When exact maps fail, regulated maps take over, paired with error bounds computed from the input data itself. Input errors, statistical or as strict pointwise bounds, carry through to the target quantities. Imposing spectral positivity tightens those bounds further. The framework lets lattice results be re-expressed for phenomenology without fresh simulations.
arxiv-2606-19603:
Zhuofan Ying, Peter Hase, and Nikolaus Kriegeskorte explain a striking pattern in linear probe comparisons in 2026. Linear probes read concepts from a model's internal activations, and researchers compare probes by cosine similarity. Mahalanobis cosine similarity refines that measure by weighting with test data covariance.

Earlier work found one probe's similarity to a reference probe predicts its out-of-distribution score almost perfectly. Ying and colleagues extend that finding across models, layers, and concept domains. They then prove the pattern in closed form for balanced classes with Gaussian projections. Both the score and the similarity become sigmoid functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio, forcing a linear link. The theory also predicts when the link breaks, and tests confirm those failure cases. Task-aware similarity thus rests on firm ground as a probe comparison tool.
arxiv-2606-20003:
Zhiyao Yang, Datong Chen, and Huangjun Zhu settle an open question in shadow estimation, a method for learning properties of a quantum state from randomized measurements rather than full reconstruction. Their 2026 paper asks how few measurement bases, the distinct settings an experimenter must use, can still deliver optimal accuracy. Protocols based on so-called 3-designs are optimal in the worst case, but nobody knew whether that forced a huge number of settings.

Yang and colleagues prove the number of bases must grow with the square of the system dimension for worst-case optimality, and they give an explicit family reaching the bound. The average case is far cheaper: any 2-design already gives strong average performance, with tight concentration for random states. Simple options such as mutually unbiased bases or shallow circuits therefore suffice for typical tasks, and the cost split guides how labs design measurement campaigns.
arxiv-2606-20203:
Ratikanta Swain, Sayantan Ghosh, and Bharat Kumar ask whether the trace anomaly still organizes the inside of a neutron star when gravity is modified. Their 2026 paper works in energy-momentum squared gravity, where the star's interior is sourced by effective variables that need not match the physical pressure and density. The trace anomaly, a QCD measure of how strongly conformal symmetry breaks, neatly orders interior profiles in ordinary general relativity. Whether that order survives the modification was unknown.

The authors keep a clean split: the anomaly comes from the fluid alone, while curvature scalars come from the variables sourcing the modified equations. For five mean-field equations of state, anomaly profiles still rose from core to surface, splitting with coupling strength and compactness. Curvature invariants still fell onto organized bands against the anomaly. The anomaly thus remains a useful label for interior geometry even in modified gravity.
arxiv-2606-20503:
Neven Gentil, Rianne Lous, and Aida Todri-Sanial build a general circuit mapping algorithm for neutral atom quantum computers. Their 2026 paper targets a compilation bottleneck: executing circuits on these machines means physically moving qubits, and every transfer costs time and fidelity.

A circuit-independent mathematical framework, built on graph-theoretic combinatorial optimization, determines the minimal number of required qubit transfers. The model captures platform constraints such as zone-limited gate operations and multi-qubit gates. The mapping problem is encoded as a nonlinear integer program and solved with a genetic algorithm. Minimizing transfers before execution should translate directly into deeper, more reliable circuits on neutral atom hardware.
arxiv-2606-20603:
Yudong Li and six colleagues survey how large language models are used to perceive and measure human psychology. Their 2026 review asks whether LLMs can accurately gauge latent constructs like personality, emotions, and cognitive states. The literature has grown faster than its organization.

The authors propose an analytical framework structured around three dimensions to organize the domain. Studies are sorted by how models perceive psychological signals and how measurements are validated. The survey turns a scattered set of demonstrations into a field with shared questions. Psychologists get a map of what these instruments can and cannot measure.
arxiv-2606-20803:
Hareesh Bhaskar, Cristobal Petrovich, and Diego Muñoz argue in 2026 that planet-planet migration predicts a link between hot Jupiter tilt and orbital period. Stellar obliquity is the tilt between a star's spin and a planet's orbit. It preserves clues about how hot Jupiters moved inward. In single-star systems, strongly tilted hot Jupiters cluster at short periods. Longer-period ones tend to align. Tidal effects in the star cannot explain that pattern.

Simulations show two routes. Short-period planets arise through a highly inclined companion mechanism, yielding broad tilts. Longer-period planets form through coplanar high-eccentricity migration over longer times, keeping low tilts. Middle periods show a moderate range. The transition is gradual, not abrupt. Obliquity surveys could therefore read migration history from period patterns, turning a puzzling trend into a test of how giant planets reach close orbits.
arxiv-2606-21003:
Kazuhiko Seki shows in a solo 2026 paper that delayed fluorescence in triplet-fusion systems displays a generalized Mpemba effect driven by magnetic fields. The Mpemba effect is known from hot water freezing faster than cold. In modern form, a state farther from equilibrium can relax faster than a closer one. Relaxation paths can cross. Seki's system uses spin-dependent delayed fluorescence instead of temperature.

A diffusion-controlled model extends the Johnson-Merrifield framework for geminate recombination. Fluorescence paths at different magnetic fields cross when geminate fusion is effective. A compact kinetic criterion for crossing is derived. It balances mid-time decay rates against long-time power-law amplitudes. Fast and slow contributions compete inside that criterion. Extending the Mpemba idea to spin kinetics links an odd relaxation puzzle to measurable light signals, giving experimentalists a new place to test when far-from-equilibrium systems recover fastest.
arxiv-2606-21103:
Nagashri Krishnakumar, Harshil Mittal, and Jayalal Sarma study reachability in 2026 on undirected graphs whose edges are labeled by elements of a monoid, an algebraic structure with an associative operation. A walk from a start node to a target node is accepted when the product of its edge labels lands in a fixed accepting set. Such problems capture space-bounded complexity classes.

When the accepting set is fixed rather than part of the input, finer bounds appear. The authors reveal upper and lower bounds and dichotomies that depend on the monoid's structure and the accepting set. Earlier work treated cases where the monoid is aperiodic or a group with a variable accepting element. Algebraic classification of reachability helps complexity theory map exactly which label structures make a search problem easy or hard for space-limited computation.
arxiv-2606-21203:
Ece Takmaz and three colleagues test coherence illusions in 2026 in Dutch language models, where a text can feel coherent for the wrong reason. Human readers fall for such illusions when a distractor matches what comes next. Texts use linking words that point back to earlier context. Six monolingual and four multilingual Dutch models are studied against human judgments and eye-tracking data.

Surprisal at the critical word tracks human acceptability. Models are more surprised by incoherent continuations. A matching distractor in prior context reduces that surprise, mirroring the illusion. Attention entropy at the critical spot identifies heads that behave differently under coherence and incoherence. Ablating those heads transfers across experiments, suggesting a shared mechanism. An energy metric from associative memory research is also introduced. Language models may thus share a human-like failure, with implications for trusting their reading of long documents.
arxiv-2606-21503:
Michele Filippucci, Stephen Thomson, Neil Lewis, and Simona Bordoni use idealized aquaplanet simulations in 2026. They ask how Arctic warming changes atmospheric blocking, the stubborn high-pressure patterns that stall weather and breed extremes. Earlier model studies found a weak, robust circulation response to Arctic amplification, but the role of east-west asymmetry was unclear. The team compares a zonally symmetric water world with one carrying a localized midlatitude storm track.

With symmetric geography, blocking grows uniformly from mid to high latitudes as the pole warms. With a storm track, the blocking maximum instead shifts upstream, to the storm track's exit. In both worlds, weaker zonal winds slow Rossby waves and cut the flow's carrying capacity, the traffic-jam mechanism behind blocking. Mean circulation shape, not just warming, steers the response.
arxiv-2606-21703:
Bruno R. R. Boaretto, Kalel L. Rossi, Lyle E. Muller, Elbert E. Macau, and Roberto C. Budzinski show in 2026 that signal delays, usually cast as a nuisance, can organize excitable networks. Neuronal communication is inherently delayed by finite propagation speeds. In their networks of excitable neurons with delayed excitatory links, the delays themselves create self-sustained oscillations, in-phase or out-of-phase.

Small changes in coupling strength or delay then trigger an abrupt, explosive jump into in-phase synchrony. The mechanism is an interplay between each neuron's excitable dynamics and the transmission lag. It survives across different network layouts, neuron models, noise levels, and even without excitation, which suggests a general principle rather than a modeling quirk. For neuroscience, the work reframes delay as a coordination tool circuits may exploit, not merely a constraint they endure.
arxiv-2606-22103:
Ding and colleagues study, in 2026, the quantitative homogenization of convex Hamilton-Jacobi equations posed in the Wasserstein space of probability measures. The solution is the value function of a mean field control problem with fast oscillations at scale epsilon. As epsilon vanishes, the authors show it converges uniformly to the solution of a limiting equation whose Hamiltonian comes from a suitable cell problem.

They also establish rates. Under general multiscale assumptions the rate is of order square-root epsilon. When the Hamiltonian depends only on the fast variable and the momentum, the sharp rate of order epsilon holds. The authors note this is the first such result extending the optimal finite-dimensional rate to the Wasserstein space. The analysis also extends to dynamic optimal transport problems with a constrained final distribution.
arxiv-2606-22503:
Xinyi Tang and seven colleagues, including Boris Malomed and Yongyao Li, study quantum droplets in this 2026 physics paper. The droplets are self-bound blobs of ultracold polar molecules that hold together without any trap. Dual microwave fields dress the dipole-dipole interactions between molecules, letting experimenters tune the droplet's shape and stability.

Working in a regime dominated by non-axisymmetric interactions, the team map where such droplets can exist. They characterize the chemical potential, total energy, effective volume, peak density, and geometric anisotropy of the states. Several quantities depend nonmonotonously on the interaction strength, rising then falling rather than moving one way. Adding more particles makes the droplets tighter bound and more anisotropic. Shrinking the s-wave scattering length instead drives a transition from stable droplets to collapse. Collisions between droplets moving along different directions vary strongly with direction, ending in quasi-elastic rebound, merger, or fragmentation.
arxiv-2606-23103:
S. Grouffal and colleagues report ten years of monitoring the HIP 41378 planetary system in a 2026 astronomy paper. Systems with several planets record how planets formed inside one shared disc of gas and dust. Known systems skew toward tight, fast orbits, so wide systems are precious. HIP 41378 hosts five transiting planets with periods up to about a year and a half. One of them is an ultra-low-density world. The two outer transiting planets still lacked firm periods and masses, leaving the system's layout only partly mapped.

Grouffal and colleagues combine radial velocity data from four precision instruments with space photometry gathered from 2015 to 2024. They detect velocity signals for every planet. Planet d favors a period near two hundred seventy-eight days, while planet e settles near three hundred ninety-three days. A new mass for the puffy planet f confirms its remarkably low density.
arxiv-2606-23403:
Prajjwal Gupta and colleagues design evaluation metrics for AI systems without any labeled data in a 2026 paper. As agent systems move into production across many domains, judging them grows harder. The deeper problem is that evaluation goals often stay implicit. Nobody states plainly what the system must do, how it can fail, or which failures matter. Metric choices then float without justification. Their system, Litmus, reads the pipeline's own source code and asks targeted questions to draw out that intent. It converts the answers into constraints for building a per-stage portfolio of metrics.

Gupta and colleagues test Litmus on three real code-defined pipelines: financial account grouping, scientific question answering, and inherent risk assessment. Against rival systems, Litmus covered the broadest set of concerns with near-zero redundancy. Its metrics ranked first in validity, judged against per-row quality labels, across all three pipelines, decisively on the science one.
arxiv-2606-23503:
Perron and colleagues build a single vision model that can read satellite and aerial imagery from almost any sensor, in a 2026 Earth observation paper. Earth observation data vary wildly in pixel size, color bands, timing, and sensing method, from ordinary cameras to radar and laser scanners. Standard vision Transformers chop images into patches with a fixed projector, a first layer that assumes one set format, so each new sensor usually forces awkward resampling or a separate model.

Their model, UniverSat, replaces that rigid layer with a universal patch encoder that maps patches of any spatial, spectral, or timing resolution into one shared space using one set of weights. Trained by self-supervision, learning from unlabeled data, on mixed collections from many sensors, it produces features that transfer across instruments. Tests on standard classification and segmentation benchmarks from GeoBench, PANGEABench, and SpectralEarth show strong results throughout.
arxiv-2606-23803:
Rampp, Rather, and Claeys repair a proposed ladder of ever weaker solvability conditions for quantum circuits, restoring exact answers everywhere, in a 2026 paper on quantum dynamics. Dual unitary circuits are toy quantum systems whose behavior can be computed exactly even though they are chaotic. Their gates are unitary in both time and space directions. A recent extension stacked weaker conditions into a hierarchy. Beyond the second level, though, it stopped being solvable everywhere.

The authors introduce a matching infinite hierarchy of solvability conditions. Combined with the earlier hierarchy, these yield circuits whose correlations and entanglement growth can be worked out exactly throughout spacetime. Circuits meeting the conditions exist at every level, so the ladder is not empty. Dual unitarity can thus be extended while keeping exact solvability.
arxiv-2606-23903:
Cui and colleagues find that repeating fast radio bursts tend to shed dispersion over time, a drift consistent with expanding debris from a young supernova, in a 2026 paper on radio astronomy. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of unknown origin. Their dispersion measure counts the electrons the signal crossed en route to Earth, and changes in it probe the burst's surroundings. The team took CHIME's sixty three monitored repeaters, kept the nineteen with more than ten bursts each, and tracked dispersion over years.

Seven sources show significant evolution, five decreasing and two increasing. A binomial test on the combined sample finds decreases significantly outnumber increases. A falling measure means the local electron density is thinning with time. Expanding ejecta from a young supernova remnant would do exactly that. The authors estimate remnant contributions for different ejected masses.
arxiv-2606-24003:
Fontenot, Kaki, and Chang present DissProve, a tool that checks safety traits of distributed protocols on its own. Such protocols, the rule sets letting many computers act as one system, are hard to verify. Messages arrive out of order, so the count of execution histories explodes. Protocols are also defined for any number of actors, so histories have no bound. Older methods demanded global invariants that describe the whole system at once. Those are painful to write even for simple protocols.

Reasoning backwards from error states is the core move. The tool proves bad states unreachable, instead of tracking all behaviour forward. Fontenot's team splits affine protocols from harder non-affine ones. Affine histories grow in length but stay within bounded rounds of communication. New goal-directed notions of materialization, causality, and summarization then let DissProve verify affine protocols with unlimited actors, with no hand-supplied global invariants.
arxiv-2606-24403:
Chawla and Shome teach robots object handling by replaying demonstrations with judgement, instead of imitating them blindly. End-to-end imitation methods, dominated by diffusion and flow models, perform well but sacrifice clarity. Their 2026 framework, RE4, repurposes principled handling theory around manipulation modes. These are the distinct contact regimes an interaction passes through. Four explicit steps compose the method.

Lightweight self-supervised training over the demo data itself yields pose estimates of the target object from images. That pose informs retrieval of the most relevant demo for the current mode. A mode aware transformation adapts it to the new situation. A replanning step connects the robot to the retrieval point, preserving mode constraints, before the transformed demo rolls out. Benchmarks on Push-T and Robomimic cover state-based and image-based settings. An adversarial benchmark targeting sparse data regions of image-based Push-T shows robustness when demonstrations are scarce.
arxiv-2606-24503:
Apredoaei expands the kernel of a Toeplitz operator whose symbol simply switches between zero and one. Toeplitz operators compress multiplying by a function into a holomorphic subspace. Here the symbol is the indicator function of a compact domain, with smooth boundary, inside a complete symplectic manifold of bounded geometry. The operator behaves almost like a projection.

An off diagonal expansion of the operator's kernel is proved. It describes behaviour away from the diagonal, where that intuition is weakest. Two results are extended from compact to non compact settings. One is the asymptotics of traces of polynomials in the operator. The other is a Weyl law counting its eigenvalues. Writing alone in 2026, Apredoaei pushes Bergman kernel style analysis, developed for compact Kähler manifolds, onto the non compact stage. Many quantum problems live there, and the marker symbol's sharp boundary makes the limits genuinely delicate.
arxiv-2606-24603:
Erben derives how wide the allowed range for the next correlation value of a random field can be, in terms of determinants. For a uniform one-dimensional random field, correlation coefficients cannot be chosen freely. Every finite Toeplitz correlation matrix must stay positive semidefinite. That fences each next coefficient into an allowed interval. The widths of those intervals are tied to determinants of main Toeplitz submatrices.

A classical determinant identity, the Desnanot-Jacobi identity, yields a simple determinant form for the interval widths directly. As a direct result, Erben recovers the product expressions for allowed interval widths stated by Schneider and Hartlap in 2009. They now sit inside the general body of classical Toeplitz determinant theory, rather than standing as lone formulas. Writing alone in 2026, Erben's short argument shows a modern result about these constraints was latent in nineteenth century determinant algebra all along.
arxiv-2606-24703:
Nicolas Gast, Bruno Gaujal, and Adrien Obrecht tackle job scheduling in a single server queue. Jobs arrive as a Poisson process and their sizes follow an unknown distribution. One server switches between jobs instantly, and the goal is the lowest expected response time. The celebrated Gittins index policy is optimal when the size distribution is known. Here it is not. The scheduler must learn the indices from samples of past job sizes instead.

Gast and colleagues discretise the bounded range of job sizes. Each sample is then shifted to the nearest grid point on its right. They prove the Gittins index of this shifted empirical distribution stays close to the true one. That closeness makes the resulting index policy asymptotically optimal as the sample count grows. Numerical comparisons with rival approaches confirm the method is efficient in practice. The construction is called the shifted empirical Gittins policy.
arxiv-2606-24803:
Grégoire Misguich wrote these lecture notes as an introduction to tensor network methods in quantum many body physics. Tensor networks compress huge quantum states into manageable pieces. The notes centre on matrix product states, the workhorse representation for one dimensional systems. Readers first learn the basic language: graphical notation, virtual indices, bond dimensions, and gauge freedom. Canonical forms follow, built from QR and singular value decompositions.

The main algorithms come next. Contractions, correlation functions, and matrix product operators lead into DMRG and time evolution methods. Projected entangled pair states extend the idea to higher dimensions, with their approximate contraction sketched. Mixed states, quantum channels, and Lindblad dynamics close the course, aimed at thermal states and open quantum systems. Short Julia code examples use the ITensor libraries throughout. The notes were prepared for the ninth Les Houches summer school on computational physics, held in June 2026.
arxiv-2606-25103:
Asymmetric Shapley values adapt feature attribution to causal knowledge: a causal graph restricts which orderings of features count. Ezequiel Companeetz, Santiago Cifuentes, and Sergio Abriola study when these values can be computed exactly and fast. In some settings where the standard SHAP computation is provably hard, they show the asymmetric version is tractable.

Equivalence classes over the orderings of the graph do the compression work. For a rooted directed tree, an algorithm computes the values in time polynomial in the number of classes. For any directed acyclic graph, the team gets close to the values by sampling orderings at random, each ordering equally likely, reusing known samplers and simpler alternatives. Tests on real world causal structures show the approach is practical.
arxiv-2606-25603:
Particle filters track hidden states by keeping many weighted guesses and resampling them, copying the good ones and dropping the poor. Conditional versions run inside Markov chain samplers, where one reference path must survive each sweep. Axel Finke, Adam Johansen, Anthony Lee, and Lawrence Murray supply in 2026 a simple framework certifying which resampling schemes stay valid in both settings. It covers systematic, stratified, adaptive, and even exotic schemes such as chopthin, whose tangled dependence used to need case by case proofs.

Conditional analogues of the standard schemes come out of the framework without shuffling ancestor indices at random, a common awkward step. The assumptions demanded are strikingly weak: neither unbiasedness at the margins nor exchangeability of offspring counts is required. For practitioners the payoff is a checklist: pick a scheme inside the framework and the resulting filter or sampler is guaranteed to target the right distribution.
arxiv-2606-25903:
Alberto Acosta Reche works in analytic number theory on the prime geodesic theorem. Closed geodesics on a hyperbolic surface play the role that primes play for integers. The theorem counts them with an error term, much like the prime number theorem with a remainder. Acosta Reche studies the count split into congruence classes inside the modular group. Luo and Sarnak, plus Soundararajan and Young, had treated parts of this landscape before.

A analogue for geodesics of the Chebotarev density theorem is the result. It holds with a specific improved exponent, stated in the paper as twenty-five thirty-sixths plus an arbitrarily small term. The same exponent then follows for the prime geodesic theorem itself. The deduction covers any congruence subgroup of the modular group. Progress here sharpens how evenly geodesics distribute among arithmetic classes. That distribution question mirrors deep problems about prime numbers in arithmetic progressions.
arxiv-2606-26303:
Alberto Paniate, Ivano Ruo-Berchera, and Francesco Monticone explain what controls photon pairs born in metasurfaces. A metasurface is a flat sheet of tiny structures that bends light in designed ways. Down-conversion inside such sheets makes entangled photon pairs in a compact device. Designers still optimize by trial and error, because the governing mechanisms are murky.

Pump shapes and measurement geometry are the levers. Each choice moves three outcomes: how many pairs are generated, which way they fly, and how many a detector can collect. The framework reads existing experiments through that lens. Two quiet knobs get promoted. Substrate thickness and multilayer stacking both tune the physics usefully. Either can raise pair output or steer emission direction. Future metasurface sources gain design rules instead of folklore.
arxiv-2606-26403:
Sriram Selvam and Anneswa Ghosh release ProfileFoundry, a generator of fully synthetic people for testing AI systems that handle personal data. Real user records are hard to share or audit safely, while randomly faked fields lack the consistency serious evaluation needs.

The fixed release holds 100,000 synthetic adult person objects across eight locales, each with a current snapshot, household and employer links, and events aligned over time. In total it carries about 709,000 events and 519,000 relationship links. The authors check population margins, per-object consistency, and provenance, while stating plainly that it is a test substrate, not a model of a real population.
arxiv-2606-26503:
Kuize Zhang formalises a layered secrecy property for finite-state automata. An automaton is a machine that moves between states as events occur. Two agents watch different subsets of its events through labels. The second agent knows exactly what the first can observe. The question is what the second agent can infer about the first agent's estimate of a past state.

Zhang calls the target property order-2 bygone-state opacity. It holds when the second agent can never be sure that the first agent pinned down a past state uniquely. He builds a verification tool from concurrent composition and the classical observer construction. The check runs in doubly exponential time, a very large but finite bound. The contribution extends inference about automata from one watching agent to two ordered agents. That ordering captures realistic settings where one observer monitors another.
arxiv-2606-26603:
Vidullan Surendran, Neehar Peri, and David Watkins study how to mix two kinds of robot training data. Handheld collection devices gather demonstrations quickly in many settings. They record what a person did, not the commands a robot controller should issue. Teleoperation records the right commands but is slow and costly. The authors examine where each kind of supervision stays valid.

Handheld data works in free-space phases, where precision is forgiving. It fails in contact phases, where stiff tracking creates unsafe forces. Their hybrid strategy teleoperates only the segments where handheld-trained policies fail. Naively mixing the two data types, though, performed worse than handheld data alone. Their BRIDGE method routes each phase to a gated expert suited to its data type. Diffusion-based experts generate the robot's actions. The combination beat either source used alone.
arxiv-2606-26903:
Xinyu Liang and five colleagues present DNSMOS-C, a compact model that grades speech quality end to end. Quality scores guide the building of speech systems, but human grading is slow. Their model extends a leaner predecessor, DNSMOS Pro, which predicts mean opinion scores directly from audio. Big pretrained encoders and multi-stage training are avoided.

A contrastive loss is the new ingredient. Triplets of clips are arranged so the latent space orders itself by perceived quality. Training learns speech features and quality regression together in one framework. Across several data sets, correlation with human scores improved over the predecessor. Gains held on hard out-of-domain test sets. Analysis of the latent space showed an emergent low-dimensional ordering by quality. That ordering aids interpretation and stabilises training, with no extra computing cost.
arxiv-2606-27103:
Fascendini and colleagues devise a sly test of flexible thinking called the riddle riddle paradigm. Each item looks like a familiar riddle, with the same teasing shape and tone. One tweak changes everything: a literal reading now gives the right answer, with no clever leap needed. Nine leading language models and one hundred human participants faced both genuine riddles and these altered twins during the 2026 experiments.

Humans and models failed in opposite directions across the two experiments. Models scored far higher on genuine riddles than on the altered ones, while humans showed the reverse pattern. Error checks sharpen the contrast. Most model errors on altered items came from inventive reasoning used where plain reading sufficed. Human errors on genuine riddles leaned the other way less often. Strong riddle scores may therefore reflect memory retrieval more than flexible strategy choice.
arxiv-2606-27203:
Terracini examines which endless algebraic fields keep number heights safely away from zero. The height of an algebraic number measures its arithmetic size. Fields with the Bogomolov property keep a positive floor under heights, apart from roots of unity. Lehmer's famous conjecture predicts such floors broadly, but endless extensions behave subtly. Galois representations, which encode symmetry actions of a field, cut out many such extensions. In the 2026 note, Terracini asks when the field cut out this way has the Bogomolov property.

Classical cases include cyclotomic and abelian extensions, plus fields from torsion points on elliptic curves. Habegger's theorem on torsion fields is a landmark the representation language naturally absorbs. Local behaviour, Galois group structure, and geometric origins all influence the answer. Framing the property this way unifies scattered examples under one question. Height floors thus become a property of symmetry data, not just of fields.
arxiv-2606-27303:
Castorena and Vite study curves lying on a special quartic surface in three-dimensional projective space. The surface is a very general smooth quartic containing a line, drawn from a Noether-Lefschetz family. The authors ask which linear systems on the surface hold smooth, irreducible curves. Behaviour inside the Hilbert scheme, the space cataloguing all curves, is the second theme, in an algebraic geometry paper published in 2026.

For most curve classes, a typical member sits as a smooth point on the expected Hilbert scheme. That smoothness means deformations behave as dimension counts predict, with no hidden obstructions. A few exceptional classes need separate care. Finally, the Rao function of every curve on the surface is computed. That function measures how far a curve is from being arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay, a strong algebraic niceness property. The results complete a picture begun by earlier classification work on such surfaces.
arxiv-2606-27403:
Ali and colleagues charge a quantum battery through a lossy bridge without losing a single photon. A quantum battery stores energy in a quantum system for later release as work. Charging through an intermediate state that radiates usually trades speed against dissipation. In their driven three-level cell, one bright amplitude feeds the decaying state, and a counterdiabatic field cancels the lone residual source driving it. In the 2026 quantum physics paper, the lossy state stays identically empty, so charging is exactly lossless at any detuning, coupling, or speed down to the rotating-wave limit.

Losslessness holds for any reservoir, Markovian or not, because the dark sector never touches the system-bath coupling at all. An exact treatment confirms the cancellation across memory times. The same dark-state structure protects stored charge, stretching self-discharge to a slow metastable lifetime. Dissipation engineering is inverted: the lossy sector is never populated.
arxiv-2606-27503:
Sabol and Yoshida study where to place a facility when distance itself is measured tropically, and data points may run off to infinity. The Fermat-Weber problem seeks a point minimising the weighted sum of distances to given sites. Their distance comes from the tropical one-infinity pseudonorm, a polyhedral gauge function with tunable asymmetry that is unchanged by constant shifts, so it descends to tropical projective space. In 2026, non-finite data, points at the boundary of that space, enter the formulation.

Several variants of the inverse problem are investigated: given a desired location, find data or weights that make it optimal. Linear programming formulations solve these inverse variants. The forward problem's known structure guides the inversion throughout. Tropical location theory thus gains both a wider data class and a design toolkit. Planners can work backwards from the answer they want.
arxiv-2606-27703:
Negami's Planar Cover Conjecture links two graph properties. A connected graph has a finite planar cover exactly when it embeds on the projective plane. The conjecture is already proved for rotation compatible planar covers. Those are covers carrying an extra condition on their rotation systems. The existing proof leans on advanced algebraic and topological methods. Shohei Koizumi, Yusuke Suzuki, and Kensuke Tamura offer another proof in 2026.

Their route is primarily combinatorial. It rests on a structural analysis built around a spanning tree of the base graph. A spanning tree reaches every vertex without cycles. Working from that skeleton, the authors rebuild the argument step by step. The new proof avoids the heavy machinery of the earlier one. It therefore makes the rotation compatible case accessible through elementary graph structure. The result itself is unchanged. What changes is the path by which readers can verify it.
arxiv-2606-28603:
Angelo Ricarte, Erandi Chavez, Franc O, and Pavlos Protopapas hunt for the observable fingerprints of flux eruption events. These are violent moments when a strongly magnetized accretion flow near a black hole expels matter through magnetic reconnection. The Event Horizon Telescope might soon image such eruptions, if astronomers know what to look for.

The team trains a neural network on simulated images to learn eruption-relevant structure, and uses it to label a larger image set. Then plain models, a random forest and logistic regression, say which visible features betray an eruption. During events, images grow more diffuse, polarization rises, and total flux dips, but weakly compared with ordinary swings. One loop diagnostic even rotates more slowly, against expectation. The forest flags candidates at about eighty percent accuracy.
arxiv-2606-29103:
Fukuyama rewrites a conjecture about the Tomimatsu-Sato solutions, a known family of exact solutions to Einstein's equations for spinning, symmetric vacuum spacetimes. The Nakamura conjecture links these solutions to the Toda molecule hierarchy, a chain of particles with exact solutions of its own. The link is the paper's focus.

The conjecture's equations mix two kinds of derivative. One kind is the Hirota bilinear form, a standard tool in soliton theory. The other is plain first derivatives, which do not fit the bilinear algebra. Fukuyama builds a reduced trilinear form, using threefold operators with three-way symmetry, cut down to a smaller sector. Both kinds of derivative can be rewritten in full inside this reduced form. The new form also keeps a Hirota-type direct method for building solutions, with new spectral factors. The result suggests the Tomimatsu-Sato system is one reduced sector of a broader trilinear theory.
arxiv-2606-29203:
Huang, Hou, and Tan study best-arm identification, the task of finding the best option among several uncertain choices within a fixed sampling budget. Their twist is abstention: the learner may refuse to recommend anything. They work in the Bayesian setting, where prior beliefs shape the problem, and measure the risk of recommending a worse arm without abstaining.

Abstention, they find, triggers a sharp phase transition. With no abstention allowed, the error probability shrinks only polynomially as the budget grows. Any small positive abstention budget switches that decay to exponential, a far faster improvement. Nearly tied arms, where the top two options almost match, drive the fundamental difficulty. Their adaptive algorithm, PGWS, spends its abstention allowance on ambiguous cases and achieves the optimal error rate. The improvement turns out to be exclusively Bayesian; in the frequentist setting, abstention changes only lower-order terms.
arxiv-2606-29403:
Berthier and four colleagues work on conformal prediction, a method that wraps a model's forecast in a set guaranteed to contain the truth at a chosen rate. That guarantee holds on average, yet pooled calibration can hide weak coverage in particular regions of the input space. In safety-critical subgroups, meaning smaller groups where errors matter most, real coverage can fall short.

Their scheme, Self-Organized Conformal Prediction, first discovers groups without labels. A Self-Organizing Map, an unsupervised grid that clusters similar inputs, defines those groups. At test time, calibration data come from the cell nearest the query, or from a small fixed neighbourhood around it. The predictor itself stays untouched. Across eight benchmarks in regression and classification, regional coverage gaps fell on seven datasets. Prediction sets grew only modestly in size, and computing overhead stayed negligible on the larger datasets.
arxiv-2606-29503:
Kaul, Kim, Khurshid, and Vishwanath name a bottleneck they call the verbose context problem. Structured medical concepts often need long, token-hungry text descriptions. In population health, analysing a cohort means reasoning over thousands of coded events in longitudinal patient records. That material can exceed four hundred thousand tokens, far beyond what a language model handles comfortably.

They present PopMedQA, a benchmark that isolates this problem with computational tasks over groups of patient records. A new library, neopatient, generates artificial patient records under controlled language rules, so no real patient data is exposed. The team runs extensive ablations, testing prompting strategies, prompt compression, and agentic decomposition, where a task is split among cooperating agents. Domain-independent methods all fail to relieve the problem. The authors conclude that large gains remain available to methods that exploit the specific structure of medical records, rather than treating the text as generic prose.
arxiv-2606-29603:
Wang proves a rigidity theorem in dynamics, the study of systems that evolve over time, for a class of maps on a torus, a doughnut-shaped surface. The maps are Anosov diffeomorphisms, smooth transformations that stretch in some directions and shrink in others everywhere.

The theorem says that if such a map's behaviour at its periodic points, points that return to themselves, matches its linear model at every such point. Then the change of coordinates linking the map to the linear model is smooth in a strong sense. The proof assumes no conformality and no simple spectrum. It works first on layers inside the map's stretching and shrinking blocks before extending to the whole. The same method gives a local result for small perturbations of the linear map.
arxiv-2606-30303:
M. Echeveste and fourteen colleagues rewrite the rules for when mass transfer between binary stars stays stable. One star overflowing its Roche lobe can feed its companion calmly or run away unstably. The stability criterion in population synthesis codes is a long-standing uncertainty. Their new criterion accounts for mass and angular momentum leaving the system. It is implemented in the SEVN population synthesis code.

The derivation starts from the Roche-lobe radius response to mass loss. Only that response term changes versus the standard approach. Population simulations then test the impact on two populations. Blue stragglers, rejuvenated stars in clusters, increase in predicted number. More of them also form in wider orbits than before. That shift helps reconcile theory with observations of blue stragglers. Binary compact objects show the strongest effects for neutron star systems. Gravitational wave progenitors grow in number under low transfer efficiency.
arxiv-2606-30603:
Jewel Mahajan and Arnab Mitra study the coefficients of symmetric power L-functions, central objects in analytic number theory that package a modular form's data into a series. They restrict attention to integers that can be written as a sum of m squares, for even m from two to twelve. Over that thin set of integers, they ask how partial sums of the coefficients behave, and how often the coefficients change sign.

The pair bound the partial sums of the coefficients themselves from above. For the squared coefficients they prove asymptotic formulas, precise growth laws, over the same sums of squares. As an application, they derive lower bounds on the number of sign changes along these sequences. Results of this kind test how randomly the coefficients oscillate, a question tied to deep conjectures about L-functions. The methods extend earlier moment calculations for these symmetric power families.
arxiv-2606-30703:
Zoey Shepherd, Ohad Kammar and Elizabeth Polgreen speed up program synthesis, the automatic search for a program that meets a specification. Search usually enumerates program syntax, and many syntactically different programs mean the same thing. A synthesiser wastes effort evaluating and rejecting each duplicate separately. Their system, NSynC, enumerates semantics instead: it searches the space of normal forms for a typed lambda calculus with sums.

Because each candidate is semantically unique by construction, every evaluation counts. A top-down, type-directed algorithm steers the search through that normal-form space. On a synthetic benchmark suite, preliminary results showed a geometric-mean speedup of about eight point nine times over the unrestricted syntax-based algorithm. The authors present the approach as synthesis by semantics, trading a harder search space design for freedom from duplicate work. The typed setting also guarantees that every candidate is at least type-correct.
arxiv-2606-30903:
James Sullivan, Roger de Belsunce and Mikhail Ivanov propose that several cosmological tensions share one mundane cause: the optical depth to reionization, tau, being higher than usually assumed. Tau measures how much cosmic microwave background light was rescattered after the first stars reionized the universe. Recent work showed that ignoring large-scale polarisation data and adopting a higher tau eases the Hubble tension, the pull toward negative neutrino masses, and hints of evolving dark energy. The authors fix a concordance tau centred on 0.11 by requiring positive neutrino masses and agreement between microwave-background and galaxy-survey values of the Hubble constant.

Inside that high-tau universe they obtain a tentative detection of the summed neutrino mass, about 0.10 electronvolts at the two-sigma level. Dark energy becomes consistent with a cosmological constant, and the Hubble tension with local measurements eases.
arxiv-2606-31803:
Curticapean and Liu resolve the complexity of counting induced subgraphs with a prescribed automorphism group. The broader problem counts vertex subsets whose induced subgraph satisfies a fixed property. Such problems are known to be either hard for the parameterized class #W[1] or fixed-parameter tractable, but a direct classification by property stayed open. Graphs with no nontrivial automorphisms were a noted holdout.

Counting induced subgraphs with no nontrivial automorphisms is #W[1]-hard, the pair show. Their proof builds clique scaffolds, restricted versions of the property that support a reduction from the k-clique problem. The argument extends further: for every finite group Q, counting subgraphs whose automorphism group equals Q is likewise #W[1]-hard.
arxiv-2606-32003:
Wafi sets two control strategies side by side for uncertain linear systems whose commands travel over a lossy, bandwidth-limited channel. One is Adaptive Quantized Control, built for unknown dynamics and using acknowledgment messages to make up for dropped packets. The other is a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient reinforcement learning controller, trained on the nominal model without acknowledgments. Mid-run, the plant also switches from a nominal unstable system to a more unstable one.

Within its training world, the learning controller responds faster and damps oscillations better than the adaptive design. Under model uncertainty, packet loss and the dynamic switch, the adaptive controller proves more robust throughout, backed by strict Lyapunov stability guarantees. Raw performance and certified robustness pull in opposite directions.
arxiv-2608-00003: AutoFOAM: The Self-Refining Autonomous OpenFOAM Agent, arXiv 2608-00003. The CFD agent. The research is preserved here. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
arxiv-2608-00103: IngMamba: Ingredient-Level Drug-Drug Interaction Modeling, arXiv 2608-00103. The drug interactions. Researchers may consult the paper. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
arxiv-2608-00403: Visualizing Placement Proposals for Window Arrangement in Mixed Reality, arXiv 2608-00403. The MR windows. Readers can access the paper here. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
barbara-blomberg-volume-03:
A singer waits in vain for praise in Volume 3 of Barbara Blomberg, by Georg Ebers. Ebers places Barbara in the chapel on a fast day, singing her best while the Emperor stays away in his rooms. The Queen of Hungary has gone hunting, and only a thin crowd of lords, ladies, priests, knights, and pages hears her at all in this volume.

Chapter XII follows the slight into the next morning's rehearsal. Praise flows there, but Barbara snaps back at the choirmaster Appenzelder even when his criticism is well founded. The bright charm of two days ago has vanished from her face. Choir boys notice her sullen manner. Under the temper sits a deep anxiety she cannot name in public: her voice, praised by the finest judges, has failed to move the one listener it was meant for.
berthollet-essai-statique-chimique-1803:
Claude-Louis Berthollet founds the study of chemical balance in his Essai de statique chimique, in French from 1803. Reactions, he argues, can run both ways and settle at a point of balance. He drew lessons from soda lakes he had studied while in Egypt with Napoleon's learned corps.

His idea of mass action changed how chemists read combinations. Strong and weak forces, amounts and heat, all weigh in his system. Rivals disputed him, yet the core insight endured and grew. The book marks the birth of thinking about equilibrium in chemistry, a notion no later chemist could afford to leave aside.
brown-carwin-1803:
Brown left Memoirs of Carwin unfinished, and the fragment dates from 1803 to 1805. Carwin, second son of a farmer in western Pennsylvania, narrates his own early life. His older brother loved the haystack and the furrow and never looked past them.

Carwin was the reverse, hungry for knowledge and restless with wonder at all things strange. His father tried to cap his learning at reading and writing, and failed. In time the boy found his odd gift for throwing his voice. That power later drives the ruin in Wieland, so this piece serves as that novel's lost opening.
bukhari-traditions-islamiques-houdas-mar:
Al-Bukhari's Sahih gathers the most trusted reports of the Prophet's words and acts, and the French translation by Octave Houdas and William Marçais began in 1903. Tome I opens the Imprimerie nationale's four-volume Les Traditions Islamiques. Al-Bukhari, who died in 870, sifted hundreds of thousands of reports and kept only those with sound chains.

Hadith scholarship treats his collection as the most authoritative in Sunni Islam, a second source beside the Quran itself. The French version made the vast work usable by European scholars at first hand. Tome I begins the long order of books, from revelation and faith onward.
butler-way-of-all-flesh-1903:
Samuel Butler wrote The Way of All Flesh in the 1870s and 1880s but kept it private during his lifetime. The novel drew so closely on his own family that he feared publishing it. It finally appeared in 1903, the year after he died.

Ernest Pontifex grows up under a harsh clergyman father and a smothering mother. He becomes a priest himself, falls into disgrace and prison, and slowly breaks free of the family grip. Butler attacks Victorian family life and church respectability with cold humor. The novel influenced a whole generation of writers who rebelled against their parents' world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-beaton-:
Archbishop of Glasgow James Beaton, also called Bethune, was born in 1517 and died on 24 April 1603. He was son of James Beaton of Balfarg and nephew of Cardinal David Beaton. He was elected archbishop in 1551 on Andrew Gordon's resignation. Not yet in priests' orders, he was ordained at Rome and consecrated there on 28 August 1552. For eight troubled years he ran his diocese and stood faithfully by Queen Regent Mary of Guise.

He backed her against disaffected Scottish nobles plotting to destroy the ancient Church and enrich themselves with its spoils. He assisted at Edinburgh's provincial council, summoned by Primate Archbishop Hamilton. That was the last such assembly in Scotland for 326 years. The events of 1560, including an alliance treaty with England, soon forced him into exile. The entry follows a bishop who carried Glasgow's archives into a long French exile.
cia-0000008703:
Photo comparison case AB 12,428 yielded its results in a CIA paper dated March 1971. The AB prefix sets this case slightly apart inside the numbered identification series. As usual, specialists weighed a possible prisoner's image against the records of the missing.

The series' scale can hide its purpose, so it helps to state it plainly: name the unnamed faces. Each result either strengthened a lead or cleared one away. Both outcomes served the accounting, which needed firm ground more than comfort. This file is one dated step in the long effort to match faces to names.
cia-0000011503:
Tito's Yugoslavia had broken with Stalin in 1948, and by September 1952 the CIA was probing Belgrade's intentions toward Albania. Albania, loyal to Moscow, sat on Yugoslavia's southern border as a hostile outpost. The paper also touches on Albanian government leaders and the small state's place in Balkan rivalries.

The study weighs whether Tito meant to pressure, subvert, or absorb his neighbor. It maps the fears of a regime caught between two larger communist powers that hated each other. The paper opens a window on the Balkans' cold war within the Cold War, fought with spies and threats.
cia-0000012003:
Egypt's war in Yemen had become a costly trap by January 1965, and a CIA paper that month weighs Nasser's problems and prospects there. Egyptian troops, tens of thousands strong, were propping up a republican regime against royalist tribes backed by Saudi Arabia. The war drained Cairo's money and army while gaining little ground in Yemen's mountains.

The paper judges how deep the quagmire might grow and what it cost Egypt at home. It also weighs Nasser's room to pull back without losing face. Analysts saw the drain clearly years before Egypt finally withdrew, beaten and poorer.
cia-0000012303:
'The Most...' begins the quoted title in a Helms memo to the DIA director from November 1961, another fragment of the Military Thought traffic. The black bars and cut titles shape what history can see of this channel. Soviet officers' own words, chosen and forwarded by the CIA's clandestine chief, reached the Pentagon's new intelligence agency week after week that autumn.

The memo adds one more veiled page to the case file. Its redactions are part of its record, marking what still cannot be said. For readers, it stands among the secrets behind the secrets, the guarded routine of the spy business.
cia-0000012403:
The day's second sitting gets its own record: meeting number fifteen, London, May 4, 1961. Penkovsky is named in the title this time. Double days were becoming the pattern that spring in London. The pattern showed how much the colonel carried in his memory. It also showed how hard his handlers pressed to draw it out before his trip ended and the door closed.

The fifteenth session's record sustains the debriefings' intensity. Morning's questions bred afternoon's, as each answer opened new ground. For readers, the page measures a source who seemed, to the men questioning him, inexhaustible.
cia-0000012803:
Small observations from Hanoi fill a CIA paper from May 1967, a notebook of the enemy capital's details. American planes bombed the north, but Americans could not walk its streets. What reached Langley came through travelers, defectors, and watchers abroad. The miscellany collects their scraps: prices, moods, uniforms, shortages. Together they form the small change of a city at war, spent daily under the bombs.

Such trivia accumulated into a portrait no single report could give. The enemy's seat was observed at one remove, and honestly labeled as such. For readers, the paper shows intelligence at its most human scale: the small things, noticed.
cia-0000013603:
Subversion in Honduras is the danger weighed in a CIA paper from January 1964. The small republic's weakness was its exposure. Honduras sat between revolutionary Cuba's admirers and nervous neighbors, with an army that ruled as much as it guarded. Its strategic spot on the map belied its size, sitting astride routes and borders that mattered to every plan Washington drew for the region.

The paper weighs the left's chances and the regime's defenses. It treats the banana republic's red scare with the seriousness of the era. For readers, it shows how thoroughly the Cold War graded even its smallest stages.
cia-0000013903: Two American prisoners were observed in Binh Dinh Province, in a CIA note dated November 5, 1967. The note is brief and gives no names in its title. Even so, a count of two at a known place helped track the southern camps. Reports like this piled up into the full prisoner picture officials worked from.
cia-0000014803: Testimony before a federal grand jury anchors an untitled CIA file dated May 2, 1950. The witness is unnamed in the title, and the case is left unsaid. Grand jury words built the spy cases in secret that spring. A scrap like this marks one step in the quiet march toward the Rosenberg arrests.
cia-0000015303: A letter to Donald Keyhoe from J. S. Harman fills a CIA file dated March 4, 1958. Harman wrote that he found nothing reflecting the point raised, per the title. Keyhoe was the loudest saucer author of the age, pressing the government for answers. A flat reply like this was the standard wall he met.
cia-0000037103: Disbursements for travel and other expenses are listed in a CIA record dated October 3, 1942, naming Cook, Dulles, Nelson, Rado, Tyler, and Foss. The page comes from the first year of the OSS, the wartime office that grew into the CIA. It sets out payments in the dry form of a ledger, name by name. Bookkeeping like this tracked the cost of building a secret service from scratch.
cia-0000045203:
Salvadoran officials reportedly negotiated the kidnapping in Panama, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1985. Panama offered neutral ground away from San Salvador's dangers. Secret talks abroad were the crisis's hidden second track.

Inside, the reported Panama channel is recorded as it leaked out. Back channels work only while they stay unspoken and unseen. Once reported in the press, they become part of the public bargaining too, whether the negotiators in Panama wished it or not at the time. The file preserves the moment the secret track surfaced, when a negotiation meant to be invisible became one more headline in a watched and worried country.
cia-0000046503: Sources in Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam, their names blacked out, spoke to the prisoner and missing-men question in a CIA item dated March 6, 1988. What people inside those countries said was the hardest kind of evidence to get and to judge. The item gathers regional voices on an issue Washington usually heard about secondhand.
cia-0000049003: A strong movement among right-wing Salvadoran officers aimed to overthrow the revolutionary government in 1980, and a CIA item from that year tracks it. The junta then ruling in San Salvador sat between a rebellious right and a rising guerrilla left. The item preserves the coup danger as watchers saw it then, from inside the files.
cia-0000049203: Senior officers of ESAF, the Salvadoran armed forces, met at a high level in 1991 to discuss the Jesuit case. A CIA item from that year preserves the meeting, kept with the Truth Commission records. By then the case was the single greatest danger the institution faced, greater than the guerrillas that year.
cia-0000049303: San Salvador, the capital, stood tense in a CIA item from 1989, kept with the Truth Commission records. Capital tense was a headline built from mood: rumors, troop movements, and a city listening for the offensive everyone expected. The item preserves the held breath of a city that had learned to read its own danger.
cia-0000049403: El Salvador Situation Report number fourteen is preserved as declassified CIA document 0000049403, dated February 3, 1983. Marked for the Truth Commission, it belongs to a numbered situation report series. The file's chief interest is serial: one dated installment in a running sequence of Salvadoran situation reports, showing the routine form of the agency's wartime updates.
cia-0000096503: Third Report to the President by the President's Board of Consultants on Foreign Intelligence Activities appears again as declassified CIA document 0000096503, dated January 1, 1959. The catalog holds several records of this same board report with different dates. Readers get another dated copy in that run, useful mainly for showing how often the report was filed.
cia-0000119203:
In August 1968 the CIA compared an unidentified prisoner photograph, numbered 109, with known photos of Roy F. Townley. The task was simple to state and hard to do: decide whether the man in the prisoner photo was Townley. Work like this sat at the center of the prisoner accounting effort.

Photo comparison was painstaking work done from grainy prints and old service pictures. A match could bring a family long-awaited news, while a wrong call could do real harm. The document preserves one such comparison, showing how analysts tried to put names to faces when the prisoners themselves could not be asked.
cia-0000119703:
A September 1952 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in the Union of South Africa. The country was four years into formal apartheid, and its government was tightening racial rule. Analysts in Washington were asked to chart where the country was heading.

Forecast papers like this one weighed a government's strength, its opposition, and the pressures that might change it. South Africa posed hard questions, since it was both an anti-communist partner and a state building open racial rule. The paper records the agency's early read on that problem. It marks the start of a long American effort to judge a regime whose policies would trouble relations for decades.
cia-0000124303: A November 1962 CIA technical report works out the sizes of Cosmos series satellites from their mass, area ratio, and brightness, adding matching figures for American satellites. Analysts sized up Soviet craft from the light they reflected. The paper shows technical intelligence at its most careful. Brightness tricks let analysts estimate size for craft they could never inspect, a standard method of the years before spy satellites could settle such questions directly.
cia-0000132203: Situation report 520, from January 1991, reports Israeli fears that Iraqi chemical attacks are imminent, with Israel misspelled in the original heading. Fear of gas-tipped missiles drove the handing out of gas masks. The report records that anxiety as filed. Israel's fear had deep roots in the gas attacks of the Iran war, and the sitrep's misspelling survives as a fingerprint of reporting done at crisis speed.
cia-0000132403: Cuba and Latin America are paired in a CIA document carrying an estimated date of January 1, 1961. The invasion at the Bay of Pigs was still three months away. Havana's revolution was already sending its example across the hemisphere. The short document covers that regional picture, as analysts watched governments and rebel movements react to the Cuban model in the new year.
cia-0000132503: Dissension inside Ecuador over policy toward Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 3, 1961. It pairs with a warning from the same month that violence might break out there over the same issue. The Cuba question was dividing governments and parties across the region that year. The short document tracks the Ecuadorian dispute and the sides forming within it.
cia-0000133203: Eighty-three photographs marked with the code name JMTIDE fill a CIA paper carrying an estimated date of January 1, 1961. The paper itself is untitled in the record. JMTIDE was an agency code name, and its meaning is not given here. The photographs form the picture file of some covert program. The short paper keeps the set in the bare form the record gives it.
cia-0000136703: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents, cataloged at 1 January 1961 with the date flagged as estimated. The new year found the brigade of anti-Castro exiles in training for a secret invasion. The record states no subject for this item. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, grouped with the other estimated New Year records in the brigade's file, and described on that basis.
cia-0000137003: Asylees sheltering in embassies create a dangerous problem in this June 1954 cable on extradition, signed under J. C. King. Through a channel, a request is made to resolve a tense and potentially explosive situation in Guatemala City, where diplomatic establishments including the Ecuadoran embassy hold asylees. If Ecuador refuses and insists on safe conduct, the asylees would have to be received by Ecuador, adding Iron Curtain trained communists and hardened criminals to its already alarming local communist situation. Prestige and precedent are both invoked.
cia-0000140403: Consultants for a hypnosis research project are recommended in this February 1952 memo. It discusses an unnamed psychologist known for his work in hypnosis. One researcher's ten-year experiments form a careful classic. His book is key reading for anyone serious in the field. He is now feeble and no longer interested. His two chief assistants remain active and valuable. Another man is very able and broad-minded. He has experience in research, lab, clinical, and business psychology. His judgment on hypnotism or drugs is trusted.
cia-03006503: THE COMMUNIST WINTER-SPRING OFFENSIVE IN SOUTH VIETNAM, a CIA assessment. The offensive analysis. This file preserves that declassified paper. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
