plaw-108-3-2003: Public Law 108-3, the National Flood Insurance Program Reauthorization Act of 2003, extends the federal flood insurance program by one year. Approved January 13, 2003, it moves the program's end dates from December 31, 2002, to December 31, 2003. The changes touch borrowing authority, the power to issue insurance contracts, emergency program rules, and money for studies under the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968. The act counts as effective on December 31, 2002, so the program never lapsed.
plaw-108-30-2003: Public Law 108-30, approved May 29, 2003, keeps money alive for a school food test program. The fruit and vegetable pilot program, run under the National School Lunch Act, gave free fruits and vegetables to students in selected schools. This law adds words to section 18 of that act. The program's funds now remain available until the close of the school year beginning in July 2003, rather than expiring sooner.
plaw-108-31-2003:
Public Law 108-31, passed in 2003, aims more foreign aid at the very poorest people through tiny business loans. It amends the Microenterprise for Self-Reliance Act of 2000 and the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. Microenterprise programs lend very small sums to poor households in developing countries so they can run small businesses.

The amendments retarget the program's language from microentrepreneurs to microenterprise households. They swap the poorest of the poor for the very poor as the named focus. A new rule requires that at least half of all microenterprise aid under the title go to the very poor. Definitions are widened so aid serves borrowers and their households together.
plaw-108-32-2003:
Public Law 108-32, the Grand Teton National Park Land Exchange Act, speeds the purchase of Wyoming land inside a famous park. The State of Wyoming owned about 1,406 acres within the boundaries of Grand Teton National Park. The land appears on a March 2001 map of private, state, and county inholdings.

The Secretary of the Interior may gain the state land in several ways. The state may donate it, the government may buy it with donated or appropriated money, or the two may swap it for federal land in Wyoming picked under the act. State lands means land and interests owned by Wyoming inside the park lines. Finishing the deal removes a patchwork of ownership from the park.
plaw-108-33-2003: Public Law 108-33, approved June 23, 2003, names a post office building in Clifton, New Jersey. The postal facility at 1114 Main Avenue becomes the Robert P. Hammer Post Office Building. The act is two sections long. The references section states that any mention of the facility in a federal law, map, or record is deemed a reference to the Robert P. Hammer Post Office Building.
plaw-108-34-2003:
Public Law 108-34, the Zuni Indian Tribe Water Rights Settlement Act of 2003, approves a settlement of the Zuni Tribe's water claims in Apache County, Arizona. Water is precious in the dry Southwest, and tribes, states, and towns often fight over river rights for decades.

The findings state federal policy: settle tribal water claims without long, costly lawsuits whenever possible. Measuring a tribe's water rights, and building the works to use them, is vital for reservation communities in arid states, Congress says. The United States set aside a reservation for the Zuni in 1984 above where the Little Colorado and Zuni Rivers meet. It was for the tribe's long-standing religious and farming life.
plaw-108-35-2003: Public Law 108-35, approved June 23, 2003, names a federal building and courthouse in Indianapolis, Indiana. The building at 46 East Ohio Street becomes the Birch Bayh Federal Building and United States Courthouse. The act follows the standard naming form in two sections. The references section deems any mention of the building in federal laws, maps, or records to be a reference to the Birch Bayh Federal Building and United States Courthouse.
plaw-108-36-2003:
Child abuse and neglect prevention is the subject of the Keeping Children and Families Safe Act of 2003, Public Law 108-36 of the 108th Congress. The law improves and reauthorizes programs under the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act, the main federal law in this field.

Title I covers the general program: a national clearinghouse for child abuse information, research and demonstration work, and grants to states and to public or private groups. Separate grant lines support state prevention and treatment programs and the investigation and prosecution of abuse and neglect cases. Title II turns to community-based grants aimed at stopping abuse before it happens. The act also sets funding levels and reporting duties.
plaw-108-37-2003: A new federal building in Omaha, Nebraska, receives its name in Public Law 108-37, passed by the 108th Congress in 2003. The building is the regional headquarters for the National Park Service in the Midwest, still under construction when the law passed. It is designated the Carl T Curtis National Park Service Midwest Regional Headquarters Building. Any reference to the building in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is to be read as a reference to that name.
plaw-108-38-2003:
Sexual assault awareness is the subject of Public Law 108-38, a joint resolution passed by the 108th Congress in 2003. The resolution states the sense of Congress on raising awareness and encouraging prevention across the United States. It supports the goals of National Sexual Assault Awareness and Prevention Month.

The opening clauses lay out the scale of the problem. Another person is sexually assaulted about every two minutes, and the Justice Department counted 248,000 victims in 2001. One in six women and one in thirty-three men had been victims of rape or attempted rape, and 44 percent of victims were under eighteen. Fewer than 40 percent of victims reported the attack, and two-thirds of the crimes were committed by someone the victim knew. Congress also notes that new DNA methods could help solve tens of thousands of old cases.
plaw-108-39-2003: Stock sale deadlines for a satellite company move under the ORBIT Technical Corrections Act of 2003, Public Law 108-39 of the 108th Congress. The law amends the Communications Satellite Act of 1962. It concerns the orderly dilution of ownership in Inmarsat by the former signatories to the Inmarsat Operating Agreement, meaning the old owners were to sell down their stakes. Two dates in the initial public offering rules shift: December 31, 2002 becomes June 30, 2004, and June 30, 2003 becomes December 31, 2004.
plaw-108-4-2003: Federal agencies keep running under Public Law 108-4, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress approved on January 31, 2003. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2003, the stopgap funding Congress uses when regular spending bills are not finished. The whole measure does one thing: it amends the earlier funding law, Public Law 107-229, by striking the cutoff date in its section 107(c) and replacing it with February 7, 2003. That buys about one more week of funding.
plaw-108-40-2003:
Welfare funding continues under the Welfare Reform Extension Act of 2003, Public Law 108-40 of the 108th Congress. The law reauthorizes the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families block grant program through fiscal year 2003. That program is the federal block grant that sends welfare money to the states.

Most amendments in the act are made to the Social Security Act, where the program lives. The central section keeps the state family assistance grant flowing for 2003. Each state's grant is set by a ratio. Its share follows the amount it was owed for fiscal year 2002 compared with the national total for that year. That ratio is applied to the amount set for the new year.
plaw-108-41-2003: Schools get help sharing life-saving information under the Automatic Defibrillation in Adam's Memory Act, Public Law 108-41 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The short law amends the Public Health Service Act. It authorizes certain grant funds to be used for a new task: setting up an information clearinghouse. The clearinghouse provides information meant to increase public access to defibrillation in schools. Defibrillators are the devices used to restart a heart with an electric shock.
plaw-108-42-2003:
A California river basin is studied under the San Gabriel River Watershed Study Act, Public Law 108-42 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The law authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to run a special resource study. The study area covers the San Gabriel River and its tributaries north of and including Santa Fe Springs, plus the San Gabriel Mountains inside a state conservancy's territory.

In running the study, the Secretary must consult the San Gabriel and Lower Los Angeles Rivers and Mountains Conservancy and other federal, state, and local bodies. The study must weigh regional flood control and drainage needs and public works such as wastewater treatment plants. A report is due within three years after money is made available for the work.
plaw-108-43-2003: A land swap revises a park boundary under the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area Boundary Revision Act, Public Law 108-43 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The recreation area lies in Utah and Arizona. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire about 152 acres of private land in exchange for about 370 acres inside the recreation area, following a map dated May 16, 2002. When the trade is done, the boundary is redrawn to match. The act also raises the area's size ceiling to 1,256,000 acres.
plaw-108-44-2003:
Wall Street's watchdog hires faster under the Accountant, Compliance, and Enforcement Staffing Act of 2003, Public Law 108-44 of the 108th Congress. The law streamlines hiring at the Securities and Exchange Commission for accountants, economists, and securities compliance examiners. Its stated aims are to protect investors, raise trust in the capital markets, and fully carry out the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002.

A new section of title 5 gives the Commission special appointment power. For those three job types in the competitive service, the Commission may appoint candidates under the looser rules of the excepted service, setting aside the normal competitive hiring rules. The law stresses that using this power does not convert the jobs themselves into excepted service positions. The Commission must report on the new hiring to Congress, starting within ninety days.
plaw-108-45-2003:
National service bookkeeping is tightened by the Strengthen AmeriCorps Program Act, Public Law 108-45 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The law improves how the Corporation for National and Community Service approves national service positions and records the money owed for them. AmeriCorps is the national service program the Corporation runs.

The act fixes the timing of approval. The Corporation must approve a position at the moment it signs an enforceable agreement with a participant. In other cases, approval comes when it awards a grant, contract, or cooperative agreement for the program. At that same point it must record an estimate as an obligation, money formally set aside. The rule applies even where it overrides parts of the National and Community Service Act of 1990 and other laws.
plaw-108-46-2003: Michael J Healy is honored by Public Law 108-46, a redesignation law passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 7401 West 100th Place in Bridgeview, Illinois, known as the Moraine Valley Post Office, becomes the Michael J Healy Post Office Building. Any later reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the Michael J Healy Post Office Building.
plaw-108-47-2003: Floyd Spence is honored by Public Law 108-47, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 1830 South Lake Drive in Lexington, South Carolina, is designated the Floyd Spence Post Office Building. Any reference to the Lexington facility in a United States law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the Floyd Spence Post Office Building.
plaw-108-48-2003: Cesar Chavez is honored by Public Law 108-48, a redesignation law passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 1859 South Ashland Avenue in Chicago, Illinois, known as the Pilsen Post Office, becomes the Cesar Chavez Post Office. Any reference to that Chicago facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the Cesar Chavez Post Office.
plaw-108-49-2003: James R Merry is honored by Public Law 108-49, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 141 Erie Street in Linesville, Pennsylvania, is designated the James R Merry Post Office. Any reference to the Linesville facility in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States is deemed a reference to the James R Merry Post Office.
plaw-108-5-2003: Agency funding is extended again by Public Law 108-5, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress approved on February 7, 2003. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2003, the stopgap funding used while regular appropriations bills are pending. The resolution amends Public Law 107-229 once more, striking the date in its section 107(c) and inserting February 20, 2003, in its place.
plaw-108-50-2003: Delbert L Latta is honored by Public Law 108-50, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 111 West Washington Street in Bowling Green, Ohio, is designated the Delbert L Latta Post Office Building. Any reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Delbert L Latta Post Office Building.
plaw-108-51-2003: Dr Roswell N Beck is honored by Public Law 108-51, a naming law of the 108th Congress enacted in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 1901 West Evans Street in Florence, South Carolina, becomes the Dr Roswell N Beck Post Office Building. Mentions of the Florence facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, and records count as mentions of the building by that name.
plaw-108-52-2003: Norman D Shumway is honored by Public Law 108-52, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 7554 Pacific Avenue in Stockton, California, is designated the Norman D Shumway Post Office Building. Under the law, references to the Stockton facility in federal records are treated as references to the Norman D Shumway Post Office Building.
plaw-108-53-2003: General Charles Gabriel is honored by Public Law 108-53, enacted by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 4832 East Highway 27 in Iron Station, North Carolina, takes the name General Charles Gabriel Post Office. Any reference to that facility in a law, map, regulation, or other record of the United States is deemed a reference to the General Charles Gabriel Post Office.
plaw-108-54-2003: Timothy Michael Gaffney is honored by Public Law 108-54, a naming law passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 2318 Woodson Road in St Louis, Missouri, is designated the Timothy Michael Gaffney Post Office Building. Later references to the St Louis facility in federal laws, maps, and records are read as references to that building name.
plaw-108-55-2003: Admiral Donald Davis is honored by Public Law 108-55, a redesignation law of the 108th Congress enacted in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 201 West Boston Street in Brookfield, Missouri, known as the Brookfield Main Office, becomes the Admiral Donald Davis Post Office Building. References to the facility in federal records are deemed references to the Admiral Donald Davis Post Office Building.
plaw-108-56-2003: Dr Caesar A W Clark Sr is honored by Public Law 108-56, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 1502 East Kiest Boulevard in Dallas, Texas, is designated the Dr Caesar A W Clark Sr Post Office Building. Any reference to the Dallas facility in a United States law, map, regulation, or other record counts as a reference to that building name.
plaw-108-57-2003: Patsy Takemoto Mink is honored by Public Law 108-57, enacted by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 120 Baldwin Avenue in Paia, Maui, Hawaii, is designated the Patsy Takemoto Mink Post Office Building. Under the law's reference rule, mentions of the Paia facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are treated as mentions of the Patsy Takemoto Mink Post Office Building.
plaw-108-58-2003: Hunger fellowships are funded through a new channel by Public Law 108-58, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The law authorizes the Congressional Hunger Center to award the Bill Emerson and Mickey Leland Hunger Fellowships for fiscal years 2003 and 2004. Money provided for the fellowships in those years goes to the Congressional Hunger Center for awarding them, setting aside the Congressional Hunger Fellows Act of 2002 for this purpose. Any amount over three million dollars in either year goes instead to the Congressional Hunger Fellows Trust Fund.
plaw-108-59-2003:
Planning for Lincoln's two hundredth birthday runs longer under Public Law 108-59, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The law extends the Abraham Lincoln Bicentennial Commission, the panel created by Public Law 106-173 to plan the commemoration. It also widens the commission's duties.

The commission must now recommend to Congress a plan for carrying out the activities it proposes, and it may run related supporting activities. One wording fix changes redesignation to rededication in its duties. The reporting schedule stretches as well: an interim report is due by June 24, 2004, and the final report, once expected much sooner, is now due by April 30, 2010. That final report must hold the commission's closing statements, recommendations, and required information.
plaw-108-6-2003: Federal judges receive a pay adjustment under Public Law 108-6, a one-section law of the 108th Congress approved on February 13, 2003. Under section 140 of Public Law 97-92, Justices and judges of the United States are authorized during fiscal year 2003 to receive a salary adjustment. The adjustment follows section 461 of title 28 of the United States Code.
plaw-108-60-2003:
A British prime minister is honored by Congress in Public Law 108-60, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The law awards a Congressional Gold Medal to Prime Minister Tony Blair of the United Kingdom. Congress finds that Blair had shown himself, in a trying and historic time for both countries, a staunch and steadfast ally of the United States.

The Speaker of the House and the President Pro Tempore of the Senate are to arrange the presentation of the medal. It honors Blair's outstanding and lasting work in keeping all freedom-loving nations secure. The Secretary of the Treasury strikes the gold medal, choosing its emblems, devices, and inscriptions. Bronze duplicates may be struck and sold at a price covering the full cost, including the gold medal itself. The medals count as national medals and as collectors' items under title 31.
plaw-108-61-2003:
Burma's military rulers are sanctioned by the Burmese Freedom and Democracy Act of 2003, Public Law 108-61 of the 108th Congress. The act aims to punish the ruling junta, strengthen Burma's democratic forces, and recognize the National League for Democracy as the rightful voice of the Burmese people.

Congress finds that the State Peace and Development Council refused to hand power to the National League for Democracy, whose candidates won the 1990 elections by a wide margin. The council also refused real political talks with the league and ethnic minorities and brushed aside United Nations mediation. On May 30, 2003, its forces attacked league supporters, killed and hurt scores of civilians, and arrested democracy advocate Aung San Suu Kyi. The findings charge the regime with grave rights abuses, rape used as a weapon, forced use of child soldiers, and ethnic cleansing against groups such as the Karen, Karenni, and Shan.
plaw-108-62-2003: A visitor center gets its road under Public Law 108-62, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The Secretary of the Interior may grant an easement to Otoe County, Nebraska. The county may then build and maintain an access road to the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center in Nebraska City, Nebraska. The road links the center with Nebraska State Highway 2 and Otoe County Road 67. No part may sit on private property, and no Interior money may be used to design, build, maintain, or run it.
plaw-108-63-2003: A historic Oregon house joins a national site under the McLoughlin House Addition to Fort Vancouver National Historic Site Act, Public Law 108-63 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire the McLoughlin House in Oregon City, Oregon, including the Barclay House and related property, from willing sellers only, by gift, purchase, or exchange. City-owned land may be taken by donation only. Once acquired, the property joins Fort Vancouver National Historic Site.
plaw-108-64-2003:
A fallen ranger is honored by Public Law 108-64, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. The law names the visitor center in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in Arizona the Kris Eggle Visitor Center. Congress dedicates the center to Eggle and to raising awareness of the dangers faced daily by public land law enforcement officers.

Congress finds that Kris Eggle, a twenty-eight-year-old park ranger at the monument, was murdered in the line of duty in August 2002 along the border between the United States and Mexico. The Secretary of the Interior must post signs at the visitor center and at the trailhead of the Baker Mine and Milton Mine Loop. The signs explain the role of law officers in protecting park visitors, and note the loss of Eggle. They record the dedication by Congress, and include a copy of the act and an image of Eggle.
plaw-108-65-2003: William J Scherle is honored by Public Law 108-65, a redesignation law of the 108th Congress enacted in July 2003. The Postal Service facility at 101 South Vine Street in Glenwood, Iowa, known as the Glenwood Main Office, becomes the William J Scherle Post Office Building. Any reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the William J Scherle Post Office Building.
plaw-108-66-2003:
Two New Mexico pueblos gain trust land under Public Law 108-66, passed by the 108th Congress in July 2003. Certain Bureau of Land Management land is to be held by the United States in trust for the Pueblo of Santa Clara and the Pueblo of San Ildefonso. The arrangement rests on a boundary agreement signed by the governors of the two pueblos on December 20, 2000.

The agreement is titled as an affirmation of the boundary between the aboriginal lands of the two pueblos within the Garcia Canyon Tract. The act defines its key terms, including the agreement, the boundary line it sets up, the governors, and the trust land itself. For Santa Clara, the federal interest in the described land, together with improvements, appurtenances, and mineral rights including oil and gas, passes into trust.
plaw-108-67-2003:
Lake Tahoe land returns to its first people under Public Law 108-67, passed by the 108th Congress in August 2003. The Secretary of Agriculture must convey certain land in the Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit, Nevada, to the Secretary of the Interior. The land is held in trust for the Washoe Indian Tribe of Nevada and California.

Congress finds that the Washoe homeland covered about five thousand square miles in and around Lake Tahoe, and the lake was the heart of that territory. In 1997, federal, state, and local governments, with many private landholders, formally recognized the Washoe as the indigenous people of the basin. The act's purposes are to return the tribe to Lake Tahoe and to let members resume traditional practices on its shore. Those practices include spiritual renewal, land stewardship, Washoe plant growing and gathering knowledge, subsistence gathering, and teaching.
plaw-108-68-2003:
Volunteer screening groups gain a liability shield under Public Law 108-68, passed by the 108th Congress in August 2003. The law amends the PROTECT Act to clarify certain volunteer liability. It adds a new subsection to section 108 of that act, which set up pilot programs for checking the fitness of volunteers.

The shield covers the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and its directors, officers, employees, and agents. They cannot be held liable in a civil suit for a call that a person is unfit to volunteer, when the call rests on the fitness rules of the program. The protection also covers most fit decisions based on criminal history records, or on the absence of such records. It falls away on proof of actual malice or intentional misconduct, and where the center knew records were wrong, incomplete, or hidden.
plaw-108-69-2003: Disaster victims get fast federal money from the Emergency Supplemental Appropriations for Disaster Relief Act, 2003, Public Law 108-69 of the 108th Congress. The act provides extra funding for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2003. Its one item adds money for Disaster Relief work under the Robert T Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act. The amount is nine hundred eighty-three million six hundred thousand dollars, available until spent, and Congress designates it as an emergency requirement under the 2004 budget resolution.
plaw-108-7-2003:
Yearly spending for much of the government is joined in the Consolidated Appropriations Resolution, 2003, Public Law 108-7 of the 108th Congress. The joint resolution makes consolidated appropriations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2003. Rather than passing each spending bill alone, Congress folded them into divisions of one measure.

Division A funds agriculture, rural development, the Food and Drug Administration, and related agencies, with titles for farm programs, conservation, rural development, and food programs at home and abroad. Division B funds the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the judiciary, and related agencies, ending with a title of rescissions that cancels earlier funding. The same division pattern continues through the rest of the resolution.
plaw-108-70-2003: James L Watson is honored by Public Law 108-70, passed by the 108th Congress in August 2003. The building at 1 Federal Plaza in New York, New York, is designated the James L Watson United States Court of International Trade Building. Any reference to that building in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the James L Watson United States Court of International Trade Building.
plaw-108-71-2003: Garner E Shriver is honored by Public Law 108-71, a naming law of the 108th Congress enacted in August 2003. The Postal Service facility at 9350 East Corporate Hill Drive in Wichita, Kansas, is designated the Garner E Shriver Post Office Building. References to the Wichita facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are treated as references to the Garner E Shriver Post Office Building.
plaw-108-72-2003:
Room for the nation's treasures is funded by the Smithsonian Facilities Authorization Act, Public Law 108-72 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The law provides added space and resources for the national collections held by the Smithsonian Institution. It amends an older facilities law, Public Law 94-98.

The Board of Regents may plan, design, build, and equip extra storage and laboratory space at the Smithsonian's museum support facility in Suitland, Maryland. The space serves the care, preservation, conservation, deposit, and study of the national collections held in trust. Funding is authorized at two million dollars for fiscal year 2003 and ten million dollars for fiscal year 2004. For each year from 2005 through 2008, whatever sums are needed are authorized.
plaw-108-73-2003: Family farmers keep a bankruptcy path under the Family Farmer Bankruptcy Relief Act of 2003, Public Law 108-73 of the 108th Congress. The law extends by six months the period for which chapter 12 of the bankruptcy code is in force. Chapter 12 is the part of the code written for family farmers. The end date moves from July 1, 2003, to January 1, 2004, with matching shifts to related start dates, effective July 1, 2003. A later 2004 law extends the same chapter again.
plaw-108-74-2003:
Children's health money lasts longer under Public Law 108-74, passed by the 108th Congress in August 2003. The law amends title XXI of the Social Security Act. It stretches the time states have to spend their allotments from fiscal years 1998 through 2001 under the State Children's Health Insurance Program, the program that covers children in working families.

For the 1998 and 1999 allotments, kept and redistributed amounts stay available through fiscal year 2004 instead of 2002. The 2000 allotment gets a new rule. Of the money a state had not spent by the end of fiscal year 2002, half remains available to that state through the end of fiscal year 2004. The rest feeds the pool of redistributed allotments for states that need more.
plaw-108-75-2003:
Mosquito control gets federal grants under the Mosquito Abatement for Safety and Health Act, Public Law 108-75 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The law authorizes grants through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for programs that fight mosquitoes and the diseases they carry.

A new section 317S is added to the Public Health Service Act. The Secretary, acting through the CDC director, may give coordination grants to states for mosquito control programs. States may use the help to pass grants down to their cities and counties. Those local grants pay for assessments of what control work is most needed nearby and for building local control programs on those findings. The section joins a wider set of disease prevention grants in part B of title III.
plaw-108-76-2003:
Students called to war get relief from the Higher Education Relief Opportunities for Students Act of 2003, Public Law 108-76 of the 108th Congress. The law gives the Secretary of Education clear waiver power to respond to a war, another military operation, or a national emergency. It works through the Higher Education Act of 1965.

Congress opens with the reason: hundreds of thousands of reservists and National Guard members from every service had been called to active duty. Service members put their lives on hold, leaving families, jobs, and college behind to serve. Congress calls supporting them through the move into and out of active service one of its highest duties. Section 2 then grants the waiver and modification power, letting the Secretary ease student aid rules for those affected by military call-ups and emergencies.
plaw-108-77-2003:
Trade with Chile is opened by the United States-Chile Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act, Public Law 108-77 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The act puts the United States-Chile Free Trade Agreement into American law. Title I approves the agreement and covers its entry into force and its relation to federal and state law.

Title II holds the customs provisions. It changes tariffs, sets rules of origin that decide which goods count as Chilean, and covers drawback, the refund of duties on re-exported goods. Other sections deal with customs user fees, false certificates of origin, and denial of special tariff treatment for wrong information. Recordkeeping duties and enforcement of the textile and clothing rules of origin close the title. Later titles handle relief from imports and other matters.
plaw-108-78-2003:
Trade with a Southeast Asian city-state is opened by the United States-Singapore Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act, Public Law 108-78 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. Like the Chile act passed beside it, this law puts a free trade agreement into force in American law. Title I approves the agreement and sets when and how it takes effect.

Title II again carries the customs work: tariff changes, rules of origin, customs user fees, and penalties for wrong information. Enforcement of the rules for textiles and clothing gets its own section, and a regulations section closes the title. Title III turns to relief from imports, the safeguards used when a surge of imports harms an American industry. The two 2003 trade acts follow the same pattern for two very different partners.
plaw-108-79-2003:
Sexual abuse behind bars is measured and fought under the Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003, Public Law 108-79 of the 108th Congress. The law provides for study of how often prison rape happens and what it does, in federal, state, and local institutions. It also provides information, resources, advice, and funding to protect people from prison rape.

Congress notes how little was known. At the end of 2001, about two million one hundred thousand people were locked up in the United States. Over ten million admissions and releases passed through prisons and jails in 1999. Experts guessed that at least thirteen percent of inmates had been sexually assaulted, but hard data was thin. The act orders national statistics and research, prevention and prosecution work, protective grants, and a National Prison Rape Reduction Commission to set standards.
plaw-108-8-2003: Small business loan costs are recalculated under Public Law 108-8, passed by the 108th Congress in February 2003. The law improves how the federal subsidy rate is figured for certain loans, the rate standing for what a guaranteed loan is expected to cost the government. For fiscal year 2003 loans under section 7(a) of the Small Business Act, the budget director may use the most recently approved subsidy model. The model keeps the assumptions and history from the 2003 budget. After notice to Congress, the rate applies from October 1, 2002.
plaw-108-80-2003: Ed Edmondson is honored by Public Law 108-80, a naming law enacted by the 108th Congress in September 2003. The United States courthouse at 101 North Fifth Street in Muskogee, Oklahoma, is designated the Ed Edmondson United States Courthouse. Any reference to that courthouse in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Ed Edmondson United States Courthouse.
plaw-108-81-2003:
Museums and libraries are funded under the Museum and Library Services Act of 2003, Public Law 108-81 of the 108th Congress. The law reauthorizes the Museum and Library Services Act. Title I sets the general rules: definitions, the Institute of Museum and Library Services itself, its director, and the National Museum and Library Services Board. It also covers awards and study of how services affect the public.

Title II covers library services and technology. It sets funding levels, reserves, and allotments, and requires state plans. Grants go to states, and national leadership grants, contracts, and cooperative deals support stronger library work across the country. Title III turns to museum services, with its own purpose and definitions. Together the titles keep one federal institute serving both libraries and museums.
plaw-108-82-2003: The do-not-call list is secured by Public Law 108-82, passed by the 108th Congress in September 2003. The short law ratifies the authority of the Federal Trade Commission to establish a national do-not-call registry, the list that lets households block telemarketing calls. It confirms that the Commission acts under the Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abuse Prevention Act when it runs and enforces the registry. The registry provision of the Telemarketing Sales Rule, issued by the Commission and effective March 31, 2003, is ratified word for word.
plaw-108-83-2003:
Congress pays its own bills in the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 2004, Public Law 108-83 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The act provides funding for the legislative branch for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2004. Title I is the legislative branch title, and it begins with the Senate.

Expense allowances come first. The Vice President, the President Pro Tempore, and the majority and minority leaders get twenty thousand dollars each. Smaller sums go to the whips and committee chairmen. The total is one hundred twenty-seven thousand five hundred dollars. Representation allowances add fifteen thousand dollars for each leader. Salaries for Senate officers and employees follow, at a little over one hundred twenty-five million dollars, including two million twenty-eight thousand dollars for the Office of the Vice President.
plaw-108-84-2003:
The government starts its new year on stopgap funding under Public Law 108-84, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress approved on September 30, 2003. The resolution makes continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2004. Agencies may keep running the projects and activities they ran in fiscal year 2003, at a rate no higher than the current rate, until full spending bills pass.

Section 101 lists the 2003 appropriations acts whose authority carries over. Agriculture and food programs lead the list, followed by the act funding Commerce, Justice, State, and the judiciary. District of Columbia funding, energy and water projects, and foreign operations are also named. The list continues through Interior, labor and health, and military construction, with a few named exceptions where older riders do not carry forward.
plaw-108-85-2003: Irrigation works change hands in Idaho under the Fremont-Madison Conveyance Act, Public Law 108-85 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The law authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to convey certain facilities to the Fremont-Madison Irrigation District, an irrigation district organized under Idaho law. Section 3 orders the conveyance to be made under the terms of a memorandum of agreement between the district and the government. The sample text ends within that conveyance section, so the facilities and terms named later in the act are not described here.
plaw-108-86-2003:
Postmasters gain a seat at the table under the Postmasters Equity Act of 2003, Public Law 108-86 of the 108th Congress. The law amends chapter 10 of title 39, the postal title. It brings postmasters and their organizations into the process for developing and planning certain postal policies, schedules, and programs.

A representation threshold is set: an organization that speaks for at least twenty percent of postmasters qualifies under the same sentence that covers the supervisors' organization. A new subsection then gives postmasters and their groups the same consultation and related rights that supervisors enjoy under section 1004. Where two or more postmasters' organizations exist, they are treated as a single organization, under arrangements the groups agree on among themselves.
plaw-108-87-2003:
The military is funded for a year by the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2004, Public Law 108-87 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. An appropriations act supplies real spending money. This one covers the Department of Defense for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2004.

Title I pays the people in uniform. Military Personnel, Army covers pay, allowances, clothing, food, travel, and retirement fund payments for soldiers on active duty, cadets, and aviation cadets, at more than twenty-eight billion dollars. Military Personnel, Navy does the same for sailors, midshipmen, and aviation cadets at more than twenty-three billion dollars. Similar accounts for the other services and the department's running costs follow through the act.
plaw-108-88-2003:
Highway and transit programs keep running under the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2003, Public Law 108-88 of the 108th Congress. The act extends highway, highway safety, motor carrier safety, transit, and other programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund. It holds the programs over while Congress works on a new version of the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century.

Section 2 handles the money as advances. The Secretary of Transportation divides the funds among the states by the same shares they held in fiscal year 2003 obligation authority for the federal-aid highway program. Within each state share, set amounts must flow to named programs. The list covers interstate maintenance, the National Highway System, bridges, and the surface transportation program. It also covers congestion relief and air quality, recreational trails, the Appalachian development highway system, and the minimum guarantee.
plaw-108-89-2003:
Welfare and other programs are extended by Public Law 108-89, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2003. The law extends the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families block grant program, along with certain tax and trade programs. Title I holds the family assistance provisions.

Section 101 keeps the program running through March 31, 2004, in the manner authorized for fiscal year 2002. Grants and payments for the first two quarters of fiscal year 2004 are made at the level of the first two quarters of fiscal year 2002. The needed sums are provided from the Treasury. Matching changes follow in the Social Security Act. Supplemental grants for states with fast population growth are adjusted. The contingency fund year moves from 2003 to 2004, and the maintenance of effort rules are rolled forward.
plaw-108-9-2003:
A former president's birthday is celebrated by Public Law 108-9, a joint resolution of the 108th Congress approved in March 2003. The resolution recognizes the ninety-second birthday of Ronald Reagan, which fell on February 6, 2003. Congress, speaking for the American people, sends Reagan its birthday greetings and best wishes.

The whereas clauses note that Reagan was the first former president ever to reach ninety-two. He had been twice elected president by wide margins, and Congress credits his leadership with renewing American growth and optimism and with helping extend freedom and democracy as the Cold War ended. His wife Nancy is praised as a gracious First Lady who led a national crusade against illegal drug use. The resolution closes by holding the Reagans in the nation's thoughts as he battled Alzheimer's disease.
plaw-108-90-2003:
The newest cabinet department is funded by the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2004, Public Law 108-90 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The act provides the Department of Homeland Security with its money for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2004. Title I covers departmental management and operations.

The Office of the Secretary and executive management receives about eighty-one million dollars, with no more than forty thousand dollars for official receptions. The Office of the Under Secretary for Management receives about one hundred thirty-one million dollars. Of that, twenty million is set aside for altering and improving facilities and for moving the department's headquarters operations. Department-wide technology investments follow at one hundred eighty-five million dollars, for information technology gear, software, and services, including the shift to narrowband radio systems.
plaw-108-91-2003:
Hospital building loans get clearer rules under the Hospital Mortgage Insurance Act of 2003, Public Law 108-91 of the 108th Congress. The law amends section 242 of the National Housing Act, which governs federal mortgage insurance for hospitals. Section 2 rewrites the standards for deciding whether a hospital is needed and workable.

The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development must require proof that the hospital sits in a state or locality with sound minimum licensing and operating standards. The Secretary must also require proof that those standards will be enforced. On need and feasibility, if the state has an official method for judging hospital need, the applicant must follow it and document the finding. If the state has no such method, the Secretary sets the means of judgment. Section 3 then provides an exemption for critical access hospitals.
plaw-108-92-2003: Federal pensions get a small lift from Public Law 108-92, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2003. The law amends chapter 84 of title 5, which runs the Federal Employees Retirement System. Some annuity calculations include at least two months of credit for a period spent receiving disability payments under the federal workers' compensation chapter. For that period, the percentage used rises by one percentage point. The change applies to annuities based on separations from service on or after the date the law took effect.
plaw-108-93-2003:
An ancient circle in Miami is studied under Public Law 108-93, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2003. The Secretary of the Interior must run a special resource study of the Miami Circle archaeological site in Miami-Dade County, Florida. The study judges the site's national significance and whether adding it to the National Park System, as part of Biscayne National Park, is suitable and workable.

The study must be finished within three years after money for it is provided, and the Secretary must consult American Indian tribes and other interested groups while doing it. Beyond the main questions, the study weighs which nearby areas should join the park. It also weighs whether more staff, buildings, or resources would be needed to run the site, and what effect joining would have on the local area. A report goes to two named committees of Congress within thirty days of completion.
plaw-108-94-2003:
A gunmaker's village is weighed for park status under the Coltsville Study Act of 2003, Public Law 108-94 of the 108th Congress. The law directs the Secretary of the Interior to study Coltsville in Connecticut for possible inclusion in the National Park System. Coltsville is the Hartford neighborhood built around the Colt firearms works.

Congress finds that Hartford, home of Colt Manufacturing Company, played a major role in the Industrial Revolution. Samuel Colt, the founder, and his wife Elizabeth inspired Coltsville, a community of Victorian mansions, open green space, botanical gardens, and a deer park. Their home, Armsmear, is a national historic landmark, and the Colt factory shapes the Hartford skyline. The findings stress that the Colt legacy is not only about firearms, but also about industrial invention and technology that changed American life.
plaw-108-95-2003: A wilderness line shifts by equal amounts under the Mount Naomi Wilderness Boundary Adjustment Act, Public Law 108-95 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. About thirty-one acres shown on the official map as Land Excluded are removed from the Mount Naomi Wilderness. In their place, about thirty-one acres marked Land Added are brought in, subject to rights already held, under the Utah Wilderness Act of 1984. The map, dated May 23, 2002, is kept with the Chief of the Forest Service, and the Secretary of Agriculture may correct it.
plaw-108-96-2003:
Runaway and homeless young people are served by the Runaway, Homeless, and Missing Children Protection Act, Public Law 108-96 of the 108th Congress, enacted in 2003. The law reauthorizes programs under the Runaway and Homeless Youth Act and the Missing Children's Assistance Act. Title I amends the Runaway and Homeless Youth Act, starting with its findings.

Congress finds that young people who are homeless, or who leave home and stay away without permission, suffer serious health and emotional problems at high rates. Living on the street for long stretches endangers them and strains the towns where they gather. Many need short-term shelter and services that fit their language and situation. Because the problem crosses state lines, Congress assigns the federal government two jobs. One is building an accurate national reporting system. The other is helping create a system of care outside welfare and law enforcement, from prevention to street outreach.
plaw-108-97-2003: Roberto Clemente Walker is honored by Public Law 108-97, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2003. The Postal Service facility at 1000 Avenida Sanchez Osorio in Carolina, Puerto Rico, is designated the Roberto Clemente Walker Post Office Building. Any reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Roberto Clemente Walker Post Office Building.
plaw-108-98-2003:
Foreign schools face tighter tests under Public Law 108-98, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2003. The law amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 on the qualifications of foreign schools. It matters because students at approved foreign schools can use federal student loans, and Congress wanted stronger proof that those schools match American colleges.

Section 102 of the education act is rewritten. The Secretary of Education must set rules for approving schools outside the United States and for judging them comparable to American institutions of higher education. Graduate medical and veterinary schools abroad are excused from one part of the standard test. For a foreign graduate medical school, loan eligibility carries sixty percent rules on who is enrolled, who graduates, and how its students and graduates perform on the medical licensing examinations.
plaw-108-99-2003: Religious workers keep a visa path under Public Law 108-99, passed by the 108th Congress in October 2003. The law amends the Immigration and Nationality Act to extend the special immigrant religious worker program by five more years. It works by a word swap in section 101(a)(27)(C)(ii): where the text said 2003, it now says 2008. The change takes effect on October 1, 2003.
plos-pbio-0020003:
Sophie I. Candille, Catherine D. Van Raamsdonk, Changyou Chen, and co-workers studied mouse coat color in PLOS Biology in 2004. Many mice have a light belly and a dark back. The team tied that top-to-bottom pattern to a gene called Tbx15.

Tbx15 helps set up body plans as an embryo grows. The study shows it also shapes where dark and light hair form along the back and belly. That is a neat case of one gene doing pattern work in both the body plan and the skin. The finding helps explain how animals gain their markings. It also links coat pattern to deeper rules of growth that shape the whole animal.
plos-pbio-0020203:
Edan Foley and Patrick H. O'Farrell ran a genome-wide screen of fly immunity in PLOS Biology in 2004. They silenced genes one by one in fly cells, then exposed the cells to bacteria. Genes whose loss changed the defense response were flagged for a closer look.

A screen like this turns a vague trait, innate immunity, into a list of working parts. The hits included genes no one had tied to defense before. Each one is a lead for deeper study in flies and, by comparison, in humans. Innate immunity is our first line against infection, and its fly version is close enough to ours to make such lists valuable.
plos-pbio-0020303:
Naomi Ward, Øivind Larsen, James Sakwa, and a huge team sequenced a methane-eating bacterium in PLOS Biology in 2004. Methylococcus capsulatus, called Bath, lives on methane as its sole food. Its full genome shows the tools it uses to do that rare trick.

Methane is a strong greenhouse gas, and microbes that eat it blunt its rise. The genome reveals genes for trapping methane, handling its toxic by-products, and taking up metals the process needs. That blueprint guides work on using such bacteria to cut methane from farms, landfills, and gas leaks. It also informs the search for life signs on other worlds, where methane plays a key role.
plos-pbio-0020403:
Barış Genç, P. Hande Özdinler, April E. Mendoza, and their team traced nerve fiber guidance in PLOS Biology in 2004. Proprioceptive nerves carry signals from muscles that tell the brain where limbs are. As embryos grow, those fibers must find their way into the spinal cord and to the right targets.

A factor called NT-3 acts as an attractant for these fibers, the team found. Without its pull, the fibers stray. Guidance cues like NT-3 are the road signs of the growing nervous system. Mapping them one by one explains how precise wiring arises. It also informs efforts to regrow nerves after spinal injury. The adult cord lacks those youthful signs.
plos-pone-0000003:
Matthew Goddard, Jessica Leigh, Andrew Roger, and co-authors studied a selfish gene in the Cnidaria, the animal group that holds jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones. A selfish gene spreads itself through a population even when it gives the host no clear benefit. The team asked how such a gene invades and then persists.

Tracking the gene across cnidarian hosts let the authors test ideas about how these elements survive over long spans of time. Persistence is the puzzle: hosts evolve defenses, yet the gene stays. The study gives a concrete case for one of evolution's stranger claims, that selection can favor DNA that looks out only for itself.
plos-pone-0000103:
Jian Li, Samuel M. McClure, and Brooks King-Casas studied economic choices over time in PLOS ONE in 2006. In their game, players adjusted their strategy as conditions changed, much as governments adjust policy in a shifting economy. The authors tracked how people update their approach after wins and losses.

People did not simply chase the last good result. Their adjustments followed patterns that simple learning rules only partly capture. Games like this are the lab bench of neuroeconomics, the study of how brains make value choices. Knowing how strategies drift in dynamic settings matters for real policy too, where each new rule changes the game it governs.
plos-pone-0000203:
Jittima Piriyapongsa and I. King Jordan published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that fine-tune gene activity. The authors identify a family of human microRNA genes that arose from miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements, small pieces of jumping DNA known as MITEs.

Genes born from jumping DNA show how genomes recycle their own clutter into working parts. The paper traces this family's origin and spread in the human genome. It adds to the evidence that transposable elements, often dismissed as junk, are a real source of new regulatory genes.
plos-pone-0000303:
Christian G. Noble and Haiwei Song published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. eIF4AIII is an RNA helicase, a motor that unwinds RNA, and a core part of a complex that marks newly made messages. The authors show that the protein MLN51 stimulates that helicase activity.

A stimulator that speeds the motor changes how the marking complex does its job in quality control of gene messages. The paper defines MLN51's role in that machinery. Such detail feeds into the study of diseases where RNA processing goes wrong. Details like these fill in the wiring of a core cellular machine.
plos-pone-0000403:
Abhaya V. Kulkarni, Jason W. Busse, and Iffat Shams asked what makes a medical paper get cited, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Citations are the currency of science: a paper that others cite shapes the field, while an ignored one sinks. The team looked for traits of papers that are linked to a higher citation rate.

Knowing which features go with influence helps readers judge a crowded literature and helps researchers report work so it can be found and used. The study is a piece of meta-research, science studying its own habits. Its lessons apply to anyone trying to tell landmark studies from the mass of published work.
plos-pone-0000503:
David C. Nickle and colleagues built statistical models of how HIV proteins change over time, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV evolves fast, dodging immune attack and drugs. Their HIV-specific probabilistic models of protein evolution capture the virus's particular patterns of mutation, which differ from the generic models borrowed from other organisms.

A model tuned to the virus reads its sequences more accurately, spotting which changes are meaningful. That helps in tracing transmission, predicting drug resistance, and designing vaccines against a moving target. The work is infrastructure for HIV research: better math underneath many other studies.
plos-pone-0000603:
Clara S.M. Tang and Richard J. Epstein reported an unexpected division in human DNA structure, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper titled A Structural Split in the Human Genome. The genome is usually described by its sequence of letters; structure here refers to larger-scale organization in how that sequence is arranged.

A split in genome structure, if real, divides the genome into two kinds of territory with different rules. Claims of large-scale order matter because they affect how genes are regulated and how variation is distributed. Short structural papers like this one stake a claim that later genome-wide data can confirm or dissolve.
plos-pone-0000703:
Hiroki Nagai and Guojun Sheng watched two chicken globin genes switch on together, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The chicken beta globin locus holds four genes. Two of them, called rho and epsilon, are expressed from the earliest stage of primitive hematopoiesis, the first wave of blood formation in the embryo. The pair sits side by side in the genome.

The authors show the two genes' transcription runs in on and off phases. During each on phase, they are cotranscribed, copied together in a shared burst. That coordination raises questions about how neighboring genes share control machinery. Blood development is a classic system for gene regulation, and this adds timing to the picture.
plos-pone-0000803:
Katsuyuki Hotta, Toshio Ogura, Kenji Nishii and colleagues evaluated a blood test for tuberculosis screening in Japanese healthcare students. The whole blood interferon-gamma assay, QuantiFERON-TB-2G, had not been fully evaluated as a baseline screening test in students about to begin clinical contact with patients. Their 2007 PLOS ONE aim was to compare the assay's results with those of the tuberculin skin test.

Baseline screening matters because healthcare workers face TB exposure, and a starting value separates old infection from new. A blood test avoids return visits and reading errors of skin tests. The comparison in a low-risk student population tests the assay where false positives hurt most.
plos-pone-0000903:
Sheila Costford, Nihan Kavaslar, Nadav Ahituv and colleagues studied a human gene change that boosts a key energy enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme, AMPK, watches over energy balance in cells and in the whole body. In muscle, switching it on guards against some effects of inactivity and poor diet.

The change they studied, called R225W, sits in the gamma 3 part of AMPK and makes it work harder. The title links it to more glycogen and less fat stored in skeletal muscle. Human cases like this are rare natural tests of what a drug target does. They show both the promise and the reach of AMPK in daily metabolism.
plos-pone-0001003:
Tom Little, Lenny Nelson and Ted Hupp found signs of fast evolution in a stress response protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some cancers grow from a mix of tissue damage, germs and local immune attack. The links in that chain are only starting to be unraveled.

Against that background, the team report a strong signature of adaptive evolution on the DNA sequence of a stress response protein. A sequence that changed faster than chance suggests it was shaped by real pressure, not drift. Which pressure, infection or damage, becomes the next question. The find ties an evolutionary pattern to a protein with a foot in cancer biology.
plos-pone-0001103:
Hiroyuki Kurata, Takayuki Tanaka and Fumitaka Ohnishi worked out how to find the critical reactions in a feedback rich cell model, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Computer simulations are needed to see how biochemical networks stay robust under stress or mutation. Sensitivity analysis links that robustness to network structure, but it usually gives only local answers.

The authors present a mathematical method to identify critical reactions in the interlocked feedback model, a standard test network full of loops. Reactions that carry robustness are the ones drugs and mutations hit hardest. A method that finds them reliably helps modelers spend experiments where they count.
plos-pone-0001203:
Knowing which genes are on in each tissue is basic reference data for biology. Henrik Hornshøj and colleagues built such a reference for the pig in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using gene expression microarrays, they profiled 20,000 genes across 23 healthy porcine tissues.

Most microarray studies chase genes tied to a disease or a stimulus. A catalogue of normal expression across many tissues is a different kind of resource: the baseline against which abnormal patterns stand out. Pigs are also a major model for human medicine and a food animal, so the profiles serve several fields at once.
plos-pone-0001303:
Knocking out a gene in a mouse and measuring which other genes change activity is a standard way to find a protein's targets. Luis Valor and Seth Grant report a caution about that method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using tissues from multiple lines of knockout mice, they found that gene expression changes cluster around the targeted gene's location.

Changes near the manipulated locus may reflect the engineering itself rather than the missing protein's function. The authors describe these clustered changes flanking targeted gene loci. Their warning affects how thousands of microarray studies in mutant organisms should be read.
plos-pone-0001403:
Ludovic Tailleux and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study that reads both sides of a TB infection at once. Gene chips let labs watch many genes switch on or off in a sample. The team used them on the TB germ and on the human cells it infects. No prior study had read both partners in this paired way.

Their paired reads map the cross talk as germ and host react to each other. Some host genes rose while germ genes shifted to meet the new state. A two sided map like this can reveal weak points on both sides. Those weak points may yield new drug or shot targets for a disease that still kills widely.
plos-pone-0001503:
Hilde Krol and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a class of brain ills tied to a stretched protein tract. In these ills, a tract of one building block grows too long in a protein. Brains show clumps of the stretched protein, which were thought to drive harm. The team tracked one such protein, ataxin-1, live in cells.

They found the stretched protein moves faster, not slower, in cells. It also did not form clumps in their tests. That breaks the simple clump tale for this protein. Harm may come from the free protein's acts, not from clumps, which shifts drug aims.
plos-pone-0001603:
Heungjeong Woo and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a mouse model of salmonella gut ill. Mice fed salmonella by mouth do not get diarrhea as people do. A dose of germ drugs first makes them prone to gut inflammation, but gene prone mice die of body wide infection first. The team built a model in hardy mice that get the gut ill.

Their mice show diarrhea with the gut harm, much like human cases. A model that mirrors the human course lets labs test vaccines and drugs with more faith. It also helps sort gut harm from body wide spread, two ills with unlike needs.
plos-pone-0001703:
Koichi Iijima, Hsueh-Cheng Chiang, Stephen A. Hearn, and their co-authors used fruit flies to test Alzheimer's-linked protein variants in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Clumping of the amyloid-beta-42 peptide in the brain is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and stopping clumping is a proposed treatment. Yet the peptide can form several kinds of assemblies, not all equally harmful.

The team made Aβ42 mutants with different aggregation profiles and expressed them in Drosophila. Different variants induced distinct pathologies in the flies, per the paper's title. The full text gives the variants, the fly brain damage, and the behavior effects. Separating which assemblies hurt most sharpens the target for anti-amyloid drugs, a field with many failed trials.
plos-pone-0001803:
Takeshi Nagashima, Takahiro Suzuki, Shinji Kondo, and their co-authors profiled gene activity in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Heregulin beta-1 is a signal that activates MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways through ErbB receptors. Those pathways can add phosphate tags to the estrogen receptor at one site, Ser-118. That raises the question of how much the estrogen receptor matters in the response.

Their gene activity analysis shows heregulin can drive genes without the estrogen receptor in MCF-7 cells. The full text gives the gene sets and the pathway tests. If heregulin drives genes without the estrogen receptor, hormone blocking breast cancer drugs may leave this route open, which matters for resistant tumors.
plos-pone-0001903:
Jenia Semyonov and colleagues asked which gene families survive genome doubling, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. At rare points in the past, whole genomes were copied at once, leaving most genes in pairs. Most spare copies are lost with time, yet some families keep theirs far more often than chance would suggest.

The team reports that genes for G protein-coupled receptors, a huge family of cell signal catchers, are kept at high rates after such doublings. That bias hints that extra copies of signal genes paid off in survival. The work helps explain how complex signal webs grew, and why some gene families are so large today.
plos-pone-0002003:
Elie Aoun and co-authors pooled past studies to decode a gene risk in a pancreas illness, in a 2008 PLOS ONE meta-analysis. Chronic pancreatitis is long-term inflammation of the pancreas with lasting harm. One gene form, the SPINK1 N34S haplotype, marks high risk, but how it interacts with trypsin-driven injury and alcohol-driven injury was undefined.

The team set out a model in which the illness can arise by several paths, then tested it against pooled data. Sorting paths matters, since care for an alcohol-driven case may differ from care for a gene-driven one. The study gives doctors a frame for a mixed-cause illness.
plos-pone-0002103:
Sara Thomas and co-authors read the genome of a versatile soil bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Anaeromyxobacter dehalogenans strain 2CP-C is a delta-proteobacterium found in many soils and sediments. Its ribosomal RNA gene groups it with the myxobacteria, social bacteria with striking traits, yet its genome is a mosaic of pieces from many sources.

As the title states, that mosaic suggests an aerobic common ancestor for the delta-proteobacteria, a group now rich in oxygen-shunning forms. A patchwork genome can record a past way of life that the modern cell has left behind.
plos-pone-0002203:
Isabelle George, Hugo Cousillas, and Jean-Pierre Richard looked for the brain basis of sound grouping in songbirds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Sorting sounds into classes is basic to thought, but finding where the brain does it is hard. Songbirds are a good test case because they sort songs and calls and learn them socially.

The team searched for a neural substrate, a brain area whose activity matches the sorting of complex acoustic signals into functional classes. A songbird that treats some calls as one kind and others as another must have circuitry that draws those lines. Locating it would link animal communication to the wider science of categorization.
plos-pone-0002303:
Thilo Lange, Kyu Kwang Kim, Rakesh Singh, and co-authors tested an iron-based compound against hard-to-treat ovarian cancer cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some ovarian cancers resist platinum drugs, the standard chemotherapy, leaving few options. The compound, iron(III)-salophene, is an organometallic molecule, built around a metal atom.

In this first study of its biological activity, the team measured its effects on viability, shape, growth. Cell cycle in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer cell lines. The compound showed selective cytotoxic and anti-proliferative effects, killing cancer cells more than ordinary ones. Early selectivity like this is what drug hunters look for before animal tests.
plos-pone-0002403:
Painter joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Corrie A. Painter, Anthony Cruz, Gustavo E. López, among others. Its subject is model for the Peptide-Free Conformation of Class II MHC Proteins. Major histocompatibility complex proteins are believed to undergo significant conformational changes concomitant with peptide binding, but structural characterization of these changes has remained elusive.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002503:
Ma led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Yanqing Ma, Craig C. Malbon, David L. Williams, among others. Its subject is altered Gene Expression in Early Atherosclerosis Is Blocked by Low Level Apolipoprotein E. Mice deficient in apolipoprotein E (apoE −/−) develop atherosclerosis.

The possible linkage between expression of adhesion molecules/cofactors and atherosclerosis was probed at the level of mRNA and protein expression. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002603:
Fishman and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Yelena Fishman, Eliahu Zlotkin, Daniel Sher, among others. Its subject is expulsion of Symbiotic Algae during Feeding by the Green Hydra – a Mechanism for Regulating Symbiont Density?. Algal-cnidarian symbiosis is one of the main factors contributing to the success of cnidarians, and is crucial for the maintenance of coral reefs.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002703:
Xincheng Zheng and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was modulation of NKT cell development by B7-CD28 interaction: an expanding horizon for costimulation. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Xincheng Zheng, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. It has been demonstrated that the development of NKT cells requires CD1d. It goes on to note a further point. The contribution of costimulatory molecules in this process has not been studied. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002803:
Qingfa Wu and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on poly A- transcripts expressed in HeLa cells. The catalog record names Qingfa Wu first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Transcripts expressed in eukaryotes are classified as poly A+ transcripts or poly A- transcripts based on the presence or absence of the 3′ poly. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002903:
Kamija Phiri, Job Calis, Brian Faragher and colleagues followed Malawian children after severe anaemia in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Severe anaemia is common in African children admitted to hospital and often proves fatal. What happens to survivors over the long term was unknown when the study began.

Early reports had warned that survivors might face later illness and death. The team tracked outcomes to test that concern with real follow-up data. Child health programs in Africa can use such results to decide whether care should extend well past discharge from hospital. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003003:
Suraiya Rasheed, Jasper Yan, Alex Lau and co-authors profiled proteins in HIV-infected cells in 2008. People with HIV develop metabolic problems including insulin resistance, fat redistribution, and abnormal blood lipids. These were tied to antiretroviral drugs, yet infected individuals also showed changes beyond drug effects.

Using proteomics, the team reports HIV replication itself raises free fatty acids, low density lipoproteins, and many key lipid metabolism proteins. Published in PLOS ONE, that shifts part of the blame from drugs to the virus. It may change how metabolic care for HIV patients is planned. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003103:
Ching-Shan Chou, Qing Nie and Tau-Mu Yi modeled yeast cell polarization under spatial gradients in 2008. Cells polarize by localizing internal components to specific locations in response to external signals. Yeast, for example, forms a mating projection toward the source of mating pheromone, a chemical gradient.

Polarization raises specific challenges in robustness: cells must aim accurately despite noise. The model weighs tradeoffs between robustness goals, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, those tradeoffs are general design principles for any cell that must sense a faint gradient, from immune cells to neurons. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003203:
Jacqueline Chevalier and co-authors track a drug pump in hospital germs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Deaths from infectious disease are set to rise as germs evolve resistance to antibiotics faster. Each new defence germs gain wears down the drugs doctors can use. Pumps that throw drugs out of the cell are one such defence.

The team compare the pump in strains of Enterobacter aerogenes taken from patients in 1995 and in 2003. Readers see how the pump changed over eight years of drug use. That record shows how treatment itself can breed harder infections.
plos-pone-0003303:
Paul C. Sereno, Ricardo N. Martinez, Jeffrey A. Wilson and colleagues report a new predatory dinosaur from Argentina in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Living birds possess a unique heterogeneous pulmonary system composed of a rigid, dorsally anchored lung and several compliant air sacs that operate as bellows, driving inspired air through the lung. Evidence from the fossil record for the origin and evolution of this system is essential.

The authors present evidence for avian intrathoracic air sacs in this new dinosaur. Readers see the bird breathing system traced into a meat-eating dinosaur. That supports a deep origin of bird-style breathing before flight itself evolved.
plos-pone-0003403:
Harparkash Kaur and colleagues checked malaria drug quality across Tanzania in this 2008 survey. Malaria care depends on pills that truly contain the stated drug. Weak or fake pills fail patients and breed drug resistance. The team bought antimalarial drugs from retail shops across the country.

Each sample was tested for what was really inside. The nationwide results showed how often buyers got poor-quality medicine. Substandard drugs are a direct threat to malaria control in hard-hit regions. The survey gave health officials hard numbers to act on. Shops, not hospitals, were where many patients actually bought their malaria pills.
plos-pone-0003503:
Hanneke K. M. Meeren and co-authors timed early vision in this 2008 study. Sorting sights into categories was thought to start well after first sight. The first hundred milliseconds were seen as an even, unsorted stage. Flipping images upside down disrupts face and object processing in known ways.

Using that inversion trick, they found category-specific activity very early. Brain responses differed by category within the first hundred milliseconds. Early vision thus begins sorting sooner than the old view allowed. The finding reshapes models of how perception builds. Faces are the test case here, but the timing claim reaches all vision.
plos-pone-0003603:
Joseph L. Mankowski and co-authors studied brain protection in virus-infected monkeys in this 2008 paper. HIV often causes neurologic disease even under treatment. Certain MHC class I alleles have been tied to AIDS outcomes. Their role in restricting brain disease was less clear.

In SIV-infected macaques, one MHC class I allele was neuroprotective. Monkeys carrying it resisted lentiviral disease of the central nervous system. Host genetics can thus guard the brain specifically. The finding may guide HIV neurology research. SIV in monkeys is the main lab stand-in for HIV in people.
plos-pone-0003703:
Raúl Y. Tito, Simone Macmil, Graham Wiley, and colleagues published this microbiome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The microbes living in the human gut differ between people and shape health in many ways. Modern samples alone cannot show what those communities once looked like. The team turned to ancient material.

They typed the microbes in two ancient human microbiomes and studied what those microbes could do. The census maps which organisms lived in people long ago and what jobs they performed. It sets a baseline for judging how modern guts, and their ills, have changed.
plos-pone-0003803:
Kaw Bing Chua, Kenny Voon, Gary Crameri, and colleagues published this virus study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Reoviruses were found in the early 1950s and named orphan viruses because no disease was linked to them. The group's earlier work had isolated the Melaka virus from a patient with acute respiratory disease.

Here they identify and characterize a new orthoreovirus from patients with acute respiratory infections. The virus expands a family once thought harmless to humans. Its characterization puts a new suspect on the board for respiratory illnesses that routine tests cannot explain.
plos-pone-0003903:
Krishnamurthy N. Rao, Stephen K. Burley, and Subramanyam Swaminathan solved shapes of ancient microbe proteins in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns a protein family found only in archaea. Archaea are microbes distinct from bacteria, and many of their proteins remain unknown. The family, called UPF0201, had no known job.

The team used X-ray methods to get the structures of four family members. Their shapes look like proteins that bind RNA, the cell's message copies. Tests still suggested these proteins are unlikely to bind RNA themselves. The work shows how shape alone can mislead about a protein's task.
plos-pone-0004003:
Eva Gross, Birgit Busse, Matthias Riemenschneider, and co-authors linked a gene variant to drug harm in cancer care in 2008. Some chemotherapy drugs, called fluoropyrimidines, can cause severe side effects. Patients with faults in the DPYD gene face high risk from them. The gene makes an enzyme that clears those drugs.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a strong link for one common variant. Testing patients before treatment could flag those at risk. Avoiding severe toxicity saves lives and hospital time. The study supports wider genetic screening before fluoropyrimidine therapy. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004103:
