Antonietta Anatriello and co-authors pool in 2026 observational evidence on whether popular diabetes and weight drugs raise the risk of eye damage. Concerns cover retinal disease, glaucoma, and a rare optic nerve stroke. Their meta-analysis gathered twenty-eight observational studies in people with diabetes, comparing these GLP-1 drugs with other diabetes treatments.

No outcome showed a clear increase in risk with the drugs. Rates of the optic nerve event, glaucoma, and new or worsening retinal disease all landed close to the comparison groups. The studies, however, disagreed strongly with one another, which weakens certainty in the pooled numbers. The authors conclude that monitoring eyes during treatment remains wise while the reassuring signal is tested in better controlled research.
pmc-13269203:
Ahmad Al Aiyan and co-authors map in 2026 the arteries feeding the horse brain, a reference long missing for veterinary neurology. They injected colored latex into the neck arteries of ten preserved adult horse heads, then dissected and photographed the vessels from many angles. Horses have large, folded brains that depend on uninterrupted blood flow.

Every specimen showed a complete, symmetrical arterial circle joining the carotid and basilar systems at the brain's base. The front artery fed the inner front cortex and the bridge between hemispheres, the middle artery fed the side surfaces, and the back artery fed the rear lobes. Small connecting variations appeared in most specimens without breaking the overall pattern. The map supports reading brain scans and planning future clinical studies in horses.
pmc-13269303:
Masamichi Isogai and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a virus-like sequence found inside gentian plants. Deep reading of small RNA from plants with kobu-sho, a serious gentian disease, turned up pieces matching a known virus family. The team checked whether a live virus was present.

The full sequence looked like a new virus, yet no free virus form was found in the plants. Instead, 1,929 short pieces of it sat spread across the plant's own genome, most far shorter than the full virus. Many pieces were broken or changed, so they can no longer copy themselves. The authors class it as a built-in, non-infectious remnant of an old virus.
pmc-13269403:
Hui Wang and co-authors investigate in 2026 damage to the blood vessel lining's sugar coat in intensive care patients with bacterial bloodstream infection. That coating, the glycocalyx, sheds a marker called syndecan-1 into blood when injured, and its loss is tied to sepsis harm. In 188 patients, the team measured twenty-four blood markers and gene activity alongside syndecan-1 levels.

Higher syndecan-1 meant higher risk of death within thirty days, independent of other factors. Illness severity explained most of the marker's variation, while the infecting germ type explained very little. Damage tracked with vessel dysfunction first, then inflammation and clotting changes, and gene data showed heightened platelet activity. The coating's state, the authors argue, reflects how sick the patient is more than which bacterium caused it.
pmc-13269603:
Mahdie Jajroudi and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 predicting how Hodgkin lymphoma tumors respond to treatment, lesion by lesion. Their method mines medical scans for thousands of measured features, varied across many settings. A deep learning network then selects features and makes the prediction.

Scans from 70 patients yielded 420 lesions and 13,790 features each. The new network scored 0.8470 on a standard accuracy curve, finding 82.2 percent of responding lesions and clearing 78.2 percent of others. It beat three standard machine learning models, including a boosting method at 0.8160. An explanation tool showed which features drove each prediction. The authors aim at more personal therapy choices.
pmc-13270403:
Zongzhi Li and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on Chinese water deer in fragmented habitats of northeastern China. The species is classed as vulnerable. Non-invasive samples from 286 deer were tested at 11 DNA markers plus inheritance markers passed through mothers, to measure diversity and movement between groups.

Diversity was moderate, and signs of inbreeding appeared within local groups. Yet overall population structure was extremely weak, and current gene flow stayed high despite fragmentation. The reason was female-biased dispersal, unusual for hoofed animals, where males usually roam. Female movement acts as a natural genetic rescue, the authors argue. They urge protecting corridors that let females travel.
pmc-13270803: Fereshteh Falah is first named author on a 2026 correction notice for an article screening yeast strains for possible probiotic use. The strains came from farm-industry and animal stomach sources. The article also named them with a DNA-based method. The correction states that Behrooz Alizadeh Behbahani was missed as a corresponding author during the production process. It says the original article has been updated. It lists contact details for the corresponding authors.
pmc-13272003:
Abdullah Faiz Zaihan and coauthors present in 2026 a case of insulinoma, an insulin-making pancreatic tumor, arising during pregnancy. Fewer than thirty such cases are reported worldwide, and pregnancy symptoms mask the low blood sugar the tumor causes. Delay risks harm to both mother and baby.

A 36-year-old woman came in at seven weeks pregnant with repeated low-sugar episodes and later weight loss. Blood tests showed insulin that stayed high when it should fall, and a scan found a pancreatic lump over two centimeters wide. Specialists deferred surgery, controlled sugar partly with octreotide, and delivered at thirty-four weeks. A guided heat ablation after birth restored control.
pmc-13272303:
Mei Hua and coauthors catalog in 2026 the fungi living in and around the roots of a critically rare wild orchid in Yunnan Province. Cypripedium subtropicum survives in tiny populations, and its root fungi likely support germination and growth. Knowing which fungi occur where is basic knowledge for saving and propagating the plant.

High-throughput sequencing of root and soil samples from twelve habitats found tens of thousands of fungal variants, with Wenshan Prefecture holding the richest communities. Fungal makeup differed clearly between the root interior and surrounding soil. Wild and introduced populations in one county held similar fungal richness, a hopeful sign for reintroduction work.
pmc-13272503:
L. Li and co-authors compared primary and recurrent luminal B-like breast cancer in a 2026 genomic study. This subtype makes up a large share of breast cancers and returns more often than the luminal A form. The team wanted to learn which changes drive recurrence and which might be treated.

They sequenced DNA from a panel of cancer genes and also read RNA in samples from 15 patients. Most mutations and copy changes were already present in the first tumor and stayed through recurrence. TP53 and PIK3CA were altered most often, while some changes appeared only later. Recurrent tumors showed more T cells, and greater unevenness in the first tumor linked to shorter time without return.
pmc-13272603:
Alfonso Alarcon leads a 2026 study of how a bacterium, Burkholderia cepacia, changes its internal chemistry while making a biodegradable plastic. The plastic group is called polyhydroxyalkanoates, or PHA, and oleic acid was fed as the carbon source. High cost is the main bar to wider use of such plastics.

Using two kinds of mass spectrometry, which sort molecules by weight, the team found 24 key metabolites by one method and 223 by the other. The changes involved fat burning, energy release, and sugar pathways. A molecule called acetyl-CoA sat at the crossroads of cell upkeep and plastic making, and shifted with nutrient changes.
pmc-13273003:
Pedro Zavala leads a 2026 cohort study of thigh strength after revision knee ligament surgery, comparing graft choices. For a second anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, surgeons may reuse tissue from the front tendon system or use hamstring tendon. Strength balance between legs at six months was the main measure in 53 patients.

Patients who switched from a front tendon graft to hamstring had the best strength balance, at 88 percent. Those who used a front tendon graft for the revision scored 69 to 70 percent, regardless of their first graft. No clear difference appeared between the two front-tendon revision groups. The authors conclude that a front graft for revision is linked to lower thigh strength at six months.
pmc-13274103:
Lukas Andreas Basedow and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on stigma toward people with cannabis use disorder. Stigma can keep people from entering treatment. The German web survey asked readers to judge short case stories about an adolescent and an adult with the disorder, meaning cannabis use they could not control.

In total, 1,603 people took part, including 501 adolescents, chosen to mirror the wider population. The adolescent case drew more stigma than the adult case. People who knew cannabis use or the disorder more closely gave fewer blaming answers. That softening effect of familiarity was stronger when the case was an adolescent rather than an adult.
pmc-13274303:
Patpong Rongkard and a large team present a 2026 case-control study on how diabetes changes the immune response in two serious infections. Diabetes raises the risk of melioidosis, a tropical bacterial infection, about twelve-fold, and of tuberculosis about three-fold. The team sequenced all active genes in blood from patients in several countries.

They studied eighty-one melioidosis patients from northeast Thailand and 151 tuberculosis patients from four other countries, plus uninfected controls. In both infections, diabetes came with an over-heated inflammatory response, with overactive clotting and scavenger pathways. In tuberculosis, diabetes also blunted interferon signaling, a key antiviral-style defense. The authors say these patterns could guide future immune-boosting treatments.
pmc-13274503:
Grace Woolway and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on the emotional cost to psychologists of hearing clients' trauma stories. Absorbing others' trauma can reshape a therapist's beliefs about self and world, a strain called vicarious trauma. The team surveyed United Kingdom practitioner psychologists who had been exposed to such stories at work.

In total, 255 psychologists completed the survey and reported moderate levels of vicarious trauma. Higher trauma scores came with higher burnout across personal, work, and client-related measures. Both burdens ran higher in psychologists scoring low on self-compassion. Self-compassion did not clearly buffer the trauma-to-burnout link, though one sub-check hinted self-kindness might soften it slightly. The authors back routine screening.
pmc-13275203:
Marcin Marciniak and colleagues present a 2026 journal article analyzing Reddit discussions of tongue-tie, a tight strip of tissue under the tongue that can restrict movement. Diagnosis and surgery rates for the condition have risen amid professional controversy. The team scraped 2,521 posts and comments from relevant subreddits between December 2018 and February 2025 and coded their themes and emotional tone.

Personal stories led the themes at 14.3 percent, then giving and seeking advice. Posters were mostly patients themselves or parents. Dentists and lactation consultants were the commonest diagnosers named. Overall sentiment skewed positive at 56.4 percent, but money worries and post-surgery symptoms scored lowest. Posting volume grew about forty-four percent every six months, signaling fast-rising public engagement.
pmc-13276103:
Douglas Blackwood wrote a 2026 commentary on Martha's Rule and what it means for surgical care teams in England. The rule is named for a thirteen-year-old who died of sepsis after her mother's warnings went unheeded. Since 2025 it has applied across English hospital sites.

The rule lets any staff member request an urgent review of a worsening patient by an independent team. Patients and families can trigger the same round-the-clock review themselves. Every inpatient must also be asked daily whether they feel better or worse, with answers recorded and acted on. Blackwood notes hospitals differ less in how often complications happen than in how fast they respond. Early data show most calls sparked by the daily question changed treatment or moved the patient to better care.
pmc-13277303:
Alysha K Lee, José-Luis Giner, and Paula V Welander identify a bacterial enzyme behind an unusual sterol shape, in a 2026 study. Sterols such as cholesterol are vital lipids, and some bacteria make versions with a rare double-bond position. No protein was known to create that arrangement.

Working in a methane-eating bacterium, the team expressed candidate genes in a test system. One reductase enzyme reshaped the sterol core, reducing one bond and shifting another into the rare position. Changing single building blocks in the enzyme showed which parts grip and transform the sterol. The gene appears only in bacteria, mainly in a few families, and likely evolved alongside a partner enzyme.
pmc-13277403:
Andrezza do Espirito Santo Cucinelli leads a 2026 image-based case report on white blood cell changes in severe COVID-19. A blood smear from a severely ill patient showed striking changes in neutrophils, a front-line immune cell type. The images show heavy toxic granules, poorly segmented nuclei, and an internal vacuole, a small empty space tied to active germ eating.

One image shows a mesh-like web of released chromatin, the cell's DNA material, outside a cell. Such webs, called neutrophil extracellular traps, can drive harmful inflammation and clotting when overproduced. Similar cell changes have been linked to disordered blood cell production in severe infection. The report uses one patient's smear to display signs of intense immune activation.
pmc-13277603:
Azade Kanat and colleagues present a 2026 case of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection with prominent rash and mucositis. The bacterium commonly causes chest infections and sometimes affects organs beyond the lungs. A rare reaction pattern, shortened to MIRM, brings striking mouth sores with sparse blistering skin lesions.

The patient was a healthy thirty-year-old veterinary surgeon treated for pneumonia in the left upper lung. Breathing symptoms improved on antibiotics, yet he returned a week later with new mucosal problems. Findings included crusted mouth lesions, inflamed eyes, and blistering spots on the trunk. The authors remind clinicians to weigh this infection when pneumonia arrives with mucositis or unusual skin signs.
pmc-13278703:
Osama Elazzouny, Joseph D Tobias, and Ibrahim Abdullah report a 2026 case where a hidden vessel variant surfaced during heart surgery. A six-month-old girl with Down syndrome was having a heart defect repaired. An ultrasound probe passed into her food pipe to watch the heart during the operation.

As the probe went in, the pressure trace from her right wrist line flattened unexpectedly. Imaging then revealed an aberrant right subclavian artery running behind the food pipe. The probe had pressed on the misplaced vessel and cut its flow signal. Such variants usually cause no symptoms at all. The authors urge teams to consider vessel anomalies when monitoring traces change without explanation.
pmc-13278803:
Kazuki Ueda leads a 2026 case report of protein-losing enteropathy cured by bowel surgery. In this condition, serum proteins leak through the gut lining, causing low blood protein and swelling. A 76-year-old woman arrived with diarrhea and edema, with a history of heart and vessel disease and past bowel cancer surgery.

Scans showed a swollen, inflamed end segment of small bowel, and a tracer scan pinpointed protein leaking there. Tissue exam after removal confirmed ischemic ileitis, damage from poor blood flow, with no cancer. Conservative care had failed, so surgeons removed the segment and later closed the stoma. Her blood protein normalized. Localized ischemic damage is a rare but treatable cause, the authors note.
pmc-13279203:
Elias Tjärnhage and colleagues published a 2026 study testing whether cancer drugs that block ALK-family kinases can be repurposed as antivirals against influenza and coronaviruses. Their target is LTK, a kinase that sits in the endoplasmic reticulum and controls how proteins are packaged for secretion from the cell. Because viruses depend on that same shipping machinery to build and release new particles, blocking it attacks the host rather than the virus, which should make escape mutations less likely.

The team evaluated repurposed inhibitors in cell cultures and in mice, and reports that dampening protein secretion reduced viral infection in both settings. Host-directed drugs could serve as a first line of defense when a new virus emerges and vaccines do not yet exist. The approach may matter most for elderly and immunocompromised people, who respond poorly to vaccines and suffer the worst outcomes from respiratory infections.
pmc-13279603:
Nafiye Koc-Inak and colleagues report a 2026 study of insecticide resistance in house flies from Turkiye. The house fly spreads many germs to people and food, and breeds fast in homes, farms and slaughterhouses. Control fails as resistance spreads. The team ran poison feed tests on five strains from slaughterhouses. They also screened gene faults tied to resistance in thirty five field samples.

Three drugs failed to kill the flies well: permethrin, deltamethrin and bendiocarb. One drug, thiamethoxam, worked in a mixed way by strain. Fipronil worked best of the set. Gene screens found high rates of two faults in the nerve channel gene that drugs target. Four faults in a second target gene also showed up. Ongoing watch of both kill rates and gene faults can steer local pest control.
pmc-13279703:
Mengting Wang and colleagues published a 2026 genomics study of orchid mitochondrial genomes and ties among recently diverged tribes of the subfamily Epidendroideae. The subfamily holds over 20,000 species, but ties among some young tribes stay disputed because flower shapes converge misleadingly. The team assembled the complete mitochondrial genome of the orchid Dendrobium chrysanthum from two sequencing technologies. They compared nine orchid mitogenomes and built family trees from mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes for ten species.

The Dendrobium mitogenome stretched to 638,041 DNA letters split across multiple chromosomes, a multichromosomal layout rather than the single circle once assumed for plants. Genome size and structure varied greatly across the orchids compared, while sequence similarity tracked known relatedness. Most branches agreed between the two trees, though some placements conflicted. The authors offer the new genomes as fresh evidence for sorting out the young tribes and as a resource for orchid evolution research.
pmc-13279903:
David Freire and colleagues present a 2026 geospatial dataset of oil wells and social risk marks in a coastal city in Ecuador. Oil well data aid study of how old hydrocarbon work shapes risk for people near by. In the coastal canton of Salinas, city growth has pushed homes, salt works, roads and fishing ports close to old wells. About two hundred twenty eight wells were drilled there since the early twentieth century.

The dataset joins well sites and technical traits with population, nature and city service data. Wells spread across urban and rural sectors of the coast. Past sets that join well and social data for coastal cities were scarce. With the join, analysts can map where old wells and weak services overlap. Town leaders can then rank clean up, health checks and land use rules by true exposure.
pmc-13280803:
Hao Cheng and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a very rare womb cancer. The cancer, called a yolk sac tumor, grows more often in the ovaries. Fewer than forty cases in the womb lining have been written up in English. Their patient was a sixty-six-year-old woman in China. She had bleeding for about two weeks and doctors found a mass in her womb.

Blood tests showed a very high level of a protein that this tumor sheds. Scans showed a mass about seven centimeters wide. Surgeons removed the womb, ovaries, and part of a fatty sheet in the belly. Lab checks confirmed the rare tumor, at an advanced stage. The blood marker fell sharply after surgery. The authors say full surgery plus drug care may give the best chance.
pmc-13281003:
Francesca Cutropia and colleagues published a 2026 study teaching a neural network to read structures as text. It predicts whether compounds disturb the androgen or estrogen receptors, hormone switches central to hormone disruption screening. Instead of computed descriptors, their bidirectional memory network ingests SMILES strings, the line notation chemists write, and learns its own features. An explanation method maps the network's attention onto the structure, coloring fragments that push a prediction toward or away from harm.

Trained on public sets of 1,664 chemicals for the androgen endpoint and 1,529 for estrogen, the models scored about 0.75 and 0.81 under cross-validation, though results varied between resamples on the androgen side. The authors emphasize transparency: regulators can see which fragment drove a flag rather than trusting a black box. They present descriptor-free reading as a practical route to faster, more readable screening of hormone-active chemicals.
pmc-13281403:
Mohammad Basheer Alameer and colleagues surveyed vape use among Syrian university students in a 2026 study. Vapes are sold as a safer, cleaner swap for smoking. Little was known about their use in Syria. The team shared a web survey on social media with twenty-six questions. More than fifteen hundred students replied. Questions covered what students know, how they feel, and whether they vape.

About one in four students vaped only, and about one in ten vaped and smoked. Friends were the top source of facts about vapes, ahead of media. Good taste was the top draw, then fun. Knowledge scores were low on the whole. Being male, having a parent who smokes, and a lax view of vaping each raised the odds of use. The authors call for awareness drives on campus.
pmc-13281703:
Wencke Walter and colleagues checked a claimed new subtype of blood cancer in a 2026 letter. The cancer is a fast leukemia of young white blood cells. A recent study had named a subtype marked by high levels of a gene called TWIST2. That subtype was tied to flaws in cell fuel enzymes. The letter writers searched their own adult records for like cases. They read gene activity in six hundred sixty cases and wider blood disease panels.

Seven of their leukemia cases showed the high gene signal. The signal also popped up in a few cases of three other blood diseases. That spread shows the marker is not unique to one subtype. Gene checks of the seven backed the fuel flaw link from the first study. But the flaw mix was varied, not one neat pattern. The authors say the subtype is real yet more mixed than first drawn.
pmc-13282003:
Öner Kilinc and colleagues compared camera angles in knee ligament surgery in a 2026 study. Rebuilding a torn front knee ligament works best when its tunnels sit where the old ligament sat. Surgeons view the joint through a slanted camera, most often at thirty degrees. A steeper seventy-degree camera exists too. The team read records of fifty-five patients from 2020 to 2024, all fixed by one surgeon with hamstring grafts. CT scans measured the thigh and shin tunnel spots.

Thigh tunnels in the steep camera group sat further back and lower. That is closer to the natural ligament's root. Shin tunnels did not differ between groups. Knee function scores at six months or later ran higher in the steep group. Thigh tunnel spot alone predicted function in deeper checks. The authors conclude the steep camera aids truer thigh placement. They note records-based work cannot fully rule out other causes.
pmc-13282403:
Elena Repges and co-authors report a 2026 study on a vitamin K recycling protein that shields blood vessel lining cells from a form of cell death. Vitamin K is known for helping blood clot in the liver. Its lesser-known relative protein, VKORC1L1, works in vessel walls. The team tested vitamin K2 in human coronary artery lining cells and in mice fed a vitamin K2-rich diet after artery injury.

Vitamin K2 raised cell survival and cut lipid peroxidation, the fat damage driving ferroptosis, that iron-linked cell death. Mice on the diet healed their artery lining faster without changes in clotting. Silencing VKORC1L1, but not its clotting relative, harmed cell growth and raised oxidative stress and inflammation. Vitamin K2 could not rescue cells lacking it, proving its role. The authors name VKORC1L1 a repair-promoting part of the vessel vitamin K cycle.
pmc-13282803:
Pengfei Luo and co-authors wrote a 2026 review proposing a framework, the neuroautophagic interactome, for how selective cell cleanup shapes brain disease. Selective autophagy is a disposal pathway that targets specific cargo, such as worn-out mitochondria and protein clumps, for breakdown. It keeps nerve cells in balance, and its failure is tied to degenerative disease, brain injury, and inflammation.

The review maps how this cleanup talks to cell death, inflammation, oxidative stress, and blood-brain barrier damage. Cleanup can protect neurons, yet in some settings it drives harm, a dual role the framework is meant to capture. Key molecular players include switches and tag-readers that interpret ubiquitin codes on cargo. The authors also weigh emerging therapies that tune the pathway to limit neuronal damage.
pmc-13283403:
Antibiotics packed into fat bubbles kill resistant gut bacteria better than free drugs, Barani Devi T's formulation team shows in 2026. Resistant Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Salmonella strains raise death risk in hospitals. Bubble carriers may push drugs past bacterial defenses more effectively.

Carriers were made by a thin-film method and loaded with three antibiotics. Sizes fell in a narrow nano range, and drug loading varied by compound. The carriers harmed kidney cells little in lab safety tests. They killed resistant strains far better than free drugs in direct tests. Release stayed steady over 24 hours, and imaging showed strong contact with bacteria. Pump-blocking effects were also probed.
pmc-13283903:
What looked like a heart tumor on ultrasound turned out to be a stomach hernia in a 2026 case from Rifah Anjum Samiha and colleagues. Hiatal hernia pushes stomach tissue up through the diaphragm near the heart. It rarely mimics a heart mass, yet location makes confusion possible.

The elderly woman had the finding during routine heart imaging at the clinic. A chest X-ray showed an air-fluid level behind the heart that hinted at hernia. Contrast CT of the chest then settled the diagnosis with clear images. The authors stress hernia as a key alternative when a heart mass appears. Simple X-ray review can prevent misdiagnosis where resources are limited.
pmc-13284303:
How teens feel after comparing upward on social media, not use itself, forecasts depression growth in a 2026 diary study by Andrea Irmer and Florian Schmiedek. Daily negative feelings that spike repeatedly may pile into disorder risk. Two hundred early teens logged experiences for fourteen days.

Ages ran from ten to fourteen years, with about half the sample female. Daily logs captured media use, upward comparisons, mood, and symptom checks. Teens whose mood dipped hardest on comparison days gained depressive symptoms. That path ran through higher average negative mood across the study. Media use coupling showed no such forecast effect. Emotional response matters more than screen time.
pmc-13284503:
Cinthia Jhovanna Perez-Martinez and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how oxidative stress may disturb a key light-sensing pathway in diabetic eye disease. Nerve damage in the retina can start early in diabetic retinopathy. The cGMP signal helps photoreceptor cells work and survive, and the enzyme PDE6 controls that signal by breaking cGMP down.

The review links reactive oxygen species from mitochondria and other sources to faults in PDE6 handling, including steps tied to AIPL1 and FAT10. Faulty PDE6 could upset ion channels and calcium balance, harming photoreceptor function. The authors frame PDE6 and cGMP as a redox-sensitive hub and a possible target for protecting vision.
pmc-13284903:
Lance M. O'Connor and colleagues report a large search, published in 2026, for microbes that live inside host cells and pass from parent to offspring in wild roundworms. The team screened three self-fertilizing Caenorhabditis species. No such inherited microbe had ever been found in free-living nematodes, even though related worms carry many other kinds of microbes.

DNA came from more than 4,000 wild strains after microbes passed between hosts had been removed. Unmatched sequence reads were sorted by type, and promising strains were checked directly with fluorescent probes. The search found no experimental evidence of inherited microbes in any strain. Readers get a careful negative result that shapes how worm biology is understood.
pmc-13286003:
Milad Dodangeh, Hamidreza Kanani, and Mohsen Soori describe a scope-based save for a stomach leak that would not close in a 2026 case report. A 33-year-old man arrived with a burst ulcer and belly-wide infection after a deliberate drug overdose. Surgeons patched the hole, yet eating too soon tore the repair and a second patch also failed to seal the leak.

With leaking fluid staying local rather than spreading, doctors threaded a camera into the stomach and placed a small curled drain across the hole. The drain gave fluid a path back into the stomach, letting the tissue heal from inside without a stent or new open surgery. Infection signs cleared within three days, and he left hospital about a month after the first operation. Checks weeks later confirmed full recovery with no return of the leak.
pmc-13286303:
Aditya Sharma and colleagues report a rare emergency in which two loops of small intestine tied themselves into a knot, cutting off their own blood supply. The 2026 case concerns a 78-year-old man with sudden bowel obstruction. Scans suggested a closed-loop blockage but could not show the knot itself, a common problem with this condition.

Emergency surgery revealed the knot and found about three feet of dead bowel near the end of the small intestine. Surgeons removed the damaged section and brought the bowel ends out through the abdominal wall as stomas. The patient recovered after the operation. The authors urge early surgical exploration when obstruction worsens fast, since delay lets more bowel die.
pmc-13286603:
Denise Lautenschleger Fischer and co-authors profile airway inflammation in young cystic fibrosis patients in a 2026 observational study. Twelve patients aged 6 to 18 gave sputum on a single test day alongside breathing tests and a cycling fitness exam. Their marker levels stood against saliva from healthy peers, and the team probed ties to lung function, fitness, and antibiotic use.

Patient sputum bristled with neutrophils and carried far more interleukin-8 than control saliva. A marker of oxidative damage also ran higher in the patient group. One interleukin tracked days spent on antibiotics closely, while interleukin-8 rose as a mid-range airflow measure fell. Fitness scores, notably, showed no link to the inflammatory markers. The pattern ties airway chemistry to lung health and illness burden even in stable patients.
pmc-13286903:
Vasileios Kapralos and Matthias Zehnder put eight pre-mixed root canal sealers sold as bioceramics through a battery of physical and chemical tests. The 2026 study checks what makers disclose, which elements the products contain, and how they behave against an international standard for flow, visibility on X-rays, and setting time.

Paperwork was incomplete: most products hid their dispersing agents, and half left cement ingredients vague. Half the sealers related to Portland cement and half were aluminum-free silicates. All passed the flow and visibility requirements, while setting times ranged from about two hours to nearly three days. Aluminum-containing products set faster and hardened more. All kept an alkaline environment for a month, though calcium release and aluminum leakage varied.
pmc-13287103:
Petra Fikrova and colleagues test which adhesion molecule really drives liver vessel inflammation in a 2026 cell study. Endoglin helps immune cells stick to vessel walls elsewhere in the body, and oxidized cholesterol builds up in fatty liver, so the pair seemed destined to interact in liver sinusoidal cells. Human cells of that type were dosed with an oxidized cholesterol compound while surface proteins and white cell sticking were measured, with blocking antibodies sorting out credit.

The treatment did inflame the cells and sharply raised monocyte sticking. But endoglin fell rather than rose, and blocking it changed nothing about the sticking. The adhesion molecule ICAM-1 climbed steeply, and blocking it alone erased the extra adhesion. VCAM-1 also fell in the pattern. The authors conclude this vessel bed runs its inflammatory sticking through ICAM-1, and warn against importing endoglin's reputation from other vessels.
pmc-13287203:
Jesus Gomez-Escudero and colleagues studied in 2026 how blood vessel cells inside mouse breast tumours change during long treatment with doxorubicin, a widely used chemotherapy drug. Tumours that first shrank and later regrew were examined for shifts in vessel cell types and the signals those cells send.

Regrowing tumours held a vessel cell group with growth and inflammatory signalling switched on. Another new group carried markers tied to clearing drugs and handling oxidative stress, which may blunt treatment and support new vessel growth. The authors argue that vessel adaptation, not only cancer cell change, helps explain why chemotherapy stops working.
pmc-13287403:
Stefanos Karakolias and Artemis Palla surveyed 120 volunteer platelet donors in 2026 across five public hospital units in Attica, Greece, in the first study of its kind there. Donations took place between February and April 2025. Donors rated access, technical care, and how staff treated them.

Overall satisfaction ran high. Staff courtesy, respect, and attention scored best, and hygiene and skill also rated well. Access scored only moderately: donors named staff shortages, short opening hours, and long waits. Repeat donors were slightly happier than first-time donors. The authors recommend fixing hours and staffing to keep donors coming back for a scarce blood product.
pmc-13288603:
Chencha Chebo and colleagues compare two chicken types in Ethiopia in 2026. The study deals with climate fit. It sampled 262 healthy adult birds. Local birds numbered 122 in the set. Sasso birds numbered 140. Three landscapes were covered.

Most blood values did not split by breed. Season and landscape shifted results clearly. Local birds held higher values in most settings. Sasso birds edged ahead in wet highland seasons. They also led in midland wet seasons. Thyroid hormones ran higher in Sasso birds. Highland birds had the top hormone levels. Breed choice should fit place and season, they warn.
pmc-13288703:
Bjorn Zethelius, Mats Talback, and Rickard Ljung pit four comorbidity scores against plain age and sex for predicting death, in a 2026 Swedish register study. Their cohort held 5,010,261 residents born in 1975 or earlier, followed for deaths from 2015 through 2019, with scores built from hospital and prescription records at several look-back lengths.

Age and sex alone beat every index used on its own, including the Nordic Multimorbidity Index, the Charlson index, and the Elixhauser index. Adding the Nordic index to age and sex helped only slightly, while simple counts such as hospital days or filled prescriptions reached similar modest gains. When full history data are missing, those simple counts may serve nearly as well.
pmc-13288903:
Naiyuan Liang, Cheng Huang, and Qiang Pan study a Chinese folic acid program. The 2009 program gave rural women free folic acid. Their 2026 study uses it as a natural test. They track 1,953 children aged 10 to 15. Data came from a 2020 family panel survey.

Girls in high-need areas scored better on memory tests. Their math reasoning was also stronger. They reported fewer signs of low mood. Boys showed no such gains. Mental health gains clustered in richer homes. Brain gains spread more widely. The authors say food aid alone cannot close gaps. Social gaps still shape who gains most.
pmc-13289003:
Cristina Fernandez Turienzo and colleagues report a blood donor project in Sierra Leone. Their 2026 report covers Kono and Kenema districts. Blood is scarce in the nation. Paid and family donors fill most gaps. Past top-down drives failed to build trust.

Local hubs led the new model. Volunteers taught peers and rallied donors. Monthly drives used non-cash rewards. The project ran for eight months. It drew 539 units from 376 donors. Repeat donors made up 43 percent of gifts. Costs per unit fell by 40 percent. Good will and public praise drove most donors.
pmc-13289103:
Rennie Viah, Rashid Ansumana, and Emmanuel Komba Finoh study care choices in Sierra Leone. Their 2026 study ran in Bo District. It drew 500 women at two sites. One site was a city hospital. One was a rural birth facility.

Nearly all women cited push factors for care. Knowledge and awareness led that list. Culture weighed more for rural women. Means to reach care split town and country most. City women had more cover and cash. Rural women leaned on social and language support. Birth problems were common in both groups. How illness swayed choices split by place, though.
pmc-13289303:
Félix K Pham and colleagues published a 2026 study on how melanoma cell states shape immune neighborhoods and response to anti-PD-1 therapy. Nearly half of patients resist these immune drugs, even though melanoma often responds well. Tumor cells can shift form, and that plasticity may help them evade immune attack in distinct ways.

Tumors came from 57 people with stage III disease, sampled before adjuvant anti-PD-1 care and split by relapse within two years. Slides with many stains plus spatial gene mapping in four cases charted tumor patches, T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and lymphoid clusters. Groups of like tumor cells formed tight patches. The team defined a plasticity ratio from patch types to link layout with relapse risk and immune layout.
pmc-13289403:
Mannon Geindreau and coauthors report a 2026 mouse study on how combined vessel and immune therapy recruits killer cells into colorectal tumors. Blocking blood vessel growth plus releasing immune brakes helps some cancers, yet early immune steps inside tumors stayed murky. The team tracked the first wave of changes after dual blockade of VEGFR-2 and PD-1 signals.

CD8 T cells reacted early to vessel blockade and released a signal called IL-10 before gaining full killing power. That signal unexpectedly pulled natural killer cells into the tumor mass. Those cells then released a factor that matured macrophages and drew in more CD8 cells, sustaining attack. Cutting IL-10 signaling or killer cell function erased the treatment benefit in mice.
pmc-13289903:
Joseph J Shearer and coauthors test a 2026 question on whether protein risk scores for death in heart failure travel across populations. Heart failure kills many patients, and scores built from hundreds of blood proteins promise sharper prediction than clinical tools alone. Three published scores, each built in a different setting with the same protein platform, were compared in one community cohort for fairness.

Scores correlated moderately with each other and spread similarly across patients in the test cohort. Each step up in any score raised death risk, even after accounting for clinical factors, though gains shrank with adjustment. Accuracy for five-year death and calibration were checked against a clinical model. Scores stayed useful across pumping strength groups.
pmc-13290103:
Rebuilding teaching for one-year medical fellows is the aim of a 2026 educational improvement project led by Romy Yun at Lucile Packard Children's Hospital Stanford. Using pediatric anesthesiology as the test case, the team replaced a traditional syllabus with a holistic curriculum built on adult-learning principles and twelve teaching formats.

Survey results from 58 of 60 fellows across 2014 to 2024 were tracked on a statistical process control chart. Scores for educational content rose after the new curriculum began in 2021-22, and ratings for diversity, equity, and inclusion training also improved, while resources showed no change. Yun and colleagues argue the model can guide other short fellowship programs squeezed by clinical demands and duty-hour limits.
pmc-13290503:
Plant healing compounds ride nanocarriers into diabetic wounds in a 2026 review by Eko Sri Wahyuningsih and colleagues. Diabetic wounds stall because tissue regrowth is weak and inflammation never switches off, while plant chemicals such as flavonoids and polyphenols fight oxidation and swelling but dissolve poorly and break down fast.

The review focuses on two carrier families: silver nanoparticles, prized for killing microbes and available through green synthesis, and chitosan nanoparticles, which are body-friendly and stick to tissue. Both protect their cargo, push it deeper, and release it slowly, strengthening protection, germ-killing, and tissue regrowth in the studies surveyed. Wahyuningsih and colleagues weigh how they work and the steps still needed before such dressings reach routine clinical care.
pmc-13290903:
A young man's leg weakness turned out to be a mycobacterial infection strangling his spinal roots, Rocco Ricciardi and colleagues recount in a case report from 2026. The 36-year-old arrived with progressive gait trouble, left facial paralysis, a month of leg numbness, and new weakness.

Spinal fluid was strikingly abnormal: yellow-tinted, packed with lymphocytes, very low in sugar, and extremely high in protein. MRI showed thickened, clumped, enhancing cauda equina roots and involvement of the facial nerve, and PET lit up in the same places. pmc-13291003: Somya Mehra, James M. McCaw, and Peter G. Taylor issued a short correction in 2026 to an earlier mathematical study of Plasmodium vivax malaria and its dormant liver stage. Only the correction notice itself is present here, so the underlying model cannot be judged from this evidence alone. One symbol in Equation (10) was printed wrongly for a mosquito-to-human transmission rate and must be swapped, and Equation (16) is missing a constant that the notice restores. Readers using the formulas should apply both fixes.
pmc-13291403:
Caitlin Hibbs and colleagues compare early symptoms of young-onset and late-onset dementia in GP records, in 2026. Dementia before sixty-five often starts atypically, which delays recognition. The case-control study pulled records for 88 young-onset cases and 174 late-onset controls, matched by sex and practice. Symptoms from the five years before diagnosis fell into eight groups.

Young-onset patients reported emotional symptoms far more often in the last two years before diagnosis. Odds ran roughly two and a half times the late-onset group's. Social warning signs, such as work or relationship trouble, appeared more often at several earlier points too. Gait problems, by contrast, showed up less in the young-onset group. The authors say mood and social changes deserve weight when a younger patient raises memory concerns. Earlier suspicion could shorten the road to diagnosis.
pmc-13292003:
Shuo Wang and co-authors trace ultrafast light behavior in a modified nucleoside aimed at cancer therapy, in 2026. The molecule, 5ph-4TU, adds a light-catching arm and a sulfur swap to a standard building block. Those changes push its absorption from ultraviolet into visible and near-infrared light. The team fired laser pulses and ran quantum calculations to map its excited states. Such states decide whether it can spawn cell-killing oxygen species.

One excited state lived unusually long, about six hundred picoseconds, and glowed measurably. A structural twist that drains energy was blocked by a barrier the arm creates. From a later state, it slips efficiently into triplet states that drive therapy. Two-photon absorption reached into the near-infrared while keeping the same pathway. In cell tests, near-infrared pulses triggered singlet oxygen and killed cancer cells, with good tolerance in the dark.
pmc-13292203:
Zachary Warren and co-authors watch a battery electrolyte form in liquid in a 2026 study. Sulfide solid electrolytes conduct lithium well, and the argyrodite family adds a halogen for stability. How the key thiophosphate unit assembles in acetonitrile was poorly known. Raman spectroscopy tracked the mixture live, and X-ray diffraction checked the recovered powders. Three lithium halides, iodide, bromide, and chloride, were compared.

A Raman band tied to the thiophosphate unit grew fastest with chloride and slowest with iodide. A solvent band shifted in step, hinting that acetonitrile coordinates around forming species. Final powders matched the speed ranking in completeness. Chloride runs reached nearly full argyrodite, bromide runs partial product, and iodide runs mostly glass. Without any halide, solvent-bound intermediate phases appeared instead. The authors link the pattern to solubility, surface reactions, and lithium coordination. Halide choice thus steers low-temperature liquid synthesis.
pmc-13292303:
Ken Niwa's team reports a 2026 high-pressure experiment using metallocenes as single-source starting materials for exotic metal phases. Ferrocene and ruthenocene pack metal, carbon, and hydrogen into one molecule at atomic scale. The team squeezed them in a laser-heated diamond anvil cell to pressures up to 68 GPa, watching with optics, Raman spectroscopy, and synchrotron X-rays.

Above roughly 20 GPa both compounds turned opaque, which let laser heating couple efficiently. Treatment beyond 30 GPa broke the molecules down and produced a face-centered cubic phase in each case. That structure signals a metallic phase stabilized by light elements drawn from the precursor itself. The authors argue organometallic precursors open a practical route to exploring metal-light element systems at extreme conditions.
pmc-13293403:
Mingqun Lin, Nan Duan, and Yasuko Rikihisa study, in a 2026 paper, how the tick-borne bacterium Anaplasma phagocytophilum escapes from human white blood cells. The germ must live inside cells, growing in sacs before mature forms break out to infect anew.

Near exit points, the cell skeleton protein actin thinned where sacs touched the cell surface. Drugs that broke actin caused early, messy release of less infectious germs. A bacterial protein called AnkA sat with actin and partner proteins that link and trim it. Cutting those partners also sped early release. AnkA thus seems to time release by steering actin.
pmc-13294003:
Jianv Wang and coauthors report a 2026 case of mycosis fungoides occurring together with squamous cell carcinoma in a young man. Mycosis fungoides is the most common skin T-cell lymphoma and usually moves slowly through patch and plaque stages. Second skin cancers in such patients often follow light therapy, radiation, or skin chemotherapy, none of which this patient had received.

The 29-year-old had a 10-year history of itchy red plaques on the trunk, with fast worsening and ulceration over 4 months. One chest ulcer measured about 15 × 15 cm. The authors warn that new growths still need cancer checks even without classic treatment exposures.
pmc-13294103:
Moirangthem Lakshmipriyari Devi and coauthors sequence the transcriptome of Zanthoxylum armatum in a 2026 study of a traditional medicinal shrub. Leaf, stem, and fruit were sampled across seasons to find genes for berberine and sanguinarine production, two isoquinoline alkaloids, plus the transcription factors that control them.

Assemblies yielded tens of thousands of unigenes per tissue, with 5,576 simple sequence repeats found overall. Pathway genes such as BBE and SOMT varied in activity by tissue and season. Large regulator families included AP2/ERF and MYB-related groups. Linking gene activity to metabolite data could guide engineered boosts in target compound output.
pmc-13294703:
Abhaya Sharma and colleagues track which coronavirus variants circulated in Rajasthan, India, during 2025, in a genomic surveillance study published in 2026. A medical college in Jaipur received 602 swabs from positive patients between late April and early September, and 373 samples with enough virus were fully sequenced. Watching the variant mix in near real time helps officials spot recombinants and judge vaccine strategy.

One lineage, XFG, accounted for nearly half of all sequences, with its sublineage XFG.3 the single largest group. PY.1 and LF.7 families made up most of the remainder, while older lines had faded. Most patients were working-age adults, about a fifth had no symptoms, and reinfections appeared in nearly three in ten cases. Three deaths were recorded. The authors argue that sustained sequencing in the state is essential for preparedness.
pmc-13294803:
Lillian Hung and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for mapping research on screen-based artificial intelligence companions for older adults. Such companions, without a physical robot body, are promoted as answers to loneliness and unmet social needs in later life. Terms and study designs vary widely, leaving the field hard to survey.

Following established scoping review guidance, the team will search major health, psychology, computing, and grey literature sources. Eligible work must involve older adults and companions built mainly for company, conversation, or social support. Two reviewers will select and chart studies independently, with findings summed up through counts and narrative synthesis to expose gaps.
pmc-13294903:
Ancy Michel and co-authors build a maths model for gallium nitride fin transistors in a 2026 article. Vertical FinFET devices made from gallium nitride suit radio-frequency and power uses, but designers need reliable physics-based models. Their model covers a narrow fin channel on a gallium nitride base with a field plate gate.

Starting from a two-dimensional charge equation, the team derived formulas for surface potential, threshold voltage, current, and on-resistance. Results were checked against detailed computer simulations of a stepped gate device. Close agreement, plus strong simulated current values, supports the formulas as a practical aid for tuning future device designs.
pmc-13295003:
Fengkai Yang and co-authors check a new climbing machine for fitness testing in a 2026 study. Measuring maximum oxygen uptake guides training and heart-lung assessment, with treadmills as the usual standard. A vertical climbing device could offer controlled workloads if its readings prove trustworthy.

Thirty-one male sports students, averaging about 20 years old, completed maximal tests on both machines. Oxygen uptake, heart rate, and breathing measures from the climber matched treadmill values closely, with average error under ten percent. Speed control was accurate and repeat results were steady across sessions. The authors present the device as a valid, reliable option for standard metabolic testing.
pmc-13295803:
Patricio Arce-Johnson and co-authors gather the human trial record on maqui berry supplements, in a 2026 systematic review. Twelve trials from 2014 to 2023 qualified. The steadiest gains sat with the eyes: more tears, milder dry eye complaints, and calmer tear chemistry. Small trials and short runs cap how firm the claims can be.
pmc-13295903:
Laura Cardoso, Rakiya Saidu and Louise Kuhn review, in 2026, single-visit screen-and-treat care for preventing cervical cancer in poorer countries. Most deaths from this preventable cancer occur where multi-visit care loses many women along the way.

Treatment offered on a positive test, ideally the same day, cuts that loss, and the review weighs testing and treatment options for real clinics. Virus testing, including self-taken samples, proved more accurate than visual checks, while portable heat treatment matched older methods without gas supplies. Treating some women needlessly remains a worry, but missing treatment is judged the larger danger.
pmc-13296103:
Kenji K Kojima and co-authors announce, in 2026, that Repbase and Dfam, the two main libraries for recognising jumping genes in DNA, will merge into one fully open resource. Repbase moves to a CC-0 release and its curators join the Dfam team.

For three decades the pair have underpinned genome assembly and gene annotation, one built on expert-curated consensus sequences, the other on statistical family models with stored evidence. The authors say a single open framework should end split curation and access limits. The merger is presented as a foundation for future work on these mobile elements.
pmc-13296203:
Bohan Zhang and Zhen Gao apply a transformer-based learning method to sort kidney cancer subtypes from whole slide images, in a 2026 study. The three main subtypes of renal cell carcinoma carry unlike outlooks and care paths, yet telling them apart takes expert eyes. The team reworked a known slide-learning system by swapping its image encoder for a Swin transformer, keeping the slide-level gathering step the same.

Training used 928 slides from 928 patients in a public cancer atlas, with labels only at slide level. Across five test rounds the system sorted the subtypes with high scores, and the rarest subtype gained most. Heat maps showed where the model looked, offered as a guide rather than proof. The authors say outside testing and calibration must come before any clinic use.
pmc-13296303:
M. Carmen Cano-Lozano, Lourdes Contreras, and María J. Navas-Martínez study violence by young adults toward their parents in a 2026 survey paper. Prevention work, the authors argue, should address parenting practices and the young person's own traits together, rather than treating either one alone.
pmc-13296503:
Dror Robinson and colleagues follow inhaled cannabis treatment for stubborn chronic low back pain over five years, in a 2026 analysis. The 241 patients had already failed at least a year of standard drug and physical therapy. Each patient's earlier year on conventional care served as the comparison for later years on cannabis.

Pain, disability, and pain-interference scores all improved markedly and stayed improved through year five. Nearly all patients were still using cannabis at the end, and very few stopped for side effects or poor effect. Use of opioids and several other drug classes fell sharply over the same period. Because patients served as their own historical controls, the authors' design cannot rule out other explanations for the gains.
pmc-13296603:
Konstantin P. Shchukin and co-authors tune a fulleride superconductor directly on a chip by driving rubidium ions into a carbon film, in a 2026 paper. Older ways of adding alkali metals give poor control over the final composition, especially in thin films. An electric current pushed the ions in gradually while the sample sat in ultrahigh vacuum.

As the formula moved toward three rubidium atoms per sixty-carbon molecule, the transition temperature roughly doubled within the measured range. Smooth control by timing the current is the key advantage. The method suits battery research and other intercalated materials as well.
pmc-13297003:
Qinyao Sun and co-authors study, in 2026, the fine geometry of brain wiring in behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, a disease reshaping personality and conduct. Some tracts showed more geometric distortion, many front-to-temporal links showed less, and patients lost brain volume while network efficiency shifted. Lower distortion tracked with worse clinical severity scores closely. The geometry measure also sat in the middle of pathways linking brain shrinkage to symptoms. The authors present it as a sensitive new marker.
pmc-13297203:
Mohammad Islamuddin and co-authors watch, in 2026, kidney macrophages regrow after selective wipeout in mice, using a switchable ablation system and gene reading at four time points. Resident macrophages guard kidney health, but how their niche refills was unclear.

Kidney tube cells quickly raised a lure signal that stayed up as macrophages returned. Newcomers shifted from stressed and inflamed toward energy-rich, dividing states steered by a shared gene module. Early chatter between macrophages and tube cells, especially through osteopontin, drove repair. The authors flag the lure, the messenger and metabolic routes as repair targets.
pmc-13298103:
Weijun Li and others introduce a sampling algorithm for quantum states that must satisfy stated inequality constraints, in a 2026 methods paper. High-dimensional state spaces have awkward boundaries, which makes random sampling with specific properties difficult. Their Sequentially Constrained Monte Carlo approach builds samples step by step while respecting those limits.

One demonstration produced thousands of bound entangled two-qutrit states within minutes, far faster than independence sampling in their implementation. Other tests sampled states from sharply peaked distributions and filled bounded regions uniformly for parameter estimation. The authors present the method as practical and versatile as system size grows, within the sizes they investigated.
pmc-13298203:
Outlining tumors in breast ultrasound scans demands both the big picture and fine edges, and Shivpratap Singh Kushwah with co-authors built a network for exactly that in 2026. On benchmark sets the model scored Dice coefficients of 82.41% on BUSI and 86.62% on Dataset B, beating several existing approaches on overlap measures as well. The authors credit the mix of global context and direction-aware decoding for the gains.
pmc-13298603:
Half of multiple sclerosis patients in Saudi Arabia's Qassim region report bladder overactivity, and similar shares report depression or anxiety, found Mohammed Alqwaifly and colleagues in a 2026 cross-sectional study. They surveyed 262 patients at a specialist hospital during 2024.

Depression affected 53.4%, overactive bladder 50%, and anxiety 43.9%; night-time urination was the commonest bladder complaint, and urge incontinence was more frequent in women. Being single and having anxiety raised depression risk, while anxiety tied to being female and to depression itself. For bladder symptoms, anxiety was the only linked factor. The authors press for routine screening and integrated care for these hidden burdens.
pmc-13300003:
Seungwon Lee and others compare low-dose radiation energies in a mouse model of Alzheimer disease, in a 2026 experimental study. Cognition tests and brain markers for inflammation, amyloid, tau, and neuron damage followed treatment.

The kilovoltage treatment clearly slowed cognitive decline on both tests and cut inflammatory markers plus amyloid and tau levels in the hippocampus. Neuron and synapse degeneration also eased. The megavoltage version produced minimal, non-significant effects. The authors advise kilovoltage energy as the preferred protocol for this emerging therapy approach.
pmc-13301003:
M J Espinosa Pascual and co-authors validate a diagnostic interval trick for hard to classify fast heart rhythms in a 2026 two-center study. The team measured the gap between stimulus to atrial timing during pacing and the ventricle to atrial interval during the rhythm. They did so in twenty cases where pacing shifted atrial timing and terminated the episode.

The twenty cases split into twelve atrial tachycardias and eight reentry rhythms of kinds. Every atrial tachycardia showed a negative value for the interval difference, averaging below zero, while every other rhythm stayed positive. A cut-off at zero separated the groups on the discrimination curve. Atrial cases also ran slower with longer ventricle to atrial intervals. The authors offer the sign of one subtraction as a reliable tiebreaker for this corner.
pmc-13301203:
L Cobarro Galvez and co-authors measure how far vein isolation lesions spill onto the back wall of the left atrium for three energy types, in a 2026 remapping study. One hundred patients returning for repeat mapping after pulsed field, cryoballoon, or radiofrequency isolation were compared on isolated back wall area and the width of surviving tissue corridors. Anyone with extra ablation or scarred walls was excluded.

Radiofrequency covered significantly less, near thirty percent, with a trend toward smaller absolute area too. The authors conclude that catheter shape and deployment mechanics, more than the energy itself, decide how much of the back wall gets caught.
pmc-13301303:
Meltem Altınsoy and co-authors test whether a blood inflammation index mirrors the injured heart muscle seen on scans in acute myocarditis, in a 2026 study. Enhancement appeared in sixty-two patients, just over a third, and that group ran hotter on nearly every inflammatory measure. The systemic inflammation response index discriminated best, with an area under the curve near 0.94 and a cutoff above 1.33 catching over ninety percent of cases. It stayed independently linked to both the presence of enhancement and how much muscle it covered, in segments and percentage terms. The authors see an admission blood score that tracks injury burden, while flagging that one center's retrospective data needs prospective confirmation.
pmc-13301603:
M Asami and co-authors follow new wall motion problems spotted right after left bundle branch area pacing in a 2026 follow-up study. Five of them, about fourteen percent, showed fresh wall motion problems right after implant, mostly in the front septal wall the lead screws into. Ejection fraction barely moved across the group.

By year three a split appeared: patients with the early problem averaged an ejection fraction near fifty-two percent, below the roughly sixty-one percent of those without it. Pacing burden was nearly total in everyone, so exposure was equal. The authors read this as possible local muscle injury or uneven motion seeded at the lead site. They argue for ultrasound checks after this pacing style, rather than assuming a clean implant scan settles the question.
pmc-13301903:

Six studies covering 88 patients tested successive versions, with the final design used in 41 people across two trials. Placement succeeded in every attempted case, and pacing capture was achieved right after the procedure in all of them. Capture thresholds rose modestly over the first two days but stayed workable. Patients treated during valve replacement had less steady capture, leading the authors to advise fixing the lead after valve work finishes.
pmc-13302403:

Device-related infections over two years occurred in just under three percent with chlorhexidine and just under four percent with povidone-iodine. That gap, about a quarter lower in relative terms, was not statistically significant. Major heart events and skin side effects also matched closely between groups.
pmc-13302803:
Vitamin K2 fed to arthritic rats spared their knee cartilage, Emre Uzun and colleagues report in a 2026 animal experiment. Treated rats received eight micrograms of oral vitamin K2 daily for twenty-eight days before tissue examination.

Cartilage damage scores in treated animals came in at 4.25 against 11.10 in untreated controls, a wide gap. Treated cartilage also kept more type II collagen staining and showed less of the matrix-chewing enzyme MMP-13. The authors read the vitamin as slowing degeneration in this induced model.
pmc-13303103:

Overall variety looked alike across the groups, and no germ passed strict checks between the two arthritis groups. Early signals, though, showed Escherichia and Shigella up while Roseburia and Ruminococcus, both makers of a helpful gut fuel, thinned out. Inflammatory germs tracked how active the disease was. The authors flag these germs as candidate markers needing bigger studies.
pmc-13303403:
Roko Šantić and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how to protect muscle and bone while patients lose weight on GLP-1 medicines. The authors separate harmless lean changes from true strength loss, noting that function often holds up better than scans suggest. Their preferred support package combines food-first counselling, enough protein, structured resistance exercise, and management of stomach side effects. Supplements from creatine to omega-3 oils are graded as secondary options with thinner proof. Trials are urged to measure strength, bone, and nutrition, not weight alone.
pmc-13303603:
Sasha A. Fleary and co-authors describe a 2026 program report on building health literacy skills in community groups during COVID-19. A federal push funded local work to improve prevention habits and vaccination in underserved city neighborhoods.

From March 2022 to June 2024, a university public health school and the New York City health department partnered with four community organizations. The groups served neighborhoods of Black, Indigenous, and other residents of color hit hard by the pandemic. Training aimed to strengthen how clearly each group communicates health guidance and how well it meets cultural and language standards in its daily work.
pmc-13303703:
Yunjuan Ji, Liping Chen, and Xiang Shi track marriage satisfaction and low mood after childbirth in a 2026 longitudinal study. The early weeks at home can strain both a partnership and a new mother's mental health.

A total of 238 women from Nantong First People's Hospital answered standard scales at one, six, and twelve weeks after delivery. Satisfaction with marriage fell steadily while depressive symptoms rose over the same span. Earlier satisfaction predicted lower later depression, but depression did not predict later satisfaction. The protective link ran strongest for women without paid work, with low household income, or after cesarean birth.
pmc-13304103:
Dongyan Zhao and co-authors study a germanium-on-silicon light detector that multiplies signal through avalanche effects in a 2026 device report. Such detectors suit low-cost silicon photonics for sensing and data links.

A layered design separating absorption, charge, and multiplication zones was driven past its normal threshold with ramped gating. A steady dark avalanche current grew in proportion to the gate and heat generation, and straight-line multiplication continued even beyond the usual Geiger point. Traps at the germanium-silicon boundary help explain the behavior. Under infrared pulses the device showed self-quenching effects tied to shifting internal fields.
pmc-13304303:
Jiahao Liu and co-authors design, in a 2026 engineering paper, a bendable antenna that sweeps its beam across a wide arc for Ku-band communications. Patterned metal stubs create a slow-wave channel whose radiation escapes at a frequency-dependent angle, giving natural beam scanning. The four-element array swept continuously across roughly one hundred degrees of arc while keeping strong gain and efficiency over half across the band. Simulations and bench measurements agreed, and performance held under different bend radii. The authors target conformal wireless systems on moving platforms.
pmc-13305503:
