Caregivers of 139 children aged three to five joined across the Midwest between 2022 and 2023. Fewer than half judged weight correctly, and nearly as many rated their child lighter than charts said. Underrating tied to looser limits on food for health and weight reasons. Overrating leaned toward tighter weight limits instead. Pressing children to eat showed no link to misjudgment.
pmc-13307003:
Franziska Eckert tracked a cell-death marker weekly during combined chemo and radiation for rectal cancer in a 2026 study. Nineteen patients with locally advanced disease gave blood samples across long pre-surgery treatment.

The marker HMGB1 was compared with tumour size on magnetic scans before treatment and at weeks two and five, plus tumour DNA levels in blood. Higher starting marker levels matched larger tumours and higher tumour DNA shares in reported links. Marker paths wobbled during care, with steady rises in four patients who later showed poor tissue response.
pmc-13307103:
Chufan Ren extracted rock outcrops from drone point clouds in a 2026 study of the southern Junggar Basin. Slanted drone photos map scattered, plant-covered outcrops for oil exploration analogues, yet manual picking is slow and rare rock classes get missed.

A cross-scale attention network built on PointNet++ adds stronger data variation, sampling, encoding and loss tuning in the reported design. The test site holds Cretaceous Qingshuihe Formation rocks near Louzhuangzi. Results judge how well the method keeps sharp rock shapes while still finding sparse outcrop patches at field scale.
pmc-13307203:
Yuting Yan followed Chinese blood cancer patients after stopping BTK inhibitor drugs in a 2026 multicentre study. Records covered 37 people with chronic lymphocytic leukemia or its small-cell form who left this common drug class.

Mean age at stopping was 62.67 years, and most patients were male in reported counts at 67.57% of the group. Resistance drove 48.65% of stops and intolerance drove 32.43% in the recorded reasons. Next treatment most often paired an anti-CD20 antibody, and median time without progression on the original drug was 19.09 months. The data may help teams plan next care steps for men and women who stop such drugs.
pmc-13307303:
Dmytro Rozov used bile duct stents off-label to fix stubborn narrowings and leaks after infant oesophagus repair in a 2026 case series. Six infants treated between 2021 and 2025 at a referral centre received fully covered expanding metal stents by endoscope.

Placement and removal succeeded in every case, and clinical success reached 83.3% in reported counts. Leaks and perforations sealed completely in all such cases, while lasting opening held in half the pure narrowing cases. One long narrowing later needed surgery, with no major adverse events over median follow-up of 2.75 years. The team says the stent route should be tried when no child sized tool can be had.
pmc-13307403:
Ana Marco-Fuertes and co-authors study in 2026 drug resistance in bacteria taken from shop eggs across four hen housing systems in Spain. Over one year they gathered 1200 eggs from major supermarket chains and tested shell and contents against 15 drugs.

They found 49 Escherichia coli isolates, all on shells and none inside the eggs. About seven in ten isolates resisted at least one drug, and close to half resisted many drugs at once. Multidrug resistance was most common in organic eggs, at 61.5 percent in that group, versus a lower share in cage eggs. Outdoor access and wildlife contact may spread resistance, so tighter farm hygiene matters.
pmc-13307603:
Jennifer Stapleton-Kotloski and co-authors test in 2026 whether COVID-19 vaccines shield the brain, using brain wave scans in female cynomolgus macaques. Animals got rising doses of a psoralen inactivated vaccine, some with a DNA vaccine boost, and then faced the Delta variant of the virus.

Scans taken 41 days after virus exposure showed far more kept brain activity in vaccinated animals than in unvaccinated ones. Higher doses kept more power, and the boosted group kept the most of all groups in the study. Brain wave scans may thus catch subtle harm that standard images miss, and they offer a way to track vaccine benefit.
pmc-13307803:
Abdulrahman M Sheikh and co-authors design in 2026 a multi part vaccine against Toxoplasma gondii, the parasite that threatens people with weak immune systems most. Their design, named USM.TOXOII, joins bits of three parasite proteins and was built with software tools, then made in bacteria and cleaned for use.

Shots in BALB/c mice raised total antibody levels and two antibody subtypes in a clear way after the course. A cell signal tied to the Th1 arm of defence rose as well, while a Th2 signal stayed flat in the mouse group. Those signs point to a mixed body and cell response, yet live parasite challenge tests must still show true protection.
pmc-13307903:
Rosaria Iardino and a regional team survey hospital vaccination services for high-risk patients in Lombardy, Italy, in 2026. Forty health bodies covering 114 sites replied to a set survey form in 2025, building on surveys from the two previous years. Hospitals see at-risk patients often, which makes them natural hubs for shots.

Nearly eighty-seven percent of sites offered shots for at-risk people in 2025. Their own pathways existed for most risk groups in over half of sites, and diabetes services were most of all common. Staff shots against flu and COVID-19 led the offers to health workers. Offers rose year by year across the three survey years. The authors describe a regional model that is taking shape, not done. Catching missed shot chances during hospital visits is the core idea behind the plan.
pmc-13308703:
I Passaris and co-authors chart in 2026 which pneumococcal types cause non invasive disease in Belgium from 2022 to 2025, a large slice of total burden. Serotype 3 led the count with 178 cases, which is 12.7 percent of isolates in the cross sectional set.

That lead type weighed less on babies under two years than on older groups in the data shown here. Newer vaccines cover roughly half to four fifths of the types in play, by the counts in this survey. Low adult uptake leaves a wide gap, so the authors press for stronger adult coverage to match the tools now on hand.
pmc-13309403:
Riya Albert and co-authors report a 2026 study on triple-negative breast cancer treated before surgery with immune therapy plus chemotherapy. This cancer type grows fast and lacks the usual drug targets. A key question is which tumors vanish fully by the time of surgery.

Charts for 187 patients treated at two hospitals between 2021 and 2024 were reviewed. Overall, 57 percent of patients had no cancer left at surgery. Tumors with many immune cells inside responded far more often than tumors with few such cells. Response rates were similar across ethnic groups. The authors argue that counting these immune cells can help predict who gains most from the regimen.
pmc-13310403:
Miao Zhang and co-authors study how inflammation and clotting interact in psoriasis with artery disease in a 2026 article. Psoriasis is a chronic skin inflammation that also stirs whole-body inflammation, thickens blood flow measures, and disturbs clotting. Those shifts feed atherosclerosis, the artery clogging behind heart attacks and strokes.

Patients with psoriasis numbered 439 at entry, joined by 198 controls, before matching narrowed the set to 206 cases and 126 controls for fair comparison in the analysis. Vessel ultrasound sorted psoriasis patients by artery disease status. The artery group showed higher fibrinogen, a clotting protein, among other shifts. The authors sketch a three-way axis linking inflammation, blood flow traits, and clotting as a joint driver.
pmc-13311103:
Tongyan Ding and colleagues map germs and drug resistance in pus samples at a Shenzhen mother and child hospital in a 2026 study. Pus tests guide drug choice for deep skin and wound infections. Local germ patterns shift over time, so five years of hospital records were pooled.

Isolates totaled 586 in number from 2021 to 2025, with gut type germs in near two thirds. Escherichia coli led, followed by Staphylococcus aureus. Cases peaked in young children and women of childbearing age. Many E. coli made an enzyme that blocks common drugs, yet strong hospital drugs still worked. Local tracking supports wiser first drug picks.
pmc-13311303:
Mobin Rasapour, Hamid Mohajer, and Erfan Sabouri report a 2026 study of gut bleeding in COVID-19 patients and what predicted death. Bleeding is a known cause of death in this illness.

Charts from one hospital in Isfahan covered admissions from March 2020 to 2022. Of 7243 patients, 107 showed gut bleeding, and 63 stayed in the study after checks. Nearly half of those 63 died within 30 days of discharge. Vomiting blood and black stools were the most common signs, and most bleeds started during the hospital stay. The analysis weighed which patient traits tracked with death. Their charts also logged blood thinners given during care.
pmc-13311903:
Jinqiu Su and co-authors, in 2026, present a lab study testing two antibody drugs, rituximab and pembrolizumab, against endometrial cancer cells. One targets CD20, the other the PD-1 checkpoint.

Gene data showed both target genes run high in these tumors. Two cancer cell lines were dosed with each drug alone and together, then checked for growth, death, and cycle stage. Each drug slowed growth, raised cell death, and stalled the cycle in a dose-linked way. The pair together suppressed growth more than either alone. The authors see a case for testing the pairing beyond the dish.
pmc-13312003:
Régis Lambrecht Andrade and co-authors write a 2026 letter on ecthyma contagiosum, or orf, in a goat farmer. The viral zoonosis passes from sheep and goats to people who handle them.

The patient, a 46-year-old rural worker, had a painful ulcer on her right thumb measuring 1.6 by 1.0 cm and a smaller crusted spot at the base of her index finger. Both appeared seven days earlier and were first blamed on a spider bite. She had tended goats with crusted mouth sores, matching the animal picture. In healthy people the illness clears on its own, though weak immunity risks large, lasting sores.
pmc-13312103:
Xianghong Liu and colleagues report a 2026 immune-response study of orvacabtagene autoleucel, a CAR T cell therapy tested in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Regulators and developers watch for antibodies against the built receptor, since such responses could blunt the treatment. Among 157 treated patients in a phase 1/2 study, anti-CAR antibodies appeared in 44.6 percent of them. Rates and levels climbed over time, prompting a closer mapping of what the immune system was attacking.

Profiling found five dominant peptide stretches inside the CAR that antibodies targeted. Both IgG and IgM antibody classes recognized them. Most positive patients also showed an unusually persistent IgM response. Antibody status did not reduce CAR T cell expansion or survival, though the cells lasted somewhat less long in positive patients. The authors attribute the muted clinical impact to patients' weakened immune systems and prior lymphodepletion. They flag the mapped hotspots for future CAR design.
pmc-13312203:
Jiaxi Chen and colleagues examine, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how physical activity connects to academic burnout in middle school students, and which emotion habits carry that link. The survey covered 1,529 students at one junior high school in Huaihua, who completed scales on activity, burnout, and two regulation strategies: thinking problems through calmly and hiding feelings.

Burnout fell as activity rose, and it was strongly tied to both strategies. A closer analysis showed that cognitive reappraisal carried part of the protective link between being active and lower burnout. Expressive suppression behaved differently, weakening part of that protection instead. The authors caution that effects were modest, yet argue the contrast matters: how students handle emotions shapes whether exercise habits translate into relief from school exhaustion.
pmc-13313203:
Chen Kai and fellow authors report in 2026 on Twf1, a protein that handles actin threads, and its role in fat cell growth. Fat tissue grows by making more cells or by swelling each cell, and failed cell making leads to swollen cells, inflammation, and poor metabolism.

Mice fed a high-fat diet and mice slimmed by eating less gave fat samples from three depots for protein surveys, and Twf1 levels were checked by gene and protein tests. In cultured precursor cells the team raised or lowered Twf1 and then triggered fat cell formation with a drug mix. They tracked cell growth, fat making, and where the Yap protein sat in the cell. The results place Twf1 as a driver that moves Yap into the nucleus, linking actin turnover to the making of new fat cells.
pmc-13313303:
Tomasz Muszyński leads a 2026 study of how stomach removal and drug care change body makeup and nutrition in gastric cancer. Cutting out the stomach reshapes how the body handles food, and patients often lose weight and lack key nutrients after surgery.

The study followed 37 patients who had surgery plus drug care around it and had no spread of disease. Before surgery and at 6 and 12 months after, the team checked body mass index, blood counts, fats, vitamins B12 and D, iron, and proteins such as albumin. They also ran body scans by bioimpedance, asked about activity and quality of life, and scored nutrition and inflammation indexes. The long view helps care teams plan diet support for the full first year after surgery.
pmc-13314403:
Basma Mortada Fouda and Mervat Medhat study how AI-run conflict handling at work spills into home life, in a paper from 2026. Hybrid work blurs the line between job and family, yet most past work on algorithmic management looked at tech or firm gains, not at stress carried home.

The team asked how three forces shape the sense of safety of hybrid staff in the United Arab Emirates. Those forces are openness about AI, fairness of its rules, and digital watching by employers. In turn, that safety shapes family life at home. They used a design that pairs survey data from 420 hybrid workers, as counted in the report, with later deeper inquiry. The frame treats trust in AI as a social matter, not just a design one. Their work speaks to firms that hand disputes to software without weighing the cost at home.
pmc-13314503:
Madison Hawthorne and colleagues measure the gap between referral and real attendance in balance therapy in a study appearing in 2026. Vestibular rehabilitation helps dizziness, yet how many referred patients show up was poorly known.

The team reviewed charts of 243 adults, aged 18 to 80 years by the entry rules, who were sent for therapy at the Miami Ear Institute from 2012 to 2022. They logged age, sex, race, ethnic group, insurance, diagnosis, and scores on a dizziness handicap scale and a gait test. Area poverty was gauged by a deprivation index for each neighborhood. The aim was to size the attendance gap and test whether social or insurance traits track with who comes and who gains. Such data can guide clinics to close an equity gap in dizziness care.
pmc-13315203:
Joanna Sajewicz-Krukowska and co-authors compared early lung gene activity in chickens and ducks infected with H5N8 bird flu in a 2026 study. Chickens often die quickly from this virus, while ducks tend to get milder or slower illness, and the reasons for that gap are still unclear.

RNA sequencing 24 hours after infection found a similar count of changed genes in both species, but the pattern differed. Chickens showed a focused response built around innate defense and swelling signals, including interferon and cytokine pathways. Ducks showed a wider, more even spread of changes across many functions. PCR checks confirmed selected genes.
pmc-13316003:
Stephen PJ Macdonald and Sandra L Peake argue in 2026 that choosing between vasopressors and fluids at the start of septic shock care is a matter of clinical judgment. Shock care still debates how much intravenous fluid to give first and which targets to chase, two decades after early goal-directed therapy entered practice.

Later trials found no gain from the full early bundle. Yet an opening volume of 3 to 4 liters became usual care. Guidelines weakly advise at least 30 milliliters per kilogram within three hours, on limited evidence. Newer observational data feed fresh doubt, and the authors weigh early pressor use against fluid loading.
pmc-13316203:
Saddam Mustafa and co-authors swapped part of wheat flour for chickpea starch in bread in 2026, at 5 to 15 percent levels, and tracked dough, loaf quality, and digestion response. The swap improved flour water uptake and helped starch granules swell and gelatinize, lifting dough elasticity.

Spectra showed protein shapes shifting from disordered forms toward ordered sheet and helix forms, steadying the dough network. Yet higher swap levels weakened gluten, making bread firmer with lower volume, baking loss, and springiness. Color and flavor improved, likely through stronger browning reactions, and glycemic response was also measured.
pmc-13316303:
Kishore A Krishnamurthy led a 2026 mouse study comparing two forms of glycogen storage disease type I, called Ia and Ib, which differ in gene faults yet overlap in symptoms. Using liver-only gene editing, the team created both forms side by side for a fair comparison.

Edited mice of both types showed big livers, low fasting blood sugar, high lactate, and raised uric acid, with signs a bit stronger in the Ia form. Fat making in the liver rose in both, while only Ia mice showed mildly higher blood fats and liver sugar phosphates. Gene and protein reads mostly matched across forms, though immune and cancer-linked paths shifted more in Ia. The work helps explain why Ia patients often fare worse.
pmc-13317303:
Kentaro Okamoto and colleagues ask, in a 2026 intensive care study, whether a red cell transfusion truly raises venous oxygen levels in heart surgery patients, a common bedside hope. The measure, SvO2, balances oxygen supply against body use, but a rise does not always mean tissues fare better.

Records covered 1,352 patients given one unit with starting hemoglobin at or above 7.5 in the study rules. Hemoglobin rose modestly, yet average SvO2 barely moved, gaining just 0.08 points in the paired figures. Patients starting with low SvO2 were far likelier to respond, and each point higher at start cut response odds. Starting level alone predicted response moderately well, guiding smarter transfusion calls.
pmc-13317403:
Mahmoud H S Daoud and colleagues report a 2026 case of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, a brain swelling disorder, triggered by kidney inflammation after a streptococcal infection in a 20-year-old Sudanese man. The pairing is rare in adults and usually appears in children.

He arrived with a sudden severe headache, two full-body seizures, and painless loss of sight in both eyes. Tests showed kidney injury, blood and protein in urine, low protective complement, and sky-high antibodies to streptococcus, while scans found the classic swelling at the back of the brain. Blood pressure drugs, seizure medicines, and brief steroids brought improvement within a day, sight returned by day five, and kidneys healed in two weeks.
pmc-13318703:
Begüm Utz and co-authors review, in 2026, diagnostic biomarkers for ischaemic stroke. Brain imaging is the standard test, but scanners are often missing before hospital arrival. A fast body-fluid test could confirm stroke and separate it from bleeding or mimics. The review sorts markers from blood, urine, and saliva by pathway.

Blood markers are the most advanced so far. One brain protein, glial fibrillary acidic protein, shows high specificity for early subtyping. Many other markers rise too slowly or lack specificity. Urine and saliva signatures exist but remain experimental and unvalidated in large acute groups. No single marker suffices, the authors conclude. They back multi-marker panels with standard methods and early sampling.
pmc-13318903:
Yaoqin Zhang offers a 2026 survey study of writing anxiety among Chinese postgraduate students who learn in English. AI tools now help with drafting and language polishing. They also bring new uncertainty for second-language writers. The study asks how views of the technology shape emotion and performance.

Zhang proposes a Technology-Emotion-Performance framework joining acceptance, social cognitive, and appraisal theories. Students rated usefulness, ease of use, and trust in AI tools. They also rated writing confidence, anxiety, and performance. Positive views of the technology linked to higher writing confidence. Confidence in turn predicted lower anxiety. Trust calmed anxiety both directly and through confidence. Worries about integrity pushed anxiety up. The author frames anxiety as an appraisal outcome, guiding teaching strategies.
pmc-13319403:
Gilles Delahaut and co-authors review what is known about how fast throat and mouth tumors grow in a 2026 article. Growth speed before care starts might hint at how long a person will live or whether the cancer will return. Past studies used varied scans and math, so a broad sweep of the field was needed to weigh the claims.

Three databases were searched for work from 1990 onward, and 13 papers fit the rules. Eight gave a true growth rate, and nine tested links to length of life. Results clashed across studies, and gaps in design blocked any pooled verdict. Growth speed may still guide personal care plans, but firm proof needs shared methods first.
pmc-13319703:
Weiqian Wang and co-authors press walnut meal protein under high pressure in a 2026 study of shape change and food use. Walnut meal is a cheap plant protein source that goes to waste, yet how hard pressing reshapes it at the tiny scale was unclear. Press levels and times were varied to map the shifts.

Strong pressing cut how well the protein dissolved, from near half to a small share at the top dose, while clumps grew and surfaces turned more water shy. Shape probes showed looser folds and more sheet like parts. At the same time, foaming, mixing, and holding of water and oil all improved. Computer models of single proteins matched the lab picture and help explain why food traits improved.
pmc-13320403:
Kevin Kim and Carly Kirshen report, in 2026, a man on a biologic drug for psoriasis who safely received a live vaccine and developed immunity. Live vaccines are normally withheld during biologic treatment because weakened vaccine viruses might theoretically cause infection. Guidelines advise pausing the drug first, though evidence for the risk is thin.

The 42-year-old had taken guselkumab, an interleukin-23 blocker, since 2020 with complete clearance of his long-standing plaque psoriasis. In May 2025 his doctor gave the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine after blood tests showed no existing immunity. He had no signs of vaccine-strain infection, and his psoriasis stayed clear. Tests in November 2025 showed reactive antibodies for all three diseases, confirming successful seroconversion.
pmc-13320503:
Anna O Norman and co-authors test a gene therapy idea in a 2026 mouse study of fragile X syndrome. The condition stems from loss of a brain protein called FMRP after a repeat fault in the FMR1 gene. The team used a harmless virus to deliver a human form of that protein into newborn mice that lack the gene.

Brain wave tests and adult behaviour checks followed two dose levels. The higher dose brought gamma wave power and sound responses closer to normal and cut excess background brain activity. Treated mice also showed normal exploring, social choice, and flexible learning. Broad spread through the cortex seemed key to the gain.
pmc-13321103:
Robin André Rørstadbotnen and Martin Landrø show how seabed fibre-optic cables can detect whales that make no sound in a 2026 study. Listening through such cables can already record whale calls and track singing animals. Silent animals, though, left no trace by that route, a gap as Arctic seas open to more shipping.

The method picked up silent blue whales within 40 metres of the fibre, using signals the animals create simply by moving through the water layer. Detecting quiet whales widens the reach of cable based monitoring beyond singers. Such tools could help map whale ranges and habitats as migration patterns shift with rapid Arctic warming.
pmc-13321203:
Noheer Hesham Mahmoud and colleagues test two gene variants in type 1 diabetes among Egyptian children in a 2026 study. Type 1 diabetes stems from immune loss of insulin making cells, and most inherited risk sits in HLA genes. Two non-HLA variants that guide insulin sensitivity and release, in PPARγ and TCF7L2, were checked for joint effects.

One hundred children with diabetes and 95 healthy children were genotyped with a targeted PCR method. The PPARγ variant was more common in patients, with the mixed CG form at 10.0 percent against 1.1 percent in controls, while the TCF7L2 variant showed no clear group gap. Diabetes control, by HbA1c, was far worse in patients, as expected.
pmc-13321503:
Cristiane B Patroclo and co-authors build a public database for records of traumatic brachial plexus injury in a 2026 data article. The injury tears the nerve network serving the arm, strikes mostly young men after motorcycle crashes, and often leaves severe loss of movement and feeling. Sharing standard data may reveal markers of recovery and new research tools.

Detailed electronic questionnaires captured background, physical, and clinical details, stored with free Neuroscience Experiments System software. Data cover 170 Brazilian adults with varied levels of impairment, collected between 2014 and 2020. Separate forms record first assessment, follow-up visits, and surgical repair, making the set reusable for later studies of this disabling injury.
pmc-13322303:
Jin Zhai and his team present, in 2026, a nanoparticle designed to deliver a chemotherapy drug and gene-silencing RNA as one package into cancer cells. Combination delivery can attack resistance pathways while the drug kills cells, but particles often stay trapped in cell compartments called endosomes, where the RNA is destroyed before it can work.

Their sphere-like particles hold doxorubicin inside a nanotube scaffold and carry the RNA on charged surfaces. The scaffold's buffering action helps burst the endosome, a proton sponge effect, releasing both cargos into the cell. In cell cultures, 3D tumour balls and mouse ovarian tumours, particles carrying RNA against a drug resistance gene plus doxorubicin silenced the target and increased cancer cell death. The authors offer the platform as proof of concept against multidrug resistance.
pmc-13323003:
Vashti Berry leads a multi-site case study of social prescribing for children and young people in England, published in 2026. Such schemes link young people to community activities, yet local services shape the core parts very differently, above all for those with mental health needs.

Five varied pathways were mapped with site leads, and 34 interviews covered referrers, link workers, managers and practitioners. Referral routes were uneven, needs centred on mild mental health concerns where statutory care had gaps, and link workers often did far more than linking. From that variation the authors build a taxonomy based on setting, referral shape, link worker role and community links, to help planners compare models.
pmc-13324003:
Tanveer Ahmed and team explored why pluripotent stem cells handle energy stress differently from most other cells. Their 2026 paper starts from a puzzle. Many cell types tolerate a blocked electron transport chain when given pyruvate or aspartate, yet pluripotent stem cells slip into a paused state even with abundant pyruvate. Because the chain regenerates NAD+, central to metabolism, the team asked what makes stem cells so sensitive to its disruption.

Blocking the chain in mouse embryonic stem cells triggered severe NADH reductive stress, driven mainly by the enzyme threonine dehydrogenase. That NADH-rich environment kept pyruvate dehydrogenase inhibited and favored cells with intact mitochondria, tracking with greater genomic and epigenetic stability. In human stem cells, blocking two one-carbon enzymes eased the stress and rescued the pause. The authors read limited redox flexibility as a conserved stem cell trait that may guard the genome at the cost of growth.
pmc-13324403:
Kunto Wibowo and co-authors describe a new shrimpgoby species from the coast of Banyuwangi, East Java, in a 2026 taxonomic paper. Two specimens ground the description of Tomiyamichthys oriens, a fish that lives alongside burrowing shrimp in tropical Indo-Pacific waters.

The new species sits closest to the Japanese T. hyacinthinus, sharing nine segmented rays in both dorsal and anal fins, plus two long filaments on the male first dorsal fin. It parts from that relative in fin ray, scale and gill raker counts and in colour pattern. Mitochondrial COI data backed the split, showing 3.1 percent genetic divergence from the Japanese species in their analysis, a gap the authors treat as species-level proof.
pmc-13325103:
Michelle R. C. Fortunato and colleagues unlock sugar from macauba seed cake with ball milling in a 2026 study. The cake left over from oil pressing is rich in the polysaccharide mannan, a feedstock for mannose and other sugars.

Chemical checks showed the cake holds 44 percent d-mannose by content. Dry grinding for up to 240 minutes broke down crystal order, and solid-state NMR tracked the change closely. Crystallinity fell from 26.6 percent in raw cake to 1.2 percent after 120 minutes of milling. Enzymes from Aspergillus niger then freed up to 76.8 percent of the mannose at that milling time. No added chemicals were needed.
pmc-13327803:
Kerem Tuna Tas and colleagues report ten years of results for single-session radiosurgery on a benign ear nerve tumor in a 2026 study. Vestibular schwannoma grows slowly, and focused radiation aims to halt it while sparing nearby structures. The single-center review covered 68 patients treated with photon radiosurgery at a mean dose of 13.1 Gy.

After a median follow-up of 68 months, tumors stayed controlled in 95.6 percent of patients, with control at five and ten years both at 98.5 percent on their time-based estimates, and scans showed shrinkage in 41.2 percent. Side effects were mostly mild and brief, and severe harm stayed under 3 percent. Lower doses under 14 Gy looked favorable, supporting radiosurgery as a main treatment choice.
pmc-13327903:
Franziska Kirstein and fellow editors introduce a research collection on robots for a sustainable future in a 2026 editorial. Climate change, shrinking resources, species loss, and growing waste call for scalable answers, and robots can watch ecosystems, save inputs on farms and in factories, and take on hazardous work. Pairing robot bodies with human judgment adds further reach.

The editors note the promise is not automatic and ask under what conditions robots truly help, across home, farm, and heavy industry settings. Contributions span drone monitoring of the environment and other field uses, weighed against economic and social effects. The collection aims to join scattered work into one cross-cutting view of robotics and sustainability.
pmc-13328003:
Desheng Zhang and co-authors test a blood ratio as a death risk marker in acute kidney injury in a 2026 hospital study. The ratio of uric acid to HDL cholesterol reflects metabolic inflammation, and kidney injury still kills many inpatients. Records covered 500 adults treated from January 2021 to January 2024, of whom 65 died in hospital.

Those who died were older, carried more hypertension and diabetes, and showed worse kidney numbers and inflammation. Each unit rise in the ratio came with a 55 percent higher hazard of death after adjustment, a hazard ratio of 1.55 in their model, and the link ran stronger in older patients and those with higher creatinine or lower urine output. A cheap ratio may sharpen early risk sorting.
pmc-13328403:
Ying Shuai and co-authors build a football emotion scale for Chinese youth players in a 2026 psychometric study. No checked tool existed for sport-specific feelings in young players, so the team surveyed players across twelve Shandong cities, using 492 in a first exploratory round and 450 in a confirmatory round.

Six emotion factors emerged, explaining 67.027 percent of total variation in the first analysis, and the confirmatory model fit excellently, with an RMSEA of 0.033 in the reported indices. The final 26-item scale held steady over repeat testing, with reliability values from 0.703 to 0.915 across its parts. Coaches and psychologists gain a sound way to track young players' emotional lives.
pmc-13329103:
Enver Ulaş and Harun Ismail Incekara study links between gaming addiction and manipulative traits in teenagers in a 2026 report. They also ask whether online bullying carries part of that link, and whether family ties change its strength. Their group was 601 high school students in Istanbul who completed standard questionnaires.

Model testing showed that online bullying sat between gaming addiction and Machiavellian traits, helping to explain their link. The tie between gaming addiction and online bullying was stronger when parent and teen ties were weaker. Fit checks supported the model as acceptable. The authors suggest that stronger family ties and less online bullying could soften harms tied to heavy gaming in teens.
pmc-13329503:
Naruenan Wongreantong and team sized up lab-grown models for studying fat metabolism in triple-negative breast cancer. Their 2026 study set chick membrane patient grafts against tissue slice models over nine days of incubation, using fat profiling. Fat metabolism drives cancer growth but is hard to model: animal models give blood fats at high cost and low speed, while cell fluids lack enough fat on hand.

Tumor fat profile gaps were driven first by built-in gaps between first and spread tumors, then by lab model. Ether-linked phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylcholine fats built up in membrane grafts from both first and spread tumors but stayed flat in tissue slices. The membrane model showed steady build-up of certain fats missing in slices, with gaps between first and spread tumors. The team flags each model's use as a sturdy, cheap path for studying the triple-negative breast cancer fat profile.
pmc-13330303:
Rilan Bai and team found a circular RNA that drives cancer growth by shielding a cancer signaling molecule. Their 2026 study found TAFCR1, a new circular RNA within the fatty acid synthase locus, formed through MBNL1-mediated back-splicing via short Alu motifs. Lipid metabolic reprogramming marks cancer, and fatty acid synthase is a key enzyme in that pathway, yet its role was unmapped.

TAFCR1 was raised in tumors and boosted cancer cell growth, invasion, and migration in vitro, while knockdown suppressed tumor growth and metastasis and prolonged survival in xenograft and lung metastasis models. TAFCR1 binds the ubiquitin-activating enzyme UBE1, disrupting UBE1-dependent, TRIM21-mediated ubiquitination of CD44 and thereby raising CD44. Raised CD44 activates PI3K/AKT signaling by suppressing the tumor suppressor PHLPP1, enhancing stemness factor SOX2, transition markers, and matrix metalloproteinase-9. The team presents TAFCR1 as a promising therapeutic target for cancers.
pmc-13330503:
Susan Hammoud and colleagues report a case of poor dental numbing in a long-term cannabis user in a 2026 article. The patient was a 34-year-old man who needed tooth extraction. Despite standard local anaesthetic technique, numbing was hard to reach and pain response seemed heightened.

The authors link the odd course to cannabis-linked shifts in pain pathways. Long exposure may heighten pain sensing, and drug handling plus blood flow effects may also play a part. No firm proof is claimed from one case. Still, dental teams should ask about cannabis use when planning anaesthesia, they argue, and be ready to adapt dosing, timing, or added pain control for such patients.
pmc-13330603:
Nilo Riva and a large team ask how patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis view feeding tube placement in a 2026 study. Tubes placed through the stomach wall help when swallowing fails, a common and severe problem in this disease. In total, 48 patients and their caregivers answered a satisfaction survey one month after placement.

Most patients, 77.1 percent in the reported replies, said they would choose the tube again, and caregiver agreement was higher still. Most patients felt feeding grew easier and wellbeing improved. Gut-related quality of life scores rose after placement and held at one month. General physical scores fell, matching disease progress. The authors read patient views as broadly positive toward the tube.
pmc-13330703:
Benjamin Rader and colleagues track United States views on generative artificial intelligence in health care in a 2026 study. Two survey waves ran in May 2023 and November 2025 on a participatory platform, with 3,130 and 3,088 adults in the reported waves. Questions covered awareness plus comfort with AI-led primary care and therapy.

Awareness rose sharply, with those hearing a lot growing from 26.5 percent to 42.9 percent across waves in the given ranges. Comfort with AI-led care barely moved overall. Trends split by politics: Republican views warmed while Democrat views cooled. Age and race gaps also widened. Fair rollout will need trust work beyond mere exposure, the authors argue.
pmc-13330803:
Mei-Jun Zou and colleagues give the synthesis and crystal structure of a mixed alkali borate in a 2026 report. Borates draw interest for ultraviolet optics, since boron and oxygen units link in many rich patterns. The new compound pairs sodium and caesium with a pentaborate unit and water, made by a solvothermal route.

Pentaborate building units join into sheets pierced by nine-membered rings, the structure work shows. Sodium and caesium ions plus water molecules fill the gaps between sheets. The unit itself mixes triangle and tetrahedral boron centres plus a hydroxyl-bearing group. Bond lengths and layout details are tabulated for other chemists. The compound adds to a family of over 3,900 known borates.
pmc-13331603:
Elsa Mazari-Arrighi and colleagues present a 2026 lab platform that builds tiny three-dimensional tubes lined with human lymph vessel cells. Lymph vessels drain fluid between tissues, watch for infection, and carry large molecules, yet lab models of them have stayed flat, short-lived, or leaky. The team used coaxial extrusion, pushing an alginate shell around a gel core, to form tubes whose width could be tuned from about 50 to about 300 micrometres.

A four-part gel let the cells join into hollow layers within a week. Those tubes stayed alive, kept lymph markers, and let large molecules pass in a selective way for at least thirty days. Gene readouts showed stronger lymph growth, matrix building, and maturation signals than flat cell layers showed. The same gel also grew long-lived blood vessel tubes.
pmc-13331803:
Ying Chen and a large team report 2026 laboratory and clinical work linking a shift in histidine handling to severe asthma. Histidine levels were markedly higher in sputum from asthma patients and rose with disease severity, worse airflow, and stronger inflammation.

Combining chemical profiling with gene activity data, they found the body making more histamine while losing carnosine, a protective compound. Blocking this pathway eased airway tightening, inflammation, and tissue remodeling in two mouse models of severe asthma. The mechanism ran through oxidative stress damaging mitochondria, which leaked their DNA and switched on signals that killed airway lining cells by necroptosis. The authors propose the histidine pathway as a drug target for severe asthma that resists steroids.
pmc-13332103:
María de los Ángeles Fernández-Ceballos and colleagues review blood tests for Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 systematic review centered on the ultrasensitive SIMOA platform. Standard diagnosis leans on spinal fluid sampling and brain scans, which are costly and invasive, so a reliable blood test could open earlier and wider detection.

The review gathers studies that measured blood levels of amyloid proteins Aβ42 and Aβ40 and their ratio. It also covers several tau forms including p-Tau181, p-Tau217, and p-Tau231, plus the nerve damage marker NfL and the glial marker GFAP. Across the disease span from silent stages through mild impairment to dementia, the combined evidence supports blood markers as a stand-in or partner for the invasive methods. The authors still require stronger validation before routine clinic use.
pmc-13332503:
Thai Duy Vo and colleagues set an ECG challenge in 2026 around an alarming heart tracing taken one hour after a pulsed-field ablation. The patient, an 85-year-old woman on dialysis, had just had her pulmonary veins isolated and a left atrial appendage occluder placed without trouble.

An hour later she became breathless with blood pressure of 210/130 mmHg but no chest pain. Her tracing showed a slow junctional rhythm, apparent ST elevation in leads V1 to V4, and broad tall T waves in the lower leads, a mix no single artery territory could explain. The answer walkthrough weighs heart attack, air embolism, ablation-related artery spasm, high potassium, and pressure effects. It lands on arterial pulse-tapping artefact, where an electrode sitting over a pulsing vessel fakes the changes. Moving the electrode normalized the tracing, and the challenge asks which bedside check should come before irreversible clot-busting treatment.
pmc-13333303:
Dorothea Gebauer and co-authors tested whether stress in early life changes how the body answers a broken bone, in a 2026 mouse study. Early-life stress burdens about 39 percent of people and raises later bone disorder risk, yet its effect on fracture healing had never been examined.

Their two-hit model separated mouse pups from their mothers to mimic early stress, then gave adults a standardized thigh bone cut fixed with an external frame, alongside behavior tests and healing measures. Three hours after the break, stressed mice showed a damped inflammatory response, with several pro- and anti-inflammatory signals significantly reduced, an effect stronger in males. By days 10 and 21, however, healing measures no longer differed between stressed and control animals. The authors conclude early stress reshapes the first immune reaction to fracture in a sex-dependent way without derailing the repair itself.
pmc-13333403:
Abdallah Ghonimy and colleagues tuned the carbon feed in shrimp biofloc tanks by water temperature in a 2026 preliminary study from China. In biofloc farming, added carbon feeds helpful bacteria that clean the water, but the recipe may need to change with the season, and harmful Vibrio bacteria are the threat to suppress.

Over 60 days with whiteleg shrimp, the team compared starch, seaweed, and a mix at 22 °C, the season's start, and 28 °C in mid-season. Chemical profiling found the warm mix tank rich in L-carnitine at 450-fold and mesaconic acid at 12-fold. That matched more Proteobacteria and less Vibrio, plus higher levels of two molecules that blunt bacterial virulence. Cool starch tanks also kept Vibrio low, while seaweed raised a candidate protective compound three-fold at both temperatures. The authors recommend starch before the season and the mix during it, and nominate several of the molecules as shrimp prebiotics.
pmc-13333703:
Yan Shi and co-authors modeled vancomycin dosing in patients with burns in a 2026 population pharmacokinetic study. Burn injuries change how the body handles this antibiotic, yet dosing guidance for this group has rested on small studies.

The team modeled routine drug monitoring data from 93 adult burn patients using nonlinear mixed-effects methods. A one-compartment model fit best, and kidney function, measured as creatinine clearance, proved the key driver of how fast vancomycin leaves the body. Clearance ran higher than in general patients. Checks by bootstrap showed the model was stable, and it predicted drug levels in nine outside patients more accurately than a standard online calculator. The model gives clinicians a firmer basis for personal dosing after burns.
pmc-13334403:
Srinivas Vinod Saladi and co-authors devised a paired drug strategy for acute myeloid leukemia in a 2026 lab study. The leukemia depends on the chromatin regulator CARM1, but no clinic-ready CARM1 inhibitor exists, so the team attacked its downstream effects instead.

They found CARM1 supports DNA repair programs tied to malignant growth, and blocking CARM1 made leukemia cells sensitive to DNA-PK inhibition by peposertib, which shuts down a major repair route. Active enhancer marks and the P300 enzyme sat at the promoters of CARM1-controlled repair genes. True to that logic, inobrodib, a p300/CBP blocker, teamed with peposertib in AML cells. The pairing exploits an epigenetic dependency from two sides and offers a reasoned pairing for a disease with poor survival, above all after relapse.
pmc-13335403:
Alejandro Herranz Berzosa and co-authors looked at polymer nanoparticles as fillers for battery electrolytes in a 2026 article. Mixed electrolytes usually rely on inorganic particles to gain strength and conductivity, but polymer bits made from dried latexes offer a tunable option.

The review first explains how sulfonamide-functional poly(methyl methacrylate) particles are made by emulsion polymerization, with size held between 20 and 100 nm and surfaces shaped at will. It then shows how these particles build composite electrolytes with better strength, high ionic conductivity, or lithium single-ion conduction. Finally it surveys how those electrolytes perform inside lithium- and sodium-metal batteries. Edges over inorganic fillers include scalable production, low density, and easy mixing into polymer matrices.
pmc-13336403:
Kyosuke Kagami and co-authors showed that a rare placental tumor can absorb genes from the mother carrying it, in a 2026 case series. Cell fusion between cancer and immune cells had been proposed to create wandering hybrids, but genetic proof in human cancer was missing.

The team followed four cases of placental site trophoblastic tumor that, remarkably, produced immunoglobulin. Three recurred and responded well to pembrolizumab. In one daughter-derived tumor that relapsed after treatment, gene profiles over time showed the tumor absorbing DNA from host maternal cells. The DNA included maternal alleles the daughter never inherited, at the immunoglobulin lambda and HLA-DQA2 loci and across wide regions. Immune-related proteins TLR10 and SIGLEC10 rose as incorporation spread, suggesting the graft taught the tumor immune tricks.
pmc-13336903:
Junming Huang and colleagues use a local tumor treatment to widen cell therapy in pancreatic cancer in a 2026 study. Pancreatic tumors carry few clear targets, starving vaccine and T cell approaches. Their ionic liquid, ILvax, injected into the tumor, kills tumor cells in a way that alerts the whole immune system.

Special dendritic cells, cDC1, carry tumor pieces to lymph organs and start a presenting cascade. That spreading taught the immune system more targets, expanded infused TCR-T cells, and shifted their fuel use toward oxygen-based burning. Both the body's own CD8 T cells and infused cells worked better together. A local jab that teaches broadly could make a hard cancer treatable by cell therapy.
pmc-13337503:
Federico d’Oleire Uquillas leads a large 2026 team mapping how the cerebellum ages across 47,000 adults in three imaging studies. This back-brain structure holds most brain neurons and supports thought as well as movement, yet its aging pattern was murky. Volume and tissue-ratio measures, backed by quantitative scans in an independent sample, charted the changes.

Aging proved uneven: association and motor-related regions declined faster with age than other lobules. Bigger cerebellar volume tracked with higher cognitive scores as age rose, suggesting reserve that protects function. In Alzheimer's patients the link held mainly at lower amyloid burden, even in high genetic risk carriers. The cerebellum emerges as an active guardian of late-life cognition, until disease overwhelms it.
pmc-13337703:
Xuqiang Wang and colleagues chart the learning curve for scope surgery to remove bleeding in the basal ganglia in 2026. The minimally invasive method is demanding, and how many cases proficiency takes was not well defined. Their data come from one experienced neurosurgeon.

Records of 120 straight cases were reviewed, with cumulative sum analysis based on operating time. A clear turning point appeared near the 25th case. Operating time fell across phases from 1.77 hours in early cases to about 1.23 hours later, as reported means show. The share of clot removed rose at the same time. Results give training programs a concrete benchmark for skill growth.
pmc-13338603:
Anthony Hauser and co-authors analyze how COVID-19 reshaped causes of death in Switzerland in a 2026 study. Weekly deaths from 2011 to 2021 were split into nine cause groups, with age, sex, and region also tracked. A Bayesian model trained on pre-pandemic years predicted what 2020 and 2021 should have looked like.

Among people aged 80 and older, non-COVID breathing deaths fell by 25 percent in the reported estimate, largely offset by COVID deaths. Only a modest overall excess remained. Hidden COVID deaths and shifted timing likely explain part of the pattern.
pmc-13341703:
Kidney failure racing ahead in tuberous sclerosis is reported by Rushuang Yang and colleagues in a 2026 case report. The 28-year-old woman moved from advanced kidney disease to no urine output and end-stage failure within 3 years, far faster than the usual slow course.

During pregnancy she showed heavy protein and blood in the urine, yet scans found no large tumors. Treatment later lapsed for financial reasons, and over about 30 months both kidneys were replaced by diffuse angiomyolipomas. Guidelines trigger preventive drugs mainly at tumor sizes above 3 cm. The authors urge watching urine markers as early alarms and involving multidisciplinary teams sooner.
pmc-13344303:
Xiaoli Zheng and co-authors review lactylation, a newer chemical tag linking lactate to gene control in cancer, in 2026. Methylation marks on DNA and RNA, histone changes, and non-coding RNAs all tune the enzymes and transporters of lactate flow. Lactylation itself writes lactate onto proteins, feeding back into growth, immune escape, and drug resistance. Mapping this loop opens treatment ideas aimed at lactate pathways, which the authors present as a promising front against stubborn tumors.
pmc-13346003:
Ibtissem Ben Bayer and co-authors present a 2026 case where freezing a tumor made the impossible operation possible. A 64-year-old woman carried a giant desmoid tumor in her chest front that caused worsening breathlessness and pain, shrugged off two rounds of drug therapy, and was ruled unresectable.

Inside a prospective trial, the team froze the mass through the skin with cryoablation. The tumor shrank markedly and its grip on nearby structures loosened, reopening the surgical door. Removal through a split breastbone achieved clean margins, with under 10 percent living tumor left in the specimen. Eight months on she remained well and recurrence-free, suggesting freezing deserves a downsizing role in selected chest tumors.
pmc-13346603:
Abdullah and co-authors propose a hybrid deep learning system, issued in 2026, for sorting gut diseases from endoscopy images. Their design joins a Vision Transformer with a layered memory network and then adds bagging and stacking ensembles to combine several model outputs.

Training used the Kvasir-v2 set of over 8,000 labelled images across eight disease classes. The system beat five named baseline models and stayed above 96 percent correct under added noise, blur, and light shifts, though such near-perfect scores merit care in new clinics.
pmc-13346803:
Tarek Hammadieh and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how common medicines and supplements can trigger glaucoma, a condition that damages the optic nerve, usually through raised pressure inside the eye. Open-angle disease develops as drainage through the eye's meshwork fails, while acute angle-closure disease strikes when a bulging iris blocks fluid outflow and can cause rapid vision loss.

The narrative review surveys which drug classes raise risk, by what mechanisms, and which patients need closer eye checks. For prescribers and eye clinicians alike, it offers a practical reminder to weigh eye safety when starting or combining long-term medicines.
pmc-13346903:
Ji Hyun Kim and colleagues issue joint guidance for Alport syndrome care in Korea, in a statement published in 2026 for two national kidney societies. Alport syndrome is an inherited kidney disorder marked by blood and protein in urine and slow kidney failure, often with hearing and eye problems. pmc-13347303:
Georgios Ktenidis and co-authors measured in 2026 how widely heated tobacco and nicotine pouches were used in the European Union in 2023. They also asked what drives people to start. These newer nicotine goods have spread fast. Yet their reach and user profiles vary a lot by land and group.

Multi-level models linked current and past use to life traits and stated reasons to start. About 1.7 percent were current heated tobacco users. Pouch use and start reasons were mapped too. The findings give regulators a base line for tracking a fast-moving market.
pmc-13348403:
Esther M. Johnston and a global team build a shared framework for training family medicine teachers, in a consensus study published in 2026. Family practice shares core ideas worldwide yet training, certification, and standing vary by region, leaving no global guide for preparing its teachers. The final frame holds three domains, covering hands-on teaching skills and knowledge, personal approach with learners, and acting as a professional role model in daily work. Built for bend, the frame can fit local systems while holding a common core, aiming for steady quality in doctors who train the next family physicians.
pmc-13350003:
Vadivel Ganapathy and Yangzom D Bhutia wrote a 2026 commentary on whether blocking STAT3 sits at the heart of how a plant compound, toosendanin, kills cancer cells. The death route in focus is ferroptosis, an iron-driven process distinct from ordinary cell suicide.

Free iron can spark reactions that burn the fatty building blocks of cell membranes, and cells survive by controlling iron levels or mopping up the damage. Toosendanin reportedly triggers ferritin eating, freeing stored iron, through a chain involving STAT3 and the cargo protein NCOA4. The authors weigh that chain and ask whether one signalling hub truly explains the herb compound's cancer effects.
pmc-13350603:
Elizabeth Thoburn and co-authors systematically weighed in 2026 the safety of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, BNT162b2, in pregnancy. Over thirteen billion COVID-19 vaccine doses have been spread worldwide, plus over five billion Pfizer doses. Yet real-world pregnancy proof varied in design and outcome definitions, with scant work by dose timing or variant span.

Most prior reviews grouped all COVID-19 vaccines together, curbing product-specific conclusions. This pregnancy-focused review, registered prospectively, synthesised studies on pregnancy-linked outcomes after BNT162b2, such as miscarriage, preterm birth, and congenital outcomes. The synthesis gives pregnant patients and clinicians product-specific safety proof at a time of lasting public worry about vaccination in pregnancy.
pmc-13350703:
Menglong Zheng and co-authors built in 2026 CT radiomics nomograms to forecast whether pulmonary ground-glass nodules are malignant and how invasive malignant ones are, a visual challenge for radiologists. Nomograms for malignancy and invasiveness were built. Among malignant nodules, invasiveness grades were forecast from radiomic patterns. The nomograms give a pre-surgery decision aid, helping surgeons pick between watchful waiting, limited resection, and wider surgery.
pmc-13351703:
Jiahui Meng and co-authors test whether salidroside can calm vessel lining injury linked to Kawasaki disease, in a 2026 combined computer and lab study. Kawasaki disease is a fever illness in children that can damage heart arteries. Salidroside comes from Rhodiola rosea and is known for anti-inflammatory effects.

Human coronary artery cells were stressed with TNF-alpha to mimic injury, and RNA sequencing tracked gene changes after treatment. Cell tests covered survival, movement, and cell death. Results point to NF-kappaB and NLRP3 pathways in the protective effect, though the work stays at lab stage.
pmc-13351903:
Jiawei Chen and co-authors review outcomes of windpipe surgery after pre-treatment in a 2026 cohort study. Complications affected 13 patients, and major ones affected 5, while no deaths occurred at 30 or 90 days. Median follow-up was 29.5 months. Join problems arose in 4 patients, so the authors weigh benefit against a real risk at the join.
pmc-13352403:

Users were grouped by record codes from the prior 2 years as nonusers, nicotine only, cannabis only, or both. Outcomes ran to 2 years and spanned nerve, surgical, and medical problems, plus pain, mental health, opioid use, and care visits. Separating the two substances lets the team judge each one's own link to recovery.
pmc-13352503:
Hsin-Yin Chuang leads a 2026 nanoparticle study aimed at calming inflammation inside atherosclerotic plaques. pmc-13352703:
Katharina Lüthy leads a 2026 mixed-methods study of how German teachers view electromagnetic field risk. About a third of each teacher group, at 32 percent and 33 percent, judged exposure below legal limits as risky. Estimates were corrected for non-response, and latent class analysis sorted teachers into perception types. How informed teachers felt and how often field questions arise at work were also mapped. Findings guide health agencies on what information teachers actually need.
pmc-13354403:
Mahnoor Sheikh and co-authors write a 2026 letter on the fast-tracked approval of orforglipron under a new FDA voucher scheme. pmc-13355003:
Aanchal Ralhan and co-authors tested in 2025 a low-cost virtual way to teach point-of-care ultrasound to rural trainees in Canada. Trainees rotated through nine hands-on stations plus one virtual station that covered the core acute care topics. Teacher and learner could each show probe placement and view the other's images. The authors present the model as a cheap, easy way to bring expert ultrasound teaching to remote sites and working rural doctors.
pmc-13355203:
Trung Dat Phan and co-authors share a 2026 dataset from a motor-driven breathing bag device built in Vietnam. The machine squeezes a standard self-inflating bag to push air, as a low-cost stand-in for a ventilator. Sensors track airway pressure, airflow, and air volume a thousand times per second.

Twelve files cover three motion patterns for each state, with motor and control signals logged alongside. The authors offer the data for building models of the device, testing control methods, and making digital copies for design work.
pmc-13359003:
Zhaoquan Wu and co-authors describe a rare but deadly side effect of targeted lung cancer drugs in a 2026 paper. They found 50 patients, with lung trouble starting a median of 50 days after treatment began. Breathlessness, low oxygen, and cough were the top signs, and scans mostly showed hazy patches. After stopping the drug and giving steroids, nine in ten patients improved, but one in ten died. The paper warns doctors to act fast on new breathlessness.
pmc-13361103:
Jaemin Lee and co-authors compare two anesthesia types for double knee replacement in a 2026 study. Spinal anesthesia numbs the lower body, while general anesthesia puts the patient fully to sleep. The team reviewed 207 patients and 414 surgeries at one center.

They compared kidney injury and blood transfusion rates between the two strategies. Many planned spinal cases switch to general midway, so the team sorted cases by the first plan and then double-checked with a second sorting. Results from single knee surgery may not carry over to this harder setting, where patients are older and stress adds up. The study gives surgeons and anesthetists direct proof for planning.
pmc-13361603:
Marzhan Nurbekova and co-authors review a class of magnetic oxide materials in a 2026 paper. Perovskite manganites mix a flexible crystal frame with manganese in several charge states. The authors survey magnetic, optical, electrical, and catalytic behavior across simple, double, layered, and thin forms of the material. Such oxides interest engineers for sensors, memory, and energy devices. The review gives newcomers a single map of a crowded field.
pmc-13364503:
Abdullah Jalal and co-workers tell a 2026 case of a six year old girl with a smooth brain birth flaw, hard seizures, and a strict fat based diet plan. Care teams cut the band that links the brain halves and swapped a nerve stim unit to calm her fits.

Care after surgery brought a rough patch: more fits at first, then a sick spell with low blood sugar, low salts, and a sky high fat burn mark. Fluids, sugar aid, and a diet shift steadied her. A gut drug then let tube feeds run smooth. The case shows the close watch such mixed care needs.
pmc-13364903:
Yiyao Liu and co-workers find in 2026 a pond mud germ that eats a harsh crab germ and may guard farmed mitten crabs. The harsh germ sickens crab farms and few safe guards exist. The team fished the hunter germ from farm mud, use the crab germ as bait, then mapped its full gene set.

The hunter held tools for move and wall break, no harm genes, and no ill effect in crabs at high dose. It slowed the target germ near to nil in glass tests and raised crab life in live tests. It also hit three more farm germs. A green farm guard may be at hand.
pmc-13365303:
Xue Yang and co-workers ask in 2026 if skill at find and judge web health facts guards Hong Kong college youth from game ill. Too much game play can harm mind health, yet few seek help. The team polls 370 students on game signs, health web skill, and help will.

Near three in ten met the bar for like game ill, but near one in ten said they had it. High web health skill tied to few game signs. It also fed help will through faith that care works. Teaching web health skill could cut game harm and lift help use.
pmc-13366203:
Emily Tilstra-Ferrell and co-workers read in 2026 the write ups made in a joint care plan for fresh sex attack harm and drink ill. The plan blends write out care for stress ill with skills for drink use, in five web calls. Ten adults in the plan gave the write ups.

pmc-13366903:
Tuoxin Cao and others showed that astrocyte-brain cells crosstalk through CSF1 and interferon-beta promotes central nervous system repair, in 2026. pmc-13371503:
Yin Yen Mun and co-authors share an eye case from 2026 on a shift in sight after lens surgery. A man aged 29 with a flat iris and long-term eye pressure trouble had his clear lens removed and tiny drains placed. Five weeks later his sight blurred and he saw double.

pmc-13373603:
Paul S. Appelbaum and co-authors asked study members what they want back from gene tests in a 2026 survey. The 149 people had taken part in a large gene study that gave back risk scores for eight common ills. Most were white, well schooled, and at ease in English.

Most said that to get their own results would weigh a lot in a choice to join a next study. Two in three gave that point the top mark. They wanted the facts to guard their own health and their kin's. Fear of harm was low, and most would share the facts. The replies can help teams plan fair returns of results.
pmc-13374203:
Pedro Henrique Takata and co-authors set lab and live tests of germ-eating viruses side by side in a 2026 study. The target germ is a tough lung and wound germ that shrugs off many drugs. Such viruses, called phages, kill one germ type and spare the rest.

Past work rarely links the two read types. A firm link would let labs screen phages in dishes with more trust in what will work in the body.
pmc-13375603:
Phuong Nguyen and co-authors give a cheap way to light up many proteins in tissue in a 2026 paper. Glow tags let staff see where each protein sits in a slice. Old two-step ways are slow and picky on host type, and one-step ways are dim and fixed.
