pmc-13377903:
Katijah Khoza-Shangase maps risks in ear and speech care in South Africa in a 2026 study. Care there runs in a thin, split health world: state wards with few tools, and paid rooms with cash strain. A total of 92 staff gave their tales in 2025.

Four risk sets came out of the talks and counts. State staff told of more cure slips and late care, most of all in far zones. Staff lack and kit breaks hit them more too. Paid staff fret more on cash swings. One risk plan can't fit both worlds, the study holds: each needs its own guard stack.
pmc-13380103:
Zhanghao Chen and colleagues present a 2026 study on capsule traps for PFAS, the long-lasting chemicals that pollute water worldwide. Inspired by cell membranes, which let only certain substances through, the team built capsules about a millimetre wide. Each has a powdery core rich in nitrogen groups and a porous plastic shell.

Tests and computer models showed the shell lets PFAS pass while keeping out other material in the water. The core then pulls the chemicals inside. By tuning the core, the team also captured short-chain forms, which are usually harder to trap. The capsules caught a wide range of these chemicals, offering a selective tool for cleaning polluted water.
pmc-13380203:
Anmar Al-Taie, Ahmed Shaheen Abdullah, and Oritsetimeyin Arueyingho wrote a 2026 scoping review of artificial intelligence in clinical pharmacy services. Such tools promise to make medicine management safer and more efficient in hospitals and community pharmacies. The review maps what has actually been tried and reported.

Following standard guidance for scoping reviews, the authors searched major databases for studies from 2010 to 2025 and included 36 publications. The largest group used these tools to detect harmful drug interactions and side effects. Other uses covered tasks across the medicine-use process. The map shows where evidence is concentrated and where pharmacy practice has yet to test these tools properly.
pmc-13382503:
Taylor and colleagues review strategies for keeping arteriovenous fistulas open, in 2026 vascular research for dialysis patients. A fistula, a joined artery and vein in the arm, is the preferred dialysis access, yet it often narrows and fails. The chief culprit is neointimal hyperplasia, inward wall thickening driven by needle sticks, shear stress, and the inflammatory chemistry of kidney failure. The authors note it contributes to over 60 percent of dysfunctional fistulas in the literature.

Balloon angioplasty, first used for stenosis in 1982, remains the first-line rescue, forcibly dilating the narrowed segment to remodel it outward. The review weighs drug-coated balloons, stents, surgical revision, and surveillance for catching stenosis before thrombosis closes the vessel, plus the biology that makes each succeed or fail. Taylor argues durable patency needs both mechanical fixes and control of the wall's fibrotic response, since dilation alone invites the hyperplasia to return at the site.
pmc-13383403:
Hanxiao Zhou and colleagues build a single-cell atlas of aging-linked markers in melanoma in 2026 work. Aging reshapes how this skin cancer grows and how well immune therapy works, but the cell-level picture was unclear. The team joined mutation, gene activity, and other data layers to find age-driving factors.

One factor, named a RevitalAge Marker, tied to younger profiles and better survival. Cells carrying the marker aided anti-tumor roles, while cells without it showed spread and immune evasion traits, especially in patients over 65. A five-gene signature predicted therapy response well, and one gene's product bound two candidate drugs strongly in docking tests.
pmc-13385903:
Romina Roozbeh, Narjes Keramati, and Mehdi Mousavi Kamazani test an amine-tuned framework material for clearing tetracycline from water in 2026 work. Their material, NH2-ZIF-11, adds amine groups to a porous crystal to grip the antibiotic more strongly. Structure checks confirmed the framework stayed intact after the change.

Under best settings, removal reached about 91 percent within an hour of contact in their tests. Capacity more than doubled compared with the unmodified parent material, a gain credited to charge, stacking, and hydrogen bond forces working together. The material kept working across three reuse cycles and the process was heat-absorbing and spontaneous.
pmc-13386203:
Hai Xuan Nguyen and co-authors isolate two new plant compounds that block the pigment enzyme tyrosinase in 2026 work. Such blockers are sought as skin-whitening agents for pigment disorders. Chemical analysis of Streblus ilicifolius stems yielded the pair, named strebluses A and B, with structures solved by spectra and light-based methods.

Both compounds beat the standard control kojic acid in lab potency tests. Computer docking placed them snugly at the enzyme's active site, touching the same key residues as the control. Stability runs backed the docking picture, and the authors offer the pair as blueprints for future cosmetic development.
pmc-13389003:
Wen-Yue Dai's team explain the puzzling variety of binary asteroids with a multi-generation model, in which repeated spin-up shedding events build satellites in stages. Simple breakup theory predicts elongated satellites on tight orbits, yet missions found oddballs such as Selam, a contact-binary moon on a wide orbit around Dinkinesh.

Simulations showed an existing moon strongly steers later moon formation through disc and moon-moon interactions, reproducing Dinkinesh and several triple systems. About forty-four percent of known binaries show signs of such multi-moon histories, hinting many more diverse configurations await discovery.
pmc-13389603:
Yaping Chen and co-authors present, in 2026, a highly unusual case of tuberculosis affecting several genital sites at once in a woman past menopause in Guangzhou, China. Lesions were confirmed on the vulva and cervix, with suspected spread to the womb lining.

The authors stress that genital tuberculosis belongs on the list of causes when a postmenopausal woman bleeds, even with no past lung tuberculosis. Sampling with acid-fast staining and culture confirmed the vulvar and cervical disease and allowed prompt cure, while suspected womb involvement still needs tissue and germ proof. Gynaecologists gain a reminder that this infection can mimic cancer and that targeted sampling settles the question faster than imaging alone.
pmc-13390003:
Cancheng Li's team presents TACMAN, a system that aligns single-cell data across species despite lab shifts and tangled gene kinship. Single-cell gene reading maps cell range at high detail, but weighing cell types between animals and people has stayed hard.

TACMAN joins a meta-path graph neural network with an encoder-only transformer. It matches shared cell types under healthy conditions while keeping living signals. Applied to human and animal data, it showed shared cell subtypes in tumours, inflammation, and infection. It even linked a worm germline tumour model to human testicular germ cell tumours, aiding translation from models to patients.
pmc-13390903:
Natalia Gattass-Ferreira and colleagues follow, in 2026, pregnant women whose early blood sugar was only mildly raised, asking whether that small rise truly signals diabetes risk. Mild fasting glucose elevation in the first trimester is sometimes labelled early gestational diabetes, which triggers treatment and monitoring.

The prospective study included 114 women whose first-trimester fasting glucose stayed below a set ceiling. Those in the mildly raised band had the test repeated after three to four weeks. Women whose repeat value fell back below the threshold formed a comparison group. That group received no treatment. Obstetric readers gain evidence on whether a mild, non-persistent rise predicts later diabetes or poor outcomes, or mainly creates needless alarm.
pmc-13392403:
Golan Karvat's team found a one-size rhythm shape of brain signals. They split brain-signal spectra from 859 people across data sets, species, techniques, ages eighteen to eighty-eight, regions, and states in health and disease. Neural signals are usually split into frequency bands, yet wobbles often appear as brief bursts rather than steady rhythms.

A rhythm measure showed two kinds. High-rhythm bands carry steady wobbles, and newly noted low-rhythm bands are ruled by brief bursts. The shape reflects two running modes, steady upkeep versus brief signals of change, giving a single system and rule-based basis for own wave definitions.
pmc-13392803:
Jimin Lee's team built an H2O2-set-off pre-drug rig that at once tackles multiple AD ills. It exploits elevated H2O2 around amyloid plaques and metal imbalance. Boron ester-masked starters stay inert in the body but undergo oxygen boron loss in H2O2, releasing redox-ready amino phenols.

Activated molecules mopped up reactive oxygen species, changed amyloid-beta residues, and shifted clumping of metal-free and metal-bound amyloid. In gene-tweaked mice, long-term BE-1 treatment converted in brain tissue, cut seahorse-shaped oxygen stress and plaque burden, and better cognition, giving an illness-ready chemical strategy for nerve wasting.
pmc-13393603:
Nathan Muci Aguiar and six colleagues publish the protocol for a systematic review asking how exercise affects pain in breast cancer survivors during chemotherapy. The review separates the immediate sting from the long-term gain. Exercise is considered safe during treatment and broadly recommended, yet a session may flare pain acutely while training over weeks could ease it. The protocol, registered in advance, follows standard reporting rules for review plans.

Searches will span five major databases for randomised trials of set exercise in adults on chemotherapy that measured pain by objective or subjective means. Two bias and certainty schemes will grade each trial and the overall body of evidence. Because studies will differ in exercise type and timing, the team pre-plans subgroup and sensitivity analyses plus structured handling of heterogeneity. The finished review aims to guide pain care during treatment.
pmc-13393803:
Yujie Yang and colleagues measure how efficiently Chinese disease control centers operate in a 2026 study covering twelve years. China has steadily raised funding for its Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but whether extra resources turned into better public health results was unclear.

Using panel data from 31 provincial regions for 2011 to 2022 plus 2022 cross-sectional data, the team applied a three-stage efficiency model to inputs, outputs, and environmental factors drawn from official yearbooks. The paper tracks efficiency changes over time and across provinces. Officials gain an evidence base for tuning funding and services in the disease control system.
pmc-13393903:
Tuan Thanh Nguyen and colleagues describe keyhole surgery for a blocked kidney junction in a horseshoe kidney in a 2026 case report and review. Horseshoe kidneys often develop ureteropelvic junction obstruction, and whether to cut the isthmus joining the kidneys during repair remains debated.

A 28-year-old Vietnamese man with recurrent flank pain and fever had a horseshoe kidney with severe right-sided swelling and a shrunken left kidney. Surgeons performed Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty combined with isthmusectomy, a minimally invasive first experience for the team. The report adds practical guidance for a rare anatomical challenge.
pmc-13394403:
Taihei Fujimori and co-authors track, in 2026, how single cells lock genes off for good. They pulled a silencer called KRAB to one test gene and watched the DNA fibre in three dimensions. Silencing left a mark named H3K9me3 and packed the fibre tight over long stretches. A second route, which strips small chemical tags, turned the gene off without such packing.

Only the packed state stayed off weeks after the silencer was removed. Over time the first mark faded while DNA methylation took its place. Models suggest packing helps marks copy themselves along the fibre. The authors saw like packing at real genes as cells took on new fates.
pmc-13394903:
Sianga Mutola and co-authors follow, in 2026, women in Zambia as they rejoin daily life after fistula surgery. Fistula, a childbirth injury, leaves women leaking and often shunned. The study tracked 2,172 women repaired at eight hospitals between 2017 and 2023. Scores blended five parts of social life, from family ties to work.

Most women left hospital dry, and dryness was the strongest driver of social recovery. Scores jumped most in the first three months, then held steady. Women still leaking gained ground too, and the gap slowly narrowed. The authors urge strong surgery plus early follow-up visits. Social support, they say, is part of the cure.
pmc-13395503:
Daniel Lowe and co-authors tell, in 2026, of stubborn belly fluid after a liver transplant that traced to a thieving spleen artery. A 65-year-old man got a new liver for alcohol-linked scarring. Fluid kept pooling, and scans showed the spleen artery drawing blood away from the liver graft. Bile ducts inside the graft also suffered from poor flow.

Two attempts to block the spleen artery from inside failed. Removing the spleen ended the fluid build-up and the bile trouble. The syndrome hides among more common causes of post-transplant fluid. The authors say surgery is a sound backup when artery blocking fails. Early scans of artery balance can speed the hunt.
pmc-13396403:
Tibebe Birhanu and Hang-Hyun Jo offer a burst-tree frame for time patterns in event runs in a 2026 paper, tried on human heartbeats. Past plain gaps between beats, bursts of fast beats split by calm spells hold layered time shapes that old gauges miss.

Burst-tree splits map an event run just right onto a tree, where each join fuses near bursts at the gap that parts them, baring layered burst shapes. Fresh gauges of burst knot, burst recall, and join kernels score ties across scales. Tried on sound and sick heartbeats, the frame bares clear layered time marks of heart health.
pmc-13397103:
Marlon Rodriguez Valladares writes a 2026 viewpoint arguing that treating appendicitis with antibiotics alone, rather than surgery, cannot simply be imported into Honduras. Trials in rich countries found the drug route fails for roughly a quarter to a third of patients within a year, yet even those results rest on supports his setting lacks.

The trials assumed early arrival, dependable imaging, a steady antibiotic supply, planned follow-up, and a surgical team on standby. At one Honduran referral center, up to 54 percent of patients arrive with dead or burst appendixes, which removes them from the antibiotic option at once. Local habits, such as abdominal massage, add further delay, he notes.
pmc-13397303:
Wei Liu and others offer a simplex-based model for nanoparticle grain naming in four-dimensional electron microscopy in a 2026 study. Naming which crystal phases fill each spot is core to stuff checks, yet grains that overlap confound stock reads.

Each simplex corner stands for a pure grain's diffraction pattern. With edges and insides standing for overlaps, and a two-stage method gauges grain shares from Bragg disk data plus a trait grid for each grain type. The method untangles grains that beat plain reads. Stuff scientists gain a shape tool for reading tangled polycrystalline nanoparticles.
pmc-13397603:
Yasuhiro Morita and others link hip abductor strength to mobility limits in community adults in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Mobility limits raise disability risk in older adults, and Japan's locomotive syndrome notion captures it, but hip abductor strength's lone role was unclear.

Among 325 community adults getting osteoporosis screening, hip abductor strength gauged with a dynamometer and scaled to body weight was tested against locomotive syndrome risk scores. Front-plane hip steadiness, not just broad strength or muscle bulk, emerged as the key factor. Screening programs gain a sharp muscle aim for keeping mobility.
pmc-13397803:
Zefeng Zhai and coauthors traced how two gene regulators shape potato tuber formation under long daylight. Their 2026 paper focuses on StAP2-13 and StAP2-18, members of the APETALA2 family that switch other genes on and off during plant growth. Tuber formation decides potato yield and quality, yet the exact role of these regulators in that process had stayed unclear.

The team catalogued 18 StAP2 genes across the potato genome and found the two candidates strongly active in leaves and developing tubers. Both followed daily rhythms and bound a key tuber regulator called StCDF1 in yeast tests, with further assays confirming control of related genes. The work maps a daylight-linked control route for tuber growth and offers breeders gene targets for yield, though field proof in varied potato varieties still lies ahead.
pmc-13398103:
Josephine D Kahn and co-authors engineer an immune signal that switches on only inside tumours. Their 2026 study tackles interleukin-12, a potent immune activator whose body-wide action causes heavy side effects that have blocked its use against solid cancers. The design keeps IL-12 tied up until the protein meets a matrix marker found across tumours, fibronectin EDB.

A two-armed antibody holds the signal in a competitive grip; crowding at the tumour marker pries it open. Computer modelling first set the binding strengths needed, then phage screening and library design produced switches with the right grip. Lab tests confirmed activation depended on the tumour marker, a step toward strong immune therapy with a wider safety margin.
pmc-13398303:
Lauren R Sastre and colleagues evaluate Fresh Start, a food-as-medicine programme for rural North Carolina adults with type 2 diabetes and thin insurance cover. Their 2026 report covers the 2021 to 2024 rollout across 15 eastern counties. The 20-week scheme handed participants 5 to 7 pounds of produce at each of nine group classes, plus phone coaching one to one.

Programme records measured whether delivery worked as planned, while surveys and interviews captured how participants received it. Before-and-after questionnaires tracked knowledge, skills and habits, and chart review followed blood sugar control through HbA1c readings. The mixed verdict (reach, response and early health shifts) aims to show funders what a produce prescription can and cannot do.
pmc-13399103:
Ji and co-authors review, in 2026, prime editing as a route to treating neuropsychiatric disorders at their genetic roots. The technology fuses a reverse transcriptase to a modified Cas9 and reads its instructions from a guide RNA template. That lets it install base substitutions, small insertions, and deletions without double-strand DNA breaks. That precision suits brain diseases caused by single-letter mutations or small indels, which often produce severe, early-onset symptoms.

Studies in cells and animals have corrected pathogenic alleles and rescued function in monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders, proof of concept. The barriers to clinic are substantial: low editing efficiency in non-dividing neurons, guide design, reverse transcription errors, vector payload limits, and crossing the blood-brain barrier. They survey fixes, including split virus delivery systems, lipid nanoparticles, peptides, and compact Cas variants, and argue translation hinges on neuron-targeted, transient delivery plus genome-wide safety checks.
pmc-13399403:
Qiongyu Zhou and colleagues compared five large language models on oncology nursing decision support tasks, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The team wanted to know how much help the five chatbots can offer. They fed every model the same prompt with exam questions and 33 case-based questions from a national training manual.

Two experienced oncology nurses scored the case answers for correctness, clarity, and conciseness, agreeing only moderately with each other. Median total scores put DeepSeek first at 11.50, followed by Qwen at 11.00, with ChatGPT and WiseDiag lowest at 10.00 on the scale. The only clear pairwise gap was between DeepSeek and ChatGPT. On the examination questions, all five models passed, with accuracy between 77 and 93 percent as tallied by the authors. The researchers conclude that the models handle structured knowledge well but falter on fast-changing clinical judgment. Their answers should support rather than replace nurses' expertise.
pmc-13399503:
Esther Omuseni and colleagues tracked COVID-19 infection and immunity across a rural community in western Kenya through six surveys, reporting in 2026. Working inside a health and demographic surveillance site of about 160,000 people, the team visited representative household clusters every two months from April 2021 to March 2022. Volunteers gave nose and throat swabs plus blood samples for neutralizing antibody measurement.

Infection detected by PCR jumped from 3 percent at the first survey to 24 percent at the second, in June 2021. It then fell to zero before rising again to 10 percent during the January 2022 Omicron wave, according to the survey tallies. Immunity climbed steadily behind it. The share of people with neutralizing antibodies rose from 18 percent to 86 percent by the final survey, and average antibody levels increased more than twentyfold. The authors say the pattern fits widespread natural exposure, while cautioning that unmeasured factors prevent crediting antibodies alone for the decline.
pmc-13399603:
Xiangyi Ma and colleagues charted how routine blood counts change with age in healthy community-dwelling Chinese older adults. Their 2026 cross-sectional study aims to map normal aging trajectories for blood cells and derived inflammation markers, evidence needed to judge immune aging and elder health. Reference patterns by age and sex had been incomplete for this population.

From 9,331 recruits, the team analyzed 1,630 healthy people aged 24 to 97. Red cells, hemoglobin, and platelets generally fell with age, while red cell size and variation rose, and monocyte share increased. Derived markers showed mixed trends, with platelet-to-lymphocyte and systemic immune-inflammation ratios falling and neutrophil ratios fluctuating. The dataset gives clinicians age-aware reference patterns, though a single-time-point design cannot track individual aging.
pmc-13399703:
Xueting Wang and Ying Zhao wrote this 2026 letter raising two methodological objections to a study that predicted loss of daily-living independence in older adults with type 2 diabetes. The original work, by Inoguchi and colleagues, found that a higher percentage of oxidized albumin, HNA%, and lower bilirubin each predicted decline in activities of daily living. The letter writers argue the analysis may have inflated the markers' apparent value.

Their first concern is competing risk. In an elderly diabetic cohort, death prevents the disability outcome rather than merely censoring it, and a standard Cox model can overstate the risk when deaths are simply censored. The original study reported 28 disability events among 101 participants without stating how many died. They recommend a Fine-Gray model for unbiased estimates. Both fixes, they say, are needed before the markers guide care.
pmc-13399803:
Ling-Ying Lu and colleagues measured a family of immune-regulating proteins called TRIM in the blood cells of people with systemic lupus erythematosus, in a 2026 study. They used quantitative PCR on peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 33 patients and 20 healthy controls. Expression was compared against disease activity, kidney involvement, symptoms, and laboratory values.

Four family members stood out. TRIM5, TRIM11, TRIM21, and TRIM72 all ran higher in patients whose disease was inactive, in those without kidney inflammation, and in those in low-activity states. Their levels also moved against clinical symptoms, though not against the standard laboratory parameters, as the analysis reports. The authors propose the four TRIM proteins as candidate activity biomarkers. They call for mechanistic work and for monitoring studies that follow patients over time before any clinical use.
pmc-13399903:
Kimia Fathalizade and colleagues report a 25-year-old Iranian man whose routine premarital screening uncovered a hemoglobin combination never previously documented, in a 2026 case report. The unexpected electrophoresis band led to full genetic testing. Hemoglobin British Columbia is a rare variant that grips oxygen unusually tightly, made by a single substitution in the beta-globin gene. The second change, IVS-I-6, is a beta-thalassemia variant that reduces how much beta-globin is made.

Capillary zone electrophoresis showed the abnormal hemoglobin making up 73.2 percent of the total. Sequencing confirmed the double inheritance: one beta-globin gene carries the British Columbia change and the other carries IVS-I-6. Despite carrying two variant genes, the man was entirely healthy, with normal blood counts and chemistry and no symptoms. The authors stress that because the rare variant can mimic common patterns like HbC, only DNA analysis settles the identity.
pmc-13400603:
Mohammad Mehdi Akbarin, Zahra Farjami and Hugo Ramírez Álvarez review, in 2026, how vitamins influence two related cancer-causing retroviruses: HTLV-1 in humans and bovine leukemia virus in cattle. Both can drive blood cancers and inflammatory disease, and no curative therapy exists. Host nutrition and immunity strongly shape how illness unfolds.

Studies link low or altered vitamin D, C and B-complex signaling with higher susceptibility, worse inflammation and more nerve or blood complications. Vitamin D pathways may help control viral load, vitamin C can push infected cells toward death in lab work, and B vitamins have improved nerve symptoms in patients. The authors map what is known in both viruses and flag gaps for future work.
pmc-13400903:
Dsouza and colleagues wire a ten step assembly line that turns glucose into isobutanol, a fuel and feedstock, while recycling its helper molecules instead of washing them away. Cell free cascades beat fermentation on control, but redox steps burn through nicotinamide cofactors. In flow reactors they drain off. Their 2026 study fuses the redox enzymes into pairs linked by peptide straps. Each strap carries one attachment point where a tagged cofactor is locked on permanently.

The machines kept working and made isobutanol in both batch and continuous flow runs with no free cofactor added. Each cofactor cycled through fourteen thousand rounds of use, among the highest counts for an anchored cofactor. Swapping in an ultrastable cofactor worked without redesign, showing its modularity. Self sufficient cascades like this, the authors argue, are a design template for cell free factories that run unattended, with the chemistry's wasteful consumable bolted down.
pmc-13401403:
Gregoire Zerr, David Eichler, Pierre Imbert, and Christian Lutz contributed a 2026 technical note on a combined knee operation. It joins anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with a lateral extra-articular tenodesis, both built from one continuous strip of the iliotibial band. A known weakness of band-based techniques is a thinner graft than hamstring alternatives.

Their modification folds a detached distal strip of the band back over the graft's central portion. This thickens the part inside the joint without harvesting any extra tendon, and it keeps the graft's natural continuity. Other teams had solved the size problem by adding a gracilis tendon graft, which the authors note is reliable but debatable. The note lays out the self-augmenting method step by step so other surgeons can reproduce it.
pmc-13401703:
Hirotaka Watase and co-authors describe DDIapp, a web application for estimating drug-drug interaction risk before clinical studies. Their 2026 paper builds the tool under the international ICH M12 guidance for static interaction assessment, using the Shiny for Python framework.

The app models enzyme inhibition, enzyme induction, and transporter effects in the gut, liver, and kidneys, and includes a net-effect model that combines inhibition and induction into one exposure ratio. It implements matrix-specific corrections for drug binding in laboratory preparations and offers flexible inputs, real-time results across scenarios, and automatic risk categories with visual cues. Equations are displayed for transparency, results export to PDF and Excel, and a glossary links to regulator resources. The tool was validated against a commercial interaction calculator under the same guidance conditions.
pmc-13402003:
Muhammad Zulqarnain and Ilyas Mukhtar recount a 60-year-old man found unresponsive in his garden on a hot summer day, with a core temperature above 42.2 degrees Celsius on first measurement by responders. Cooling and supportive care woke him quickly. Blood tests then showed raised high-sensitivity troponin T, a heart injury marker, yet his heart tracing showed no clear heart attack pattern.

Because he had heart risk factors and no clear cause for the collapse, doctors treated him as a non-ST-elevation heart attack case. A heart ultrasound showed one wall segment moving poorly, and an angiogram found tight narrowing in the proximal left anterior descending artery, treated with a stent procedure. The case warns that heat stroke can raise heart markers while real artery disease hides underneath, so both need checking.
pmc-13402103:
Xiao and colleagues mine a loneliness survey to test a theory of ageing. How older people judge their loneliness, and what meaning they make of it, decides whether age brings more of it. Gerotranscendence theory sees late life as a shift in outlook, not decline. Their 2026 study analyzes the BBC Loneliness Experiment, with 6,875 aged sixteen to ninety four. It mixes regression, models for younger and older adults, and topic mining of text.

Loneliness followed an inverted U, peaking near age thirty nine, not in old age. In the older group, two factors carried age's effect: self-stigma about being lonely, and the meaning assigned. They softened how strongly loneliness struck, though not length. Nothing appeared in the younger group. The text split into two themes, limited social function and unsatisfying relationships, weighted differently by age. Uniform interventions, the authors argue, will miss what changes with age.
pmc-13402703:
Wang and co-authors present, in 2026, Model Predictive Task Sampling, a way to choose which tasks a learning system should practice so it adapts well to new cases. Hard tasks build resilience to distribution shifts, but ranking task difficulty requires expensive testing through environment trials or model passes. Their method uses a small generative model that predicts each task's adaptation risk and ranks tasks from that.

The method ranks task difficulty while spreading the testing cost. It plugs into zero-shot, few-shot, and supervised fine-tuning pipelines for foundation models and general policies. Across experiments in pattern recognition with foundation models and in sequential decisions, the approach improved adaptation strength on tail-risk and out-of-distribution tasks. It beat baselines such as CVaR subset selection, and improved learning efficiency. They position predictive sampling as a tool for learning to adapt under safety, labeling, and compute limits.
pmc-13403603:
Masao Shioda led a 2026 case of repeated neck bleeding in a man with a genetic disorder that weakens blood vessels. The 67-year-old arrived with sudden neck swelling and no injury at all. Scans showed a large blood pocket pushing his windpipe aside and an active leak from a small artery branch.

Doctors sealed the leak from inside the vessel with a medical glue. Bleeding returned the next day from two other artery branches, so a second sealing session was done. No more bleeding followed, and he recovered with basic support care. Early close watch after the first fix is the core lesson.
pmc-13403803:
Jahnelle Jackson and Jonathan S. Berg argued in 2026 that smart gene screening policy needs solid records of how rare single-gene diseases unfold over a life. Gene reading keeps getting cheaper and faster, yet knowing a variant is not the same as knowing when illness starts. Onset age, reach, and severity vary a lot between conditions.

Such natural history facts decide what to screen for and when screening can help or harm. Rare diseases hit few people each, yet together they affect about 300 million people worldwide. Half show signs early in life, often before age five. Careful records of disease course can sharpen both screening plans and bedside choices.
pmc-13404003:
Saif Ali Malik headed a 2026 case of a woman who developed a runaway immune storm after a liver transplant, then a fatal fungal invasion. The 30-year-old received a new liver for sudden liver failure of unknown cause. Fever, low blood counts, and a faltering graft are warning signs of the storm state, called HLH.

Such signs have many causes after transplant, which makes the call hard. Standard scoring tools can speed the diagnosis when used early. Immune calming treatment then raises the risk of deep fungal spread. Her course turned fatal through that fungal disease. Outlook stays poor once such infections join, the authors warn.
pmc-13404303:
Alejandro Vega-Muñoz and colleagues retested in 2026 whether a popular student engagement scale truly holds three parts or just one. The scale asks about vigor, dedication, and absorption in study life. Their group held 755 Chilean university students who filled in both long and short forms.

A general engagement factor explained about 85 percent of shared answer spread in both forms. The three named parts kept almost no reliable spread of their own once the general factor was counted. The long form also wobbled in tests, with one model failing to settle. A single total score from the short nine-item form looks most defensible for campus well-being checks.
pmc-13405003:
Chalachew Abiyu Ayalew and a large team measure vitamin and mineral shortfalls among pregnant women in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, in 2026 work. Poor micronutrient intake in pregnancy harms mothers and babies, yet local levels were not well documented. The study ran in public clinics from January to March 2024.

About 420 women aged 18 and older who attended antenatal care took part. Each woman recalled everything she ate and drank in the previous 24 hours. Nutrient values were computed with Ethiopian and world food tables, then scored with adequacy ratios. Statistical modelling searched for predictors of inadequate intake, giving local planners a picture of which women need dietary support most.
pmc-13407403:
Lan Sun and co-authors, in 2026, watched how three kinds of carbon nanoparticle get inside cervical cancer cells grown in dishes. Activated carbon particles interest the group as possible drug carriers. The team compared them with carbon nanotubes and quantum dots. Entry routes, cell damage, and final particle locations were all tracked.

All three slowed cell growth more as dose and time rose. Under microscopes, treated cells shrank, lost grip on the surface, and showed membrane damage that differed by particle type. Flow tests and DNA assays found raised cell death and DNA injury across the board. Electron images caught carbon particles crossing into the cytoplasm and even the nucleus. Internal structures swelled as a result. Blocking entry routes or chilling cells stopped nanotube uptake. That points to an active swallowing process.
pmc-13408203:
Yufei Luo, Xiang Gu, and Jian Sun present a 2026 computational method for predicting the fleeting midpoint structures of chemical reactions. Those transition states set reaction speeds and reveal mechanisms, yet they vanish too quickly to observe and are costly to compute conventionally. The authors recast the prediction problem in terms of distances between atoms instead of fixed coordinates.

Their generative flow model learns to evolve a starting guess along a transport-inspired path toward chemically sensible structures, using a two-branch network. On benchmark reaction sets it produced starting structures closer to the true transition state than coordinate-based rivals, sped up later refinement, and handled reactions it had not seen in training. Chemists gain a faster front end for reaction modelling and catalyst design work.
pmc-13408403:
Reham Samir Hamida and co-authors describe in 2026 a greener way to make silver nanoparticles, using a newly characterised cyanobacterium as the factory. Silver particles this small can kill bacteria and cancer cells, yet chemical production routes are harsher and harder to control. The strain used, Cyanobium gracile PCC 6307, supplied both biomass extract and spent growth medium for two preparations.

Both products came out small, round, and evenly sized, coated in algal compounds identified by spectroscopy. In dishes they slashed colon cancer cell survival at the highest dose while sparing normal fibroblasts more, halted several staphylococcus species, and showed modest antioxidant activity. The medium-based particles were the smaller and more antibacterial of the two. Readers in nanomedicine get a sustainable synthesis route with a full biological activity profile.
pmc-13410603:
Dinkal Kasundra and Paresh Patel synthesize in 2026 a family of new compounds joining pyrene to pyrazole rings and test them against germs. Pairing the two ring systems could yield fresh antimicrobial leads at a time of rising drug resistance. Each compound was checked with standard spectra to confirm its build.

The set was screened against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria plus fungi. Activity swung widely with small changes in attached groups and their positions. One member, labeled 4h, stood out, clearing wide zones against two bacterial species. Computer docking placed that compound neatly into a bacterial enzyme pocket with the best binding score of the set. Its fat-liking balance also looked drug-like on paper.
pmc-13410803:
Xinglong Li and co-workers uncover in 2026 a protein that worsens liver damage when blood flow returns after surgery. Such injury follows liver transplants and major liver operations, driven by sterile inflammation with no good drug fix. The protein, RGS16, rose sharply in patient livers after surgery.

Mice engineered to lack the protein in liver cells suffered less inflammation and cell death, while extra protein made injury worse. Deep molecular profiling fingered a signal called CXCL1 as the protein's main tool. That signal kills liver cells and calls in neutrophils, which cast sticky DNA traps that add harm. Blocking the signal or dissolving the traps eased injury in mice, pointing to fresh drug targets.
pmc-13411103:
Matthias Elstner and a large team describe in 2026 a newly recognized brain inflammation syndrome tied to an antibody against a protein called copine-5. Many cases of autoimmune brain inflammation lack any known antibody, leaving diagnosis shaky. Routine testing flagged an unusual binding pattern in four patients.

Protein fishing and mass measurement named copine-5 as the target, confirmed with lab-made protein tests. Patients showed confusion, psychosis, seizures, movement problems recalling parkinsonism, and pain including cramping spasms. Scans lit up deep brain hubs and the temporal lobe. Stunningly, all four patients had melanoma, the skin cancer, with the primary tumor hidden in three. Steroids and antibody infusions formed the main treatment reported.
pmc-13412603:
Emaan Salam, VonPatrick Soliman DelaRosa, and Manish Trivedi describe in 2026 an unusual flare of alpha-gal syndrome presenting as acute diverticulitis. The syndrome is an allergy to a sugar found in red meat, triggered by tick bites, and usually causes delayed allergic reactions after eating. Gut-only presentations are increasingly recognized, the authors note, and can be mistaken for other bowel diseases.

Their patient, a 38-year-old woman with known alpha-gal syndrome, developed inflamed sigmoid colon with a pelvic abscess they judged likely tied to her condition. Broad intravenous antibiotics alone did not settle her severe pain, prompting a camera inspection of the abdomen. Bowel removal was avoided, and continued antibiotics brought complete recovery by follow-up. The case widens the syndrome's gut spectrum.
pmc-13413803:
Joan A. Ramos-Olvera and co-authors review in 2026 the case for mangiferin, a mango-family compound, as a multi-level lever on metabolic syndrome. The syndrome bundles obesity, insulin resistance, blood pressure, and lipid problems behind much chronic disease. Their synthesis searched three databases for work from 2016 to 2025 and graded how strong the support was behind each claimed effect of the C-glycosylated xanthone.

Mangiferin switches on the energy-sensing AMPK pathway and calms inflammation by freeing Nrf2 while suppressing NF-kappaB and messengers such as IL-6 in the studies reviewed. It also nudges fat and appetite signals, including leptin and adiponectin, in favourable directions. Nearly all support comes from computer, dish, and animal work, with few human observations. The authors call for trials tying blood levels of the compound to gut and metabolic effects.
pmc-13416903:
Signe Højstrup Bessing and colleagues study blood markers in women who once had preeclampsia, a dangerous rise in blood pressure during pregnancy, in a 2026 report. Such women face two to four times the heart disease risk in later years. The team asks whether vessel growth markers track with plaque in the heart arteries.

The group held 892 women from the Capital Region of Denmark, scanned up to 28 years after the affected pregnancy. One marker, placental growth factor, ran higher in women with artery plaque, though the link weakened after adjustment. Other marker levels did not differ. The authors treat the result as a lead for more work.
pmc-13418503:
Minwoo Jang and colleagues use mechanical bending to rescue photocurrent in a ferroelectric thin film solar material, in a 2026 physics study. Barium titanate films can generate voltage beyond normal solar limits, yet carriers are lost at interfaces, throttling current. Strain gradients from controlled loading create a flexoelectric effect, an electric response to uneven bending.

The gradients rebuilt the electric landscape at the interface, strengthening the field that sweeps carriers out. Photocurrent rose about 35 fold. Modelling reproduced the thickness dependence and showed structure, electrostatics, and material traits jointly govern extraction. Deliberate strain design may unlock thin film devices based on this effect.
pmc-13418603:
Areli Guadalupe Flores-Carrillo and colleagues describe one stage surgical care for a child with many trapped teeth, in a 2026 case report. The 10 year old boy had delayed eruption, several retained and impacted permanent teeth, an extra tooth, and a cyst in the lower jaw. Three dimensional scans showed badly angled teeth threatening neighbouring roots and blocking eruption paths.

Under general anaesthesia the team removed teeth with no eruption potential, took out the cyst, and exposed salvageable teeth for later orthodontic pulling. Recovery went well. Early detection, three dimensional planning, and teamwork across dental specialties are highlighted for such complex cases.
pmc-13418703:
Lucas Grape and co-authors hunt remaining barriers to flu and COVID vaccination among high risk patients in northern Sweden, in a 2026 study. Six hundred emergency department patients gave interviews and record data, with community factors linked from national registers. Four hundred fifty were eligible for both vaccines, which are free for risk groups in Sweden.

Coverage was only about half for each vaccine, though people who took one almost always took both. Lower uptake tracked with male sex, younger age, smoking, reduced independence, and eligibility by age alone. Extra conditions did not raise uptake in multimorbid patients. Community factors mattered little. Personalised risk communication and joint administration are proposed.
pmc-13419303:
Nimasha Ekanayaka and colleagues report a 2026 case of wild temperature swings after a high neck spinal cord injury. Temperature control is a known yet underreported danger of such injuries, since damaged autonomic nerves can drive the body from deep cold to dangerous heat within hours.

A 55-year-old man found unconscious in rain arrived at 31 degrees with slow pulse and low blood pressure, was rewarmed and stabilized, then spiked to 42.2 degrees without sweating despite cooling, ending in cardiac arrest. The case urges continuous temperature monitoring after high cervical cord injury, since neurogenic fever can kill fast.
pmc-13420303:
Gu and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of a COPD flare striking minutes after a breathing tube was removed following kidney stone surgery. The patient was a 70-year-old man with a heavy smoking history and newly found moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term lung condition that narrows the airways. He had only one day of breathing preparation before surgery to crush a kidney stone.

Gu describes how surgery under general anaesthesia ran about five hours with the patient face down. Two minutes after the tube came out, his oxygen crashed, wheezing began, and heart rate and blood pressure spiked. Emergency drugs and suction steadied him within half an hour, and symptoms cleared by evening. The authors argue one day of preparation is not enough for such patients, and they urge longer preparation, protective ventilation during surgery, and a ready rapid-response plan after tube removal.
pmc-13420603:
Manpreet K. Singh and colleagues argue that child and adolescent mental health research stands at a turning point and must innovate past new drugs alone. The burden of youth mental illness is global and shifting, while published proof stays thin and slow to reach families. Their piece sets out what the field's journal will prize: work that generates hypotheses, shows its methods, and informs care at once.

New treatments in the pipeline include ketamine, magnetic brain stimulation, digital tools, and intensive prevention models. Circuit-based therapies now must prove they engage their target brain circuit, not merely that symptoms move. Design, measurement, and spread of research all need the same inventive push as treatment itself. The agenda speaks to funders and health systems as much as to bench scientists.
pmc-13421303:
Anna Aichinger and seven co-authors describe, in a 2026 nationwide study, the Austrian children who needed intensive care for invasive group A streptococcal infection during the surge that began in late 2022. All 13 Austrian paediatric intensive care units took part, collecting standardised records for confirmed cases admitted between September 2022 and March 2024.

Seventy children were included. Chest infections dominated: pleural empyema appeared in about half, pneumonia and sepsis in just under half, and septic shock in a quarter. Over half carried another viral or bacterial infection at the same time. Nearly three quarters needed breathing support, half needed drugs to support circulation, and one in ten received extracorporeal therapies such as ECMO.
pmc-13421503:
Melissa Kilus and co-workers tested a natural plant compound, benjaminin, in 2026 against breast cancer cells, testing tumor MCF-7 cells against normal MCF-10A breast cells. Standard chemo drugs harm healthy tissue, so plant compounds offer a possible picky option, yet benjaminin's breast-cancer effects were new.

Benjaminin killed only cancer cells while sparing normal cells, halted them in the G1 phase, set off cell death through a DR6 and Bax pathway. It blocked spread by breaking the cell frame. The paper provides the first joined-up pathway for benjaminin in breast cancer, supporting further study beyond cell dishes.
pmc-13421603:
Di Tang leads a nine-author systematic review, published in 2026, asking whether taking part in esports helps or harms health. Public debate often lumps competitive gaming together with ordinary video gaming, and earlier findings conflict, so the team set out to compare esports participants with non-participants directly.

Searching seven databases to May 2026, they gathered 53 studies covering 86,652 people, with 36 feeding meta-analyses. At first pass, participants and non-participants did not differ significantly on physical activity, body mass index, sleep, anxiety, depression, stress or grip strength. Careful sensitivity analysis then revealed slightly lower depression among esports participants. Subgroup checks separated professionals from amateurs. The authors call the overall health picture more neutral than popular concern suggests.
pmc-13421803:
Ignacy Stadnicki and four colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether city life changes the eggs of great tits. Birds in towns differ from country birds in many ways. Snails, the usual calcium source for shells, are scarce in cities. So the team expected smaller eggs, more heavily speckled, signalling thinner shells.

They photographed and scored 718 eggs from ninety clutches across eight sites in a city mosaic over two breeding seasons, measuring built-up surface around each nest from satellite images. Egg volume and pigmentation were then set against that urbanisation measure. Egg size and speckle patterns, it turned out, did not follow the urban gradient at all, a null finding the authors set against clear city effects reported for other traits.
pmc-13422303:
James S. Ford and four colleagues track, in a 2026 study, a decade of American hospitals' compliance with the federal sepsis care bundle, SEP-1, against national sepsis deaths. Sepsis drives one in three hospital deaths in the United States. The bundle was introduced for reporting in 2015. It becomes a pay-for-performance measure in 2026, amid fierce argument about whether it saves lives.

Using public data from Medicare and the CDC, the team compared hospital compliance rates with mortality across the bundle's first ten years. The backdrop matters: a recent review of the studies found no solid proof that compliance lowers mortality. The authors offer their national trend analysis to inform the policy fight over the measure's future.
pmc-13422703:
Kyra Guy leads a twelve-author team examining, in a 2026 study, what helps and hinders smoking-cessation help inside HIV clinics in Uganda and Zambia. Tobacco compounds the health risks of people living with HIV, and a tailored programme, Quit4life+, was being tried across sixteen clinics — the team mapped its implementation against a standard framework.

Evidence came from site-visit reports, health-system assessments, interviews with fourteen clinic providers and focus groups with fifty-five patients. Adapted message libraries and nicotine replacement therapy won acceptance, while costs fought adoption. Seasonal farm work, civil unrest and other outer pressures also weighed on delivery. The authors organise the findings by framework domain so future programmes can plan around the same obstacles.
pmc-13422803:
Huiping Li leads a nine-author team testing, in a 2026 real-world study, whether a Chinese parent-training programme for autism can live inside routine child healthcare. Behavioural help is the bedrock treatment for autism's core symptoms, and STPAC — built by Chinese clinicians — teaches parents in groups to coach their own toddlers.

Between mid-2023 and mid-2025, 128 families with children aged eighteen to fifty-four months joined at two child healthcare sites. The eight-week course mixed lessons, video modelling and individual coaching. Parents were assessed before and after on their intervention knowledge, their children's communication development and their own stress. The authors frame the single-arm design honestly: it tests feasibility and within-group change inside real services, not superiority over alternatives.
pmc-13423803:
Barragán Fonseca and colleagues test in 2026 whether leftovers from insect farming can feed crops as a sustainable fertilizer. They used exuviae, the shed outer skins of farmed insects, worked into farm soil.

In a two-year field experiment, mustard plants in the treated soil grew as well as or better than plants given reference organic fertilizers. They grew taller and wider, made more flowers, drew more pollinator visits, and produced more seed than untreated plants. A parallel greenhouse study found richer and steadier communities of root-associated microbes in the treated soil, including several bacteria known to promote plant growth. The authors present the waste stream as a way to support circular farming.
pmc-13424303:
Tushar Dudeja and colleagues tested explanation maps in 2026 for semiconductor wafer defect classification, asking whether Grad-CAM points at the true defect. On 3828 held-out wafer maps from the WM811K set, baseline localization accuracy was low, at 0.129 on a top-10-percent overlap measure.

Both Grad-CAM and its variant showed a consistent radial bias, suggesting the model's learned features rather than the explanation math cause the skew, and a radial suppression fix lifted accuracy by 19.4 percent, mainly for edge-ring defects. Chip inspectors gain a caution and a correction for trusting explanation heatmaps on wafers.
pmc-13424403:
Matthew L Brengman, Prajakta H Waghmare, and I-Fan Shih compare robotic-assisted and laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, the classic weight-loss operation, in a large United States hospital database covering 2020 to 2023. Matched cohorts of adults with a body mass index of 30 or more let the team weigh surgical approach against early outcomes.

Robotic cases converted to open surgery half as often, reached intensive care less, and needed fewer transfusions. Stays skewed slightly shorter and return visits within thirty days were a little rarer. The trade-offs were real, though: operating time ran 17.5 minutes longer and bowel obstruction was somewhat more frequent. Other complications matched between the approaches.
pmc-13424603:
Yunus Emre Gemici and four colleagues run an emergency-department trial asking whether a fast bolus of fluids protects the kidneys from scan contrast as well as the traditional slow drip. Prolonged hydration clashes with emergency care, where imaging is urgent and monitoring time is short, so a noninferiority design tested the shortcut head-on.

Between August 2024 and April 2025, 257 patients with raised baseline creatinine were randomised before contrast CT scans. The bolus group received a litre of fluid around the scan, half before and half over two hours after; the continuous group received a slower infusion spanning ten hours. Kidney injury within three days was the main outcome, with thirty-day survival and dialysis need also tracked.
pmc-13424803:
Kalinchuk and colleagues mapped in 2026 gene activity where tumor and support cells touch directly inside breast cancers, comparing the hormone-driven luminal type with the triple-negative type. They used spatial transcriptomics, a method that reads gene activity at mapped spots across a tissue slice, on samples from ten luminal and nine triple-negative patients. Spots holding both cell types were set against tumor-only spots.

Kalinchuk found the contact zones switched on invasion-linked genes in both cancers, including matrix-cutting enzymes and shape-change programs. Luminal contact zones showed a wider menu of signal pairs passing between cells. Triple-negative contact zones stood out for a stem cell marker and a signal that restrains shape change. Shared themes covered growth signal cascades, cell death control, and sticking and movement. The authors say reading the tumor-stroma border helps explain how cancers organise their spread.
pmc-13425403:
Chad Cook and coauthors wrote a 2026 commentary on how to test whether manual therapy works through the mechanisms clinicians claim. Most earlier studies showed outcomes without proving that a proposed step actually caused the change. The authors set out to name research designs able to support causal claims about force-based treatment mechanisms and to illustrate each design with published examples.

Five designs are outlined, starting with mediation analysis, each bridging laboratory science and everyday practice in a different way. Clinicians and researchers gain a menu for building studies that can separate true mechanisms from plausible stories about treatment effects.
pmc-13425503:
Hirokazu Miyoshi and Masahiro Fujiwara report a 2026 experiment on separating tritiated water, called HTO, from ordinary water by membrane distillation. Removing HTO matters for handling radioactive materials and for securing fusion fuel. Their earlier device used water-soaked glass fibers for gas-liquid exchange, and the new work swaps in water-soaked clays and other porous materials instead.

Montmorillonite clay performed best among sepiolite, palygorskite, synthetic zeolite, and mesoporous silica. Adding 4 milliliters of water to 1 gram of montmorillonite lowered the tritium ratio in collected water by about 10 percent, showing clay choice and water amount both matter. The team also notes that cost, time, and ease of use all shape which route a plant or lab may pick for this task.
pmc-13425603:
Köklü and colleagues published a 2026 study on smoked sea bass cooked in sealed bags. Sous-vide cooking holds fish at a steady, gentle heat in its own juices. The team flavored fillets with liquid smoke and cooked them at three heat levels. Each batch then sat in cold storage for 32 days of checks.

Tasters liked the batch cooked at 65 degrees best of the three. That middle heat also balanced safety and texture across the storage period. Germ counts passed safe limits near day 28 for the cooler batches. The warmest batch held its germ counts lower but pleased tasters less. The team set shelf life at 24 days for the winning batch. Chemical freshness scores stayed in the good range through the full month.
pmc-13425903:
Rashima Prem and colleagues rewired a mitochondrial enzyme to uncover hidden lipid trafficking steps in a 2026 cell biology study. Mitochondria build phosphatidylethanolamine using Psd1, an inner membrane enzyme facing the space between membranes, fed by phosphatidylserine shipped from the endoplasmic reticulum. Whether Psd1 acts after transport across that space or at the outer membrane contact sites was unresolved.

Their two-pronged rewiring strategy was designed to bypass known carriers such as Ups2 and Mdm35, or contact site machinery, and observe which routes remain. Results expose trafficking steps that earlier models had not accounted for in mitochondrial membrane assembly.
pmc-13427603:
Tuna Aras and co-authors reply, in 2026, to commentary on their case of an unusual aortic arch, the big artery leaving the heart. Their patient had two shared trunks, one feeding both neck arteries and one feeding both arm arteries. That pattern is often called avian-type, after birds. The reply accepts a pooled rarity estimate from the commentator and then questions the name itself.

Birds, they note, carry paired trunks that each split toward head and wing, so the human pattern only partly matches. The reply ranges across frogs, crocodiles, and fish to show how arch layouts serve each animal's life. A shared question remains open: whether stress on the artery wall in this variant raises tear risk, as seen in a commoner pattern. Rare anatomy, handled carefully, can sharpen basic questions.
pmc-13427703:
Anna J. Esser-Seraphin and a large German team lay out, in a 2026 protocol, a long-term study of eating disorders in elite athletes. Sports that prize leanness can raise risk, and reported rates vary wildly, from about 1 percent up to 28 percent. Eating disorders damage bones, energy, mood, and performance, and their signs can hide inside normal training demands. The ENHANCE study will follow 300 elite athletes across four waves of assessment.

Athletes come from weight-sensitive sports like ballet and bodybuilding and from less sensitive ones like soccer and basketball. A further 300 non-athletes serve as controls, and 90 athletes will also sit for clinical interviews. The team will test which sport-related signs best flag risk and how accurate screening tools are. Better early spotting could get help to athletes sooner.
pmc-13428703:
Daniel Rusu and co-authors track how often lateral compression type 1 pelvic fractures, a common break pattern from side impacts, were treated with surgery in the United States. Their 2026 study uses the National Inpatient Sample for the years 2003 to 2018.

The data covered 43,743 older adults aged 60 and above and 29,024 younger adults. Surgery was used in 3.2 percent of older patients and 20.2 percent of younger patients. Operative care rose steadily, by 5 percent per year in older adults and 2 percent per year in younger adults. Over the same period, hospital stays shortened and deaths fell in both groups. Older surgical patients, however, became slightly less likely to be discharged home. The authors document a clear shift toward operating on these fractures.
pmc-13429903:
Srikanth Sadhu and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, a plant alkaloid that fights Salmonella by arming the host rather than poisoning the germ. Salmonella hides inside cells, where antibiotics reach poorly and resistance grows. The compound, fangchinoline, comes from a traditional medicinal plant. In macrophage dishes it sharpened bacterial killing, and in mice it improved control of infection through the gut.

The effect hinged on nitric oxide, a gas immune cells use as a weapon. Blocking its production erased the benefit, and mice lacking the enzyme that makes it gained no protection. Blood chemistry shifted in ways consistent with making more of the gas. The compound also paired well with a low dose of a standard antibiotic and left a memory-like T-cell imprint that resisted later infection. Host-directed therapy is the pitch.
pmc-13430203:
Bell Xi Wu and colleagues use, in a 2026 study, mice carrying human immune cells to test combination therapy for small cell lung cancer. This cancer comes in four molecular subtypes with distinct immune surroundings, and humanized mice let researchers watch human T cells meet each subtype. Tumors grown from cell lines of all four subtypes drew different levels of T-cell infiltration. The inflamed subtype admitted the most T cells, matching its name.

Infiltrating killer T cells quickly raised exhaustion markers, echoing patient tumors. Checkpoint therapy alone controlled only the inflamed line's tumors. Adding a DNA-repair-blocking drug plus radiation changed the chemistry: tumors released T-cell-attracting signals and raised the checkpoint target itself. Previously cold tumors then responded, and their T cells looked more tumor-focused and less worn out. A platform for testing immune combinations is the wider offer.
pmc-13430303:
Anas Ali Alhur and Nouf Khalid Al-Kahtani presented a 2026 interview study on how health informatics students in Saudi Arabia use generative artificial intelligence in their studies. Thirty undergraduates from six public universities took part. Each student had already used such tools for school work, and talks ran over two months in person and online.

Students said the tools help them sum up readings, grasp hard ideas, plan tasks, and draft assignments. They also raised worries about leaning on the tools too much, learning less on their own, copying, and unclear sources. They noted that rules from their schools remain vague. The authors call for clear guidance, training in sound use, and careful steps to bring the tools into course plans.
pmc-13430803:
Alayne Gatto and colleagues test a website, Baby-Feed, that gives caregivers live feedback on infant diets in the United States. Infant diet advice is often missed, which can lower diet quality and raise later obesity risk.

The site was built on trusted behaviour-change ideas, showing current advice, scoring each diet, and tracking progress. Primary caregivers who read English or Spanish, had internet access, and could receive texts joined a parallel-group randomised trial. Diet quality was scored with a total index from a baseline near four months of age.
pmc-13431703:
Fazal Ur Rehman and co-authors built a three-layer solid filler in 2026 for lithium-metal batteries, aiming to block spiky metal growth while letting charge flow fast. Solid fillers promise safer, denser batteries, yet spikes of lithium, weak seams, and slow flow have held back sales. Their design stacks two soft outer skins over a stiff core.

The core blends a plastic host with ceramic grains wrapped in a sticky coat, plus a stretchy partner that soaks up stress. The coat helps the grains spread evenly and cuts seam drag. The grains open fast paths for lithium ions and loosen the plastic's stiff order. The best mix flowed charge near four times faster than the plain plastic and held up across a wide voltage span. Full cells kept most of their charge after a thousand rounds.
pmc-13432903:
Yang and colleagues studied in 2026 whether flu vaccination is linked to lower stroke risk in older adults with diabetes. Using a regional health platform, they followed 131,045 diabetic adults aged sixty or more for about seven months. About four in ten had received the 2021/22 seasonal flu vaccine.

Vaccinated adults had about fifteen percent lower risk of a first stroke over the follow-up than unvaccinated peers, after adjustments. The link held across flu activity phases and was strongest when the vaccine matched the circulating flu strain well. It was especially marked in patients who also had coronary heart disease. A negative control vaccine against pneumococcus showed no such link, which supports a specific flu effect. They call for randomised trials to prove cause.
pmc-13433403:
Marko Balan and colleagues scope published work on greening intensive care, where the environmental cost of critical care is only beginning to be measured. They searched four databases for studies published before October 2024 on intensive-care sustainability and carbon footprints, hand-checking selected journals.

The search found 1,967 potentially eligible articles, with 149 read in full and 99 meeting the criteria. Studies fell into five domains, led by waste management with 31 and carbon footprint with 20, followed by sustainable medication practice with 9 and energy delivery with 4, plus other topics. ICU leaders get a map of where green evidence is thick and where it thins to anecdote.
pmc-13433803:
Farida Seduk and co-authors found in 2026 that a soil germ's breath enzyme cannot work alone: it must dock in rows on a tube built by a partner protein. Breath enzymes of this kind feed cell power by passing electrons to pool oils in the skin. Stock reads cast this one as a lone skin-sitter, which the new work upends.

Cuts of either partner killed the fuel burn in full. Cold-scope frames show the partner wound into a tube, with enzyme units parked at set gaps by their tail ends. The tube runs near a hundred body lengths long and holds a greasy run of oils that mimics skin. Kin hunts show the pair arose in one germ order alone, poached from a sulfur crew.
pmc-13434003:
Anjun Song and co-authors built a needle patch in 2026 that parks buzzing mineral frames on skin tumors to cut the nerve chatter that shields melanoma from immune attack. Nerves that creep into tumors sway cell shows, T cell fire, and spread. The frames wear coats from nerve cells to home on pain nerves in the tumor.

One patch dose settles the frames at the spot in female mice. Mild sound shakes make the frames drag a heat gate inside pain nerves and wake a DNA alarm road, which trims the nerves' flow of two calm-down scraps. With that chatter cut, the tumor's immune room heals and nerve creep shrinks. The authors pitch nerve-aimed patches as a fresh lever for immune care.
pmc-13434203:
Rongxiang Zhang and colleagues build a full chromosome map for Lycopus lucidus, a healing plant with many chromosome sets that grows widely across China. Plants gain sets and then shed them, yet how uneven set evolution shapes adaptation to place was little known.

The map shows a recent tripling of the whole genome. Its three sets differ sharply in jumping-gene load, gene keeping, and speed of change. Set B held steady under strong purifying selection, while sets A and C reshaped fast, with rapid gene turnover, gene decay, and lopsided selection. Gene data from sixty plants split into four lineages that match geography, giving breeders a map of local adaptation.
pmc-13434403:
Lucia Varbaro and coauthors report a rare effect in a nickel based superconductor in 2026. The material carries current with no loss, then loses that trait in a magnetic field, then gains it back as the field grows. Europium added to the layers plays a key part in the odd return.

Voltage tests and models of the loss point show two rare earth ions pulling in rival ways. Their pull is felt only once a field lines them up. The balance lets the no loss state return at high field. The result helps physicists test how nickel layers pair with cuprate cousins.
pmc-13434503:
Joseph Lim, Jaeso Cho, and Hunmin Kim discuss brain network markers for children whose epilepsy resists drugs in 2026. Early brain growth builds the white matter links that wire large networks. Lasting seizures in those years may bend that growth and shape later thinking skills. Usual pre surgery checks count seizures and drug load but say little about network change.

The piece weighs a study that reads routine brain scans for network flaws tied to weak thinking in these children. Past work shows epilepsy scrambles network order well past the seizure zone. Scan based markers may sort which child needs which support path. The next step is proof in larger groups.
pmc-13434603:
Do and colleagues published a 2026 study on what shapes newborn size in Vietnam. Birth weight and length predict health in the first years of life. The team read records for 198 full-term babies born at one Hai Phong hospital. They weighed mother, father, and care factors against the babies' measures.

Longer pregnancy and heavier mothers before pregnancy predicted heavier babies at birth. Protein supplements during pregnancy also nudged birth weight upward in the model. Father's height was the strongest single predictor of baby length overall. Mother's height and weight added their own share to length predictions. Care before birth should involve both parents, the authors argue. Family context belongs in prenatal checks, not mother-only screening alone.
pmc-13434803:
Nancy E. Rodas De Leon's team asked in 2026 whether a lifetime of using two languages reshapes how the brain pays attention. They recorded brain waves and reaction times from young adults with varied language histories. The volunteers watched a visual oddball task, a setup known to trigger a brain wave called P3b when a rare target appears. Language history was scored from a background questionnaire, and childhood family income level was held steady in the checks.

Greater bilingual experience went with a larger P3b response, even though behavior on the task did not differ and family income did not explain the link. The paper argues that long bilingual use may tune the neural side of attention, not just test scores. Brain teams get a careful, controlled link between language life and attention circuits.
pmc-13435003:
Traxler and colleagues ran a randomized controlled trial in Germany testing whether a single in-person seminar could reduce stigma toward people with skin diseases among health and personal care workers. Cosmeticians, hairdressers, nurses, and physiotherapists often work in close body contact, and patients with visible skin conditions report avoidance and humiliation in exactly those settings. Results of the 2026 study were published in German.

Traxler assigned 64 workers to the anti-stigma seminar, which combined self-reflection exercises, factual teaching, and a meeting with a patient, while 65 controls attended a workplace health seminar instead. The seminar group showed clear drops in false beliefs about skin disease and in agreement with negative stereotypes, measured right after the session and three months later. The wish for social distance fell in both groups after their seminars but returned to starting levels by follow-up, suggesting belief change lasts longer than distance change.
pmc-13435903:
Gui and colleagues analysed in 2026 whether government health spending improves health outcomes across China's thirty-one provinces, using panel data from 2008 to 2023. They applied fixed-effects models with statistical instruments to limit bias, then tested indirect pathways and threshold effects. Outcomes were maternal deaths, deaths around birth, and life expectancy, set against the national Healthy China strategy.

Spending significantly cut maternal and perinatal mortality, but showed no significant effect on life expectancy. One pathway backfired: the sheer count of health institutions carried a negative mediating effect. Effects also depended on context. In low-income settings, extra spending could even produce worse outcomes. As regional income and health resources grew, the same spending turned clearly positive. Most pharmacology so far comes from the sponsor. The authors argue the drug's handling suits kidney patients, while warning that a biased partial agonist should not be assumed to copy peptide drugs.
pmc-13458103:
Xinyue Hou and colleagues test nano additives in steel fibre concrete in a 2026 study. Steel fibre concrete resists cracking better than plain concrete, yet nano silica and nano titanium carbide may further lift strength and freeze-thaw durability. Single additions of nano silica at 1, 2 and 3 percent and nano titanium carbide at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 percent were tested at 7 and 28 days, with mixed additions and freeze-thaw checks following.

Single additives barely changed 7-day strength but improved 28-day compressive, splitting and flexural strength, with nano silica best at 2 percent and nano titanium carbide best at 1 percent. The best mix, 2 percent nano silica plus 0.5 percent nano titanium carbide, optimised pore structure and improved freeze-thaw resistance. Builders gain a tested dosage sweet spot, though gains varied widely across mixes, so site trials remain wise.
pmc-13458403:
Trojnar and colleagues turned in 2026 a cancer drug's worst side mark, skin burn in light, into its mode of attack. The drug hugs a knot form of DNA found at gene starts and strand caps. In bare brew it makes both kinds of harsh air bits when lit. Bound to the knots, its light math flips: one kind fades, and free rad sparks take the lead. The team read the sparks, then dosed cancer cells and mice.

Lit drug killed cancer cells at up to a hundredth the dark dose. Harm marks stacked in the cell's code, and the knots them selves came loose. In mice, lit doses shrank tumors and stretched life. Dead cells wailed in ways that wake guard cells, a plus for joint care. The team pitches light aim at tumors as the path to use a known drug anew.
pmc-13458503:
Lola P. Lozano and colleagues test whether low testosterone helps explain why some men's urethras scar shut. Most anterior urethral strictures arrive with no known cause, although testosterone builds the male urethra before birth and aids its healing afterward. Their 2026 secondary analysis draws on a prospective multicenter study of 154 men having urethroplasty, measuring five blood hormones against nine men having vasectomies.

Free testosterone, the available fraction, ran at barely half the control level in stricture patients, 1.08 against 2.13 in the reported units, and each unit increase cut the adjusted odds of stricture by 67 percent. Among patients, longer strictures paired with lower free testosterone. Total testosterone and the other hormones, estradiol, progesterone, and cortisol, showed no such pattern, and hormone levels did not track inflammation. The authors suggest that scarce free testosterone leaves the urethra unable to repair everyday micro-injuries, letting scar win, a theory awaiting proof.
pmc-13458603:
Nicholas Gillman and Eric Chung place eleven erectile dysfunction guidelines side by side and note where the world's experts actually disagree.
