Thresholds and sequencing should adapt to regional practice and to the individual patient, rather than treating any single guideline as universal law.
pmc-13458903:
Jin and colleagues argue that a thickened heart wall, found on ultrasound, should start a diagnosis hunt rather than end one. Left ventricular hypertrophy means a wall thicker than set cutoffs. It most often comes from high blood pressure. But it can also signal inherited muscle disease, amyloid deposits, or Fabry disease, a storage disorder. Their 2026 article warns that wall thickness alone cannot tell these apart, yet the right label matters, since each cause now has its own therapy.

Delays are long: amyloid heart disease takes five to six years to name, and Fabry disease more than thirteen years, by the authors' figures. They propose a two step pathway guided by the pattern of clues. Frontline care gathers family history, body signs, heart tracings, and imaging red flags. These split plain pressure effects from suspect cases. Specialist centers then confirm the cause so treatment can start early.
pmc-13459203:
Mohd Aizuddin Mohd Zulastri and co-authors report a 54 year old Malaysian woman whose hidden lung cancer first announced itself through fluid squeezing her heart. She arrived with three weeks of productive cough, low fever, and breathlessness on exertion. She was first treated for pneumonia with fluid around one lung. In their 2026 case report, the authors describe how her symptoms persisted despite antibiotics and drainage. A scan then revealed fluid completely surrounding the heart with signs of cardiac tamponade, dangerous pressure on the heart, even though her blood pressure stayed normal.

An urgent needle drainage removed 600 milliliters of blood stained fluid, and lab analysis of that fluid found malignant glandular cancer cells. Body imaging then revealed a right upper lung mass with spread to the chest lining, pericardium, bones, adrenal glands, and skin. The authors stress that early heart ultrasound and fluid testing are essential when effusions remain unexplained.
pmc-13459603:
Yang Niu and co-authors examined how stroke type affects thinking and speech, using artificial intelligence to analyze patients' voices for diagnostic clues. Their 2026 study compared 117 people at a hospital in Anhui, China, in three groups: lacunar infarction, where tiny deep vessels block; larger non-lacunar infarction; and healthy controls. Everyone took a standard cognitive screening test and described a standard picture aloud, generating speech recordings from which acoustic features were extracted.

Both stroke groups scored lower on cognition than controls, and the non-lacunar group performed worst overall. The gap showed clearly in fluency tasks, where the non-lacunar group differed most from controls, and in memory tasks, where both stroke groups lagged. The speech analysis also found acoustic features that differed between the two stroke types themselves. Voice features could help distinguish small deep strokes from larger ones, the authors suggest, cheaply and non-invasively.
pmc-13460103:
Hao Chen and a Beijing team compared in 2026 two strategies for repairing disease of the aortic arch, the curved top of the body's main artery. Hybrid repair reroutes the branches above the arch and then relines the aorta from inside, while the frozen elephant trunk operation replaces the arch in open surgery. Records for 785 patients treated at Beijing Anzhen Hospital from 2015 to 2023 were analyzed, with statistical weighting to balance the groups.

Hybrid patients were older and carried more diabetes and lipid problems before adjustment. Even so, their operations involved less blood loss and quicker recovery than the open procedure, advantages that persisted after weighting. The study weighs those perioperative gains against later outcomes such as death, stroke, and repeat intervention, informing choices for patients unfit for the bigger operation.
pmc-13460203:
Josefina Principe and Facundo Iriarte review in 2026 an uncommon surgical route for closing bronchopleural fistula, a leaking airway stump left after a lung is removed. Rather than reopening the original chest incision, surgeons approach through the breastbone and the sac around the heart, reaching the central airway from the front. The review gathers case series and technical reports on who qualifies, how the closure is reinforced, and what outcomes follow.

The front route avoids dissecting through an infected, scarred chest cavity, and published series report durable closure with acceptable complication rates in chosen patients. Results vary widely, reflecting differences in patient condition, fistula size, infection, and earlier failed repairs. Bronchoscopy and camera assistance are emerging helpers, yet the research base remains small and retrospective.
pmc-13461503:
Hikmat Abdel-Razeq and colleagues report in 2026 germline genetic findings from 652 Jordanian men diagnosed with cancer at age fifty or younger. Inherited risk is often suspected in this group yet rarely mapped outside Western populations. Every man in the King Hussein Cancer Center program received multigene panel testing of inherited DNA regardless of tumor type, stage, or family history, and results were sorted against standard testing criteria.

Ninety men, about fourteen percent, carried a clearly harmful inherited variant, and a third carried an uncertain one. Yield ran far higher in men meeting standard criteria, and youngest patients, those diagnosed between eighteen and thirty, showed the richest haul at over a quarter testing positive. Colorectal cancer dominated the case mix and the positive findings, with six genes recurring most often.
pmc-13462003:
Lindsey Vilca and co-authors examined the internal structure of the PHQ-4, a four question anxiety and depression screener, across four Latin American countries using network psychometrics. That newer framework treats symptoms as a web of interacting items. Whether the scale forms one dimension or two, anxiety versus depression, has been argued from older methods. In their 2026 study, 1,887 adults aged eighteen to forty from Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru completed the questionnaire. Community detection analysis mapped how the four items cluster in each country.

In all four countries the four items formed a single community with large network loadings, supporting one unified dimension of distress rather than separable clusters. Redundancy analysis confirmed every item contributed uniquely to the network in each national sample. The structure held consistently across countries with different sample sizes. For Latin American screening practice, the authors conclude, the PHQ-4 works best scored as one total.
pmc-13462403:
Cheng and co-authors proposed a 2026 review framing inflammatory bowel disease as a disorder of chemical conversation between gut microbes and the body. Microbes release metabolites, small molecules such as short-chain fatty acids and bile acid products, that shape the gut barrier and immune activity. The authors call the lasting imprint of those signals microbial metabolic memory.

Cheng argues that helpful metabolites dwindle while inflammatory ones build up, breaking immune tolerance and weakening the barrier even during remission. Inflammation then reshapes the gut environment, which pushes microbes to make yet more inflammatory products, locking in a feedback loop. That loop may explain why the disease keeps relapsing after symptoms settle. Treatments discussed include adding back helpful metabolites, blocking harmful signals, engineered probiotics, and diet guided precision care.
pmc-13463503:
Gavin Haines and three co-authors review nitrate poisoning in cattle and other ruminants, in a 2026 paper on farm animal health. Forage can build up nitrate under drought, frost, or heavy fertilizer use. Once eaten, that nitrate can turn to nitrite in the rumen and block the blood from carrying oxygen well.

Guidance for safe intake levels varies a great deal between sources and between states, the authors show. Much of the base research is old, and fresh work since the 1970s has been thin. Their review sorts the factors that drive buildup and risk, then presses for clear, proof-based limits. Ranchers and vets get a plain map of where the rules agree and where they still clash.
pmc-13463603:
Mohammad Faraz Zafeer and a large team study how a distant gene switch controls GDF6, a gene needed to build the cochlea. The cochlea is the snail-shaped hearing part of the inner ear. Switches far from a gene can still turn its activity up or down.

Deleting the switch stretch in mice, or muting it with CRISPR tools, cut GDF6 activity sharply. Ear tissue then failed to mature, and hair-like hearing cells never formed. Human ear organoids, small lab-grown ear models, showed the same dependence on the switch. The findings help explain deafness in patients who lack this stretch of DNA.
pmc-13463703:
Ana María Quirós and colleagues profiled the nutrition of a Costa Rican cricket powder to judge its value as human food. The cricket belongs to the genus Gryllus, though its form hints it may differ from described species.

Corrected for shell fibre, the protein content reached about 61.5 grams per 100 grams of dry powder, with fat near 11.7 grams. Essential amino acids made up about 56.5 percent of all amino acids, a strong share, though lysine ran short against world reference patterns. The powder was rich in potassium, phosphorus, and calcium, and its fats were mostly the heart-friendlier unsaturated kinds. Quirós concludes the cricket could complement other proteins in sustainable foods, best paired with lysine-rich partners.
pmc-13464403:
Al-Hatab and colleagues built in 2026 a light computer pipeline that sorts brain MRI scans into four stages of Alzheimer's disease, from no dementia to moderate dementia. Sorting stages accurately helps plan care, but heavy deep-learning systems demand costly hardware. The team wanted a lean method that still scores high.

Their pipeline pulls features from scans with a compact pre-trained network, then shrinks the feature list with principal component analysis, a method that keeps the most informative parts. A hundred kept components held nearly all the signal. Several classifiers were then tested, and a fuzzy neural method called EFMM won, scoring about 97 percent accuracy on held-out scans and about 98 percent across repeated validation folds. The authors present the pipeline as a fast, low-cost aid for staging the disease.
pmc-13466903:
Marta Carnovali and colleagues feed zebrafish a diet laced with PFOA, a persistent industrial chemical. Their 2026 study watches what happens to the fish's bones and to their offspring. Exposed young adult fish grew shorter and lighter than unexposed controls. Their scales, which soak up the chemical into the mineral layer, shrank in area.

Bone-building cells in the scales worked less while bone-eating cells worked harder, especially at the scale's center. The inner skeleton showed malformations across spine, ribs, fins, and jaw structures. Embryos from exposed parents were also checked for viability and development, extending the harm picture across a generation.
pmc-13467003:
Tingting Wen, Bing Xiong, Chengjie Mei, and Shengwen Song present four anesthesia patients who inhaled stomach contents and were treated by washing the airways through a scope, in a 2026 case series. Aspiration during anesthesia can be life-threatening, and whether washing helps or spreads contamination further has long been debated. The four were high-risk patients who had inhaled large amounts of fluid, solid food, or bile.

After washing with a quarter to over two thirds of a liter of saline into the affected lung sections, every patient's oxygen levels improved at once and airway pressures fell. None developed severe pneumonia or lung failure, and follow-up scans showed no spread of contamination. One patient even had pre-existing lung injury from pancreatitis and still recovered well.
pmc-13467103:
Boyi Wei and colleagues designed a foldable honeycomb material studded with resonators that blocks low-frequency waves and softens impacts. The structure builds on the Miura-ori fold pattern, adding tuned vibrating masses inside a polygonal honeycomb.

Analysis and lab tests found two complete bandgaps, frequency ranges no wave can cross, in the low-frequency zone. Widening the resonators merged two narrow gaps into one broader gap, giving designers a tuning knob. Under impact pulses, the material cut peak reaction force by 43.43 percent versus the same honeycomb without resonators. The peak force also arrived 26 milliseconds later, spreading the blow over more time. Eight resonators per cell proved the best balance of performance and light weight, Wei reports.
pmc-13467803:
Li, Lan, and Yao primed a 2026 study of sweet sorghum seed soaked in gibberellic acid, a plant hormone, to harden seedlings against drought. How the leaf cuticle, the waxy skin that seals in water, responds to such priming was unclear. A screening test first picked the dose that helped growth most under dry conditions.

Ten milligrams per litre proved optimal, lifting height and biomass while cutting markers of oxidative damage in droughted seedlings. Under drought, primed plants boosted leaf alkanes and primary alcohols sharply, and one waxy compound rose more than four fold. Li found primed plants also lost water from leaves most slowly, matching their heavier cuticle deposits. The work used a single sorghum genotype under controlled conditions, so field confirmation remains open.
pmc-13467903:
Gan and colleagues describe an unusual cancer case in this 2026 report: a palate tumor that returned as neck lymph node metastasis more than a decade after seemingly successful treatment. The tumor type was mucoepidermoid carcinoma, the most common cancer of the salivary glands, in this instance arising in the hard palate of a 47-year-old woman.

Her original, well-differentiated tumor was removed surgically, and she stayed clear for 11 years before lumps appeared in the right side of her neck. Surgeons at Guangxi Medical University removed the neck mass completely along with the surrounding lymph nodes, and pathology confirmed the same carcinoma had spread. Eleven months after the second operation she remained under follow-up. The authors stress that even low-grade palate tumors keep a long tail of metastasis risk, so close surveillance should extend for many years.
pmc-13468003:
Weixuan Liu and colleagues review in 2026 how quantum dots, tiny semiconductor crystals, can push perovskite solar cells closer to their theoretical limits. Perovskite cells already exceed 26 percent certified efficiency, yet they still fall short of the maximum possible and degrade too fast for the market. Quantum dots bring size-tunable energy levels, bright light output, and easy solution processing to that fight.

The review examines four ways of adding the dots: modifying the charge transport layers, doping the active layer, converting ultraviolet light into usable light, and serving as sub-cells in tandem stacks. It compares the mechanisms behind each, from defect repair to slowing ion drift. It also names the open problems, including toxic lead and cadmium in many dots and the lack of standard stability tests. The framework helps cell designers pick the right dot strategy for each layer.
pmc-13468103:
Sakhile T. Dube, Lindelani Q. Qwabe and Holger B. Friedrich published this 2026 review on turning waste glycerol into glycerol carbonate, a useful chemical for solvents and plastics. Glycerol floods the market as a biodiesel by-product, so upgrading it adds value. The route reviewed reacts glycerol with alkyl carbonates, helped by catalysts made from mixed metal oxides. The authors examine how these catalysts work, aided by computer modelling.

Catalysts pairing metals such as magnesium with aluminium, iron, zirconium or barium converted over 90 percent of the glycerol fed in. Of the product, 90 to 96 percent was the carbonate, often without solvents. Modelling showed the secret is teamwork between basic sites, which strip a proton from glycerol, and acidic sites, which activate the carbonate partner. The review also covers microwave and ultrasound heating to speed the process. The authors map what blocks scale-up, including catalyst fouling and metal loss.
pmc-13469303:
Ya-Nan Zhang and co-authors build in a 2026 letter a safer screening system for hunting drugs against Mayaro virus. The mosquito-borne alphavirus causes fever, headache, joint pain, and rash much like chikungunya. The virus is classed at biosafety level 3, which makes live-virus drug screening slow and restricted, and no approved vaccine or specific treatment exists. Their solution is a replicon: a stripped viral genome that copies itself inside cells without producing infectious virus.

The replicon carries a drug-resistance marker and a light-producing reporter gene, and it was installed in a stable hamster cell line kept under puromycin selection. Compound activity then reads out as fading light, enabling high-throughput screening in ordinary containment. A screening platform that removes the dangerous virus from the assay lets many more laboratories join the search for Mayaro antivirals.
pmc-13469603:
Kengo Utsunomiya and colleagues examined retinal age gap in 2026 among glaucoma patients, testing whether eye factors distort an AI ageing marker. Retinal age gap, the gap between AI-guessed eye age and real age, tracks whole-body disease, yet eye influences were unclear. The study reviewed 283 eyes photographed at Yamanashi Hospital from 2010 to 2025, estimating retinal age with a deep learning model.

Mean true age was 65.5 years against predicted 59.9, giving a mean gap of negative 5.7 years. Lens status mattered most, with natural-lens eyes showing larger gaps than artificial-lens eyes, while worse vision and farsightedness also raised gaps. Overall glaucoma severity did not track the gap, except in natural-lens eyes, so clinicians must adjust retinal age readings for lens status and vision.
pmc-13469703:
Mariko Takeuchi found a paired lethal target in 2026 for cancers missing both SMARCA4 and SMARCA2 DNA shapers. Dual-loss tumours, including lung cancer subsets and ovarian small cell cancer, resist current paralog plans. Genomic analysis fingered the CHD3/NuRD complex as a gene-switch brake at the PARD3B booster in these cancers.

Cutting CHD3 freed PARD3B through DNA opening, and PARD3B build-up killed cells while dampening MYC marks without breaking MYC protein. CHD3 loss shrank dual-lacking tumours in mice, proving the route in vivo. The gain-of-poison route offers a fresh treatment avenue for treatment-stubborn dual-loss cancers.
pmc-13470403:
Shanshan Liu tested cracked sandstone in 2026 under cyclic loading and unloading for deep building safety. Cracked rock in tunnels, mines, and caverns faces complex stresses, and its failure ways govern frame safety. Lab tests, CT scanning, and number runs traced fissure growth under one-way and then two-way cyclic loads.

Under one-way cycles, peak strength and elastic modulus rose with fissure angle, while crack start stress first fell then rose, and damage grew with angle. Under two-way cycles, angle barely changed strength or modulus but worsened shear-ruled failure, with higher start stress, wider spread, and severer damage than one-way cases. The checked model supports safety review for cracked rock masses.
pmc-13471303:
Xiang and an international team showed in 2026 how black soldier fly larvae staff their gut with microbes to digest tough plant waste they cannot break down alone. Larvae raised germ-free barely degraded the fiber at all, while larvae with gut microbes degraded about a third. The team mapped immune activity and sugar-coating genes along the gut, profiling microbe communities in each section.

The gut runs a dismissing-then-recruiting strategy: the front midgut bristles with antimicrobial weapons, a selective barrier killing most arrivals. The rear midgut lowers its immune guard and ramps up genes coating surfaces with sugars, a four-to-fivefold rise. Those sugars feed exactly the symbionts thriving there, microbes armed with fiber-cutting enzymes. The rear gut thus farms its workforce rather than tolerating it. The authors say the principle could improve industrial waste conversion with these larvae, already farmed for protein and waste processing.
pmc-13471403:
Wang and co-authors searched for a way to make kidney tumors that resist PARP inhibitors, a class of DNA-repair-blocking drugs, vulnerable to them. Their 2026 laboratory study screened DNA-damaging alkylating agents for synergy with PARP blockade in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the subtype behind about 80% of kidney cancers. Tumors with normal BRCA genes, usually unmoved by these inhibitors, were the specific target.

The effect depended on SLFN11, a protein missing in about 45% of cancer cells, which marked which tumors responded. Combinations shrank tumors in mouse xenografts and in patient-derived tumor grafts, and every drug involved is already approved for cancer treatment.
pmc-13471503:
Han and co-authors pooled trials of online advance care planning decision aids, websites that help cancer patients record future care wishes. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered 12 studies, including 10 randomized trials, mostly from the United States, searching the literature through March 10, 2026.

The programs worked where it matters most administratively: patients using them were about twice as likely to have planning documented, with an odds ratio of 2.06 in the pooled analysis, and engagement scores rose by 0.28 points on average. But completing an advance directive itself did not significantly improve, with an odds ratio of 1.37 whose interval crossed no effect. Satisfaction, decisional conflict, and anxiety also showed no clear change.
pmc-13471603:
Feyissa and colleagues asked new mothers in Adama town, Ethiopia, whether they could recognize the warning signs that a newborn needs urgent care. Their 2026 cross-sectional study interviewed 426 postpartum women at public facilities during April 2022, testing recognition of nine World Health Organization danger signs with prompted yes-or-no items.

Three quarters scored well: 75.5% of mothers showed good knowledge by the study's cutoff, far above the 20.3 to 67.1% range reported in earlier Ethiopian studies. Education drove the gap, with college-educated mothers at 4.83 times the adjusted odds of good knowledge and secondary schooling at 3.10 times the odds. Caesarean delivery, at 2.47 times the odds, and having given birth before also helped, which the authors link to longer contact with health staff.
pmc-13472003:
Baptiste Ganachaud and colleagues review in 2026 how gut microbes and the gut own nervous system interact in the digestive troubles that shadow autism. The enteric nervous system, the nerve web governing gut movement, sits exactly between those microbes and gut function.

Evidence from patients and mouse models shows both partners changed in autism, and the review focuses on microbe derived mediators that can steer the development and daily work of the enteric nerves. Serotonin related and metabolite pathways feature heavily in that traffic. The authors suggest the gut nerve interface may also feed back on behavioral severity, making it a therapeutic target worth testing rather than a curiosity.
pmc-13472803:
Ren and colleagues present a 2026 comprehensive review of blood-based monitoring of ESR1 mutations in advanced breast cancer that is hormone-sensitive and HER2-negative. First-line treatment pairs hormone therapy with CDK4/6 inhibitors, but resistance grows, and mutations in the estrogen receptor gene ESR1 are a central escape route. Tumor DNA circulating in blood lets doctors track these mutations without repeat biopsies.

The review weighs the value of ESR1 mutations found before treatment and during it: they forecast worse outcomes on standard therapy and can signal when to switch to newer receptor-targeted drugs. Because mutation levels rise and fall with treatment, they act as moving decision points rather than fixed labels.
pmc-13473003:
Ladányi and colleagues report a 2026 study of tumor-infiltrating immune cells as predictors in melanoma patients given PD-1 inhibitor drugs after surgery. These drugs cut recurrence, yet many patients still relapse within two years. The team stained pretreatment tumor samples from 48 patients for seven immune markers and measured how densely each cell type packed the tumor.

Eighteen of the 48 patients relapsed during follow-up. Densities of specific immune subsets, counted before treatment began, associated with how long patients stayed recurrence-free. A tumor's immune mix at surgery thus carries information about whether adjuvant therapy will hold.  Such markers are urgent because the drugs are costly and can cause lasting side effects.
pmc-13473503:
Hafsa Khan and colleagues put forward a neural network method in 2026 for equations with memory and delay effects. Such equations model odd spread patterns, memory circuits, and swirling fluid motion. The new method, called PINN-CF, trains a network to honor the physics rules inside the equation itself. It uses a smooth memory kernel that avoids sharp faults found in older forms.

Four test problems checked the method, from delayed growth rules to circuit models. Error levels stayed very low across the tests, near the floor set for the runs. Charts of error over training backed up the headline scores. The work gives modelers a flexible solver for systems where the past shapes the present.
pmc-13473703:
Erdoğmuş and colleagues in Türkiye tested in 2026 whether a folk herb, Anchusa azurea, can speed wound healing when packed in tiny fat bubbles. The alcohol brew held more shields and fought rust harder. Both brews left skin cells unharmed in dish tests.

The brews were then sealed in nanoliposomes, fat bubbles a hair across, which leak their load in two waves. On cut wounds in rats, the bubbled forms beat the plain brews and the bare controls. Wounds shrank faster, and tissue checks showed more collagen, more new blood paths, and quicker new skin. The alcohol brew and its bubble form led the pack. The team backs them for wound care goods.
pmc-13473803: Correction notice: Sylvain Rama, Thomas P. Jensen and Dmitri A. Rusakov correct Figure 2 of their 2026 article on glutamate imaging in the giant mossy fiber boutons of the brain's CA3 region. The figure appeared heavily distorted in the online version, and the notice supplies the corrected version, which also appears in the PDF. The figure shows distinct glutamate release sites inside single large boutons, with line-scan traces capturing releases that are not synchronised between sites, including spontaneous events. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13474003:
Phillips and co-workers in Australia read in 2026 the files of a state body that runs a new web of help hubs for the families of people with mental ills. The hubs, called Connect centres, are staffed by folk who have cared for kin in the same straits. The lead body, Connect Coordination Victoria, is run by such carers too. The team read 41 files from two of its shared works, a set of teach meets and a show case day, and coded what the words showed.

Four core values stood out: connection, responsiveness, consistency, and flexibility. The hubs gain from a lead body that shares their lived roots, the authors say. Its meets gave a far flung new workforce a place to swap craft and feel one team. The authors set out steps that like bodies can use to name their own work values.
pmc-13474703:
Xuhao Liu, Minfeng Chen, and Yi Cai test chatbots as teaching aids in 2026 for prostate cancer training of urology residents. Three leading models answered a forty-item question bank and were graded blind by experts. The top scorer then joined a small randomized teaching trial with thirty-four residents. Both trial groups got the same lectures, with one group allowed model help for study questions.

One model, DeepSeek R1, ranked first, with an edge on higher-order and creative questions. The aided group scored about ten points higher on a closed-book exam. Gains concentrated in choice questions and research items, not in team case review. Teachers and students both rated the aid well, which supports careful classroom use.
pmc-13474803:
Song and co-authors studied in 2026 which psoriasis patients test positive on the interferon-gamma release assay, a blood test for latent tuberculosis that guidelines recommend before starting biologic therapy. A positive result can delay treatment, yet the factors behind positivity in this population were poorly characterized. The team reviewed records from a single dermatology center and built a statistical model of the associations.

Of 1,126 patients without prior tuberculosis, 285 tested positive, an overall rate of 25.3 percent that climbed steeply with age, from 8.2 percent in those thirty or younger to 45.6 percent in patients over sixty. Older age, pulmonary nodules, and a higher eosinophil percentage each independently raised the odds of positivity, while prior biologic exposure lowered them, likely through selection effects. The eight-variable model discriminated acceptably. The authors say it adds context but must not replace standard tuberculosis assessment.
pmc-13475703:
Chunming Tan and seven colleagues published this 2026 food science study on how vacuum-packed marinated silver carp, a popular Chinese freshwater fish product, spoils over 60 days of storage. The team tracked appearance and taste acceptance, spoilage markers, flavour compounds and the bacteria living on the fish, tying the threads of spoilage into one story.

By day 60 the fish looked and smelled clearly worse. Protein and fat oxidation advanced together, shown by rising spoilage nitrogen and fat breakdown values, falling protective sulfhydryl groups and rising carbonyls. Five signature aroma compounds, including eugenol, nonanal and linalool, escaped or faded, draining the flavour. The bacterial mix flipped: Bacillus, dominant early, gave way to Enterococcus, and twelve genera were flagged as likely spoilage promoters feeding on amino acids and sugars. The authors offer the combined picture as a basis for keeping fish fresh.
pmc-13475803:
Lin Chen and seven colleagues published this 2026 case report of one patient, a 64-year-old man whose heart artery procedure caused a tear that spread into the aorta. During treatment of his right coronary artery, the tear began as a Dunning class II dissection. It resisted the rescue attempt: standard drug-eluting stents failed to seal the backward tear into the aortic root, and it progressed to class III.

The operators then placed a covered stent at the artery's opening, halting the dissection's advance. Strict blood pressure control and a surgical team on standby backed the rescue. The case is presented as the first report of this percutaneous strategy for this complication. The authors argue covered stents deserve a defined bailout role when standard stents cannot seal tears, avoiding emergency open-heart surgery in stable patients.
pmc-13476703:
Latika Singh and co-authors build a two-in-one antibody in 2026 that blocks a checkpoint and traps a calming cytokine at once. Treated T cells resisted IL-10 damping and fired up more strongly than with either part alone. Helper immune cells also shifted toward a mature, active state. Killer T cell activation beat checkpoint care alone and beat the loose mix of parts. Dual targeting may rescue patients whom single checkpoints fail.
pmc-13476903:
Kai Tsugaru and colleagues studied d-serine, a mirror-form amino acid, as a hidden brake on the immune attack against stomach tumours. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, and the d-form is the flipped twin of the usual l-form.

In mouse tumours, d-serine weakened killer T cells and boosted suppressive macrophages, the immune cells that calm attacks down. Blood, urine, and stool levels of d-serine ran higher in stomach cancer patients than in 87 healthy controls. Higher blood levels tracked later disease stages across the patient groups studied. Patients with high levels also answered poorly to a standard immune therapy drug, marking d-serine as a warning sign.
pmc-13478603:
Kefan Chen and colleagues report a 2026 climate study reconstructing the Atlantic overturning circulation across the last preindustrial millennium. This circulation moves heat northward and shapes climate worldwide, yet its past behavior and causes stayed disputed. The team combined indirect natural records, several climate models, and a data assimilation method that merges both.

Their reconstruction shows the circulation slowly weakening from the year 850 into the Little Ice Age, losing roughly 0.7 sverdrups, about four percent of its flow. Explosive volcanic eruptions emerge as the main cause. Each eruption briefly strengthened the circulation, then left a century-scale weakening as cold stored in the deep Atlantic fed back on surface climate. The work offers a physical explanation for a long-debated trend.
pmc-13479203:
Dalibor Procházka and coauthors published a 2026 computer-model study of driverless ground craft for battlefield medical rescue runs. Speed from the point of injury to a casualty pickup point strongly shapes survival, and combat units now handle this leg with one armored vehicle per pickup point under current doctrine. The team modeled a possible fleet of robot craft.

Data on injury timing and place came from computer-aided drills, and the test used agent-based models mixed with discrete event models. Spread-out unmanned transport worked better because the wounded could be served by injury class first rather than in simple order. The authors stress the idea stays on paper for now. Benefits depend on AI support plus live data on each wounded soldier's state from body sensors.
pmc-13479503:
Mika P. Nadvornik and colleagues published a 2026 protocol for comparing antiseptic irrigation fluids in patients with abdominal abscesses drained through the skin. Drainage is the standard treatment, and saline rinsing cleans mechanically but kills no germs. Hypochlorous acid, an antiseptic the body itself produces, offers broad germ killing with good tissue tolerance.

The study exploits a hospital practice switch on the first of December 2025, comparing patients treated before and after in one center. Main questions are whether the antiseptic shortens drain time and the course of systemic antibiotics. The ambispective design combines records already collected with prospective follow-up. The authors pre-register their methods so the eventual results can be judged against a fixed plan.
pmc-13479703:
Angelika Lahnsteiner and coauthors published a 2026 analysis of how metabolic disease gene variants may act by breaking tiny folded DNA structures called G-quadruplexes. These four-stranded knots sit in gene control regions and tune how strongly genes are read. Genome studies have tied thousands of variants to metabolic diseases, yet most have no known mechanism.

Between about one and two percent of metabolic disease variants fell inside predicted quadruplex motifs, depending on the prediction method. The team tested how those variants change the structures' stability and shape, and whether they sit in alternative promoters also seen in cancer. A variant that collapses a quadruplex could raise or lower a gene's output, offering a concrete mechanism for otherwise mysterious statistical associations.
pmc-13480103:
Aman Shrestha and co-authors offer a 2026 pooled review of elder abuse among older adults living at home in South Asia. The team searched six databases plus grey sources and kept 33 studies from five countries, with most from India and Nepal. Adults aged sixty and above counted, and abuse within family or community settings formed the focus.

Across studies, about thirty-two percent of older adults reported abuse, though results varied so widely that the pooled figure needs care. Nepal showed the highest share near fifty percent, while India sat near twenty-six percent. Women faced abuse more often than men. Neglect by caregivers and emotional abuse were the most common forms, each near twenty percent. Three countries in the region had no usable studies at all. The authors call for country-level research and for community programs that fit local family norms.
pmc-13480203:
Yue-Loong Hsin and Min-Fei Chuang report a 2026 study of frailty among older adults admitted to hospital with epilepsy. The team drew on a national United States inpatient database spanning 2005 to 2022. Adults aged sixty and above with epilepsy as the main diagnosis numbered near 177,000 stays, and a standard frailty index sorted patients into frail and non-frail groups.

Nearly fifty-eight percent of stays counted as frail. After matching patients on other traits, frailty linked to more major complications, more urinary infections, longer stays, and more discharges to care settings rather than home, plus higher hospital costs. Oddly, frail patients showed lower death rates during the stay, which the authors tie to discharge patterns rather than protection. Spotting frailty early may help teams plan support and discharge for this group.
pmc-13481403:
Muyang Liu and Xiaojun Shen report a 2026 study of a stitch that may cut fluid build-up after keyhole groin hernia repair. Large hernia rings leave a pocket where fluid gathers after surgery. The team reviewed 162 patients with wide rings at one Chinese hospital across a year, half with the inner ring stitched shut during repair and half without.

Fluid pockets at one week struck under nine percent of the stitched group against over twenty-eight percent of the rest. At one month the gap held, near two percent against fourteen percent. By three months both groups matched. Surgery ran about three minutes longer with the stitch, while pain, other side issues, and early hernia return matched across groups. Closing the ring seems a cheap win against early fluid trouble.
pmc-13482303:
Abdullahi and colleagues propose a faster solver in 2026 for large systems of nonlinear equations, the kind that arise when cleaning up signals and restoring damaged images. Their method blends four existing conjugate gradient algorithms, a family of step-by-step solvers prized for low memory use, into one hybrid with a restart rule. Whenever progress slows, the search direction resets instead of dragging old information forward into the next step.

The hybrid inherits the strengths of its parents while keeping two safety properties, a guaranteed downhill direction at each step and bounded step sizes throughout the run. Under standard assumptions the authors prove the method converges globally and estimate how fast that convergence should be for large problems. On benchmark problems it reached solutions faster and more accurately than the existing methods it was compared against, and the paper points it at signal processing and image recovery tasks.
pmc-13482403:
Xiao and Zheng build an automated simulation system in 2026 for incremental launching, the method that slides a bridge into place segment by segment over its supports. Curved city bridges launched in linked sections strain older analysis tools, which miss working conditions and distort the geometry. Their system pairs quick one-dimensional models with detailed three-dimensional mapping and writes the simulation commands itself through a Python program.

They validated the approach on the Guangzhou-Shenzhen Expressway reconstruction, running 771 distinct working conditions across the whole launching sequence for the project. The system extracted support reactions, hinge shear forces, displacements, and stresses at each stage, and measured how deck curvature and twisting change those forces during the slide. The authors say the automated pipeline fixes the efficiency and coverage gaps of hand-built models and gives engineers a safer basis for launching bridges in tight urban sites.
pmc-13483603:
Liu and co-authors built a two-step deep-learning system that finds and labels each vertebra in chest and abdomen CT scans. Accurate labels matter for planning spine surgery, yet vertebrae look alike and span a long column, which trips up single-step software. Their 2026 framework first outlines the whole spine roughly, then pinpoints each bone's center with a coordinate-predicting module built for three-dimensional images.

The system lifted correct identification from about 81 percent to about 96 percent against the baseline approach compared. Average position error shrank from 7.6 millimeters to about 2 millimeters, a gain that matters when surgeons plan screw placement near nerves. The method beat current rival approaches on the test data used. Liu presents the two-stage design as a robust aid for spinal diagnosis and surgical planning.
pmc-13483903:
Ahmadullah and co-authors calculated how desert dust changes the right size for a home solar-plus-battery system in Saudi Arabia. Dust films steal sunlight, so a system sized for clean panels under-delivers once panels dirty. Their 2026 study examined real dust under microscopes, measured how it dims glass at three coating levels, then ran an economic model for a typical household that must never lose power.

Dust grains averaged about 50 micrometers across and cut glass light transmission to roughly a third at the heaviest coating tested. A clean-condition home system needed 21 panels and five batteries at the lowest electricity cost figure computed. The heaviest dust case demanded double the panels, nine batteries, and raised the cost figure by about 82 percent. Ahmadullah argues planners in arid regions must budget for dust or for cleaning.
pmc-13486103:
Dilson Lobo and co-workers measure each source of error in a diode tool that checks radiation dose inside the body. The dose is given in cobalt-60 brachytherapy, where seeds sit close to a tumor. For this 2026 study, the tool is tuned in plastic models of the body. Straight-line response is checked from 1 to 8 Gray. Slabs like bone, lung, and soft tissue are placed in the beam path.

Repeat reads swung by less than 2 percent across runs. Drift across piled-up doses stayed under 2.5 percent. Response stayed straight across the whole dose span. More results on tissue-like slabs sit in the full text. A bedside check guards patients only if its own error size is known. This work turns a neat tool into a trusted safety net.
pmc-13486503:
Samuel I Zapata-Valencia and others build a faster microscope that records both an image and a full spectrum of colours at each point. In 2026, the platform replaces slow spectrometers with a high-speed line-scan camera that captures dispersed light in parallel, using single-pixel imaging with coded patterns. Commercial hyperspectral microscopes remain slow, expensive, and inflexible by comparison.

Full scans of sixty-four by sixty-four pixels finish in under a second, yielding up to seventy-three spectral bands at four-nanometre resolution. Fusing those data with high-resolution monochrome images expands reconstructions to over six hundred pixels square while preserving spectral detail. Testing covers reflected light and fluorescence, so the system offers a scalable, cheaper route to rapid spectral microscopy.
pmc-13486803:
Hashii and colleagues report a phase 2 trial of a cancer vaccine for children whose leukaemia returned or resisted treatment. Their 2026 paper tests WT1 peptide vaccines given after a donor stem cell transplant, called allo-HSCT. WT1 is a protein found on leukaemia cells, and the vaccine aims to train the immune system to attack leftover disease without harming healthy tissue.

Children at three Japanese hospitals who had reached remission after transplant received the vaccine into the skin, weekly at first and then less often, for up to three years. Three years after treatment, 70.6 percent of vaccinated patients were alive, a share the authors contrast with about 30 percent in historical comparison patients. They conclude the maintenance vaccine appears both effective and safe in this hard-to-treat group.
pmc-13487303:
Jang and colleagues discovered that a long RNA molecule in liver cells has its own tumor-blocking job, separate from the famous small RNA it was thought merely to precede. The long form, lnc122, was dismissed as a raw intermediate for microRNA-122, a known liver guardian. Their 2026 study silenced the long form in liver cancer cells and mouse livers while leaving the small form's supply intact, then watched cancer-relevant pathways.

Silencing lnc122 let the growth-driving protein MYC accumulate, because lnc122 normally stabilizes the machinery that tags MYC for destruction. That machinery, built around the UBR5 protein, sits beside MYC in the genome and is co-amplified in over forty percent of human cancers. In a mouse liver tumor model driven by MYC, lnc122 held back tumor formation. Jang argues the long RNA deserves study as a cancer actor in its own right.
pmc-13487803:
Willem H Collier and co-workers test a ranked joint score for child cancer support care trials. Such trials juggle many key results at once, which clouds what a result means. A ranked joint score stacks results by clinical weight, so a win on life trumps a win on comfort in one sum. This 2026 work re-runs two large phase three trials from a US child cancer group with that lens.

The ranked score proved more apt to catch true gains than one-result reads. It also gave clear calls when a care step helped on one front yet hurt on the next. Fever bouts, drug use, blood infection, and death show the layers such trials must weigh. The team backs set use of the score when new trials are drawn up, not just in hindsight checks.
pmc-13488203:
Xiaojing Chen leads a large team studying a stress signal protein called GDF-15 in a 2026 analysis of United Kingdom Biobank data. Nearly thirty thousand people with early stages of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, a grouping of linked heart, kidney, and metabolic risks, had the protein measured. The team tracked who developed fatty liver disease linked to metabolism, or atherosclerotic heart and vessel disease, where fatty deposits narrow arteries.

Higher GDF-15 tracked with worse overall syndrome health, most strongly with kidney function measures. Each step up in the protein came with higher risk of both outcomes and of having both together in the reported models. Transitions ran both ways between the diseases. The authors test whether the marker sharpens risk prediction beyond standard factors.
pmc-13488303:
Sarah E. Philo and colleagues trace which bacteria carry antibiotic resistance genes through water reclamation plants in a 2026 study of three sites in North Carolina, Texas, and California. Samples of incoming wastewater, treatment sludge, and cleaned outflow were collected over three spring weeks. A sequencing method called Hi-C links DNA pieces that sit inside the same cell, revealing whether a resistance gene rides on a movable plasmid or sits on the chromosome.

The team found 244 distinct resistance genes, with seven present in every sample. Resistance genes were more often plasmid-borne in incoming water and more often chromosomal in sludge. Seventeen bacterial hosts still carried resistance genes in treated outflow. Four bacterial families accounted for over half of all host links.
pmc-13489703:
Samantha A. Swanson and a large team test copper feeding levels in young and growing pigs in a 2026 study with two experiments. Added copper can boost growth, and the trials used about 150 milligrams per kilogram of feed from different copper sources. The nursery trial followed more than two thousand small pigs for thirty-eight days across feeding phases, while the finishing trial followed a similar number of larger pigs for one hundred ten days.

Nursery pigs gained faster on added copper during the middle phase, yet overall performance did not differ between feeding schedules in the first experiment. Finishing pigs on added copper grew faster in the first half of the second trial, with no advantage later and no difference between copper sources in the reported results.
pmc-13490603:
Korczyńska and team read the gene activity of womb-lining tissue from women with two common benign growths, fibroids and polyps, comparing diseased-looking and normal-looking patches side by side. Both conditions impair fertility, yet their molecular footprints on the lining were unmapped. Their 2026 study sequenced paired samples collected during hysteroscopy from women before and around menopause, then contrasted the patterns statistically.

Normal-looking lining barely differed between the two conditions, with only nine genes separating the groups in that comparison. The lesional tissues diverged sharply instead, with 398 genes differing between fibroid and polyp samples in the reported analysis. Further contrasts within each condition traced how each growth remodels its own neighborhood, with fibroid tissue leaning on matrix and survival genes the authors name. Korczyńska concludes the two growths imprint distinct molecular signatures despite their shared benign label.
pmc-13490903:
Tjampakasari and colleagues profiled the resistance genes behind treatment failure of an antibiotic pairing in urinary E. coli from Indonesian patients, in a 2026 gene study. The drug pairing trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is increasingly defeated by acquired genes named dfr and sul, which bacteria trade between themselves. From 678 urine samples the team got a culture-positive set and studied eleven E. coli isolates in detail, with eight resistant ones.

Tjampakasari used DNA amplification and sequencing and found the resistance genes spread unevenly: some isolates carried dfrA5, one carried dfrA1, several carried sul2. Sul1 appeared unchanged from the version. Sequencing exposed amino-acid changes inside the dfr and sul genes, though no change explained resistance in all of them. One resistant isolate carried none of the targeted genes at all, pointing to other routes. The authors present the survey as gene evidence and call for studies with whole-genome sequencing and tests.
pmc-13491603:
Jessica J Wong and ten colleagues publish a 2026 scoping review on why older adults with low back pain struggle to reach rehabilitation care. Rehabilitation helps people function better despite health problems, yet access depends on far more than clinic availability. The reviewers mapped structural barriers and supports reported in qualitative research on adults aged fifty and older.

From 8,550 citations, sixteen studies qualified, covering low back pain and lumbar spinal stenosis in middle- and high-income countries. Cost and insurance gaps, distance and weak transport, and limited knowledge or stigma around certain treatments came up most often. Some patients met ageism from providers who treated pain as normal aging. Findings shifted with rurality, income, and disability, and no studies came from low-income countries.
pmc-13491703:
Weizhen Liu and seven co-authors introduce in 2026 a method for outlining plant structures inside CT scans without any training data or hand labeling. Standard deep learning approaches demand large sets of painstakingly labeled images for each new species, which slows cross-species research. Their system, DiffPlantCT, borrows visual features from a pretrained image generation model and combines them with the scan's own gray levels.

Each two-dimensional slice is segmented by unsupervised clustering, and the slices are then stacked back into a three-dimensional result. Tests ran on walnut fruit and barley spike datasets plus self-collected wheat and rice material. The method beat the best previous unsupervised approach by a wide margin on overlap scores. The authors present it as the first proof that plant CT segmentation can work with neither annotations nor training.
pmc-13491803:
Natalie Erickson and four colleagues profile in 2026 how a human gene variant linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder changes the protein makeup of young brain cells. The variant, an inverted copy of CHRFAM7A carrying a two-letter deletion, dials down a nicotine-responsive receptor. The team grew neural progenitor cells from stem cells that either carried the variant or lacked the gene entirely.

Mass spectrometry compared thousands of proteins between the matched cell lines. Some 129 proteins differed, clustering in pathways that build the matrix around cells, make collagen, and glue cells to their surroundings. Direct adhesion tests confirmed that cells with the variant gripped their matrix differently from gene-free cells. The authors propose that faulty cell anchoring may be one route from this variant to brain disease.
pmc-13492003:
Hassan Boskabadi and others compare neurodevelopment in newborns with jaundice from ABO versus Rh blood group incompatibility. In 2026, the study follows infants referred to a Mashhad teaching hospital from 2017 to 2019, eighty-three with ABO incompatibility and eighty-one with Rh incompatibility. It assesses development with the Denver screening test over the first three years.

Bile pigment levels, age, birth type, and sex did not differ clearly between groups, yet developmental results diverged sharply. Nearly nine in ten ABO-group infants showed near-normal development, against under half in the Rh group, where moderate-to-severe delays were more frequent. The authors conclude that Rh-mediated hemolysis carries greater neurodevelopmental risk despite similar bile pigment and treatment.
pmc-13493903:
Fei Wei leads an eleven-author team uncovering in 2026 how a little-known surface protein helps liver cancer grow, and how to drug it. The protein, LY6H, sits anchored on cell membranes and appears at abnormally high levels in hepatocellular carcinoma, the dominant liver cancer, where patients carrying more of it die sooner. Laboratory and animal experiments traced its grip on the cell's recycling system, autophagy.

LY6H grabs a key signaling subunit and shields its activated form from destruction, keeping a growth pathway switched on and autophagy humming. Blocking that pathway or silencing LY6H stalled tumor cells, confirming the chain of command. A screening hit, the compound NSC243928, shut down LY6H-driven recycling and tumor promotion in dishes and in animals. Tumors co-expressing the whole axis predicted the worst outcomes, marking both a prognosis tool and a target.
pmc-13494403:
Guglielmelli and colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about an inherited DNA pattern that shapes polycythemia vera, a blood cancer where the marrow overproduces red cells. Most cases carry the JAK2 V617F mutation. A common inherited haplotype called 46/1, a set of neighbouring DNA variants, makes that mutation more likely. Their letter analyses 756 patients with the mutation, asking whether inheriting the haplotype from both parents changes the disease's face or course.

Patients homozygous for the haplotype showed a distinct clinical picture and carried a heavier load of the cancer mutation in their blood. They also faced a higher risk of venous thrombosis, dangerous blood clots. That risk stayed significant even after accounting for the mutation load itself. A nearby immune gene's behaviour offers one possible explanation, since the same haplotype has been linked to higher expression of the PD-L1 checkpoint protein.
pmc-13495203:
Zhenyu Zhu and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, that a gene called ThASR4 helps plants withstand salty soil. ASR genes switch on under stress and during fruit ripening, yet their role in Tamarix hispida, a salt-tough shrub, was little studied. The team cloned six family members from the shrub and found salt switched them on, with ThASR4 answering most strongly in shoots and roots.

Moved into a model plant, ThASR4 raised seed sprouting, root length, and weight gain under salt. Both the model plant and the shrub carrying extra copies held less harmful oxygen waste and less cell damage, while their protective enzymes and a stress amino acid rose. Silencing the gene in the shrub flipped every result. The gene also woke partner genes for waste cleanup and salt defense. The authors frame ThASR4 as a useful lever for breeding salt-tough crops and shrubs.
pmc-13495303:
Sara A Kohlbeck, Jacey M Kant, and Katherine A Quinn explore, in a 2026 study, what they call the school-to-suicide pipeline among Black youth. Suicide in this group has risen, and the authors stress that race itself is no risk factor; social conditions and school settings shape the risk. The team gathered records for county residents who died by suicide across ten years and interviewed school psychologists and social workers.

The records covered 293 deaths, most of them Black residents, and school issues counted as a contributing factor for several. Interviews yielded four themes, with exclusionary discipline, such as suspensions, standing out for its harm to mental health. Staff also described thin resources for supporting Black students. The authors urge trauma-informed, restorative, and non-punitive ways of handling behavior in schools, above all for minoritized students, and frame the change as urgent suicide prevention.
pmc-13495403:
Ayşe Karacalı Tunç and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, silver nanoparticles brewed with an extract of Stachys spectabilis, a mint-family herb, against germs and their biofilms. Biofilms are slimy germ cities that shrug off many drugs. Green brewing uses plant chemistry to form the particles, avoiding harsh reagents. The team made the particles and checked them against four hospital germs.

On agar plates the particles barely spread, so zones stayed tiny. In liquid tests a clear dose pattern emerged: the staph germ was most sensitive, and killing doses sat above stopping doses. The particles also cut biofilm mass sharply in all four germs, by about half in three of them and two fifths in the fourth. The authors conclude the brew works in liquid settings despite its poor spread on plates, and merits work toward wound or surface uses.
pmc-13495903:
Fabricio O Lima leads the RESILIENT investigators asking, in a 2026 analysis, whether age changes who gains from clot removal after a major stroke in Brazil. Trials in rich countries found the catheter treatment helps old and young alike, but proof from poorer health systems is thin. The team reexamined their randomized trial of 221 patients treated in Brazil's public system, splitting patients at seventy and eighty years.

Age itself predicted worse recovery across everyone. The treatment's edge also shrank steeply with age: patients under seventy gained a strong benefit, while those over seventy and over eighty showed little or none. Statistics confirmed the split as real. The authors caution that results from rich systems may not travel to stretched public hospitals, and call for work on why the benefit fades and whether older patients there still gain.
pmc-13500203:
Carlsen and colleagues tested how the brain's quieting of the motor pathway before a movement depends on the task, in a 2026 neuroscience experiment. Before a go signal, magnetic stimulation of the motor cortex evokes a shrinking muscle response. That suppression is thought to stop release of a prepared action or to sharpen signal detection. Participants performed simple, choice, and go/no-go reaction tasks while stimulation probed excitability.

Carlsen found responses shrank toward the go signal in all three tasks. Suppression ran deeper in the simple and go/no-go tasks in the last fifty milliseconds before and at the signal. The timelines diverged in the final stretch, with choice reactions, which cannot be prepared, plateauing earlier. The authors conclude suppression is multifactorial: an early phase shared across tasks likely aids initiation, while a late phase reflects preparation and inhibition tuned to what the task demands.
pmc-13500503:
Shafique Ahmed Memon and co-authors propose in 2026 a method for explaining medical AI predictions through counterfactuals, changes that would flip a prediction, tuned by multi-goal optimisation. Doctors distrust black-box models, and plain explanations rarely show how features combine or offer realistic alternatives. Their two-phase method first trained a random forest classifier on a chronic kidney disease dataset. Candidate counterfactuals for one patient profile were then generated with an established generator and with their evolutionary algorithm approach.

Both methods produced fully valid counterfactuals, meaning every suggestion changed the model's prediction for that test case. The comparison weighed how few features each method changed against confidence and clinical plausibility, with a kidney specialist judging relevance in a first review. The optimised approach was designed to balance those rival goals better, tackling the problem that many equally valid accounts can conflict with each other.
pmc-13500703:
Shima Tavoosi and colleagues test in 2026 whether infecting leukaemia cells with a harmless bird virus can make them easier targets for the immune system's natural killer cells. Killer cells suit cell therapy because they attack tumours and tolerate donor mismatch, yet acute myeloid leukaemia often evades them. Laboratory lines and fresh patient cells, from new diagnoses and relapsed disease alike, were infected with a non-destroying Newcastle disease virus strain. They were then mixed with killer cells at several ratios while killing and immune signals were measured.

Infected leukaemia cells displayed a viral surface protein that acts as a danger flag for killer cell receptors in the reported experiments. Killer cells responded with stronger specific killing and released more interferon gamma plus the toxic proteins perforin and granzyme B. The authors propose sequencing treatment, virus first to sensitise the cancer, then an infusion of expanded killer cells to finish it.
pmc-13500803:
Yasir Almukhlifi leads a six-author team with a 2026 survey of safety knowledge among emergency medical services students in the Makkah region of Saudi Arabia. The cross-sectional study questioned 96 students at three schools with a structured form covering background, hazard knowledge, safety measures, and where students get their information. Paramedic trainees face physical, biological, chemical, and mental risks during training, yet how far knowledge becomes safe behaviour was unclear.

Students showed moderate to high knowledge overall, strongest for hand hygiene and protective equipment. Physical hazards were recognized by 83.3 percent and chemical hazards by 81.3 percent, while ergonomic risks were spotted by only 26.0 percent. About 63.5 percent had faced aggressive patients at least once a year. Progress through the programme showed no clear link with knowledge, and the link between knowledge and reported safety behaviour was weak.
pmc-13501303:
Peng and colleagues built ViralQC, a quality-control tool for viral genome fragments pulled from metagenomic sequencing, in a 2026 paper. Such samples yield mostly microbial DNA. Would-be viral sequences often carry host material or are partial, so judging their quality is needed before listing new viruses.

Peng combined DNA and protein foundation models, large pretrained neural networks, into an ensemble that flags microbial contamination inside supposed viral sequences. It estimated completeness from how the encoded proteins are arranged. Benchmarked against CheckV, the current standard tool, ViralQC detected contamination more sharply in fragments longer than ten thousand bases while keeping similar accuracy. Its completeness estimates were more accurate for fragments that were more than half complete. The authors offer the tool as a sharper filter for the flood of new viruses from such studies, with source code posted openly.
pmc-13501603:
Yoconda Arias leads a ten-author team with a 2026 feasibility study of combined exercise and brain training at a community aging centre serving a low-income area. Fifty adults over 55, living at home, enrolled after medical and mental health screening, and 46 finished with final testing. Sessions lasted one hour on alternate days for four months, rotating between structured physical exercise and supervised thinking activities. The study's main questions were practical ones of recruitment, retention, adherence, and safety.

Retention reached 92 percent, and no adverse events were blamed on the programme. Average attendance totalled 18.7 hours, though it ranged widely across people. Walking capacity improved strikingly: the six-minute walk distance grew by an average of 140 metres, a large effect, while blood pressure and oxygen responses stayed stable. Global cognitive scores rose modestly. Because the study had no comparison group, the authors treat the gains as early hints.
pmc-13501703:
Weiwei Zou leads a thirteen-author team reporting a 2026 study of spinal cord repair that began by watching what transplanted stem cells switch on inside an injured cord. Human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells were placed into rats with a cut spinal cord, retrieved, and profiled by RNA sequencing. One gene stood out: Neuroligin 3, a cell adhesion molecule better known from synapses. Screening confirmed it drove much of the transplant benefit, and restoring Neuroligin 3 in neurons alone matched the effect of the cell therapy itself.

Protein fishing experiments showed Neuroligin 3 recruiting two partners, Sar1a and Hspa8, proteins tied to synaptic vesicles. Restoring Neuroligin 3 together with either partner repaired the injury better than any single component, pointing to a noncanonical three-protein complex that tunes synaptic strength. Behavioural tests and motor evoked potentials backed the anatomical gains. The authors propose combination gene targeting of this complex for spinal cord injury.
pmc-13503903:
Nyssa K Krull leads a large team presenting IDBac, a free web platform that names bacteria from their protein fingerprints, in a 2026 paper. The method, mass spectrometry biotyping, is fast and fine-grained, yet it stayed in clinics for lack of a shared public library of fingerprints. IDBac aims to fill that gap.

The platform holds crowd-sourced protein signatures from seven bacterial groups. Users can match an unknown germ against the library, sort how strains in a collection relate, and compare the small molecules each strain makes. Worked examples show each use in action. The team invites labs worldwide to add their data, which would widen the library's reach for research outside hospital walls.
pmc-13505103:
Dongyang Wang leads a team mapping why Chinese teens with alcohol use disorder injure themselves without intent to die, in a 2026 interview study. The two problems often arrive together in adolescence, yet how they feed each other in daily life was little explored. The team traced the journey across home, hospital, and return home.

Eighteen diagnosed teens took part in deep interviews. Three nested themes emerged: a hunt for emotional numbness, a tunnel of narrowed thinking once alcohol loosens control, and a loop kept turning by shame after each episode. The mapped journey showed a hidden build-up before hospital, a stark closed-ward phase, and isolated recovery after. Teens felt most bare of support during late-night crises at home. The authors urge trauma-aware care and digital safety nets.
pmc-13506203:
Arif Khan, Rashmi Prakash, Anshu Arora, and Aishwarya Prasad argue that psychiatry's neuron-only picture of mental illness is too narrow. More than sixty approved drugs exist, yet their benefit over placebo stays modest and side effects are heavy. Surprising mood and reward effects from GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, large molecules once feared to mimic starvation's mental harm, pushed the authors to question synaptic models built on small transmitter molecules.

Psychiatric disorders run in families without following simple inheritance patterns, and symptoms vary widely, which weakens explanations based on DNA sequence alone. Drawing on Alan Turing's chemical-gradient ideas about development, the authors highlight astrocytes, support cells long treated as background. They review astrocyte variety across species and brain regions and propose that neurons and glia work as joined networks whose shared molecules produce mental function. Drug development, they suggest, should target those combined networks and the molecules glia release.
pmc-13507203:

Scores reached high levels for accuracy and related measures, with response latency near twenty-six milliseconds and few false alarms. pmc-13507303:

pmc-13508403:

pmc-13509603:

pmc-13511203:

pmc-13511703:

pmc-13512303:

pmc-13514803:

pmc-13515603:

pmc-13517203:

pmc-13518603:

pmc-13518903:

pmc-13519003:

pmc-13520303:

pmc-13520403:

pmc-13520503:

pmc-13521103:

pmc-13521903:

pmc-13522003:

pmc-13522603:

pmc-13522803:

pmc-13523203:

pmc-13523703:

pmc-13524003:

pmc-13524903:

pmc-13526803:

pmc-13527103:

pmc-13527903:

pmc-13528003:

pmc-13529603:

pmc-13530803:

pmc-13531503:

pmc-13531803:

pmc-13531903:

pmc-13536703:

pmc-13536803:

pmc-13538203:

pmc-13538303:

pmc-13538403:

pmc-13538503:

pmc-13539703:

pmc-13540203:
Taraneh Rezaei and four colleagues explore, in a 2026 cell study, how male and female sex hormones affect liver cancer growth, since this cancer strikes men far more often. Two human liver cancer cell lines with different levels of aggression were exposed to estradiol and testosterone.

In the calmer HepG2 line, both hormones lowered division-driving Aurora kinases, raised GATA3, and paused the cell cycle. The aggressive Huh-7 line moved the opposite way, speeding through early division stages. Small regulatory RNAs shifted in matching patterns in both lines. The authors conclude that the cell's character, not the hormone, decides whether the signal restrains or encourages growth.
pmc-13540903:
Nagasundaram Nagarajan and three colleagues combine, in a 2026 study, single-cell gene data with machine learning drug screening to find targets shared by lung cancer and its spread to brain and bone. Non-small cell lung cancer kills largely through such spread, and few drugs work across all sites.

Gene profiles from primary tumors and matched metastases highlighted eight candidate targets. Three proteins, ARPC2, PSMB4, and RAC2, stayed elevated everywhere and sat in key cancer pathways. Prediction models trained on chemical activity data screened millions of compounds per target with strong accuracy. Docking and simulations produced one stable lead pairing for each target, ready for laboratory testing.
pmc-13542103:
Tara Chand Yadav and colleagues mapped the shifting immune-attack toolkit for acute myeloid leukemia. Published in 2026, the review surveys new-wave immune treatments aimed at leukemia blast cells. AML is fast, varied, and marked by rogue blast growth plus niche remaking, and older treatments falter against shifting stubborn forms.

The review walks through CAR-T cells, checkpoint blockers, drug-linked antibodies, and antibody-based drugs, weighing how each hunts blast cells. It also weighs hurdles like drug fight-back, relapse, and graft-versus-host risk that shadow donor-cell attacks. Breakthroughs and open gaps get equal airing, with an eye to safer, sharper patient-matched use. Readers get a current field guide to immune options beyond chemo and transplant.
pmc-13543503:
Shanza Waseem's team published a 2026 case-based review of placenta accreta spectrum at its most dangerous: a 54-year-old woman with an IVF twin pregnancy and two previous caesarean births. In this disorder the placenta grows too deeply into the womb wall and cannot come away at delivery, risking massive bleeding. Her scans showed the most invasive form, placenta percreta, and she was taken in for a planned birth with a full specialist team.

Acute bleeding forced emergency surgery: a standard caesarean hysterectomy with partial bladder removal, backed by arterial balloon occlusion, clotting drugs, salvaged blood, and a massive transfusion protocol. Blood loss reached four and a half litres, and both twins lived after intensive care. The authors present the case as hypothesis-generating: older age, IVF, and uterine scarring may demand early imaging, delivery at top-level centres, and blood planning from the start.
pmc-13543603:
Qinyuan Yang and colleagues published a 2026 study of treating pelvic floor dysfunction in postmenopausal women at community clinics. The clinics replaced a distant specialist hospital, with a digital service package wrapped around electrical stimulation therapy. Two hundred women took part in a non-randomised comparison lasting one month. The community group received the stimulation locally plus digital support, while controls received standard stimulation at a tertiary hospital. Statistical methods tried to balance the self-selected groups.

Muscle-strength gains in the community group fell within the study's prespecified exploratory margin of the hospital group's, suggesting comparable short-term effect. Symptom severity ratings did not differ, yet the community group reported much better adherence, far greater health knowledge, and higher quality of life, and rated the digital tools highly usable. Because allocation was not random, the authors present every result as exploratory rather than proof.
pmc-13546603:
Jean-Baptiste Demigné and co-authors checked in 2026 how reliably HER2 status, a treatment-guiding marker in stomach and junction cancers, survives the trip from biopsy to surgery. Their single-center review covered 57 patients with localized disease who had curative surgery between 2017 and 2021, most after pre-surgery chemotherapy. Biopsy and surgical samples were tested with the same staining rules.

Agreement between the two samples was high, near 88 percent. Still, among twelve tumors that started HER2-positive, five lost that status by surgery, and half of the treated positive cases showed the loss. Taking more biopsy fragments did not reduce the mismatch. The authors suggest rechecking HER2 on the surgical specimen after pre-surgery treatment.
pmc-13546703:
Fahima Israt and colleagues evaluated in 2026 whether black soldier fly larvae, raised on organic waste, could replace commercial feed for Nile tilapia in Bangladesh. Larvae were reared on a mix of four waste types, and their yield, waste reduction, and nutritional makeup were measured across months. Thirty young tilapia were then split between tanks fed entirely on commercial feed and tanks fed entirely on larvae.

Larvae proved richer in protein, fat, and ash than the commercial product, and April was the peak production month. Fish on the all-larvae diet grew about as well as the control group, with a slight edge, while feed cost per kilogram fell to less than half. The authors present insect larvae as a cheaper, waste-fed protein source for local fish farming.
pmc-13547203:
Céline Augière and co-authors used genetically altered mice in 2026 to show that tiny hair-like structures in the male reproductive tract are essential for fertility. The efferent ductules, small tubes carrying sperm from the testis, are lined by cells with beating cilia that move fluid and by cells with single sensing cilia that absorb fluid. Removing the gene IFT88, needed to build both kinds, let the team test their combined role.

Mice without the gene developed shortened cilia, disorganized lining, and poor fluid balance. Males became infertile early, with swollen tubes, clumped sperm, and a blockage that left no sperm in the semen. Estrogen signaling fell, and a key water channel was misplaced. The authors credit sensing cilia with keeping the absorption machinery in place.
pmc-13547303:
Fei Han and colleagues tackled in 2026 a communications problem inside underground coal mines. Tunnel walls, rough surfaces, and coal dust scatter radio signals so badly that estimating the channel becomes unreliable. Their method designs the pilot signals and the estimator together inside one attention-equipped neural network, instead of optimizing each separately as older approaches do. Attention blocks learn which features and which frequencies deserve focus.

In simulations of harsh fading, the method cut estimation error by about 87 percent against the standard least squares approach. It beat a strong image-based rival by about 41 percent, nearing the best classical estimator at a fraction of its computing cost. Removing parts one at a time showed the pieces reinforce each other. The authors recommend real tunnel trials next.
pmc-13548003:
Sven Voigtländer and the ALSTER working group charted in 2026 colorectal cancer in Germans under fifty, using pooled cancer registry data from 2003 to 2023. They wanted to see whether the rises reported abroad apply at home. Rates were standardized for age and broken down by sex, age band, tumor site, and tumor features, with American registry figures for comparison.

Incidence rose modestly for both sexes, by just under one percent a year on average, and the increase concentrated in the twenties and thirties age bands. Appendix cancers rose in every under-fifty group. Growth was strongest among cancers with favorable features, such as neuroendocrine type, small size, and low grade. Germany started far below American rates and climbed more slowly. The authors say the causes remain unclear and monitoring must continue.
pmc-13548703:
Stephen Vreden and colleagues describe how Suriname guards its newly won malaria-free status, in a 2026 analysis. The World Health Organization certified the country malaria-free in June 2025 after local transmission had already stopped for nearly four years. The danger now is importation: gold mining draws intense cross-border movement from neighbors where malaria still circulates, and about sixty imported cases surface each year.

The national program layers proactive, reactive, and passive case hunting over more than ten thousand blood slides annually. Recent additions include giving antimalarial drugs to targeted individuals and presumptive treatment for likely carriers. A long-standing elimination task force steers the effort and adapts tactics as import patterns shift. The authors stress that Suriname cannot hold the line alone: the whole Guiana Shield needs a joint regional push.
pmc-13549703:
Jorge Briceño and colleagues linked a hair-and-teeth gene variant to ancestry mix in Latin Americans. Published in 2026, the study gauged ancestry shares with 446 marker gene variants and modeled EDAR rs3827760 types. The EDAR gene shapes skin-outgrowth structures like hair, teeth, and sweat glands, and its variant runs common in East Asian and Native American peoples.

Native American roots tracked more GG types, while European roots tracked fewer, a clear split in both single and joint models. The variant swaps one protein building block and boosts signal strength, tied to thicker straighter hair, shoveled front teeth, and denser sweat glands. The authors read ancestry shares as shaping this gene type's spread in Latin America. Readers get a clear ancestry map for a famous human trait.
pmc-13551403:
Mojca Bizjak-Suran, Manca Marčun, Mitja Košnik, and Dejan Dinevski published a 2026 retrospective study of patch testing for suspected allergy to dental materials.
