No European standard series exists for this problem, so one center reviewed 439 adults tested between 2016 and 2025 with its own 24-allergen series of metals, methacrylates, and other substances. Reactions were read at day three and again at day six or seven.

Half the patients reacted to at least one allergen, and nickel and palladium led the metals. Among methacrylate-positive patients, nearly half reacted to two or more substances, and many were negative for the usual marker HEMA. About a fifth of all positive reactions appeared only at the late reading, so the authors stress keeping it.
pmc-13551703:
Shiqing Lyu, with ten colleagues, published a 2026 study of surgeon skill in a hard ovarian cyst case. The cysts, tied to endometriosis, can burst and cause sharp pain. Swelling and scar tissue make the surgery tough. The team reviewed 122 patients treated in Beijing from 2012 to 2022. Cases were split by whether a specialist team operated.

Crude recurrence was lower after specialist surgery, at about half the other rate. That simple gap was not firm in the reported tests. A time-based analysis did show lower ten-year recurrence for specialist cases. An adjusted model landed just short of firm. Pregnancy rates did not differ between groups. The team frames skill as a likely edge that needs more proof.
pmc-13552603:
Anna Bjerager Arnesen and ten colleagues measure sepsis and antibiotic use in extremely preterm infants in Eastern Denmark. Few population-based studies cover this group. Their 2026 study includes all liveborn infants from 23 weeks to 27 weeks and 6 days of gestation from 2019 to 2021. Early-onset sepsis means onset within 72 hours of birth, and late-onset means onset from day 3 to day 90.

Within six months, 187 of 232 infants, or 81 percent, got intravenous antibiotics. Empirical treatment started for early-onset sepsis in 71 percent and for late-onset sepsis in 51 percent. Late-onset sepsis made up 90 percent of proven sepsis, and its antibiotic use ran three-fold higher than early-onset use. Sepsis caused two deaths. Suspected early-onset sepsis drove most starts, but late-onset sepsis drove most proven cases and drug exposure.
pmc-13553003:
Ikuma Ogura, with Hirofumi Miwa, Tetsuro Kobayashi, and Yuko Kasuya, compares ways to measure political outlook across nations in a 2026 study. Large cross-country surveys often use the same labels and questions everywhere. The team ran polls before and after votes in seven Asian and Western lands. They set shared measures of belief against ones built for each country alone.

Country-built measures held steadier over time than shared ones. Labels made for home use were also grasped better by those polled. Home measures linked more tightly to each other and guessed vote choice more often. Scores for strong views tied differently to faith in fair rule under each method. The authors advise using local measures in cross-country work.
pmc-13553303:
William Newell and three colleagues describe a 2026 effort to make a workhorse yeast live on formate, a simple carbon feed made from waste gas and power. No yeast grows on formate in nature, so the team first modelled which routes might work in Yarrowia lipolytica. Tests with labelled carbon showed the wild yeast already burns formate and shares it with glycerol through a ring-shaped one-carbon route.

Guided by the model, the team bred the yeast in the lab until a strain grew on formate alone. Gene activity scans pointed to shifts in energy use and stress handling. Further tweaks to those systems lifted growth to about a tenth of the best yield theory allows. The strain also made an orange pigment, beta-carotene, from formate.
pmc-13554903:
Pramod Tulsidas Gitte leads a five-author team reporting a heart attack at age twenty that exposed an inherited cholesterol disorder in a 2026 case report. The young man arrived with four hours of rest pain and sweating. Blood tests showed cholesterol levels many times the normal range, with the harmful fraction especially extreme. Scans found narrowing just above his aortic valve plus disease in all three heart arteries.

Gene testing confirmed the homozygous form of familial high cholesterol, with both copies of a key gene faulty. Surgeons bypassed his blocked arteries and widened the narrowed aorta with a patch in the same operation. The authors urge suspicion of this disorder in any very young heart attack patient with severe cholesterol readings or a matching family history.
pmc-13555903:
Nail Tekin Önder leads a nine-author team testing clove oil as a protector for frozen honeybee drone semen in a 2026 study. Freezing drone semen suffers from ice damage and oxidative stress, hurting fertility for breeding programmes. Pooled semen was split among extenders holding three clove oil doses plus a plain control. Movement, membrane health, and energy machinery were scored after thawing.

Two higher doses beat the control on swimming strength and membrane protection. The top dose guarded the sperm cap best and left the least oxidative damage marker. Antioxidant defences also ran strongest at the top dose. Oil levels needed to block microbes were measured as well. The authors back clove oil dosing for drone semen banks, with the middle and top doses close in merit.
pmc-13556003:
Sucheta Telang and ten colleagues reported in 2026 on a metabolic weak point in oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer. Drugs that block the cell-cycle proteins CDK4 and CDK6 are widely used in this disease, but tumours adapt. The team asked how these drugs change the way cancer cells burn glucose, focusing on an enzyme called PFKFB3 that speeds up sugar breakdown and is switched on by oestrogen signals.

Using flux analysis, metabolite profiling, and labelled glucose tracing in cell lines and patient-derived tumour grafts, they found that CDK4/6 blockade raised glycolytic activity. Removing or blocking PFKFB3 blunted that response. The results suggest that pairing a PFKFB3 blocker with standard CDK4/6 drugs could strengthen treatment, a combination the authors put forward for further testing.
pmc-13557903:
Hata and a large team compare two first-line plans in this 2026 retrospective study of EGFR-mutated lung cancer complicated by malignant pleural effusion, fluid flooding the chest cavity. Across fourteen Japanese centers, 421 patients starting treatment with the fluid present received either osimertinib alone, the modern standard, or the older drug erlotinib combined with a blood-vessel-blocking agent that dries effusions.

Overall the plans tied: adjusted analyses found no significant gaps in time to effusion return, progression-free survival, or overall survival. Mutation subtype split the result, though. In patients with exon 19 deletions, osimertinib cut effusion recurrence risk sharply, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.38 against the pairing, while L858R carriers showed no difference. Severe side effects were commoner on the combination, at 38 versus 21 percent, though osimertinib caused more lung inflammation overall.
pmc-13558703:
Anji Ayman Hamwi and Meenakshi Mittal proposed in 2026 a federated learning system that detects denial-of-service floods without gathering everyone's network data in one place. Each participating site trains locally and keeps a digital twin holding snapshots of its model, so a poisoned update can be rolled back for that client alone. A four-stage defence pipeline purifies updates, adds differential privacy noise, aggregates adaptively, and traces suspicious contributions, with every event written to a permissioned blockchain.

Tests on a standard attack dataset used thirty percent malicious participants throwing label-flip, gradient-noise, and backdoor attacks. The defended system kept test accuracy near ninety-nine point nine eight percent in each scenario, well above the stalled undefended baseline, and the ledger saved every run completely. Layered purification scores varied by attack type. The authors argue that twins plus layered defence make federated detection recoverable rather than brittle.
pmc-13559103:
Qin and co-authors build a bedside warning score for refractory Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia, in this 2026 study. That is the stubborn form of a common childhood lung infection. It resists standard antibiotics and can cause severe complications. They compared children whose pneumonia stayed ordinary, 56 cases, with 34 who progressed to refractory disease at their hospital during 2023 and 2024.

Six admission features independently predicted progression. They were fever lasting at least seven days before arrival and two inflammation and clotting markers above set thresholds. A collapsed lung segment on imaging and a drug-resistance mutation in the bacterium completed the six. Combined into a zero-to-twelve-point score, they separated future refractory cases with an AUC of 0.892 in the analysis. At the chosen cutoff of six points, the score caught 85.3 percent of progressors. It cleared 82.1 percent of non-progressors. High scorers developed refractory disease at a rate of 70.8 percent.
pmc-13559503:
Lisa M Fahey and colleagues summarize a multi-stakeholder meeting on speeding up clinical trials for coeliac disease drug development. Their 2026 review article reports on a May 2024 gathering convened by the Beyond Celiac Coalition. Patients, academic experts, drug industry staff, and US Food and Drug Administration participants discussed what future trials should measure and how they should run.

Speakers stressed that a gluten-free diet, still the only management, helps inconsistently and burdens daily life, leaving real need for drug therapies. Regulators pressed for trials showing both symptom relief and intestinal healing as paired primary endpoints. Practical obstacles included the mismatch between symptoms and tissue damage, patchy biopsy sampling, and unsettled definitions of meaningful healing. Controlled gluten exposure was debated as a way to make results easier to read. The authors frame the meeting record as guidance for designing trials that regulators can accept.
pmc-13560203:
Yang and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a PERMA-based program, built on positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and achievement, eases post-traumatic stress in newly qualified operating room nurses. These nurses face frequent verbal violence and heavy stress early in their careers. The study first surveyed 178 operating room nurses for probable PTSD, then ran an eight-week program for the 27 who screened positive, tracking symptoms and well-being to three months.

About one in five nurses met the probable PTSD threshold, and every one of them reported verbal violence exposure. Specific workplace fears predicted the condition, and risk climbed steeply with each added stressor, a clear dose-response pattern. After the program, symptom scores fell significantly, while general well-being scores did not change. The authors urge targeted psychological support and anti-violence policies, and call for a full randomized trial to confirm the early signal.
pmc-13560403:
Sharon J. Elliot and colleagues use a special mouse model to split hormone-based from chromosome-based reasons why men scar their lungs more in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Their 2026 study deploys the Four Core Genotypes model, which uncouples gonads from sex chromosomes in aged mice, then injures lungs with bleomycin. Scarring, hormone receptor signaling, and gene activity were tracked across all pairings.

The worst scarring showed in mice carrying XY chromosomes with ovaries, paired with high estrogen receptor alpha and a skewed receptor ratio. XX mice with testes showed the highest protective receptor beta levels and the mildest fibrosis. Removing gonads exposed both lasting and instant hormone effects, tangled with the chromosome set. Two small RNAs under chromosomal control linked dosage to a receptor and growth-factor pathway driving tissue change. The authors argue sex-informed targets should weigh chromosomes, not hormones alone.
pmc-13561703:
Wei Zuo and colleagues map the worldwide literature on robot-assisted reconstruction of the upper urinary tract. Their 2026 bibliometric analysis gathers 1,104 publications from the Web of Science and charts output, countries, institutions, authors, journals, and keywords. Robotic platforms have spread into these operations for their precision in tight anatomical spaces.

Publication grew steadily, then rapidly after 2020. The United States leads output and collaboration, with China second and rising fast. The University of Chicago, New York University, and Peking University top the institutional list, and one specialty journal leads the outlets. Classic topics center on pyeloplasty and childhood reconstruction, with the most cited work on junction obstruction repair. The frontier has shifted toward complex ureteral work: strictures, graft-based rebuilding, and single-port systems. The authors also flag sparse collaboration between leading clusters as a structural weakness.
pmc-13562103:
Marie Dreger and colleagues analyze what drives electroconvulsive therapy use across Germany, testing whether it follows patient need or local habit. Their 2026 nationwide study uses 2023 billing data from the psychiatric payment system, covering 837,762 ward stays plus day hospital figures. Over sixteen thousand cases received the treatment, with more than seventy-two thousand procedures logged.

Treatment rates by region showed almost no link to how often the relevant diagnoses occurred there. Supply bunched in larger institutions. Depression, catatonia, schizophrenia-spectrum and bipolar disorders, female sex, and older age all raised the odds of receiving treatment in layered models. Even after adjusting for case mix, huge gaps remained between institutions, with a median odds ratio above twenty. The authors read the pattern as structural inequity in access to an effective therapy, shaped more by where a patient lands than by what they need.
pmc-13562503:
Firoz Kanti Borah and two colleagues present a faster way to compute how waves scatter from very rough surfaces. Radar and light bouncing off the sea, soil, or snow underpins remote sensing, yet exact calculations break down when bumps grow tall and steep. Their 2026 method, a multilevel sparse-matrix scheme, solves the full wave equations for three-dimensional surfaces. It handles bump heights up to three wavelengths and patches as wide as 256 wavelengths square. Those scales run about ten times rougher and far larger than earlier full-wave work managed.

Five test cases show the range: boosted backscatter and absorption from fractal surfaces, cross-polarised returns from windy ocean, and soil readings at radar bands used by satellites. Snow-covered soil was modelled up to the Ku band at 17.2 gigahertz. The authors offer the framework as a general tool for wave problems that older theories cannot reach.
pmc-13562703:
Elsebeth Staun-Ram and four colleagues document how multiple sclerosis in Israel has become, increasingly, a disease of older people. Longer survival has quietly built a patient group whose needs were never mapped. The 2026 population study used records from the country's largest health organisation, tracking prevalence and new cases from 2003 to 2022. Rheumatoid arthritis patients served as a comparison group. Among people aged 60 and over, multiple sclerosis prevalence climbed from 4.6 to 18.2 per 10,000 people, with the steepest rise in older Jewish women.

By 2022, patients over 60 made up 31 percent of all cases, lifting the average age of the whole group. New-case rates in older adults stayed flat, so longevity, not fresh incidence, drove the change. Older patients with either disease carried more extra conditions, from stroke to osteoporosis, and used far more hospital and specialist care than matched peers. The authors press health systems to plan for this older, medically complex population.
pmc-13563703:
Hunbo Shim and six colleagues gather every reported case of bone cement reaching the heart after spine-strengthening procedures. Cement injected into a fractured vertebra can slip into veins and harden inside the heart, an accident that falls between spine and heart specialties. Their 2026 review searched three databases through 2025 and, after duplicate checks, kept 116 cases. The typical patient was 69, and 75.9 percent were women. Vertebroplasty preceded 67.2 percent of events and kyphoplasty 26.7 percent.

Chest pain and breathlessness were the commonest complaints. Heart ultrasound and CT scanning found the cement in over nine cases out of ten, while X-rays missed far more. Long, thin fragments were the dangerous shape, linked to perforation in 46.6 percent of cases, most often through the right ventricle wall. Surgeons retrieved cement in 65.5 percent of cases with no operative deaths, while delay or refused treatment proved fatal elsewhere. Early recognition, the authors stress, is the hinge.
pmc-13563903:
Maoyuan Li and ten colleagues test whether artemisinin, the antimalarial from wormwood, can push the overgrown lining of rheumatoid joints into iron-driven death. In rheumatoid arthritis, fibroblast-like synoviocytes multiply like a tumour and erode cartilage. Their 2026 study treated cells in culture and tracked the machinery of ferroptosis, a death by rusting membrane fats. Artemisinin lowered the guard proteins, GPX4 and SLC7A11, let lipid peroxides pile up, and made the cells more sensitive to ferroptosis triggers. Drugs that block this death cancelled the effect.

The pathway ran through p53, the tumour suppressor, which rose and squeezed the SLC7A11 supply line. In mice with collagen-induced arthritis, artemisinin eased damage by sensitising synovial tissue to the death, and ferroptosis blockers abolished the benefit. They propose repositioning a cheap, familiar drug to prune the lining, with the p53 axis as the lever to watch in dosing studies.
pmc-13569703:
Kawin Atipas and colleagues compare, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, the Eustachian tube, the channel that ventilates the middle ear, in children with and without cleft palate. Twenty-five children in each group, aged four to twelve, had camera examinations through the nose during care, with findings checked against ear outcomes.

A ridge beside the tube opening was abnormal in over half the cleft palate group, always on its rear lip, against a fifth of other children. Adenoid size and how visibly the tube opened tracked with middle ear disease and ear surgery in the cleft group. The exam details could help tailor ear follow-up for children born with cleft palate.
pmc-13571603:
Yunwei Wang and a large team test, in a 2026 study, tiny packages released by fat-derived stem cells grown in a three-dimensional self-feeder system as a treatment for diabetic wounds. The work centers on aging of the small blood vessel lining cells in skin, a driver of poor healing, rather than on generic vessel cells.

In dishes, the packages eased sugar-driven cell aging, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial trouble while restoring vessel growth, acting through a named signaling chain that controls protein production. Animal work covered both fat graft behavior and diabetic wound healing. Rejuvenating the microvascular lining, the study suggests, may unlock healing where current diabetic foot treatments stall.
pmc-13572503:
Stefano Parolai and colleagues built a new earthquake catalogue for Italy that captures shaking energy better than the standard magnitude. Moment magnitude measures the static size of a rupture, but it misses how violently the fault actually moved. Their 2026 data paper applies a high-frequency magnitude, m3Hz, derived from ground motion above the source's corner frequency, to intensity data from the Parametric Catalogue of Italian Earthquakes.

The resulting ICEM catalogue covers 1,951 earthquakes from 1117 to 2020, each with a quality index. By complementing moment magnitude with a measure tied to rupture dynamics, the catalogue should sharpen seismic hazard estimates. The authors offer it as a resource for hazard studies that need more than a single static number per event.
pmc-13574803:
Christine D. Wu, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of cranberry juice against dental plaque in adults and children. Cranberry compounds are known to block plaque germs in lab dishes. The open question was whether a real drink, taken by mouth, still slows the acid those germs make on teeth.

Two crossover trials ran, one with eight adults and one with fourteen children. Each person rinsed with pure unsweetened cranberry juice, a sweetened cocktail version, or water on set days. Plaque was swabbed before and half an hour after drinking. Pure juice cut later plaque regrowth and acid output in both age groups. The sweet cocktail and water did nothing clear. The authors float pure juice as a healthier swap for sugary drinks.
pmc-13575103:
Fanrui Zeng leads a 2026 study on tiny packages released by neural stem cells and their role in healing radiation damage to the brain. Radiation can break down the blood-brain barrier, the wall that shields brain tissue. The packages, called exosomes, carry signals between cells and may aid repair.

In a rat model, exosome treatment boosted stem cell traits and guided new cells toward becoming astrocytes, a support cell type. Mitochondria worked better and harmful oxygen by-products fell. Treatment also calmed a signalling route involving HMGB1 and TLR2. Forcing HMGB1 higher weakened the benefit, while lowering TLR2 restored it. The authors propose exosomes as a route toward treating radiation brain injury.
pmc-13575203:
Nan Ma and four colleagues combine three deep learning models to find clouds in satellite images in a 2026 paper. Cloud detection underpins many uses of remote sensing data, yet single methods mistake bright land for cloud or miss thin cloud. Their fix is an ensemble that weights each model by its F1 score, a balanced accuracy measure.

The three models were first scored on Landsat-8 images, then blended with those weights into one cloud probability. On held-out test images the blend beat majority voting by 4.7 points of F1 score and a Bayesian averaging method by 1.9 points. Errors fell across varied landscapes. The authors offer the weighted ensemble as a sturdy option for large-scale cloud mapping.
pmc-13576103:
Min Xu and five colleagues build a deep learning model that reads thyroid ultrasound images to tell cancerous nodules from harmless ones, in a 2026 study. The cancer in focus is papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer. Their model mixes image features with clinical details and uses attention methods borrowed from transformer networks.

Data covered 491 patients from two hospitals, split into training, checking, and outside test sets. After comparing 34 network designs and four classic models, the team's fused design scored 0.986 on the standard accuracy curve in the outside test set, with sensitivity of 96.4 percent and specificity of 96.7 percent in the same test. Explanation tools showed the model focused better on the nodule area once clinical features were added. The authors present the system as support for ultrasound diagnosis.
pmc-13576303:
Kenichi Takeshita, Ana G Jop Vidal, and Jorge E Vidal study a metabolic switch in a pneumonia bacterium that still causes severe disease despite vaccination, in a 2026 paper. Serotype 3 Streptococcus pneumoniae resists immune clearance well. The team focused on two enzymes at the pyruvate crossroads of the cell's energy system.

The wild strain grew poorly at airway oxygen levels, a burden lifted when one enzyme gene, spxB, was removed. In mice, the normal strain caused severe lung infection with pus, bleeding, and tissue swelling. The mutant strain spread more wildly and inflamed more, yet lacked a striking feature of the normal infection: bubble-like host membrane pouches stuffed with bacteria on airway surfaces. Gene activity data tied the normal strain to dampened T cell activation. The authors read the pouches as a new immune evasion trick.
pmc-13579803:
Michael Fridén and colleagues question whether lumping all ultra processed food together helps diabetes policy, in a 2026 review joined with a Danish cohort check. Six cohort studies covering more than six hundred thousand adults were sorted into eight food subtypes and followed for type 2 diabetes. Ready meals, processed meats, and sweet drinks mostly raised risk. Dairy items and sweets mostly pointed the other way.

In the Danish data of fifty two thousand adults, the team built a mock bad food group that included vegetables for illustration. The blend looked harmful overall, while vegetables alone looked protective, showing how a coarse label can bury a good food. Bias in the source studies ran moderate to high. The authors argue policy aimed at subtypes beats policy aimed at the whole shelf.
pmc-13583003:
Jone Razquin and colleagues built a mouse model of early Parkinson's by overloading one brainstem hub with alpha-synuclein. The locus coeruleus, a noradrenaline centre, is among the first regions hit in prodromal Parkinson's and may drive early non-motor symptoms, but its causal role was unclear. Their 2026 study used a viral vector to overexpress human alpha-synuclein selectively in locus coeruleus neurons, then tracked mice at one and three months.

Protein built up in cell bodies and projections, noradrenaline and serotonin fell early without neuron loss, and brain excitability shifted transiently by sex, while dopamine systems stayed unchanged. Mice showed lasting cognitive and emotional changes, and females showed colon shortening. The authors present the hub as a candidate target for early intervention.
pmc-13584303:
Simin Tahmasbi, Amir Faraji, and Azam Alavi examine why patients with high blood pressure in Iran do or do not take their pills as directed. The 2026 study surveyed adults in Izeh County, in town and village clinics, during 2024. After dropping incomplete forms, 530 patients remained, each rating the support they felt from others, their own resilience, and how faithfully they took their medicine.

Modeling of the answers put resilience in the middle of the story. Feeling supported did not lift pill taking on its own, yet it strongly raised resilience, and resilience in turn raised faithful use. Family support scored highest of all support kinds. The authors argue that care plans in poor regions should build patients' support networks and coping strength, not just hand out prescriptions.
pmc-13589903:
G R Warman joins three colleagues in a 2026 review of how the body clock shapes care with anaesthesia, the drugs that keep patients free of pain in surgery. The clock runs on a near 24 hour cycle and changes how the body handles many drugs. Timing a dose can thus change how long pain relief lasts and how fast a patient wakes.

Warman and the others also warn that anaesthetic drugs can disturb the clock and sleep, which may add to confusion after surgery. They point to steps that may help, such as melatonin before and after an operation. Stronger daylight in wards and drugs like dexmedetomidine may also aid sleep and recovery.
pmc-13591303:
Lin Wang leads a large team checking a short activity questionnaire used in British GP clinics, here in adults one year after a hospital stay for severe COVID-19. Clinics need fast ways to spot inactive patients, since inactivity worsens recovery. A total of 752 people filled in the form and wore wrist motion sensors for two weeks. The team tested the form's structure, fairness across groups, and match with sensor readings.

The form held together well and sorted people into activity grades that tracked health measures. It caught inactive people reliably, with high accuracy for that group, yet missed many active ones. Wang and the team call it a handy, cheap screen for inactivity, best paired with device measures when precision matters.
pmc-13591803:
Arthur Comte and seven colleagues use smell receptor science to name the main sex scent of the lily moth, a species never charted before. Female moths release scent blends that draw males of their own kind, and pinning down the blend normally needs live insects at the right hour. The team instead read the moth's genome for kin of known pheromone receptors, modeled their shapes, and predicted which scent molecule would fit.

Computer docking pointed to one compound, and lab tests on the receptors agreed. Chemical analysis of female scent glands then found that compound as the main component. Antenna tests and field behavior showed it alone can draw males. Comte and the team offer receptor guided hunting as a shortcut for other unstudied insects.
pmc-13592303:
Adam Šrut and four colleagues give, in 2026, a spatial map for a paired chemical event: a proton and an electron moving together. Such coupled moves cut energy costs in fuel and biology chemistry, yet textbook square diagrams say nothing about which atoms actually move. Their method picks real space coordinates for the proton hop and the electron hop, then rebuilds the energy landscape over that grid.

Landscapes for two rival flavors of the event, concerted transfer and hydrogen atom transfer, showed telling shape differences. Those contrasts may let scholars tell the flavors apart from data rather than by guesswork. Šrut and the team offer the mapping as a bridge between abstract energy bookkeeping and the physical motions that carry these reactions.
pmc-13592403:
Inose and colleagues reported in 2026 on a method that releases nitric oxide inside a single living cell without shining light straight on that cell. Direct light can harm cells by making reactive oxygen species or heat. Their method uses a metal nanowire coated with a porous framework that stores the gas. Light applied far away launches a wave that travels along the wire to the target point.

Inose showed that the travelling wave triggered a light-based release reaction at the far end, freeing nitric oxide inside one human smooth muscle cell. They confirmed the dose was biologically active by watching brief changes in calcium levels inside the cell. The system gives timed, precise delivery at the single-cell scale. The authors present it as a gentler tool for cell surgery and for probing how signals work in living systems.
pmc-13592703:
Karen A. Sullivan and two colleagues survey how the public reads concussion coverage inside live sport broadcasts. Such broadcasts reach huge audiences, so their injury talk shapes what families and junior coaches believe and do. An online survey of 163 people mixed fixed choice and open questions about how broadcasts portray concussion and how that portrayal should change. Answers were compared across backgrounds such as personal concussion history.

Half or more of respondents backed twelve of thirty statements about the portrayal, including that it should improve. Ten of twelve fix ideas won agreement, led by putting player health first. Background made no clear difference to views. Sullivan and the team say community backing exists for broadcasts that teach more and dramatize less.
pmc-13593703:
L Katugampola and co-authors studied what dimethyl sulfoxide, a solution flushed into the bladder to treat bladder pain syndrome, does to the bladder wall itself. Their laboratory work used strips of muscle and of inner lining tissue from pig bladders, with some muscle tests repeated on human tissue.

The solution shut down contractions in both tissue types, and at the strongest concentration it abolished them completely. Washing the tissue for a few hours restored muscle responses in full. The lining behaved differently: within about twenty-five minutes of washing, its spontaneous contractions not only returned but overshot their starting level, and responses to a stimulating drug grew stronger too. That rebound in the bladder lining may explain why some patients flare with worse symptoms right after treatment, the authors suggest.
pmc-13593803:
Enzo Zini Moreira Silva and colleagues studied how three microcystin toxins harm liver cells and whether they differ in cancer risk. Microcystins, blue-green algae toxins in water and food, threaten the liver, but their workings and cousin gaps were unclear. Their 2026 study exposed HepaRG liver cells to microcystin-LR, -LA, and -RR, tracking enzyme action, cell growth, and gene readouts.

All three toxins alike blocked PP2A, yet only LR and LA clearly boosted cell growth. Gene readouts for LR and LA matched closely, while RR hit fewer genes and matched weakly with the others. Only LR and LA upset liver harm pathways linked to liver cancer, bile blockage, and scarring. All three shifted cancer-linked tiny RNAs, with no steady pattern. The authors stress one-to-one toxin harm driven by uptake and clean-up gaps.
pmc-13594603:
Kori Puspita Ningsih, Hartono Hartono, and Nur Hafidha Hikmayani built and validated an instrument for judging the quality of clinical coding. They worked in casemix payment systems. In those systems hospitals are paid by standardized case groups. Coding errors distort both payment and health statistics. Their methodological study was set in Indonesia's national casemix scheme.

The finished tool covers seven domains, from how diagnoses and procedures are documented to whether codes comply with rules and were chosen correctly, expressed through eleven assessment items. Expert review rated its content validity very high, and answers proved highly consistent internally, though agreement between individual raters varied by item. The authors present it as an initial, multidimensional way to audit coding beyond simple accuracy, and they call for testing in more hospitals and against real casemix outcomes.
pmc-13597503:
Guodian Xiong leads a thirteen-author team that found a single amino acid acting as a master dimmer for a whole family of dangerous viruses. Orthobunyaviruses number more than one hundred thirty species. No broad treatment or vaccine exists for them. Their copying enzyme carries one lysine residue conserved across every serogroup. The team flipped that residue to its opposite charge in 2026 experiments.

The swap crippled the enzyme and weakened Ebinur Lake virus badly, cutting replication, cell damage, and lethality in mice. The same trick attenuated the family's prototype virus and a relative from another serogroup, showing the effect is general. Detective work traced the loss mainly to a broken grip between the enzyme and the viral genome's end, with a new chemical bond possibly adding to the sabotage. The authors propose the residue as a rational basis for weakened vaccine strains.
pmc-13599203:
Maryam Jafar Sameri leads a five-author team reviewing how well treatment centers for substance use disorder work around the world. Published in 2026, their systematic review asks what signs show that treatment has succeeded, and which kinds of care help people most. Success, they note, is judged in many different ways, which has kept the field from agreeing on shared standards.

Two reviewers screened 4,234 records and kept 28 studies, checking quality with standard risk-of-bias tools. Useful signs of success fell into three groups: body health, mental health, and social life, such as holding a job. Medicines like methadone and buprenorphine cut drug use and relapse, while talking therapies lifted quality of life. Care that joined both did best. Most studies came from four rich countries, and few followed patients past one year, so long-term proof stays thin.
pmc-13600303:
Juan García-Bernalt Diego and colleagues investigate why one West African Ebola variant spread so efficiently. During the 2013 to 2016 epidemic, the Makona variant picked up a change in its surface glycoprotein, its cell-entry protein. The change, known as A82V, appeared early and was linked to faster spread, but the host-side reason stayed unclear. The team focused on DC-SIGN, a receptor on immune cells.

Using harmless lab-made virus copies, the team showed the changed glycoprotein infects dendritic cells and macrophages better, only when DC-SIGN is present. Two sugar attachment sites helped it grip the receptor, and its sugar coat carried more of a tag called Lewis X. Blocking that tag cut infection, confirming its role. The findings name DC-SIGN as a key helper in Makona transmission and show how sugar coating can sharpen a virus's spread.
pmc-13602803:
Yoonju Na and four colleagues use co-design in 2026 to reshape a remote therapy program for preterm babies after intensive care. Babies born early face motor, cognitive, and social risks, yet families often cannot reach rehab services once home. The team applied a five-stage experience-based co-design method, interviewing five mothers who had used remote rehabilitation and four professionals, then workshopping findings with thirteen stakeholders.

Three themes emerged. Parents were motivated and valued the access, but preparing each session was demanding. Professional feedback built confidence, while the screen created pressure and lost the hands-on touch. Printed materials alone did not support practice between sessions, and paperwork hurt adherence. The redesigned model mixes 15-minute live video sessions with in-person training before discharge, replayable video resources, video progress checks, and a messaging channel. Content widened beyond movement to feeding, sleep, parent-baby interaction, and parental well-being.
pmc-13604003:
Runmin Jiang and colleagues built a light-label pipe for 3D scan cuts that needs far less hand-marked truth. Full-label scan cuts eat hours of hand work, most of all in 3D. Their chance-aware pipe makes thick fake labels from thin marks, reads traits with a chance-aware transformer net, and trains with a loss that heeds mark trust.

On CT and MRI sets, the pipe matched full-label work and beat past light-label work, with Dice gains up to 18.1 percent for some organs. By heeding doubt all through training, the pipe cuts bias from noisy fake labels. Open code invites wide tests in clinic scan work.
pmc-13612703:
Madeline Marie Marello Havn and colleagues launch the Aarhus Bereavement Study, the first grief group picked from state files and tied to a long grief poll with non-grief peers. Grief lifts risks for death, body ills, and mind ills, with the fresh prolonged grief ill in the mix. The full group of 68,960 folks is tracked in Danish state files from start through 2030.

State files hold jobs, pay, aid, school, body ills, mind ills, drug sales, and death causes for widowed mates, matched peers, and all their kids. A poll of 1,227 fresh spouse- and parent-loss folks in Aarhus had a 54 percent reply rate. It adds life ways, drug use, traits, big life shifts, and mind scores in eight waves over five years. A ten-year poll wave is set for 2027.
pmc-13613803:
Anita Monteverdi leads a team using virtual brain models and brain-wave scans to explain memory changes in mild cognitive impairment, a stage of thinking decline that can precede Alzheimer's disease. The condition varies a lot between people, and brain scans alone have not explained who loses memory and how fast. The team studied 30 patients, 18 with markers of Alzheimer's proteins in the brain and 12 without them.

Each person's scan data fed a personal virtual brain, sometimes called a digital twin, that mimics how brain regions talk to each other. Brain-wave readings added detail on each region's rhythms. The team then matched model traits against thinking test scores. Virtual brain traits did not split the two patient groups cleanly, yet linking models with brain waves still helped account for differences in memory.
pmc-13614803:
Simmi K. Ratan leads a team reporting a 2026 study of two blood markers as early warnings of poor outcomes in newborn babies who need surgery. Infection after surgery is a leading threat to such babies. The markers, procalcitonin and a sensitive form of C-reactive protein, both rise with infection. The team enrolled 120 operated newborns in a surgical intensive care unit and drew blood at admission and again 24 hours after surgery.

Outcomes counted as good if the baby went home, and bad if care reached the most severe complication grade or the baby died. The authors tested how well each marker level, along with white cell counts and blood cultures, separated the two paths and where the best cut-off sits. A reliable early warning could let teams act before a fragile newborn slips into severe infection.
pmc-13615703:
Ahmed Higazy and colleagues report a 2026 study of what predicts success in a prostate operation designed to spare ejaculation. The operation trims the enlarged prostate through the urinary passage while preserving a centimetre of tissue around a key landmark, so semen can still move forward. The team followed sexually active men having the procedure, recording symptom scores, sexual function surveys, and ultrasound measures of prostate shape before surgery.

In total, 108 men were counted in the final analysis, with checks three months after the operation. Symptoms improved clearly after surgery. Modelling searched for which traits, such as prostate size, a lobe pushing into the bladder, or the length of tissue above the landmark, forecast preserved function. For men who rank sexual function alongside relief of urinary trouble, such predictors sharpen the choice of operation.
pmc-13616403:
Yi-Ming Liu and colleagues engineer an injectable gel depot that starves large liver tumours of glutamine while carrying two attack payloads, aiming to fix the uneven cooking of microwave ablation. Big liver tumours often survive ablation because heat spreads patchily and the leftover zone suppresses immunity. The gel forms in place through a catalytic setting reaction and holds a glutamine-blocking drug plus a sound-activated agent.

Under microwave heat plus ultrasound, the depot cuts the tumour's antioxidant defences and its energy supply lines at once. The combined stress wrecks the power plants, the protein workshop, and the DNA of cancer cells, triggering a mixed death program and waking immune alarms. Full coverage of a large tumour, not just its centre, is the prize: fewer survivors left to regrow.
pmc-13617103:
Zhenxing Wu, Yuxin Ye, and Huifeng Huang study patients with gastric ulcer, a chronic stomach sore that needs long-term self-care, and ask how food knowledge turns into healthy action. They surveyed four hundred eighteen patients at two large hospitals in Zhejiang Province, China, in March and April 2026. The survey measured food and nutrition literacy, nutrition awareness, and proactive health behavior.

All three measures rose together. Nutrition awareness partly carried the effect of literacy on behavior, meaning knowledge helped most when it first raised awareness. Sorting patients by literacy level produced four groups, from low to high, and the groups differed clearly in awareness and behavior. The authors propose layered education programs matched to each literacy group, using awareness as the key middle step toward better daily habits and ulcer management.
pmc-13618403:
Max Little and two colleagues write a commentary warning that machine learning on voice recordings cannot yet be trusted to characterize Parkinson disease objectively. Voice and speech falter in most patients, making recordings a tempting, noninvasive data source. A paper by Shukla and colleagues in August 2026 showed naive statistical analysis of such data can mislead badly. The problem, the commentators argue, lies in how the datasets are usually collected.

Ad hoc observational collections quietly contain spurious associations. Cases and controls may differ in age or recording environment enough that a benchmark using only those background facts can beat predictions from the audio itself. Sophisticated algorithms do not rescue flawed design. The authors argue that explicit mechanistic causal analyses, and ultimately interventional diagnostic clinical trials, are required to prove a direct link between the disease and what an algorithm predicts.
pmc-13618903:
Nianbo Xu and thirteen colleagues teach AI to read womb lining tissue and predict whether an in vitro fertilization cycle will end in a live birth. Judging endometrial receptivity by eye is subjective. They compared a conventional deep network trained end to end with a pipeline built on UNI2-h, a large pathology foundation model used as a frozen feature extractor. Training used natural-cycle biopsies, with testing on held-out patients.

The conventional whole-slide model looked good internally but fell to near chance on an external test of cycle timing, a warning about overfitting. The foundation model pipeline was steadier, with moderate discrimination for live birth internally and strong discrimination of cycle phase externally. Models focused on the luminal epithelium, the embryo's landing surface, kept comparable accuracy on less data. Combining tissue scores with clinical data beat clinical data alone, and the tissue signal dominated the weighting.
pmc-13619703:
Tuna Aras and a large surgical team describe cadaver training for one of trauma surgery's rarest emergencies: bleeding from the large vein behind the liver. Total hepatic vascular exclusion, clamping every vessel into the liver, can stop such bleeding, but the exposure steps are hard to rehearse on living patients. The team practiced a five-step sequence on nine adult cadavers.

Control of the ligament at the liver's entry point rated easiest. Steps repeated across donors felt simpler over time. Reaching the vein above the liver from below the diaphragm stayed demanding, while a route through the diaphragm into the sac around the heart rated clearly easier. The authors are careful: steps ran in a fixed order and scores came from team consensus, so the study cannot prove the heart-sac route is truly safer or better in real surgery.
pmc-13619903:
Isabela Pádua Zanon and ten colleagues hunted drug-resistant bacteria on chicken carcasses at a Brazilian slaughterhouse that supplies home and export markets. Brazil leads world chicken exports, and poultry can carry bacteria that threaten human health. The team sampled thirty carcasses with visible gut contamination and thirty clean-looking ones, then tested the isolates and sequenced the genomes of nine representative strains.

Salmonella Minnesota dominated the salmonella finds, and E. coli plus several notorious hospital pathogens turned up as well. Roughly half the salmonella and E. coli isolates made enzymes that defeat whole families of antibiotics, and resistance genes of clinical concern appeared in the genomes. Some strains matched high-risk clones known worldwide and sat close genetically to bacteria from human infections. The authors call for steady resistance monitoring along the whole poultry chain.
pmc-13623403:
Wei Ren Ng and colleagues present a six-case series on tubular adenoma, a rare benign breast tumour hard to tell from the common fibroadenoma by feel or scan. Firm diagnosis needs tissue under the microscope. The series gathers clinical, imaging, and pathology details of each patient to draw management lessons.

Patients ranged from twenty-two to sixty-two years old. Ultrasound in every case showed a smooth-edged, darker-than-surrounding lump with varying blood flow inside. Core needle biopsy, which samples tissue with a hollow needle, made the diagnosis in all six. Four patients had surgery, which confirmed the benign finding, and two were watched with scans after biopsy and imaging agreed. No lump grew back, enlarged, or turned malignant during follow-up. Because rare reports place cancer next to such tumours, the authors advise biopsy proof in all cases, watching only when results agree.
pmc-13624303:
Byung Jun Lee and colleagues dissect why a promising new memory technology wears out in two opposite ways. Selector-only memory stores data in a single two-terminal device made of a glassy chalcogenide material, attractive for dense memory arrays, yet its failure physics was murky. The team stressed germanium-antimony-selenium devices and probed them with chemical and electrical tools.

Repeated switching drained selenium from the material, pushing its internal charge traps toward shallow states, so the switching threshold sagged and the margin between states shrank until the device failed. Resting and heating did the reverse: the glassy structure relaxed into deeper traps, and the threshold crept upward over time. Worse, cycling damage made the relaxation faster, a self-reinforcing spiral. The authors unite both failure modes in one trap-based framework, giving engineers specific levers, such as protecting the selenium content, for longer-lived devices.
pmc-13624703:
Grace Noonan and three co-authors present a newborn girl whose skull bones carried many hollow gaps, a rare pattern called lacunar skull. The condition usually appears beside spine or brain defects, so a healthy baby with no partner problems is unusual. She was born at term after a smooth pregnancy, and routine checks found a soft, boggy swelling over the right side of her head.

Scans with three-dimensional rebuilding showed uneven see-through gaps in the skull, strongest at the back and right side, while her brain, spine, and skull seams looked normal. No other defects turned up, so the team chose watchful waiting over surgery. At six weeks she fed, moved, and developed normally, a gentle course worth recording for other clinicians.
pmc-13626403:
Maria Matsangidou and co-authors design an augmented reality aid for the hardest corner of cancer surgery: liver, pancreas, and bile duct operations. Planning these cases strains spatial sense and team talk, and patients' feelings rarely enter design rooms. Between February 2024 and September 2025 the team ran co-design workshops and interviews. Fourteen clinicians and ten patients took part. The team then built a prototype and tested it with ten liver specialists in mock tumor board meetings.

Clinicians rated the system through a standard usability scale while observers logged where it helped or snagged. The study's point is method as much as gadget: patients and psycho-oncology voices shaped the tool beside surgeons. An AR overlay that respects emotion and teamwork, the authors argue, stands a better chance of entering real operating workflows.
pmc-13629103:
Jia-min Yan and five colleagues asked if keeping up hobbies guards older adults against high blood pressure. Their 2026 study used two large ageing cohorts. One in China held over seven thousand people. One in the United States held nearly five thousand. All were aged fifty or over at entry.

People with hobbies developed high blood pressure less often than those without. The guard was strongest in people who kept their hobbies going across visits. That held in both lands. In the Chinese cohort, hobby activity also came with a slow yearly fall in blood pressure readings. The authors suggest health programmes for ageing people should treat hobbies seriously. Steady hobby activity is a true preventive tool, not a pastime.
pmc-13630403:
Junsik Sung, Gargi Digholkar, and Ryan Pearson describe in 2026 a nanoparticle treatment designed to calm cytokine storm, the runaway immune reaction behind sepsis deaths. Their design copies natural fat particles from a plant root that were known to soak up harmful immune messengers.

The synthetic particles gather a coat of blood proteins that traps several inflammatory messengers at once rather than blocking just one. They also carry dexamethasone, a calming steroid, inside. In tests the particles lowered two key inflammatory signals, raised a calming one, and quieted a master inflammation switch. In mice with a lethal bacterial toxin challenge, treated animals kept healthier organs and survived far better. The authors frame the platform as a two-layer defense against severe inflammation.
pmc-13630903:
Melanie Bathon and eight colleagues reviewed a decade of care for liver cancer at a German university hospital, asking whether the flood of new drug treatments actually changed outcomes. They split 1,288 patients diagnosed between 2013 and 2022 into an earlier and a later group, divided at 2020 when a leading immunotherapy combination won European approval.

Charts showed the later patients arrived with earlier tumours and healthier livers, and practice shifted away from catheter-based chemotherapy toward systemic drugs. Headline survival matched across eras, and immunotherapy's apparent edge over older targeted pills vanished once baseline differences were adjusted for. Liver function, the authors stress, outweighed tumour stage in predicting who lived longest.
pmc-13631303:
Wing Lam Tiffany Yip and colleagues systematically reviewed trials of AI-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety and depression, a 2026 assessment of a fast-growing but thin evidence base. Human therapists are scarce and access barriers are wide, so chatbots and other AI tools that mimic conversation promise scale. The team searched three databases for randomized trials from 2016 onward, screening 208 studies and keeping sixteen, with quality judged by a standard bias tool.

Results were sobering. Only one of fourteen studies showed significant anxiety improvement, and only four of sixteen showed significant depression improvement. Third-wave approaches that stress mindfulness and acceptance, and programs aimed at younger people, looked somewhat more promising, while older adults seemed to benefit least. Personalization and human support did not reliably improve outcomes, and study quality raised concerns.
pmc-13631403:
Ekaterina Borozdina challenges the standard story about vaccine hesitancy. In that story, mothers are cast as lone decision-makers. Their personal choices explain why children go unvaccinated. Drawing on interviews with vaccine-hesitant Russian mothers, she moves the decision inside families. She also places it inside a particular healthcare system.

Beneath the talk of single maternal duty, she finds choices negotiated across a web of kin. Commitments to family frame the talks. The Russian setting mixes Soviet-era structures with strong state control. Newer market-style demands for personal duty sit awkwardly beside them. Where the system preaches self-reliance without steady support, distrust grows. Family involvement then becomes the practical way parents navigate doubt.
pmc-13632003:
Two new ultrasound measures for spotting a severe brain malformation before birth are tested by Li and colleagues. Holoprosencephaly, a condition where the developing forebrain fails to divide fully, can be hard to confirm early, even with modern scans. The researchers measured an angle and a distance between the forehead and a front brain artery, using microvascular flow imaging, a sensitive Doppler method that shows tiny blood vessels.

Reference ranges came from 462 healthy fetuses between twelve and thirty-four weeks of pregnancy, while the tests were also tried in fetuses with holoprosencephaly and in fetuses with look-alike brain findings. Every affected fetus scored at or below the fifth percentile on both measures. The angle measure caught all cases in the comparison group, which suggests these simple, objective readings could sharpen early prenatal diagnosis.
pmc-13633503:
Auguste Hassler and five colleagues tested whether calcium chemistry in reindeer bones can count how often a female nursed during her life. Reindeer and caribou herds are shrinking under climate pressure, and knowing past breeding rates would help explain their history. Milk feeding leaves a chemical fingerprint because calcium atoms come in slightly different weights. The team measured those weights in teeth and jawbones from five reindeer whose life histories were fully documented.

No clear nursing signal appeared in the jawbone readings, contrary to the team's hope. Bone calcium may simply turn over faster in reindeer than expected, washing out the record. One animal's data instead hinted at an undiagnosed bone-thinning illness. Other readings offered clues about seasonal diet and weaning habits. The authors judge the nursing-counting idea unproven, while calling the method promising for studying ancient diets and disease. They outline the controlled studies needed next.
pmc-13637303:
Yue Yuan and nine colleagues published this 2026 study hunting for gout warning signs in people whose uric acid reads normal. Gout care today waits for high urate or the first painful attack, which misses people who develop gout at normal levels. The team mined blood protein data from more than thirty-three thousand UK Biobank participants with normal urate. To avoid algorithm quirks, they ran hundreds of model setups and kept only what survived them all.

A ten-protein signature predicted future gout with strong accuracy. People scoring high carried well over four times the risk, independent of urate and standard factors. The proteins' levels in future cases drifted apart from controls ten to fifteen years before diagnosis. The same signature barely predicted osteoarthritis, the control condition, which supports its specificity. The authors offer the panel as an early stratification tool that opens a decade-wide window for prevention.
pmc-13637403:
Nurul Haniyah Rosslan and three colleagues published this 2026 analysis of harsh discipline against toddlers and preschoolers in Malaysia. The data come from the country's 2022 National Health and Morbidity Survey, a nationally representative household study. Caregivers of more than thirteen thousand children aged one to just under five reported discipline used in the past month. Psychological aggression meant harsh scolding or hurtful name-calling. Physical punishment covered shaking, spanking, and hitting with a hand or object.

Well over half the children had faced psychological aggression in that month, and two in five had been physically punished. Both forms climbed steeply with the child's age across the toddler years. Boys received physical punishment more often than girls. The authors recommend folding proven positive-parenting programs into routine maternal and child health services and community platforms. Their figures give Malaysian policymakers a national baseline for tracking whether gentler discipline spreads.
pmc-13642103:
Guanhua Yang led a 2026 study showing that twisting a photonic crystal can flip topological bands built on bound states in the continuum, a mechanism for trapping light with long lifetimes. Such bound states hide inside the radiation continuum yet do not leak, making them prized for lasers and sensors. Steering their band topology in momentum space remained unsolved. The team twisted photonic crystals so that zone folding moved every high-symmetry point to the center, splitting each band into three linked to bound states or resonances.

Tuning the twist angle controlled how those folded bands interacted. At a critical angle, p-like and s-like bands met in a Dirac cone. Further twisting broke that cone, flipping band topology through a parity exchange and a conversion between guided-resonance and bound-state character. Experiments matched simulations. Twist angle thus becomes a new knob for tailoring light trapping on a chip.
pmc-13642903:
Yubo Hu and four colleagues present a 2026 study of post-traumatic stress in aged rats, with attention to sex differences. How PTSD works in the elderly brain, and why women face higher lifetime rates, remains poorly mapped.

Fifteen-month-old rats went through prolonged stress plus footshock, then received behavior tests, brain glucose imaging, hormone profiling, and gene analysis. Females showed more severe PTSD-like behavior, and their fear circuits, spanning prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala, shifted glucose use more strongly. Brain glucose burning fell overall, and insulin and AMPK signaling pathways reprogrammed in a sex-dependent pattern across regions.
pmc-13643003:
Osamu Baba and Koh Ono present a 2026 review of ATP, the cell's energy currency, as both fuel and signal in atherosclerosis, the artery-hardening disease behind most heart attacks and strokes. Inside cells, ATP levels reflect the balance between two energy pathways and differ by cell type.

Outside cells, released ATP docks onto purinergic receptors and steers inflammation, vessel tone, barrier function, cell growth, movement, and calcification. The review covers how ATP is measured in plaques and what it does in lining cells, macrophages, and muscle cells. The authors close with measurement challenges and treatment ideas aimed at each ATP role.
pmc-13643203:
Cohen and colleagues published a 2026 modeling study on how parasites spread unevenly between hosts. Hosts differ in how easily they catch and pass on parasites. The twist is whether a host's infectiousness is fixed by the receiver or set by the giver. The team compared these two extreme stories in spread models.

Under receiver control, spread hinged on how catchability and infectiousness paired up. Under giver control, the single most infectious host drove overall spread. Each story leaves its own fingerprints in outbreak data patterns. Real systems likely sit between the two poles, the authors note. Knowing where a system sits sharpens control plans for outbreaks. Field data that separate the two stories are now a priority.
pmc-13645403:
Pia Vuola led a 2026 Finnish register study tracking deformational plagiocephaly and brachycephaly, flattening of an infant's skull from external pressure, between 1987 and 2010. Unlike craniosynostosis, where skull sutures fuse early, these deformities come from pressure during growth, shaped by factors such as sex, prematurity, twin birth, and prolonged back sleeping. The team analyzed 1,453,780 births from national registers, confirming diagnoses against medical records and excluding craniosynostosis.

Only 467 children were diagnosed, yet prevalence rose from 1.7 per 100,000 live births in 1987 to 136 per 100,000 in 2010, with the steepest climb after supine sleep guidance was formally revised in 2000. Among moderate-to-severe cases, boys predominated at 69 percent, right-sided back flattening led at 56 percent, and twins were overrepresented. Clinicians get a national picture that mirrors international trends, arriving later in Finland, and a reminder that back sleeping's benefits come with a head-shape trade-off to monitor.
pmc-13648303:
Norbertus A. Ipenburg and two colleagues, in a 2026 study, hunt for the cause of allergic skin rash from hearing aid ear moulds. They reviewed patients tested at Amsterdam University Medical Center from 2022 to 2025. Rash from moulds is rare in print, yet moulds sit in the ear canal for hours a day.

Of 20 patients with suspected mould allergy, eight had patch tests that pointed to mould chemicals. All eight reacted to one chemical, tetrahydrofurfuryl methacrylate. Three of them also reacted to a second one. A third chemical, long blamed in such cases, caught no one at all. The authors say the first two should join the test list when mould rash is checked.
pmc-13649103:
Nike Klun and Manca Tekavčič Pompe report in 2026 on clearing clouded vision after childhood cataract surgery using a laser procedure performed with children lying on their backs under general anaesthesia. Young patients cannot sit still at the standard laser machine, so the team adapted the posterior capsulotomy to the supine position.

Thirteen eyes of nine children treated in Ljubljana between 2019 and 2025 were reviewed. The laser opening succeeded in every eye, and average corrected vision improved significantly over a median follow-up of about two years. Three eyes needed a repeat treatment, and two had brief pressure rises that settled with drops. The authors show the adapted position is feasible for children.
pmc-13649403:
Yulong Liu and three colleagues report a 47-year-old woman whose heart artery tore on its own, a rare cause of heart attack seen most often in women. Care teams first treated her as a standard heart attack case and gave clot-busting drugs. Sound-wave scans inside the artery then showed a tear plus a large blood pocket in the wall of two linked artery segments.

Since her blood flow stayed stable and pain did not persist, the team chose watchful care over a stent or surgery. Scans three months later showed the tear and blood pocket had healed on their own. She stayed free of chest pain for about six years of checks. The authors stress that one healed case does not prove a treatment works.
pmc-13649703:
Karan Singh and three colleagues found a way to turn heart tracings into pictures that image-based learning tools can read. Heart data come as one-dimensional lines from twelve leads, which fits poorly with vision models built for photos. Their method uses a math transform to fold a full tracing into one two-dimensional image, in a way that can be reversed.

Tested on large public heart datasets, the picture form scored on par with top models, from deep networks to transformers and one-dimensional rivals. Key timing and cross-lead detail survived the fold, at least up to a final smoothing step. The authors pitch the trick as a bridge from raw body signals to standard image tools.
pmc-13650003:
Sun-Joon Yoo and five colleagues use computer simulation to compare two ways of anchoring the top of a long spinal fusion in adults with spinal deformity. The junction above the fused section often fails because stiffness changes abruptly there. Screws grip the top vertebra directly, while hooks that wrap a bony side process may give a gentler landing, and hook direction could matter.

A three-dimensional model built from one patient's spine tested screws against hooks facing down and hooks facing up under load and bending. Hooks preserved more motion at the top segment and lowered joint loads in most directions, though one hook direction raised loads when the spine bent backward. Screw pull-out risk looked high in forward bending for the screw design, while hooks carried lower breakage risk but shifted stress to the level below. The authors advise matching the choice to each patient's bone quality.
pmc-13651103:
Tevfik Koçak and four colleagues separate two faces of orthorexia, the preoccupation with healthy eating. One face is a harmless, positive interest in eating well; the other is a compulsive control that damages mental health and social life. Their survey asks which life circumstances and food attitudes feed each face.

Over a thousand adults completed a battery of scales covering eating behaviors, processed food intake, food security, label reading, food choice motives, and the obesogenic character of their surroundings. Healthy interest rose with sustainable eating habits, label reading, and motives around health, natural ingredients, weight, and ethics, and fell with price and familiarity motives. The pathological form shared some drivers, such as weight-control and ethical motives, yet diverged on mood-driven choices and health motives, which pulled in opposite directions. Food insecurity severity tracked with both. Because the design is a snapshot, the authors avoid causal claims.
pmc-3466303:
Choi, Sims, Murphy, and co-authors present a method for predicting the functional effect of amino acid substitutions and small insertions or deletions. Modern sequencing projects now produce genome-wide variation data on a massive scale. Tools are needed to predict which variants change function and to narrow the search for disease-causing ones.

Their predictor, PROVEAN, scores a change by how much it disturbs related protein sequences. Harmless changes leave conserved patterns intact; damaging ones break them. Such scores help clinicians and researchers triage thousands of variants down to the few worth laboratory testing.  Rare disease clinics use such scores when a patient's variant list arrives.
pmc-3965103:
Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones updated miRBase in 2014, the main public store for microRNA sequences. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces that help control which genes are turned on. Deep sequencing, which reads huge numbers of RNA pieces at once, had sharply raised the flow of new finds.

Release twenty, from June 2013, listed loci from more than two hundred species and tens of thousands of mature microRNA products. The update stresses high confidence, so weak or doubtful entries are marked with care. Labs use miRBase names and sequences as a shared reference, which keeps studies across the world easy to compare.
pmc-5388903:
The GBD 2015 Mortality and Causes of Death Collaborators reported in 2016 on life expectancy and causes of death worldwide. Extending life in every population takes timely, robust local data on who dies, of what, and how that changes. Without such evidence, health policy flies blind.

The study assesses deaths overall and by cause, for hundreds of causes, across the years from 1980 to 2015. It estimates life expectancy at global, regional, and national levels. The results show where gains are fastest and where causes such as conflict or epidemics reverse them. These figures anchor global health planning and funding decisions.
pmc-6145203:
Jayanta Patra, Gitishree Das, Leonardo Fraceto, and a large team reviewed nano drug delivery systems in 2018. Nanomedicine uses particles of tiny scale to carry drugs or imaging agents. Controlled release at a chosen site is the central promise.

The review surveys particle types, from lipids and polymers to metals, and how each is made. It weighs gains in targeting and dose control against safety and manufacturing hurdles. Many systems work well in animals yet stall before human use. Readers get both the excitement and the sober list of what must still be solved.
pmc-6323903:
John Tate, Sally Bamford, Harry Jubb, and coauthors described the COSMIC cancer mutation catalogue in 2018. COSMIC collects somatic mutations found in human cancers. It is the most detailed resource of its kind.

The release described here holds millions of coding mutations drawn from tumor samples and curated papers. Users can browse by gene, cancer type, or single mutation and see drug links. Expert curation keeps entries tied to real evidence rather than raw dumps. Drug developers consult COSMIC early when judging whether a mutation is worth targeting. A genome browser view lets users move from a mutation to its surrounding genes in one step.
pmc-7199903:
Yasunori Watanabe, Joel Allen, Daniel Wrapp, and coauthors analyzed the sugar coat of the SARS-CoV-2 spike in 2020. Vaccines focus on the spike, the protein that starts infection. Each of its three parts carries many sites where sugar chains attach.

The team mapped which sites actually carry sugars and what those chains look like. The coat shields much of the protein surface from antibodies, but leaves the receptor-binding area fairly open. That pattern is hopeful for vaccine design, since key targets stay reachable. The maps became a reference for antigen engineering.
pmc-7201103:
Jian-Min Jin, Peng Bai, Wei He, and coauthors compared COVID-19 severity between the sexes in 2020. The new outbreak recalled the SARS outbreak years earlier, where men fared worse. The authors set out to test whether the same pattern held.

Pooling case series and public data from China, they find men develop severe disease and die at higher rates than women. The gap persists after broad age patterns are considered. Possible reasons include smoking rates, other illnesses, and immune differences. The analysis helped establish sex as a routine factor in COVID-19 risk reporting.
pmc-7205903:
Bo Diao, Chenhui Wang, Yingjun Tan, and coauthors studied T cells in COVID-19 patients in 2020. T cells are central to antiviral defense. Their numbers and working state in the new disease were still unknown when the study began.

Blood tests on patients in Wuhan showed sharp drops in T cell counts, above all in severe cases and older patients. Remaining cells carried markers of exhaustion and worked poorly. The pattern tracks with worse outcomes, suggesting immune collapse helps drive severe disease. The findings pushed T cell support into early treatment discussions.
pmc-7312803:
Giuseppe Genchi and co-authors reviewed in 2020 the health effects of cadmium, a toxic metal that human and animal bodies have no use for. Cadmium reaches people mainly through food, drink, and tobacco smoke, and it also enters air, soil, and water from farms and industry. Once inside the body it leaves only very slowly, so exposure builds up over a lifetime.

The review describes how cadmium damages the kidneys, bones, lungs, and other organs, and how it can help set cancer in motion. The authors also cover where exposure comes from and which workers and communities face the most of it. Their summary is a reference for doctors and safety officials who must judge how much cadmium is too much.
pmc-7447603:
Jesus Banales and a broad team of specialists reviewed in 2020 where research on cholangiocarcinoma stands and where it should go next. These are cancers that arise somewhere along the bile ducts, the network that carries bile from the liver. They form a varied group of tumors, their numbers are rising worldwide, and they now account for a notable share of primary liver cancers.

The authors survey what is known about how these cancers develop, how they are found, and how they are treated. They also map the open questions, from earlier detection to drugs matched to each tumor's molecular traits. For a cancer that is often caught late and resists standard therapy, the review sets a shared agenda for the next wave of work.
pmc-8450103:
Patricia Chan and colleagues released tRNAscan-SE 2.0 in 2021, an improved version of the standard tool for finding transfer RNA genes in genome sequences. Transfer RNAs are the small molecules that carry amino acids to the protein building machinery, and spotting their genes is a basic step in reading any genome. The original tool had served for over twenty years, since the first genomes were decoded.

The update handles the flood of newer genomes, which are far more numerous and come from a far wider range of species. It also classifies the genes it finds by their likely function. The authors show the gains in accuracy and speed that justify the new version's place in annotation pipelines.
poe-works-raven-edition-1903:
Edgar Allan Poe's works fill this Raven Edition volume, edited by Stedman and Woodberry in 1903. The landmark set of 1902 to 1903 was the first scholarly complete Poe in print. This volume gathers the great tales and the Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym as well.

Readers find tales of horror, detection, and wild fancy in Poe's best-known prose pieces here. The Pym narrative sails to mutiny, shipwreck, and a strange white world at the pole. Poe's poems and essays in the full set show his theory of beauty and effect. Editors' notes trace his hard life and the texts' tangled printing history in detail. For a century this edition anchored Poe study in schools and libraries alike.
prof-cavanagh-s-phrenological-chart-1903: Scanned pages in rough shape present a seller of head readings explaining phrenology. The writer calls it a system of mental philosophy proved by facts. Heads, he says, are measured rather than felt for bumps, so strong and weak parts of character can be marked on a chart. Three kinds of examination are offered, from a spoken reading to a marked chart with private secret advice. The pages read partly as teaching and partly as a trade card, showing how head reading was sold.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-159-19:
Charivaria leads Punch for November 3, 1920, in volume 159, with brief jokes on Ireland, coal, and the navy. The column's dry tone turns even a lost battle into a jest.

Asked why Ireland should not have a parliament like England's, the column calls the idea retaliation. The miners' strike has inspired a ragtime song, to Mr. Smillie's innocent surprise. The Admiralty will publish no official account of the Battle of Jutland, cigars seized in New York are found to contain only tobacco, and the Premier's hair is reported bobbed. Water, a council member says, is being sold at a loss.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: For volume three of The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte, the front pages consist of a standard publisher's header and nothing else. Constant is named there as the author, the title is given in full, and the text is stated to be English. Readers who open this part find no narrative waiting in the pages shown: there is no first chapter, no list of contents, and no note by any editor or translator. Only the bare facts of title, author, language, and volume number three can be reported.
richard-carvel-volume-03:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel reaches its third volume with Mr. Allen Shows His Hand, the chapter that opens the pages shown. The volume's list adds The Volte Coupe, a rector worsted, things made clear, South River, and The Black Moll. A Man of Destiny is named at the list's end.

Richard reports that Dorothy's beauty had taken London by storm, as it had conquered Annapolis. Talk of a duke for her troubles him, for a duchess's coronet would end his hope. Dr. Courtenay arrives late at an assembly, proud of a private letter he will not show. Fotheringay swears the doctor is a sly dog with reasons of his own.
rousseau-confessions-1903:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote his Confessions late in life, and the book appeared after his death, in 1782 and after. The English text here is the Aldus Society edition of 1903, in an unsigned translation. Rousseau promised to show a man in all the truth of nature, himself, without excuse.

Across twelve books he tells of his boyhood in Geneva, his thefts, lies, and shames. He recalls masters, lovers, patrons, and the making of his famous books. Sweet scenes of youth sit beside acts he plainly regrets. Rousseau hides little, and that candor was new in life writing. The Confessions founded modern autobiography and shaped how later writers told the truth about themselves.
royce-outlines-psychology-1903:
Outlines of Psychology, published in 1903, is Royce's short treatise on the mind, written for students. An idealist among laboratory men, he treats mind as purpose at work in experience: attention, habit, and will shaping a world of meanings.

The book covers sensation, perception, memory, feeling, and choice in Royce's clear lecture style. Throughout, he resists reducing mind to mere mechanism, insisting that purpose is the key idea. The book served Harvard classrooms in the years when James and Royce made its psychology famous. It remains a readable record of that school at its most confident.
russell-principles-mathematics-1903:
Bertrand Russell published The Principles of Mathematics in 1903, his first major work of philosophy. Russell defends logicism, the view that mathematics rests on logic alone. He studies number, quantity, order, and infinity with fresh rigor. A famous appendix discusses the paradox that bears his name.

The book launched analytic philosophy as a movement. Russell's clear style set a new standard for argument in English. Work with Whitehead on Principia Mathematica grew from this start. Mathematicians and logicians still respect its bold program, even where later results limited it. It remains a landmark of modern thought.
savigny-recht-des-besitzes-1803:
Savigny's Law of Possession, published in German in 1803, was his first masterwork, written when he was only twenty-four.
